News.title: Two guilty of stabbing unarmed teen dad to death with zombie knives in ‘vicious’ seaside town attack
News.content:
BLADE HORROR Two guilty of stabbing unarmed teen dad to death with zombie knives in ‘vicious’ seaside town attack







Next

TWO men have been found guilty of stabbing an unarmed teen dad to death with zombie knives in a “vicious” seaside town attack.

Emergency crews rushed to respond to Whitstable, Kent, in the early hours of Friday, April 3, after receiving reports of a serious assault.



Young dad Ashton Harrington, 19, was found at the scene suffering from stab wounds.

An air ambulance was scrambled and medics battled to save the teen’s life but despite the best efforts of paramedics he was sadly pronounced dead at the scene.



Kieron Barnes, 19 at the time, and Tobias Agbaje, also 19 at the time, were arrested in the wake of the attack.

The duo had used large blades to assault Ashton in a 20 second attack that left him with a stab wound to the heart.

Appearing in court, Barnes accepted stabbing the young dad in the groin while Agbaje accepted inflicting the wound that killed Ashton – a 20cm deep stab to the heart.

Ashton, who died at the scene, was described by his family as “loyal and bubbly with an infectious laugh.”



Following the brutal attack Agbaje and Barnes fled the scene and discarded their weapons.

They hid in an unoccupied property in Sittingbourne, Kent, where they were arrested when police raided the empty home.

The duo – both drug dealers – pleaded guilty to an offence of having a bladed article.

They denied murder however and claimed self-defence, saying they attacked Ashton out of fear of being stabbed themselves.

A jury at Canterbury Crown Court unanimously found both guilty of murder.



Judge Simon James adjourned sentencing until Friday, saying: “You have both been convicted of murder.

“In those circumstances there is, in respect of both of you, only one sentence which will involve your detention or imprisonment for the rest of your life.

“However, I must set the minimum period that you must serve before you are entitled to be released.”



The verdict brought members of Ashton’s family to tears as they watched on from the public gallery.

As the two killers were led from the court room, Barnes looked to Ashton’s family and smiled.

On the night of the attack, the court was told Ashton had been with friends Cameron Neal and Tom Lilley.

The three boys went to Belmont Road at approximately 2am so Mr Neal could sell cocaine in a pre-arranged deal.

They crossed paths with Barnes and Agbaje who passed them in a three-door Citroen DS3.



Barnes and Agbaje doubled back after spotting Ashton and his friends and stopped in the street.

Barnes leapt from the motor in an “angry and agitated” state, the court was told.

The duo then launched their attack on Ashton which was captured on a security camera outside Whitstable Football Club.

Mr Neal and Mr Lilley said Barnes was wielding a “horrible, massive” knife and denied being armed themselves.

Barnes claimed that Mr Neal had been armed with a flick knife however and said he had punched him.



Agbaje, described as a frequent buyer of knives, claimed to have been punched and put in a headlock by two men before Ashton ran at him.

He told the jury that his knife “unintentionally ended up” in the teen’s chest as he tried to “warn him off.”

Both defendants had bought their knives just a day earlier from a shop in Herne Bay.

They said they carried the weapons for protection and denied involvement in a joint enterprise “murderous” attack.

Prosecutor Mark Fenhalls KC said their claim of self-defence was “absolute nonsense.”



The defence argued Barnes had already stabbed Ashton and was on his way back to the Citroen when Agbaje inflicted the fatal injury.

Barnes and Agbaje had previous convictions for possessing knives, heroin and cocaine.

Kent Police had intelligence from November 2025 that Ashton often carried a kitchen knife concealed in his waistband.

But the only “weapon” found at the scene was a razor found in Mr Lilley’s car.

Speaking after the verdict, Detective Chief Inspector Emma Lawry said: “Attacking an unarmed man with zombie knives was a cowardly action by Kieron Barnes and Tobias Agbaje.



“They ran from the scene, tried to evade police and then in court were not even brave enough to face up to what they had done.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Officers put together a strong case made up of compelling evidence, to ensure these two offenders were identified and brought to court.

“We will never be able to mend the loss felt by Mr Harrington’s friends and family, but I hope they will feel reassured by the support that was provided by the public and media during the investigation to see justice done.”

News.title: Lucy Letby trial jury was NOT told that senior doctor who gave vital evidence was BANNED
News.content:
Next

A SENIOR doctor who gave vital evidence in baby killer Lucy Letby’s trial was banned — but the jury was not told.

Prof Peter Hindmarsh was removed from clinical practice by University College London Hospitals seven months before the case began.



A UCLH medical director told the General Medical Council he appeared to pose a “risk” to children and young people.

An independent ­tribunal ruled he could continue working under supervision but UCLH had already barred him.



Letby trial prosecutor Nick Johnson KC introduced children’s hormone specialist Prof Hindmarsh as “the pre-eminent expert” on insulin.

He helped convince jurors that Letby had injected insulin into intravenous fluid bags to poison two babies.



There was no direct or forensic evidence anyone had done so.

Her solicitor Mark McDonald called his ­evidence “pivotal”.

He said the insulin claims were “the cornerstone” of the prosecution’s case.

He said: “It shaped the jury’s perception of Lucy.



“It provided the lens through which they were invited to view every other ­allegation.”

The CPS said it had met its “disclosure obligations”.

Prof Hindmarsh’s representative declined to comment.

Former neonatal nurse Letby, 36, is serving 15 whole-life sentences for murdering seven babies and trying to murder seven others at Countess of Chester Hospital.

News.title: Man ‘killed former stepdaughter, 23, with a hoe’ before going on the run as brutal details of killing emerge
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

‘BLOOD EVERYWHERE’ Man ‘killed former stepdaughter, 23, with a hoe’ before going on the run as brutal details of killing emerge







Next

A MAN has been arrested on suspicion of killing his stepdaughter with a hoe, leaving blood everywhere, before fleeing.

Maely Delfino Amaro, 63, allegedly tried to look at Phâmella Barbosa Silva, 23, while she was taking a shower, sparking a fight.



Cops arrested Amaro on Tuesday after he allegedly fled the scene in Itapemirim, southern Brazil.

Police alleged he brutally murdered young Phâmella with a hoe on Sunday after she rejected his advances.



Family members said he had been hitting on her before trying to look at her while she showered.

Witnesses said a fight erupted, and Phâmella’s mum tried to break it up.

But the young woman was allegedly thrown against a wall and fell.

Police said her stepdad then struck her repeatedly over the head with the hoe.

She was rescued and rushed to Hospital Evangélico Litoral Sul, before being transferred to another hospital in critical condition.

Phâmella died from her injuries hours later at Santa Casa de Misericórdia de Cachoeiro Hospital.



Cops were called to the family home to a report of attempted murder.

But when they arrived, suspect Amaro was nowhere to be seen.

Police searched the property to find a bloodstained hoe and bloodstains scattered across the floor and porch.



But after a thorough search of the home and yard they still could not find the suspect.

Patrol cars searched the area for two days, issuing an arrest warrant.

He finally turned himself in to the police station on Tuesday and was immediately arrested.

Amaro is being investigated on suspicion of femicide.

He is being held in custody.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Family members said Phâmella’s mum and the suspect had separated before the alleged murder, but still lived together.

The investigation has been handed to the Regional Police Station.

News.title: Why Burnham’s Europe fixation will NOT solve Britain’s major problems or connect with majority of voters
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Why Burnham’s Europe fixation will NOT solve Britain’s major problems or connect with majority of voters







Next

ANDY Burnham is putting Europe at the heart of his premiership, staking his hopes on closer ties with Brussels to fix Britain’s problems.

The PM has claimed exports had been hit and were down since the country left the EU – which Brexiteers yesterday claimed was false.



Ministers are expected to sign Britain up to EU rules on food, carbon trading and youth mobility at a crucial summit on Friday.

And earlier this week he said Brexit was exactly what “our enemies wanted”, insisting it was the “first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism”.



Mr Burnham likes to see himself at the heart of European decision making, where he will even travel to Berlin for a meeting of the Coalition of the Willing when American, Chinese and Russian premiers hold their summit in Shenzhen.

But whipping up his core supporters will unlikely solve the country’s problems or connect with the vast majority of voters.



Brits rank the cost of living and immigration as by far the two biggest issues facing the country, followed by defence and security.

Meanwhile, just 11 per cent name Britain’s relationship with the EU as one of the most pressing issues facing the country.

Labour MPs are becoming increasingly energised by Europe, with ex-deputy PM David Lammy the latest to argue that ‘Rejoin’ should be on the ballot at the next election.

But their fixation will unlikely do nothing to cut energy bills, which are set to soar by £443 from January.



It will unlikely control Britain’s borders, with more than 20,000 migrants crossing the Channel since the start of the year.

And it won’t cut a benefits bill set to top £400billion by 2030.

Even a new report by Alan Milburn, if followed to the letter, will only start bringing it down by 2036.

Whipping up his core supporters into a frenzy who deeply care about Europe may work in the short-term.

But none of this will address major problems facing the British economy.

News.title: Lefties ‘nervous’ about dealing with men’s issues, minister admits as Labour vows ‘national reckoning’ summit
News.content:
Next

LABOUR have been too timid and nervous about addressing issues facing men and boys, a minister has admitted.

Justice minister Jake Richards said a “national reckoning” summit on men and boys will take place next year, as he claimed the Left has dodged the issue for too long.



Politicians plan to team up with TikTok and YouTube influencers to reach millions of men, with stars from sport, music and gaming set to front content on being a good male role model.

The Government wants to hand the stage to these figures instead of MPs.



Justice minister Jake Richards told The Sun that left-wingers have traditionally been “nervous” about tackling men and boys’ issues.

He claimed Andy Burnham was a “long champion” of men’s issues, despite being the most Left-wing PM in decades.



Speaking ahead of International Men’s Day at a school in North London, he said: “I think traditionally on the Left we have been nervous about talking about men and boys issues.

“Because we have got, understandably, in a right moral campaign to end the gender pay gap, to tackle violence against women and girls, and that’s absolutely right at the heart of what this government is trying to do.

“But the other side of that coin is to make sure that we offer the environment, the opportunities for young men and boys to grow up to be decent men, like the vast majority of people do.”

Mr Richards said he wanted there to be more of a focus on why young lads were disproportionately on the dole and out of work.



On the upcoming summit, the Labour minister said: “I want it to be a real moment for the whole country, a national reckoning where we kind of talk about some of these issues that, frankly, for too long, politicians haven’t spoken about.

He added: “Why is it that suicide is the biggest killer of men aged under 50 in England?

“That’s a really shocking statistic, which should be right at the top of what we’re thinking about as a country. Why is it that boys do far, far worse than girls at school?”

“Why is it that you know youth unemployment a big issue this week? Boys are hugely disproportionate in that NEET number. So we’ve got to talk about that.”

The upcoming men and boys summit will take place in a series of events across the country and outside of London.

News.title: Read the room Burnham and fix the issues that REALLY matter to Brits rather than reopening Brexit wounds
News.content:
Leave it out







Next

AFTER years of bitter division and political paralysis, reopening the Brexit wounds is the LAST thing Britain wants.

But don’t just take our word for it.



A new poll shows that barely one in ten Brits think it is a priority.

Cosying up to Brussels barely scrapes in at ninth position on the public’s to-do list.



Hard-working families are far more worried about our moribund economy, soaring bills and out-of-control mass immigration, according to a new poll.

Yet barely a day goes by without Andy Burnham lecturing 17.4million Leave voters that they got it wrong.

And tomorrow the Prime Minister is off to Brussels for a “surrender summit” to hand more power back to the EU.

Yesterday, former Deputy PM David Lammy let the cat out of the bag when he admitted fighting the next election on a second referendum would help shore up his left-wing base.

What he conveniently ignored was that it would drive away millions of “Red Wall” voters who have zero appetite for a return to toxic Brexit battles.

Burnham would do well to read the room — and fix the issues that really matter.



Out of tune

MINISTERS care deeply about cultural enrichment for illegal migrants — yet their generosity stops at our own school gates.

Taxpayers are footing a scandalous £90,000 bill for art and music lessons at an asylum camp in East Sussex.

Meanwhile, half of secondary teachers say their pupils NEVER sing together, just 15 per cent learn an instrument and GCSE music entries have plunged by 27 per cent since 2010.

More than a third of English schools don’t even offer the subject.

Hard-pressed parents must dig into empty pockets for private lessons while Whitehall splashes out for new arrivals.



When it comes to our own kids’ futures, ministers are completely tone deaf.

Sub-standard

BRITAIN’S nuclear submarines are called “the silent service” for a reason.

Their whereabouts and crew details are top secret to keep us safe.

Try telling that to our TikTok- obsessed Government.

Top Brass are furious after Cabinet bigwigs showed shocking carelessness as HMS Vengeance returned from a record 217-day patrol.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Moments after it docked at Clyde, ministers — including First Secretary Louise Haigh — were posting vanity snaps on social media, tearing up rules designed to protect our kit and brave personnel.

It just about sums up Andy Burnham’s Government. More interested in showboating than getting the job done.

News.title: Britain must press ahead with drilling at Rosebank oil field to boost energy security, says US diplomat
News.content:
Next

BRITAIN must press ahead with drilling at the Rosebank oil field to boost its energy security, the US Ambassador to the UK says.

Top diplomat Warren Stephens is calling for new North Sea extraction despite as many as 100 Labour MPs including one Minister opposing the plans.



Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh has already given the green light to the Jackdaw gas field but is understood to be more sceptical about Rosebank.

Mr Stephens said he was pleased the government took a “practical approach” to Jackdaw despite coming more than four years after it was first approved.



He said: “But one month later, gas is already flowing from the site, providing cheap and efficient energy for UK businesses and consumers.

“It shows how quickly business can move once it receives direction from government.



“And this is true in many industries.

Speaking at the Prosperity Institute event, he added: “We hope approval for Rosebank will follow, and that the UK continues to take this pragmatic approach towards energy security.”

The oil field is situated about 80 miles northwest of the Shetland islands and could contain as much as 300 million barrels of oil, creating some 1,600 jobs.

News.title: Fury at Burnham’s ‘Brexit sell out’ after it emerges he’s ready to slash tuition fees for EU students from £38k to £10k
News.content:
Next

ANDY Burnham has been accused of a Brexit sell-out after it emerged he’s ready to slash tuition fees for EU students.

The UK has reportedly offered to make the annual charges the same as those paid by British undergraduates — a cut from £38,000 to £9,970.



Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith accused the PM of “putting foreign students ahead of our own young people” though the potential agreement would include a reciprocal deal for UK students in the EU.

Mr Burnham travels to Brussels tomorrow for the UK-EU summit and is expected to give away Brexit freedoms, signing Britain up to EU rules on food, carbon trading and youth mobility.



But a YouGov poll shows Brits think closer ties with Brussels is a low priority.

Just 11 per cent named it as a big deal — putting it ninth on a list of 14 issues.

The economy was first on 52 per cent, followed by immigration on 49 per cent.

Meanwhile, former Foreign Secretary David Lammy urged the PM to fight the next election on rejoining the EU, despite dismissing such calls six months ago.

Reform’s education spokesperson said: “Why is Burnham cutting tuition fees for EU students but not British students? His focus should be helping our own youngsters.

“EU students still owe the British taxpayer £6billion in unpaid fees and this will only rise.”



The PM travels to Brussels on Friday where he is expected to give away hard-won Brexit freedoms, signing Britain up to EU rules on food, carbon trading and youth mobility.

News.title: This is a remarkable diplomatic moment for China's Xi - but it comes with pitfalls
News.content:
Xi Jinping will believe he has achieved something no other world leader could in securing a historic summit with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump in Shenzhen.

For decades, Washington and its western allies shaped the world order.

Yet it is China that has orchestrated the remarkable diplomatic spectacle of three of the world's most powerful protagonists sitting around the table.

And surrounding it all is the futuristic display that is Shenzhen, with driverless cars cruising past as drones fly overhead and robots - literally - dance in the streets.

Ostensibly, this is an economic summit for Asia Pacific leaders. But for Xi, it is also a demonstration of China's grip on the global economy and world politics.

His country is no longer just reacting to decisions made in Washington, London or Brussels - instead Beijing is at the heart of conversations which are reshaping the international order.

But this meeting is not without its pitfalls for Xi as there are many things he does not appear keen to discuss with Putin and Trump.

News.title: McDonald's sex abuse: 'They were waiting for the younger girls to turn 18'
News.content:
A former McDonald's worker who says a manager failed to protect her when she was being sexualised by customers, has called on the firm to âchange the way they treat younger employeesâ.

Hope, who worked at a branch in the West Midlands in 2023, also told BBC News she saw older colleagues eyeing up 16- and 17-year-old workers, and talking about wanting to sleep with them when they turned 18.

Hope is one of hundreds of workers bringing a discrimination claim against McDonald's. This week, a judge ruled against McDonald's attempt to have their claims struck out, a move that Hope welcomed.

McDonald's said: "Ensuring a safe, respectful and inclusive working environment across our restaurants and offices remains a fundamental priority."

The latest developments come after a BBC investigation in 2023 which heard that workers, some as young as 17, were being groped and harassed.

Last year, McDonald's staff told us they still faced sexual abuse and harassment.

Hope, who is now 22, says that her branch of McDonalds had a very sexualised, "toxic" environment.

She spoke of a time a manager came up behind her and put his hands on her shoulders. From then on, whenever she saw him coming over, she says she "moved quick" to get away from him.

"I got the hell out of there," she says.

News.title: 'Feudal' leasehold system set to be scrapped in England and Wales
News.content:
The government is to introduce new laws to scrap the way flats are built in England and Wales.

Under the proposed bill, most new leasehold flats will be banned and replaced with commonhold, where residents collectively own and manage their buildings.

Matthew Pennycook, the housing minister, said the current leasehold system was "blighting lives" and was an "anachronism in the twenty-first century".

The legislation follows Labour's 2024 election manifesto to "bring the feudal leasehold system to an end" - with further details expected to be set out later.

However, freeholders argue the policy is "unjust" and will have a detrimental impact on investment markets.

News.title: Can Anthropic's record-breaking IPO stop the AI bubble bursting?
News.content:
It was during November 2020 that somewhere in San Francisco, a woman called Daniela Amodei phoned a friend, asking for advice.

Daniela oversaw safety and policy at OpenAI, one of the most talked-about AI companies in the world.

But Daniela and her brother Dario - who worked there too - had misgivings over safety levels at OpenAI and thought it could be time to walk away.

So she did what many do when we can't make a decision about something, she phoned a friend. The friend's reply was direct and to the point: "You don't need to be on the phone with me. You already know the answer."

The Amodei siblings and a handful of other colleagues quit. Together, they set up a rival â Anthropic.

Six years on and Anthropic, the maker of leading AI model Claude, has predicted revenues of $52bn in 2026 and $135bn in 2027, according to analyst estimates.

It is about to sell shares to the public for the first time in what's known as an Initial Public Offering or IPO, aiming for a valuation of an estimated $1.4tn (Â£1tn), which would propel it straight into the top 10 of the most valuable US companies.

News.title: Crew unaware of risks before Bayesian yacht accident, say investigators
News.content:
In the early hours of 19 August 2024 the Bayesian was anchored outside of Porticello port, on the north coast of Sicily.

With thunderstorms rapidly coming in, wind speeds went from 8 knots to about 70 knots (80mph) within minutes. The weather forecast had only predicted gusts of up to 27 knots (31mph).

The MAIB report stated that with no sails set Bayesian was vulnerable to being knocked over in severe winds.

A study commissioned by the MAIB indicated that, in the conditions assessed, Bayesian was vulnerable to extreme winds at the vessels widest point, known as the beam.

It also found that any knockdown - where the boat was suddenly tipped sideways - would be "irrecoverable once the yacht passed the angle of vanishing stability", assessed in the study as being 73 degrees. Once the vessel passed this angle it could not right itself.

In addition, the centreboard, which provides stability when a ship is under sail, was raised. The report said the centreboard was not needed when the Bayesian was using its motors and was rarely lowered at anchor. The way the boat was loaded, and the angle of the wind, also contributed to the accident.

Inspectors said a "downburst of hurricane-force winds" was the most likely cause of the ship keeling over.

They happen when cold, dense air plunges rapidly, sending out violent winds across the surface.

The MAIB said that none of risks were covered in the UK training syllabus, nor in published guidance available to crew.

Once the vessel was on its side, it rapidly filled with water and sank.

News.title: Prince Harry says he would rejoin army as he warns of Russia threat
News.content:
The Duke of Sussex, who carried out a surprise visit to Ukraine at the weekend, has said he would rejoin the military if asked, as he warned of the threat from Russia.

He told the Telegraph, external he thought people were right to be nervous in the current international political climate and said it was time to "double our support" for Ukraine.

There appeared to be warnings about President Trump - with Prince Harry saying there was a big separation between what the American public thinks about Ukraine and the administration's attitude.

Prince Harry, able to speak more freely than working royals, said he hoped after the US mid-term elections it would be "fantastic to have more American support" for Ukraine.

Speaking to the Telegraph's Dominic Nicholls, Prince Harry said he thought the threat to Europe had been there for the past 15 years - and he felt like it had been at war for the past decade.

"Just because there's not drones, bullets, and rockets flying at us, it doesn't mean that we're not at war," said Prince Harry.

Prince Harry had been in Lviv in Ukraine on Saturday and Sunday - and had told the BBC and journalists at events that he thought the "rest of the world will continue to support" Ukraine.

He had told his Ukrainian hosts, about a conflict with Russia that has already lasted more than four years: "You're going to win the war."

In his Telegraph podcast, he called for a similar unity that was being shown by Ukraine, and feared that Europe could be divided and could "turn on itself".

He addressed the shifting position of US President Trump in a way that is unusual for a royal.

"I think there's been a big separation between what American society feels regarding support for Ukraine, which I think is incredibly high and always has been, compared to a certain group, or in, in this case, an administration that was perhaps thinking about it differently," said Prince Harry.

"As of January, things are going to change, so I think we should all be looking forward to that," he said, referring to the US mid-term elections, which saw significant setbacks for President Trump.

The BBC has approached the White House for comment.

Having served in the military in Afghanistan, Harry said he would return if needed for a future conflict: "If asked to sign up again, if the need is there, then I will 100% be there to serve my country alongside my fellow veterans and service personnel."

Prince Harry had received an enthusiastic welcome when he visited Lviv in Ukraine at the weekend, meeting Ukrainian competitors taking part in his Invictus Games.

There were emotional scenes as he was applauded by injured service men and women, some of the 150,000 seriously wounded war veterans in the country.

His visit had been carried out with a press blackout for security reasons - and the night before journalists arrived in the city to cover the visit, there had been air raid warnings that had forced Prince Harry's planning team to head for the shelters.

"Ukraine now is experiencing elements of war that no other country has experienced before," Prince Harry had said, including inventing new ways of treating the growing number of injured casualties.

"War is a terrible thing," he said in Lviv, but hailed the resilience of the Ukrainians who had been badly wounded in their defence against Russia's invasion.

News.title: Google rejects UK request for Russell Brand YouTube video to be removed, sources say
News.content:
Google has refused a government request to remove a YouTube video posted by jailed rapist Russell Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

The Prison Service of England and Wales submitted the request. A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said "it was only right" to ask for content that was "distressing for victims" to be removed.

The comedian is currently serving a 10-and-half-year prison sentence after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

There was no immediate comment from Google when approached by BBC News.

On Sunday, his wife Laura had shared a video on their YouTube channel and read out a handwritten message from Brand in which he claimed: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The MoJ spokesperson added that while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

The Prison Service of England and Wales formally requested that the video be removed on the basis that they believed it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken.

Brand's message prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against him, said she found the message shared on the couple's Sunday Service show "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC Radio 4's Today programme this week.

She is one of the women who made allegations against Brand in 2023 as part of a Times, Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches investigation.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised media outlets earlier on Wednesday for playing extracts of the message, saying they should not have "amplified" his words.

Speaking to LBC, she described Brand as "someone who's not showing a jot of remorse, a jot of any sensitivity at all to their victims".

In 2023, YouTube suspended Brand's channels from making money from adverts for "violating" its "creator responsibility policy", shortly after he was accused of rape and sexual assaults between 2006 and 2013.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site.

Meanwhile, his social media accounts on Meta platforms - Instagram, Facebook and Whatsapp - were disabled last week.

News.title: Is your child lying to you? That might not be a bad thing
News.content:
When drawings appear on the wall or biscuits disappear from the tin, your child might blame the dog or claim there was a ghost - even if they are clutching crayons or covered in crumbs.

Children telling fibs is something most parents experience, but such dishonesty and deception is an important part of mental development.

"It's actually a skill that they're developing and that they will play with in order to get better," clinical psychologist Dr Jade Redfern tells the CBeebies Parenting Download podcast.

Here, experts explain why learning to lie is a sign of healthy behaviour - and how to help encourage honesty.

News.title: Council wins legal fight against flags on lamp-posts
News.content:
Birmingham City Council has won a High Court injunction preventing unauthorised flags being attached to lamp-posts and other highway infrastructure across the city.

The authority sought the order after thousands of St George's flags and union jacks were put up by supporters of anti-migrant group Raise the Colours from summer 2025 onwards.

Council lawyers argued the displays created safety risks and fuelled tensions, while campaigners said the move would restrict freedom of expression.

Judge Emma Kelly said there was a "compelling need" to grant the interim injunction.

In her ruling, the judge said it would last until trial or further order of the court.

The order applies to Raise the Colours' leader Ryan Bridge; Ben Cullen, who is also associated with the group; and persons unknown from attaching flags to street furniture and highway infrastructure.

It also grants a power of arrest against Bridge and persons unknown, meaning police could arrest someone without a warrant if they are suspected of breaching the injunction.

The council said anyone who breaches the order could be jailed for up to two years, fined or have their assets seized for contempt of court.

The local authority sought the injunction after thousands of St George's flags and union flags were attached to lamp-posts and bridges in Birmingham from summer 2025 onwards.

Lawyers acting for the council argued the displays could pose safety risks, obstruct visibility and contribute to tensions and disorder. The application also referred to reported incidents of alleged intimidation, harassment and obstruction connected to flags being put up in the city.

The court heard that, on one occasion, a man suffered a broken leg when he was struck by a cherry picker being used while flags were being installed.

The case followed similar legal action in Oxfordshire, where the county council secured a permanent injunction against four named individuals over flags attached to lamp-posts and other highway structures.

News.title: Typical energy bill forecast to go up by £443 a year from January as inflation rate rises again
News.content:
Gas and electricity bills for a typical household are forecast to jump by Â£443 a year from January as the inflation rate rose to its highest level in a year.

A typical annual bill is predicted to rise by 26% in the new year, according to consultancy Cornwall Insight, ahead of the official announcement next week.

Some households will get a Â£100 payment to help with the rising cost of living, a policy which was announced in the Budget.

Prices rose 3.6% in the year to October, up from 3.5% in September mainly because of higher petrol and diesel prices, official figures show.

Inflation has been driven higher in recent months as the US-Israel war with Iran has driven up the cost of energy and fuel.

In response to prices surging, the Bank of England raised interest rates for the first time in three years earlier this month, in a bid to slow inflation to its target of 2%.

Interest rates increased from 3.75% to 4%, and the Bank signalled a further rise could be likely unless the conflict in the Middle East is resolved.

Higher interest rates lift the cost of borrowing for some mortgages, loans and credit cards, but can also lead to a better return on savings.

Emma Reynolds, chief secretary to the Treasury, said the government was providing help for households with energy costs.

VAT has been cut on electricity bills to zero until next July and the government will also hand Â£100 to 20 million homes in January.

But with annual household energy bills forecast to reach Â£2,166, Cornwall Insight's retail markets principal, Craig Lowrey, said that "ultimately this support can only chip away at the edges of a bill that continues to be pushed up by events in the Middle East".

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, said: "Affordability is my number one priority, and I will continue driving towards cheap, clean power."

News.title: Police investigate death of boy, 3, after nursery incident
News.content:
An investigation has been launched into the death of a three-year-old boy following an incident at a nursery in Greater Manchester, police said.

The boy became critically ill at Cosy Toes Nursery in Middleton shortly before 16:00 GMT on Monday 2 November.

He was rushed to hospital, where he died three days later.

Greater Manchester Police said his family were being supported by specialist officers.

Det Ch Insp Claire Brennan said: "This is an incredibly tragic development in a deeply upsetting incident and our thoughts remain with the boy's family."

Police said an investigation had been launched in line with standard procedure following a child's death in a care setting.

No arrests have been made at this time.

News.title: Regulator mistakenly sent complaints about doctors to newspaper
News.content:
The doctors' regulator the General Medical Council (GMC) has apologised after it mistakenly sent information about more than 220 doctors to a national newspaper.

The information included summaries of complaints alleging antisemitism or Islamophobia against the doctors.

For some of the medics involved, it was only when the GMC alerted them to the data breach that they discovered a complaint had been made about them.

The GMC says it is "very sorry" for the incident and has reported itself to the Information Commissioner's Office.

The GMC - an independent body that regulates doctors, physician associates and anaesthesia associates to protect patient safety - sent the information about 223 doctors to a journalist at the Times newspaper.

While no names were revealed, GMC identification numbers were included, which would easily allow doctors to be found on the regulator's register.

Some doctors have also raised concerns that their ethnicity was included in the data breach.

All the medics involved have been the subject of a complaint involving either antisemitism or Islamophobia, dating from the Hamas attack on Israel in October 2023 to September 2026.

The GMC says it has a legal and statutory responsibility to investigate such claims.

Meanwhile, the Times is understood to have promised not to make any of the leaked details public, but has said it will not delete the leaked information.

News.title: Police chief says racists and misogynists working inside force
News.content:
The chief of Wales' largest police force says he is working to root out racists and misogynists from his organisation as part of efforts to improve trust in officers.

Chief Constable Jeremy Vaughan had responded to a question from MPs about how he and other police chiefs were clamping down on staff misconduct "in a post-Sarah Everard era".

The South Wales Police chief said: "Do I think I've got racists, misogynists, working for me? Yes. Do I think my work is to find them and excommunicate them from policing? Absolutely yes."

He appeared in front of the Welsh Affairs Committee on Wednesday, along with Wales' three other police bosses, as part of its inquiry into the future of policing.

One of the issues being examined by the committee, made up of Welsh MPs from the UK Parliament, is a UK government proposal to reduce the number of police forces in England and Wales.

Committee chairperson, Newport West and Islwyn MP Ruth Jones, had asked the chief constables of all four forces how they were evaluating their forces' performance when it came to addressing misconduct.

Jones noted in her question that "we're still in a post-Sarah Everard era", referencing the 33-year-old woman who was abducted, raped and murdered by serving Met police officer Wayne Couzens in London in 2021, and that "there have been issues across Wales".

Vaughan said that 126 people had been dismissed from the force under his watch since he started his role six years ago, and that he believed it had been "significantly higher" than under his predecessor.

Saying he believed improvements to vetting and training meant his organisation was now "more upstanding than by-standing than ever before", he noted that 22 people within it were currently suspended - which he said was a "low proportion of the workforce".

He said that identifying and sacking racists and misogynists from within South Wales Police was a "whole-organisation leadership effort".

News.title: Raise The Colours member guilty of dancefloor murder
News.content:
A member of activist group Raise The Colours has been found guilty of murdering a pub landlord who died after being punched in the neck on the dancefloor at a bar.

Matthew O'Gara, 44, was attacked by Billy Allison at Rico and Loren bar in Lichfield, Staffordshire, on 24 May.

Allison was also found guilty of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to O'Gara's friend Adam Cooper, 62, who was punched twice and was left with a fractured eye socket and nose.

O'Gara, who ran The Plough on the outskirts of Lichfield, suffered two broken bones and a split artery in his neck, which caused a massive bleed and rendered him unconscious until he died in hospital two days later, Stafford Crown Court heard.

The trial was told the punch could be heard over the bar's DJ sound system.

Allison, who had been drunk and had taken cocaine during the day, had admitted manslaughter ahead of the trial, but denied murder.

He appeared shocked by the verdict, sighing and holding his head in his hands and seeming to cry as he left the dock without being granted permission by the judge.

News.title: Thousands regain water supply after major outage
News.content:
Most residents in Stourbridge, in the West Midlands, should start to see their water supply return to normal after a major outage, according to Severn Trent.

The firm said it expected customers to be back on supply during Wednesday evening.

"We have had a huge number of specialist teams working hard in the area, who have been moving water through the network and using a fleet of over 30 tankers to restore supplies," the firm said.

It comes after thousands of properties were without water on Wednesday morning as teams worked to locate a burst pipe.

"We're thankful to the local community who have been supportive, unbelievably understanding and patient given the circumstances," a Severn Trent spokesperson added.

"Our priority will now be making sure the last few remaining customers are also back on as quickly as possible."

Ridgewood High School and Ashwood Park Primary School remained closed on Wednesday, and residents said they were unable to cook, wash or flush their toilets.

Emergency bottled water stations were operating since 08:00 GMT, although supplies temporarily ran out at one site before a fresh delivery was arranged.

On Wednesday morning, it was reported that 6,000 homes and businesses were without water, but by lunchtime that had risen to 8,500 as engineers attempted to find the source of the leak.

Earlier, Howard Perry, head of water quality at Severn Trent had warned some residents might be without water for four days.

"We are very hopeful we can get customers back on supply before that," he said.

News.title: 'Good for the people' if politicians stopped doing media, says NI secretary of state
News.content:
The secretary of state for Northern Ireland has said that if politicians stayed off the media for a month it would "probably be very good for the people".

Sir Chris Bryant said it breaks his heart that because of the crisis over agreeing a budget he can't get round to issues like violence against women and girls, or resolving community tensions.

He told a committee of MPs that was "one of the symbols of the kind of complete abnormality that now seems to pervade Northern Ireland politics".

In response to the comments, Stormont's Finance Minister John O'Dowd said that Sir Chris had continued to respond to "cold hard facts and figures with bluster and theatrics".

Ministers on the Stormont executive say they can't strike a budget without additional money from the Treasury.

The government has offered around Â£1.5 billion in extra funding over the next three years but ministers say they need more.

It means Northern Ireland faces the prospect of strikes by public sector workers because there is no way of meeting pay claims.

Asked by the committee chair Tonia Antoniazzi how much money ministers required he said: "Oh I mean it changes every week. One version is another billion pounds."

He added that some politicians "won't sit in the same room as each other".

He told members of the Northern Ireland Affairs Committee: "The point is that Northern Ireland is getting fair funding, and whatever the envelope is, if you were a councillor, you would have to set a legal budget.

"You just have to make the sums add up. And what really frustrates, I think, all of us is, I've tried processes of adjudicating between the different parties, because let's face it, the parties aren't talking to each other at the moment."

News.title: Fiji declares national disaster after El Nino-driven drought causes ‘prolonged dry conditions’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Fiji has declared a national state of disaster after an El Nino-driven drought caused widespread water shortages, with the Pacific nation's weather bureau forecasting below-normal rainfall until at least April.

In a national address on Wednesday, prime minister Sitiveni Rabuka said ⁠the declaration would allow his government to scale up its response by mobilising resources and coordinating assistance as conditions continue to worsen.

"Families across Fiji are concerned about the availability of water and the effects of prolonged dry conditions on their daily lives," Mr Rabuka said.

"Farmers ​are ⁠worried about their crops and livestock, while communities, particularly in remote and maritime areas, face growing pressure on their water ⁠supplies. These concerns are real."

Mr Rabuka said his government has set aside 20 million Fiji dollars ($8.5m) for the national response, redeployed from existing funds, to ensure emergency water supplies for families and farmers. The state of disaster has been declared for ‌one month, with the government able to extend ‌or revoke it based on the advice of the National Disaster Risk Management Council.

Illustration showing a magnifying glass placed over a map of equatorial Pacific Ocean sea surface temperature anomalies, made in Paris, France, on July 10, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

El Nino is a natural climate pattern in which surface temperatures in the central `and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, causing weather extremes around the world, including drought in some regions and flooding in others. Some scientists say global warming may increase its intensity.

The US Climate Prediction Center said last week that El Nino is strengthening, with a greater than 79% chance of a strong-to-very-strong event through January to March. ‌Australia in June said El Nino could intensify in the ​second half of 2026 to become one of the strongest ‌in seven decades.

Fiji's national weather bureau warned in October that strong El Nino conditions persist across the tropical Pacific. Rainfall is likely to remain below normal from November through April, ‌while daytime temperatures ​are expected to exceed normal levels through ‌January across most of the ​country, the Fiji Meteorological Service said.

News.title: Inside Greenland’s push for fine dining, from polar night logistics to 'kaffemik' traditions
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Greenland, a vast Arctic territory of about 56,000 people, is perhaps better known for its icebergs, polar bears, rare minerals and geopolitical tensions than its cuisine.

But a new generation of chefs is working to change that, transforming traditional Inuit ingredients into modern fine-dining experiences.

Greenland’s food culture has long been rooted in hunting and fishing, with local ingredients ranging from ptarmigan, reindeer, musk ox and lamb to capelin, shrimp, snow crab, whale and halibut.

Restaurant Ulo opened two years ago in Hotel Arctic, believed to be the world’s northernmost four-star hotel, in Ilulissat, a town of 5,000 that sits about 300 kilometers (about 186 miles) north of the Arctic Circle.

The restaurant takes its name from the “ulo,” a traditional crescent-shaped knife used by women for hunting and food preparation.

“There is no fine-dining culture here,” said executive chef Sudarshan Sundararaj. “We wanted to do the fine-dining culture here in a modern technique with modern cookery, gastronomy style with mainly Greenlandic items — so that was the challenging part.”

“It’s about creating something to reveal Greenland, to experience Greenland for whoever is coming for a visit,” said Sundararaj, who moved to Greenland from his native Sri Lanka six years ago.

Ulo's 13-course meal puts local produce center stage and — like many things in far-off Greenland — comes at a steep price: 3,900 Danish kroner (about $570) per person with wine included.

Focusing on what makes Greenland special

The fluffy starter dish known as “rekling” reimagines air-dried halibut as a delicacy distinct from the dried fish familiar to many Greenlanders.

"We thought, ‘okay, what makes Greenland special?’” said Danish sous-chef Esben Staun-Olsen. "There are a lot of things that make Greenland special, but part of it is really, really good protein.”

Running a fine-dining restaurant on the edge of the world comes with unique challenges: Every year, Ilulissat is plunged into 44 days of polar night, fresh ingredients are difficult to grow, and frozen harbors can prevent supply boats from reaching town.

Most vegetables on Ulo’s menu are imported, and supplies are often unreliable because of the weather, said Sundararaj.

Other upscale restaurants are beginning to appear across the Arctic territory.

Restaurant Sarfalik, in the high-rise Hotel Hans Egede in the capital, Nuuk, offers a changing menu of freshly-caught fish with views of the fjord and nearby mountains.

In the southern town of Qaqortoq, newly-opened bistro Tamassa serves reindeer steak, lamb chops and traditional Greenlandic soup.

A ‘kaffemik’ tradition in the homes of locals

Ulo’s chefs believe fine dining doesn’t require imported luxuries like caviar or truffles. But understanding Greenlandic food culture means going beyond restaurant kitchens and into people's homes.

At its heart is “kaffemik” — which roughly translates as “with coffee” in Greenlandic — a traditional social gathering centered around coffee, food and community that’s often an all-day affair, bringing people together to celebrate a new baby, a birthday or other special occasion.

For Greenlander Kathrine Johansen, it’s more than just a gathering; it’s a treasured tradition.

“It means a lot to me, because I grew up in a big family where we had a lot of kaffemiks,” she says. “That is our way of living with those traditions.”

One delicacy on the menu is mattak, a traditional Inuit dish made from raw whale skin and blubber.

“It’s a tradition in many years that we have been eating this kind of food. I really like it,” says 24-year-old tour guide Niklas Johansen, savoring the small cubes of raw whale at Johansen's home. “I usually eat it this way, when it’s fresh.”

News.title: Young people around the world want marriage and children – they just can’t afford them, UN warns
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Young people around the world are struggling to achieve the traditional milestones of adulthood, from financial independence and stable employment to marriage and parenthood, according to new research by the United Nations Population Fund (UNFPA).

Despite being better educated and more connected to information than previous generations, millions are finding it harder to secure the jobs, housing and financial stability needed to build the lives they want.

The pressures are particularly acute in sub-Saharan Africa, where limited economic opportunities and rapid population growth are presenting governments with mounting challenges, according to UNFPA’s the State of World Population report, published on Thursday.

Young people face significant barriers to entering the workforce, with more than a third of Senegal’s young people unemployed in 2024, and 30 per cent in Mali.

Globally, one in five young people are not in employment, education or training, while four in five young adults in low-income countries do not have a secure paid job.

What is a neets crisis? Are young people struggling to find jobs in the UK?

“The gap is not in young people's ambition, it is in their opportunity,” said Diene Keita, UNFPA's executive director, adding that today's young people are better educated than previous generations, have grown up with more access to information and have been taught that they have human rights.

“They can expect to live longer, thanks to decades of progress in public health, economic development, and breathtaking advances in technology,” Ms Keita told a press briefing. “But all these measures, they should be the most successful generation of young adults in history, but many are not yet seeing the gains they were promised.”

The report, which draws on a survey of more than 100,000 young adults across 73 countries and territories, challenges the idea that younger generations are increasingly rejecting marriage and parenthood.

More than 90 per cent of respondents said they wanted at least one child, while 70 per cent said marriage was their ideal relationship arrangement. Financial insecurity was the most commonly reported obstacle to finding a partner, cited by more than half, with almost three quarter saying it was a barrier to having children.

Congo’s Ebola outbreak tops 10,000 cases as authorities race to slow the spread in African countries Show all 4

Nearly nine in 10 respondents said financial security was a precondition for feeling ready to become a parent.

The report highlights the particular challenges facing girls in sub-Saharan Africa, where poverty, child marriage and adolescent pregnancy continue to restrict access to education.

In Benin, only about one in three girls completes the first cycle of secondary education, with financial difficulties, early marriage and pregnancy among the main reasons. In Chad, secondary school enrolment rate is just 41 per cent, while over 60 per cent of women were married before the age of 18.

The report also points to examples of progress, however, with Nigeria girls' secondary school completion rates rising by a quarter between 2018 and 2024. Child marriage is also falling following investment in free schooling, school meals and safe spaces.

The challenges facing young people also extend to conflict, with the number living within 50km of an active conflict more than doubling since 1990, to 340 million.

Cuts to international aid are also risking progress in healthcare and education, while UNFPA warned there could be as many as 22 million additional preventable deaths by 2030 if the reductions continue.

News.title: North Korea is expanding its original uranium enrichment facility, IAEA chief says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex, the head of the U.N. nuclear watchdog said, in yet another sign that the North is delivering on its vow to bolster its nuclear weapons program.

The assessment by International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi came as U.S. President Donald Trump expressed his eagerness to meet North Korean leader Kim Jong Un while he was in Asia for a regional forum in China.

“Since mid-September 2026, a further extension to the original Yongbyon enrichment facility has been under construction with the new extension externally complete by late-October 2026,” Grossi said in a statement Wednesday to the IAEA’s board of governors. “The ongoing expansion of the DPRK’s uranium enrichment program remains a cause for serious concern.”

DPRK stands for Democratic People’s Republic of Korea, North Korea’s official name.

The IAEA has not had access to Yongbyon or other locations in North Korea since the country kicked out the agency’s inspectors in 2009. The IAEA has said it uses satellite imagery and open source information to monitor developments in North Korea’s nuclear program.

North Korea has called its Yongbyon complex “the heart” of its nuclear program. Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon.

Observers say North Korea has taken steps to build additional uranium enrichment facilities at Yongbyon and elsewhere since Kim’s earlier high-stakes nuclear diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. Last year, South Korea’s Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day.

While Trump expressed interest in meeting with Kim, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio later said no meeting was yet scheduled for Trump’s China visit with Kim but he said the president is prepared to begin a new dialogue with Pyongyang.

North Korea hasn’t responded to Trump’s fresh overture. Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the U.S. drops its “hostile policy” against his country and respects what he calls the North’s status as a nuclear state. Experts say North Korea is eager to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of U.N. economic sanctions.

News.title: Anthropic to debut on Wall Street with a $1.5 trillion valuation in the biggest IPO of all time
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Anthropic priced its initial public offering at $83 per share Wednesday, valuing the artificial intelligence giant at $1.5 trillion in the biggest Wall Street debut of all time.

The pricing above the range initially projected by the company signals broad investor enthusiasm for AI stocks even amid some uncertainty in the market stemming from the ouster of Nvidia's CEO and worries about an AI bubble.

Anthropic said the offering consists of 980 million shares, roughly 956 million sold by the company and the rest by selling stockholders. Proceeds totaling $81 billion put Anthropic's IPO ahead of SpaceX, which raised about $75 billion in June.

The San Francisco-based maker of the Claude AI tool is set to make its debut Thursday on Wall Street. The company had set a price range of $70 to $78 per share, initially offering 825 million shares. The stock will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol “ANT.”

Anthropic decided to barrel ahead with the IPO despite jitters among some investors over market volatility, a potential regulatory crackdown by a Democratic-led Congress next year and growing anti-AI sentiment among the public. Then there's the spectacular downfall of one of the industry's biggest cheerleaders, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, over extramarital affairs, including one with an alleged Chinese spy.

“This is strong appetite for this major AI IPO in Anthropic, and it’s a big win for the tech sector after a white-knuckle time with Nvidia. The pricing shows strong demand among investors,” said Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co.

The company’s rival, OpenAI, is not planning to go public until next year.

IPO offers a way to raise money without going deeper into debt

Anthropic already has taken on $6.2 billion in debt, which it acknowledges in financial filings is “substantial.” Adding to the strain, the company is unprofitable, at least under standard accounting rules, suggesting that its resources to pay interest and principal are limited.

While the company has ample cash for now, it will likely run through it quickly if it cannot raise more soon, given its outsize spending plans. The company said it has already signed leases and other deals requiring it to spend $900 billion on computing power and infrastructure in the coming years, including $70 billion in the next 12 months.

An IPO is essentially a way to raise money, instead of going into further debt. And borrowing has gotten more expensive. That’s partly due to inflation fears and partly due to the sector’s massive cash needs, which have drawn comparisons to the Gilded Age splurge on railroads. Lenders fear that AI companies have taken on too much debt to expand while having no clear path to profitability.

Anthropic's IPO also means its employees can begin to sell their vested stock, a payout that will make many of them millionaires. The IPO could also give Anthropic enormous resources to accelerate its expansion and potentially add billions of dollars to the fortunes of CEO Dario Amodei and his sister and co-founder, Daniela Amodei.

The offering consists of 980,000,000 shares of Class A common stock, 956,351,354 of which are being sold by Anthropic and 23,648,646 of which are being sold by certain selling stockholders.

AI industry faces concerns about data centers, a possible bubble and regulations

Formed in 2021 by former OpenAI leaders, Anthropic is locked in a fight for dominance with that company. But both companies have plenty of other competitors, including Google, startups in the U.S. and China and SpaceX, which has an AI business.

Anthropic, OpenAI and SpaceX’s AI division have all lost more money than they’ve made because of the huge costs associated with building AI. That has fueled growing concerns about a bubble forming in the sector.

Dario Amodei cautioned in September that the AI industry should slow its fast-moving development to give safety measures time to catch up. Without such a slowdown, Amodei warned, AI could be capable of letting loose a swarm of agents that could take over the internet within months.

Amid those fears, the regulatory environment could also change for Anthropic once the new Congress is in session. Newly elected Democrats are vowing to crack down on the industry amid a backlash against data centers. And two big states offering incentives for data centers, Texas and Georgia, just elected Democratic governors vowing to stop new construction.

Adding to the pressure is the possibility that demand for AI shares could drop or even collapse. Investors have become anxious about the massive financing needs of the sector, and several tech companies have pulled IPO plans recently.

Investors will have less control in Anthropic's unusual structure

The goal of most companies, above all, is to do well for their owners. Usually that means making profits and growing the business. Anthropic says it too will consider its stockholders, but it will balance their interests against another fundamental goal: “the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity.”

Like its rival OpenAI, Anthropic is a public-benefit corporation, a legal designation used by companies that pledge to balance shareholder interests with the public good. How that will play out for companies worth potentially trillions of dollars is uncharted territory.

Anthropic has set up a long-term benefit trust that will have the ability to elect or remove a majority of the company’s board of directors. The trust will not run the day-to-day operations of Anthropic. But its influence means the company could opt for strategies that may not make the most money for investors.

Market valuation for AI companies is going to be “up and down for many years to come, but more up than down,” said Rich Lesser, the global chair and former CEO of Boston Consulting Group.

“Exactly what the flow of that will be, it’s very hard to predict,” Lesser said in an interview with The Associated Press on Tuesday at the Semafor Silicon Valley & The World forum. “There’s no question what Anthropic and OpenAI and Google and a number of the other players in this industry have done is pretty remarkable.”

___

Associated Press business writers Bernard Condon, Kaitlyn Huamani and Michelle Chapman contributed.

News.title: England feast on Australia chaos to land early Ashes blow
News.content:
Good morning from idyllic Hobart, where there is not a cloud in the sky, and England are having a belting time batting first.

They zipped along all day in lovely batting conditions, moving to 137 for two from 20 overs.

The wickets to fall have been Tom Banton, well caught by a juggling Mitch Marsh running back from mid-off, and Joe Root, who had a horrible heave at Matt Renshaw, and was bowled. He has never made an ODI hundred on Australian soil and is unlikely to get another chance.

Ben Duckett initially cruised along in Banton’s slip stream, but has hit a blaze of boundaries since. He has feasted on some Australia’s bowling and fielding that has been pretty ordinary, as they say in these parts. Duckett was the beneficiary of a terrible drop at square leg by Alex Carey, who is back in the side but not keeping.

The other big talking point, inevitably, is sandpapergate. Usman Khawaja, who lit the fire for the reopening of the public debate, is here commentating, and Cricket Australia have announced an independent forum for players and staff from the tour of South Africa in 2018 to come forward and share their memories. CA will not be reopening the investigation, and or issuing any new punishments, though. They haven’t even decided how much of forum’s findings they will make public. So it is unclear exactly what the point of the whole thing is.

News.title: Households face back-to-back interest rate rises
News.content:
Mortgage borrowers face another rise in interest rates before Christmas after official figures showed inflation rose to its highest level in a year.

The Bank of England is expected to raise borrowing costs again in December, after increasing rates for the first time in three years earlier this month.

It comes after consumer prices index (CPI) inflation rose from 3.5pc in September to 3.6pc in October, according to the Office for National Statistics.

In a rare intervention after the publication of inflation data, the Bank underlined its commitment to slowing down the pace of price rises.

A spokesman for the Bank said: “The conflict in the Middle East has caused energy prices and inflation to rise in recent months, and inflation is expected to rise further by the middle of next year due to cost pressures already in the pipeline.

“The Monetary Policy Committee raised Bank Rate two weeks ago to limit how much higher energy costs affect other prices, and will continue to set interest rates to make sure inflation returns to the 2pc target and stays there.”

Rob Wood of Pantheon Macroeconomics said it was a “very close call” over whether policymakers raise rates in December or February, but favoured a jump before Christmas.

Traders are betting there is a 74pc chance of a December rate rise, down from 77pc on Tuesday, after services inflation rose slightly less than expected to 3.7pc in October.

Mr Wood said: “The headlines provide some relief, but underlying inflation remains too high, and airfares may be beginning to show some effect from higher energy costs.

“We expect at least two further rate hikes and now bring our calls forward to December and February, from February and April.”
