News.title: ‘No guarantees’: Sierra Leone’s struggle to stop women dying in labour
News.content:
As she comes face to face with her newborn baby girl for the first time, young mother Adama Gomes smiles with relief.

Standing before a row of brand-new incubators in a spotlessly clean neonatal intensive care ward, Adama, 23, cradles her tiny one-day-old daughter with even more trepidation than most novice parents.

During an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems, she often doubted this blissful moment would happen.

Had she reached term a year ago, Adama, who has sickle cell anaemia, could have died from the significant complications she faced.

Adama Gomes, who has sickle cell anaemia, endured an anxious pregnancy fraught with health problems Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Thankfully, however, the first-time mum from a village in Sierra Leone’s Kono region gave birth at the recently opened Maternal Center of Excellence, a state-of-the-art hospital that would be the envy of the NHS.

As she bonds with her yet to be named first child, who has been kept in one of the incubators overnight, Adama and her tiny daughter embody the impressive transformation in Sierra Leone's maternal health over the last decade.

Maternity staff help Adama with her new baby Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I am so happy that me and my baby are healthy,” she declares. “It was hard getting here for check-ups during the pregnancy but I’m so glad I did.

“I know that it’s only because of the treatment I received that I am here now. They checked my body very thoroughly and gave me the tablets that I needed.”

Midwife Gloria Nanah Kamara explains that Adama needed medication to prevent pre-eclampsia. The risk was great enough for doctors to insist her baby be delivered by caesarean section.

“Pre-eclampsia is very common, probably the leading cause of death during pregnancy in this country,” Kamara explains.

“The only way of ensuring that the mother and baby survive is to do a caesarean, which they cannot do in a local clinic.”

Adama Gomes watches over her newborn baby in an incubator Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Before the creation of the new hospital, which opened in February this year, the treatment Adama received would have been inconceivable for a mother from an underdeveloped region in Sierra Leone.

Two decades ago, amid the smouldering wreckage of a brutal war, the West African nation held the dubious distinction of having the worst maternal mortality rate in the world.

Around 2,000 women were dying for every 100,000 children born, a damning statistic for a country trying to rebuild.

Since then, the prospects for expectant mothers in the West African nation have improved dramatically.

Sullaymata Saffa with her one-day-old baby girl, after travelling across Sierra Leone to use the new maternal facility Credit : Simon Townsley

According to official figures from its Ministry of Health released last month, there are now only 354 maternal deaths per 100,000 live births, a 74 per cent reduction.

While any progress is welcome, the latest data show that globally 260,000 women died during pregnancy and childbirth in 2023. The vast majority of deaths in low and middle income countries are due to infection, haemorrhage and hypertensive disorders such as pre-eclampsia – and they are entirely preventable.

Reducing these risks does not require expensive or hi-tech kit – instead access to antenatal care, emergency obstetric care and postnatal follow up could all help save women’s lives. When a mother survives childbirth, her child is significantly more likely to live, receive an education, and break out of generational poverty, strengthening the community around him or her.

An expectant mother receives an ultrasound scan at an MSF hospital Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Sierra Leone’s success is largely due to the roll-out of free healthcare to pregnant women and children in 2010, and a more recent push to reach zero preventable maternal deaths. The 300 days of Activism for Triple Zero campaign – which also aims to tackle preventable child deaths and unvaccinated children – began in March.

According to the government, maternal deaths have dropped by 31.4 per cent since last year. There remains, however, deep inequality for pregnant women, mostly because of geographical inequity.

The United States charity Partners in Health, the lead funder for the Maternal Center of Excellence, points out that women in Sierra Leone have a one in 74 chance of dying in pregnancy or childbirth in their reproductive years. By comparison, the risk for UK women is around one in 7,500.

Despite the unparalleled progress of recent years, the happy ending which Adama and her baby have experienced is by no means universal across Sierra Leone.

A mother and her newborn recover from birth at the Maternal Center of Excellence at the Koidu Government Hospital Credit : Simon Townsley

Accounts of pregnant women dying before reaching hospital are commonplace, with deplorable road conditions and poor facilities in rural clinics often to blame.

Last month, a woman in the remote Falaba district in the far north of the country died while being taken to the local state hospital.

The first ambulance dispatched to transport her became stuck on the road, forcing health authorities to send a second ambulance. Sadly, the woman died while being transported in the replacement vehicle.

During visits to villages in the diamond-producing Kono district, the Telegraph observed how the positive official statistics do not always reflect the reality on the ground.

The busy waiting room at Koidu Government Hospital, in the east of Sierra Leone Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

The contrast between the gleaming new hospital in the regional capital Koidu and the primitive clinic in the village of Ponduru is jarring.

Our journey provides a snapshot of how arduous it can be for expectant mothers living in distant communities to reach a decent maternity unit.

For the first hour, the spine-shaking terrain prompts me to contemplate how much more painful the same trip would be for a heavily pregnant woman.

Women wait for ante-natal examinations Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Afterwards, the churned-up mud track is so bad that we have to abandon the vehicle and walk the final mile.

Motorcycles skid and swerve through the sticky clay, but are the only form of transport for people living several hours further down the treacherous route, including pregnant women.

An ambulance that was due to visit the village during our visit never arrives because the driver is afraid it will get stuck.

It is evident that a woman needing a team of midwives and expensive monitoring equipment to assist with a complicated birth can be totally cut off during the rainy season.

On our hike, we pass women washing clothes in a flooded river while, further along, a group of men escapes the full blast of the sweltering heat in the shade of a mango tree.

Betty Abu prepares for the birth of her third child; Only two of Isha Sheriff’s four children survived Credit : Simon Townsley

Nine-months pregnant Betty Abu, 26, is sheltering inside the village clinic, preparing to give birth for the third time.

“I walked here from my own village because the road is so bad,” Betty tells me. “It took me three hours. I’ve been doing the same thing regularly for appointments because I’ve had a lot of pain.

“Even though it’s not great here it’s better than where I come from. Many women there have had miscarriages and stillbirths.”

Beside her, 29-year-old Isha Sheriff echoes this view, testifying that only two of her four children were born alive. Isha, like others, bears her tragedy with stoicism, recognising her own survival is entirely thanks to modern medicine.

Sebatu Kamara with baby Moses Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I had a blockage in my stomach, which caused the baby to die inside me. I also had sepsis,” explains Isha, a teacher in the village school. “They had to operate on me.

“My whole body was swollen. I could barely walk because I was so weak. But I know that I definitely would have lost my life without the treatment I was given in hospital.”

As we leave the village, I meet 23-year-old Sebatu Kamara carrying her eight-month-old baby Moses in a sling on her back.

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu faces the prospect of motorcycle transport Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“I feel very lucky to have got through my pregnancy,” admits Sebatu. “There are no guarantees in a place like this. Now I can focus on my child.”

Heavily pregnant Betty Gbortu, 19, is less settled, desperately hoping that she can avoid an excruciating motorcycle trip to Koidu. She counts down the days to her admission into Ponduru’s delivery room.

If she does stay, the facilities in the clinic will be minimal. The village has a pump from a borehole, but no running water.

Community midwife Margaret Messie Seppeh admits the power supply is so unstable that she regularly depends on mobile phone torches to see during a nocturnal delivery.

The Maternal Center of Excellence is now the country’s main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

For those with the means to get there, the Maternal Center of Excellence, which is five and a half hours from the capital and biggest city Freetown, offers exemplary care.

Attached to the existing Government Hospital, it is now the main referral centre for high-risk pregnancies and obstetric emergencies for the whole country.

From the six-bed delivery ward to the intensive care unit, every part of the hospital boasts the latest foetal and maternal monitoring technology.

The facilities are so much better than other regional delivery wards that some patients travel for days on the back of a motorbike taxi to use it, including some from neighbouring Guinea. Admission is free of charge, mostly thanks to financial support from Partners in Health.

The centre boasts state-of-the-art hospital facilities Credit : Simon Townsley

Nearly half of the 2,375 women to give birth in the Maternal Center of Excellence since it opened have had emergency caesarean sections, for which a blood transfusion is routinely required.

The reason for this is that many patients – often still teenagers – have had no check-ups, so potential complications are only identified as they go into labour.

Nurse Kamara says another significant challenge is that the majority of expectant mothers have been subjected to female genital mutilation, making a natural birth more problematic.

Midwife Fatu Josephine Musa with foetal heart-rate monitors in the centre’s delivery suite Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most mothers who come here have undergone this procedure,” she explains. “We can have up to 14 c-section operations a day, not including emergencies.

“Many of them had no antenatal appointments so when they arrive it is already too late for a natural birth.

“The young mothers often just don’t know what they are doing. They arrive here with a variety of obstetric problems. They are usually exhausted from the long journey too.”

A mother watches over her newborn in Sierra Leone’s first-ever neonatal intensive care unit Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Another issue which affects maternal health is the nutritionally limited diet of mothers who depend on staples like cassava and plantain. A lack of vitamins and minerals can increase the risk of anaemia, pre-eclampsia and complications after delivery.

Lack of income prevents many from making the long journey to Koidu. For them, motorcycle taxi fares are unaffordable.

But for now, the successful results of the facility mean pregnant women are gravitating there. With no equivalent anywhere nearby, it could soon be over-capacity.

In the antenatal ward, Kadiatu Jawara, 26, says it has taken her two days to reach the sanctuary of the region’s outstanding maternity hospital from her village in Guinea.

After suffering a miscarriage in her first pregnancy, she was desperate for the reassurance it provides.

“The pregnancy has been fine, but I know there is always risk,” admits Kadiatu. “I will need a caesarean, so I feel much more confident about it being here.”

Blood donors in Ponduru – including the village chief (centre) – play a crucial role in maternal healthcare Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

At the heart of the multi-pronged approach to tackling maternal deaths in Sierra Leone is blood donation.

A scheme called Gi4SaveLife is addressing postpartum haemorrhage – when a mother loses a large quantity of blood after delivery – one of the leading causes of maternal death.

Clinics previously relied on blood donated by family members for transfusions.

Community blood donors in Ponduru Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

This precarious dependence was further complicated by cultural suspicion around blood donation in the rural areas where it is most needed.

Now, instead of desperately finding relatives willing to accompany a patient to give blood during an emergency, villages are building up their own supply.

Isatu Jimmysam, 27, discloses that she is alive only because she received two pints of blood from stocks donated by her neighbours when she delivered her baby boy Hassan earlier this year.

At a blood drive in another village outside Koidu, backed by the local Lifeline organisation, 28-year-old Kadaitu Balgale tells me she feels obliged to donate following her own experience during childbirth.

“I was given a transfusion because of complications when I had my baby,” she reveals. “My pressure went right up during labour and I collapsed. The nurses had to perform a C-section.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village after losing his sister to childbirth Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Now my baby is three and we are both healthy. I was lucky. I’m very happy to give blood to make sure there is enough stock for other women who have the same problem.”

“I’m doing this to help save pregnant women and their children,” affirms Osman Kamara, 32. “I have been several times after the daughter of our village chief became very ill and needed blood during labour.”

In Sierra Leone’s most isolated places, however, keeping a stock of blood is simply not feasible.

Maya died aged 25, along with her infant, after losing too much blood to be resuscitated Credit : Collect

Refrigerated storage requires stable electrical power but 95 per cent of rural areas remain off grid. Solar panels are used but are not always reliable, especially during the rainy months.

Moses Kpovuwa, 45, is one of the most vocal advocates for blood donation in his village.

His sister Maya died aged 25 after losing too much blood to be resuscitated. She had been pregnant with her third child.

“Both her and the baby died,” states Moses. “She was very strong and healthy but developed serious complications which led to her bleeding profusely. There was nothing that could be done in time.”

The introduction of portable monitoring systems which enable rural midwives to assess maternal and foetal heart rates has also brought positive results. A trial of a device called the Cradle-5, backed by King’s College London and local NGO Wellbodi Partnership, improved detection of complications such as haemorrhage, sepsis and pre-eclampsia.

In the fishing village of Tombo, a complementary endeavour linked to the blood drives has led to a steep drop in maternal and perinatal deaths.

A pregnant teenager in the isolated Ponduru village, Kono district Credit : Simon Townsley

2YoungLives is a nationwide mentoring scheme for pregnant teenagers which recruits respected older women to mentor pregnant adolescents from pregnancy until a year after birth.

Mother mentors take girls to antenatal appointments, negotiate with families, recognise danger signs, accompany them during labour and help them return to education.

Before it started, many young women were ejected from their family homes after becoming pregnant.

Ostracised from the traditional support network, they were less likely to seek medical attention until too late.

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

Mother mentors with their charges and the babies in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

A 2015 survey showed one in ten pregnant teenagers had died during pregnancy or during delivery.

According to a paper published in The Lancet, 2YoungLives has reduced the number of maternal deaths, stillbirths and neonatal deaths in some areas since its creation in 2017. More than 900 pregnant young women have been mentored.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, who founded the project with Lucy November, a midwife research fellow at King’s College London, said it started because so many of Sierra Leone’s maternal deaths were among those aged under 20. Many were also victims of sexual assault, she explains.

Dr Mangenda Kamara, one of the project’s founders Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

Having become pregnant at 16 herself but then encouraged to continue school by her supportive father, Dr Kamara, now 45, is familiar with the predicament others fall prey to.

“Those who were dying were frequently from rural areas,” Dr Kamara explains. “They were often girls who were forced into sex. For example, it might be that a man would tell a girl he could help her avoid the long queue for water in return for sex.

“There are also stories of teachers and motorbike taxi riders abusing their positions in this way too. When they become pregnant, these teenagers become stigmatised and avoid seeking help.

“I took in a girl who became pregnant after being raped by her stepfather. She stayed with me until she gave birth so I could ensure there were no problems. That’s how this started.”

“Pregnant girls here are very vulnerable,” says mother-of-four Margaret Mansaray, 65, who has been part of the mentoring scheme since it started. “Their boyfriends abandon them and their families drive them out.

Margaret Mansaray, 65, has been part of the mentoring scheme since it began Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“Most of these pregnant girls don’t want to go to clinic appointments because they are embarrassed, so one of our main jobs is to ensure that they do.

“We make sure they are tested for conditions like malaria and hepatitis, as well any issues with the pregnancy.”

Margaret has been mentoring around 10 girls every year, significantly diminishing the skyrocketing maternal death rate in Tombo.

Pregnant Saodatu Fofana, 17, with her mother-mentor Margaret Mansaray in Tombo Credit : The Telegraph/Simon Townsley

“There were so many girls dying in the past,” she continues. “My own niece died from bleeding because she was not taken to hospital in time.

“Because of that, I was very happy to do this. I knew there was a desperate need. We used to go into the communities to search for abandoned pregnant girls but now people are aware of us. They see us as role models. Some of the girls even name their children after me.”

Gathered around Margaret are the local teenagers whose lives she has protected. Mums Adama Sesay, 17, and Rahmatalai Bah, 16, sit on a stone wall holding their babies.

Although abandoned by the men who got them pregnant, they can at least look forward to watching their children grow up.

Additional reporting by Saidu Bah

News.title: Testosterone ads banned over low sex drive claims
News.content:
Five adverts that claimed symptoms such as low energy and lack of sex drive were linked to low testosterone levels have been banned by the UK’s advertising watchdog.

An investigation by the Advertising Standards Authority (ASA), published on Wednesday, found that the adverts exaggerated the link between low testosterone and several common symptoms, including loss of motivation and changes in mood, which could have many possible causes.

The adverts, which included three posters and two paid-for Facebook ads, were created by Voy, an online health platform and prominent seller of weight loss jabs like Mounjaro and Wegovy.

The ASA said: “While some symptoms may be more closely associated with the condition, others were much less specific and shouldn’t have been presented as strong indicators of low testosterone in isolation”.

It also ruled that one Facebook ad, claiming that low testosterone affects one in four men over 30, was “misleading and not supported by the evidence Voy provided”. Voy disputed this.

“We’ve banned the ads and have told Voy to ensure that future ads don’t mislead people about the symptoms or prevalence of low testosterone,” added the ASA, who launched its investigation after receiving multiple public complaints.

Catherine Drewett, investigations manager at the ASA, said: “People should be able to trust the health claims they see in ads. This ruling makes clear the standards we expect from advertisers promoting health tests and services and the importance of ensuring their claims are supported by strong evidence”.

In response, Voy said the language in the ads was “deliberately conditional”, arguing it “did not state or imply that the advertised symptoms were definitively caused by low testosterone”.

Voy said the ads were retracted while the investigation was underway, adding that they will not run them again.

Dr Earim Chaudry, Chief Medical Officer at Voy, said: “Every patient decision at Voy is clinician-led and these campaigns were developed to align with UK advertising standards. We keep all our advertising under continual review to ensure it meets any updated guidance”.

News.title: Saucepan racks, fitted sheets and dehumidifiers: Your tricks for drying laundry in winter
News.content:
As temperatures drop and laundry piles up, drying clothes indoors can become a headache. But when Laura de Barra gave her verdict on the best heated clothes airers, Telegraph readers had a lot to say. So, we asked you what works in your homes.

While some of you have relied on heated airers for years, others have found a standard clothes horse or an overhead airer paired with a dehumidifier preferable. Several of you argue that you can’t beat the efficiency of a tumble dryer.

Here are your tried and tested tips...

Heated airers

These readers explain why they’ve relied on their heated airers for years, offer advice on what makes a good model and how to avoid damp and mould problems.



After seeing a review for the Lakeland heated airer printed in The Telegraph in 2008, Clive Ruffle, 67, from Surrey, felt enticed to buy one. “It had a price offer and a coupon to send to the newspaper,” he recalls.

“It’s still going strong and has been very useful to us,” he says. “I was quite surprised to see the dryer we bought those years back still available.”

The options to fold the airer away flat and use only half of it, where one side is folded down, are the two major features that attracted Clive to the product.

“The drying speed is good, and we’ve never felt frustrated by it,” he says. “The heated bars are very effective and if we choose to heat, clothes are usually done in the day. They take a bit longer without the heater.”

To avoid damp or mould problems, Clive keeps his upstairs windows open, “even on the coldest days,” he adds.

For a more affordable option, Caroline Morrell, 65, from Greater Manchester, recommends buying a tiered Minky heated clothes airer, which she uses with a Beldray cover.

News.title: ‘I lost my family when I contracted HIV’: why virus is still taboo in Iraq
News.content:
Hassan Mehdi never imagined that telling his family he had contracted HIV would cost him his home and his family.

The initial symptoms of the virus weren’t too worrying: a skin allergy, a rash, and swollen lymph nodes in his neck. The dermatologist told Mehdi, not his real name, that he was probably suffering from a seasonal allergy. But he then began to think about his dating and sexual history and did an HIV test at home. A faint line appeared, indicating it was positive. “I tested once again at home and got the same result,” he said.

His worst fears were then confirmed by doctors at a public HIV centre.

“Mentally and psychologically, I collapsed,” Mehdi told The Telegraph, his voice thick with pain. “I decided to take a break and leave my job as a graphic designer, and I shut myself in my room.”

The doctor urged Mehdi to tell his family about the diagnosis. He also asked him to sign a paper promising to disclose his status if he married, not to stop treatment and not get a tattoo. It also warned that he could face legal consequences if someone accused him of spreading the virus.

When he finally broke the news to his mother, he hoped she would support him. But instead, he was met with hostility.

He said: “After informing my mum, she started to spread the news with my relatives, and they warned her that if I stayed at home and mixed with them, I would infect them all. Additionally, my elder brother heard and told me: ‘If I see you in the street or anywhere else, I will kill you.’ That was the last sentence I heard from him before I packed my bag to leave home forever,” he said.

“I lost my family when I told them I had HIV,” he adds. “To a religiously extreme family, HIV/Aids is taboo,” he added.

To fight the virus and adjust to a new life away from the town where he grew up, he immersed himself in gym workouts, a strict diet, and his treatment regimen. Close friends, social gatherings, and special cultural events became his sanctuary.

News.title: Bosses ‘increasingly reluctant’ to hire as employment costs soar
News.content:
Job vacancies fell to their lowest level in 12 years outside the pandemic as employers braced for the impact of the Government’s workers’ rights reforms.

Vacancies dropped by 22,000 to 690,000 in the three months to October, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS).

This was the lowest since February to April 2021 – and the worst performance since the three months to September 2014 when taking out the impact of Covid lockdowns.

Bosses are grappling with higher employment costs in addition to the Government’s looming deadline to implement the Employment Rights Act on Jan 1. Under the changes, a cap on claims for unfair dismissal will be scrapped and the time a worker needs to have been employed before they can make a claim will be cut from two years to six months.

Martin Beck, the chief economist at WPI Strategy, said: “The problem isn’t that businesses are firing workers. It’s that they’re increasingly reluctant to hire them.”

Sports.title: Leicester City terminate contract with main sponsor after it named porn star as ambassador

LEICESTER CITY have dropped their main shirt sponsor over its relationship with a porn star.

BC Game has sponsored the League One outfit since the start of the 2024-25 season, but will be immediately removed from the kit after naming Eva Elfie as a brand ambassador.



Fans’ group The Foxes Trust put pressure on the club after the move earlier this month and terms have been reached to end the partnership.

Fans who bought merchandise from the club shop will be able to return their shirts.



A statement revealed: “Leicester City Football Club and BC GAME have reached a mutual agreement to conclude our commercial partnership with immediate effect.

“The decision follows constructive discussions between both parties in recent days, during which we recognised our differing commercial priorities moving forward.



“We would like to thank BC GAME for its support throughout its two-and-a-half-year association with Leicester City and for the constructive approach taken in reaching this agreement.

“Supporters who have purchased a BC GAME-branded replica shirt through official LCFC retail channels within the last 28 days (since 21 October, 2026) can return it for a full refund or exchange (subject to availability) by Wednesday 2 December. Proof of purchase will be required.

“This enhanced returns policy includes shirts that have been worn or personalised, which would not ordinarily qualify under our standard returns policy.

“Returns can be in-person at the Foxes Fanstore at King Power Stadium or via post.



“If supporters return their items via Royal Mail standard delivery, the cost of the return postage will be refunded by the Club via the payment method used for the original purchase.”

Elfie is a 29-year-old Russian, whose real name is Yulia Romanova.

She won the AVN Award for Best New Foreign Starlet in 2021.



The social media sensation has 4.9million Instagram followers and has made headlines in football before.

In 2021, she presented Venezia’s football kit after the club ended a 20-year absence from Seria A.

Elfie has also offered to fund esports prizes and featured in an ad campaign for Aurora Gaming’s Counter-Strike 2 team.

“Now it’s not time to think about rest, it’s not time to think about sleep. It’s about being ready and to prepare everything to be sure that we are going to compete in the best condition at Anfield.”

His appointment was announced last Friday, just over 24 hours after United had confirmed the sacking of Michael Carrick following the Red Devils’ worst start to a campaign since 1986.

‌



On Tuesday night, Pochettino asked fans to “give him time” to make United the city’s dominant club again after his last match in charge of the United States. Told by former Manchester City loanee DaMarcus Beasley that “Manchester is blue, it will always be blue” in the TNT Sports US studio after the second leg of the Nations League tie against Haiti, Pochettino responded: “You will see. Give me time.

View 2 Images Pochettino beat Haiti 2-0 in his final game with the USMNT (Image: Omar Vega/USSF/Getty Images)

‌



“The new challenge is a big challenge, but at the same time it’s adrenaline you want to feel.

“We need to add our common sense… we know the situation is not a situation that deserves to be a club like Manchester United, the fan base is amazing.”

‌



Pochettino then gave a very short interview to United club staff after arriving at Carrington. “Very excited to be here,” he said.

“It’s an honour. It’s a privilege to be in this amazing club. Yes, looking forward to start to work.”

‌



He added in a later club video directed at fans: “I am looking forward to meeting you guys. I hear so many good things about you. I hope we bring all the happiness working together and connecting together.

“This is going to be a special season to support and to make our players fight on the field and to get the results that we deserve.”

Sports.title: Arsene Wenger left red-faced as 'daylight' offside proposal set to be axed
Sports.content:
Arsene Wenger left red-faced as 'daylight' offside proposal set to be axed

A new offside proposal from the legendary former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is now unlikely to be given the green light after an underwhelming trial in Canada

View 2 Images Arsene Wenger's daylight offside rule has not impressed (Image: Jean Catuffe/Getty Images)

The proposed new 'daylight' offside rule proposed by Arsene Wenger is set to be scrapped - with even the legendary former Arsenal manager not impressed after it was implemented in a trial.

‌



‌



The Canadian Premier League was chosen as the testing ground for the proposal, which works on the basis that there must be clear daylight between an attacker and a defender for the former to be declared offside.

‌



Although Wenger's proposal had the potential to wipe out tight offside calls in the future, The Times report that it will not be recommended for use by the International FA Board.

‌



Results from the trial, which spanned 108 games, were presented to the game's law-makers, who discovered that the altered rule only 'made things worse', with most teams adopting deeper defensive lines to combat the proposal.

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



While the number of offside decisions fell by more than half, there was no significant increase in goals scored. Only 13 goals were scored by players who would have been deemed offside outside of the daylight trial.

As well as confirming even Wenger failed to be impressed by the results of the trial, a source told the outlet: “The consensus was that the daylight offside doesn’t work. The defences dropped much deeper and there were not many more goals scored - and some of those that were scored looked weird.

‌



“It was frustrating for the players too. This is not the way forward.”

View 2 Images Wenger has been tipped to rival Gianni Infantino for the Fifa presidency in recent weeks (Image: ANP/Shutterstock)

‌



Wenger, who won three Premier League titles during his historic Arsenal tenure, became Fifa's head of global football development back in 2019.

He had recently been touted as a potential rival to Gianni Infantino for the top job at Fifa following a chastening year for the incumbent president. However, it emerged earlier this week that Wenger has opted against rivalling Infantino in his bid to be re-elected.

Article continues below

Wenger would have received the backing of Uefa had he decided to run for the presidency after they called on Infantino to resign earlier this year. Instead, Philippe Diallo, the president of the French football federation, will be Uefa's preferred candidate.

Sports.title: The cost of Arsenal's great player retention drive - and what comes after
Sports.content:
Regardless of what transpires between now and May, nobody can accuse Arsenal of standing still in the wake of their Premier League success last year.

The Gunners have followed up on their first domestic title in more than two decades by positioning themselves even further ahead of their elite rivals. Already, they are the overwhelming favourites to lift English football's most coveted prize aloft at the end of the season. And they once again look a real force on the continent after the most heartbreaking of conclusions to their bid to seize a maiden European crown last time out.

A major factor of Arsenal's current rude health is the shrewd work they have undertaken in terms of managing their contract churn. A flurry of renewals has strengthened Mikel Arteta's hand no end as the Gunners chase greatness.

Bukayo Saka is the poster boy for the movement: a top-class, homegrown player committing his prime years to the club in exchange for handsome renumerations in the region of £300,000-a-week. But Arsenal's operation preceded him; Gabriel and William Saliba, the cornerstone of Arsenal's imperious defence, signed on again last year. Myles Lewis-Skelly has also re-signed. And it emerged this week that Declan Rice will also enter the upper echelons of the club's pay bracket after agreeing a new deal. which brings him almost in line with Saka. David Raya, Jurrien Timber and Piero Hincapie are also poised to follow suit. Others are likely to follow, if you don't get the picture by now.

‌



That leaves Arteta very much looking like the cat who got the cream. The nucleus of a title-winning team all locked down as they approach their prime? We're approaching Football Manager territory.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

The caveat to this impressive operation of player retention - which will at some point bite - is the cost associated with such a strategy. Even a goliath of the game such as Arsenal cannot ignore the numbers and enhanced contracts for so many key figures, not to mention a meaty new reported £20million salary for their title-winning manager, too, is quite the significant outlay. And that's without taking into account the natural side-effects of a team growing older together.

‌



Player trading may seem like the obvious answer to offsetting the cost of these significant contracts. But that is not without risks. It will undoubtedly lead to difficult decisions in terms of personnel - and potentially sooner rather than later given the ages of some of the key players Arsenal have yet to lock down to fresh terms.

View 3 Images Declan Rice and Bukayo Saka have both agreed lucrative new contracts with Arsenal (Image: Stuart MacFarlane/Arsenal FC via Getty Images)

Captain Martin Odegaard is a prime example. Turning 28 next month and with 18 months remaining on his deal, it is effectively stick or twist time for the Norway international. If Arsenal decide Odegaard will not be joining his peers in having his terms extended, then selling your captain in his prime - and just as he appears to have rediscovered top form - is a hard sell. But it's a scenario they may have to play ball with if they are to remain in a position of power long-term. Particularly as they will need to rebalance their squad in future transfer windows with new heroes as father time joins the Premier League elite in chasing their current stars.

Another element is Arsenal's track record in sales. It is, perhaps, the one area the club have failed to substantially improve upon in the years where they have re-established themselves as a leading force in the game.

‌



Arsenal have simply generated nowhere near enough from selling players in the past, particularly when you compare their activity to their elite rivals in the Premier League. That Gabriel Martinelli became the club's record sale at £55.7million when he departed for Al-Hilal in the final hours of the summer window is telling. The fact that prior to his move Arsenal's sale high was £35m is an even more damning reflection on their previous body of work in the market. If it continues, Arsenal will have no wriggle room in those challenging decisions.

View 3 Images David Raya is among a group of Arsenal players who are expected to follow Rice and Saka in signing new deals (Image: Julian Finney/Getty Images)

Andrea Berta will be the man primarily responsible for transforming the club on that front. Their recent success should naturally translate itself to more lucrative sales, with successful players more likely to prove far more desirable to potential suitors. But it would be naive just to expect the issue to simply solve itself based off the team's continued success alone. Arsenal will need to be more savvy in the market in the future to sustain their recaptured influence and power. And once a club has a reputation in the market, be it cheap sellers or over-payers, it can be hard to shift, as other English clubs have discovered.

Arsenal felt like a club operating in the here and now in the summer; the failure to land the world-class attacker Arteta craved may have stung, deals but for Ezri Konsa and Bruno Guimaraes were not done to lay foundations for the future. Not with the next five years in mind, rather the upcoming 18 months.

‌



There is nothing wrong with that approach. And given the current status of Arsenal's elite rivals in the Premier League, it may even be very likely to yield further titles and accolades. And for Arteta to create the dynasty he craves.

But the picture for the future will have to come into sharper focus soon - and one that is considered carefully given the vast sums of money tied up in this team.

Arsenal may very well be approaching a new golden era; one that maybe even lives up to the glorious Arsene Wenger days of old. What comes after won't be straightforward or cheap.

Sports.title: Premier League sent clear 'justice' warning over Man City appeal after sponsor threat
Sports.content:
Premier League sent clear 'justice' warning over Man City appeal after sponsor threat

The Premier League will meet with representatives of its clubs on Thursday amid the threat of legal action from Manchester City's sponsors, which could drag the saga on even longer

View 3 Images Chief executive Richard Masters is the face of the Premier League's battle against Manchester City (Image: Getty Images)

The Premier League has been warned that it needs to deliver "justice" in the Manchester City scandal as quickly as possible, or risk damaging its product.

‌



‌



City were found guilty in September of breaking the Premier League's financial rules over a nine-year period. An independent commission found them guilty of 114 of the 115 charges levelled against them, finding they had used "sham" contracts to inflate revenues or reduce costs by more than £900million.

‌



City have always insisted upon their innocence and have launched an appeal, which could be heard in December, ahead of a verdict in the New Year. The implications are huge, with punishments including relegation, a significant points deduction, a huge fine and a transfer ban on the table if the appeal fails.

‌



It emerged this week that the Premier League's board of directors will ask its clubs at a meeting on Thursday for legal protection should City's sponsors decide to sue them personally. The possibility of Etihad Airways and Etisalat taking action after the appeal's verdict means the process - which began in February 2023 when City were charged - could rumble on even longer.

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



Emanuel Macedo de Medeiros, the co-founder and global chief executive of Sport Integrity Global Alliance (SIGA), says sponsors are "entitled to protect their reputation and pursue legitimate legal remedies". But he has warned the Premier League that the eyes of the world are upon them and a definitive conclusion is needed.

“Whatever the final ruling will be, the process must follow applicable rules, established findings and due process," Medeiros told Mirror Football. "What is also indisputable is that football – and not just the parties involved – needs an outcome that is reasonable, credible and capable of commanding confidence.

‌



"Because there is no doubt that there’s been rivers of ink and controversy around this case. I think that justice needs to prevail on its own terms without any constraints, but also with the notion that for justice to be justice, it needs to be served swiftly. That is very important."

View 3 Images Etiihad Airways have threatened legal action against the Premier League. (Image: James Gill - Danehouse, Getty Images)

‌



Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

The Premier League season is continuing while the appeal is ongoing, creating a great deal of doubt over the events on the pitch, where City sit third in the table, six points adrift of defending champions Arsenal. The significance of the case is therefore heightened even further.

‌



Medeiros said: “The longer it takes for the final decision, the more controversy it will grow, but I want to believe that the end is close and there will be no margin for doubt at the end because no formality was overlooked or neglected and everyone had the chance to present their case. Whether it will be the last word, it is yet to be seen. Law is not an exact science."

View 3 Images Manchester City could be relegated from the Premier League if their appeal fails (Image: Getty Images)

‌



He added: “The process is still ongoing and every procedure must be exhausted. The decisions must be clear and unequivocal, beyond any doubt, so it leaves no room to surpass any formality, or constitutional right that parties involved legally enjoy."

The looming threat of legal action complicates matters after Etihad Airways said it was considering its options and Etisalat called the commission's findings relating to the telecommunications company "entirely false and defamatory". Medeiros says it is imperative that the Premier League can fulfil its duties without feeling in any way intimidated.

‌



"The wider principle is that football must retain the ability to investigate and enforce its rules, including when powerful commercial interests are involved – from sponsors, investors, or clubs themselves," he said.

"Access to justice and independent enforcement are both essential and neither should depend on which party has the deepest pockets or the greatest power in the media or the public sphere."

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino officially begins as Man Utd manager after gruelling flight
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino officially begins as Man Utd manager after gruelling flight

Mauricio Pochettino has officially started work at Carrington as Manchester United boss, having flown over the Atlantic following his final game in charge of the United States

View 2 Images Mauricio Pochettino has arrived at Carrington to start work (Image: Eamonn & James Clarke)

Mauricio Pochettino has touched down at Carrington to start his tenure as Manchester United's new head coach, mere hours after wrapping up his previous position as manager of the United States.

‌



‌



The 54-year-old arrived on a private aircraft at Manchester Airport at 11.32am on Wednesday following a seven-hour journey from the US, where he concluded his time as USMNT boss with a 2-0 victory over Haiti in Cincinnati.

‌



Pochettino was greeted at the airport by United security personnel and taken directly to Carrington, reaching the club's training complex shortly before 12.30pm for his opening day in the post.

‌



The Argentine will link up with his trio of staff who touched down in Manchester on Sunday, while also meeting the broader team and settling into his new surroundings. He is set to oversee his first training session on Thursday.

Pochettino is wasting no time in getting started, with his maiden match in charge coming against Liverpool at Anfield on Sunday. He will have just three training sessions to get ready for that fixture.

Sports.title: Oddball Gary Neville doesn't know what Grand Theft Auto is - and we love him for it
Sports.content:
Oddball Gary Neville doesn't know what Grand Theft Auto is - and we love him for it

OPINION: Gary Neville doesn't know what Grand Theft Auto is - and that's barely in the top 10 weirdest things about him

View 2 Images Oh Gary, you do make us laugh... unintentionally (Image: Stick to United podcast)

There's a video currently doing the rounds that serves as a beautiful, pristine reminder of exactly who Gary Neville is.

‌



The context, as you may well know, is that Grand Theft Auto (GTA) 6 drops on Thursday and the entire civilised world is vibrating with anticipation - including grey-haired schoolboys pushing 50 like Mark Goldbridge, who grew breathless with excitement while attempting to discuss this impending cultural monolith with the former Manchester United right back on this week's Stick to United podcast.

Neville, it quickly transpired, has absolutely no earthly idea what GTA is. When gently informed of the acronym's meaning, his brow furrowed with the earnest, uncomprehending confusion of a Victorian vicar confronted with a disposable vape. "So," he deduces, the gears grinding visibly behind his eyes, "is it just about... nicking cars?" Well, yes, Gary. Yes, it is. But it gets better.

Neville then casually reveals that he has never played a computer game in his entire life. Not one. Except, he concedes after a moment of heavy thought, for a brief dalliance with "the game where, do you know where the shapes come down and you try to fit them in?"

Make sure you don't miss sport's biggest stories and breaking news by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

Mauricio Pochettino's Man Utd inbox has five pressing jobs as staff fly in to begin work READ MORE :

Tetris. The man is describing Tetris as if it were a rare, highly classified Soviet psychological experiment he was subjected to in 1989.

He then goes on to express his lingering, puritanical disgust for his former team-mates who used to stay up until 2am mashing buttons on a PlayStation. To Neville, that was an act of profound, unforgivable unprofessionalism. You can practically see the ghost of Sir Alex Ferguson nodding approvingly over his shoulder as Neville condemns the pixelated sins of his peers.

But really, none of this should surprise us. We're talking about Gary Neville, a man whose public existence is essentially a long, fascinating exhibition of delightful oddness. He isn't wired like the rest of us. He's an intense, hyper-focused organism entirely lacking the gene for normal human function.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Take, for example, his now-legendary admission about taking "mini-retirements." A few years ago, Gary earnestly explained his revolutionary strategy for avoiding burnout on The Diary of a CEO podcast.

He described, with the unblinking, evangelical zeal of a Silicon Valley tech bro, how he takes a "mini-retirement" for three days, usually to Spain or Italy, to recharge his batteries before diving back into his 85 different jobs.

The rest of the world, upon hearing this breathtaking lifestyle hack, had to gently point out to him that he had simply discovered the concept of a weekend break.

Then there was his legendarily peculiar pre-match ritual during his playing days. Straight after Ferguson's team talk, Neville would pull on his kit, walk into the players' lounge toilets, sit on the exact same cubicle with the lid down, and read the matchday programme in complete silence for 15 minutes like a medieval monk studying an ancient parchment in a bleach-scented sanctuary.

He used to zigzag-sprint off the training pitch every Friday - leaving baffled team-mates like Cristiano Ronaldo and Carlos Tevez staring at him as if he were actively evading a swarm of invisible wasps.

He also spent years trying to build an £8million, underground, petal-shaped eco-mansion in Bolton - a turf-roofed hobbit hole that locals gleefully dubbed the "Teletubbies house" before he finally abandoned the scheme.

View 2 Images Gary Neville isn't normal... but that's why we love him (Image: Getty Images)

And who could forget his viral A-level results day phone call, where he comforted a devastated teenager who had just flunked his exams with the immortal wisdom: "Life's like a game of football. You win some, you lose some, and you draw some"? Ah yes. I fondly remember grinding out a few gritty, backs-to-the-wall 0–0 draws in my own exams.

Throw in the involuntary, strangled-badger "goalgasms" he emits in the commentary box whenever Fernando Torres rounds a goalkeeper, and you have a genuine British original - a relentless joy-proof Spartan who happily tucks into a bowl of plain pasta for Christmas dinner and is fast asleep by 8pm every New Year's Eve.

Modern football is infested with media-trained mannequins reciting sanitised platitudes. Neville is the glorious, bewildered antidote - a man who genuinely believes stacking descending geometric blocks is the zenith of digital entertainment, and we are infinitely richer for it.

Sports.title: JJ Gabriel has gambled his bright future by forcing through messy exit from Man Utd
Sports.content:
JJ Gabriel has gambled his bright future by forcing through messy exit from Man Utd

JJ Gabriel has taken an extraordinary approach to achieving his dream move from Manchester United to Real Madrid and once the saga is over he may find the grass isn't greener in Spain

View 3 Images JJ Gabriel has announced his departure from Manchester United - which was news to the club

The JJ Gabriel saga saw a development on Tuesday night which perfectly summed up the mess it's become.

‌



A 16-year-old player, who has never made a first-team appearance for Manchester United, took to social media to release a glossy video announcing his departure from the club.

Using phrasing more befitting of a club legend, Gabriel said he'd grown as a player and a person at Carrington and would forever treasure his time there. He then issued his thankyous ahead of his "next chapter".

‌



Which is all well and good, except for the fact that his "next chapter" has not been rubber-stamped. Despite his confident declaration of departure, Gabriel remains registered to Manchester United. Despite his own mind being made up, he is not a Real Madrid player.

Gabriel and his advisors, who most prominently include his father Joe O'Cearuill and new agent Ali Barat, have taken a forceful approach to getting what he wants.

Black Friday special! Click here to sign up to Mirror+ for just £1 a month!

‌



JJ Gabriel confirms Man Utd exit despite potential legal action over Real Madrid move READ MORE :

First he went AWOL from United in September, cutting off all contact from the club he's spent six years with. Then they went on a tour of Europe, courting interest from Barcelona, Bayern Munich and Paris Saint-Germain before settling on Real Madrid.

Gabriel then moved to Madrid to train solo while Barat negotiated a deal with the Spanish giants which, according to reports in Spain, is a three-year contract worth more than £850,000 (€1m) per season.

‌



Now, armed with a European Union passport, and like a breakaway region declaring independence from a country, he has self-determined his next step. Goodbye Manchester United, hello Real Madrid.

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



View 3 Images JJ Gabriel has forged his own path and it might bring a legal dispute (Image: Manchester United via Getty Images)

Once boasting the best academy and with a clear pathway to the first-team, United have evidently lost what made them the great at youth development. But its hard to imagine a saga like Gabriel's in a previous era either.

‌



Gabriel has 892,000 followers on Instagram, with the online hype machine driving incredible interest in his career. He told Marca recently that his decision to leave United in partly driven by his desire to win the Ballon d'Or.

And while times have clearly changed, the words of a previous United wonderkid still ring true. "Sometimes you have to be patient," Ryan Giggs said in early September. "You need to play games and it's difficult because if you're in squads for the first team you're not going to turn that down, but also you need minutes on the pitch."

‌



Gabriel has not played a game of competitive football since September 10, when he scored a hat-trick for United in their 5-0 win over Sabah in the UEFA Youth League. He has sacrificed minutes in pursuit of the move he has dreamed of. He is running before he can walk.

View 3 Images JJ Gabriel was hugely impressive for Manchester United's youth teams (Image: Alex Livesey/Getty Images)

‌



His dream move is not going to pan out as he envisioned it. United are poised to pursue legal action, having still not received any sort of contact from Gabriel, his family or representatives, or Real Madrid. If they find any evidence of Real tapping up the youngster while he was registered with United, then the battle could get even uglier.

Even if things go as smoothly as possible then Gabriel still won't be able to play a competitive game of football for some time. Having featured for United in the Youth League, he is ineligible to play for Real in the competition this season.

‌



If they can register him in the January transfer window then Real reportedly plan to place him in their Castilla reserve team. It doesn't seem like the grass is greener on the other side just yet.

Having frustratedly walked away from United when on the brink of making his first-team debut, Gabriel may well find things much tougher going in Madrid, where expectations are even higher. Many wonderkids have found the Real environment too fierce.

This messy saga is just the start of his gamble - and the way he's gone about things have certainly raised the stakes.

Sports.title: Man Utd training ground improvements could be derailed by BATS after complaint made
Sports.content:
Man Utd training ground improvements could be derailed by BATS after complaint made

EXCLUSIVE: Manchester United have made a planning application to Trafford Council, hoping to build floodlights and upgrade a pitch, but are facing objections from a local campaign group

View 3 Images Manchester United are facing objections to their training ground plans (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

Manchester United could be prevented from upgrading their training ground due to bats.

‌



‌



United submitted a planning application to Trafford Council on September 30 in a bid to build new floodlights at their Carrington training base, as well as replace a grass pitch with a synthetic one. But the request to erect eight new 18.3 metre-high floodlights has prompted an objection which could derail United's plans.

‌



Friends of Carrington Moss, a local campaign group who are trying to protect the peat bog on which United's ground sits, have raised concerns to the council. They claim there are "several unresolved issues" with United's application, which seeks to improve three of their 14 pitches at Carrington.

‌



"The proposal’s effects on Green Belt openness, landscape, lighting, ecology, biodiversity and drainage are not acceptable," their letter to Trafford Council says.

Black Friday special! Click here to sign up to Mirror+ for just £1 a month!

Get YOUR Mirror Football Newsletter Get our comprehensive football coverage, with news, updates, opinions, analysis and everything that matters to you, straight to your inbox. To get it, it's a quick and easy one-two: 1. Head THIS WAY 2. Enter your email and hit Subscribe

‌



A particular concern regards the impact that the additional floodlights would have upon the local pipistrelle and Myotis bat population, "particularly as the anticipated operational use (up to 9pm) overlaps with dusk foraging, when bats are most active.”

United have commissioned a biodiversity net gain assessment as part of their application and plan to purchase "off-site habitat units from a habitat bank" in order to offset the impact of the works. The club are aware of the objection and feel they have properly considered all the impacts to the landscape and ecology.

‌



Trafford Council refused to comment on the application but confirmed that a decision will be made "in the next few weeks".

Make sure you don't miss the best Man Utd coverage by making the Daily Mirror one of your Google preferred sources.

‌



View 3 Images Manchester United want to make improvements to their training ground (Image: Ash Donelon/Manchester United via Getty Images)

United have been at Carrington for 26 years and the facilities underwent a £50million makeover in the summer of 2025. The upgrades for the men's, women's and academy teams included the addition of cryogenic chambers plus improved changing rooms, gym, pool and medical and massage areas.

‌



"It’s disappointing that Manchester United, who consider themselves to be world class, are not making more effort to be sustainable," Marj Powner, chair of Friends of Carrington Moss, told Mirror Football.

"The lights are 18m high, they’re going to be massively visible from everywhere around and will disturb the wildlife. I don’t think they’ve properly considered an alternative, including lower lighting.

‌



View 3 Images The planned new floodlights could affect bats (Image: Getty Images)

"I get that it’s more convenient to have artificial grass and 18m-high lighting poles, but a truly world-class sustainable organisation wouldn’t be looking at their personal convenience, they’d be looking at what they can do to help encourage nature’s recovery, instead of helping to make it decline further."

Article continues below

This is not the first time that United have upset Friends of Carrington Moss, having received permission from Trafford Council to use a car park near Old Trafford earlier this year, despite their objections over sustainability issues.

Sports.title: Van Gerwen: I need my A-game to beat Wade at Grand Slam
Sports.content:
Michael van Gerwen believes James Wade is "in some of the best form of his life" and says he'll need to bring his "A-game" in order to win their second-round meeting at the Grand Slam of Darts.

Their clash on Thursday night - live on Sky Sports+ and Main Event from 7pm - is a rematch of the 2016 final, in which Van Gerwen claimed the second of his three consecutive titles.

But it's Wade, a three-time runner-up at the event, who is the form player of the pair leading into the last 16 matchup, having dropped only one leg across his two group-stage wins.

Van Gerwen, contrastingly, saw both his wins over Henry Coates and Jeffrey de Graaf come down to last-leg deciders. He averaged 100 against Coates, but that dropped to 90 against De Graaf, a match in which he missed seven match darts.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Twenty-year-old Henry Coates hit TWO huge finishes against Michael van Gerwen at the Grand Slam of Darts

"It wasn't a good game at all," Van Gerwen, seeded 10th at the tournament, told Sky Sports after his victory over De Graaf.

"Sometimes you're not doing what you want to do. That's frustrating, because I know I'm capable of doing a lot more.

"What can I say? I am through to the next round - that's all history now - and it's onto the next one."

The former world No 1 added: "James Wade is playing some fantastic darts, you can't deny that. He's probably in some of the best form of his life.

"I need to make sure I play my A-game if I'm going to beat him - simple as that."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Matt Edgar backed James Wade to make his return to the Premier League in 2027

Wade has been in sensational form across 2026, making it to the final of the UK Open, winning the Australian Masters, Flanders Darts Trophy, and the opening Players Championship event back in February.

He knows that, with his form at the minute, he has the game to beat anyone, especially if the contest is a bit of a grudge match.

"I think I am way better than the top 10 but I have had to bumble along," said the seventh seed, who has averaged over 100 in both of his Grand Slam group stage wins against Cam Crabtree (5-1) and Ricky Evans (5-0).

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cam Crabtree landed a brilliant 151 checkout for his only leg won against James Wade, who could only applaud!

"I think if I was probably a little bit more consistent, I would be better than I am.

"But talk is cheap and all that rubbish. I think I am good enough to beat anyone at the moment, because I like a scrap and no darts player wants to have a scrap.

"Most of them just want to have a little gallivant along the meadows and stuff like that, but I am quite happy to take them to a place where most of the younger players don't want to go and that is when I win games."

Luke Humphries, the 2023 Grand Slam champion, is also in action on Thursday night, against Tom Sykes, while Gian van Veen faces Martin Schindler and Nathan Aspinall takes on Gabriel Clemens.

Mardle: I don't get Van Gerwen at the moment

Sky Sports' Wayne Mardle:

"There has been so much made of James Wade's form. He is playing great.

"I don't really get Michael van Gerwen at the moment. A couple of weeks ago he was playing in a Pro Tour event and was averaging 114, 115. He also looked great in his opening group game here, but then looked really edgy in his second.

"Having said that, normally with Michael, the longer the format the less edgy he looks. I'm not saying he'll beat James, but I don't buy into this narrative that Michael is off. He's just not as consistent as he used to be.

"He portrays a lack of confidence at times with what he says, which I don't like.

"I believe he is capable of growing into a game. His confidence grows after a couple of decent legs.

"But if James Wade gets on top of him, I don't like Van Gerwen's chances from there."

Gabriel Clemens v Nathan Aspinall

Gian van Veen v Martin Schindler

Luke Humphries v Tom Sykes

James Wade v Michael van Gerwen

Sports.title: Wattimena wins hearts with win vs Littler: 'Beat him, the crowd loves you'
Sports.content:
Jermaine Wattimena put in a stunning performance to come up with a 10-8 win and dump Luke Littler out of the Grand Slam in the second round; you can watch the Grand Slam of Darts in Wolverhampton live on Sky Sports until November 22

Jermaine Wattimena wins Wolverhampton hearts with victory over Luke Littler: 'You beat him, the crowd loves you'

Highlights of the second-round match between Luke Littler and Jermaine Wattimena at the Grand Slam of Darts

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player

Jermaine Wattimena was visibly emotional following his massive 10-8 win over Luke Littler in the last 16 at the Grand Slam of Darts, taking in the moment as the Wolverhampton crowd sang his name.

An English crowd chanting so heartily for a Dutch player is somewhat of a rarity, especially when they are taking on an Englishman, but it was the sensational manner of his victory over the world No 1 and back-to-back Grand Slam champion that won them over.

Littler was aiming for a Grand Slam three-peat after his wins in 2024 and 2025 but with the Dutchman prevailing, it is still only Phil Taylor and Michael van Gerwen who have achieved such a feat.

Wattimena led 3-2 before running away to get 7-2 up against Littler. He then held on as Littler fought back to 9-8 and pinned 77 on tops for what is now the biggest win of his career.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Luke Littler is out of the Grand Slam of Darts after being beaten by Jermaine Wattimena in round two

It was made all the sweeter given the fact Wattimena has felt the pain of a massive Littler comeback before. He was 7-2 up against 'The Nuke' at the Matchplay in 2025 before eventually being beaten.

"Brilliant. One word needed, brilliant," Wattimena said.

"To be honest, I was thinking about the Matchplay in 2025 when I was 7-2 up. Now I am feeling that again but then the 77 goes in.

"I beat Luke Humphries in the European Championship and this is a bigger win than Luke Humphries then.

"I think you have seen me playing and I played with a lot of confidence. I was really concentrating in the match and I think I can go further than this.

"To be honest, I always play well against Luke Littler but to finally beat him on stage, I am really happy with that.

"I think my scoring power was better than his scoring power. He had to do it against me as well, but I don't think he did.

"They sang my name and I was emotional. That was really brilliant.

"If you beat Luke Littler then the crowd loves you."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player An emotional Jermaine Wattimena gives his reaction to his win over Luke Littler at the Grand Slam of Darts

Wattimena beat Littler back in August on the way to picking up a Players Championship title.

It was that win that reinforced for Wattimena that he could do the same again on the TV stage.

"I think (that win) gave me some confidence and then you know that he is not unbeatable as well. He is a human, he is not a robot," he added.

"He is a good player, he's an amazing player, everyone knows it but I am more than happy to beat him here at the Grand Slam.

"He got me here two years ago with a high score, but now I got one back.

"When you go to a tournament, you have to think that you can win the title, to be honest.

"You play tournaments to win something. It is a long way to go, but I am here for a win.

"I have got a day off tomorrow, so I have got nothing to do. I will be jumping in the jacuzzi, jumping in the swimming pool, so I'm all relaxed tomorrow."

Sports.title: Chelsea snatch late winner vs PSG to move top of WCL table
Sports.content:
Veerle Buurman's late winner snatched a late 1-0 win for Chelsea against Paris Saint-Germain to move them to the top of the Champions League table.

Sonia Bompastor's side looked as if they were heading to back-to-back goalless draws, following the 0-0 draw with BK Hacken last time out in Europe, until Buurman was able to bundle her effort home at the near post in the 88th minute.

The hosts had been the dominant side throughout but were thwarted by Katarzyna Kiedrzynek on more than one occasion.

Alyssa Thompson had come close to breaking the deadlock just before the break after seeing her initial shot and follow-up effort smothered by Kiedrzynek.

Image: Alyssa Thompson went close for Chelsea

The corner for Buurman's timely winner arrived after the PSG goalkeeper got down well to her right to keep Sjoeke Nusken's header out.

Lucy Bronze's delivery and a slight touch on the way through sparked panic among the PSG defence and it was Buurman who reacted first to sweep home the winner, sending her side to the top of the table with one league phase game to go.

The Blues remain unbeaten in Europe, winning three of their five games so far, and are well placed to qualify for the last 16 through the top four automatic qualification spots. They face OH Leuven in their final game, where they will go into it as strong favourites.

Bompastor praises resilient team performance

Chelsea boss Sonia Bompastor speaking to UEFA:

"I like the resilience from my team. Believing until the end of the game we could score that important goal and it was really important for us to win tonight.

"What I like in my team and squad is the fact they are really flexible; they are really open-minded to changing systems sometimes, adapting to what is happening on the pitch.

"They understand really quickly. I think it was good for us to be able to change, to go to a back four. We wanted to have the width to destabilise them more than we did in the first half."

On her side potentially finishing in the top four: "We knew we had two games left and getting two wins will help us to probably secure top four.

"So we still have things under control and that was why it was really important for us to win."

Buurman on 'important' win for Chelsea

Chelsea defender Veerle Buurman speaking to Disney:

"It was really important we scored the goal. Winning and three points was really important, especially after the last Champions League game where we drew against Hacken.

"A good team performance. We tried really hard and that I can score a goal is really important for the team."

Walsh: We are in a good place in WCL

Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh speaking to UEFA:

"We spoke about it before the game about wanting to finish the evening on top. We are in a good spot going into the last game.

"It was a massive win. It was tough for us tonight. They defended really well and they're aggressive.

"It was a difficult game physically but to get the win was really important. Hopefully it will push us into the top four."

Key moments from The Cherry Red Records Stadium

43: SO CLOSE! Thompson has an initial shot and a second effort saved by Kiedrzynek from close range.

53: SAVE! Kanjinga makes space to shoot, but Hampton keeps her effort out at the near post.

67: CLOSE! Buurman meets the corner and glances her header towards goal but it is saved by Kiedrzynek again.

86: ANOTHER SAVE! Nusken's header looks destined for the bottom corner until Kiedrzynek dives to claw it away.

87: GOAL! Chelsea finally break the deadlock as Buurman scores late winner at the near post.

Sports.title: Cadillac confirm Bottas to stay with team for 2027
Sports.content:
Cadillac have confirmed Valtteri Bottas will stay on at the team for the 2027 Formula 1 season, ending speculation about the Finnish driver's future.

Bottas returned after a year's absence from the grid for this season, Cadillac's first in the sport, as one of two hugely experienced drivers for the all-new American team's first line-up alongside Sergio Perez, who signed a contract extension last month until at least 2029.

But, Bottas' future has been up in the air recently as Cadillac pushed for American Formula 2 driver Colton Herta to earn a Formula 1 super licence, which he secured two weeks ago, by running him in practice sessions.

The team have committed to Bottas for another year though, citing the 37-year-old's "extensive Formula 1 experience, technical insight and race-winning pedigree to the team".

"To whom it may concern, I'm staying!" said Bottas, in reference to his team radio after winning the 2019 Australian Grand Prix with Mercedes.

"I'm excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn't going to be easy, but that's exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We've laid the foundations, we're learning and improving, and there's still plenty more to come, I'm hungry for more, and I believe in what we're building together. The story is only just getting started."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Cadillac driver Valtteri Bottas talks about why he decided to cycle from Malaysia to Singapore between those two races

Newcomers Cadillac are yet to score a point in their maiden campaign but Bottas is ahead of Perez in the Drivers' Championship due to countback, as his 13th place result at the Chinese Grand Prix is the team's highest result.

But, Perez has generally outpaced his team-mate which, with the links of Cadillac potentially keen for an American driver in Herta, led to speculation about Bottas' future.

Cadillac F1 CEO Dan Towriss said: "Valtteri's experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team.

"Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1. On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."

Cadillac say they will announce their 2027 F1 reserve and test drivers in "due course".

Just one seat left to be filled on 2027 F1 grid

With Bottas' future secured and Racing Bulls confirming last week that Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad will be their line-up once again in 2027, only Haas are yet to complete their driver pairing for next year.

Last month, Haas announced Rafael Camara will drive for the team in 2027, having already made an early F1 debut in Brazil and will compete again this weekend in Las Vegas, after Esteban Ocon was dropped following a dispute at the Mexico City Grand Prix.

But, Oliver Bearman has not been confirmed, although is expected to keep his seat once a "few bigger-picture things that we're working on" have been resolved according to the British driver.

Haas team principal Ayao Komatsu furiously dismissed reports claiming that contract extension talks with Bearman are being held up by the British driver demanding a £5m annual salary.

"I have no idea where that comes from," he said in Mexico.

"I've experienced this sometimes this season as well. People say there's no smoke without fire but really some people will invent a story."
