It will be fascinating to see if they gain access to his inner sanctum at United.

The club have had to double their media commitments this season as a result of the streaming deal, although they have been reluctant to organise sitdown interviews with players, telling Amazon that they must establish their own rapport for those.

Some clubs have been known to give their content away for free, with Sky Sports taking two seasons of Mission to Burnley without paying. The driving force behind those moves is to promote brands. Under Alan Pace’s premiership, Burnley are staring at potential relegation to League One.

Vincent Kompany, then the Burnley manager, is understood to have been vexed at his portrayal as a hot-headed screamer. Brendan Rodgers cannot have been overly pleased with Being: Liverpool, which ended in public ridicule and comparisons to David Brent. Players at other clubs have confided that they hid from cameras.

‘You can’t be yourself, you never forget the cameras are there,’ says Grayson of his season alongside the makers of Sunderland 'Til I Die

Salford's co-manager Anthony Johnson gives his players a dressing down in the BBC documentary

Joey Barton, meanwhile, is still waiting for his moment – and may be for some time. Fleetwood Town commissioned their own team to chart his start in management and streaming giants Dazn purchased the rights.

It was so close to being aired that Fleetwood held a premiere at Highbury Stadium for 100 supporters including the local mayor, only for one of Barton’s brushes with law enforcement in the intervening days to suspend the broadcast. Prolonged legal proceedings meant the idea was canned and Dazn’s licencing period expired.

It was later resurrected, focusing in part on then Fleetwood owner Andy Pilley’s fraud trial – a crew followed him into court on day one – but was then shelved when a guilty verdict was handed down. Cameras are following clubs up and down the EFL from Birmingham to Cambridge via Sheffield Wednesday.

Grayson, for his part, refused to share his drive home from training with the crew and now admits that the ultimately unfavourable edit may have been a result of him not giving the production company what they wanted.

‘I did a presentation with the players with a flip chart and everybody thought it was an hour before kick-off of a league game,’ he says. ‘It was actually done at 11:30am before a pre-season game!

'That’s why I let them film it, because it was a pre-season game, and it had no real meaning. But they presented it in the doc as if it was before the first game of the season.

'Part of the severance when I was sacked was that I still needed to do some work for them. I did three different (choreographed) interviews in a London hotel with different shirts on after I’d been sacked, done as if they were filmed at the time.

‘People said, “You didn’t come across that passionate about the club when you were talking about it”. Well, why would you when you were filming in November after you’d already been sacked? We were talking about deadline day in one of them. I’d already done something on that in August.

‘I think they had sympathy with me, but also if they’d had more sympathy, they wouldn’t have even asked me to do it. I’ve spoken to managers since and they’ve gone, “F***ing hell, you did well to put up with that".'

Grayson only ever watched four episodes back and has heard his successor, Chris Coleman, was also dealt a raw deal.

Fabian Delph leads a Manchester City inquest during an FA Cup defeat at Wigan - the only scene from the dressing room that made it into Amazon's documentary on the 2017-18 season

Mauricio Pochettino banned cameras from his office in his final days at Tottenham. Will he do the same at Manchester United?

By his own admission, Johnson enjoyed the process more than Grayson did. One ex-Salford player claimed that nothing was really cut from the show other than a fight on a team-bonding night out. It was authentic, no-holds barred.

Until the end of Johnson and Morley, that is.

‘We won the league and we ended up getting sacked anyway,’ Johnson says. ‘We went to meet Gary (Neville) and the board. We went upstairs in Hotel Football and a cameraman followed us. Obviously they knew what was going on. When we got to the room for the meeting, they wouldn't let the camera in.

‘I'm actually smiling thinking about it. The documentary followed me and Bern everywhere, eating food or whatever, and then when the day comes to sack us, they didn't want the camera in the room!

‘The conversation was fine in the room itself but I think the perception from the outside world looking in would've been: "What the f*** is that all about?”’

Sports.title: NFL slams 'inappropriate and offensive' Hitler joke about Patriots coach Mike Vrabel's mustache
Sports.content:
NFL slams 'inappropriate and offensive' Hitler joke about Patriots coach Mike Vrabel's mustache

The NFL has publicly rebuked Pro Football Talk's Mike Florio over his controversial comment about Mike Vrabel and the mustache he grew before the New England Patriots' recent trip to Germany.

The Patriots suffered a 35-10 loss to the Detroit Lions in Munich, which was the team's third in its last five games, and Vrabel has naturally been the target of criticism in the days since. Some of that criticism touched upon Vrabel's new mustache.

'If you're in Germany, you've got to be careful trimming that thing,' Florio said during a recent PFT Live podcast.

Florio's producer, Gary Carter, took issue with the joke, which many interpreted as a reference to Hitler's infamous mustache.

'It's funny, Gary. It was 80 years ago. Let us have some fun for crying out loud,' Florio said in response.

Now Jeff Miller, the NFL's EVP of communications, public affairs and policy, has weighed in, calling the comment 'inappropriate and offensive' in a statement provided to Front Office Sports.

New England Patriots head coach Mike Vrabel pictured at a press conference on Sunday

NFL Insider Mike Florio seemingly made an Adolf Hitler joke at Vrabel's expense

The 61-year-old Florio did not immediately respond to The Daily Mail's request for comment, although he and co-host Chris Simms did issue a joint apology on Wednesday.

'On yesterday's PFT Live show, we made comments that some found offensive and we apologize,' Florio and Simms wrote in a statement distributed by his employer, NBC Sports.

A former West Virginia lawyer, Florio has been covering professional football since the early 2000s.

His comments went viral on social media, with many fans ripping into him for the distasteful on-air remark.

Meanwhile, it was a disastrous trip to Europe for Vrabel and the Patriots, who are now 5-5 and in danger of falling out of the playoff picture.

Patriots quarterback Drake Maye is set to undergo further tests on an apparent ankle injury

To make matters worse, quarterback Drake Maye appeared to suffer a season-ending injury after getting sacked by Lions star Aidan Hutchinson.

After receiving medical attention, Maye headed straight for the locker room. He was initially questionable to return before being ruled out of the game a short while later.

Speaking after the game, Vrabel offered an update on Maye amid major concern from Patriots fans over the extent of the injury: 'Obviously [he] wasn't able to finish the game, so we'll have to get some more tests run when we come back what it ends up being, the severity of whatever injury he has.'

NFL Insider Adam Schefter later added that Maye will undergo those 'additional tests' once the team returned to Foxborough.

The Patriots now welcome their Week 11 bye, which could help provide extra recovery time for the 24-year-old signal-caller.

New England returns to action on November 29 against the Los Angeles Chargers.

Sports.title: Mykhailo Mudryk reveals he spent 'MILLIONS' on legal bills to fight doping charge as he blames his stint with Ukraine for two-year ban in tell-all interview
Sports.content:
Mykhailo Mudryk reveals he spent 'MILLIONS' on legal bills to fight doping charge as he blames his stint with Ukraine for two-year ban in tell-all interview

Mykhailo Mudryk has blamed his stint with the Ukrainian national team for the failed doping test which cost him two years of his career and revealed how fighting his case personally cost him millions of pounds.

The Chelsea winger, who is now on loan with Tottenham Hotspur, has opened up for the first time since he returned to football in the summer when his suspension was suddenly lifted.

It was in a two-hour interview with Ukrainian journalist Dmitry Gordon via his YouTube channel. While the title of the video mentions ‘suicidal thoughts’, Mudryk clarifies during the conversation that he did not consider committing suicide despite being in a dark place. ‘Kill myself – no, that’s not a way out,’ he said when asked that question.

But he did discuss how Chelsea broke the news of his failed test to him, whether they helped their £89million signing from Shakhtar Donetsk during his ban, his belief that the drug meldonium entered his system while he was in Ukraine, and why he is now with Tottenham. He further claimed that he has faced threats from gangsters, and admitted his dream is to someday win the Ballon d’Or.

On the Ukrainian national team and their federation, the Ukrainian Association of Football, Mudryk said: ‘I’ll be honest, it pretended to help. But in reality, there was no help. They created more problems than they solved. Especially when we needed help the most, they turned their backs on us.

'I just would like, for the future, everyone to understand that you can only rely on yourself.'

Mykhailo Mudryk has spoken publicly for the first time about the doping case that cost him two years of his career

Mudryk has criticised the Ukrainian Association of Football over their support during his case

Daily Mail Sport contacted the Ukrainian Association of Football for comment.

Continuing, Mudryk said: ‘The UAF is afraid of being left to blame in this situation, and afraid of the criticism or whatever else might come raining down. Distancing themselves from their own player, not helping, pretending to help, and in the end, first they drag the case out for months without really helping the case in the end. But at least the UAF isn’t to blame.’

Mudryk was handed an initial four-year ban after being charged by the Football Association for failing a doping test, with his last appearance prior to that coming in November 2024 in the Conference League away at Heidenheim. He scored in that 2-0 win for Chelsea. He was able to return when a seismic resolution was struck after changes to the 'scientific reporting standards'. Mudryk appeared for Chelsea during their pre-season tour before joining Tottenham on loan.

On how and why he failed his test, Mudryk said: ‘I had never heard of a drug like meldonium, never seen it, never come across it in my life. I only learned about it when they told me the news. I definitely have ideas. It’s a drug you can only get in Eastern Europe.

‘This drug could only have got into my body where I was, and that’s Ukraine. There are no such drugs in England. It supposedly stimulates your heart and helps you, as far as I understand, handle physical load better.

‘I was at home and Chelsea’s management came to see me and they said we needed to talk. Then they say you’ve returned a positive doping test and now you’re facing a ban.

‘You can’t believe it’s true. You can’t believe this is happening to you. If I’d ever taken anything anywhere, I’d have understood that this conversation might happen one day.

‘At least I’d have understood it was possible. But when you spend a huge pile of money on watching your diet, on a nutritionist, on a chef. When you spend that much money every year on all these things, that’s the last thing you expect. Because it speaks for itself: that you take things very seriously, like nutrition, everything that goes into your body, you watch it very closely.

‘Otherwise there’d be no need to spend money on it, because you could manage without it. They tell you this news, and you sit there, and you kind of listen to them but don’t hear them.

Mudryk returned to action when his ban was lifted in August, with the winger revealing Xabi Alonso told him to get game time and that he was 'counting on him'

The Ukrainian joined Tottenham on loan but has seen injury restrict his involvement to date

‘At some point you just go into a trance. It feels like you’re falling in a dream off a skyscraper. You’re flying down, you feel yourself flying down, and only in a dream do you wake up when you hit the ground, but in real life you don’t wake up, you just keep falling. It hits you very hard mentally. At that moment the tears came later.’

Mudryk revealed how ‘the figure is in the millions’ when asked about the lawyers fees which were needed to fight his case. He confirmed he paid for that himself, along with the personal trainers and massage therapists he used to maintain his fitness while suspended. However, Mudryk did add that Chelsea continued to pay his salary during his time out of football.

On joining Tottenham and being reunited with Roberto De Zerbi, who formerly managed him at Shakhtar Donetsk, Mudryk said: ‘It’s a perfectly logical decision. The club (Chelsea) has a new coach (Xabi Alonso), he sees football his own way. He sees the players he needs for that football. He came up and told me straight to my face: “You’d better go and play, get some game time, and then come back to Chelsea. I’m counting on you.”’ On De Zerbi, he added: ‘We met and he says: “Are you happy? Come on, we’ve still got a lot of work to do together.”’

Mudryk added how difficult it was after switching to England and, along with encountering issues with his former representatives who encouraged him to move to Chelsea rather than Arsenal, he said: 'They give you ultimatums, you know. That’s how it is.’

Sports.title: Anthony Joshua becomes a father for the second time: Boxing star welcomes baby girl in secret with mother of his son and says it was his 'duty' after death of best friends in car crash
Sports.content:
Anthony Joshua becomes a father for the second time: Boxing star welcomes baby girl in secret with mother of his son and says it was his 'duty' after death of best friends in car crash

Anthony Joshua has revealed he is a father again, welcoming a new baby girl into the world with Nicole Osbourne.

Former heavyweight world champion Joshua, who is gearing up to fight long-term rival Tyson Fury at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff, already has a son with Osbourne called JJ, aged 11.

Now JJ is a big brother, with Joshua deliberately not finding out the sex of his newborn during pregnancy.

His daughter is yet to be named but was born on November 14, weighing 5.5lb.

'It's been amazing, a big blessing, and I can't believe I'm a girl dad. I didn't want to find the sex out during the pregnancy,' the 37-year-old told The Sun.

'I love boys but as soon as I found out we had a little girl I said, "No more Fifa, no more motorbiking, no more PlayStation!".

Anthony Joshua has announced that he is a father again, welcoming a baby girl into the world

The ex-heavyweight world champion already has a son called JJ who is now 11 (duo in 2021)

'I'm going to do it all, so you might see me with some eyeshadow on, some nail polish on, drinking some tea in a doll's playhouse and just trying to do the right thing by her, you know? I will change nappies, I've gotta go through all that stinky bum time again!

'Now I've got a daughter, I will get an insight and a bit more understanding of what it means to be a woman, and how I can be supportive.

'My daughter will give me a first-hand experience of the power of a woman - I've spoken to all the women in my family, and it's amazing the amount of support that women give each other.'

Joshua is yet to meet his daughter as he is in Marbella preparing for his long-awaited showdown with Fury in the early hours of December 12, but will meet and hold his newborn after the fight. In the meantime, there have been FaceTime calls with Osbourne to see their daughter.

'This past year has been incredibly tough, I realised how precious life is, and how short it can be. I’m just going to live my life by duty, and even having a baby girl was part of my duty. I wanted to bring life in, it was a conscious decision, 100 per cent. If something happened to me, I didn’t want JJ to be out here alone,' he added.

The wholesome news comes less than a year after Joshua was devastated by the loss of his best friends Sina Ghami and Latif 'Latz' Ayodele last December, after the trio were involved in a car crash near Lagos.

Joshua has been deeply affected by the death of his friends and surviving the fatal crash himself, with the accident coming just ten days after he took down YouTuber-turned-boxing star Jake Paul.

Upon his return to the ring in late July with his fight against Kristian Prenga, Joshua broke down during his post-fight interview as he credited Ayodele and Ghami for getting him through a tough first round.

The 37-year-old is preparing to fight long-term British rival Tyson Fury in Cardiff next month

'I don't want to talk about it anymore,' Joshua had said quietly as he let out his emotions.

Earlier in the evening he had stepped into the ring wearing his friends' names on pennants pinned to his chest and had admitted before the fight that he had spent months suppressing the pain of their loss.

Joshua was being driven along one of Nigeria's deadliest roads in December when his SUV crashed into a stationary truck on the Lagos-Ibadan Expressway.

He is thought to have narrowly escaped major injury or worse after having switched to sit behind the driver in the back seat on the left-hand side of the car.

Joshua was admitted to hospital with 'minor injuries' after being pulled from the wreckage of the crash.

In February, Joshua added the names of 'LATZ' and 'SINA' to the tattoo outline of Africa he sports on his bicep.

Sports.title: The six biggest bombshells in Cameron Bancroft's damning Sandpapergate verdict that tore Australia apart: How Steve Smith will now be hounded, the brave voice they all ignored... and how two English cricket figures are mired in scandal
Sports.content:
The six biggest bombshells in Cameron Bancroft's damning Sandpapergate verdict that tore Australia apart: How Steve Smith will now be hounded, the brave voice they all ignored... and how two English cricket figures are mired in scandal

Just five days after Pat Cummins addressed the public with the intention of closing the uncomfortable rub of Australian cricket’s sandpaper chapter once and for all, Cameron Bancroft threw the book at the entire Test squad and its entourage.

Enraged by Cummins’ hour-long sermon last Friday, proclaiming his own innocence, Bancroft took to the pages of the West Australian to eviscerate the argument that three players alone knew of the ball-tampering ploys of 2017-18 in a 4,500-word response.

Usman Khawaja’s chronology of events in his recently-released autobiography Sabr had lightened his burden, but ‘the final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins’ press conference,’ he revealed. ‘It made me feel angry, betrayed and alone.’

Perhaps pre-empting what was to follow later on Wednesday, Cricket Australia attacked the issue for the first time since the scandal’s second coming aired earlier this month, promoting an in-house amnesty for those involved during the South Africa tour of 2018 to provide their recollections.

If this was designed to neuter an arsenal of testimony that features David Warner and Chadd Sayers aligning to that of Khawaja, it was like firing a popgun at someone armed with a bazooka.

Cricket Australia chair David Boon and CEO Todd Greenberg (left) announced the new forum in Hobart just hours before Cameron Bancroft's bombshell

For the force of Bancroft’s allegations has turned up the heat on the governing body to upgrade an independent forum into a new probe and for Cummins to revisit the conversation, having dismissed Khawaja’s words as ‘complete and utter nonsense.’

Here are the key takeaways from his bombshell essay...

Now the heat is on Smith and Cummins

Bancroft says he will attend the forum but has ‘reached a point where continuing to protect an incomplete account of events feels more damaging than the truth.’

And that rather than continuing to hold his tongue, perpetuating the theory that then captain Steve Smith, Bancroft himself and Warner were the sole perpetrators in the ball-tampering scandal, he believes it is important that the country’s cricket-loving public are given transparency.

Bancroft played 10 Tests for Australia but just two were after the sandpapergate scandal

Pat Cummins (left) and Steve Smith will now face questions after Bancroft's claims

Of receiving a nine-month ban and a permanent smear on his reputation as the tamperer-in-chief eight years ago, Bancroft wrote:

‘This was a burden which was heavier than my capacity and I took the bullet for everybody, and it was my choice.

‘However, in 2018 not the entire truth was told. I have never been completely honest about what happened.

‘It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team.

‘When I was questioned during Cricket Australia’s investigation, I did not give a complete and truthful account. I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

‘I did this to protect Cricket Australia’s investigation and not implicate others around me.’

Bancroft’s sharing of the finer details will intensify pressure on others to confirm or deny his portrayal of events, with Smith certain to be hounded by questions on his return from his New York home to play for New South Wales this weekend.

As for Cummins? His series of denials over knowledge of sandpaper entering the field of play, stretching back to the original inquiry including putting his name to a joint letter - alongside those of fellow attack members Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon - refuting it in 2021, and culminating in last week’s press conference, will not make this go away.

He must surely now reconsider his position as Australia’s captain.

How Bancroft felt forced into abetting senior stars

Bancroft backed Khawaja’s allegation in Sabr that Australia were doctoring the ball throughout the 2017-18 Ashes by lifting the quarter seam, an illegal tactic to encourage reverse swing.

‘I remember during my first Test match being instructed, along with other members of the team, to push the quarter seam of the ball together after the team took a wicket,’ he recalled, reflecting on how doing anything to gain an advantage over the opposition had been normalised within the Australian team environment.

David Warner (left), Bancroft and Smith were the only three players punished for their role

And so, according to Bancroft, when Warner - who had been in charge of the ball during the 4-0 win over England - suggested sandpaper could be used to rough up one side of the ball in the second Test versus South Africa in Port Elizabeth, he took over the role.

Having entered the match with a 1-0 series advantage, Australia were dismissed for 243 and had seen South Africa close to within 90 for the loss of two wickets by tea on the second day.

Cue the team talk in which Warner’s proposal was aired..

‘I was asked whether I could carry out the task. I felt uncomfortable and compromised. I knew it was wrong. I knew that using sandpaper was not simply pushing the boundaries of the laws of cricket. It was cheating.'

‘But I also saw an opportunity to contribute. I was a youngster playing in his seventh Test match. If you asked me to run through a brick wall at that time I would have.

‘That’s how naive and impressionable I was. I just wanted to be accepted by my teammates beyond the runs and catches I took. This was an opportunity for that.’

Inexperienced in such practice, Bancroft - then 25 - said he looked for reassurance.

‘I recall conversations with all the fast bowlers Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Marsh about whether it was reverse swinging enough. All the bowlers gave me feedback if my work on the ball was working. It was helpful.’

The moment umpires confronted Bancroft at Cape Town over his use of sandpaper on the ball

Australia took four wickets for 28 runs during the evening session. St George’s Park is a ground renowned for reverse swing due to its warm cross breeze, but this was a particularly fruitful session for the tourists’ attack.

The fact that Bancroft thought he was giving his side an advantage emboldened him to tamper with the ball habitually in the field from that point in what was a second Test defeat until being caught in Cape Town.

The coaches in England implicated in the crime and cover-up...

‘I remember bowling coach David Saker being involved in those conversations. Coach Darren Lehmann was also present.'

In Bancroft's account of the tea-time plot he also claims that after being rumbled by the television cameras shoving the sandpaper down his trousers at Newlands, Australian 12th man Peter Handscomb ran out at the drinks break with clear instructions.

‘He said to me: “I think it’s time I take that off you now”. And Pete was doing his job after Boof (Lehmann) shouted to him on the walkie talkie “get the f***ing sandpaper off Bangers now”.’

This version of events contradicts the one logged in CA’s 2018 inquiry which logged Lehmann as having said: ‘What the hell is going on?’ Or words to that effect.

‘It has been documented that a coach approached me during our fielding innings telling me that I needed to do more with the sandpaper on the ball to get it to swing. That coach was David Saker and it is true.’

Furthermore, he said Saker was the one who instructed him not to mention sandpaper back in the post-Cape Town media conference.

Australia's bowling coach David Saker went on to work with Ben Stokes at England

This leaves English cricket in something of an awkward spot. Daily Mail Sport is aware that Northamptonshire quizzed Lehmann - who has consistently distanced himself from the scandal - over his involvement when interviewing him for the position of head coach two years ago.

They were satisfied with his response then, and were unconcerned when it re-surfaced recently. Happy with his transformation of the club’s fortunes - they won the Twenty20 Blast for a third time last summer - they extended his initial two-year contract until the end of the 2027 season.

Saker, meanwhile, has worked as England’s fast bowling coach on multiple occasions either side of the sandpaper affair, finishing on the winning side of the Ashes divide in both 2010-11 and 2013 during his initial spell and returning, after leaving his Australian team post in February 2019, on multiple consultancies in the past four years, starting with the Twenty20 World Cup win in 2022, and also including the 2023 and 2025-26 Ashes.

Saker’s most recent assignment was with Brendon McCullum’s white-ball team in Pakistan last month, but the ECB are not intending to use him in the near future.

Lehmann is said to have left his commentary position with ABC radio at England’s win over Australia in Hobart early to consider a response to the allegations.

Northamptonshire quizzed Darren Lehmann before appointing him in 2025

The lowdown on how they tried to get away with it

Bancroft elaborated on the timing of his actions, touched upon in Khawaja’s book, evading suspicion by working outside of TV’s glare.

‘When we returned to the field after the break, the umpires would leave the ball on the outfield, a short distance away from the boundary line. From a broadcast perspective we knew that the cameras didn’t pan onto us as a team until we were about halfway out.'

'This was because the country logos would pop up on the telecast as an intro to the session. This is common practice. We’ve seen this before. Dave (Warner) explained to me why that presented an opportunity. It was also what seemed to be the safest time to do it. Others in the group agreed and gave their opinions on this.’

Such detailed communication about the 30-second windows in which they could operate to avoid detection highlights the depths the Australian team had delved in creating their win-at-all-costs culture.

Traditional methods of trying to get the ball to deviate through the air - of polishing it on trousers with the use of then permitted agents like saliva or sweat - had been ditched just a third of the way into a Test.

And what Bancroft says had been a team culture of fiddling with the quarter seam against Joe Root’s England on home soil weeks earlier had descended into something much more devious.

A brave dissenting voice that everyone ignored

‘Our media manager, Kate Hutchison, expressed her objection to what was happening. I recall her making it clear that she believed it was wrong, that she wanted nothing to do with it, and walking away from the discussion.

‘I will never forget that. Somebody had spoken up. Somebody had demonstrated that being part of the team did not mean having to accept everything the team was doing. And I ignored it.’

Referring to an Australian team meeting on the third morning at Port Elizabeth, Bancroft is talking about media manager Hutchison who left the organisation in April 2018, just days after Lehmann resigned as Australia coach. She has since held positions with Swimming Australia and in Australian rules football.

Australia's former media manager Kate Hutchison with Shane Watson (left) and Xavier Doherty

Usman Khawaja reopened the wounds of sandpapergate with his autobiography

The death knell for Bancroft's international career

‘My cricket career has been destroyed and I have never been able to play for my country since Justin Langer was coach in 2019.

‘I believed that, with time, my performances and conduct might earn me another opportunity to represent Australia.

‘Selection is complicated. There are cricketing reasons, competing players, different conditions and decisions that I have not been part of. For many years I believed I would be selected because I trusted the selection process.

‘But I would be lying if I said I had never wondered whether the unresolved tension surrounding these events in South Africa had played a part.’

Indeed, following two underwhelming performances at the start of the 2019 Ashes, the 33-year-old has finished within the top six Sheffield Shield run scorers for four of the past six seasons and is sixth this year too after four appearances for Western Australia.

Yet whatever he goes on to achieve on the field, it is for his damning revelations off it that he is destined to be remembered.

Sports.title: Mauricio Pochettino's Man United rallying cry: New boss promises fans it will be a 'SPECIAL' season - despite club sitting in drop zone - as he gets straight to work after flying from US
Sports.content:
Mauricio Pochettino has issued a rallying cry to Manchester United supporters, promising that this is going to be a 'special season' despite their dismal start which sees them 18th in the Premier League with just one win from their opening 10 games. The new Red Devils head coach landed in Manchester on Wednesday morning, hopping straight off a private jet to meet his new players, hours after leading the USA in his final game as their boss. And during a busy first day among his new surroundings, the Argentine sent a direct message to the club's fanbase as he preached for unity. 'Hi Reds, here's it's Mauricio Pochettino,' he said via a video posted on United's X account at 7.15pm on Wednesday evening. 'I am looking forward to meeting you guys. I hear so many good things about you. 'I hope we bring all the happiness working together and connecting together. Mauricio Pochettino addressed Manchester United fans directly on Wednesday evening after starting work officially as their new head coach The new Red Devils head coach has promised a 'special season' in a direct message to fans Pochettino poses at his unveiling with United director of football Jason Wilcox on Wednesday 'This is going to be a special season to support and to make our players to fight on the field and to get the results that we deserve.' In a second message in his native Spanish, Pochettino expanded further: 'This message is about being united, like the name Manchester United. We all need to work together. 'I hope to bring the happy moments that this club deserves and create the unity that every team needs so that the players can be at their best on the pitch.' Those messages came less than eight hours after arriving in England. He landed in Manchester at 11.32am on Wednesday and immediately headed to their Carrington training base where he took a tour and met players and staff. Speaking to the club's media channels earlier on Wednesday, Pochettino said: 'Thank you so much, I'm very excited to be here. It's an honour, it's a privilege to be in this amazing club. I'm looking forward to starting work.' The club then officially welcomed the new manager on their website, writing: 'Mauricio Pochettino has officially started work as Manchester United head coach, marking the start of a dream role for the Argentinian. 'Pochettino is joined at United by a team of loyal staff he has worked with at Espanyol, Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur, Paris Saint-Germain, Chelsea and USA. Join us in welcoming Jesus Perez, Miguel D’Agostino, Toni Jimenez, Alec Scott and Sebastiano Pochettino.' Pochettino had made a promise to end Man City's dominance as United manager in his last interview as United States national team coach on Tuesday evening. He took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet chartered by the club after his final match on American soil, which saw the US beat Haiti 2-0 in Cincinnati. But before becoming airborne, Pochettino had time for a final statement Stateside, after being taunted that 'Manchester is blue, and will always be blue' by one of his interviewers. Earlier on Wednesday, Pochettino made his way to Carrington straight after landing in Manchester, meeting players and staff and taking a tour The Argentine took off from northern Kentucky in a private jet last night and landed at 11.32am The manager shared a picture from his journey as he prepared to touch down at the airport (Source: Instagram/Mauricio Pochettino) 'No way,' he shook his head. 'You will see.' 'Give me time. Give me time and then that - that's going to change.' Pochettino also shared a poignant farewell message to his US set-up, days after breaking down in tears in a press conference ahead of his penultimate time in charge. Man United fans may also have been pleased to read of Pochettino's new-found love of John Denver's song Country Roads in his goodbye message, a song which is played before kick-off at Old Trafford. 'It is never easy to say goodbye, especially after everything we experienced together.' Pochettino captioned a carousel of photos of his time in the role. 'I always wanted the opportunity to coach in the USA, and I was very happy to have this chance with the national team. Two incredible years, with so many great moments and experiences that will stay with me always. 'From the challenges we faced at the Gold Cup to the excitement of the USA hosting the World Cup, and now finishing our time by reaching the semi-finals of the Nations League, I am proud of what we achieved. 'When we arrived, I wanted us to believe that we could compete with anyone. I hope today that belief is stronger, not only with the players but with everyone who supports this team. Not everything in football can be measured by results, and I believe we have helped build something important for the future of soccer in this country. The plane believed to be carrying Pochettino and his staff was hired by Manchester United 'This experience has re-energised me and given me so much, both in football and personally. I have discovered a wonderful country, made new friends and enjoyed so many of the traditions. Every time I hear Country Roads, I will forever think of all of you with a smile. 'Thank you to the players, staff, everyone at (the US national team) and all the supporters. Especially to those who believed in us and gave us this opportunity. 'Leaving is tough at this moment, but sometimes in football an opportunity comes that is impossible to say no to. I have always believed in following my heart, even when it means leaving a place where I have been very happy. 'I hope this team continues to grow and achieves all the success it deserves. Thank you USA.' Pochettino had previously explained his emotions as stemming from how difficult the decision had been to leave the national team and re-start at Old Trafford. ‘I haven't prepared a speech, I'm talking with my heart,’ he said on Friday. ‘It's difficult for me to talk now because I am a very emotional guy. ‘When these moments arrive, it is always tough. Normally it is the opposite – you have been sacked! You cry because you want to stay. ‘I think it was one of the most difficult decisions of our career, but you have to move forward. ‘Not too many opportunities can happen in your career with a side like Manchester United. That is difficult to turn down when it arrives. ‘In some part it’s a very sad decision, in another part we are professional and we are trying to make our dreams come true. We are excited for that step forward.' Man United first made contact with Pochettino following their breathless 4-4 draw against Aston Villa in their last match before the international break. The Man United hierarchy had previously given former head coach Michael Carrick a stay of execution amid a worrying start to the season, but as they prepared to head into the two-week pause in the relegation zone, the board became keen to make a change. An agonising wait for Carrick followed, with the club legend taking training for multiple sessions at the start of the week as his future was openly mulled by executives including CEO Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox. After the duo returned from Monaco, where they had flown to speak to co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe about Carrick's future, the 45-year-old was finally dispatched last Thursday morning. In their statement regarding Pochettino's arrival on Wednesday, United also confirmed the exits of Carrick and Co, writing: 'The club can confirm the departures of Travis Binnion, Jonny Evans, Steve Holland, Craig Mawson and Jonathan Woodgate alongside Michael Carrick. 'We would like to thank the group for their total commitment, dedication and professionalism, and we wish them all good luck for the future.' Pochettino's United States farewell match went off in pitch-perfect style, which allowed thoughts to quickly move to the next task at hand after the final whistle. Christian Pulisic helped make sure that Pochettino's reign in charge ended on a high note The manager will now focus his attentions on getting Man United out of the relegation zone 'When you finish the game, you start in your mind to think about different things,' Pochettino said after the win. 'Of course, it's tough because it's emotional. Because I really love these guys, and I love the players. I love the staff. I love the fans and everything.' Travelling with Pochettino were outgoing USMNT first-team coach Miguel D'Agostino, strength and conditioning coach Silvia Tuya and analyst Alec Scott, while his assistant Jesus Perez, goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez as well as Pochettino's son and fitness coach Sebastiano have already begun preparing for Sunday's matchup with Liverpool at Anfield. Man United paid a staggering £10million to cleave Pochettino and his staff away from the United States, after the head coach signed a new contract with the national team in the wake of this summer's World Cup. The quick turnaround means Pochettino will be able to work with the players as they begin reporting back from international duty. Furthermore, he is expected to speak to club media before conducting his pre-match press conference around lunchtime on Friday. Before boarding his flight, Pochettino not only waved to his adoring fans, but took a photo with staff and players on the pitch in Cincinnati. 'It's impossible not to cry, but that is because we care about the people and the people care about us,' he told reporters. 'When that happens, it's normal to show your emotions, no? Because we are human. We are no robots.'

Sports.title: Lionesses star Chloe Kelly cuts a glamorous figure in see-through dress at GQ awards night - hours after being left out of the England squad again
Sports.content:
Lionesses and Arsenal star Chloe Kelly stole the show at the GQ Men of the Year Awards on Tuesday night, going braless in a see-through dress just hours after missing out on Sarina Wiegman's latest England squad. The two-time Euros and Champions League winner arrived on the red carpet in a long-flowing navy dress, showing off her toned body and glamorous long blonde hair. She was joined by former England stars Mary Earps and Alex Scott. Kelly was once again left out of Wiegman's selection for the play-offs against Ukraine due to a hamstring injury, as the winger's battle to make the plane for next summer's World Cup continues. Wiegman announced her squad on Tuesday morning, turning to England's younger generation for the double-header against Ukraine. Izzy Goodwin is the latest emerging talent to receive a call-up to the Lionesses squad, after Lexi Potter, Erica Meg Parkinson and Freya Godfrey won their first caps in the previous round against Greece. The 23-year-old London City Lionesses striker scored the equaliser against Kelly's Arsenal last weekend at the Emirates, with the home side dropping points yet again. Chloe Kelly looked glamorous in a long-flowing navy dress at GQ Men of the Year 2026 The 27-year-old missed out on Wiegman's England squad for the second time in a row Arsenal have had an underwhelming start to the season, with just three wins in 10 games, and they currently sit in sixth place in the WSL table. Kelly was dropped for the first time by Wiegman for the previous qualifiers against Greece, alongside fellow forward Ella Toone. 'The main reason is that I think the levels weren't what I expect from them on the pitch,' Wiegman explained at the time. Toone has returned to the latest squad, with Wiegman praising her reaction to being dropped last time out. 'She responded really well (to being dropped last camp),' Wiegman said: 'Working really hard, she came in and was ready straight away. Going back to club she's done well and that's what has been fed back to me, too.' As for Kelly, however, it has since been confirmed that she has been struggling with a hamstring injury which has kept her from competitive first-team action since the end of September. The winger has started just one game for Arsenal, a 0-0 draw with Crystal Palace, and has not registered any goals or assists. She has yet to complete 90 minutes in the WSL this season. She was previously omitted from Wiegman's squad in 2025 for a lack of playing time as she fought with Mary Fowler for minutes - a disappointment that inspired her move to London from Manchester City. Kelly was joined by former Arsenal and England legend Alex Scott Kelly has been battling a hamstring injury that has plagued her since the end of September Known for showing up in big moments, it was a gamble that paid off and Kelly scored the winning penalty against Spain to win Euros 2025, earning her the nickname Chloe 'clutch' Kelly. Now, she faces fierce competition from new German signing Lisa Baum, with other talented wingers Caitlin Foord and Olivia Smith refusing to roll over. Kelly will have to steal the spotlight yet again to get a glimpse of Wiegman's England side.

Sports.title: Legendary commentator MARTIN TYLER on taking the Premier League plunge in 1992, Arsene Wenger's fury, his love of Woking - and THAT Sergio Aguero moment
Sports.content:
Two football images adorn the walls of Martin Tyler’s new home or at least they will when everything is in order. Tyler has recently moved house and the large, framed photograph of Teddy Sheringham scoring for Nottingham Forest against Liverpool, the only goal of the first Premier League game broadcast live by Sky is still on the floor by the front door. From wherever it ends up, it will project a moment in time when everything changed for Tyler, having walked away from a steady job at ITV and taken a leap of faith as lead commentator for the new satellite channel. 'A new frontier,' admits Tyler, the undisputed ‘Voice of the Premier League’ by the time he left the role at Sky, more than 30 years later. 'We didn’t know where it would take us, so that was a special day. Feeling a bit like a pioneer. Wondering whether we were all on a fool’s errand. Some people turned down the job I accepted because of the risk. My kids were four and two at the time. 'We used to travel to the games by train in those days, and we would look out of the window and count the satellite dishes as we passed through a big town. We didn’t know whether it was going to work. I wasn’t sure anybody would be watching. Legendary football commentator Martin Tyler has released a book: TALES FROM THE GANTRY Tyler was the undoubted 'Voice of the Premier League' by the time he left Sky Sports in 2023 'It was slow off the ground and there was a feeling within the game against live football, that people wouldn’t go to the games if they were televised live, and it ended up the opposite. Attendances have gone up, an amazing paradox. Now you can’t get a ticket.' Televised football has come a long way since Tyler’s first commentary game, Southampton v Sheffield Wednesday in the old Division Two in 1974, shot with just four cameras for Southern Television. 'Now if you don’t have 24 cameras you can feel a bit short-changed,' he laughs. 'I worked at ITV for about 17 years, most of it commentating and you would get a crew on match day who had been doing Coronation Street or Emmerdale Farm in the week and a match director from light entertainment.' The Premier League has come a long way, too. Some might argue too far. It has led football from its roots as the working man’s game to a place where clubs are owned by nations states and mired in the legal complications of the Manchester City case. Tyler wants to reserve comment on City’s financial offences until sentencing is passed, aware he is inextricably bound to their success because of his iconic commentary for Sergio Aguero’s winner in the 93rd minute against Queen’s Park Rangers to snatch the Premier League title from Manchester United in 2012. 'I’ve always said you won’t see anything like it again, and I stick to that,' he says, although he the 'Aguero moment’ as it has become commonly known probably means less to him than it does to others. He is proud to deliver the words but insists those moments belong to the players, the clubs and the fans, not to him. Ask about his favourite game from three decades in the Premier League and Tyler instinctively pulls Liverpool’s 4-3 comeback win against Newcastle in 1996 from the thrillers he has called. His own footballing background, meanwhile, could hardly be any further from the Premier League’s glitzy, moneyed elite. Tyler has always supported Woking and played as an amateur for Corinthian-Casuals. 'The law was you couldn’t get paid,' he says. 'We were on expenses only and they weren’t dodgy expenses. If I went on the tube to Leytonstone, I got the tube fare repaid and no more. 'I played for five years at that level and never got a penny because that was the rule. I played my last game in 1973 and within two years’ they got rid of it because so many people were bending the rules. An opposition player told me their team were on £75 a game.' Tyler reflected on his time in the game as a player, coach and commentator with Daily Mail Sport's Matt Barlow He was famously on commentary for Sergio Aguero's title-winning moment in 2012 From a cricketing family, Tyler was on the books at Surrey where he twice served as 12th man and lived for a time with Bob Willis, who became one of England’s greatest fast bowlers after moving on to Warwickshire. His manager for a time at Casuals was Surrey legend Micky Stewart, who had also played for the famous amateur football club before turning professional at Charlton. In those days it was possible for the multi-talented to hold down a decent career in two sports. An afternoon in Tyler’s company is just as likely to involve digressions into non-league football, where he worked as an assistant to Alan Dowson at clubs including Woking and Hampton & Richmond, as it is into the Premier League. He might regale you with a story about Arsene Wenger and the time, on the way to the gantry at Wigan Athletic, he slipped deeper than he realised into long conversation with the then Arsenal boss about rioting in Paris and almost missed his pre-match slot. And he might pivot from there into Wenger’s fierce rivalry with Sir Alex Ferguson. 'I have seen Arsene very, very grumpy,' says Tyler. 'When he lost the FA Cup semi-final when Dennis Bergkamp missed the penalty and Ryan Giggs scored. 'I have never seen a manager so angry because he knew he had handed over not only an FA Cup final place but also the domination they enjoyed at that time. They had done the Double in 98 and he felt that was not only about losing a match but losing their psychological edge over their greatest rivals. He was livid. Talk about winning and losing with dignity.' But there’s every chance he will reminisce about the time when, as a schoolboy Woking supporter in the terrible winter of 1962-63 he was rewarded for volunteering to paint the stands with an invitation to travel on the team bus to an Amateur Cup tie at Lydbrook Athletic. 'We left Woking at seven on the morning of the match for a two o’clock kick-off in Gloucestershire and by nine we were digging the bus out of a snowdrift on the A4,' says Tyler. 'We got there at four, no floodlights, and they had marked the lines on the snow with blue soap powder but there was no way we could play. We turned around to go back, got stuck in Cheltenham and had to stay for the night.' The only other footballing image on display in Tyler’s home is a photograph of him and Dowson celebrating as the final whistle confirmed their Hampton & Richmond side as Isthmian League champions in 2016. Tyler has had a hugely varied career, all the way from grassroots level right to the top Tyler even worked as an assistant coach to Alan Dowson at several Non-League clubs TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE After collecting the trophy, Tyler jumped into his car, drove north and less than 24 hours later was at the King Power Stadium to see Leicester crowned champions of England. 'The greatest fairytale story in the Premier League,' as he says. 'I had sampled that in a tiny non-league way, then taken those feelings with me to Leicester where it was multiplied a million times, but I could tell the world a tiny bit about how wonderful they must be feeling.' The range of his experience is vast. From amateur football in the 60s, through regional television and ITV to Sky’s Premier League revolution. He commentates regularly and coaches at Woking’s academy and has written a book. It is a wonderful compilation of 110 essays, the reflections on his lifetime in football. 'The random thoughts of a football obsessive,' as he likes to call it. TALES FROM THE GANTRY: Letters from a Lifetime in Football by Martin Tyler is published by Pitch and out now HERE
