Sports.title: Cadillac completes F1 2027 driver pairing
Sports.content:
Incumbent Valtteri Bottas will remain with the Cadillac Formula 1 team through 2027 after the US-owned team decided against fast-tracking American test driver Colton Herta to a race seat.

Bottas will stay on board with Cadillac alongside Sergio Perez as initially planned, with both race-winning veterans having signed a multi-year deal when they initially joined F1's 11th team.

But after struggling for pace against the Mexican, Bottas’ seat came under increased scrutiny within the organisation and majority owner TWG Motorsports, led by CEO Dan Towriss, weighed up whether to give Herta a chance as early as 2027.

After all, the team had spared no expense readying the former IndyCar star for racing in F1, including a tough F2 campaign and an increasing number of FP1 outings to ensure the 26-year-old Californian would reach the required threshold of 40 FIA superlicence points.

Bottas' fortunes were not helped by a series of performance, reliability and parts consistency issues with the rookie team, which has made the Finn's form harder to judge fairly.

And with Cadillac still far removed from being a frontline F1 operation, Towriss and team principal Marcin Budkowski now appear to have agreed that Bottas' vast F1 experience - which currently spans 265 grand prix starts - is what will benefit the team the most in 2027.

Cadillac said on Wednesday: "The announcement provides continuity and stability as Cadillac builds on its first season on the grid. It continues its long-term ambition to establish a competitive team at the pinnacle of global motorsport.”

Valtteri Bottas, Cadillac Racing Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

This now completes the 22-car grid next year with Cadillac yet to issue an update on what's next for Herta, saying "reserve and test drivers will be announced in due course”.

Bottas, 37, who has 10 race wins, said: "To whom it may concern, I’m staying! I’m excited to continue this journey with Cadillac into 2027. We knew building a new Formula 1 team from the ground up wasn’t going to be easy, but that’s exactly what makes this challenge so special.

"We’ve laid the foundations, we’re learning and improving, and there’s still plenty more to come, I’m hungry for more, and I believe in what we’re building together. The story is only just getting started."

Towriss added: "Valtteri’s experience, perspective and commitment are important strengths for our team. Continuity gives us a strong platform as we continue developing the team and working toward our ambitions in Formula 1.

“On the eve of the Las Vegas GP, everyone in the team is pleased to have Valtteri locked in for 2027 alongside Checo and look forward to the next stage of our journey together."

Sports.title: F1 to showcase driver health data in new partnership
Sports.content:
Formula 1 has signed a deal with wearables company WHOOP which will see a number of drivers wear the company's health trackers and showcase their data on the TV broadcasts in 2027.

WHOOP will become an Official Partner of F1 in a deal that will see an increasing number of drivers start wearing tech bracelets provided by the company while inside the car. Per F1's plans, that data such as heart rate, will then be fed to into its storytelling, ranging from graphics on social media to overlays that can be used during the live TV broadcast as early as 2027.

F1 did not disclose how many drivers will use the wearables from next season, as it is understood to be in the process of finalising deals on a case-by-case basis, but at least a handful of drivers have already signed up to the programme.

Earlier this year, WHOOP signed a deal with Ferrari, making the devices available to team members to monitor their wellbeing throughout a demanding season. The wearables are able to chart metrics like heart rate and heart rate variability, sleep quality, and VO2 Max. F1 hopes the deal will better be able to showcase the physical demands of racing.

Its announcement read: "Through this groundbreaking partnership, utilising WHOOP's industry-leading wearable technology and combining it with the sport’s award-winning broadcast, fans will gain a deeper understanding into what the critical moments they witness over a grand prix weekend require both physically and mentally.

"A cornerstone of the partnership will be the development of new broadcast storytelling experiences, featuring select insights delivered in the right way in collaboration with the drivers to provide fans with a real-time window into the physical realities of racing. These innovations will help showcase the human side of the sport in ways never seen before."

Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc are already using WHOOP's wearables. Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

WHOOP CEO Will Ahmed added: "WHOOP is bringing an entirely new dimension to Formula 1 by revealing the human performance behind the wheel.

"For decades, fans have had incredible insight into the cars, but less insight into the impact that races have on the drivers. Now, for the first time, we can show what happens inside a driver's body during the most intense moments of a race. This will change how fans experience Formula 1 and ultimately deepen our understanding of human performance."

F1 CEO and president Stefano Domenicali said: "The opportunity to uncover new insights, tell new stories and showcase the world-class athleticism that goes into making F1 one of the most extreme and exciting sports in the world, is truly groundbreaking.

"I can't wait to see these insights come to life through our broadcasts, giving fans a completely new way to experience Formula 1 while highlighting the incredible strength, resilience, and determination required to compete at the highest level of motorsport."

Sports.title: The factors behind the abortive 2030 F1 rules announcement
Sports.content:
Famously, when the papal conclave gathers to elect a new pope, a successful vote is communicated to the huddled masses via smoke from the Sistine Chapel chimney as the chemically impregnated ballot papers are burned: white smoke signifies a decision, black means yet another round of voting. The practice derives from the 13th century, when the cardinals took three years to debate a successor to Clement IV, prompting the frustrated local faithful to lock them inside the palace with only bread and water to subsist upon.

All this came to mind when Monday's much-anticipated meeting between the engine manufacturers, the FIA and the commercial rights holder to discuss the next generation of Formula 1 engines was followed by the 21st century F1 equivalent of white smoke billowing from the chimney: an Instagram post by FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem.

“You spoke, we listened. V8s coming soon,” he wrote underneath the ‘asset', an FIA-branded graphic illustrating sound waves and accompanied by the unmistakeable scream of a high-revving V8 engine.

And then, almost within the blinking of an eye, the white smoke turned black. Various related promulgations on the FIA's other social media channels were deleted, kept for posterity only by those with the foresight to screenshot them.

Ben Sulayem has been among the most vocal exponents not only of a return to ‘purer' racing engines than the current turbocharged hybrid V6s, but also of an earlier timing for that change. Although the balance of electrical deployment to internal combustion engine power is shifting over the next couple of seasons, the essential concept is due to remain in place until 2031.

Speaking earlier this season, the FIA president made it clear he wants to bring forward a new generation of engines in 2030, and would use all the powers at his disposal to make it so. But while it is within Ben Sulayem's bailiwick to set the F1 technical rules, whether the other stakeholders in grand prix racing would sign up to that is another matter, and bound into the commercial settlement known as the Concorde Agreement.

Realistically, Ben Sulayem requires a consensus between the FIA, the teams, the manufacturers and the commercial rights holder. Aligning these parties – some of whom are in competition with one another – is usually a process that is both tormented and tormenting.

It's in that context we must view this week's announcements and their subsequent striking from the record.

What is understood from various briefings is that there was broad agreement for a turbocharged 2.1-litre V8 with a smaller electrical element. Even to get to this point has required a great deal of compromise, since Ben Sulayem's spoken preference was for naturally aspirated V8s with token electrical input, similar to the Kinetic Energy Recovery System (KERS) first seen in 2009.

The president sees simplification as the way of creating a virtuous circle: manufacturing and development would cost less, potentially opening the way for non-manufacturer engines, while the engines themselves would be lighter. This would make a lower minimum weight for the cars realistically achievable.

This met with considerable resistance from the car manufacturers – although, to complicate the debate further, these are not all aligned with one another. Ford and Cadillac, for instance, with their broader focus on the US market, are understood to have been supportive of dropping turbos and having a smaller but still significant electrical element. At the other end of the scale, Audi and Honda saw natural aspiration as a deal-breaker and were insistent on a strong element of hybridisation.

Adding two cylinders was much less of an issue since V8 engines still figure largely in several key road car markets. In racing terms, V6s make a much less inspiring noise owing to their ugly firing order, even when not breathing via a forced induction system which mutes the soundtrack.

Nico Hulkenberg, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Brett Farmer / LAT Images via Getty Images

Although the principle of turbocharging will most likely remain, it will be based on smaller compressors running with lower boost pressures, which will reduce lag. The electrical motor's output will be reduced from the current maximum of 350 kilowatts (kW) to 100kW in general running, with another 100kW available to augment overtaking.

While this was the understanding, it's clear now that several of the parties in Monday's meeting emerged with a different perception to the governing body about what had actually been agreed.

This isn't necessarily a setback to the process, even though it has exposed a certain lack of consensus as we approach the point where the rules must be set. One thing all the manufacturers appear to agree on is that they need clarity by the end of this year to have enough development runway for a 2030 introduction.

To that end, the FIA wants to present a definitive 2030 regulatory framework to the World Motor Sport Council meeting in Shanghai on 10 December. This, though, would essentially be a rubber-stamping process. The real agreement must be secured before then.

This week's premature celebration suggests that this agreement is close enough to have the press releases written, but not yet at the point of clicking ‘send'. Perhaps we should lock the stakeholders in a nearby palace and feed them only bread and water until unanimity breaks out?

Sports.title: What McLaren has learned from a tough 2026 as it aims for a return to glory in 2027
Sports.content:
McLaren's 2026 Formula 1 season has been characterised by a recovery effort that never quite came to fruition.

Yet, team principal Andrea Stella insists the reasons for this are well understood, so he can be optimistic about 2027: "We are in a completely different place compared to the start of the season," he told Autosport.

Whenever it seemed to have caught its rivals, McLaren found itself falling behind once again. A difficult start, followed by progress that culminated in a period of the championship when the MCL40 appeared capable of setting the technical benchmark, then a gradual decline in competitiveness and a return to the front at the Brazilian Grand Prix. This trajectory is not easy to interpret.

Stella has an explanation that goes beyond the performance of individual upgrades. He traces the team's 2026 difficulties back to what happened during the previous season, identifying three decisive factors: a delay in developing the new car, the consequences of the demands placed on the team by the 2025 championship battle, and the disadvantages of being a Mercedes customer team at the beginning of the new regulatory era.

"I don't think there have been any upgrades this season, at least among the top teams, that haven't worked," Stella explained. "Even when we introduced some new parts in Baku, after which it appeared that we had taken a step backwards, that wasn't actually the case. Competitiveness has to be assessed in relation to your rivals, not simply by looking at your own progress in absolute terms. And from that perspective, I don't believe we ever took any steps backwards during the season."

The distinction is fundamental. McLaren improved gradually throughout the season, but not enough to compensate for the progress made by its rivals. Above all, it had to recover from an initial deficit that was considerably greater than anyone might have imagined.

A three-month development deficit

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Clive Mason / Getty Images

"We established that, at the start of the season, we were three months behind in terms of development," said Stella.

This is a significant admission, particularly because the Italian makes clear that this was not an assessment made retrospectively by translating the gap in lap times into months of work. McLaren had already identified the problem by analysing its development trends during 2025.

Stella acknowledges the impact of what happened during the previous championship battle. McLaren had planned to gradually redirect its resources towards the 2026 project, but Red Bull's resurgence in the second half of the championship meant it had to maintain a strong focus on the MCL39 which was still competing on track.

On top of this came an especially complex management challenge: supporting the championship ambitions of both Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri while maintaining an internal balance that would not jeopardise the team's future.

"For me, it was probably the season in which I worked harder than in any of my 26 seasons in F1," said Stella. "Every day, you had to pay attention to managing the team's environment, as well as the technical and operational aspects."

This is one of the less visible aspects of McLaren's story. The team had to devote its energy not only to developing the car and defending its competitiveness, but also to managing a delicate sporting situation. This effort, combined with the technical difficulties, contributed to slowing preparations for 2026.

The customer-engine factor

Mercedes' double championship demonstrates that it's now more challenging for engine customers to be competitive with their suppliers Photo by: Hector Vivas / Formula 1 via Getty Images

There is, however, a second element Stella considers decisive. For years, McLaren had demonstrated that a customer team could win a world championship using the same power unit as a works outfit. In 2026, that situation changed.

"In 2025, I was often asked whether not being a works team was a problem," said Stella. "I always said no, and in fact it had never been a problem until the end of last season."

With the introduction of the new power units, the situation became considerably more complicated. Integrating the engine into the car and optimising energy-management parameters took on decisive importance. Mercedes HPP, tasked with developing a competitive and reliable power unit, had to establish its priorities.

"When you're a customer team, you're not the priority," Stella acknowledged. "When it came to understanding the engine's power curves, certain cooling aspects or optimising the integration, we arrived a little late."

One concrete example involved the gearbox ratios, which had been defined using power curves that did not perfectly match those subsequently observed on track. These might appear to be marginal differences, but under the new technical regulations they can translate into significant disadvantages.

"In such a competitive F1 environment, you cannot afford to give away one or two tenths as a structural disadvantage simply because you're not in a position to be at the cutting edge of development timing," he added.

The most sensitive issue, however, concerns the tools used to optimise the power unit's operation. Some software developed jointly by Mercedes HPP and the works team contained proprietary elements that could not be shared with McLaren.

"They told us that these tools contained a significant amount of Mercedes intellectual property and that they couldn't give them to us," Stella said. "I didn't have particularly strong arguments with which to say, 'You have to give them to us anyway'."

The solution was to develop equivalent tools with HPP, essentially repeating some of the work that had already been carried out between Brackley and Brixworth. This process took time, and it is only in 2027 that McLaren will have full access to the same optimisation capabilities.

Nevertheless, Stella avoids any criticism of his engine provider. He acknowledged the difficulties faced by HPP, including those relating to reliability, and ruled out any deliberate attempt to disadvantage McLaren. The working relationship has remained positive, but that has not eliminated the structural disadvantage.

A recovery effort that wasn't enough

Developments have added performance, but not enough to ensure consistent winning form Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

McLaren attempted to make up the lost ground via the upgrades introduced throughout the season. The developments brought to Miami and Hungary produced clear improvements, but they were not enough to close the gap consistently.

"Every time we brought an upgrade, we saw a step forward, but we also saw that our rivals weren't standing still. The other teams brought their own upgrades too, and we weren't able to close that gap," Stella admitted.

Baku is a particularly telling example. At a circuit where electrical energy management is crucial, McLaren paid the price for its difficulties in optimising the power unit: "We weren't able to deploy all the battery energy from the final corner in Baku all the way to the end of the main straight.

"At that point, you're carrying a crucial disadvantage at a circuit that is so sensitive to power."

The problems had already emerged in the opening races. In Melbourne, the team discovered how a single suboptimal parameter could compromise energy management for an entire race, while reliability issues in China prevented both cars from starting.

The complexity of the new regulations had been anticipated, but not to this extent. Stella admits that McLaren underestimated just how decisive the power unit would become and how high the price would be for every parameter that wasn't perfectly calibrated.

The return to winning ways in 2027

Lando Norris, McLaren Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

The 2026 season hasn't diminished McLaren's ambitions, though. Stella believes the team now has a much deeper understanding of the car and, above all, of the Mercedes power unit.

"I'm optimistic about 2027," he said. "Compared with the start of the season, we're in a completely different place in terms of how we're using the power unit."

The technical relationship with HPP is also set to change. The tools that were unavailable at the start of 2026 will be fully accessible next season, albeit a year later than for the official Mercedes team.

There is another factor that Stella considers important: with 2026 being less demanding in terms of sporting management than the previous season, McLaren's leadership has been able to devote more energy to technical work and preparing the new car. The aim is to avoid starting next year's championship with the same deficit that has hampered the team this season.

"We are a team that, over three years, has had a rate of development that has taken us to two consecutive constructors' championships," he said. "We cannot now back down and say that finishing third or fourth is good enough. Our ambition is to remain world champions."

McLaren therefore ends 2026 with a different perspective from the one it had at the beginning of the season. Stella made no attempt to hide the mistakes and delays, but he stands by the quality of the work carried out throughout the year.

The challenge now is to turn what the team has learned into a competitive advantage, and to look back on 2026 as a transitional year that laid the foundations for a future back at the forefront of F1.

Sports.title: The Antonelli you don't know: Daily life with F1's newest champion
Sports.content:
There is one thing that physiotherapist Sergi Avila took a little while to understand. When Kimi Antonelli finally found himself with a free weekend, after weeks being spent between circuits, airports and training, the most logical choice would have been to stay at home: sleep a few extra hours, meet friends and switch off. Antonelli, instead, got in the car and went to a race track - perhaps to watch karting or MotoGP.

At first his performance coach inevitably tried to dissuade him, but then he understood that he was making a mistake as for Antonelli, simply going to a track does not mean working, but returning to the place where he feels happiest.

“The track is his natural habitat,” said Avila, “the place where he feels most at ease, where he can be completely himself. At first I thought it would be better to stay at home, rest, sleep a bit more. Then I understood that for him the balance is positive. Going to the circuit gives him something he would not have by staying at home.”

It is a small detail, but perhaps it is one of the best ways to begin getting to know the new Formula 1 world champion. Not the one witnessed on television, talking to the engineers and celebrating on the podium, but the one known by the people who live alongside him, sharing with him much more than the 24 Sundays of an F1 campaign.

The first time in F1: “How can he already brake like that?”

Riccardo Musconi, now chief engineer, virtual world at Mercedes, was one of the men tasked with accompanying Antonelli for the testing programme organised in 2024 to prepare him for his F1 debut. His first memory, however, dates back a few years earlier, during a single-seater presentation at Silverstone.

“I had heard about Kimi,” said Musconi. “I saw him in the garage and asked him if it was him. He answered me in English, so I explained that I was Italian too. Then I spoke with his father Marco. He told me how the conditions had come about for Kimi to enter the Mercedes programme. It seemed as if all the planets had aligned.”

Riccardo Musconi, Brazil 2022 podium Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

When the time came to start testing, Musconi found himself facing a boy who was not yet 18 years old. The first episode he remembers, however, does not concern a single-seater, but a van. “We were at the Spielberg circuit,” he recalled. “He took us for a lap of the track, in heavy rain - well, I didn't imagine a van could go that fast! He scared us to death. It didn't last long, because the brakes were already cooked after a couple of laps.”

Then came the moment to get into the Mercedes. In that case too, the track was wet. Musconi had at his disposal the reference data from the single-seater previously used by grand prix winner Valtteri Bottas and was impressed.

“It was his first run in the wet and he immediately found himself close to Valtteri's references at Spielberg that they had on file,” he added. “I wondered how it was possible. He had never driven a Formula 1 car: how could he already brake in that way? How did he know where to put the car in the wet? That left me speechless.”

The subsequent tests, including the one at Imola, confirmed the engineer's assessment, and he prepared a report intended for Mercedes' technical management. “After three tests I had understood that this boy was a phenomenon,” said Musconi. A conviction that would make it even more difficult to understand what would happen the following season.

A plan completed ahead of schedule

Bradley Lord, deputy team principal of Mercedes, remembers the first time he saw Antonelli in the team's garage. It was the 2018 Monaco Grand Prix, when the Italian was only 11 years old and so small that he could barely see over the workbench.

Eight years later, that child has won the F1 title. But when Mercedes decided to give him the seat vacated by seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton, the objectives were different. “We hoped to develop a driver who could help us win the constructors' championship in 2026,” Lord explained. “The plan envisaged a 2025 of learning, to put him in a position to contribute significantly the following year. Obviously Kimi accelerated the programme.”

Bradley Lord Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

The choice had been a brave one. Mercedes was losing Hamilton, the most successful driver in F1 history, and instead of looking for a conservative solution, it preferred to open a new chapter. “It would not have made sense to look for a half-copy of Lewis,” said Lord. “We had to do something different, start a new story. But in the end what really matters is only speed, performance and potential. Everything else can be managed.

“Last year he learned in one season what is normally learned in three years. He had a good start, a difficult middle part and a positive finish. But above all he found the way out of the difficulties on his own. In a certain sense, for me this is his fourth season, not his second.”

Five minutes that reveal a person

Rosa Herrero, senior public relations manager, knows another Antonelli. This is the one that she has to accompany from one interview to another, protect from constant requests and guide through the commitments of a day that often does not even leave time to breathe. After 10 years spent alongside Hamilton, the switch to Antonelli was a discovery for her too and a strong bond of trust has developed between them.

But there is a small secret in Herrero’s schedule. When she plans a meeting for Antonelli with Italian journalists, she sets aside 20 minutes, but only communicates 15. The other five are a safety margin. “I know that when the interview ends he will still stay to talk, to say hello to everyone,” she revealed. “I don't want to be the one who comes in and keeps saying that we have to leave. So I leave him those extra minutes.”

It is not an occasional concession, as Herrero knows his difficulty in pulling himself away from a conversation. “He has an incredible memory for names,” she said. “You introduce him to someone and the next time he already knows who they are. He says hello to everyone, he stops to talk. I think it is something that comes from his upbringing, from his family.”

Lord also recognises in this spontaneity one of the driver's most valuable traits, revealing a surprising detail. “In all the years we have worked with him, we have done one day of media training,” he revealed. “Just one! We want authentic personalities, not robots. Kimi is himself, he is honest, transparent, open. It is one of his superpowers.”

One of the group, without needing to play a role

Kimi Antonelli and Peter Bonnington Photo by: Zak Mauger / Motorsport Images

Peter Bonnington has worked with some of the strongest drivers in F1 history, from 2009 title holder Jenson Button to seven-time world champion Michael Schumacher. For 12 seasons he was also Hamilton's race engineer and when he left Mercedes in 2025, a new chapter also opened for Bonnington. His particular challenge was building a relationship with an 18-year-old sensation, who suddenly found himself occupying one of the most important seats in the series.

The first time he met Antonelli, in Monaco, Kimi was still a child. Toto Wolff introduced him, announcing, almost as a joke, that one day he would be his race engineer. Bonnington smiled, without imagining that prediction would become reality.

The professional relationship grew alongside the human one. “Kimi brought a dimension of spontaneous fun into the garage, almost like a playground,” said Bonnington. “That doesn't mean there was a bad atmosphere before, absolutely not. But this boy arrived and immediately broke down certain barriers. He is one of the group, we work hard and have fun together.”

It is above all that expression, “one of the group”, that describes the way Antonelli experiences life at Mercedes. He has not tried to create distance between himself and the people who work on his car, but he prefers to sit on a stack of tyres and talk with the mechanics, share a joke and even stop when his commitments suggest going elsewhere.

It is behaviour that Lord traces back to his origins. “He grew up in racing teams thanks to Marco and Veronica, he knows what it means to be part of a team,” he said. ”You see that every day.”

Antonelli has known that world since he was a child. He learned early that behind a single-seater there are people, even before roles and responsibilities. And today, despite having become world champion, he continues to behave as he always has without needing to continually prove he is the most important driver in the garage.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images

The salmon, the desserts and the little secrets of hospitality

There is, however, one place at Mercedes where the world champion goes back to simply being a 20-year-old. It is the hospitality kitchen, where Zugel works as the chef who prepares meals for Antonelli and his team-mate George Russell.

Zugel has known Antonelli since his Formula 2 days and since his arrival in F1, he has started to take direct care of his nutrition, following Avila's instructions. But Antonelli is not always willing to respect the programme.

“Sometimes he tries to be smarter than Sergi, to get around the rules to eat something he shouldn't,” said Zugel with amusement. “In Singapore he came into the kitchen without me seeing him. He touched my shoulder, I turned around and found him in front of me. He asked me for a double portion of salmon. I thought it had all been agreed!”

“About 10 minutes later, Sergi arrived and asked me if Kimi had ordered anything special. I told him about the double portion. Only then did I understand that it was not authorised.” There was even another occasion in which Antonelli had attended the buffet to serve himself a steak, ignoring the menu prepared for him. And when he sees a particularly inviting dessert, he tries to convince the chef to save him a portion. “He tells me to keep something aside for him for later, but not to tell Sergi,” chuckled Zugel.

Those are small acts of complicity that have built a special relationship. Zugel now knows Antonelli’s tastes, the way he prefers his pasta and which dishes make him happiest. “Through food you learn to know a person from a different point of view,” he claimed. “You try to prepare what he likes, you change something according to his tastes and little by little you build a relationship. In the end he spends so much time here that this has almost become a second home.”

The chef, too, has been struck by Antonelli's growth. “It is impressive to see the maturity he has reached, especially mentally,” he reckons. “He doesn't seem to feel the pressure and yet, despite everything that has happened, he has remained the same boy.”

When talent was not enough

Austria 2025 Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

Antonelli's rookie campaign was far from easy. Following an encouraging start, the summer of 2025 represented the most difficult moment of his journey and Musconi does not hide that that period profoundly surprised him.

“If you ask me what surprised me most in these two years, I would answer that it was the difficulties of last year,” he said. “After three tests I was convinced he was a phenomenon. At a certain point I was asking myself: what is happening? How is it possible that he cannot express what we have seen?”

The answer, at least in part, came from comparing notes with some engineers used to working with young drivers. “They pointed out something we had underestimated,” he added. “Working with a rookie is different from working with an experienced driver and I realised that many of the engineers following Kimi had never worked with a debutant.”

It was a reflection that shifts part of the attention from the driver to the structure that had to support him: Antonelli needed to learn, but Mercedes also had to adapt its working method. Lord confirmed how difficult it was to face that situation: “Only some drivers can withstand the pressure of going directly into a top team. Kimi felt the responsibility towards everyone, also because of the fight in the constructors' championship. It was an enormous weight.”

Herrero remembers Spa above all. After a particularly difficult session, she was supposed to take him in front of the television crews for the customary interviews, but she understood that he was not ready. So, she took him back to the engineers, gave him time to speak with the team to regain a little serenity. “I knew he needed time,” she said. “I kept telling him that he had to believe in himself. When you are nineteen it is difficult to bear the weight of an entire world judging you and today everything is amplified by social media.”

Bonnington also remembers that period. Mercedes had introduced modifications to the rear suspension that had not helped Antonelli, but external judgement inevitably fell on the driver. After Monza, the race engineer felt the need to have a frank conversation with him, as there were things that were not working and they had to improve.

Monza, 2025 Photo by: Simon Galloway / LAT Images via Getty Images

It was the beginning of a rebuilding process. Lord identified the meeting after Monza and the Baku weekend as the moment when the Italian began to find his own way. The team had not stopped believing in him. And Antonelli was learning to react.

The maturity he had acquired emerged in 2026, especially when the run of success was interrupted. “I was impressed by the way he managed the disappointment,” Lord said. “In the moment he was angry, emotionally involved, but shortly afterwards he had already turned the page and was focused on the next race.”

In Singapore, after a difficult Friday, he continued to work until he rediscovered a very high level of performance. At Austin he did even better and Lord remembered the calm he showed during qualifying in Texas. “He knew he was putting the pieces of the puzzle together and when the decisive lap came, he put them all in the right place,” he said.

A maturity that also surprises Bonnington. “The way he reads a race, picks up on the small details, describes the behaviour of the car during debriefings, they are all things you would expect from a driver with 10 years of experience,” he said. “And many of them you cannot teach. They come naturally to him.”

The champion who thinks he is only at the beginning

There is a conversation that Avila has remembered with particular pride. After the Hungarian Grand Prix, when Antonelli had already shown he could compete with the best drivers in the world, Antonelli confided to him that he still felt far from his own potential.

It was not a technical assessment. It was the awareness that he still had to learn, especially in direct confrontations with experienced rivals and in race situations he had never faced. “He told me he still needed to expose himself to many different scenarios, to gain experience. For me, hearing him talk like that was wonderful,” he said.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bagnall / Sutton Images via Getty Images

From karting to single-seater racing, Antonelli had never contested two seasons in the same category before F1, so constantly had to learn something new. Even with 2026 to an extent, considering the regulation change which represented a new challenge.

But today he is a world champion. He has achieved the goal he had pursued since he was a child, yet those close to him describe a boy who does not seem to consider anything concluded.

Rosa will continue to leave him five extra minutes in the schedule. Zugel will probably still have to defend a few desserts from the raids of his most famous guest. Bonnington will try to preserve that direct and spontaneous relationship he has built with his driver and Sergi, perhaps, will no longer try to convince him to stay at home on free weekends.

They are small details, far from the stopwatches and the standings, but they say something important. Antonelli has become world champion without losing the curiosity, lightness and need for authentic relationships that belong to his age.

Lord, who has known him since he was a child unable to see over the garage table, now watches with pride the driver he has become. “Out of the car he is fantastic,” he said. “But when he gets into a single-seater he is a monster. A good monster, but a monster!"

Sports.title: Piastri to receive 10-place grid drop at Las Vegas GP
Sports.content:
McLaren driver Oscar Piastri is set for a 10-place grid drop at the Las Vegas Grand Prix for exceeding his engine allowance in the 2026 Formula 1 season.

The 25-year-old was already on the limit of four internal combustion engines for the campaign, but will need a fifth Mercedes V6 engine to finish 2026.

As it is the first time he is exceeding his ICE allowance, Piastri will be docked 10 places on Las Vegas' starting grid on Saturday night local time.

McLaren said: "Oscar will take a new Internal Combustion Engine in Las Vegas after a reliability issue. As it is his fifth of the season, he will take a 10-place grid penalty, but he has a good chance to recover positions with overtaking in Saturday's race."

The Woking squad also confirmed it will take Mercedes' upgraded turbocharger, which the manufacturer developed under the FIA's so-called Additional Development and Upgrade Opportunities (ADUO) catch-up mechanism.

McLaren added: "Both cars, as with the other HPP-powered cars, will be fitted with a new ADUO-enabled turbo specification: the expected performance benefit is relatively small."

Oscar Piastri, McLaren Photo by: Michael Potts / LAT images via Getty Images

The Mercedes works team will trial the new turbo on Kimi Antonelli's car, while George Russell will stay on the original specification to avoid a grid drop, as Russell had already reached the limit of his allowance.

Mercedes boss Toto Wolff said: "We will have the ADUO-enabled turbo specification available from this weekend. This is primarily about proving out the development in race-weekend conditions, with the expected performance benefit relatively small.

"We anticipate running it with Kimi, whilst with George our priority is protecting his grid position with the performance benefit likely too limited to justify taking a grid penalty."

Sports.title: Mercedes’ technical director explains how Antonelli leapt ahead of Russell in 2026 | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Andrea Kimi Antonelli scored less than half as many points as his team mate in his first season of Formula 1 last year.

But he turned that around in his second season which put him in position to clinch the world championship as Mercedes produced the car to beat.

James Allison, Mercedes’ technical director who led development of their first world championship-winning car for five years, believes a shift in the handling balance arising from this year’s new technical regulations explains why George Russell lost the edge he had over his team mate.

“I would say that George – I’m more or less quoting George here – when he has been prospering, it is at a track where you can make a lot of difference from the apex and out of the corner,” he explained in a video released by the team.

“George is good at getting on the power and getting a strong exit from a corner. That certainly was true of last year’s cars and George was very strong relative to Kimi in last year’s car.

“I think this car is a little bit more conventional as a car, where a lot of the lap time is in trusting the car and the combined brake and steer on the way in: So, delivering the car to the apex, leaning on the front, trusting that the rear is not going to punish you and then arriving at the apex just that little bit quicker so you don’t have to be so aggressive on the exit.”

Antonelli’s stronger performance on the way into corners gives him an advantage when looking after his tyres, says Allison.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

“That, in the race, tells because you are using less of the rear tyre. You get less tyre degradation and that – if you want to see the standout performances of Kimi this year, it’s 20 laps in when everyone else has peeled into the pits and his lap times just go level.”

Lewis Hamilton, whom Antonelli replaced at the team in 2025, has also benefited from the same change, Allison believes.

“I think that’s one of the reasons why Lewis is having something of a sort of Indian summer in his career, because that was always Lewis’s great strength is hurling the car to the apex, trusting that he’s going to manage the thing as it gets to the apex.”

Allison said he is impressed by Russell’s focus on addressing where he has fallen short compared to Antonelli this year.

“He does not hide from his own deficiencies,” said Allison. “He’s one of the most honest drivers I’ve ever had the good fortune to work with.

“He can see the areas where Kimi has been quicker than him this year and he knows that those are things that he needs to bring to the table to compete on equal or better terms with this precocious young talent. I do very much admire the fact that he looked straight down the barrel of that and I’m pretty sure that we will see, we have seen in the last couple of races some very, very strong performances from him.

“I’m pretty sure in the last three we’re going to see him, without all the burden of these championships still on any of our shoulders, looking to build the platform that is going to let him have a run at it next year, alongside an amazingly talented team mate.”

Sports.title: An early season finale? Five talking points for the 2026 Las Vegas Grand Prix | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 heads to Las Vegas this weekend for what is supposed to be the first of three consecutive race weekends – but doubt still hangs over the following two events in the Middle East.

Here are the talking points for this weekend’s Las Vegas Grand Prix.

McLaren’s upgrade

Fresh from the team’s third victory of the season in Brazil, McLaren is bringing another upgrade for its MCL40 this weekend. However this latest package is aimed more at laying the foundations for 2027, when it hopes to reclaim the championships it lost to Mercedes last year.

The Las Vegas Strip Circuit has not been a kind venue to the team in recent years. They are yet to score a top-five finish at the track: although both cars took the chequered flag inside the top five last year they were later disqualified for excessive plank wear.

Will Lando Norris be back among the victory contenders this weekend – and will team mate Oscar Piastri get a better grip on a car he’s struggled with all year?

Alpine’s last chance for a result?

Alpine’s bright start to 2026 raised hopes at the team that, having sunk to last place in 2025, they would immediately rebound by finishing in the top half of the championship this season. That looks increasingly unlikely as the team has taken only a single point over the last six rounds, allowing Racing Bulls to open up a 45-point lead in pursuit of their best-ever championship finish.

The best hope for Alpine is a repeat of the windfall result they enjoyed in the closing stages of 2024, when its drivers pulled off an unlikely double podium finish in Brazil. But if that’s going to happen anywhere for them, Las Vegas might just be the place.

The track’s long straights favour aerodynamic efficiency and straight-line speed. Pierre Gasly showed Alpine have that in abundance when he claimed a surprise pole position at Monza earlier this year. He’s shown some form at this track too, putting his Alpine third on the grid for this race in 2024.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Here to stay

Formula 1’s ambitious plan of racing on the Las Vegas Strip did not make an especially auspicious start when practice for the inaugural 2023 race was badly disrupted after a drain cover caused significant damage to Carlos Sainz Jnr’s Ferrari. At the time F1 only had an agreement to race at the circuit for three years and it remained to be seen whether the city would embrace the race for the long-term.

Now they have: this will be the first Las Vegas Grand Prix since the promoters announced a new, 10-year contract. F1’s belief it could establish a foothold in Las Vegas has been vindicated.

The new Las Vegas Grand Prix is undoubtedly more impressive than its dismal eighties predecessor and has clearly served as a useful promotional vehicle for the sport. But it’s also an event where the show unquestionably comes first and the contest feels like an afterthought. Will that change now the event’s future is assured?

Speeding down the Strip

If the Las Vegas race represents everything Liberty Media wants Formula 1 to be, it’s rather unfortunate that its latest generation of cars appear so ill-suited for the track.

F1’s energy-starved power units will have to wait a long way between recharging opportunities on the Las Vegas Strip, not to mention the other long acceleration zones dotted around the circuit.

All year drivers have been frustrated at how constrained they are by their power units, notably in Mexico, another track featuring a long acceleration zone but otherwise blessed with many other recharging opportunities. Expect the problem to be especially acute this weekend.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

The last F1 race of 2026?

Since the previous round in Brazil, F1 has abandoned its contingency plan to race at Imola if the final two races in the Middle East cannot go ahead. Andrea Kimi Antonelli can therefore forget about signing off his dream, championship-winning second season on home ground.

Instead the series will cross its fingers and hope for the best when it departs Las Vegas for Qatar and Abu Dhabi. Moto GP raced at Losail two weekends ago, though one manufacturer stayed away, deeming it too risky.

While F1 team bosses have publicly expressed faith in the FIA’s judgement over the races, they are also taking seriously the possibility they may not happen. So far all bar three* teams have confirmed they will satisfy their commitment under the rules to run four inexperienced drivers in practice by this weekend.

There is a financial incentive for F1 not cancelling two of its most lucrative races. But are all the teams and drivers satisfied this is a risk worth taking? And if not, will any be bold enough to speak out?

*Update: Ferrari have now joined Haas in confirming they will run a practice driver this weekend, leaving just two teams yet to officially announce their plans.

Sports.title: Hamilton tells F1 to spend £50 million in promoting under-represented talent | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has called on Formula 1 to publish data revealing how far the championship is representative of people from different backgrounds.

The seven-times world champion founded Mission 44, an organisation to promote black and other under-represented groups, in 2021.

Hamilton said polling conducted by the organisation shows support among fans for broadening representation. Almost two-thirds of 3,000 people polled across the UK, US and Brazil said F1’s leadership should do more to widen participation, while 55% agreed the series “talks about inclusion more than it delivers”.

In order to promote new talent in the championship, Hamilton’s review made three recommendations. These include a commitment to invest £50 million over five years promoting new talent.

The organisation’s review, called Igniting Inclusion, also recommends the series, the FIA and all 11 teams report data on representation to an independent organisation for tracking. The data would include “who joins, who is promoted and who leaves, by gender, ethnicity and socio-economic background.” This partner would “publish one, sport-wide picture each year” and give annual awards recognising progress made by teams.

Igniting Inclusion also urges teams to create a published number of early-career places each year which would “build thousands of paid routes into motorsport by 2030.”

“Formula 1 is inspiring millions of young people around the world,” said Hamilton. “But inspiration means nothing without opportunity. We can’t tell young people to dream big and then not open the doors when they try to make those dreams a reality.

“F1, the FIA and every team must push harder and move faster. We need real investment, more opportunities and greater accountability. We’ve shown that change is possible. Now we need to go further. The talent is out there, and the future of our sport depends on unlocking it.”

Sports.title: O’Shaquie Foster May Have to Earn Shakur at 140
Sports.content:
O’Shaquie Foster is still pushing for a fight with Shakur Stevenson, but his path to getting it likely runs through a credible light welterweight contender first. Shakur is focused on lucrative matchups, and Foster brings a sharp counterpunching style capable of spoiling his night on the scorecards without generating the ticket sales or viewership to make the gamble worthwhile.

Foster revived the callout after Stevenson reached out to congratulate him. While Foster acknowledged the gesture and praised Stevenson as a great fighter, he made it clear that their fractured relationship keeps the matchup personal for him.

“We had a good relationship back then, but it’s where it’s at now,” Foster told Fight Hub TV. “So, you know, we still need to make that happen across the ring from each other.”

According to Foster, “stuff was said” and “the lines was crossed.” Still, the push for the bout has come almost entirely from his side. Stevenson’s message gave Foster an opening to put his name back in the mix, while Shakur has shown minimal public interest in taking the bait.

If Shakur ever warms up to the idea, he will almost certainly demand the fight at 140. That puts the pressure on Foster to move up from 130 and handle the extra weight. Foster has the patience to make Stevenson lead and work harder than he wants to, though proving he can hold his ground and make his counters hurt against natural junior welterweights remains an unanswered question.

Stepping up to 140 will make the fight against Shakur possible, and beating an established name in the division would give Foster real leverage at the negotiating table. The catch is that he would be taking on a dangerous opponent with no promise that Stevenson waits on the other side. Foster has the personal motivation to take that chance, yet Stevenson still requires a payday large enough to justify risking an upset.

Sports.title: No Handouts: Crawford Demands Canelo Shot for Lester Martínez After His Own Shortcut
Sports.content:
Terence Crawford wants to know why Lester Martínez is still waiting for a shot at Canelo Álvarez, though he is overlooking the business and boxing realities that put Christian Mbilli in line first.

Mbilli held the full WBC super middleweight title, which Canelo won from him by decision on October 31. Martínez holds only the interim belt and does not bring the leverage, name value, or resume needed to force his way into a massive payday.

Crawford and Martínez trained together under Brian “BoMac” McIntyre, who still coaches Martínez and prepared Crawford for his 2025 victory over Canelo. Loyalty to a former gymmate clearly played a role when Crawford focused on WBC president Mauricio Sulaimán on X, pointing out that Mbilli and Martínez fought to a draw:

“I don’t get it. It’s crazy how the @wbcmoro say Lester not good enough to fight @Canelo but Mbilli was. This the type of stuff I don’t like with these sanction bodies, they pick and choose. How being the interim champion not good enough for a chance at the championship.”

What Crawford leaves out is how Canelo’s career actually operates at this stage. Canelo is being paid enormous money by Turki Alalshikh, and Turki is focused on global spectacles, not charity mandatories for fighters the casual public has never heard of. Outside of hardcore boxing circles, Martínez is virtually unknown, and complaining on social media will not talk him into a fight he has not earned.

There is also a glaring double standard in Crawford’s complaint. Crawford himself received a massive shortcut in 2025 when he was allowed to skip the entire 160-pound division and jump straight to the front of the line to challenge Canelo for the undisputed 168-pound championship without facing a number one contender or grinding through the mandatory path. Nothing about that was fair.

Crawford got the fight because Turki liked him, and he was lucky to even arrive there undefeated after struggling badly in his previous bout against Israil Madrimov. Many fans felt Crawford lost that fight, yet he escaped with the decision, bypassed the sharks at middleweight and super middleweight, and walked straight into a title shot he had not earned in the division.

Even after winning the belts, Crawford did not rush to defend them against dangerous, low-reward fighters like Martínez or IBF champion Osleys Iglesias before stepping away.

Now Crawford is upset that his former gymmate is not receiving the same special treatment. Martínez has none of Crawford’s star power or backing, and his thin resume does not justify a handout. He did not look impressive in his interim title bouts against Immanuwel Aleem in March or Luka Plantić over the summer, and he was fortunate to escape the Mbilli fight with a draw after leaning heavily on excessive shoving while the referee let it slide.

If Crawford wants his former gymmate to land a fight with Canelo, the answer is simple: tell him to go earn it in the ring. Martínez needs real wins over legitimate opposition like IBF champion Osleys Iglesias, Darius Fulghum, Bektemir Melikuziev, or top middleweights moving up like Janibek Alimkhanuly and Carlos Adames. Until he beats serious threats and builds a case the public cares about, Canelo has no reason to give him the time of day.

Sports.title: Devin Haney Says Shakur Stevenson Fight “Has to Happen”
Sports.content:
Devin Haney is already talking about a fight with Shakur Stevenson like it’s a sure thing, claiming it “has to happen.” Looking at the rest of the welterweight division, you can’t blame him for eyeing that payday.

Outside of a Ryan Garcia rematch, nobody else brings the kind of money and spotlight that Stevenson does. The problem is that Haney is looking way too far ahead. He still has to survive Liam Paro first, and Garcia is lurking right behind him.

“I think that it has to happen. I think it’s just a big fight,” Haney said during an appearance on Shannon Sharpe’s Club Shay Shay. “I think that he’s going to keep winning. I’m going to keep winning, and eventually we’re going to have to meet.”

Realistically, Teofimo Lopez is one of the only other fighters who can help Haney sell a massive event. Conor Benn might get there if he keeps stacking wins, and Keyshawn Davis is still building up to that level of star power.

Guys like Richardson Hitchins, Rolly Romero, and Brian Norman Jr. would all make for solid matchups, yet none of them spark the kind of heated debate that Haney versus Stevenson does. Fans have argued for years over who has the sharper skills, and they will gladly open their wallets to settle it.

The problem Haney has is that there’s no way of knowing whether Shakur’s career will go downhill. He’s already lost almost an entire year on his extended victory lap after beating Teofimo last January. What we’re seeing here from Shakur is his chase of exclusively big paydays sidelining him, causing him to lose out on that great gig he had with Zuffa.

Haney needs to focus on putting the fight together with Shakur as soon as possible while he’s still in demand. The way his career looks now, it’s following in the same direction as the Charlo brothers. Jermell and Jermall went from headlining major events to sitting on the shelf for roughly three years, and by the time they finally resurfaced, the sport had moved right past them. Now they are stuck fighting on undercards for a fraction of what they used to make.

If Stevenson walks away from the Raymond Muratalla purse bid over low money, he is heading straight down that exact same path. That puts the pressure squarely on Haney to push for this fight immediately before Stevenson tanks his own value.

Sports.title: Chisora Claims Sparring Beating Drove Opetaia Out of Wilder Fight
Sports.content:
Derek Chisora is disputing the reason Jai Opetaia pulled out of his December 11 bout against Deontay Wilder, claiming a rough sparring session forced the Australian out of the fight while offering to step in as a replacement.

“Opetaia is not injured. He had a bad experience,” said Chisora, according to Desai. Chisora claimed the heavyweight got the better of Opetaia so badly that he left the gym and never returned. He went further, saying Opetaia couldn’t step up to heavyweight.

The massive purse for his previous fight against ‘The Bronze Bomber’ Wilder completely wrecks any realistic chance of Chisora getting the call. If $4 million to $6 million is his baseline asking price, the math simply does not work for an undercard slot as the replacement.

Fury vs. Joshua is already going to eat up the vast majority of the budget for that December 11 stadium show in Cardiff. Organizers are not going to blow another $5 million on a co-feature rematch that Wilder already won cleanly over 12 rounds back in April, especially when Chisora is demanding an eight-round cap.

From a business standpoint, paying A-side money for an aging veteran who does not move the needle on PPV buys or ticket sales makes zero sense. They can find a younger, hungrier heavyweight willing to fight 12 full rounds for a fraction of that purse. Chisora can keep floating sparring rumors all he wants, but he is pricing himself right out of the conversation.

If Chisora actually wanted the fight instead of just a headline, he would be publicly undercutting the market instead of telling gym stories.

Floating a discounted substitute rate of a few hundred thousand dollars would immediately get the organizers’ attention. On a massive stadium show where Fury and Joshua are soaking up almost the entire purse budget, promoters are looking for cheap, recognizable names to fill out the undercard without blowing up their overhead.

By demanding “the right money” while simultaneously asking for an eight-round cap, Chisora is playing his hand completely backward. He has zero leverage here. He is coming off a clear 12-round loss to Wilder in April, and nobody is clamoring to see a rematch.

If he came out and said he would take $300,000 to save the December 11 co-feature, his phone would actually be ringing. Instead, talking trash about Opetaia while pricing himself at millions just ensures the organizers move right down the list to someone hungry enough to take the smaller check.

Sports.title: Teremoana Teremoana Stops Hemi Ahio in Two
Sports.content:
Teremoana Teremoana dropped Hemi “The Heat” Ahio twice and stopped him at 1:36 of the second round to win the vacant IBF Inter-Continental heavyweight title on Wednesday at Pullman Melbourne Albert Park. The scheduled 10-round main event aired on DAZN, with Eddie Hearn’s Matchroom Boxing and Peter Maniatis’ PM Events promoting the card.

The much taller Teremoana (13-0, 13 KOs), of Brisbane, caught Ahio (25-2, 19 KOs), of Auckland, with a left to the chin midway through the first round. Ahio got up and took an eight-count from referee Ignatius Missaidis. Teremoana dropped him again with a right to the chin in the second. Ahio beat the count, but Missaidis waved off the fight.

Joel “Came KO” Camilleri (39-1, 15 KOs), of Melbourne, won the vacant IBF Australasian middleweight title with a unanimous decision over fellow Melbourne fighter Mitchell Leek (14-1, 8 KOs). The judges scored it 96-93, 96-93 and 95-94 for Camilleri.

Camilleri had a strong second round, but Leek dropped him in the third for an eight-count from referee Brett Manton. Leek also suffered a cut over his right eyebrow in the third. Camilleri appeared to be ahead after seven rounds. Leek pressed for a stoppage in the tenth and won the round on this writer’s card, but Camilleri made it to the final bell.

Ky “Hit Man” Hodgson (8-1, 6 KOs), of Melbourne, stopped Victor “The Tank” Adis-losifidis (3-1, 1 KO), of Victoria, at 2:30 of the third round to win the vacant Australasian super welterweight title. The taller Hodgson outlanded Adis-losifidis in the first. Adis-losifidis had more success in the second, though his right eye began to swell. Hodgson landed six unanswered punches in the third, prompting Manton to stop the scheduled 10-round bout.

Omar El-Abdallah (7-0, 6 KOs), of Melbourne, knocked out late replacement Nick “The Brick” Benn (5-3, 5 KOs), of Tauranga, New Zealand, at 0:37 of the seventh round of a scheduled eight-round bout. El-Abdallah outlanded Benn through the first four rounds and dropped him with a lead right to the chin in the seventh. Missaidis waved it off without a count.

Melbourne’s James Noonan (1-1-1) and Victoria’s Matt Faron (2-0-1) fought to a four-round draw in a middleweight bout. All three judges scored it 38-38. Both southpaws switched to orthodox and back in the opening round, which Faron appeared to edge. Noonan had the better of the second, and Manton warned Faron for holding in the third. Noonan appeared to take the fourth by outworking Faron.

Sports.title: Derek Chisora Still Waiting for the Right Wilder Money
Sports.content:
Derek Chisora says he still hasn’t been offered enough to fight Deontay Wilder again on the December 11 Tyson Fury vs. Anthony Joshua undercard in Cardiff. He’s willing to step in for Jai Opetaia, but says he’ll stay home if the offer falls short. Asked how much it would take, Chisora kept the figure to himself.

“They already asked me, and I already told them, ‘Yes, give me the right money.’ So now we’re just talking about money,” said Chisora on talkSPORT. Pressed for a figure, he said, “A good number. A very good number.”

Given that Chisora reportedly earned between $4 million and $6 million for his first bout with Wilder, it is hard to see how he commands even a tiny fraction of that amount today. At 42 years old with 14 losses on his record, Chisora no longer has the O2 Arena farewell narrative he used to sell out London back in April.

If Dana White were running these negotiations, he wouldn’t just balk at a steep asking price; he would laugh Chisora right out of the room and refuse to even entertain the idea of using him.

If Chisora’s price stays inflated, the promoters have every reason to walk away and look at a younger heavyweight instead. Bringing in someone like Bakhodir Jalolov would give viewers a fresh matchup and let fans see how Wilder handles a younger southpaw with deep amateur credentials at a fraction of the cost.

Putting Chisora in the co-main slot drags down the broadcast quality rather than adding value.

To younger American fans, Chisora is basically invisible. He hasn’t been a relevant force on U.S. television in years, and casual viewers tuning in for Fury and Joshua aren’t going to care about an aging British domestic attraction who already lost to Wilder seven months ago.

Hardcore boxing fans aren’t clamoring for it either, because everyone already knows exactly what Chisora brings to the table at this point in his career.

The bigger problem is how weak it makes the top of the card look. When you pair a faded Chisora with a 41-year-old Wilder who has lost four of his last six fights, you end up with a co-main event featuring zero top-five contenders. Following that up with Fury and Joshua means the final two bouts of the night are built entirely on nostalgia rather than elite, current division talent.

If the promoters want the card to have actual credibility with hardcore fans and younger American viewers, they need a legitimate threat or a rising contender across from Wilder, not a recycled eight-round exhibition.

Jim White wrapped up the radio segment by noting that Chisora is holding out for his magic number, prompting Simon Jordan to joke about the veteran being a “greedy little swine.”

Sports.title: Teremoana Teremoana Calls For World Title Shot After Stopping Ahio
Sports.content:
Teremoana Teremoana dropped Hemi Ahio with right hands in both rounds and stopped him at 1:36 of the second to win the vacant IBF Inter-Continental heavyweight title on Wednesday, November 18, at Pullman Melbourne Albert Park in Melbourne, Australia.

Teremoana (13-0, 13 KOs) kept his perfect knockout record intact against the most experienced opponent of his professional career. Ahio (25-2, 19 KOs) got up from both knockdowns, but referee Ignatius Missailidis checked him in the corner after the second and waved off the scheduled 10-round fight.

After the fight, Teremoana said he would take a shot at a world heavyweight title in his next bout if the opportunity came up. His goal is to fight for one within the next 12 months.

Teremoana Drops Ahio in Both Rounds

Ahio came forward from the opening bell, looking to get inside Teremoana’s jab and trade at close range. Teremoana made him pay for the approach within the first minute, catching the New Zealander with a hard right hand as he tried to close the distance. Ahio got to his feet and took more punches in combination before making it out of the first round.

The second opened at a slower pace, with some clinching and work to the body. Teremoana found room for his right hand again and hurt Ahio before putting him down with another right. Ahio beat the count, but Missailidis ended the fight after looking him over in the corner.

“I knew if I stayed close, he’d try and hit me; that’s why I stayed long. I think I handled myself well,” said Teremoana after the fight.

At 6’6″ and about 269 pounds, Teremoana had six inches in height and roughly 37 pounds on Ahio at the weigh-in. His jab made the shorter man start his attacks from farther out, and the right hand caught Ahio on the way in. Ahio kept pressing after the first knockdown, but he never found a way to get inside consistently enough to keep Teremoana from throwing at full extension.

The 28-year-old Brisbane heavyweight represented Australia at the 2024 Paris Olympics, where he lost to eventual gold medalist Bakhodir Jalolov in the super heavyweight quarterfinals. He had stopped his first 12 professional opponents inside two rounds. Ahio, 36, came in with 26 professional bouts and 19 knockouts of his own. Even with that experience, he became the 13th opponent to fall before the third round.

Matchroom Boxing CEO Frank Smith praised Teremoana for dealing with an opponent who kept coming forward. Teremoana mentioned the Anthony Joshua vs. Tyson Fury undercard as a possible place for his next fight and said he would leave the decision to his team.

In the co-feature, Joel Camilleri dropped previously unbeaten Mitchell Leek in the opening round and won a unanimous decision to claim the vacant IBF Australasian middleweight title. The judges scored it 96-93, 95-94 and 96-93.

Omar El-Abdallah knocked out Nicholas Benn in the seventh round, and Ky Hodgson won the vacant Australian super welterweight title with a third-round TKO of Victor Adis-Iosifidis. James Noonan and Matt Faron fought to a unanimous draw, with all three judges scoring it 38-38.

Sports.title: Jorge Linares Facing Deportation After El Paso Airport Arrest
Sports.content:
Former three-division world champion Jorge Linares is sitting in federal custody in El Paso, Texas, after immigration officers arrested him at the airport on Sunday. The 41-year-old Venezuelan retired in 2023, and now he is stuck in a legal battle outside the ring that looks far messier than anything he ever dealt with between the ropes.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement told reporters that Border Patrol and ICE agents picked up Linares at El Paso International Airport. According to the agency, Linares entered the United States on October 26, 2023, on temporary admission and stayed past his allowed time. ICE confirmed he will remain locked up at the El Paso Service Processing Center while his removal case moves forward.

His attorneys at Wilner & O’Reilly are fighting the government story. In a statement on Tuesday, his legal team insisted Linares is authorized to be in the country and has cooperated fully with officials. Still, his lawyers refused to say what exact status or paperwork he holds, leaving fans wondering how a former star ended up in detention after attending a ProBox TV card in town.

Linares broke the news himself on Sunday with a short Spanish post on X saying ICE had him in El Paso. WBA president Gilberto Mendoza confirmed the arrest on Monday and said he is staying in regular touch with the fighter’s family.

Fans remember Linares best for winning world titles at featherweight, super featherweight, and lightweight before retiring after his 2023 loss to Jack Catterall in Liverpool. He famously dropped Vasiliy Lomachenko at Madison Square Garden in 2018 before getting stopped by a body shot, and he hurt Devin Haney late in their 2021 title bout. Now, instead of enjoying retirement, Linares is waiting on immigration judges to decide if he can stay in the United States.

Ghana News.title: GoldBod looks beyond 2 refineries to expand local gold processing – Dr Manteaw
Ghana News.content:
The Chief Executive Officer of the Gold Board (GoldBod), Sammy Gyamfi

The Ghana Gold Board intends to work with more refineries and is considering building its own facility to expand local gold processing, Dr Steven Manteaw has said.

The Co-chair of the Ghana Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (GHEITI) said he believed GoldBod was currently working with two refineries.

He said plans to involve other facilities were part of efforts to increase refining capacity.

Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he said the expansion was necessary to support Ghana’s ambitions for local gold refining.

“I know they have the intent of expanding that to other refineries. They are also thinking about building their own refinery.”

The government’s 2027 budget targets 100% local refining of artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold by 2028.

During the interview, host Evans Mensah cited Gold Board reporting that 30% of ASM gold was currently refined locally. He asked whether Ghana could raise that share to 70% by next year, given the required infrastructure.

Dr Manteaw said capacity would have to grow to achieve that target.

“We definitely will have to increase that capacity, and I know GoBod is working towards that,” he said.

Asked whether such an expansion could be delivered within a year, he said Ghana could draw on existing infrastructure while developing additional facilities.

“Oh, it is possible,” he stated.

He argued that working with available refineries offered a practical starting point. New capacity could then be added as the expansion progressed.

“So you work with the existing refineries, and there are quite a few of them.”

Despite his confidence, Dr Manteaw said the implementation roadmap needed to be made clear. He urged the government to explain how it would translate its commitments into increased processing capacity.

“You don't just make promises, but you show how you're going to do it, and it is the how that is not apparent to us.”

He maintained that the industry’s existing infrastructure provided grounds for optimism.

“But knowing what we know in the industry, we know it's possible,” he said.

Ghana News.title: NYA to hold maiden graduation ceremony for National Apprenticeship Programme tomorrow
Ghana News.content:
The National Youth Authority (NYA) is set to hold the maiden graduation ceremony for beneficiaries of the National Apprenticeship Programme (NAP) on Friday, November 20, 2026.

The ceremony, scheduled for 8:00 a.m. at the forecourt of the State House in Accra, will mark the graduation of the first cohort of beneficiaries under the programme, which is aimed at equipping young Ghanaians with practical and employable skills.

It will be held under the theme, “Skills for Prosperity: Empowering Ghana’s Future,” reflecting the programme’s focus on skills development, vocational training and creating opportunities for young people to improve their livelihoods.

President John Dramani Mahama is expected to attend the ceremony, alongside the Ga Mantse and President of the Ga Traditional Council, His Royal Majesty King Tackie Teiko Tsuru II, and the Minister for Youth Development and Empowerment, George Opare-Addo.

The Chief Executive Officer of the National Youth Authority, Osman Abdulai Ayariga, is also expected to participate in the event, which forms part of efforts to promote skills acquisition and youth empowerment.

The National Apprenticeship Programme is designed to provide young people with practical training and skills to enhance their employability, support entrepreneurship and contribute to Ghana’s economic development.

Ghana News.title: Government must show how it will deliver gold refining target – Manteaw
Ghana News.content:
Dr Steven Manteaw has urged the government to explain how it will deliver its gold refining targets, saying the ambition is achievable but the implementation roadmap remains unclear.

The Co-chair of the Ghana Extractive Industries Transparency Initiative (GHEITI) said expanding local refining requires more than a promise. It needs a clear plan for securing the necessary capacity.

Speaking on Joy News’ PM Express on Wednesday, he called for that explanation while expressing confidence in the industry’s potential.

“You don't just make promises, but you show how you're going to do it, and it is the how that is not apparent to us.”

The government’s 2027 budget targets 100% local refining of artisanal and small-scale mining (ASM) gold by 2028.

During the discussion, host Evans Mensah cited Gold Board reporting that 30% of ASM gold was currently refined locally. He questioned whether Ghana could expand its infrastructure sufficiently to reach 70% by next year.

Manteaw said the increase would require additional refinery capacity. He indicated that GoldBod was already pursuing options to support that expansion.

“We definitely will have to increase that capacity, and I know GoBod is working towards that.”

He said he believed GoldBod was currently working with two refineries and understood that it intended to involve other facilities.

“They are also thinking about building their own refinery.”

When asked whether the expansion could be achieved within a year, Manteaw said existing facilities could provide a starting point.

“Oh, it is possible,” he stated.

He proposed using available refineries while adding new infrastructure. That would let Ghana expand processing through existing facilities as it builds more capacity.

“So you work with the existing refineries, and there are quite a few of them.”

His call for a roadmap therefore centres on how the government will bring those options together to meet its targets.

Manteaw maintained that industry knowledge supported confidence in the ambition.

“But knowing what we know in the industry, we know it's possible.”
