Ghana News.title: Oil prices settle lower as traders weigh surplus supply outlook
Ghana News.content:
Oil prices fell more than 1% on Wednesday after US crude and fuel inventories rose more than expected, according to the Energy Information Administration, adding to expectations of a supply surplus.

Brent crude futures fell $1.19, or 1.28%, to $91.95 a barrel. US West Texas Intermediate futures settled down $2.75, ‌or 3.2%, at $83.26, their lowest since August 26.

Brent fell more than $2 a barrel during the session, while WTI lost more than $4.

US crude inventories rose 3.4 million barrels to 417.8 million barrels in the week ended November 13, the EIA said, compared with analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll of a 58,000-barrel rise.

US gasoline stocks rose 5.2 million barrels in the week to 215.9 million barrels, the EIA said, versus analysts' expectations in a Reuters poll for a build of 1.6 million barrels.

Distillate stockpiles, which include diesel and heating oil, rose by 1.6 million barrels in the week to 104.9 million barrels, versus expectations for a 1.3 million-barrel rise, the EIA data showed.

Those stock increases renewed selling pressure, Gelber & Associates analysts said, adding: "Attacks involving Iran and commercial shipping ​still threaten deliveries through the Strait of Hormuz, but those risks have provided limited support against the growing expectation of a global surplus."

Meanwhile, both Brent and US crude ​futures contracts were on track for declines of about 20% this month on rising exports from the Middle East, as signaled by plummeting shipping rates.

The Brent/WTI spread was trading at its widest in around two weeks on Tuesday, LSEG data showed, with WTI logging steeper declines during trading on Wednesday.

"WTI arbitrage trades have been shut to Asia and Northwest Europe, thus WTI correcting more ​than Brent is the expected price movement to allow the arbitrage window to open again," said June Goh at Sparta Commodities, adding that rising US Gulf Coast ​crude stocks are further contributing to the widening spread.

US-IRAN CONFLICT CONTINUES

But the continuing Iran war and the risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz curbed price declines.

Iran said it attacked US ‌drone and ⁠missile sites in Kuwait overnight after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz. It was Iran's first attack on the US-allied Gulf state since September. Bahrain, home of the US Navy's Fifth Fleet, said it intercepted Iranian attacks.

Both oil benchmarks had settled higher on Tuesday as attacks on ships in the Middle East intensified, even as talks continued between Iran and mediators from Oman and Qatar.

ADNOC L&S of the United Arab Emirates said on Wednesday that one crew member was missing and 11 ​injured after one of its vessels was ​attacked in the Strait of Hormuz ⁠on Tuesday.

An LPG tanker was also struck by a projectile off the coast of Oman on Monday, prompting its crew to evacuate the ship.

"Although regional supply may continue to recover through alternative routes, the latest vessel data suggests that normalization of flows ​through Hormuz is still not possible under current conditions," LSEG analysts said on Tuesday.

Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis said on Tuesday ​that they launched five drones ⁠toward two pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline, which has been used to bypass the strait.

Saudi Arabia is preparing for the conflict with the Houthis to stretch well into next year, said two Western officials briefed on the plans by Saudi officials.

Meanwhile, US President Donald Trump is expected to hold bilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China ⁠on Thursday, ​in addition to the trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, US and Russian officials said.

Trump's ​envoys have intensified diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with discussions that are also set to involve European leaders focused on post-war security guarantees and economic recovery planning.

Ghana News.title: Cocaine and millions of pills seized in eastern Libya, officials say
Ghana News.content:
File photo

Eastern Libyan authorities said they seized more than 4 million narcotic pills and 29 kilograms ​of cocaine and hashish in the coastal city ‌of Derna on Tuesday.

Members of a drug-trafficking gang were arrested in the city, the interior ministry's General Administration for ​Combating Drugs said in a statement.

Pictures posted by ​the administration showed piles of blocks of hashish, ⁠boxes and transparent bags containing white tablets.

"We will ​show no leniency toward anyone who dares to compromise ​the security of our youth or the future of our country," the agency's director, Major General Ahmed Al-Shamikh, said in a ​video statement posted late on Tuesday.

Libya has become ​a major regional transit hub for synthetic drugs and other narcotics ‌on ⁠their way to local users and other parts of North Africa and the wider continent, according to a UN report released in January.

Drug gangs have been ​taking advantage of ​the tumultuous ⁠situation in the country since 2011, said the report by the United Nations ​Office on Drugs and Crime. That year, ​Gaddafi was ⁠toppled in a NATO-backed uprising, plunging Libya into a prolonged period of internal conflict and division.

Three years later, ⁠a ​civil war broke out between ​armed factions vying for power and divided the country between eastern and ​western administrations.

Ghana News.title: Russia’s A7 payment network plans further expansion in Africa, executive says
Ghana News.content:
Russia's A7 international payment system plans to expand further in Africa, after opening in Nigeria and Zimbabwe, to build banking infrastructure around growing Russian investment, company executives said at a forum in Moscow on Wednesday.

The company is pushing ahead with the expansion despite US sanctions imposed last month after the Treasury said it was ​being used by Iran. A7 denied any links to Iran.

A7 deputy managing director for sales Stanislav Lazarev told the RBC Foreign Trade Forum that A7 intends to serve local exporters and importers interested in cross-border transfers, as well as Russian businesses.

Russia ​has sought to expand its influence in Africa, culturally and through investment, as it looks for new markets and partners amid strict Western sanctions.

Most payments processed by A7 go to countries with strong ties to Moscow. China and Hong Kong accounted for most A7 ⁠transactions from January to September, at 55%, followed by the United Arab Emirates. It has around 15,000 clients, most of them exporters in the agricultural and metallurgy sectors.

ALTERNATIVE PAYMENT METHODS

A defence-sector-focused bank PSB developed the platform in 2024, and it plays a key role in Russia’s cross-border payments market.

A7's agent-based payments in third countries offer Russian businesses an alternative way to make payments under Western sanctions and foreign currency restrictions, Finance Minister Anton Siluanov told the "Vesti" television news programme on Tuesday.

The value of payments processed via the A7 system rose 54% year on year over January-September, while the number of payments rose 83%, Lazarev said.

Ghana News.title: 94.6% of ASM Gold purchased in October was locally refined – GoldBod
Ghana News.content:
The Media Relations Officer of Ghana Gold Board (GoldBod), Prince Kwame Minkah, says the institution is making significant headway in its drive to keep more of the value generated from the country’s gold resources within the economy, with nearly 95 per cent of its artisanal and small-scale gold purchases in October 2026 processed locally.

He cited figures announced by GoldBod Chief Executive Officer Sammy Gyamfi at the African Minerals Policy Forum’s Mining in Motion conference in October. suggesting that, out of the 5.7 tonnes of gold bought by the Board during the period, 5.4 tonnes had undergone local refining, representing 94.6 per cent of the total.

Speaking on Joy FM’s PM Express on Wednesday, November 18, he said the achievement reflected the growing capacity of Ghanaian refineries to handle gold purchased by the Board.

He attributed the progress to partnerships with two privately owned Ghanaian facilities - Gold Coast Refinery and Royal Ghana Gold Refinery - which have entered into refining arrangements with GoldBod.

The two facilities, he explained, each had the capacity to process about 2,000 kilogrammes of gold weekly, provided the necessary logistics were available.

Gold Coast Refinery has also partnered South Africa’s Rand Refinery, which is the only London Bullion Market Association (LBMA)-accredited refinery in Africa, a relationship expected to support efforts to meet international refining standards.

Both Ghanaian refineries are working towards securing LBMA accreditation within the next three to five years, with regulatory guidance from GoldBod.

The Board is also planning to establish its own state-of-the-art refinery as part of a broader strategy to expand domestic processing capacity and reduce dependence on foreign facilities.

GoldBod has also introduced a mandatory local refining requirement for self-financing aggregators.

The directive, which took effect on September 1, 2026, requires gold doré purchased under approved offtake arrangements to be refined in Ghana before export. Unrefined doré is no longer approved for export under the arrangement.

The policy forms part of the government’s ambition to move Ghana away from exporting raw minerals towards achieving zero raw mineral exports by 2030.

Ghana News.title: Emirates boss says fuel, not demand, squeezing airline profits
Ghana News.content:
Emirates, the Middle East's largest airline, is seeing strong demand on routes to China, Russia, and Africa, but is feeling the squeeze from high fuel prices linked to the Iran war, its President, Tim Clark, told Reuters on Wednesday.

The Dubai-based carrier reported a 66% drop in first-half net profit this month after airspace closures and disruptions from the nearly nine-month conflict hit travel across the Middle East and drove up oil and jet fuel prices.

Dubai International Airport said on Tuesday that passenger traffic fell 28.1% in the first nine months of the year, but added that traffic is recovering.

Brent crude traded as high as $120 a barrel earlier this year, but ⁠has eased to about $93 in recent weeks on hopes of de-escalation.

"The industry needs to have oil back at $70," Clark said in ​an interview at his office in Dubai International. "That's the rate in which people can trade. The global economy will move, the airline ​industry will be in a better place."

Clark said that higher costs could trigger bankruptcies across the airline sector, though he added that state-owned Emirates remained profitable despite narrower margins.

"We managed to make money in the first half. Not bad at all, given fuel is at the level it is; that's the real kicker," Clark ​said. "It's fuel, not people. We're filling the airplanes."

Gulf carriers have gradually restored operations, but recent attacks on Saudi Arabia by Yemen's Iran-aligned ​Houthis have clouded prospects for a full recovery.

STRONG DEMAND FROM RUSSIA, CHINA, AFRICA

Emirates said this month it had restored operations across 91% of its ‌network by ⁠the end of September. Its passenger seat factor, a measure of how many seats are filled, fell to 72% in the first half from 79.5% a year earlier.

Clark said strong traffic on some routes was helping to offset weakness elsewhere.

"It's very strong. If you look at the Russian market, you look at the some of the African points that we're serving. Look at Asia, China is full," ​he said, adding meanwhile that ​Oceania "needs a little bit of ⁠help".

The Emirates Group had 54.1 billion dirhams ($14.7 billion) of cash at the end of September, down 5.5 billion dirhams from six months earlier as it drew on reserves to support operations.

Clark said the ​company was closely monitoring cash flow but remained "in good shape" and had no immediate need to ​raise debt.

"Now if ⁠something adverse happens, we will recourse to the debt markets. But at the moment, we're not there," he said.

Clark also said there were no plans for an initial public offering of the airline and that the Dubai government would decide on any listing.

"At the enterprise ⁠value level, ​we are, I would say, probably in about $120, $130 billion if you look at ​the multiples of EBITDA," he said, adding that a listing could raise significant proceeds.

"It's a question they (the government) have asked themselves in the past. I don't think ​with any degree of seriousness."

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from their Shenzhen meeting?
World.content:
The US, Chinese and Russian leaders are to hold their first three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

Share What do Trump, Putin and Xi want from their Shenzhen meeting? on social media

US President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin will hold a three-way meeting on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, the first ever between the leaders of the world’s three most powerful militaries.

The meeting, which will take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, has drawn comparisons with the 1945 wartime Yalta conference at which the United States, United Kingdom and then-Soviet Union agreed on the post-war order. But those powers had been allied during a world war. Analysts say the three men meeting on Thursday are arriving with very different goals, and that few concrete outcomes can be expected.

“It’s a summit of Trump’s ego, Putin’s tactics, China’s strategy,” Scott Lucas, professor of international politics at University College Dublin, told Al Jazeera.

So what does each leader want from this meeting?

What is this meeting about?

The trilateral meeting is taking place on the sidelines of the APEC leaders’ summit, which China is hosting in Shenzhen on November 18 and 19. Trump travelled to China after attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) meeting in Manila.

The White House has said that Trump plans to discuss the war with Iran as well as a possible three-way agreement on nuclear armament with Xi and Putin. Ukraine is not expected to be on the formal agenda, as Xi is understood to be reluctant to be drawn into what he views as a European matter.

The meeting comes as Trump has strained ties with traditional US allies, at times floating troop withdrawals from South Korea and cuts to assistance for Japan, while his administration continues to describe China as Washington’s main geopolitical rival.



Vuk Vuksanovic, a lecturer in foreign policy and grand strategy at the Department of War Studies, King’s College, London, cautioned against viewing the summit as a new “carve-up” of the world order, however.

“It is a far cry from being a new Yalta,” he said. “In Yalta, you actually had the idea about how the world was going to look, and where the demarcation line would potentially be between the superpowers. We don’t have anything similar, not even the contours of that, in the making at this moment.”

At the Yalta Conference in February 1945, US President Franklin D Roosevelt, British Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Crimea to shape the post-war order, agreeing on the division of Germany and setting the stage for Soviet influence over Eastern Europe.

Where do China-Russia-US relations stand?

There are competing interests at play here.

US and China

Trump landed in Shenzhen on Wednesday, with Xi greeting him at the airport. This is their third in-person meeting since they paused their bitter trade war late last year. At its height, US trade tariffs on Chinese goods reached 145 percent, with China retaliating with tariffs of 125 percent on US goods, before a temporary truce agreed in Busan, South Korea, in October 2025, when tariffs were relaxed. Xi also agreed to pause new restrictions on exports of some rare earth metals which are crucial for manufacturing technology from smartphones to fighter jets. Soon after that, Trump relaxed restrictions on the sale of some Nvidia AI-related computer chips to China.

The truce has since been extended to January 10, 2027 to allow for broader trade talks.

Friction remains, however.

China’s rare earth mineral exports to the US are still about 75 percent below normal levels, according to the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

A scandal over Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data centre company accused of diverting Nvidia chips to China in breach of US export controls, has also strained ties, as has the recent scandal over Nvidia’s former CEO, Jensen Huang’s extramarital affairs, including with a woman the US has accused of spying for China.

Beijing rejects all spying allegations as “baseless”, and Trump has said he does not plan to raise the issue at this meeting.

Expectations are low for a major thawing, however: Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, told Al Jazeera that a handshake without incident would be seen as a win.

US and Russia

Trump’s special envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, have brokered talks between Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, the first in direct format since February. The pair have visited both Kyiv and Moscow to promote these talks in recent days.



Days before they travelled to Moscow on Thursday last week, Trump said Washington and Moscow were close to a “big, beautiful agreement” covering not just Ukraine but “all of Europe”.

Trump’s rhetoric towards Putin has softened greatly in recent months, as it has hardened against Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whom he has publicly admonished for targeting Russian energy facilities, driving up the global cost of oil and diesel. Trump has also called for Zelenskyy to step down and has paused some sanctions on Russian oil, much to the anger of many in his Republican Party.

Some analysts are concerned that US negotiators may offer Russia concessions on NATO in return for peace, including pushing a deal that allows Russia to retain land it has seized from Ukraine in the past four years – a prospect that alarms European leaders.

Russia and China

China has become Russia’s top trading partner since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, weeks after the two had declared a “no limits” partnership.

At a summit in Beijing in May this year, Xi and Putin signed more than 40 cooperation agreements and hailed growing energy trade.

Russian oil exports to China rose 35 percent in the first quarter of 2026, according to a Kremlin aide. China has also ignored Western demands to stop supplying high-tech components to Russia’s weapons industry.

Chinese President Xi Jinping called for China and Russia to “lead and advance the trend towards a multipolar world” after holding talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

The two leaders also met on Wednesday in Shenzhen.

Putin addressed the summit after Xi. He described Western powers as “former hegemons” and said Europe was experiencing a “humiliating decline”.

What does Trump want?

Analysts say Trump is the leader most eager to walk away with something he can present as a “win” from this trilateral meeting.

Vuksanovic said Trump is arriving “wounded domestically” following his Republican Party’s crushing defeat at the US midterm elections, which have seen the Democratic Party gain control of both US Houses of Congress. Trump’s legacy, Vuksanovic added, has been damaged by the war on Iran, particularly in light of Trump’s pledge not to drag the US into another “forever war” during his presidential campaign in 2024.

The deadlock that currently exists between the US and Iran has been described as a “frozen war” by observers.

“[Trump] hopes that he can get some quick-fix deal on something, at least, which he can then try to spin and sell to his base in the US as an enormous accomplishment,” Vuksanovic said. But he added that he doubts Trump could secure anything beyond “something very symbolic”, noting that the agenda of the meeting has remained opaque.

One issue Trump may push for is a trilateral agreement on nuclear armament. The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty (New START) between Russia and the US lapsed in February. It was first signed in 2010 and caps US and Russian strategic nuclear arsenals.



Trump previously rejected Russia’s proposal to extend the treaty after it expired, demanding instead a “new, improved and modernised” deal that includes Beijing. However, Xi is understood to be unenthusiastic about joining a treaty that China had no part in writing.

Lucas said Trump is there largely “for the photo opportunity”. But he drew a distinction between Trump and his administration, which he said wants to “regain their footing a little bit in terms of leadership” on China.

Washington’s China policy, Lucas said, has been “a disaster”. The administration launched a tariff war that saw duties climb as high as 145 percent, before Beijing retaliated by squeezing exports of rare earth minerals, forcing a truce.

“They’ve got to try to say: ‘Look, we’re leaders. Look, we have a firm policy on China, but one that’s not confrontational,'” he said.

That balancing act is complicated at home, Lucas added, with Republicans in Congress pushing for a tougher line on Beijing as the administration’s position weakens.

What does Putin want?

For Putin, the meeting is above all about the war in Ukraine and ending Russian isolation as a result of European and US sanctions.

“Putin and the Kremlin want cover for the invasion of Ukraine, because they’ve got some serious problems with it,” Lucas said. Moscow wants to keep the Trump camp on side, gain more Ukrainian territory and see Washington withdraw support for Kyiv, he added, while securing at least political backing from Beijing.

Lucas said Russia also wants to break “the notion that it’s isolated” after years of sanctions and the costs of a nearly five-year war that has not delivered victory. Putin is eager to prevent the US sanctions bill, which Trump has paused – and which would impose steep tariffs on Russia and on buyers of its goods, including China – from being implemented.

Vuksanovic said the optics alone, therefore, will be a prize for Moscow. After decades of complaining about US dominance, he said, Russia and China can now argue that “the power gap is not as great, so now we can sit at the table with the US”. That image of great-power status, he added, is “particularly appealing” to Putin.

Lucas added that Putin is unlikely to give up his leverage relating to Iran, and will resist offering Washington any binding promise that Moscow will not cooperate with Tehran.

What does Xi want?

For Xi, the host, the meeting is a chance to secure the space to pursue China’s long-term interests without interference.

“China wants the space to pursue its political, economic and military goals,” Lucas said. Beijing, he added, already has what it wanted in terms of recognition: “Now he’s on the same level with Trump and with Putin.”

What Beijing wants next, Lucas said, is no return to the tariff wars, no opposition to its alternative economic model, recognition of its primacy in rare earth minerals and technology, and no US pushback over Taiwan, which it regards as part of its territory.

China does not want anyone challenging its regional military presence, he said, including the Quad grouping of the US, Japan, India and Australia.

Vuksanovic described China as a rising superpower that is nevertheless “much more inward-looking” and focused on a vast process of internal reform. “They actually much rather prefer to be patient and to think long term, rather than to go for anything which is diplomatically grandiose,” he said.

He argued that China is “probably the biggest winner” of the wars in Ukraine and Iran, which have kept Washington distracted from the Asia Pacific. Beijing’s main worry, he said, is the risk of energy markets collapsing.



“Minus that economic risk, they’re still happy that the US is bogged down in two major wars which Washington does not know how to disentangle itself from,” he said.

Will this meeting change anything on Iran or Ukraine?

Observers are not expecting any sort of a breakthrough from this meeting.

On Iran, Lucas said the US administration would like Beijing to “privately urge the Iranians to make compromises”. But US-Iran talks remain stuck on whether to address the Strait of Hormuz and financial incentives for Tehran first, or its nuclear programme.

Vuksanovic said he is “very dubious” that China would take on a major mediating role. Beyond brokering the Saudi-Iranian rapprochement in 2023, he said, Beijing has preferred to be “diplomatically skilful rhetorically, without sticking out as a major conflict mediator”.

On Ukraine, Vuksanovic said Moscow sees the war as existential and believes it can win through attrition. Russia, he said, will not give up its minimum demands of full control of the Donbas and Ukraine renouncing its bid for NATO membership.

“I don’t think that this meeting will have any bearing on the outcome of the Ukraine war, which will not be resolved at a diplomatic table, but on the battlefield,” he said.

Lucas said Russia will instead try to keep Washington focused on what the Kremlin calls a Europe-wide security architecture, a framing that sidesteps a ceasefire, the territorial question and security guarantees for Kyiv.

Where Moscow and Beijing do agree, Lucas said, is in wanting the US to confine its ambitions of dominance to the Western Hemisphere. But he warned against seeing the summit as a carve-up among equals. “It’s much more a dynamic process where power is shifting, and where these leaders and their administrations are trying to preserve or even regain power,” he said.

What is the rest of the world hoping for?

Above all, stability, Lucas said.

Governments do not want Trump, weakened by the midterms, returning to a tariff war with China or disrupting their own economic ties with Beijing. The European Union faces a looming decision on its own economic relationship with China, he noted, while Canada, under Prime Minister Mark Carney, and the Gulf states are already recalibrating their approach.

“They would like a little bit of space themselves where they’re not having to respond to self-inflicted crises,” Lucas said. “So they’ll want Trump to behave.” They will also hope Putin is open to some pullback in Ukraine, and that China uses its power responsibly.

Vuksanovic said countries of the Global South will welcome the three powers talking, which fits their thinking on multipolarity. But they will also bring “a healthy degree of scepticism”.

“They will primarily observe whether there is any tangible outcome which impacts their own respective interests,” he said, from conflict resolution to the global economy, energy and new technologies.

World.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar
World.content:
The Gambia accused Myanmar of genocide following a 2017 military crackdown displacing over 730,000 Rohingya.

Share ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar on social media

The International Court of Justice (ICJ), the United Nations’ highest court, is set to rule in a landmark case accusing Myanmar of committing genocide against its Rohingya minority.

The reading of the judgment will begin at 10am (09:00 GMT) on Thursday at the Peace Palace in The Hague and is expected to last up to 90 minutes.

It could be the first time the court rules that a state has committed genocide.

The ruling is final and cannot be appealed, but the court has very limited means of enforcing it. If Myanmar ignores it, The Gambia could ask the UN Security Council to act.

What is the case?

The Gambia, a Muslim-majority West African country, brought the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation.

It argues that Myanmar bears state responsibility for genocide resulting from a 2017 military offensive that drove at least 730,000 Rohingya, who are mostly Muslim, from Buddhist-majority Myanmar into Bangladesh.

Survivors have recounted killings, mass rape and the burning of villages. A UN fact-finding mission concluded that the campaign included “genocidal acts”.

Myanmar denies genocide and says its forces responded legitimately to attacks by armed groups. It argues there is no direct evidence of an intent to destroy the Rohingya.

Why is it significant?

Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, genocide requires proof of the specific intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, ethnic, racial or religious group.

The ICJ has never held a state responsible for committing genocide. In 2007, it found that Serbia had failed to prevent the 1995 Srebrenica massacre in Bosnia, in which more than 8,000 Muslim men and boys were killed, but ruled that Serbia had not itself committed genocide.



The judgment could also set precedents for other cases, including South Africa’s case accusing Israel of genocide in Gaza.

The ICJ settles disputes between states, so it can find Myanmar responsible but cannot try individuals, which is the duty of the International Criminal Court.

The Gambia has asked the ICJ to order Myanmar to prosecute those responsible, make reparations and ensure the Rohingya can return safely. Myanmar disputes The Gambia’s right to seek reparations on their behalf.

About 1.2 million Rohingya live in the Cox’s Bazar refugee settlement in Bangladesh, where many will follow the judgment, the Reuters news agency reported. Roughly 550,000 remain in Myanmar, with restrictions on their movement, healthcare and livelihoods.

World.title: Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide
World.content:
A new report alleges that injuries on Epstein’s body were overlooked by medical examiners during his 2019 autopsy.

Share Why a trio of experts alleges Jeffrey Epstein did not die by suicide on social media

A trio of experts has released a report casting doubt on whether convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein died by suicide in his jail cell in 2019, as a medical examiner in the United States previously ruled.

In documents obtained by Al Jazeera and other media outlets, Michael Freeman, Anders Eriksson and Itiel Dror – a forensic scientist, a forensic pathologist and a cognitive scientist – said the injuries on Epstein’s body were “most consistent with homicidal strangulation”, not suicide.

“The pattern, distribution, and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging,” their report reads.

Instead, they suggest Epstein was first assaulted and then strangled, providing an alternative narrative to the medical examiner’s 2019 report.

The cause of Epstein’s death has long been a source of controversy and conspiracy theories.

A wealthy businessman, Epstein cultivated a range of high-profile relationships with leaders in politics, industry, academia and the arts. His network of contacts included US presidents Bill Clinton and Donald Trump.

Those connections have raised questions about whether there was a cover-up of Epstein’s crimes – or whether some of his associates knowingly turned a blind eye.

In 2008, Epstein pleaded guilty to the solicitation of a minor for sex as part of a plea deal that saw him serve 13 months behind bars. Later, in 2019, he was arrested on federal charges of sex trafficking, with prosecutors accusing him of having “sexually exploited and abused dozens of underage girls”.



He died in a New York City jail while awaiting trial.

A controversy over cause of death

Medical examiner Kristin Roman performed the autopsy on Epstein’s body. She and New York City’s Chief Medical Examiner Barbara Sampson ultimately ruled that the evidence pointed to a suicide by hanging.

Other experts have sided with their ruling, pointing out that, while the circumstances of Epstein’s death were unusual, they are not necessarily inconsistent with suicide.

But Epstein’s brother, Mark, has long doubted the medical examiner’s findings. He gave Freeman, an Oregon-based forensic scientist, access to the death records.

Freeman has consulted in trials where families have questioned the narratives put forward by law enforcement about how someone died, including in high-profile cases like the murder of George Floyd.

Eriksson, meanwhile, is a Sweden-based forensic pathologist who has researched issues like shaken baby syndrome, a controversial diagnosis used to prosecute some adults for abuse of young children.

He and Freeman worked alongside Dror, a cognitive scientist who studies biases in forensic science.

At the time of his death, Epstein was a well-known figure, and Dror said the investigators handling his case would have been subject to significant political pressure.

“It’s so obvious this played a critical role in the examination of the body,” Dror told Al Jazeera.

“There was at stake a lot of emotion, a lot of people involved, a lot of politics involved, so many factors. You can list them for an hour, and all of those interfered and biased and influenced what should be a scientific decision.”

Dror explained that he and his colleagues pored over photos and records related to Epstein’s death and concluded that the medical examiner had wrongly ruled it a suicide.

Points of concern raised

In their report, the trio noted a number of issues with the initial investigation.

The prison personnel who found Epstein’s body did not take any photos before moving it, for instance. Investigators also failed to identify the ligature, the object that was actually around Epstein’s neck, they said.

They allege that some avenues of investigation went unexplored. The prison guard who first came across Epstein’s body initially refused to be interviewed, according to the report, and the medical examiner who determined the case was a suicide was not allowed to visit the prison.

The report also disagrees with the medical examiner’s assessment of Epstein’s injuries.

Marks left by the ligature on Epstein’s neck, the researchers said, were not slanted in the way that would be expected if his body had been hanging from the bedpost in his cell.



They observed bruising on Epstein’s back, shoulder and neck that they said was not acknowledged in the medical examiner’s original statements.

Those injuries, their report said, are “most consistent with homicidal strangulation from behind, most likely using a narrow knotted fabric ligature”.

Freeman, Eriksson and Dror believe either that the prison guard who found Epstein was lying about finding his body hanging in the cell, or that the body was deliberately put into that position to make it seem like a suicide had taken place.

World.title: 'The drones don't fly here' - BBC reports from Ukraine's new front line
World.content:
There's a new front in the war in Ukraine, and it is underground.

For the past seven months Ukrainian forces have been living and fighting Russian troops in an old Soviet gas pipeline in the north-eastern Kharkiv region.

With a diameter of just over a metre there is enough room only to crawl. But it is relatively safe from the drones that now saturate the skies above the front line â and make it nigh-on impossible for either side to advance.

Going underground is now the "only option", says Zanuda, who has helped plan Ukraine's tunnel operation and calls it a new world of fighting. But, he acknowledges, it is hard.

"On the surface you always have some room to manoeuvre, but here you can only engage the enemy head-on."

The journey to get to this subterranean battleground in the Kharkiv region only reinforced the dangers on the ground: a high-speed move by vehicle across open fields, followed by a long march across muddy ground â accompanied by Ukrainian troops with their weapons loaded, ready to shoot down Russian drones.

World.title: Myanmar faces historic genocide verdict at UN court over Rohingya massacres
World.content:
When the judges of the International Court of Justice read out their verdict in the seven-year-old genocide case filed by The Gambia against Myanmar on Thursday, they could make history.

In the years since the Genocide Convention was signed in 1948, after the Nazi Holocaust, dozens of individuals have been successfully prosecuted for the crime of genocide, in conflicts such as those in Rwanda and the former Yugoslavia.

But no state has ever been found guilty by an international court of committing genocide.

"It would be a judgment of landmark importance if The Gambia were to win this case," says Arsalan Suleman, the lawyer leading the case against Myanmar at the court. "It would give renewed vitality to the 1948 Genocide Convention and to the notion of international legal accountability for crimes committed by a state."

The mass expulsion of the Rohingya population of Rakhine State in August and September 2017 was without question a military operation of exceptional brutality.

I was among a very small number of journalists who witnessed the deliberate burning of Rohingya villages in Rakhine, and also the dreadful human suffering of the hundreds of thousands who fled to neighbouring Bangladesh.

Their accounts of killing, torture and mass rape by Burmese soldiers have been thoroughly documented by human rights groups and a United Nations fact-finding mission, external.

I have on many occasions interviewed ethnic Rakhine people about their animosity towards the Muslim population, and I have documented the systematic obliteration of what remained of Rohingya villages by the Myanmar state.

But the question posed at the UN's top court, the ICJ, is whether all of this amounted to genocide.
