World.content:
Anthropic has seen its value jump to as much as $1.5tn (Â£1.14tn) as its shares are set to start trading on the stock market on Thursday.

The artificial intelligence (AI) company behind the popular chatbot Claude said its shares will be priced at $83 each when it lists on the Nasdaq, a tech-focused stock exchange based in New York.

That will make it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

Anthropic's stock market debut will make it the first US firm focused exclusively on AI to go public. It will also mark a crucial test for the fast-growing industry, which faces questions over whether the huge amounts of money being poured into the technology will be profitable.

The firm said earlier this month it would offer its shares for between $70 and $78 each, which valued the company at up to $1.3tn.

But demand for Anthropic's stock debut - commonly referred to as its initial public offering, or IPO - is very high, according to one early investor in the company who spoke with the BBC on condition of anonymity.

The person said shares were more than 10 times oversubscribed ahead of the public listing, meaning demand for Anthropic shares exceeded the number of shares available.

If that turns out to be the case, Anthropic's valuation could quickly blow past its target on Thursday when trading begins.

World.title: Van Gogh painting sells for record $190.4m after row over its Nazi history
World.content:
It was not immediately clear who purchased the painting. The BBC has contacted Sotheby's for comment.

The oil painting, which was estimated to carry a value of $180m (Â£136m) prior to the sale, was put up for auction as part of a set called the Blaquier-Arrieta Collection.

Sotheby's announced in the hours before the auction that it had resolved a dispute between the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the heirs of the Fischer family - the prior German owners of the work - regarding the sale.

Representatives acting for heirs of the Fischer family had claimed the painting may have been sold under duress during the rise of the Nazis.

A lawyer for the family's heirs reportedly wrote to Sotheby's on their behalf, telling the auction house that the painting was sold in Amsterdam before World War Two because of financial losses the Fischer family's publishing company suffered under the Nazis. The BBC has contacted the lawyer for comment.

"In recognition of the painting's complex Nazi-era history and the suffering endured by the Fischer family during the Holocaust, the two families have reached a mutually satisfactory resolution and the work will be sold pursuant to their agreement," Sotheby's said on Wednesday.

Sotheby's website details the provenance of the oil painting and how it has researched the artwork changing hands since 1890.

It says Samuel Fischer - a famous German publisher - acquired it 1909 before it was passed down in his family after his death in 1934.

The painting was deposited with Paul Cassirer in Amsterdam in 1932 or 1933 before it went to Henriette and Marcel Kapferer in Paris in 1936, Sotheby's said.

Four other owners then had the painting.

The Blaquier family acquired it in 1975 and owned it for more than half a century before the latest sale, the auction house said.

World.title: Crimean Bridge attacked again, Russian official says
World.content:
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked by Ukraine for the third time this week, a Russian official has said.

The Moscow-installed head of Crimea, Sergei Aksyonov, confirmed that traffic was temporarily suspended following another strike on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea.

The critical bridge had already been hit twice earlier in the week resulting in severe damage and part of the bridge collapsing into the water.

The important infrastructure has long been targeted by Ukraine because of its significance as a logistical and symbolic asset to Moscow's war effort.

World.title: Israeli military launches rare ground operation in Gaza beyond Yellow Line
World.content:
Israeli ground forces have launched a rare operation in part of the central Gaza Strip outside their control, after issuing evacuation orders for residents.

Witnesses said tanks advanced east of Nuseirat refugee camp and rolled onto the territory's main north to south road under the cover of artillery strikes.

The Israeli military said the "targeted" operation aimed to dismantle a "terror tunnel" west of the so-called Yellow Line, which marks the more than 60% of Gaza's territory occupied by Israel.

The Palestinian armed group Hamas, which controls the rest of Gaza, accused Israel of a "flagrant violation" of the October 2025 ceasefire agreement.

Violence has continued in Gaza over the past 13 months, with near-daily Israeli strikes, and living conditions for the 2.1 million people there remain dire.

Early on Wednesday afternoon, Israeli military body Cogat's Arabic spokesperson announced the start of the incursion and warned Palestinians living in an area north of Nuseirat and Bureij refugee camp to stay away for their own safety.

It also said a section of the north to south Salah al-Din road that passed through the area would be closed to traffic.

Later, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it had begun a joint operation with the Shin Bet security service "to dismantle a terror tunnel west of the Yellow Line that posed an immediate and direct threat to IDF troops".

"IDF troops under the Southern Command are deployed in the area in accordance with the ceasefire agreement and will continue to operate to remove any immediate threat and thwart attempts by the Hamas terrorist organisation to harm Israeli civilians or IDF troops, or to violate the agreement," it added.

Hamas warned in a statement that the advance of Israeli military vehicles beyond the Yellow Line and the evacuation of residents constituted "a dangerous development and a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement".

Footage published by Palestinian media outlets and on social media showed families fleeing areas near Nuseirat camp following the announcement.

In one video verified by BBC Verify, a man can be seen ducking after hearing artillery fire and then running along Salah al-Din road, about 1.5km (0.9 miles) west of the Yellow Line. "The Israeli occupation now is firing randomly near the houses and tents of people," he says.

Automatic gunfire can be heard in another video filmed just to the south-east.

A resident of Nuseirat who was forced to flee told BBC Arabic's Middle East Daily programme: "The situation is now extremely dire, with Israeli forces firing indiscriminately at areas where displaced people have sought shelter."

"We couldn't take any of our belongings with us - not even our blankets, pillows, or clothes. We had no choice but to leave everything behind."

A second resident also reported "indiscriminate gunfire and shelling" and said there had been "numerous casualties, including fatalities".

Asked about reported fatalities, the IDF sent a general statement about the operation.

World.title: Elon Musk says record spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
World.content:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX CEO was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (Â£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.

Democrats won control of the both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.

The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.

Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.

He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.

In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.

Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.

The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.

Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.

Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

World.title: 2027: Tinubu expands campaign visits to 19 states, FCT
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has expanded his planned appearances at the All Progressives Congress (APC) presidential campaign rallies ahead of the 2027 general elections, increasing the number of states he intends to visit from 12 to 19, alongside the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

The revised campaign timetable shows that Mr Tinubu is now expected to attend 20 of the 37 rallies scheduled across the 36 states and the FCT, with the programme running from October 2026 to January 2027.

The updated itinerary, released by APC National Publicity Secretary Felix Morka, adds several locations to the president’s original campaign schedule, including Katsina, Taraba, Zamfara, Imo and Kwara, as well as Abuja.

The revised programme also incorporates Akwa Ibom, Jigawa and Kebbi, where Mr Tinubu has already attended campaign rallies.

The president visited Uyo, Akwa Ibom State, on 6 November, where he attended an APC rally and inaugurated projects executed by the administration of Governor Umo Eno.

He subsequently attended rallies in Port Harcourt, Rivers State, on 7 November, Dutse, Jigawa State, on 10 November, and Birnin Kebbi, Kebbi State, on 17 November.

These appearances were not included in his original personal campaign itinerary.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Under the revised schedule, Mr Tinubu is expected to attend the APC rally in Katsina on 2 December, Kano on 17 December and Jalingo, Taraba State, on 19 December.

He is also scheduled to attend the rally in Abuja on 21 December, followed by Gusau, Zamfara State, on 28 December and Owerri, Imo State, on 30 December.

The president’s January campaign appearances will begin in Yola, Adamawa State, on 4 January 2027, followed by Sokoto on 5 January, Ilorin, Kwara State, on 8 January, Asaba, Delta State, on 11 January and Lagos on 13 January.

Other states on his revised itinerary include Kaduna, Plateau, Oyo, Borno and Enugu.

The revised timetable also changes some dates in the original schedule. The rally in Bauchi, initially scheduled for 29 November with the president expected to attend, has been moved to 1 December, with no indication that he will be present.

The Sokoto rally has been shifted from 4 December to 5 January 2027, while the Asaba rally has moved from 12 December to 11 January. The Lagos rally, initially scheduled for 9 January, will now be held on 13 January.

Regional distribution

The North-west has the most states on the president’s revised campaign itinerary, with seven: Kaduna, Jigawa, Kebbi, Katsina, Kano, Zamfara and Sokoto.

The North-east and South-south follow with three states each. They are Borno, Taraba and Adamawa in the North-east, and Akwa Ibom, Rivers and Delta in the South-south.

The North-central, South-west and South-east have two states each: Plateau and Kwara; Oyo and Lagos; and Enugu and Imo, respectively.

The expansion represents a departure from the original itinerary announced by the APC in October, which listed 12 states for the president’s personal appearances while other party leaders were expected to represent him at rallies in the remaining states.

PREMIUM TIMES reported on 16 October that the APC’s proposed nationwide campaign programme would cover all 36 states and the FCT, with the president initially scheduled to attend rallies in 12 states.

At the inauguration of the APC Presidential Campaign Council at the Presidential Villa in Abuja, Mr Tinubu said he would not attend every campaign rally because he did not want to abandon governance.

He, however, promised to make time to engage Nigerians directly as party leaders took the campaign to different states and local government areas.

World.title: FIFA names Amokachi, four others to NFF normalisation committee
World.content:
FIFA has appointed Super Eagles legend Daniel Amokachi and four others to the Normalisation Committee mandated to oversee the affairs of the Nigeria Football Federation (NFF) and implement reforms ahead of fresh elections.

In a letter dated 18 November, FIFA named reputable lawyer Sampson Ebomhe as chairman of the five-member committee, following consultations with the Confederation of African Football (CAF).

The other members are respected journalist and sports administrator Godwin Enakhena, former Nigeria captain and two-time FIFA World Cup player Amokachi, Amina Yerima and Joe Abah.

According to the NFF Communications Department, FIFA’s Chief Member Associations Officer, Elkhan Mammadov, communicated the appointments in a letter to Acting General Secretary Emmanuel Ikpeme.

The members are expected to assume their responsibilities immediately, subject to eligibility checks by the FIFA Review Committee in line with FIFA’s Governance Regulations.

FIFA said their confirmation would depend on the screening process.

The world football governing body also reiterated that none of the committee members would be eligible to contest any position in the forthcoming NFF elections, even if their appointments were revoked or they resigned.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Committee’s responsibilities

Beyond managing the federation’s affairs, the committee has been given a broad mandate to review the NFF’s governance structure and electoral framework.

Its responsibilities include managing the federation’s daily affairs and reviewing the NFF Statutes to increase stakeholder representation, promote a more inclusive Executive Committee, and reduce its membership.

The committee will also work with FIFA and CAF to determine whether certain provisions of the NFF Electoral Code require amendments to strengthen governance and improve the credibility of the electoral process.

It is further expected to develop proposals for additional governance reforms involving the NFF, state football associations, leagues and other relevant football stakeholders.

These reforms will subsequently be supervised by the newly elected NFF leadership.

Another major responsibility is to organise elections for a new NFF leadership team under the revised statutory framework and under the supervision of the federation’s electoral committees.

FIFA has also asked the current NFF administration to cooperate with the committee as it begins its assignment fully.

The committee’s mandate will end once it completes its responsibilities, but no later than 31 May 2027.

Background

FIFA’s announcement marks another significant step in efforts to resolve the leadership crisis that has unsettled Nigerian football administration since August.

On 22 October, the Bureau of the FIFA Council approved the appointment of a Normalisation Committee to manage the NFF until fresh elections are held for its Executive Committee.

The development followed the mass resignation of NFF President Ibrahim Musa Gusau, General Secretary Mohammed Sanusi and members of the federation’s Executive Committee on 27 August.

ALSO READ: NFF suspends two referees as crackdown continues against bad officiating

The resignations disrupted preparations for the NFF elective congress scheduled for 27 September in Lafia, Nasarawa State, prompting FIFA and CAF to intervene in the electoral process.

Emmanuel Ikpeme was subsequently appointed acting General Secretary to oversee the NFF Secretariat while consultations on the federation’s future continued.

The crisis also coincided with renewed calls for reforms in Nigerian football. President Bola Tinubu, on the day the NFF leadership resigned, directed the National Sports Commission to work with the federation and relevant stakeholders on comprehensive reforms covering governance, administration, domestic competitions and accountability.

A Nigerian delegation led by NSC Chairman Shehu Dikko had earlier met FIFA officials in Zurich on 1 September to discuss the crisis and a roadmap for reform.

The appointment of the five members now provides a clearer picture of the committee’s structure and responsibilities, and it is expected to steer the federation toward fresh elections within FIFA’s stipulated timeframe.

World.title: Nigerian govt approves establishment of public relations university
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has approved the establishment of the University of Public Relations and Leadership in Gudi, Nasarawa State.

The president announced the approval on Wednesday while delivering an address on the fourth day of the ongoing World Public Relations Forum in Abuja.

Mr Tinubu, who was represented by Vice-President Kashim Shettima, said the institution would contribute to human capital development and provide opportunities to train a new generation of communication leaders equipped to respond to the demands of a rapidly changing global environment.

“In this regard, I am pleased to formally approve and support the establishment of the University of Public Relations and Leadership, a first-of-its-kind initiative designed to advance specialised education, research, professional development and leadership training in public relations, strategic communications and related disciplines.

“Establishing this specialised institution represents a forward-looking investment in human capital and the future of the communication profession. It will provide opportunities to develop a new generation of communication leaders equipped to respond to the demands of a rapidly changing global environment,” he said.

He commended leadership of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), the Federal Ministry of Information and National Orientation, and the Nasarawa State Government for their collaboration and commitment towards making the university a reality.

The president urged relevant stakeholders to support the institution to ensure that it develops into a centre of excellence with national, continental and international recognition.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“I encourage all relevant stakeholders to work together to ensure the university develops into a centre of excellence with national, continental and international recognition,” he said.

The university approval comes amid the federal government’s efforts to halt the proliferation of higher institutions in the country, referencing concerns about inadequate funding, duplication of academic programmes, under-utilisation of existing facilities and declining standards of education.

In August 2025, the Federal Executive Council (FEC), presided over by President Tinubu, approved a seven-year moratorium on the establishment of new federal universities, polytechnics and colleges of education. The Minister of Education, Tunji Alausa, said the government wanted to redirect resources towards strengthening existing institutions, improving infrastructure and addressing shortages of academic staff.

The government subsequently extended the restriction to private tertiary institutions in March 2026, making the president’s latest announcement particularly significant.

However, the University of Public Relations and Leadership is a project of the Nigerian Institute of Public Relations (NIPR), rather than a conventional federal university. The institute had earlier in July 2025 signed a memorandum of understanding with the Nasarawa State Government for the establishment of the institution in Gudi, Akwanga Local Government Area. The state government reportedly provided 101 hectares of land for the project.

Aside from the policy implications, the proposed institution is expected to provide specialised academic and professional training in public relations, strategic communication and leadership, areas that have become increasingly important in the digital age.

Public relations professionals play a significant role in shaping public perception, managing institutional reputations, communicating government policies and building trust between public institutions and citizens. With the increasing spread of misinformation and disinformation, particularly through social media, specialised training could help produce professionals better equipped to promote credible information, manage communication crises and strengthen public engagement.

The NIPR has said the project is intended to bridge the communication gap between leaders and the public while deepening the practice and development of public relations globally.

Call for investment opportunities

Mr Tinubu also urged delegates, particularly those from other countries, to explore investment opportunities in Nigeria.

“Distinguished delegates, as you participate in this forum, I invite you to take a second interest in Nigeria beyond the conference programme. Look beyond the discussions in the hall and discover the opportunities that our country offers.

READ ALSO: Tinubu receives state police bill after approval by all 36 State Assemblies

“Explore our investment potentials: vibrant entrepreneurial ecosystem, creative industries, rich cultural heritage, tourism assets and the ingenuity of our people – the can-do spirit. Of the ten unicorns in Africa, six are in Nigeria: Flutterwave, Opay, InterSwitch, Moove, Moniepoint. That Nigerian spirit, that resilience, we are loud.

“I’m a swashbuckling capitalist. Africans are by nature a humble and self-effacing people, but Nigerians, no. I beg to disagree. We are loud. We are confident, and of course, we are extremely hardworking people. Nigeria is a country of enormous possibilities. We’re a nation of diverse cultures, talents and ideas, with a youthful population, a dynamic private sector and a strong determination to build a more prosperous future,” he added.

Mr Tinubu predicted that Nigeria’s population would surpass that of the United States by 2050, making it the world’s third most populous country, with an estimated 440 million people.

He also praised Nigerians for their achievements in business and other fields, referencing the country’s representation among the world’s wealthiest Black people.

“One out of every four black men is a Nigerian. By 2050, one out of every three black men will be a Nigerian. We will surpass the United States and become the third most populous nation on earth, with a population of 440 million people. And by the end of the century, Nigeria will be the most populous nation on earth. So we have every reason to play Nigeria. I encourage you to engage with our institutions, interact with our businesses.

“The richest black man on earth is a bloody Nigerian. The second richest black man in the world is another bloody Nigerian. The third richest black man in the world is also a bloody Nigerian. I encourage you to engage with our institutions, interact with our businesses, establish vocational relationships and explore opportunities for partnerships and investment. Nigeria goes beyond the stories we tell and what you read on the social media.

“The most outwardly mobile immigrant community in the United States are the Nigerian Americans. Sixty per cent of them have college degrees. So Nigeria goes beyond 419. Nigeria is much more bigger than that. We want you to leave Nigeria, Prof Justin Green, not only with new professional knowledge and friendships, but also with a deeper appreciation of our country and a renewed interest in its prospects. We hope that your experience here will encourage you to return, invest, collaborate, and become ambassadors of Nigeria’s positive story,” the president said.

World.title: Consent, not defence in sex with minors, police warn
World.content:
The Police Command in Lagos State has warned that sexual intercourse with anyone below 18 constitutes a felony punishable by life imprisonment under the state’s Criminal Law.

SP Abimbola Adebisi, the police spokesperson in Lagos, gave the warning in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria in Lagos on Wednesday, while highlighting measures to prevent child sexual abuse and protect minors.

“Consent was not a defence in cases involving sexual intercourse with a child, irrespective of whether the offender described the child as a girlfriend or boyfriend.

“The law recognised anyone below 18 as a child and criminalised sexual intercourse with such an individual, regardless of gender,” she said.

The spokesperson advised parents to introduce sex education early, particularly when children began communicating their needs and interacting with others.

She said children should be taught about their bodies, how to identify their private parts and understand that nobody had the right to touch them inappropriately.

According to her, parents should also explain the difference between appropriate and inappropriate touching to help children recognise potentially abusive situations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ms Adebisi, a police superintendent, urged teachers and school guidance counsellors to intensify sensitisation and provide age-appropriate sex education, stressing that parents had the primary responsibility for educating and protecting their children.

She also called on community members to remain vigilant and report suspicious situations involving minors to their parents to ensure their safety.

The spokesperson advised parents to be cautious about individuals granted access to their children, including domestic workers, caregivers and others entrusted with their supervision.

She urged parents to regularly monitor their children’s activities and interactions with such individuals and understand their experiences while in their care.

Ms Adebisi further emphasised the need for open communication between parents and children, urging parents to create an environment where children could freely share their experiences without fear of being dismissed or reprimanded.

She said parents should listen attentively to their children and encourage them to speak out whenever they experienced or noticed inappropriate conduct or anything that made them uncomfortable.

According to her, such openness will give children the confidence to report suspicious behaviour and enable parents to take timely action to prevent sexual abuse.

World.title: Electricity worker stabbed to death over power disconnection
World.content:
The Benin Electricity Distribution Company (BEDC) says five suspects have been arrested in connection with the killing of its worker, Oscar Eze, in Umunede, Delta, on Monday, over electricity disconnection.

The Acting Managing Director of BEDC, Jonathan Lawani, disclosed this on Wednesday in Benin during a news conference at the company headquarters.

Mr Lawani alleged that Mr Eze, a 38-year-old staff member, was stabbed to death for carrying out an official assignment in the community.

The incident, he alleged, occurred after the deceased disconnected a property over an outstanding electricity bill of nearly N300,000.

According to him, some people allegedly traced Mr Eze to a house in the community and stabbed him repeatedly, leaving him dead at the scene.

Mr Lawani said the disconnection was carried out in line with the regulatory framework governing electricity distribution.

“The only instrument approved by NERC to demand payment from those who refused to pay their monthly electricity bills is disconnection,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The BEDC boss condemned the killing, stressing that electricity workers should not be attacked for performing their official duties.

“The fact that we come to your house to demand payment for the service we have rendered, irrespective of your dissatisfaction with our service, does not give you the right to attack,” he said.

Mr Lawani said the company’s management visited the Assistant Inspector–General of Police’s office, the Divisional Police Officer in Umunede and the scene of the incident on Tuesday.

He disclosed that while five suspects had been arrested, others were still at large.

The acting managing director said the deceased left behind a son from an earlier marriage, a wife he married four months ago and an elderly mother.

He called on the Delta State Government to provide adequate security for electricity workers, warning that continued attacks could threaten BEDC’s operations in the state.

“We believe that the government should provide an enabling environment for people to work, and for a critical sector like electricity, we should be protected,” he said.

Mr Lawani said the company would pursue the case until justice is served.

“We cannot recover his life. We can never take his life back to his people but one thing is that we must get justice, for him,” he said.

State governments urged to protect electricity workers

Also speaking, Abel Enechaziam, head of Maximum Demand Customer and acting chief commercial officer of BEDC, urged state governments to protect electricity workers across the states where the company operates.

READ ALSO: UCH installs new power substation amid recurring electricity crisis

Mr Enechaziam said the company could no longer tolerate attacks and harassment of personnel providing electricity services.

“We cannot continue to tolerate this kind of event. It is very sad,” he said.

He urged the public to stop molesting and harassing service providers in the electricity sector.

He advised customers, dissatisfied with BEDC’s services, to use the company’s complaint channels or approach the relevant electricity regulatory authorities for redress.

He urged electricity consumers to resolve disputes through established channels rather than resort to violence against workers.

(NAN)

World.title: PREMIUM TIMES editor-in-chief Musikilu Mojeed, lawyers, others honoured at Gavel International awards
World.content:
PREMIUM TIMES Editor-in-Chief, Musikilu Mojeed, and late journalist and publisher, Oladotun Oladipo, were among the recipients of awards at the 2026 Gavel International Annual Lecture and Awards in Lagos on Tuesday.

Mr Mojeed received the Ernest Sesei Ikoli/Gavel International Media Achievement Award in recognition of his work in journalism, investigative reporting and media development, as well as his mentorship of young journalists.

In a letter dated 14 September, the organisers commended his professionalism and commitment to public-interest journalism.

They also cited his leadership at PREMIUM TIMES, contribution to online journalism, role in establishing the Guild of Corporate Online Publishers (GOCOP) and presidency of the International Press Institute (IPI), Nigeria.

The award is named after Ernest Sesei Ikoli, a pioneer Nigerian journalist and the first managing director of the Daily Times.

Mr Oladipo received a posthumous Distinguished Merit Award for his contributions to ethical and credible online journalism. His wife, Taiwo, collected the award on his behalf from Maureen Chigbo.

Mr Oladipo founded The Eagle Online and worked with Newswatch, The Punch, Nigerian Tribune, Nigerian Compass and The Sun. He was also politics editor of The Punch and served as GOCOP president from 2017 to 2021.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He died in Lagos on 25 August, aged 56, after nearly three decades in journalism.

Other award recipients included senior lawyers Bayo Ojo, Olisa Agbakoba, Tayo Oyetibo, George Etomi, Kayode Filani and Iniruo Wills.

The event, held at the OPTS Hall of the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry in Alausa, Ikeja, featured a lecture by retired Court of Appeal Justice Oludotun Adefope-Okojie on the role of the judiciary in Nigeria’s electoral process.

Speaking on the theme, “Electoral Process in Nigeria: Managing the Boundaries of Judicial Intervention”, Mrs Adefope-Okojie urged courts to intervene when political parties breach their constitutions or violate electoral laws.

“The courts must no longer refuse to intervene where political parties violate their own constitution and ‘rubbish’ the Electoral Act. They must intervene to sanitise the system,” she said.

She cautioned, however, against courts declaring candidates who lost elections as winners. Where the lawful winner could not be established, she said, a fresh election should be held to allow voters decide the outcome.

Mrs Adefope-Okojie said 1,209 petitions were filed over the 1,280 elective positions contested in the 2023 general elections, but only 103 succeeded. She said the high number of petitions reflected a lack of confidence in the country’s electoral process.

She also pointed to disputes arising from flawed party congresses, the imposition of candidates and unlawful substitutions as sources of election litigation.

Citing the Supreme Court’s 30 April 2026 decision in PDP v. Sule Lamido, she argued that courts should not use the doctrine of party autonomy as a reason to avoid examining alleged breaches of party constitutions and electoral laws.

The retired justice also raised concerns about the burden of proof in election petitions. She said petitioners often face difficulties proving irregularities polling unit by polling unit and securing the testimony of electoral officials.

She called for clearer rules on electronic evidence, particularly evidence from the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System and the INEC Result Viewing Portal. She said uncertainty over what amounts to communication failure could complicate disputes over the electronic transmission of election results.

Mrs Adefope-Okojie outlined four approaches to electoral justice: corrective, protective, substitutive and abdicative. She described corrective justice as addressing electoral wrongs and protective justice as ordering a fresh election where the rightful winner cannot be established.

She said substitutive justice occurs when courts declare candidates who did not receive the voters’ mandate as winners, while abdicative justice describes situations where courts decline to examine credible allegations of malpractice because of procedural or evidential obstacles.

She urged judges and election petition tribunal members to protect voters’ rights and remain within the limits of their judicial responsibilities.

“The Constitution places sovereignty in the people and makes the Courts the guardians of that sovereignty, not its holders,” she said.

She stated that the aim of electoral adjudication should ultimately be to make court intervention less necessary by ensuring that elections are decided by voters.

“The final aim of electoral adjudication should be its own decline: a democracy in which elections are won and lost at the ballot box, not in the courtroom,” she said.

The chairman of the occasion, Anthony George-Ikoli, SAN, said the judiciary had a duty to protect electoral integrity without taking over the responsibilities of voters and electoral bodies.

“The judiciary must neither become an alternative electoral commission nor abdicate its responsibility as the ultimate guardian of electoral legality. That is the delicate boundary we are here this morning to interrogate,” he said.

He noted that judicial restraint should not prevent judges from addressing electoral violations, just as their willingness to intervene should not lead to overreach.

“Judicial restraint should not amount to judicial retreat, just as judicial courage should not degenerate into overreach,” he said.

Another speaker, Femi Falana, SAN, called for reforms to electoral litigation to reduce the burden on the Supreme Court.

He proposed a return to the previous arrangement for appeals in governorship election disputes and criticised the different appeal procedures for presidential and legislative election petitions. He said efforts to address the problems had stalled since 2011.

Gavel International publisher, Mustapha Ogunsakin, praised Mrs Adefope-Okojie’s judicial career, including her role in a 2005 tribunal set up to investigate security breaches at the Ikeja High Court.

He said the tribunal’s report was commended by Bola Tinubu, then governor of Lagos State, and helped establish a framework for court security in the state.

Gavel International, a legal and justice news platform, began its annual lecture series in 2015.

World.title: Motsepe arrives Abuja for 48th CAF Ordinary General Assembly
World.content:
The President of the Confederation of African Football, Patrice Motsepe, arrived in the Federal Capital, Abuja, on Wednesday to a rousing welcome ahead of Saturday’s 48th CAF General Assembly, which Nigeria is hosting.

Mr Motsepe was received on arrival at the Presidential Wing of the Nnamdi Azikiwe International Airport by the Chairman of the National Sports Commission, Shehu Dikko; Mr Motsepe’s Special Advisor and former NFF President Amaju Pinnick, CAF Secretary General, Samson Adamu, CAF’s Project Lead for both the OGA and the CAF Awards Christian Emeruwa, Nigeria’s Project Lead for both events Ademola Olajire, and other top CAF Management and staff members.

His private jet touched down at the airport at 5:51 p.m., and his entourage immediately left for the Transcorp Hilton Hotel, where all VVIPs, delegates, CAF Management and Staff, invited Guests and other stakeholders are lodging for Saturday’s General Assembly.

It is the first time in 17 years that Nigeria is hosting the CAF General Assembly – the biggest gathering of football administrators and stakeholders in the African continent, bringing together the leaders and managers of the Confederation of African Football, CAF Executive Committee members, Presidents and General Secretaries of all of CAF’s 54 Member Associations, special guests from FIFA including the FIFA President and General Secretary, special guests from other Confederations of FIFA, and other stakeholders of the game globally.

This year is also the first time that one country is hosting both the General Assembly and the CAF Awards – which is the biggest football-centred awards ceremony in Africa, and brings together the best actors of the past (legends) and present, as well as CAF chieftains, guests and stakeholders.

The CAF Awards will take place in Lagos on Wednesday, 2nd December

While the OGA is scheduled for the Bola Ahmed Tinubu International Conference Centre, the CAF Awards will take place inside the expansive Wole Soyinka Centre for Culture and Creative Arts, formerly known as the National Theatre.

World.title: CCB official testifies on Useni’s controversial acquisition of London property linked to Ozekhome
World.content:
An official of the Code of Conduct Bureau (CCB) has shared fresh findings regarding the late Jeremiah Useni’s London property, which is at the centre of the criminal trial involving senior lawyer Mike Ozekhome, who is facing charges of forging documents to claim the house.

Testifying as a prosecution on Wednesday, CCB official, Raaji Babatunde, pointed out a discrepancy between Mr Useni’s acclaimed value of the property and the official value quoted in a UK property tribunal’s judgement given last year in a legal dispute over the ownership of the asset.

According to Mr Babatunde, an assistant chief Superintendent with the CCB, while Mr Useni “put the figure for the acquisition of the property at £79,000 in 1992”, the tribunal judgement in London disclosed the purchase price of the property that year as £200,000.

Also, the CCB official, who said he processed Mr Useni’s asset declaration as incoming senator representing Plateau South in 2015, testified that the late military general acquired the assets with an amount of money beyond his earnings as a public officer.

These details add another layer to the controversy that has characterised the property since it became a subject of public attention last year.

The London property, held under shadowy ownership for decades, is at the heart of the forgery case instituted against Mr Ozekhome and the late general’s son, Ponfa Useni.

The Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) filed the charges after the lid on the mess surrounding the property was blown open in a London property tribunal judgement.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

In the trial, Mr Ozekhome and Ponfa face charges of impersonation and forgery of a Nigerian passport presented before a London tribunal to support Mr Ozekhome’s failed bid to claim the London property.

The older Mr Useni, who died in January 2025, acquired the property at No. 79, Randall Avenue, London NW2, United Kingdom, under the fictitious name Tali Shani in 1992.

This was during his active years as a military officer when he took political offices, including the FCT minister, under the military regime.

His purported attempt to transfer its ownership of the London property to Mr Ozekhome allegedly led to the presentation of documents, which the property tribunal in London found to be forged to support the false identities of Tali Shani.

On 27 February, the office of the EFCC arraigned Messrs Ozekhome and Mr Useni’s son, Ponfa, on 12 counts of forgery and impersonation.

According to the charges, the defendants conspired in 2020 alongside the late Useni, a retired general, and made a false Nigerian passport with the number A07535463 and the name Tali Shani, supporting it to be issued by the Nigeria Immigration Service, to claim a property in the United Kingdom.

Similarly, the prosecution charged them with “using a false passport to facilitate the claim of the property.”

The prosecution also alleged that Mr Ozekhome helped Ponfa Useni to impersonate Tali Shani in 2020. Together, they allegedly created a fake “Irrevocable Power of Attorney” to help Mr Ozekhome claim the property.

They denied all the charges.

Process of asset declaration

Led in evidence on Wednesday by the Director of Public Prosecution of the Federation (DPPF) Rotimi Oyedepo, Mr Babatunde said he personally attended to the late general when he went to the CCB to declare his assets in 2015.

The witness said the late Mr Useni cited salaries and sale of property as the source of the funds for the purchase of the disputed property.

Two years after Mr Useni’s asset declaration, Mr Babatunde said he was directed by his superiors to analyse the asset declaration form.

He said the amount of money paid for the acquisition of the property “was far in excess of what is fairly attributed to the income of the public officer and his position.”

Mr Babatunde said Mr Useni declared £18,000 as his annual income, while he claimed to have acquired the property for £79,000 in 1992, although the UK tribunal judgement put the value at £200,000.

He said he wrote a request to the Revenue Mobilisation and Fiscal Commission (RMFC) and got a response as well as a net-worth analysis, which Mr Oyedepo, a Senior Advocate of Nigeria (SAN), submitted as evidence.

He also presented the order and decision of London’s first-tier Tribunal Property Chamber Land Registration in the case between Tali Shani and Mr Ozekhome.

Summarising the CCB’s findings on the property, the witness said, “Because of the inconsistency we noticed between the asset declaration form and the judgment of the tribunal, specifically the price of the acquisition of the property and the owners of the property, while the declarant confirmed that he is the owner. The judgment of the London Court named Tali Shani as the owner.

“Secondly, the record from RMFC places a substantial gap between the lawful income of the late Jeremiah Useni and the value of the property.”

Due to the disparity, the CCB got the property documents in the United Kingdom, and the judgment of the London court, and “the property was confiscated to the Federal Government of Nigeria,” the witness testified.

Defence pokes holes into prosecution’s case

Under cross-examination by Mr Ozekhome’s lawyer Paul Erokoro, a SAN, the witness said he told the EFCC his findings but did not write a statement. He also said he was not sure if the EFCC officer who questioned him wrote down any statement.

He also could not recall the name of the officer or the time and date he was questioned.

Mr Babatunde also said he did not know the late Mr Useni’s rank in the military. He insisted that the general made the declaration as an incoming senator in 2015.

He said he did not issue the late general the acknowledgement slip of the asset declaration form but insisted that he attended to him.

Mr Babatunde acknowledged that the issuing authority on the asset declaration form is Sam Saba.

The witness also said the original asset declaration form was in safe custody in the strong room in the office of the CCB’s chairman.

Mr Erokoro then asked the witness to show the court the letter the CCB wrote to their legal partner to obtain the London Court’s decision; the witness said it was in the office.

However, he said he could not remember the name or address of the lawyer. He also denied knowing the value of the pounds to naira as at 1992.

The witness affirmed that the late Mr Useni had shares, stocks and bonds.

Thereafter, trial judge Chizoba adjourned the case till 23 November.

Highlights of previous testimony

The first prosecution witness, a Nigerian Immigration Service (NIS) officer, testified in March that a passport with the name Tali Shani was fake.

Akim Aridegbe, a principal staff officer to the Comptroller-General of the NIS, said the passport was not issued by the NIS.

Despite the passport sharing features of a genuine copy, it has no record in the NIS database, Mr Aridegbe said.

A forensic examiner, Bamaiyi Mairiga, also told the Court that the passport with the name Tali Shani was forged.

Backstory

Mr Ozekhome’s prosecution in Nigeria stemmed from a London Tribunal’s judgement that blocked him from claiming a property in North London in September 2025.

In August 2021, Mr Ozekhome sought to transfer the property to his name, claiming it was a gift from a man who presented himself as Tali Shani in appreciation for legal services.

But this was challenged in September 2022 by Westfields Solicitors, claiming to represent “Ms Tali Shani,” who insisted she was the registered owner of the property since 1993 and had never signed any transfer.

Ruling on the dispute, Judge Paton of the UK Tribunal ruled that the house was secretly bought in 1993 by the late Mr Useni, former Nigerian Minister of the Federal Capital Territory, using a false identity.

According to the tribunal, Mr Ozekhome’s steps to claim the property were built on a network of fraud, impersonation, and forged documents. Still, it concluded that the late Mr Useni, former Minister of FCT, was the genuine purchaser of the property in 1993.

Similarly, the London tribunal uncovered fraudulent Nigerian identity records, including a passport, a National Identification Number (NIN), and a Tax Identification Number (TIN) allegedly generated with the connivance of corrupt officials at the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), the Immigration Service, and the Federal Inland Revenue Service.

In November 2025, CCB obtained an order of the Federal High Court in Abuja to freeze the property on the basis that it was shadily acquired by Mr Useni.

The CCB reported to the court in a filing in January that the property remained unclaimed weeks after a newspaper publication invited anyone with a legitimate claim to it to step forward.

The court subsequently ordered the property’s final forfeiture to the federal government.

Meanwhile, the Legal Practitioners’ Privileges Committee has since placed Mr Ozekhome’s SAN rank under suspension pending the outcome of his ongoing trial.

World.title: SIFAX boss advocates adequate storage to boost food production
World.content:
By Kafayat Kokumo

Chairman of SIFAX Group, Dr Taiwo Afolabi, has called for adequate infrastructure for storage and distribution in order to increase the economic benefits of increased food production.



He made this call at the 2026 Annual Strategy Retreat of the Odu’a Investment Company Limited held at the International Institute of Tropical Agriculture (IITA), Ibadan.



Represented by the Deputy Director, Strategy and Operations, Oliver Omajuwa, SIFAX Group, Afolabi said that investments in agricultural logistics were critical to connecting production centres with processing facilities, retail markets and export channels.

He said: “Increased production would yield limited economic benefits without adequate infrastructure for aggregation, preservation, storage and distribution.



“Cold rooms, temperature-controlled transportation and strategically located warehouses are critical investments capable of connecting agricultural production to processing facilities, retail markets and export channels.”



The SIFAX boss identified warehousing, transportation, agricultural aggregation, cold-chain services, technology and specialised logistics as viable investment opportunities, urging investors to identify gaps across the value chain before committing resources.

He also advised Odu’a Investment Company Limited to assess the transportation, storage and distribution needs of its portfolio companies, noting that their combined requirements could provide a foundation for a shared logistics platform.



On port logistics, Afolabi said investment opportunities extended beyond terminal operations to cargo handling, freight forwarding, customs clearing, equipment maintenance, storage and export consolidation.

He said: “Integrating these services would improve cargo movement, reduce operational complexities and enable customers to access multiple logistics solutions without engaging several service providers.”

He further urged investors to explore greenfield developments, acquisitions and strategic partnerships with established operators, depending on their financial capacity, technical expertise and market opportunities.

Afolabi also highlighted the importance of technology-driven solutions, including cargo tracking, inventory management and operational monitoring systems, in improving efficiency, visibility and service delivery across the logistics value chain.

However, he cautioned investors against making decisions based primarily on asset ownership, stressing that acquiring trucks, constructing warehouses or purchasing equipment did not automatically guarantee profitability.

World.title: Unilorin student seeks N43m for kidney transplant
World.content:
… Family spends over N20m, sells property to sustain treatment

By Chioma Obinna

The family of Olajide Victor, a 200-level student of the University of Ilorin, Kwara State, has appealed for N43 million to fund a kidney transplant for him after he was diagnosed with Stage V end-stage renal disease.



Victor is expected to undergo the life-saving procedure at Newhaven Specialist Hospital, Lagos, as his family struggles to meet the cost of his treatment.



He said his health challenges began in November 2025 after he sustained a minor fracture in his left leg while playing football at the university’s sports complex. Weeks later, his face and legs became swollen, prompting medical examinations.



Following several tests, including kidney function investigations, he was diagnosed with Stage V kidney disease at Taiwo Hospital, Ilorin.



A medical report signed by Dr S. Alagbe, Consultant Nephrologist, indicated that Victor requires continued haemodialysis twice weekly.



His mother, Comfort Adesanya, said the family had spent over N20 million on his treatment and sold their land, house and other valuables to keep him alive.



She appealed to individuals, corporate organisations and well-meaning Nigerians to help raise the N43 million required for the transplant, saying the family could no longer cope with the rising cost of treatment.



Donations can be made to Victor Adekunle Olajide, UBA, Account Number: 2458216260 or call Victor on 09018866426.

World.title: Food security: Nigerian farmers risk wasting billions on fertilisers without soil testing, experts warn
World.content:
By Adeola Badru & Cynthia Alo

Nigeria’s quest for food security may continue to suffer setbacks unless farmers move away from indiscriminate fertiliser application and embrace soil testing and crop-specific nutrient management, agricultural experts have warned.

The experts, who spoke at the 2026 South-West Nigeria Fertiliser and Soil Health Summit in Ibadan, Oyo State, cautioned that increasing fertiliser consumption without understanding the specific nutrient requirements of farmland could undermine agricultural productivity, weaken farmers’ incomes and worsen soil degradation.

They argued that the country’s approach to fertiliser management must go beyond distributing inputs to farmers and focus on ensuring that the right fertiliser is applied to the right soil, for the right crop and at the appropriate time.

The position formed a major highlight of the communiqué issued at the end of the summit, organised by the Institute of Agricultural Research and Training (IAR&T), Obafemi Awolowo University, Moor Plantation, Ibadan, on Tuesday.

With the theme, “Fertilisers and Food Security in South-West Nigeria: The Journey So Far,” the summit brought together more than 150 scientists, farmers, policymakers, fertiliser manufacturers and distributors, agricultural extension professionals and development partners to examine the challenges confronting fertiliser utilisation and soil health in the region.

The participants expressed concern that the continued reliance on blanket fertiliser recommendations failed to address significant differences in soil fertility, acidity, phosphorus fixation, nutrient depletion and other soil-related challenges across different agroecological zones.

According to the communiqué, “The predominance of blanket fertiliser recommendations does not adequately address the variations in soil fertility, soil acidity, phosphorus fixation, nutrient depletion and other soil constraints across different agroecological zones in the region.”

The experts maintained that fertiliser recommendations should increasingly be based on soil testing, crop requirements, prevailing agroecological conditions and economically viable nutrient management practices.

They also identified high fertiliser prices, inadequate distribution networks, limited access to credit and inconsistent availability as major constraints preventing smallholder farmers from accessing and effectively utilising the agricultural input.

The summit further warned that declining soil organic matter, nutrient imbalance, erosion and other forms of soil degradation continued to undermine fertiliser-use efficiency and agricultural productivity.

To address the situation, it called on research institutions to strengthen soil fertility mapping and develop crop-, soil- and location-specific fertiliser recommendations for major crops cultivated across South-West Nigeria.

It also urged governments and relevant agricultural institutions to facilitate affordable and accessible soil testing services to enable farmers to understand the condition of their farmland before applying fertilisers.

The participants advocated integrated soil fertility management, involving the combination of mineral fertilisers with organic resources, crop residues, compost, animal manure and biological inputs, as a more sustainable approach to improving soil health and agricultural productivity.

The summit also called for stronger collaboration between fertiliser manufacturers and research institutions to develop formulations capable of addressing specific soil deficiencies, including phosphorus fixation and shortages of secondary and micronutrients.

On the impact of climate change, the experts noted that irregular rainfall patterns and increasing incidences of drought required farmers to adopt climate-smart fertiliser management strategies.

They recommended that fertiliser application guidelines should take rainfall variability, planting dates, crop water requirements and appropriate application methods into consideration.

The communiqué also raised concerns over the circulation of adulterated and substandard fertiliser products, calling on regulatory institutions to intensify inspections, product certification, market surveillance and enforcement of existing standards.

It further recommended greater investment in digital soil maps, fertiliser recommendation platforms, mobile advisory services and precision nutrient management technologies to improve fertiliser distribution, application and monitoring.

The summit stressed that sustainable fertiliser management should not be measured solely by increased crop yields but should also take account of environmental protection, farmers’ economic returns and the long-term preservation of soil health.

It called for a coordinated monitoring framework to assess the impact of fertiliser interventions on crop productivity, farmers’ income, fertiliser-use efficiency and soil health.

The summit acknowledged previous interventions by regional governments, research institutions and development partners to strengthen fertiliser and soil health systems but maintained that significant gaps remained in ensuring that fertilisers were affordable, accessible, appropriate, balanced and efficiently utilised.

It warned that increased fertiliser use alone could not guarantee food security, insisting that sustainable agricultural production required sound soil health management, scientifically informed recommendations, effective extension services, quality assurance and supportive government policies.

Earlier in his address, the chairman of the occasion and the Vice-Chancellor of Obafemi Awolowo University, Ile-Ife, Prof. Simeon Bamire, who was represented by the Dean of the Faculty of Agriculture, Prof. A.O. Ajayi, emphasised the need to redirect attention from fertiliser distribution to fertiliser-use efficiency, describing it as a critical pathway to achieving food security.

In his remarks, the Director of IAR&T, Prof. Gabriel Oluwatosin, noted that one of the key resolutions reached at the summit was the need to organise zonal fertiliser summits across the country, adding that without proper soil health management and fertilizer use, as the population is growing, farmers would not be able to secure their food food security.

World.title: 655 tribunal registrars swear oath of secrecy ahead of 2027 election cases
World.content:
By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

With just 58 days to the general elections, the Court of Appeal on November 16 administered the oath of secrecy to 655 clerks and Deputy Chief Registrars selected to serve on the various election tribunals.



The oath was administered under the supervision of the President of the Court of Appeal (PCA), Justice Monica Dongban-Mensem.



It specifically invoked the provisions of Section 1(1) of the Official Secrets Act, which concerns the protection of official information. Under the Act, a person commits an offence if they transmit classified matter to a person to whom they are not authorised, on behalf of the Government, to transmit it.



The Act also provides that a person is guilty of an offence if they obtain, reproduce, or retain classified matter which they are not authorised, on behalf of the Government, to obtain, reproduce, or retain, as the case may be. The officials were warned that the oath would remain binding even after their assignments at the tribunal ended, with the PCA vowing to hand over defaulters to security agencies for prosecution.



“Is there anyone among you who did not read the oath form, or who signed it and now wants to withdraw from the assignment?” Justice Dongban-Mensem asked, as the weight of the oath dawned on the officials.



“I am asking because you have just signed evidence against yourselves. Anyone we find doing what we have asked you not to do will be handed over to the Police for prosecution.



“I am taking all the forms you signed to the secret registry of my office, and I will lock them in my safe. In case some of you are not aware, I began my tenure as President of this Court by handing some people over for prosecution, and they were duly prosecuted.

“It is because people are not made to face the consequences of their actions that we have so many problems in this country. But at the Court of Appeal, we give you every opportunity to abide by your oath, and when you don’t, we prosecute.

“Some of you may be approached and asked to give details of the tribunal members’ discussions. You will start eavesdropping to get information to pass on to them. “But when you eavesdrop, you can never get the full details. That is how, before you know it, false judgments start flying around. It often comes from the registry.

“We are watching you, and many other people will be watching you too. Be very careful, be committed to the nation, and let’s get it right,” the PCA warned.

Election Petition Tribunals are established to hear and determine petitions arising from the conduct of elections into political offices.

Section 285(1) and (2) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, empowers the President of the Court of Appeal to constitute an Election Petition Tribunal in each State of the Federation and the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja.

Section 134(3)(a) and (b) of the Electoral Act, 2026 further provides that these Tribunals shall be constituted not later than 30 days before the election, and shall open their registries for business seven days before the election.

The registry is a very important organ of an election petition tribunal, and its administrative duties include receiving petitions and other court processes for filing, serving court processes on parties in a timely manner, issuing hearing notices, preparing court proceedings and orders, keeping the tribunal’s documents in safe custody, and compiling records, among various other duties and responsibilities.

The effectiveness, quality, efficiency, transparency and speed of the registry have a direct impact on the performance and justice delivery of the election tribunal.

According to Section 285(5) of the 1999 Constitution, as amended, a candidate aggrieved by the outcome of an election must file a petition at the registry of the appropriate tribunal or court within 21 days of the declaration of results by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

While the tribunal is statutorily mandated to deliver its judgment within 180 days from the date the petition was filed, any appeal arising from the tribunal’s or the Court of Appeal’s judgment must be filed and disposed of within 60 days from the date of the lower court’s decision.

Addressing the 655 tribunal officials at the commencement of a two-day capacity-building workshop that followed their oath-taking session, Justice Dongban-Mensem noted that modern registry practices demand more than manual filing and routine administrative work.

She said they demand a new mindset and the adoption of electronic filing and case management systems that allow for easy tracking and retrieval of cases.

“They demand proper documentation, accurate and systematic archiving. They demand timely service of processes and effective scheduling that respects the strict timelines prescribed by law for election petitions. They demand confidentiality, integrity and professionalism.”

She said the workshop, themed: “Modern Registry Practices for Effective Election Petition Tribunal Administration,” was designed as a platform to equip the participants with hands-on knowledge of the use of technology in case management, best practices in records keeping, and the ethical standards expected of tribunal staff.

Emphasising that the integrity of the judiciary was on the line, the PCA cautioned the court’s registry staff against exploiting their election tribunal assignments for financial gain.

“It is part of your obligation to discharge your duties with utmost good faith and not be carried away by little advances.

“Your integrity and that of the Tribunal and its members are in the public searchlight. You must therefore ensure that you are not used as tools to derail the process.

“Ensure that you live above board so that you do not bring the Judiciary into disrepute. Do not see it as an opportunity to enrich yourselves, but rather go there to build your name and your future, as it is said that a good name is better than silver and gold.

“The Court will not hesitate to deal with anyone found wanting in this regard,” she added.

For his part, the Chief Registrar of the Court of Appeal, Mr. Umar Bangari, said the tribunal officials must be conscious of the fact that “the spotlight of the entire nation will turn on the Judiciary” after the elections.

He maintained that the success, efficiency, and credibility of every Tribunal rests heavily on the shoulders of the registrars and backroom staff.

“You should be aware that you are the custodians of all the processes filed at the Tribunal, the managers of strict statutory timelines, and the primary administrative interface between parties on one hand, and the Bench on the other.

“Accordingly, you are hereby placed on strict notice against engaging in any form of misconduct, including but not limited to collusion, conspiracy, or conniving with any party to manipulate court processes, alter records, or confer an unfair advantage upon one party to the detriment of another.

“You must also avoid file tampering and leaking confidential internal communications, draft rulings, panel deliberations, or privileged case information to unauthorised persons, among so many other acts of misconduct.

“We shall entertain zero tolerance towards any breach of neutrality or ethical standards. Any secretary or staff member found to be conniving with any party or counsel to subvert the course of justice will face severe consequences,” Bangari added.

Noting that election adjudication is sui generis and strictly bound by constitutional and statutory timeframes, the Court of Appeal Registrar implored the participants to adhere strictly to timelines.

“As we all know, a single administrative lapse, delayed endorsement, or misplaced process can occasion a damaging miscarriage of justice. You must treat every filing, service of processes, and transmission of records with utmost urgency and precision.

“Avoid shady practices, such as giving litigants or counsel advance copies of processes. You should also avoid backdating processes in order to bring them within the prescribed time for filing.

“Treat all Panel members of the Tribunal, as well as counsel and litigants, with courtesy, impartiality and professionalism. You are the first point of contact for litigants and counsel.

“You manage the registries, receive and process filings, maintain accurate records, issue hearing notices, and ensure that the strict statutory timelines governing election petitions are never compromised,” he added.

The Deputy Chief Registrar of the Court in charge of the election petition tribunals, Mrs. Maitumbi Altine, disclosed that a total of 223 of the participants have previously served in tribunals, while 432 of them are first-timers.

She said it was the first time in the annals of the court that such training had been organised for staff members who will serve the various election tribunals.

With the earlier inauguration of 375 judges who will serve on various tribunals across the country, the judiciary has clearly sent a loud message that it is ready for the aftermath of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: AI, fake voter records raise new risks for 2027 elections
World.content:
…Why media must not rush to publish election claims —Tech players

By Juliet Umeh

As Nigeria prepares for the 2027 general elections, voters may face a new kind of deception.



The society is now rife with images, videos and audios that appear authentic but have been fabricated or altered.



The concern has grown after the Independent National Electoral Commission, INEC, said it removed 1,609,553 records from the voters’ register following a technical assessment. The review examined suspected multiple registrations, unusual registration patterns, substituted photographs and irregularities linked to registration transactions.



INEC also found cases in which some registration personnel deliberately bypassed established procedures, including provisions for exceptional circumstances involving persons with disabilities. The commission is investigating some flagged records.



The findings have prompted questions about how the irregularities occurred and whether synthetic images or other AI-generated material could be used to undermine confidence in the electoral process. There is, however, no evidence in the material available that AI-generated images caused the irregularities in the register.



Olaronke Alo of the BBC Disinformation Unit while speaking on Arise Television said its initial verification found that some of the images circulating online were present in the INEC register.



She said: “What we did was to do the initial verification. We went into the INEC portal and began to trace some of the names and pictures being posted on social media. We found that these images were on the INEC register.”



The unit also examined claims about inconsistent records, including one instance in which the same photograph appeared against different names.



Alo said it found examples of apparently incomplete or unusual names and records alleged to belong to deceased people, including former President Muhammadu Buhari.



She said the unit’s task was to verify claims circulating online, rather than assess whether INEC’s response was adequate.

False claims can travel fast



The risks extend beyond the voters’ register. AI tools can generate convincing images, videos and audio of people appearing to say things they never said. A fabricated statement attributed to a political figure could spread rapidly before voters have time to verify it.



INEC has dismissed a social media poster and accompanying text claiming the commission had reaffirmed the leadership of the African Democratic Congress. The poster carried INEC’s logo and an image of National Commissioner Mohammed Haruna. With the matter before the courts, false claims styled as official announcements could mislead the public.



Other risks include political messages tailored to specific groups of voters, fabricated result sheets, screenshots purporting to show updates from INEC’s results portal, or cloned voices announcing false outcomes. Such material could create confusion and deepen doubts about the credibility of the process.



There is no evidence that these tactics have affected election results in Nigeria. But the possibility of manipulated content increases the work required of election officials, journalists and voters as the poll approaches.



Alo urged voters to examine the details of material they encounter online, asking who posted it, why it was posted and whether credible sources have confirmed it.



She cited a video appearing to show Burkina Faso leader Ibrahim Traoré addressing President Bola Tinubu in English. Viewers, she said, should consider whether the language matches what is known about the speaker and whether the video appeared through official channels.

She said: “If a president is addressing another president, it is expected that the national broadcaster of that country is picking up those broadcasts.”



Viewers can also look for inconsistencies in speech, mouth movements, skin tones and framing, she said. Reverse image searches may help establish whether a picture has appeared elsewhere and how it was originally used. People should also check official channels and note when platforms label content as AI-generated.



No single clue proves a post is fake. But checking the source and seeking confirmation before sharing can slow the spread of misleading claims.



Technology needs scrutiny



At a panel discussion on science and technology during election season, speakers said the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System, BVAS, and INEC’s Result Viewing Portal, IReV, could improve transparency. They cautioned, however, that technology alone could not guarantee credible elections.



Head of Research and Programmes at Kimpact Development Initiative, Oluwafemi John, said BVAS and IReV have different functions.



“BVAS helps with verification and accreditation,” he said, explaining that the device checks voters through fingerprints or facial recognition. After ballots are counted, the presiding officer uses BVAS to transmit an image of the polling-unit result sheet, Form EC8A, to IReV.



He noted: “IReV is not a collation point. We should not mix it up.”



He said questions remained about the legal and evidential status of some election technology records, and urged the public to distinguish between uploading results for viewing and formally collating them at designated centres.



A research analyst at the Centre for Journalism Innovation and Development’s Digital Technology, AI and Information Disorder Analysis Centre, Sanusi Sanusi, said online access to polling-unit results had enabled independent scrutiny.



He said: “Technology has really helped make election results transparent. If you know your polling unit, you can trace it on IReV and look at the result.”



But he raised concerns about BVAS devices’ age and performance, citing reports of accreditation difficulties and compatibility problems. He also questioned how differences between electronically generated figures and figures on physical forms were reconciled.



“If there is a disparity between the electronically generated figures and the physical figures, what is the reconciliation process?” he asked. “There is no guideline anywhere to explain that.”



Sanusi said inconsistencies in voter figures and reports of missing ballots needed investigation and clear explanations. He cautioned that discrepancies should not automatically be called evidence of rigging without further verification.

Verify before publishing



For journalists, the challenge is not only interpreting results but also assessing suspicious digital material before it reaches the public.



“Don’t run into publishing,” Sanusi said. “You need to develop your sense of doubt and figure out when something is worth investigating.” Tools that assess potentially AI-generated videos may offer clues, he said, but not definitive proof. “Always use multiple tools to verify.”

World.title: Army seeks land for armoured corps training in Bauchi
World.content:
File image.

…Commends Bala Mohammed for supporting military operations, infrastructure development

By Christopher Ameh

The Chief of Army Staff, Lieutenant General Waidi Shaibu, has appealed to the Bauchi State Government to allocate land for the establishment of a dedicated training facility for the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps in the state.

Shaibu made the appeal during a courtesy visit to Governor Bala Mohammed at the Government House, Bauchi, where he commended the governor for supporting the Nigerian Army and promoting infrastructural development in the state.

The Army Chief said the request had become necessary following the expansion of the Nigerian Army from eight to 12 divisions, a development that had increased the number of officers and soldiers requiring specialised training.

He explained that Bauchi had remained a major training centre for armoured officers, noting that military personnel usually begin their professional careers in the state through the Young Officers’ Course and other specialised programmes.

According to him, armoured officers spend more than 15 years of their military careers attending various courses in Bauchi before moving to other locations as they advance in rank.

He said the proposed facility would provide a dedicated centre for the continuous training of officers and soldiers throughout the year.

Shaibu disclosed that the Corps Commander of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps would formally present the request to the governor, urging him to give it favourable consideration.

“With this expansion, a lot of officers and soldiers have been coming into the Corps, and they will require this training consecutively throughout the year. Once that proposal comes, I crave your indulgence to please consider it,” he said.

The Army Chief appreciated Mohammed for his administration’s support for the Armoured Corps, particularly the establishment of some military units in Alkaleri as part of efforts to expand the Army’s operational capacity.

He also commended the governor’s infrastructural development efforts, describing the transformation of the Government House as remarkable.

“Being an armoured officer myself and having started my career from here in Bauchi, I must acknowledge the massive infrastructural development taking place here. In fact, I did not recognise the Government House when I was coming,” he said.

Shaibu further disclosed that he was in Bauchi to attend the grand finale of Exercise Mugunbugu, conducted in the Alkaleri general area.

He described the exercise as the Nigerian Army’s major end-of-year training activity, designed to consolidate the various military exercises conducted throughout the year.

The Army Chief also attended the maiden edition of the Nigerian Army Armoured Corps reunion and pulling-out ceremony, which attracted more than 100 retired senior officers.

He said the reunion would provide an opportunity for retired officers to reflect on their contributions to the development of the Corps and share experiences that could strengthen the institution.

Shaibu reiterated the appreciation of officers and soldiers of the Nigerian Army to the Bauchi State Government for its continued cooperation and support, expressing optimism that the partnership would further enhance military training and operational effectiveness.

World.title: 2027: Reject corrupt candidates, end imposition, Maho tells parties
World.content:
By Favour Ulebor, Abuja

Ahead of the 2027 general elections, political analyst and lecturer at the International Institute of Journalists, Dr Austin Maho, has urged political parties to reject corrupt candidates, end the imposition of party leaders and introduce strict disciplinary measures to strengthen Nigeria’s democracy.
