Maho made the call on Wednesday in Abuja at the International Stakeholders Engagement Forum on Anti-Corruption, Party Building and Democratic Governance, organised by the Diplomatic Correspondents Association of Nigeria (DICAN).

The forum had as its theme, “Nigeria’s 2027 Poll: Promoting Party Organisation, Discipline and Anti-Corruption Reforms: Lessons from Xi Jinping Thought.”

Presenting a paper at the event, Maho called on political parties to introduce anti-corruption agreements for candidates, establish independent disciplinary committees and maintain credible membership registers to promote transparency and accountability.

He warned that Nigerian political parties had increasingly become platforms for winning elections rather than institutions founded on ideology, discipline and national development.

Maho also faulted the high cost of nomination forms, saying it was shutting out credible Nigerians from elective positions and encouraging money-driven politics.

He said, “In China, the Party is an organization first, an election machine second.

“In Nigeria, our parties are election machines first, and organizations almost never.

“When we sell forms at that price, we are telling thieves to come and buy the ticket, because only thieves can afford it.”

He urged Nigerian political parties to draw lessons from China’s approach to party organisation, discipline and anti-corruption while preserving the country’s multiparty democratic system.

According to him, parties must strengthen their grassroots structures, ensure transparent congresses and sanction members found guilty of corruption, irrespective of their political influence.

Also speaking, the Counsellor at the Chinese Embassy in Nigeria, Dong Hairong, said China remained committed to its anti-corruption campaign, disclosing that 8.1 million cases had been filed since 2012.

She said 7.92 million officials had received disciplinary and administrative penalties, including more than 900 officials at vice-ministerial level and above.

Dong explained that China’s anti-corruption drive was aimed at strengthening public trust, improving governance and ensuring accountability among government officials.

She reaffirmed China’s willingness to share its governance experience with Nigeria and deepen cooperation between both countries.

In his goodwill message, the Minister of State for Foreign Affairs, Ambassador Sola Enikanolaiye, said strong political parties and effective anti-corruption measures were essential to democratic development.

Represented by the Assistant Director, Administration, in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mahmud Aliyu, the minister said democracy should go beyond periodic elections to encompass transparency, accountability and respect for the rule of law.

He urged political parties, civil society organisations and government institutions to strengthen democratic values and promote responsible leadership.

Similarly, the Executive Chairman of the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission, Ola Olukoyede, called for greater public participation in the fight against corruption.

Represented by the commission’s Head of Media and Publicity, Dele Oyewale, Olukoyede described corruption as a major challenge undermining Nigeria’s development, security and democratic institutions.

He disclosed that the commission had secured 10,872 convictions and recovered N1.23 trillion within the 34 months of his leadership.

He said, “The best diplomatic statement that we can make to the rest of the world is our commitment to the fight against corruption.”

Earlier, DICAN Chairman, Idehai Frederick, said the forum was organised to stimulate discussions on strengthening political parties, tackling corruption and improving democratic governance ahead of the 2027 elections.

He said Nigeria could draw lessons from China’s experience in party discipline and institutional development without abandoning its multiparty democratic system.

Frederick urged stakeholders to develop practical recommendations for strengthening democratic institutions and promoting accountability in governance.

World.title: 2027 countdown: Tinubu approves establishment of Kebbi inland dry port
World.content:
…Tells Kebbi voters allow me complete 8 years

..North firmly represented in decision-making — Shettima

By Omeiza Ajayi

ABUJA — President Bola Tinubu has appealed to Kebbi State voters to give him a second term to complete his eight-year tenure, promising that it would be their turn to produce the president thereafter.



“This time, I am before you to seek your support for the second time to complete what I have started. It will be your turn next time,” Tinubu told supporters at the All Progressives Congress, APC, presidential campaign rally at Haliru Abdu Stadium, Birnin Kebbi, yesterday.



The President said he returned to the state to thank the people for supporting him and other APC candidates in the 2023 elections.

“You voted for me, you voted for Kaura Gwandu, you voted for our senators. Now I have come back to say thank you. May God bless you and answer your prayers,” he said.



Seeking assurances of their support in 2027, Tinubu asked the crowd whether they had their Permanent Voter Cards, PVCs, and were ready to vote.



“Are you ready to vote? Do you have your PVC? Raise your hand if you have your PVC. Are you going to come out and vote? Thank you very much. I can go home comfortably and sleep. I know you will come out to vote from top to bottom,” he said.

Tinubu also announced approval of a long-awaited inland dry port for the state.



“I understand your request on the inland dry port. That is a given. Kebbi needs it and it is approved,” he declared.

He said requests by Governor Nasir Idris, including road projects and the reconstruction of a road damaged by flooding, were receiving attention.



“All the requests of the governor are before me here. I have listed them carefully. We are working together,” he added.



North at decision-making table



Vice President Kashim Shettima, in his remarks, said the North was adequately represented in the Tinubu administration, citing key appointments in the security and defence architecture.



He named the Minister of Defence, General Christopher Musa; Minister of State for Defence, Bello Matawalle; National Security Adviser, Nuhu Ribadu; and Chief of Naval Staff, Vice Admiral Idi Abbas.



“The North sits comfortably at the table where decisions are made,” Shettima declared, adding that “a vote for His Excellency President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and for me as your Vice President is a vote for the preservation of the North.”



He recalled Tinubu’s support for the North during the APC presidential primary, saying the President stood by the late former President Muhammadu Buhari’s preferred candidate.



“He stood by the man who told delegates that he would never buy their votes with dollars. He made sure that the favourite of the North, the late General Muhammadu Buhari, became our party’s choice,” he said.



Shettima said the North rewarded Tinubu in 2023 with 60.2 per cent of its votes and expressed confidence that the region would repeat the gesture in the 2027 election.



On security, he said Tinubu had approved an increase of up to 80 per cent in the salaries of armed forces personnel. He also disclosed that the President had assigned him to chair a committee for the procurement of N200 billion worth of fertiliser for distribution to farmers during the dry season.



Listing federal projects in Kebbi, Shettima cited the Sokoto-Badagry highway, with 258 kilometres passing through the state, describing it as the longest stretch in any state. Others include a 3.5-megawatt solar project in Ambursa and the upgrade of the Federal Medical Centre, Birnin Kebbi, to a teaching hospital.



He said the College of Nursing and Midwifery, Ambursa, had been commissioned, while Kebbi State University, Aliero, received N693 million in student loan funding through the Nigerian Education Loan Fund, NELFUND.



Shettima urged residents to vote for Tinubu on January 16 and return Governor Idris for a second term on February 6.

APC leaders rally support

Minister of Budget and Economic Planning and former Kebbi governor, Atiku Bagudu, said the APC was entering the 2027 election with greater unity than in 2023.

“We are a more united Kebbi State here today, and we are facing the 2027 election more united than we did in 2023 under the able leadership of our governor,” he said.

Bagudu credited Tinubu with bringing party leaders together, saying the President encouraged them to work together because the coming political task required “more hands rather than less”.

The Director-General of the APC Presidential Campaign Council, Senator Abdulaziz Yari, urged opposition parties to learn from the large turnout, claiming that no previous administration had invested as much in Kebbi and the North as the Tinubu government.

APC National Chairman, Professor Nentawe Yilwatda, said Tinubu deserved another term to consolidate his development projects across the country. The Speaker of the House of Representatives, Tajudeen Abbas, and Deputy Senate President, Barau Jibrin, also canvassed support for Tinubu and Idris.

Former Governor Adamu Aliero praised Tinubu for approving the deployment of an armoured brigade to strengthen security in the state. Yobe State Governor, Mai Mala Buni, and former Kebbi governor, Usman Saidu Dakingari, also urged support for the President.

Tinubu arrived at about 1.35pm, accompanied by Shettima, Yilwatda, Yari and serving and former governors. Thousands of supporters from the state’s 21 local government areas attended the rally, where northern pro-Tinubu singer, Adamu Dauda Kahutu, popularly known as Rarara, entertained the crowd.

The rally followed an empowerment programme organised at the instance of the First Lady, Senator Oluremi Tinubu, which benefited at least 2,000 women in the state.

World.title: What Makes ADCCE So Important in Today’s World?
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Oluwadunsin Sanya

When you think of having a destination wedding, your dream vacation, or your home away from home, what locations or countries come to mind? Santorini? Bali? Maldives? Paris? Canada? These locations are great but what if you begin to consider African countries: Nigeria, Namibia, Zambia, Kenya, Uganda, and more?

Have you ever been curious about African destination sites so much that you wish to celebrate your milestones there? If you have not, maybe it is time to look within rather than outside. That is where ADCCE, founded by Jackline Nantenza, comes in.

This year, I joined the Board of Directors of Africa Destinations Celebrations Conference and Expo (ADCCE) – a Pan-African platform trying to redefine Africa as the world’s premier destination for milestone celebrations and experiential travel.

This year’s edition took place in Uganda at the Speke Resort, Muyonyo under the theme: Events in The Wild. We brought together global wedding and event planners, destination management companies, hospitality leaders, travel curators, creative entrepreneurs, policymakers, investors, and media to showcase the continent’s most extraordinary celebration destinations and cultural experiences.

The conference and expo had event industry stakeholders from across Africa and beyond discussing how the continent can compete more effectively in the global destination celebrations market.

What makes ADCCE particularly important in today’s world is how it is challenging conventional perceptions of African destinations, and the work it is doing to help the world see African countries and their diverse cultures beyond news headlines.

But it doesn’t start with the world, it starts with us Africans. To explore African destinations is to first take pride in where we exist, make efforts to appreciate its landscapes, explore its depth, and embrace its culture.

Christine Ogbeh of The Wedding Guru, in her keynote speech, said we cannot attract the world to African destinations unless Africans are willing to travel to these destinations, celebrate their milestones there, and are loud about their experiences there. Often, we are prompted to look out but what if we begin to look within?

The Journeys Through Uganda

During my trip to Uganda, we visited the Lake Victoria Serena golf resort and spa. It has the perfect serene environment for someone looking for a home away from home, and one of the prettiest halls I have seen for a night-time event.

If you don’t want to have your event in a hall, you could consider having it in the wild – which is exactly what we did when we visited Entikko Safari Lodge. If you love being around nature and animals. If you are curious about seeing how they exist in their natural habitat, hearing the lions roar, the birds sing, watch how majestically giraffes walk or how overprotective elephants are of their young ones, then a safari trip would heal your inner child.

Or you could have your celebration at the most powerful falls in the world. And, yes, it is in Uganda. Murchison Falls is a waterfall on the Victoria Nile in northwestern Uganda, famous for being one of the world’s most powerful falls.

Can Africa Sustain its Destination Sites?

One of the most important questions raised is infrastructural development when we talk of having destination celebrations. It is not enough to have stunning landscapes that are tourism worthy, what of the infrastructure that makes logistics easier and the experience memorable? Is there a great road network, security? Constant power supply? Can someone from Botswana travel to Kajuru Castle in Kaduna and be assured of their safety and comfort? Can I or other Africans travel to South Africa and be assured of my safety? Is the trip to Zanzibar easy for non-Tanzanians? How easy is the visa application process within African countries?

Poor infrastructure defeats the purpose of destination experiences. So as we sell African destinations, these are some questions that need answers.

Is there a market for African destination events?

The Nigerian wedding industry is regarded as one of the largest and fastest-growing wedding and social event markets in Africa. It also cuts across other industries and vendors – beauty, decoration, catering, hospitality, entertainment, photography, event production, media, and more.

People are willing to travel to Nigeria for weddings, just as much as Nigerians are willing to travel to other countries for their destination weddings and events. The big question is whether these countries will be in Africa. Can African countries become preferred destinations for Africans travelling for weddings, celebrations and lifestyle experiences, rather than having these travellers look towards destinations outside the continent?

There is already an established, commercially active market for African destination events. But there is room for businesses that connect these industries and infrastructure that make it easier for people to discover and travel to events across Africa.

That is what we are trying to achieve through ADCCE.

We not only had conversations about African countries and potential destination sites, but there were first-hand destination experiences in Uganda. And by combining these two, ADCCE 2026 highlighted the possibilities for a more connected African celebrations industry, one that encourages Africans to explore more of the continent and then invites the world to discover Africa destination sites as places to celebrate your milestones.

*Oluwadunsin Sanya is an Editorial and Digital Content Strategist with 8+ years’ experience leading editorial strategy, digital campaign content, storytelling, audience growth, and high-performing content teams. She currently serves as Head of Editorial & Innovation at BellaNaija, one of Africa’s leading digital media platforms. With a career dedicated to telling impactful stories and amplifying the best of Africa, she has been instrumental in driving editorial excellence and innovation at BellaNaija, and leading digital content for some of its most impactful campaigns. She is a 2023 Fellow of the EJCP at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism in New York and a 2024 Fellow of the MTN Media Innovation Program at Pan-Atlantic University in Lagos. She was a speaker at the News in The Digital Age Conference, hosted by FT Strategies in London, and currently sits on the Board of Directors of the Africa Destinations Celebrations Conference and Expo in Uganda. Her work sits at the intersection of storytelling, solutions journalism, digital media content development, strategy, growth, and innovation, contributing to the future of digital media in Nigeria, and beyond.

World.title: Access to Medicine Index: How Nigeria, Uganda, Kenya Face Gaps in Affordability, Availability of Essential Drugs
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Despite progress in pharmaceutical research and access planning, patients in Nigeria, Uganda and Kenya continue to face significant barriers to affordable and reliable medicines, particularly for diabetes, cancer and other critical health conditions. In a virtual interview with Access to Medicine Foundation’s Chief Executive Officer, Jayasree K. Iyer and the foundation’s Director of Research, Claudia Martínez, on the 2026 Access to Medicine Index, the foundation examined the gaps in access, the commitments required from pharmaceutical companies and governments, and the role of local manufacturing, partnerships and measurable patient-focused targets in ensuring that medical innovations reach underserved populations. Chiemelie Ezeobi brings excerpts

With 95% of projected diabetes growth expected in low- and middle-income countries, what concrete commitments will pharmaceutical companies make to ensure that GLP-1 medicines and insulin become affordable and reliably available to patients in Nigeria, beyond simply registering the drugs?

We do not have Nigeria-specific data on the concrete plans pharmaceutical companies have made to ensure newer treatments are available.

However, a key finding from the Index highlights that access plans for diabetes treatments in the pipeline tend to focus on more commercially attractive emerging markets, with limited attention to low-income countries such as Nigeria.

For GLP-1s that are already on the market, some companies are adopting second brand strategies to launch more affordable versions of their products in certain LMICs, however we did not identify any such strategies for Nigeria.

What measurable targets will pharmaceutical companies set to demonstrate that their access-to-medicine commitments are translating into improved patient outcomes in these countries, and how will they be held accountable for meeting those targets?

The Index has consistently highlighted the importance of pharmaceutical companies setting clear, measurable and time-bound goals for patient reach, and systematically measuring and reporting progress against these goals.

Pharmaceutical companies should establish clear, measurable and time-bound patient reach targets to ensure their access commitments translate into tangible benefits for patients. These targets should be informed by factors such as disease burden, treatment eligibility, and the specific needs of each market. Companies should also systematically measure and report patient reach across their products, countries and target populations. Reporting should be sufficiently disaggregated to show which products, countries and populations are benefiting, providing greater transparency on where progress is being made and where gaps remain.

In terms of accountability, several companies have linked executive compensation to patient reach or other access-related metrics, making progress on access part of how leadership performance is assessed. There are also examples of companies, such as Novartis and Sanofi, linking patient reach commitments to sustainability-linked bonds. These arrangements create an additional incentive for companies to deliver on their targets.

The 2026 Access to Medicine Index shows that access plans now cover 69 per cent of late-stage pharmaceutical pipeline candidates, more than triple the figure recorded in 2018. However, access to essential medicines remains limited in many low- and middle-income countries. What are the major obstacles preventing pharmaceutical companies from translating these access plans into actual availability and affordability of medicines, particularly in countries like Nigeria?

While more companies are planning for access during drug development, having an access plan does not necessarily mean a medicine will become available or affordable. The quality of these plans varies, and some focus primarily on regulatory registration without addressing affordability or sustainable supply. Key barriers include limited healthcare financing, fragmented regulatory and procurement systems, and gaps in health infrastructure. Lower purchasing power and uncertain demand can also make these markets less commercially attractive for pharmaceutical companies.

In Nigeria, economic conditions have affected how pharmaceutical companies supply medicines. In 2023, GSK and Sanofi, both assessed in the Index, announced they would end direct commercial operations there and move to third-party distribution. GSK cited foreign exchange shortages and high operating costs as barriers to supplying medicines, while Sanofi also highlighted currency instability and foreign exchange challenges.

The report highlights persistent gaps in access to insulin despite growing investments in diabetes research, particularly in newer GLP-1 treatments. What specific measures should pharmaceutical companies and governments take to ensure that essential medicines, especially insulin, remain affordable and accessible to patients in low- and middle-income countries?

As newer insulins and GLP-1 therapies emerge, companies and governments must ensure continued access to established essential treatments, particularly human insulin. Key priorities include:

Maintaining affordable and reliable insulin supplies: Companies should protect access to human insulin while expanding access to analogue insulins where they offer additional clinical benefits.

Setting measurable commitments: Companies should establish transparent targets and indicators for maintaining insulin supply and improving affordability across LMICs.

Prioritising underserved populations: Greater attention is needed for LICs, children and young people with type 1 diabetes (T1D), and populations facing unreliable or unaffordable insulin supplies.

Strengthening local manufacturing: Companies and governments should leverage manufacturing partnerships to improve regional production, supply security and affordability.

Improving monitoring and accountability: Governments should track insulin availability, affordability and access across populations and regions to ensure progress.

With cancer products accounting for about half of pharmaceutical clinical candidates and GLP-1 drugs dominating diabetes research, how can pharmaceutical companies ensure that medical innovations reach patients in low- and middle-income countries rather than remaining largely accessible to populations in wealthier markets?

Companies should integrate comprehensive access planning during R&D (from phase II onwards), anticipating and proactively addressing the main barriers to access of innovative products in LMICs, including availability, affordability and sustainable supply.

While innovation in oncology has delivered significant public health advancements, innovative therapies can present significant access challenges in low-resource settings. For example, their high prices can pose affordability challenges without appropriate equitable pricing considerations that take into account countries’ and patients’ ability to pay.

Furthermore, different anticancer targeted therapies require diagnostic testing to identify whether a specific patient population is eligible to benefit from the treatment. Yet, few companies are considering diagnostic access as part of their access planning.

Similarly, expanding access to GLP-1 therapies will require companies to develop robust regulatory strategies that include LMICs early in their registration plans, establish appropriate affordability mechanisms, and ensure a reliable and sustainable supply, particularly in the context of high demand in high-income markets.

What does the 2026 Index show has improved for Ugandan patients since the previous assessment?

The 2026 Access to Medicine Index highlights pharmaceuticals companies’ efforts to address barriers to medicine access across underserved markets, including Uganda. While the Index does not present findings on a country-by-country basis, several examples throughout the report illustrate company initiatives and activities taking place in Uganda.

Additional details are also shared with the Index under a non-disclosure agreement. This is why the Index places greater emphasis on transparency, encouraging companies to regularly publish patient reach data and disaggregate these figures to provide a clearer picture of who is benefiting from their programmes.

Examples

Registration, Uganda has highest number of filings (6) for newer* products among the 26 low-income countries assessed. Uganda also had the highest number of filings for newer* products of all LICs in the 2024 Index, highlighting continued efforts to register products in the country. Whilst registration alone does not guarantee patient access, it is an important first step.

*Products that received their first marketing authorisation within the last 5 years.

Diabetes: Novo Nordisk’s Changing Diabetes® in Children programme, In Uganda, the programme expanded from reaching around 200 children and young people with type 1 diabetes in 2009 to approximately 4,000 in 2025. However, ensuring continuity of care as young people transition out of these programmes remains an important challenge.

Oncology: Bristol Myers Squibb’s collaboration with the Uganda Cancer Institute has supported publicly funded procurement of nivolumab, demonstrating efforts to expand access to innovative cancer treatments.

Your report highlights publicly funded access to nivolumab at the Uganda Cancer Institute. How many patients have benefited, who qualifies, and what costs do patients still face?

While detailed data on pricing, procurement and number of patients reached, remains under an NDA, the 2026 Index highlights efforts and progress made by Bristol Myers Squibb in expanding access to immuno-oncology treatments, primarily nivolumab (Opdivo) through its Innovative Medicines Access Programme (IMAP), part of its broader ASPIRE strategy. Through IMAP, BMS is working to expand access to nivolumab and other immuno-oncology treatments to more African countries, in both public and private oncology settings.

Nivolumab has been supplied to the Uganda Cancer Institute (UCI) through publicly funded procurement mechanism, a change from 2024 when the company was still exploring potential cancer institutes to collaborate with. This is positive progress as immuno-oncology medicines like nivolumab can be expensive and would be financially inaccessible to many patients in Uganda. UCI is the main national cancer referral and treatment center; the agreement therefore opens a channel for patients who previously could not afford it to receive it through the public system. Further details that determine access to the product such as patient’s eligibility criteria, enrollment and funded indications are not publicly available at this stage.

The report identifies Roche cancer trials involving Uganda. What commitments ensure that participants can continue receiving treatment after trials end and that successful medicines become affordable to other Ugandan patients?

There are several pathways to facilitate access to medicines after clinical trials are conducted, including post-trial access, registration preparation, and affordability considerations. Roche, for example, has a post-trial access policy, and a public commitment to register where clinical trials are conducted. Most of the companies analysed in the Index have similar commitments.

The Index assesses whether companies are taking these components into consideration when developing access plans. However, often the number of countries in scope of these access plans are limited: approximately 2% of oncology projects assessed include Uganda, for example. Addressing the referred components in a country-specific manner from the outset will be essential to guarantee access to innovative products.

Pathways for facilitating access

Post-trial access: companies can commit to providing access to patients benefiting from the trial drug after the trial is concluded, given specific criteria are met. Named patient or compassionate use programmes can also provide additional pathways for patients to access medicines.

Registration preparation: companies can start preparing for regulatory registration while these are still ongoing. Although this ensures availability when the product is approved, more measures are required to guarantee access.

Affordability: companies can start early to consider countries’ ability to pay and developing equitable pricing plans.

Only 19% of the cancer products assessed had access strategies covering low-income countries. What would persuade more companies to make these treatments available and affordable in countries such as Uganda?

The opportunity to create sustainable business would persuade more pharmaceutical companies to make treatments available in LICs including Uganda.

Three things are particularly important: predictable demand, effective pooled procurement mechanisms and a supportive regulatory environment. Aggregating demand across countries can create economies of scale, reduce transaction costs and give companies greater incentives to offer more affordable prices. Longer-term purchasing commitments and streamlined regulatory processes can further reduce the risks and costs of entering these markets.

However, product availability and affordability alone are not enough. Many LICs face wider health system barriers, including gaps in diagnostics, treatment infrastructure and healthcare financing. Addressing these requires collaboration between pharmaceutical companies, governments and local organisations.

This year’s Index highlights progress by AstraZeneca, BMS and Roche in expanding access to oncology products in underserved settings, including Uganda. Their approaches demonstrate the importance of addressing barriers across the patient pathway, not just access to medicines, and the value of partnerships in building more sustainable access.

The challenge is to create conditions where commercial sustainability and affordable access go hand in hand, ensuring that companies can reach viable markets while more patients benefit from the medicines they need.

For a Ugandan family paying for diabetes care out of pocket, what are manufacturers doing to reduce the total cost of insulin, injection supplies and blood-sugar monitoring?

There are multiple mechanisms in which the three diabetes-focused companies (Novo Nordisk, Eli Lilly and Sanofi are engaging in initiatives to reduce the price paid by governments and wholesalers in Uganda.

Examples of existing initiatives:

Novo Nordisk’s Access to Insulin Commitment is an inter-country equitable pricing strategy that targets the public sector in LMICs, under which the ceiling price per human insulin vial is set at 3 USD. Additionally, through its Changing Diabetes® in Children programme, the company provides insulin, syringes and glucometer test strips free of charge to young patients across multiple lower-middle-income countries and LICs.

Eli Lilly, utilises technology transfer and supplies its active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) for insulin at a significantly reduced price to EVA Pharma. Lilly has provided a pro-bono technology transfer to enable EVA Pharma to formulate and fill and finish insulin vials and cartridges. This collaboration is part of the Lilly 30×30 initiative. Lilly’s Life for a Child program supports children and youth with diabetes in resource-limited settings by providing insulin, delivery devices, monitoring supplies, medical care, diabetes education, complications screening and management, and advocacy.

Sanofi, considers partnerships through its Global Health Unit (GHU). For example, in partnership with mPharma it addresses access pricing and bundled care. Through mPharmas’ Mutti+ platform, diabetes patients obtained medicines at access prices, including selected Sanofi products, alongside free blood glucose testing, consultations and dietary coaching. The program ran from December 2022 to December 2025 that benefitted 387 diabetic patients.

At the same time, some companies are slimming down their insulin portfolios and scaling back production of older products and formulations. Examples of implemented approaches include

Your report warns that some manufacturers are reducing production of older insulin products. Could this affect supplies to Uganda, and what commitments are companies making to prevent treatment interruptions or forced switches to more expensive products?

There is a potential risk to insulin supplies in Uganda. The World Health Organization has warned that manufacturers are phasing out certain older insulin products and formulations, raising concerns about access to affordable treatment in low- and middle-income countries. While Novo Nordisk has committed to maintaining low-cost human insulin supplies, including through a USD 3 per vial ceiling price, this does not cover all discontinued products or guarantee uninterrupted supplies. It is essential that companies work with governments to ensure affordable alternatives are available before products are withdrawn, so patients are not left without treatment.

What support is available to Ugandan children with type 1 diabetes, and how can access to insulin be maintained when they become too old for programmes supporting children?

In Uganda, children and young people with type 1 diabetes can access support through programmes such as Novo Nordisk’s Changing Diabetes in Children and Life for a Child, supported by Lilly, which provide insulin and essential supplies. Our 2025 report Access to diabetes care for children and young people, highlights how the government provides one free vial of insulin per person per month, but patients needing more must pay for additional supplies. It also finds that these programmes only reach a fraction of those in need, and ensuring continuity of care when young people age out remains a significant challenge. Life for Child (supported by Lily) extended its age limit from 26 to 30, including in Uganda, to help maintain access for longer. However, donations are not a sustainable and long-term solution. As outlined in the 2026 Access to Medicine Index, pharmaceutical companies should identify and prioritise insulin access for underserved populations including children and young people with type 1 diabetes, this includes working with partners such as governments to strengthen national health systems and ensure insulin and essential supplies remain affordable and accessible throughout patients’ lives.

What concrete plans do manufacturers have to make newer diabetes medicines, including GLP-1 treatments, affordable in Uganda, beyond simply registering them for sale?

We do not have Uganda-specific data on the concrete plans pharmaceutical companies have made to ensure newer treatments are available.

However, a key finding from the Index highlights that access plans for diabetes treatments in the pipeline tend to focus on more commercially attractive emerging markets, with limited attention to low-income countries such as Uganda.

For GLP-1s that are already on the market, some companies are adopting second brand strategies to launch more affordable versions of their products in certain LMICs, however we did not identify any such strategies for Uganda.

Will the insulin manufacturing partnerships in Egypt and South Africa supply Uganda, and is there evidence that patients will benefit from lower prices or more reliable availability?

The insulin manufacturing partnership in Egypt does report Uganda as one of the targeted beneficiary countries of the initiative, although clear timelines and supply goals are not reported on a country-level. As for the partnership in South Africa, Uganda is currently not mentioned as a supplied country, although the collaboration is reported to supply additional countries after the initial phase.

It is early to say how these two partnerships will directly impact patients. Over time, technology transfers can potentially create conditions for lower insulin prices and improved access. Regional manufacturing can translate into tangible benefits for patients by creating a stronger regional market capable of producing quality medicines competitively, with the potential to improve affordability and availability and ensure supply during global supply chain disruptions. These partnerships have the potential to improve availability and affordability for patients; however, patient-level price and affordability impact data following such initiatives may take time to actualise. Companies should collect and share this data to demonstrate the impact of these partnerships.

How do you assess whether these programmes reach low-income patients and people outside Kampala, and what can patients do to find out whether they qualify for support?

Local manufacturing initiatives and other partnerships can help support products reach low-income patients by increasing product affordability. Partnerships with local manufacturers have the potential to improve affordability by reducing supply-chain and production costs, strengthening local capacity and supply security, and enabling higher-volume, more predictable production tailored to local and regional demand.

Two examples of supply chain capacity building with the aim of improving last-mile delivery and supply to hard-to-reach areas include initiatives from Takeda and Novo Nordisk. Takeda partners with VillageReach in five countries, including Uganda, to strengthen transport systems of products and diagnosis patient samples. Through Changing Diabetes, Novo Nordisk is strengthening cold chain supply mechanisms in Uganda for insulin so that these products can better reach those in hard-to-reach areas. This initiative also involves the distribution of free human insulin for children and youth.

Your report highlights promising sickle cell treatments. Is Uganda included in their access plans, and how can companies support affordable access to established treatment while newer medicines are being developed?

Yes, in the 2026 Index, Uganda is explicitly included in access plans for two the late-stage sickle cell disease (SCD) candidates assessed. Six companies are currently developing eight projects for SCD. Of these, six are in late-stage development (Phase II onwards), with evidence of access planning for five of the six (83%). These plans typically address multiple access components, including registration plans in low-and middle-income countries, equitable pricing and supply and demand planning. It is important that innovation includes children, especially as new gene therapies remain prohibitively expensive in low-resource settings. Yet only half of candidate drugs for sickle cell disease in the 2026 Index are being tested in children under 12 years of age.

Ensuring continued and equitable access to established treatments remains essential. For example, Novartis’s sub-Saharan Africa business unit continues with its sickle cell disease (SCD) programme in Uganda in collaboration with the Ministry of Health and other key stakeholders.

Mental health has some of the weakest access planning in the Index. What would it take to ensure that Ugandans with conditions such as depression, bipolar disorder and schizophrenia can obtain affordable treatment consistently?

Recognising that access to mental healthcare requires a holistic approach considering many components including disease awareness, workforce capacity, timely diagnosis and ultimately the availability and affordability of pharmacological treatment, the Index highlights significant gaps in mental health innovation pipelines and access planning.

Access planning for projects in the pipeline covers only 5/13 (38%) of late-stage projects, focusing mainly on registration and including on average one country in scope. None of the access plans includes Uganda.

Future access plans will need to be implemented early and move beyond registration to address affordability for lower-income groups and consider partnerships that can support appropriate uptake and use.

Which emerging malaria treatments and HIV-prevention options highlighted in the report could be most relevant to Uganda, and what needs to happen before patients can realistically access them?

The 2026 Key Finding for access planning identifies two emerging treatments for HIV prevention and malaria that are relevant to Uganda.

Ganaplacide/lumefantrine (Novartis/Medicines for Malaria Venture (MMV)), is an antimalarial in Phase III trials that could offer an important alternative to existing treatments as resistance to current antimalarial medicines becomes an increasing concern.

For HIV prevention, MSD’s alimatravir could offer a promising option as a potential first long-acting oral PrEP option, which could simplify administration (compared with injectable options that are currently available), while supporting adherence.

As highlighted in the Index, both developments are comprehensively targeting access barriers, the former through a partnership with MMV and the latter through a non-exclusive voluntary licensing agreement (NEVL) with generic manufacturers, one of which is based in Uganda (Qcil). However, the NEVL is only the first step, and access ultimately depends on successful approval registration and affordable supply in Uganda. Pharmaceutical companies have a responsibility to ensure their products are registered, affordable, and reliably supplied. However, more broadly speaking, effective distribution networks, access to diagnostics and a well-functioning health system are also needed to overcome barriers on the ground. Therefore, working with partners including governments is crucial to reach patients, particularly those in underserved communities.

What specific commitments on prices, supply, patient access and measurable improvements should we expect companies to demonstrate within a year?

While progress within a year may be difficult to assess, the Index looks for the evidence of measurable impact on people living in LMICS. Companies should go beyond reporting on commitments and initiatives to provide evidence of their impact, including patient reach, improved affordability and availability, and sustained access over time. Build on existing progress in tracking the outcomes by reporting how many patients are being reached, with which products and in which countries, enables a more transparent assessment of whether companies are reaching their intended access goals and targets.

Additionally, the Foundation looks for evidence of expanding access in low-income countries (LICs): At current, only 36% of assessed products have a country-specific access strategy in LICs, compared with 80% in lower-middle-income countries (LMICs) and 85% in upper-middle-income countries (UMICs).

Based on our analysis, the Index identifies tailored opportunities for each company that set guidance and expectations for increased access over the coming 2 years. They highlight current gaps and build on existing work and initiatives undertaken by the companies and/or their commercial presence. 9 out of the 20 companies (in the 2026 Index) have opportunities that focus on Africa/SSA, indicating that Africa, and especially Sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), continue to have long standing gaps. The potential to close the gaps lies in these opportunities, from broader registration to local manufacturing.

Novartis has maintained its top position in the 2026 Index, with GSK ranking second. Beyond these rankings, how can we measure whether pharmaceutical companies are genuinely improving access to medicines for patients in African countries such as Kenya?

The ranking and company report cards provide a comprehensive overview of progress in improving access to medicine, assessing company (and industry) efforts across the spectrum, from governance and research and development (R&D) to product delivery. To gain a deeper understanding of how companies are translating these efforts into improved access at the country level, the Index collects and evaluates company-reported data against a range of indicators.

In R&D, Kenya, alongside South Africa, stands out for its inclusion in clinical trials, helping to promote more equitable access to innovative medicines and support the development of locally informed clinical guidelines. This is particularly evident in Roche’s work, recognised as a Best Practice for expanding the geographic reach of its oncology clinical trials. In addition, 5 companies provide Kenyans access to products through inclusive business models, designed to support the sustainable availability of selected company products for populations in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) who are unserved by existing business models. These approaches aim to address access barriers through partnerships, often combining affordability strategies, local manufacturing and tailored procurement pathways. For example, In June 2025, the Kenyan Ministry of Health and Pfizer launched the Accord in Kenya, enabling the Kenya Medical Supplies Agency (KEMSA), the medical logistics provider for the ministry’s public health facilities and programmes, to procure Pfizer’s full portfolio of medicines and vaccines on a not-for-profit basis.

The Index shows that pharmaceutical companies are making progress in developing cancer medicines, but access remains uneven, particularly in lower-income countries. What practical measures can be taken to ensure that cancer patients in Kenya benefit from these innovations, especially given the high costs of diagnosis and treatment?

Firstly, companies can embed high burden countries early in oncology R&D by co-designing access plans with LMIC research partners and clinical trial centres. Secondly, expand the depth and geographic scope of access planning and strategies. Plans should look beyond registration and post-trial access to address barriers across the product pathway – including inclusive clinical trials, diagnostics and biomarker testing, affordability, reimbursement and reliable supply. Companies should also make greater use of mechanisms that can enable affordable access at scale, including voluntary licensing, which remains underused for relevant products.

Finally, build towards sustainable and equitable delivery at scale. This can be done by forming partnerships with national and local stakeholders to address needs across cancer care, including screening and diagnosis, affordability and treatment. Start by identifying existing cancer programmes and treatment centres in LMICs, and partner with them to strengthen and build on these initiatives, for example, through affordability measures targeted at underserved patients, and training of healthcare workers. Successful approaches can then be scaled more broadly.

The report highlights growing investment in GLP-1 medicines for diabetes, yet access to affordable treatment remains a challenge. At the same time, GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Mounjaro are becoming increasingly popular for weight loss, including here in Kenya. What are pharmaceutical companies doing to address this growing demand while ensuring that patients who need these medicines for diabetes treatment can still access them affordably and consistently?

While pharmaceutical companies cannot directly control which patients are prescribed GLP-1 medicines, they do have a responsibility to ensure that growing demand does not come at the expense of equitable access. Our 2026 Index shows that companies are investing heavily in GLP-1 medicines, but more needs to be done to ensure they are affordable and accessible. Only two of the 10 access plans assessed for late-stage diabetes treatments included equitable pricing measures, and none covered low-income countries. While some companies are adopting strategies to improve affordability, such as introducing lower-priced second brands, access to these medicines remains limited in many low- and middle-income countries. As demand grows for both diabetes and obesity treatment, companies need to expand sustainable supply and introduce affordable pricing strategies to ensure these medicines reach patients who need them, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.

The report highlights the potential of local pharmaceutical manufacturing and partnerships to improve access to essential medicines, particularly insulin. What opportunities exist for Kenya and the wider East African region to strengthen local pharmaceutical manufacturing? What role should global pharmaceutical companies play, and what concrete steps should the Kenyan government, particularly the Ministry of Health, take to support local production and improve the affordability and availability of essential medicines?

Kenya has an ongoing pharmaceutical manufacturing partnership between Universal Corporate Limited and Merck KGaA for the manufacture of pediatric praziquantel for schistosomiasis. This is a unique partnership between one of the large pharmaceutical companies and East Africa, especially for the manufacture of insulin. To meaningfully build lasting capacity, global pharmaceutical companies can build partnerships with local manufacturers with the aim of manufacturing priority products and with the goal of sustained independence for the local partner.

The Kenyan government plays a key role in identifying products that are viable for local production, and in creating an enabling environment for it. The Kenya Health Products and Technologies Local Manufacturing Strategy 2026-2030 shows strong commitment to support local manufacturing over the next years. The Ministry should ensure that this strategy translates into implementation through commitment and policies that support procurement from local manufacturers and continue to support the country in reaching WHO Maturity Level 3 status. Government investments and policies should also help establish the necessary workforce and infrastructure needed to take up and sustain local production. Pharmaceutical companies can also weigh in here, for example by supporting Universities in providing courses in pharma manufacturing.

World.title: How Tantita is Investing in Host Communities’ Development Beyond Oil Assets Protection
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

For Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited (TSSNL), protecting Nigeria’s oil and gas infrastructure goes beyond securing pipelines and curbing crude oil theft. It also involves improving the welfare of host communities through investments in education, infrastructure, livelihoods and social amenities. This commitment was recently demonstrated through a 2026 Back-To-School CSR programme, undertaken in collaboration with other stakeholders, which provided educational materials to more than 2,653 pupils and students across 11 communities in Imo and Rivers States. Bukola Lasisi reports

For Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, the protection of Nigeria’s oil and gas infrastructure should include investments in the welfare and development of host communities.

That explains why the company in collaboration with other stakeholders, recently carried out an extensive 2026 Back-To-School CSR programme across Imo and Rivers States. The educational support programme was designed to support pupils and students with basic educational materials, promote learning, and strengthen the relationship between the company and its host communities.

For many right thinking organisations, their operations and the communities in which they conduct their business should always collaborate to drive growth and development.

Hence, they see Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) as core to their business existence because a company is only as successful as the communities where it operates.

For Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited (TSSNL), providing good things of life to the host communities remains a priority. Its efforts in this direction was recently demonstrated with the provision of soal ammenities to host communities.

As a responsible organisation, the company believes that the government has a major role to play in making life better for the populace. It further thinks private organisations and business enterprises can partner with government in solving societal problems, especially as it concerns the environments where they operate.

Therefore TSSNL has CSR initiatives that are tailored towards meeting these needs of the society.

Taking CSR Initiatives to Host Communities

Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited and Maton Engineering joined Target Energy Limited, one of the companies sub contractor within the central Corridor to carry out an extensive 2026 Back-To-School CSR programme across Imo and Rivers States.

The educational support programme was designed to support pupils and students with basic educational materials, promote learning, and strengthen the relationship between the company and its host communities.

The programme was held recently in 11 communities cutting across Oguta, Ohaji/Egbema, and Ogba/Egbema/Ndoni Local Government Areas of Imo and Rivers States.

Items including school bags, exercise books, pens, pencils, and erasers where distributed to over 2,653 students in community primary and secondary schools. In addition, Target Energy is expanding the impact with over 300 classroom desks being distributed to schools across its ten (10) host communities.

Tantita’s Community Relations Department was represented at the programme to witness its implementation, engage with the school authorities, and assess the impact of the intervention. Distributions were conducted through classroom visits and school assemblies, allowing direct interaction with pupils, students, teachers, and school administrators.

This intervention follows Tantita’s CSR policy and mandate for all subcontractors to contribute to sustainable community development in the region, adding to Tantita’s already robust educational support projects, including new constructions and renovations of classroom blocks, fully equipped computer centers, and donation of modern ICT gadgets and solar power systems to support students, schools, and promote education as a catalyst for development across the Niger Delta.

How it started

President Bola Ahmed Tinubu had appointed Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited (TSSNL) led by High Chief, Dr. Government Oweizide Ekpemupolo, alias Tompolo, to protect Nigeria’s oil assets in the Niger Delta region.

The apointment was to enable TSSNL, through its security operations, support the national economy in getting the full benefits of oil resources.

The TSSNL works in collaboration with other security outfits to achive its goals of securing oil assets and ensuring peace and stability in the Niger Delta region.

Tantita’s operations had ensured the security of oil pipelines, ensuring the uninterrupted flow of petroleum resources, and ensuring that Nigeria migrated from a position of constant loss management to stability, planning, growth and development.

The TSSNL operations have transformed the oil and gas landscape and allowed Nigeria to expand oil production quota and significantly cut rampant oil theft.

Its track record in mitigating risks associated with oil pipelines has positioned it as a reliable partner in preserving Nigeria’s economic backbone.

Beyond these milestones, the company has in partnership with Grosvenor Global Services Limited, commissioned solar-powered boreholes and street lights in several communities in Delta State.

The commissioned projects include solar street lights in Ajomata, Ikweghwu and Ibada-Amukpe communities, as well as solar-powered boreholes in Ibada-Elume, Oyohen, Amukpe and Adagrassa communities.

Speaking during the commissioning, the Community Relations Manager of Tantita, Pastor Seimode Akposafagha Benedict, said the projects were part of efforts to improve living conditions in communities connected to the company’s operations.

Representing Tantita’s Managing Director, High Chief Engr. Kestin Ebimorbowei Pondi, Seimode said the facilities were provided by Grosvenor Global Services Limited, one of Tantita’s subcontractors, under its Corporate Social Responsibility programme.

He said the protection of Nigeria’s oil and gas infrastructure should include investments in the welfare and development of host communities.

According to him, Tantita encourages its partners and subcontractors to support projects that address the needs of residents and promote peaceful coexistence.

“As we commission these projects today, let us continue to strengthen the bond of trust, cooperation and mutual respect that has made our collective successes possible,” he said.

Seimode urged the beneficiary communities to protect and maintain the facilities to ensure their sustainability.

Chairman of Ajomata Community in Sapele Local Government Area, Mr. Cyril Omor-Oba, said the street lights would improve security and movement at night.

He appealed for additional lights to cover other parts of the community and assured the companies that residents would safeguard the facilities.

Community representatives in Ibada-Amukpe and Ikweghwu also said the new street lights had improved visibility along major roads and public areas.

The Chairman of Ibada-Elume Community, Mr. Friday Omerhiowan, described the solar-powered borehole as a timely intervention that would improve access to clean water for residents.

The projects are expected to support safer movement, improve access to potable water and encourage social and economic activities in the beneficiary communities.

For the company, security further means solar classrooms, rehabilitated roads, rice farms, police stations, and scholarships—thanks to Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited (TSSNL), founded by High Chief Government Oweizide Ekpemupolo (Tompolo).

The company manages private pipeline surveillance and asset protection for critical oil infrastructure in the Niger Delta.

Its operations target crude oil theft, illegal bunkering, and pipeline vandalism to help boost national production.

However, beyond pipeline surveillance, Tantita has in recent years emerged as a leading corporate citizen, focusing on livelihoods, infrastructure, education, security, and climate initiatives. Its approach is clear: “you cannot police poverty out of a community; you must actively replace it.”

Some of its key projects include the Sustainable Rice Farming Programme in Torugbene, created with SDN and Ecosus Pro Nigeria, which has offered legal employment for youths previously involved in oil bunkering.

Tantita invested N2.53 billion over three years in irrigation, training, and cooperative management, aiming for 100,000 hectares under cultivation.

Infrastructure initiatives include the Bendel Estate road rehabilitation and a new police headquarters in Ugborikoko, improving safety and mobility.

Education interventions span the Delta State College of Nursing Sciences, with solar panels, computers, and buses, and FUPRE, where scholarships and reading clubs boost academic performance.

Tantita also champions carbon capture projects, turning mangroves into carbon sinks, potentially generating over $300 million annually for local communities.

Praised by officials, civil society, and youth groups, Tantita’s initiatives provide tangible development and security, showing that in the Niger Delta, safety and progress go hand in hand, offering communities real, grounded hope.

Operational efficiency with tech

Tantita, recently contracted a hi- tech security company, Textron Systems, to deliver three uncrewed aircraft that would enhance the company’s capacity to carry out its surveillance operations on Nigeria’ s oil

Under the contract agreement, which was signed and sealed late last year, mandates Textron Systems, USA, to deliver three Aerosonde Mk. 4.7 vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) uncrewed aircraft systems (UAS) to the surveillance company.

The systems will be delivered in a fully ITAR-Free configuration designed for ease of export to international customers. These aircraft will significantly enhance security operations for the protection of Nigeria’s vital oil and gas infrastructure.

The sale also includes options for training and additional aircraft to support planned capability expansion, building on a previous Foreign Military Sale (FMS) contract to the country.

What stakeholders are saying

Chairman of the House Committee on Host Communities, Dekor Dumnamene Robinson had said the contributions of Tantita and its leadership to national security deserve appreciation.

Also, in one of the strongest endorsements yet of the firm’s operations, lawmakers under the Joint Committee of the House of Representatives on Host Communities and Public Petitions and other stakeholders also commended Tantita for what they described as effective and patriotic service in safeguarding Nigeria’s critical oil infrastructure.

They specifically cited the recovery of crude oil production, reduction in pipeline vandalism and restoration of relative peace in oil-producing communities as major achievements recorded under the leadership of High Chief Government Ekpemupolo, popularly known as Government Ekpemupolo.

“Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited, in partnership with NNPCL, has rendered demonstrably effective service in the protection of crude oil pipelines and the recovery of national crude oil production,” they stated.

The Joint Committee subsequently passed a unanimous vote of confidence on the company and called on the Federal Government and NNPCL to approve a long-term renewal of the surveillance contract to consolidate gains already achieved in the fight against crude oil theft and illegal bunkering.

“Tompolo and his team have served this country at great personal risk. They have kept the economic lifeline of the nation running and restored peace to communities that had not experienced peace in decades,” he said.

The National Chairman of Host Communities of Nigeria Producing Oil and Gas (HOSTCOM), His Highness Benjamin Style Tamaranebi JP

had further commended President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for the confidence he has reposed in Tantita as a critical part of the security apparatus for protecting oil assets in the Niger Delta.

“Let us be clear: Destroying our oil assets is economic suicide. It’s a direct attack on the very lifeline of our communities. Our host communities have endured environmental degradation, economic hardship, and neglect for decades. The passage of the Petroleum Industry Act (PIA) was a turning point, ensuring that our communities finally receive direct benefits from the resources extracted from our land,” he said.

He said that Tantita Security Services and other security outfits are crucial in safeguarding Nigeria’s oil assets. Their presence has helped to curb oil theft, improve production levels, and stabilise our national economy.

He said: “HOSTCOM believes that the unique understanding of the Niger Delta terrain by Tantita and its personnel is vital for effective onslaught against oil theft, and it’s imperative that our security agencies and other critical stakeholders in our region recognise the selfless contributions of Tantita and its main promoter, our own indefatigable Niger Delta crusader for better life for our people and champion of equitable and fair distribution of the nation’s resources, High Chief, Dr. Government Oweizide Ekpemupolo, alias Tompolo, the Ibe-Ebidouwei of Ijaw Nation and support them”.

A Lagos-based social analyst, Jamiu Idris, said to appreciate the current stability in the Niger Delta region, one must recall the state of near-collapse that defined Nigeria’s oil industry just a few years ago.

“Before the implementation of the Tantita Security Services Nigeria Limited (TSSNL) framework in late 2022, the nation faced an existential threat. Oil production had cratered to a historic low of 1.015 million barrels per day (bpd) in September 2022-a staggering decline that jeopardised the federal budget, weakened the naira, and pushed the economy toward the brink of insolvency,” he stated.

World.title: Beyond the Spectacle: The Technology Shaping Nigeria’s Live Experiences
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Oladapo Adeniyi

Nigeria’s entertainment and events industry has undergone a remarkable transformation over the past two decades. From conventional sound systems and basic stage lighting to sophisticated LED displays, immersive visual productions and integrated event technology, the industry has evolved into an increasingly important part of the country’s creative economy.

Behind the spectacular concerts, corporate events, cultural celebrations and major productions lies an ecosystem of technical professionals whose expertise brings creative visions to life. While audiences often remember the performers, speakers and memorable moments, the technical infrastructure that makes these experiences possible is rarely given the same attention.

As expectations for live experiences continue to rise, the role of event technology companies has become increasingly significant. Success is no longer measured simply by the equipment deployed, but by the creativity, technical precision and seamless integration required to deliver exceptional experiences.

For companies operating within this space, the evolution has required continuous investment in technology, infrastructure and specialised expertise. Mobile Screens and Sound Limited (MSS), which recently marked its 20th anniversary under the theme The Art of Experience, offers a perspective on how the sector has developed and the changing demands placed on businesses working behind the scenes.

One of the most visible aspects of this transformation has been the advancement of display technology. Twenty years ago, projectors were among the preferred options for displaying visuals at events, while LED screens were relatively unfamiliar and expensive. Their adoption required event technology providers to demonstrate their value to a market that was accustomed to more conventional solutions.

Today, large-format LED displays have become a familiar feature of concerts, conferences, exhibitions and brand activations. Their flexibility, brightness and ability to accommodate different configurations have expanded the possibilities available to event organisers, allowing visual elements to become an integral part of production design. What was once considered a specialised addition is now an important component of many large-scale events.

Sound and lighting technology have undergone similar developments. Modern productions increasingly rely on sophisticated sound reinforcement systems, coordinated lighting designs and advanced control systems to create environments that respond to the scale and nature of each event. These technologies work together to influence how audiences see, hear and experience a production, making technical integration an essential part of event planning.

However, access to advanced equipment does not automatically translate into successful production. Behind every functioning display, coordinated lighting arrangement and balanced sound system are professionals responsible for installation, operation, monitoring and troubleshooting. Sound engineers, lighting designers, LED screen technicians, camera operators, rigging specialists and production managers all contribute to the delivery of a seamless experience.

This has also changed the expectations placed on event technology providers. Rather than sourcing individual equipment for different aspects of a production, organisers increasingly require integrated solutions that bring together multiple technical disciplines. The ability to coordinate sound, lighting, staging, visual technology and power infrastructure can significantly influence production efficiency, consistency and quality.

This shift is reflected in the development of businesses such as MSS, whose operations have expanded from specialised LED screen provision into a broader range of event technology solutions, including sound, lighting, staging, live production and experiential event management. Such integrated capabilities reflect the direction in which the industry is moving, as increasingly ambitious productions require providers with the technical capacity to manage multiple elements of the event environment.

Beyond the technology itself, the growth of the sector raises an important question about the availability of skilled professionals. As productions become more sophisticated, the demand for people who can operate and manage specialised equipment continues to grow. Technical competence in areas such as sound engineering, lighting control, camera operations, LED screen engineering and rigging requires both structured learning and practical exposure.

Developing this workforce is therefore an important consideration for the industry’s long-term sustainability. Recognising the need for specialised training, MSS established the MSS Event Tech Academy in partnership with KolaDaisi University. Its 10-week programme combines technical instruction with practical experience across six areas: LED Screen Engineering, Sound Engineering, Camera Craft and Video Production, Lighting Design and Control, Event Management and Production, and Rigging and Trussing.

The inaugural cohort comprised more than 60 students, with participants gaining practical exposure through involvement in live projects and productions. Five graduates secured employment with MSS upon completing the programme. The initiative reflects the growing importance of professional development within an industry where the quality of a production depends heavily on the knowledge and capabilities of the people delivering it.

Looking ahead, the opportunities for Nigeria’s event technology sector extend beyond entertainment. Corporate conferences, exhibitions, product launches, cultural festivals and large-scale brand experiences continue to create demand for sophisticated technical solutions. The growing ambition of event organisers, alongside changing audience expectations, presents opportunities for specialised providers to develop new capabilities and support increasingly complex productions.

There is also considerable potential for growth across the African market, where the expansion of the creative economy and demand for large-scale live experiences create opportunities for businesses with the infrastructure and expertise to deliver integrated production solutions. Realising this potential will require sustained investment in technology, talent development and operational capacity.

For MSS, its 20-year milestone represents an opportunity to build on its experience within this changing landscape. With ambitions centred on deeper innovation, expansion across Africa and continued investment in technical talent, the company enters its next chapter at a time when the demands on the event technology industry are continuing to evolve.

Ultimately, the success of a live experience is often determined long before the audience takes their seats. It depends on the systems, people and technical decisions working together behind the scenes. As Nigeria’s entertainment and events industry continues to grow, the expertise and infrastructure powering these experiences will remain central to how far the sector can go.

*Oladapo Adeniyi is a Freelance Sound Engineer.

World.title: RIBADU’S SECURITY DIPLOMACY
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Nuhu Ribadu’s quiet diplomacy is increasingly turning voices of dissent into partners in nation-building, writes YAKUBU DATI

Though the concept of security diplomacy evolved over the years between countries as a measure of managing security threats across the globe, its adaptation in internal crises has proven that the idea can be internalised in nations undergoing security threats to deescalate the tendencies of groups taking up arms against the state and threatening communities at will as was the case in Nigeria.

Since Malam Nuhu Ribadu assumed office as the National Security Adviser to the President, his method for conquering threats such as terrorism, insurgency, banditry and other forms of violent crimes have come under scrutiny.

Used to military engagements, people expected a continuation of the kinetic methods which over the years, rather than lessen the reign of terror, has made it to spread to other parts of Nigeria and even to neighbouring African countries.

It was when the results of the Ribadu approach began to manifest in the North East, North West, North Central, South South and South eastern parts of the country which were ravaged by security threats that many began to admit there are better ways of handling the security situation in Nigeria.

It is obvious that Ribadu, who has served as chairman of Nigeria’s topmost anti-graft agency had from experience reasoned that some levels of investigation, penetration, consultation and confrontation can serve a more effective purpose in dealing with such crimes hence domesticated the principle of security diplomacy.

Security diplomacy by its literal definition is the concept of managing international relations to prevent conflict, lower tensions, and keep countries or groups stable, using talks and negotiations to deal with threats like armed attacks, terrorism, and the spread of dangerous weapons.

This involves the blockage of arm routes, stoppage of supply of victuals to armed groups and setting up of direct communication with groups to make them see the futility of their actions and bring them to surrender.

It however does not imply the total jettisoning of physical combat engagements, but makes it applied only when necessary to reduce civilian casualties and address the cause of the criminal acts from the roots.

While military force may contain threats, sustainable peace often requires understanding the motivations, grievances and aspirations of affected communities.

While military engagement can reduce immediate tensions, unresolved grievances, unemployment, poverty, environmental degradation and perceptions of injustice can undermine peace over time.

Just like in international disputes, security diplomacy reduces the risk of mistakes or accidental war and turns potential conflicts into opportunities for discussion, and reducing the chances of spread.

In Nigeria’s complex political and security landscape, where conflict, agitation and mutual suspicion have repeatedly tested national cohesion, Nuhu Ribadu’s quiet diplomacy has offered an intriguing narrative of political transformation, turning voices of dissent into advocates of peace and former agitators into partners in nation-building.

From the creeks of the Niger Delta to the expansive Arewa hinterland, dialogue and reconciliation have increasingly become indispensable instruments in addressing Nigeria’s multifaceted security challenges.

Ribadu’s strategic positioning within President Bola Ahmed Tinubu’s security architecture has provided an opportunity to explore how engagement, political inclusion and relationship-building can complement conventional security operations.

The potential of former agitators becoming Renewed Hope Champions has come to represent a significant political development, suggesting that individuals once alienated from mainstream governance can find pathways towards constructive participation, community leadership and national development.

This aligns with President Tinubu’s Renewed Hope agenda, particularly its emphasis on security, stability and economic prosperity. Yet, political symbolism alone cannot establish the success of such a transformation.

Nigeria’s experience with amnesty programmes, negotiations and reintegration initiatives offers important lessons.

The Niger Delta illustrates both the possibilities and limitations of reconciliation. Although dialogue and intervention programmes have contributed to periods of relative stability, questions surrounding environmental restoration, equitable resource distribution and sustainable livelihoods remain significant.

Similarly, the insurgency-affected communities of the North require more than political engagement. Rehabilitation, justice, security, education, economic opportunity and the restoration of public confidence are essential to preventing renewed violence.

The measurable improvements in security, governance and in the lives of ordinary Nigerians makes the Ribadu method highly commendable.

Dati can be reached on Yakubudati@gmail.com

World.title: ELECTIONS ARE WON BY VOTES
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Stone-pelting and booing may make dramatic television footage, but they do not win presidential elections. Some of the scenes witnessed at political gatherings may be genuine expressions of frustration by Nigerians who are unhappy with the government, while others may be politically sponsored, deliberately organised or amplified for propaganda purposes. Whatever the motivation, however, the sight of angry crowds should not be confused with an electoral result. Elections are not won by the loudest boos, the most viral videos or the number of stones thrown at a political convoy. They are won by votes, and votes are secured through political structure, organisation, mobilisation, candidate appeal and, increasingly, a record that voters can evaluate.

This distinction is important as Nigeria moves towards the 2027 presidential election. The political atmosphere is already becoming increasingly heated, with opposition parties and supporters of the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) seeking to demonstrate momentum. There is nothing unusual about this. Elections are contests of narratives. One side wants to convince Nigerians that the government has failed and must be removed; the other wants to demonstrate that its reforms are working and deserve continuity. But beyond the noise, the more important question is this: which political force possesses the organisation, geographical spread, grassroots machinery and presidential candidate capable of converting political sentiment into actual votes?

At present, the APC has a formidable advantage. The argument that political structure does not matter in a presidential election is difficult to sustain in Nigeria’s political environment.
