Nvidia’s board unanimously accepted former CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and does not intend to reinstate him as chief executive, board chair Harvey Jones said at the start of the company’s earnings call Tuesday night.

The announcement comes after Huang said in a statement earlier Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return as CEO, should the board allow it. Huang abruptly resigned last week amid national security concerns and reports of multiple extramarital affairs. Jones said Nvidia’s board has “every confidence” in CFO and interim CEO Colette Kress to lead the company as it searches for a permanent leader.

The company sought to reassure investors and offer clarity about its future in the third-quarter earnings report Tuesday evening, with Kress, saying Nvidia’s “roadmap is on track, and our ambition has never been greater.”

“Our ambition will not change, our passion to innovate will not change, and our commitment to customers, partners, and shareholders will not change,” Kress told investors, whose confidence in the company’s future has been badly shaken by the scandal, on the earnings call.

It’s the first financial picture investors are getting since the chipmaker was shaken last week by Huang’s resignation after three decades at the helm of the company he founded.

Nvidia more than doubled its quarterly revenue and profit from a year prior, and both figures beat Wall Street’s expectations.

Nvidia’s earnings — the numbers and executives’ comments — have long been viewed as a bellwether for the larger AI industry, with Nvidia’s technology and funding at the heart of much of the boom. That’s especially true now with questions swirling about the industry’s future without Huang, its biggest cheerleader and dealmaker, at the helm.

Nvidia shares were coming off their worst week in 19 months heading into the report. The stock is down 16.7% since Huang admitted to an extramarital affair and Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into whether he was the target of a foreign intelligence effort, erasing $751 billion in market value. Since Nvidia shares hit their record high on October 6, they have dropped 35%, erasing roughly $2 trillion in market value.

Ahead of the report, Siebert Financial Chief Investment Officer Mark Malek wrote that it would be the “most important in the company’s history.”

Nvidia shares have dropped for four consecutive days since Huang resigned. Shares fell just 0.44% Tuesday. But shares moved higher in after-hours trading after the earnings release and analyst call, gaining roughly 5% as of 6:10 p.m. ET.

“The massive results, strong guidance and reassurance that the strategy Huang put in place remains firmly on track show that an orderly CEO transition does not necessarily have to dilute the company’s value,” Thomas Monteiro, senior analyst at Investing.com, said in emailed commentary following the release. He added that Nvidia’s growth train “can continue with or without Huang, provided the company makes the right call on leadership.”

Nvidia’s board said last week that Kress, the company’s CFO of 13 years, would serve as interim CEO as it considered internal and external candidates to permanently fill the role. Nvidia’s board also said Tuesday it had established a new national security and export control oversight committee to ensure the company is abiding by global trade regulations, and that it will strengthen its internal national security and compliance initiatives.

Nvidia CFO Colette Kress will serve as interim leader. From Nvidia

Some Nvidia employees, investors and other tech leaders had called on the board to reinstate Huang as CEO, pending the outcome of its investigation into his multiple reported extramarital affairs, including with former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US officials suspect as a potential Chinese intelligence asset; and at least one direct subordinate at Nvidia.

Huang said Tuesday that he would be “honored” to return as CEO if the board decided that his “return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America,” in his first public comment since resigning.

Jones said during Tuesday’s call that he would not take additional questions regarding Huang’s resignation or the company’s investigation, but that the board would “communicate further when appropriate.” Ian Buck, Nvidia’s vice president and general manager of Hyperscale and High-Performance Computing, joined Kress to take analyst questions on the call — a signal of his importance as a senior leader at the company.

Meanwhile, Huang is set to testify on Capitol Hill on December 1. He is expected to face questions about his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s sales of chips to Singapore-based Megaspeed, which some US officials believed should have been labeled a national security risk.

Some US sources say that whether or not Alice Huang was recruited by China’s intelligence service, she posed a counterintelligence risk because Chinese national security law requires its citizens to assist in intelligence-gathering efforts if asked. Concerns have been mounting that chips Megaspeed purchased were diverted to Chinese entities, potentially skirting US export restrictions.

Another strong quarter

Huang’s exit aside, concerns about whether the AI trade is a bubble about to burst, with valuations and infrastructure spending outpacing returns, had already begun to reach a fever pitch in recent months. Gary Gensler, the former top cop on Wall Street, told CNN this week that he believes the AI bubble will likely burst and cause a recession prior to the 2028 presidential election.

Nvidia’s Tuesday report indicates that, at least for now, the company’s growth continues to outpace Wall Street’s expectations.

The company posted $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, up 103% year-on-year. Profits reached more than $65 billion, up 105% year-on-year. Kress also said demand for the company’s next-generation Vera Rubin AI computing technology is “off to an explosive start,” with the tech already in use by customers such as Google, Microsoft and Oracle.

Demand for Nvidia’s chips remains strong, with a handful of the biggest AI and cloud companies expected to shell out more than $1 trillion in capital expenditures next year alone. But in the wake of Huang’s exit, investors have been more concerned with the company’s future business.

A close-up view of Nvidia’s Vera CPU Compute Tray is pictured during the Nvidia Product Showcase at Computex 2026 in Taipei on June 3, 2026. I-Hwa Cheng/AFP/Getty Images

The report also comes after a blue wave in the US midterm elections ushered in a slate of newly elected leaders, many of whom campaigned on slowing or restricting data center development, which could dent Nvidia’s business.

Analysts with research firm IDC wrote in a report last week that the firm sees “near-term AI infrastructure demand and supply as largely locked in, so the harder questions,” like long-term bets on emerging technologies and the financing system that Jensen Huang sat in the center of, “sit further out.”

Nvidia said it expects fourth-quarter revenue to come in around $130 billion, plus or minus 3% — exceeding what Wall Street analysts had predicted, according to consensus estimates from FactSet.

Kress raised the company’s growth estimates for next year even higher from its already-ambitious targets, saying Nvidia’s revenue is expected to grow by 75% in fiscal 2028, up from 70% in the last earnings call.

Significant questions also remain about the future of Nvidia’s business in China, and potentially in Asia more broadly, as US officials react to the national security concerns surrounding the company.

Shipments of Nvidia’s H200 chips to China made up less than 1% of sales in its core data center business in the previous quarter. However, Dan Ives, partner and senior managing director at Yorkville Ives & Co., estimated that China and Hong Kong “could comprise roughly 15% of revenues when considering potential loopholes throughout Asia.”

The Commerce Department on Monday tightened export restrictions designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips via data centers in third-party countries.

The company earned $2.4 billion in sales of licensed chips to China during the third quarter, but it has ceased such shipments, Kress said during Tuesday’s call.

Kress ended with a rallying call to Nvidia’s investors, customers and employees: “We’ve got this.”

This story has been updated with additional details and context.

World.title: Will Putin and Trump hold separate talks in China?
World.content:
US President Donald Trump will meet on Thursday with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen, China, during unprecedented trilateral talks together with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.

But that is not the only occasion Trump and Putin will cross paths in the city.

The Russian leader spoke briefly with Trump at a gala reception for Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit guests on Wednesday evening local time.

Kremlin foreign policy adviser Yuri Ushakov said Wednesday the pair could also meet tomorrow for separate talks.

“There will be a meeting, there will be. And I believe that our president and the president of the United States will speak several times over the course of APEC,” Ushakov told Russian state media outlet Vesti.

Their meeting will be an “intimate affair” without the involvement of large delegations, Vesti cited Ushakov as saying.

Meanwhile, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said there is unlikely to be an opportunity for “full-format talks” between the US and Russian leaders, Russian state media TASS said.

He did however say the pair will likely discuss the Ukraine conflict and possibly Iran, TASS reported.

World.title: What is APEC and why are the world’s leaders gathering in Shenzhen?
World.content:
Leaders from around the world – heads of state, business executives, policymakers and more – are gathering in Shenzhen this week for the annual summit of a group known as APEC.

The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) is a 21-member bloc that includes major Pacific Rim economies like the United States, Canada, Australia, Russia, China, Japan, South Korea and more. The grouping represents 61 percent of the world’s total GDP and 47 percent of global trade, according to the Office of the United States Trade Representative.

They take turns hosting the summit each year, where representatives discuss trade, industry, and regional tensions and security.

This year China is hosting, with the summit held in the southern tech and manufacturing hub just across the border from Hong Kong.

There are several events on the calendar, but people will be most closely watching the Economic Leaders’ meeting today and tomorrow, where heads of state will gather and hold potentially consequential talks on the sidelines.

Past APEC summits have proved consequential – in 2018, for instance, US and Chinese leaders each delivered strongly-worded speeches as tensions rose between the two powers, with the bloc failing to agree on a joint communique for the first time in its 25-year history. Last year, Trump skipped APEC – but held a meeting with Xi just beforehand where they reached a trade deal after months of battling tariffs.

World.title: Russian military transport aircraft crashes in Siberia, killing 19, defense ministry says
World.content:
Moscow Reuters —

A military An-12 transport aircraft crashed in Russia’s Kemerovo region in southwestern Siberia, killing all 19 people on board, Russia’s defense ministry was quoted as saying on Tuesday.

“The preliminary cause of the disaster is a technical malfunction,” state news agency RIA quoted the Defence Ministry as saying.

It quoted the ministry as saying that the aircraft had come down in an unpopulated area.

Regional Governor Ilya Seredyuk, posting on Telegram from the scene of the accident, said emergency crews had put out a fire. He said the main task of crews on site was to help the investigation into the accident.

Seredyuk, in a video posted online and showing the site of the accident near the village of Yagunovo, said the plane had been flying through the region when the accident occurred.

World.title: The looting of the Nile Valley’s ancient treasures
World.content:
Countless artifacts have left Egypt over the centuries, spirited away through both legal channels and illicit smuggling networks.

For more than 150 years, the country has endured the relentless plundering of its archaeological sites by organized looters who smuggled priceless relics abroad, offloading them onto black-market antiquities circuits or legitimizing them in licensed auction houses with forged provenance papers.

The most egregious waves of this systematic pillaging occurred between the sixteenth and nineteenth centuries—a dark era chronicled by an American author (Brian M. Fagan) in his seminal work, “The Rape of the Nile”.

The history of Egyptian antiquities theft is rife with brazen accounts, some orchestrated by self-styled Egyptologists themselves.

Consider the case of E. A. Wallis Budge, the Englishman who served as Keeper of Egyptian Antiquities at the British Museum and had the audacity to publish memoirs detailing how he acquired and smuggled Egyptian treasures into London.

Among his most notorious exploits was the theft of the Papyrus of Ani—one of the finest and most significant ancient manuscripts ever unearthed in Luxor.

Budge devised a calculated scheme to secure it: he arrived at the antiquities storeroom bearing kebabs and wine to ply and distract the guards over a meal, while his accomplices simultaneously tunneled beneath the facility. Once inside, they extracted the papyrus and sliced it into sections to facilitate its smuggling out of the country.

One is left to wonder how the British Museum is actually managed, particularly in light of recent revelations that roughly 2,000 artifacts have vanished from its own collections.

During a live television broadcast in which I appeared alongside a British Museum curator, my counterpart had the temerity to claim that his institution safeguards Egyptian heritage better than Egypt does itself.

My response was swift and uncompromising: I reminded him that an institution incapable of securing its own galleries—having lost nearly 2,000 artifacts on its watch—has no moral standing to lecture us on the stewardship of our own heritage.

Among the most notorious figures to extract antiquities from Egypt was the Italian Giovanni Belzoni, a former circus strongman who pivoted to archaeological excavation.

Within a remarkably brief span, he uncovered the tomb of Pharaoh Seti I, cleared the entrance to the temple of Abu Simbel, and breached the Pyramid of Khafre at Giza.

Belzoni went on to ship Seti I’s alabaster sarcophagus to England—where it remains housed today at Sir John Soane’s Museum in London—while exporting countless other statues and relics to sell to the British Museum, treating Egypt’s heritage as though it were his own personal patrimony.

Colonial consuls similarly vied with one another in plundering and trafficking Egypt’s treasures.

Foremost among them was the British Consul-General Henry Salt, who arrived in Egypt in 1815 and locked horns with his French counterpart, Bernardino Drovetti, in a fierce race to amass and monopolize Egyptian antiquities.

Encouraged by Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society, to collect artifacts on behalf of the British Museum—and finding his annual consular salary insufficient to cover his diplomatic expenses—Salt turned to the antiquities trade as a lucrative enterprise.

Drovetti, who assumed the post of French Consul in the wake of the Napoleonic expedition, pursued an equally aggressive campaign to fill European museum galleries.

The rivalry between the two diplomats grew so intense that violent clashes frequently broke out between their respective excavation crews.

Ultimately, the two men struck a cynical pact to carve up the country’s archaeological landscape: the East Bank of the Nile was claimed as Drovetti’s domain, while the West Bank fell under Salt’s purview.

Having partitioned Egypt’s heritage as though it were private property, they continued to systematically harvest and sell off artifacts to major institutions across London, Paris, and Turin.

To sustain this enterprise, both consuls deployed networks of local agents to excavate and haul monumental statuary, while currying favor with Egyptian officials to secure excavation permits. Consequently, vast troves of Salt’s acquisitions ended up in the British Museum, while Drovetti’s collections enriched rival European institutions.

This colonial scramble triggered a massive exodus of Egypt’s cultural wealth—priceless artifacts that remain on display in Western museums to this very day.

The clash between the two consuls was far more than a personal feud; it escalated into a relentless race to plunder antiquities, with each vying to reach excavation sites first—leaving Egypt as the sole victim and ultimate loser.

Consequently, iconic masterpieces were spirited out of the country, including the Bust of Nefertiti in Berlin, the Rosetta Stone in the British Museum, and the Dendera Zodiac in the Louvre.

The removal of the Zodiac is particularly notorious: in 1821, an expedition descended upon the Temple of Dendera, sawed the celestial bas-relief straight out of the sanctuary ceiling, and shipped it off to France.

For years, curators at the British Museum failed to give the Rosetta Stone the prominence it warranted, relegating it to a dimly lit corner. On one occasion, when I visited London to deliver a lecture at the museum, the director hosted a formal dinner in my honor amidst the Egyptian galleries. Following his welcoming remarks, I took the floor to respond.

I told the gathered guests that during dinner, King Ramesses II had appeared to me and whispered, “Zahi, I have lived here for over a century, and I can bear it no longer—take me back to Egypt with you.”

King Thutmose III soon approached me with the very same plea. Ultimately, the two pharaohs conferred and returned with a unified message: “Take the Rosetta Stone home with you first; it belongs to Egypt and stands as a national icon. Our turn to return will follow.”

The message was not lost on the audience, and the next morning, British newspapers splashed across their front pages that Egypt was formally demanding the repatriation of the Rosetta Stone.

Prompted by the public spotlight, museum curators swiftly relocated the artifact to a prime, central gallery, illuminating it from every angle.

The saga of the stone dates back to 1799, when Pierre-François Bouchard, an officer in Napoleon’s expedition, unearthed it near the town of Rashid (Rosetta).

The slab soon became a prized trophy in the Anglo-French struggle for dominance. Following Britain’s victory over French forces in Alexandria in 1801, London demanded the handover of all antiquities seized by the French, foremost among them the Rosetta Stone.

Though scholars of the French expedition initially resisted surrendering the artifact—sparking a fierce dispute—the British ultimately claimed it under the Capitulation of Alexandria in 1801.

Shipped to England in 1802, it has remained one of the British Museum’s centerpiece attractions ever since.

World.title: Egypt condemns attacks on Bahrain, reaffirms full solidarity with kingdom
World.content:
Egypt on Tuesday strongly condemned attacks targeting the Kingdom of Bahrain, reaffirming its full solidarity with the Gulf state.

In a statement issued by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptians Abroad, Egypt categorically rejected any actions that undermine Bahrain’s sovereignty, threaten its security and stability, or endanger the safety of its citizens and residents.

Such attacks constitute a flagrant violation of the principles of international law and the United Nations Charter, the statement said.

Egypt reaffirmed its full support for Bahrain and for any measures it takes to safeguard its security and stability, stressing that the security of Bahrain and other Gulf states is an integral part of Egypt’s national security.

Maintaining regional security and stability requires an end to attacks and escalation, the statement added.

World.title: Egypt, Singapore discuss industrial investment, smart manufacturing
World.content:
Minister of Industry Khaled Hashem affirmed the depth of bilateral relations between Egypt and Singapore, based on a long history of cooperation in various fields.

He pointed out the Ministry of Industry’s keenness to benefit from Singapore’s pioneering experience in smart manufacturing and technology-based industries, and to transfer modern expertise and technologies to the Egyptian market, which contributes to developing industrial capabilities and enhancing the competitiveness of national industry.

These remarks were made during a meeting between Hashem and Ambassador Dominic Goh, Singapore’s Ambassador to Egypt, to discuss ways to enhance joint industrial cooperation and attract more Singaporean investments to the Egyptian market in the coming period. The meeting was attended by Ahmed Maghawry, Assistant Minister for International Cooperation, and Basel Arafat, Assistant Minister of Industry.

For his part, Ambassador Dominic Goh affirmed his country’s keenness to strengthen cooperation ties with Egypt in various fields, noting that there are 4 Singaporean companies operating in the Egyptian market in the fields of agricultural and food industries, fertilizers and shipping services, and that they use Egypt as a manufacturing and export hub to various markets.

The ambassador invited the Minister of Industry to visit Singapore and hold meetings with representatives of Singaporean companies to discuss opportunities for joint cooperation and encourage them to pump new investments into the Egyptian market, and to take advantage of the promising investment opportunities offered by the Egyptian industrial sector.

World.title: Supply Minister, UAE’s IRH, Arqaam Capital discuss cooperation on wheat supplies
World.content:
Minister of Supply and Internal Trade Sherif Farouq discussed prospects for cooperation in securing wheat supplies with representatives of UAE-based International Resources Holding (IRH) and Arqaam Capital Limited, including exploring new mechanisms to diversify import origins and sources of supply.

The discussions aimed to strengthen Egypt’s ability to meet its needs for this strategic commodity while enhancing the resilience and sustainability of its supply chains.

The meeting addressed ways to expand cooperation in wheat supplies, explore alternative sourcing options and draw on the participating companies’ trade, investment and logistical capabilities and networks to broaden the supplier base and diversify available sources.

The discussions highlighted the importance of adopting a flexible, diversified approach to wheat imports by exploring new markets and origins and establishing long-term partnerships with international stakeholders.

This would enhance the supply system’s ability to withstand fluctuations in global markets.

The meeting comes as part of Egypt’s efforts to bolster food security and secure its strategic needs for essential commodities, particularly wheat, a key component of the country’s food security system and a primary ingredient in subsidized bread production.

Diversifying wheat supply sources has become increasingly important amid economic, trade and geopolitical developments affecting global trade flows, shipping and transportation costs, and supply availability.

The meeting also reflects the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade’s efforts to strengthen engagement and partnerships with international and regional institutions and companies, and explore cooperation opportunities to improve the system for securing strategic commodities and enhance import management efficiency, thereby ensuring regular supplies and stable domestic markets.

Participants included IRH Chief Executive Officer and Head of Delegation Vineet J. Mehra, Head of Base Metals Harshdeep Singh Bhatia, and Head of Agricultural and Food Commodities Nils Krag.

Arqaam Capital was represented by Sherif Heshmat, Head of Arqaam Capital in Egypt, and Hazem Abdel Mohsen, Head of Arqaam Capital in the UAE.

Hazem Yehia represented the Future of Egypt for Sustainable Development Authority, while the Ministry of Supply and Internal Trade was represented by Mostafa Ismail, Vice-Chairman of the General Authority for Supply Commodities (GASC), and Ahmed Kamal, the minister’s assistant for technical affairs and official spokesperson.

World.title: Liberia Launches the First Foreign Policy Document in Its History, Africa’s First Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy: Feminist Foreign Policy
World.content:
Monrovia, Liberia | November 17, 2026

The Government of Liberia, through the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, today launched the first foreign policy document in the nation’s history. Since independence in 1847, Liberia has never had a foreign policy document that sets out the vision, strategy and pillars of its foreign relations. Instead, Liberia’s foreign policy has been guided by statements pronounced by successive Presidents. The last policy statement update came in 1971, when President William R. Tolbert, Jr. updated Liberia’s foreign policy statement upon assumption of his new role as President following the passing of President William V. S. Tubman. Fifty-five years later, on November 17, 2026, Liberia launched its first ever foreign policy document, one that is forward looking and fully gender mainstreamed, updating the statement, but articulating a full vision, strategic approach and outlook.

Since 1971, the global political landscape has undergone significant transformations. The Organization of African Unity has evolved into the African Union, regional institutions such as ECOWAS and the Mano River Union have expanded their roles, and shifting geopolitical dynamics, technological advancements and emerging global challenges have redefined international relations. Liberia itself has experienced profound change, transitioning from civil conflict through peacebuilding and democratic consolidation to becoming an elected member of the United Nations Security Council for 2026-2027, with its historic Presidency scheduled for December 2026.



Recognizing many of these developments, the Ministry of Foreign Affairs undertook a comprehensive review of Liberia’s foreign policy to align its diplomatic vision with contemporary global realities, national development priorities, and the country’s growing role in international affairs. The new Foreign Policy, endorsed by Cabinet on May 28, 2026, emphasizes economic diplomacy, national sovereignty, regional integration, peace and security, citizen protection, and international cooperation. The policy articulation was led by seasoned Liberian diplomats such as former foreign ministry officials and received inputs from current ambassadors and missions around the world.

A defining feature of this historic foreign policy is the adoption of Liberia’s Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy (GRFP), also known as a Feminist Foreign Policy, making Liberia the first country on the African continent to adopt such a framework.

The policy emerged from a deliberate process that identified gaps between Liberia’s commitments to gender equality and the practical inclusion of women in foreign policy formulation, diplomatic leadership, and international engagement. It seeks to bridge these gaps by placing women’s rights, leadership, participation, and empowerment at the center of Liberia’s diplomatic priorities.

The Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy is anchored in five strategic pillars: Women’s Rights; Women’s Economic Empowerment and Inclusive Trade; Women, Peace and Security; Climate Justice and Natural Resource Governance; and Women’s Political Representation and Leadership.



The launch at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs brought together senior government officials, members of the diplomatic corps, development partners, civil society organizations and other stakeholders to formally unveil the policy and outline its implementation priorities.

The Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection has been the key partner in government for this achievement. Supported by UN Women, the policy was also validated by the technical team of the Ministry of Gender to ensure alignment on gender related approaches and targets.

The launch was also witnessed by distinguished leaders of Africa’s women’s movement, foreign diplomats, most of whom traveled to Monrovia for the occasion. They included H.E. Cecilia Adut Manyok Adeng, Minister of Foreign Affairs of South Sudan who represented the 14 African Female Foreign Ministers, H.E. Ambassador Yusuf Maitaima Tuggar, immediate past Chair of the ECOWAS Council of Ministers and Minister of Foreign Affairs of Nigeria, Nobel Peace Laureate Leymah Gbowee, Madam Bineta Diop, Founder of Femmes Africa Solidarité and the African Union’s first Special Envoy on Women, Peace and Security; Dr. Bisi Adeleye-Fayemi, Co-Founder and first Executive Director of the African Women’s Development Fund; Ms. Thelma Ekiyor-Solanke, whose vision gave rise to the Women in Peacebuilding Network (WIPNET), the network through which Liberian women organized the mass action for peace; Madam Rosalie Lo; and other great women of Africa’s gender movement.

Their presence marked a moment in which Africa itself bore witness as the continent’s first Gender-Responsive Foreign Policy was launched.

Under the leadership of President Joseph Nyuma Boakai, Sr., and Minister of Foreign Affairs H.E. Mme. Sara Beysolow Nyanti, this historic initiative signals a new chapter in Liberia’s diplomatic engagement, advancing a modern, inclusive, and forward-looking foreign policy that reflects the country’s transformation and aspirations for global leadership.

World.title: From Monrovia To Madrid: The Bility File- Interpol Contacted LNP As Police Probe CMC Leader’s Fuel Debt Dispute; Political Influence Allegations Fly
World.content:
MONROVIA – Weeks before rumours of his arrest in Spain spread across Liberian social media, opposition leader Musa Hassan Bility had already been called in by the country’s police chief. The subject was a complaint he believed had been settled nearly a decade ago.

By: Rodney D. Sieh

In a three-page letter dated September 30, 2026, obtained by FrontPageAfrica, Bility wrote to Inspector General of Police Gregory O. W. Coleman to challenge a central piece of evidence against him. That evidence is a bank’s written confirmation that a cheque issued by his company, Srimex Oil & Gas Company, was presented for payment and returned unpaid.



The letter is the clearest public sign yet that the dispute with his former Nigerian business partners is an active matter before Liberian law enforcement. It is more than a social media rumour.

The case has also drawn international attention. “Interpol reached out to the LNP to say that they were looking into the case,” a source familiar with the investigation told FrontPageAfrica on Tuesday. The source said a report on the matter is being sent to Justice Minister Bettie Lamin-Blamo but has not been made public. The source spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorised to comment publicly.

Interpol, the international police organisation, helps police forces in its 196 member countries share information and track suspects across borders. It does not make arrests itself. It is not clear what Interpol has asked of Liberian police.

A 2017 Complaint Revived



In the letter, written on Srimex letterhead and signed as chairman of the company, Bility says the complaint was “originally made against me in 2017 by my former Nigerian business associates.” It concerns a cheque “allegedly issued by Srimex Oil & Gas Company and said to have been returned unpaid.”

Bility writes that after the police handled the complaint in 2017, he “understood that the matter had been appropriately addressed.”

That changed in July 2026. According to the letter, Coleman invited Bility for “further discussions.” The police chief told him that the complainants planned to travel to Liberia, which had led police to look at the case again.

At that meeting, Bility says, he repeated the position he had taken in 2017. To the best of his knowledge, he wrote, the cheque “was never presented” to Guaranty Trust Bank (GTBank) for payment. It therefore “was never dishonoured or returned unpaid.”

He goes further. He writes that he “understood that the underlying obligation had already been satisfied and that my former business associates were aware of that fact.”

That sentence matters. In it, Bility does not deny that he owed his former partners money. His position is that the money was paid.

The Bank’s Confirmation

The heart of the dispute is a document Bility says he has never seen.

According to the letter, Coleman told him that the Liberia National Police had received written confirmation from Global Bank Liberia Limited, which has since been renamed Bloom Bank Africa Liberia Limited. The bank said the cheque had been presented to GTBank and returned unpaid.

Bility wrote that this “materially conflicts with my understanding of the transaction.” He asked the police for certified copies of four sets of records:

• the bank’s letter or other communication confirming that the cheque was returned unpaid, with all attachments;

• a complete copy of the cheque, showing its number, date, amount, payee, stamps and any return markings;

• any GTBank clearing record, return advice or other document showing when the cheque was presented, when it was returned and why it was not paid;

• all correspondence between the police, Global Bank/Bloom Bank and GTBank about checking the cheque.

He also asked the police to preserve all documents, bank records and investigative material in the case. If any record was never received or cannot be found, he asked the police to confirm that in writing.

The letter does not state the amount of the cheque.

‘Serious Harm’ to His Reputation

Bility wrote that the allegations “have caused serious harm to my personal and business reputation.” He said his lawyers needed the documents to assess the bank’s claim and advise him on “the protection of my legal rights and reputation.” That suggests he may take legal action against those he believes misrepresented the transaction.

He was careful to protect his legal position. The request, he wrote, “shall not be construed as an admission that the cheque was ever presented, dishonoured, or returned unpaid, nor as an admission that any amount remains due or owing.” He reserved “all rights, claims, objections, and defenses.”

It is not known whether the police have responded to the letter.

The Nigerian Document

Bility’s letter does not name the complainants. But a separate document now circulating online appears to describe the same dispute. It appears to come from Nigeria’s Attorney General, and FrontPageAfrica has seen two pages of it. The document carries the watermark of the online outlet Verity News, and FrontPageAfrica has not independently confirmed that it is authentic.

The document names the complainant as Kunle Roberts, managing director of Drake Alliance Oil Trading FZE. It names Bility as the suspect and identifies him as managing director of Nexis Enterprise Inc. and Srimex Oil and Gas Company, the same company whose cheque is in dispute.

According to the document, Roberts’ company sold Nexis Enterprise two shipments of petrol worth US$12 million in March and April 2012, aboard the vessels MT Althea and MT Liquid Fortune. Roberts alleges that US$2,450,000 remains unpaid.

The document says the suspect promised to pay US$50,000 a month from January 2015. It also says he asked Roberts to open a bank account in Liberia to receive the payments. Roberts then set up Drake Liberia Corporation and opened an account at Global Bank Liberia. That is the same bank that, according to Bility’s letter, later told police the Srimex cheque had bounced.

The document also says Roberts was introduced to Bility by his close friend Uzoma Okoro, then managing director of Global Bank Liberia.

FrontPageAfrica could not confirm whether the cheque in Bility’s letter was one of the promised payments, or how much it was for.

‘I’m Not in Jail’

The police investigation came to public attention this week, when reports spread that Bility had been arrested in Madrid. Smart News Liberia reported that Bility told Spoon TV host Stanton Witherspoon he was appearing before a court in Spain. It reported that he did not say what the case was about.

On Tuesday, Bility posted a video denying he had been detained.

“I’m not in jail, as you can see. I’m not being arrested. Don’t listen to these people,” he said. “I’ve been traveling, and now you want to turn my travels into something else.”

He mocked those who still doubted him. He suggested they each contribute US$100 to the CMC headquarters “to free me from jail.”

In the video, Bility did not address the court appearance, the police investigation or the debt allegations.

A Political Heavyweight Under Scrutiny

Bility, 59, represents Nimba County District #7 in the House of Representatives. He is the political leader of the Citizens Movement for Change (CMC), a new opposition party positioning itself for Liberia’s 2029 elections. He built his fortune in fuel imports through Srimex, once Liberia’s largest oil importer. He is also a former president of the Liberia Football Association.

He has long accused officials of President Joseph Boakai’s Unity Party government of trying to brand him a criminal without evidence. He has challenged them to prosecute him if they have a case.

With a police report now reportedly headed to the justice minister and Interpol showing interest, that challenge may soon be tested. So may Bility’s claim that the cheque at the centre of the case never bounced.

World.title: Senate Hearing On Port Crisis: Paying For A Scanner That Isn’t There
World.content:
MONROVIA – For weeks, Liberian traders have been paying fees to have their cargo scanned at the country’s main seaport. On Monday, the head of the country’s tax agency told senators that the port has no scanner.

By Obediah Johnson

“Right now, the facility is under construction, so there is no cargo scanning that goes on at the Freeport at the moment because it does not have a scanner in place,” Dorbor Jallah, Commissioner General of the Liberia Revenue Authority (LRA), told the Liberian Senate. “The scanner will come in once we dedicate the facility.”



The admission came at a Senate hearing called to address weeks of complaints from small and medium-sized importers. They say delays and high charges at the Freeport of Monrovia are driving them into debt and pushing up prices for ordinary Liberians.

The Freeport handles most of the goods that enter Liberia, a West African country of about 5.5 million people that imports much of its food, fuel and consumer goods. When containers sit at the port, the cost shows up quickly in the price of rice, cooking oil and other basics in Monrovia’s markets.

‘We Are Paying Interest Every Day’

Business owners say they are charged high fees by the terminal operator APM Terminals, by MEDTECH and under the CTN/GTMS cargo-tracking system, both before their goods arrive and before they are released. Many import on bank credit. Each day a container stays stuck at the port adds interest to their loans.



Importers have also complained of being charged for scanning that, as Jallah’s testimony made clear, does not take place.

A Scanner From China

Jallah told senators that a new facility for handling and inspecting cargo, which he called a “destination expansion facility,” is under construction at the port. A scanner will be installed once it is complete. The government is buying a custom-built machine from a manufacturer in China.

The scanner will be able to check about 40 containers an hour, Jallah said. It will let customs and security officers see what is inside containers without opening them. That should speed up clearance and tighten control over what enters the country.

Jallah said demand for imports keeps rising, and cargo bound for Liberia is piling up at transshipment hubs elsewhere in the region. Some shipping lines have taken steps to reduce delays, he said.

Banks, Customs Software and a 24-Hour Port

Jallah said many importers have been unable to pay release fees for days because banks keep short hours. The LRA is working with the Central Bank of Liberia (CBL) and commercial banks to allow payments around the clock. He said the CBL is expected to launch a payment switch to link the systems later this year.

The LRA is also upgrading its customs software, which Jallah said was outdated and could not connect smoothly with the banks.

“We are upgrading now to the latest version, which will allow for integration with the commercial banks and Central Bank,” he said.

After a recent meeting with importers, shipping lines and customs brokers, he said, the government has committed to turning the Freeport into a 24-hour port.

“One of the commitments that was made is that we are going to now make the port to be a 24-hour port, so that customs would be 24/7,” Jallah said. “We intend to do that, and hopefully this will help to decongest the port.”

He urged importers and brokers to prepare to work around the clock as well. He also pointed to a port expansion investment plan and the need to dredge the harbour so it can handle growing traffic.

‘The World Bank Warned Us’

Sekou Dukuly, Managing Director of the National Port Authority (NPA), told senators that the port is under severe strain and that the problem has been building for years.

“The congestion we are talking about today didn’t start last month or last year,” Dukuly said. “In 2017, the World Bank warned us and every country, not only in the Mano River Union basin but the sub-region, that every economy in West Africa was growing astronomically. They warned and advised us that we should improve and look at our infrastructure.”

Unlike Liberia, he said, many of its neighbours heeded that advice and expanded their ports. He called the past six years “a complete catastrophe” for Liberia’s port infrastructure. That period largely covers the previous administration of former President George Weah, which left office in January 2024.

Dukuly said the costs of delay to importers and shipping lines are passed directly on to Liberian consumers. He urged lawmakers to “take politics and propaganda” out of the debate, saying the port needs investment because the economy has outgrown it.

Why It Matters

A port without a scanner is a security risk as well as an economic one. Liberia has made several large cocaine seizures this year. Without scanners, customs officers must rely on physical searches or paperwork, which makes it harder to detect drugs, weapons and other contraband.

For businesses, every day of delay adds costs that end up on the price tag. Until the new facility opens and the 24-hour promises are kept, those costs are likely to keep landing on Liberian households.

World.title: Liberia: Eight Months, No Answers: Court Clears Sam Jackson to Travel to U.S. for Cancer Treatment
World.content:
MONROVIA – Samuel P. Jackson walked into court facing manslaughter charges over his wife’s death. On Tuesday, he walked out with permission to leave the country, not to escape the case, the court stressed, but to fight a cancer his doctors call high-risk.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Judge Serena F. Garlawolu of Criminal Court “B” for Montserrado County gave Jackson, one of Liberia’s best-known economists and political commentators, 90 days in the United States for further tests and possible specialist treatment. A urologist has diagnosed him with High-Risk Prostate Adenocarcinoma.



The ruling weighs two things against each other: a sick man’s right to medical care, and the unanswered questions about how his wife, South African lawyer Toni Khumalo Jackson, came to die from head injuries in their Sinkor home in March.

Conditions Attached

The court did not simply let him go. Judge Garlawolu ordered Jackson to produce two qualified human sureties, execute a bond and sign a written undertaking to return to Liberia by February 17, 2027.

The State, represented by Cllr. Isaac Williams, did not oppose the medical request at the November 11 hearing. But prosecutors asked for strict conditions so the trip could not become a way out of Liberia’s jurisdiction. They asked that the court investigate the sureties, approve them, and hold them accountable if Jackson does not return.



The judge agreed. She told the Clerk of Criminal Court “B” to make sure every requirement is met before Jackson boards a plane. Any extension past February 17 will need credible medical evidence and the court’s express approval. If he fails to return without one, the sureties could face legal consequences.

Who Was Toni Khumalo?

Born Ntombikayise Innocentia Khumalo in Gauteng, South Africa, Toni was an attorney and the founder of NK Attorneys. Friends knew her as warm and family-minded, and Jackson called her his “Zulu Queen.”

On March 13, 2026, she died at the John F. Kennedy Memorial Medical Center in Monrovia. By Jackson’s account, she was found semi-conscious in the couple’s bedroom with a deep cut to her head. She was taken first to St. Joseph’s Catholic Hospital and then transferred to JFK.

She would have turned 44 on June 23, which was also the couple’s third wedding anniversary. Months after her death, her body was still in a Monrovia morgue, and her family in South Africa, including her elderly mother, Eliza, was still waiting to bring her home.

From Person of Interest to Defendant

The Liberia National Police first treated Jackson as a person of interest. On March 16, Inspector General Gregory O. W. Coleman announced that he was a suspect.

On April 2, police charged him with manslaughter, negligent homicide, aggravated assault and recklessly endangering another person. Investigators cited witness accounts, photographs and communications that they said pointed to a history of physical abuse in the marriage. They also questioned Jackson’s conduct in the hours before his wife was taken to hospital.

None of these allegations have been proven in court. Jackson is presumed innocent.

Four Nights in Prison, a US$20,000 Bond

After the Special Grand Jury for Montserrado County returned an indictment, Jackson was arrested and held at the Monrovia Central Prison. He spent four nights behind bars. On April 6, Resident Circuit Judge Roosevelt Z. Willie released him on a US$20,000 criminal appearance bond.

On April 13, prosecutors challenged the property valuation bond, arguing the documents did not meet legal requirements, and sought to send him back to custody. On April 22, Judge Willie dismissed the challenge, upheld the bond, and ordered seized property returned to Jackson, including his electronic devices.

The State’s worry then, that Jackson stay within the court’s reach, is the same worry behind this week’s demand for two extra sureties.

The Autopsy That Didn’t Count

The defense’s biggest setback concerned the forensic evidence. Criminal Court “A” had authorized forensic investigator Dr. Rockefeller F. Cooper II to work on the case for the defense. Prosecutors argued that his registration as a Forensic Medico-Legal Death Investigator did not make him a licensed pathologist.

On May 26, Judge Willie agreed. He declared Dr. Cooper’s autopsy null and void and inadmissible. He let stand the rest of Dr. Cooper’s work, including crime-scene documentation, evidence collection, materials analysis, and witness interviews.

The ruling did not settle the main question. The prosecution still has to prove, with admissible evidence, what caused Toni’s injuries and whether anything Jackson did legally contributed to her death.

Waiting for the Reports

The State has also been criticized for delays. On June 23, the day that would have been Toni’s birthday and their anniversary, Jackson publicly demanded the official autopsy and toxicology reports. He said the families could not repatriate her remains without them.

On July 24, prosecutors reportedly asked Criminal Court “A” for more time, saying the reports were not yet in their case file. The delay raised questions about how ready the State was to prosecute such a serious case.

For Toni’s family, the need is simple: to know how she died, and to bury her.

Jackson’s Defense

Jackson has consistently denied causing his wife’s death. He has suggested that some of her injuries may have come from cardiopulmonary resuscitation by medical staff. He has questioned the credibility of the investigation and said authorities are targeting him because he criticizes the government.

Those are defense claims. They do not resolve the charges. The burden remains on the prosecution to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt.

A Test for the State

The 90-day leave is a test for the prosecution and for the courts. By demanding enforceable guarantees, the State has shown it takes the risk of Jackson not returning seriously. The court has made clear the trip is not a way out of the criminal process.

The larger task falls to prosecutors: keeping the case moving, securing the forensic evidence and making sure Toni’s family is not lost among the procedural fights.

Access to medical care is a fundamental right. So is the public’s right to a credible justice process, in which a woman’s violent death is fully investigated and decided on the evidence.

Jackson is due back by February 17, 2027. Until then, Republic of Liberia, by and through the Ministry of Justice, versus Samuel P. Jackson remains pending before Criminal Court “B.” The allegations are unproven, and Toni Khumalo Jackson’s family is still waiting for answers.

World.title: COP31 Cover Draft Raises Climate Finance Questions as Liberia Seeks Support for Implementation
World.content:
Delegates gather for negotiations at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, where countries are discussing climate finance, adaptation and the transition away from fossil fuels. Photo: UNFCCC

Summary

A draft COP31 political agreement proposes raising annual adaptation finance to US$120 billion by 2035, while countries remain divided over funding and fossil fuel commitments.

African negotiators are pressing for climate finance promises to be adequately funded, transparently tracked and delivered on fair terms.

Liberia faces questions over implementation, with about US$360 million in climate finance commitments under its previous climate plan still undisbursed as of December 2024.

By Aria Deemie

A draft political agreement at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference proposes that developed countries keep their promise to increase annual adaptation finance for developing countries to US$120 billion by 2035, accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels and expanding electricity’s share of global energy use.



The document , known as a cover decision, is intended to capture the conference’s broad political priorities. Its first draft, released by the COP31 presidency on November 16, also proposes a global target for electricity to account for 35 percent of final energy use by 2035. However, the text contains competing formulations on fossil fuels and other issues, and the presidency has stressed that it does not represent an agreed position.

“Africa is not here to renegotiate promises; we are here to ensure they are delivered. Every climate finance commitment must be adequately funded, transparently tracked and delivered on fair terms,” Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, said in a statement published on the group’s official Facebook page .

Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, has called for climate finance commitments to be adequately funded, transparently tracked and delivered on fair terms. Photo: AGN

The remarks come as the African Group of Negotiators continues to push for stronger climate finance commitments at COP31. Amoah had been scheduled to brief journalists on November 14 on the first week’s negotiations and Africa’s expectations for the second week, but the planned press conference was cancelled.

As negotiations enter their second week in Antalya, Türkiye, Liberia is pressing for predictable climate finance and adaptation support. Civil society groups are questioning whether the proposed cover decision will help secure those commitments or distract from the detailed negotiations needed to deliver them. For Liberia, the issue is especially urgent because much of its climate target depends on international support, while funding for existing commitments remains undelivered.



The US$120 billion adaptation finance proposal is among the most significant parts of the draft. It seeks to give a specific annual amount and a 2035 deadline to the previously agreed goal of tripling adaptation finance. The draft also proposes a time-bound pathway for delivering the target and a method that accounts for the grant value of climate finance, rather than treating loans as equivalent to grants.

The scale of the need is much greater. The draft cites an estimated US$305 billion in annual adaptation needs for developing countries by 2035. International public adaptation finance stood at between US$28 billion and US$32 billion in 2024. Even reaching US$120 billion would therefore cover less than a third of the estimated requirement.

The draft also calls for faster action to phase out fossil fuels, including an immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems. It welcomes roadmaps developed under Brazil’s COP30 presidency for the transition away from fossil fuels and ending deforestation. But it also includes language reaffirming the earlier commitment to transition away from fossil fuels, leaving room for disagreement over how strongly the final decision should address the issue.

The proposals are not final decisions. In an accompanying note, the presidency said the draft was intended to reflect the range of views expressed by countries, not consensus. It added that every element remained open for discussion, including whether it should appear in the final document.

The disagreement is not only about what the document says, but whether attention to a broad political declaration is taking negotiators away from the formal discussions where countries are expected to resolve outstanding issues.

“We think that this cover decision is directing us, and the parties more importantly, towards the wrong place instead of the decision-making rooms, or instead of the negotiation rooms,” said Jacobo Ocharan, speaking at a media briefing organized by Climate Action Network International , a global network of civil society organizations working on climate change.

The network warned that the focus on the cover decision could divert attention from negotiations on climate finance, adaptation and a just transition. It also raised concerns that announcements presented as climate finance during the first week had brought very little new public funding.

Rebecca Thissen, who spoke on climate finance at the briefing, said developed countries were expected to present new climate finance plans after the previous funding period ended in 2025. She questioned whether the Climate Finance Work Programme would focus on developed countries’ obligations under the Paris Agreement or broaden into discussions about private investment and contributions from other countries.

The African Group of Negotiators has also been pushing for climate finance to remain central to the conference outcome. In a November 12 interview with the group’s chair, Amoah said the group wanted progress on the finance work program and the goal of tripling adaptation finance. He said countries had already established plans and processes for climate action, but implementation depended on finance, technology and capacity.

The group had submitted three proposals for separate agenda items at COP31, including one on tripling adaptation finance, one on trade-related climate measures and another on financing arrangements under the Green Climate Fund. None was adopted as a standalone agenda item, although the presidency indicated that some issues would be considered through other negotiating tracks.

Amoah also questioned the proposed 35-by-35 electrification target, saying a global target should account for countries’ different starting points. He said the African group was not opposed to electrification but wanted access to electricity to be prioritized alongside the transition to cleaner energy.

“For us in Africa, access to energy is the most important thing and then clean energy under this goal,” he told African Arguments.

For Liberia, the debate over finance is not abstract. The country’s updated climate plan targets a 64 percent reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2035. But 54 percentage points of that target depend on international support, making external finance and technical assistance essential to delivering much of the commitment.

About US$360 million in climate finance commitments under Liberia’s previous climate plan remained undisbursed as of December 2024. The outstanding amount raises questions about whether new commitments made at COP31 will translate into projects and support on the ground.

“COP31 for Liberia is more about implementation,” said Benjamin S. Karmorh Jr., the Environmental Protection Agency’s Chief Technical Advisor, at a meeting at the Liberia Pavilion on Monday, November 16.

Members of Liberia’s delegation brief journalists on the week’s developments and Liberia’s participation at COP31 during a meeting at the Liberia Pavilion on Monday. Photo: Aria Deemie

Arthur Becker, the agency’s Director for Multilateral Environmental Agreements, said Liberia was seeking predictable funding to support adaptation and accelerate preparation of its National Adaptation Plan, which sets out how the country will prepare for climate risks.

Becker said Liberia had been informed during a side event involving the United Nations Development Programme, the National Adaptation Plan Global Network and Brazil’s COP30 presidency that it was among countries included in a three-year funding window for adaptation planning, supported by Ireland, Germany and Canada. Details on the amount available to Liberia and when the funding would be disbursed were not provided.

But planning is only part of the challenge. Liberia has also faced delays in projects intended to strengthen its response to climate impacts, including the Climate Information System and the Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project, which includes coastal protection work for vulnerable communities.The effects of inadequate adaptation support are already visible among communities exposed to flooding and unpredictable rainfall. Farmers who depend on rainfall need timely weather information to make decisions about when to plant and how to protect their crops. At COP31, an Environmental Protection Agency official announced plans for about 10 new automated weather stations in agriculture-producing counties over the next 12 months.
