Becker said Liberia had been informed during a side event involving the United Nations Development Programme, the National Adaptation Plan Global Network and Brazil’s COP30 presidency that it was among countries included in a three-year funding window for adaptation planning, supported by Ireland, Germany and Canada. Details on the amount available to Liberia and when the funding would be disbursed were not provided.

But planning is only part of the challenge. Liberia has also faced delays in projects intended to strengthen its response to climate impacts, including the Climate Information System and the Monrovia Metropolitan Climate Resilience Project, which includes coastal protection work for vulnerable communities.The effects of inadequate adaptation support are already visible among communities exposed to flooding and unpredictable rainfall. Farmers who depend on rainfall need timely weather information to make decisions about when to plant and how to protect their crops. At COP31, an Environmental Protection Agency official announced plans for about 10 new automated weather stations in agriculture-producing counties over the next 12 months.

Farmers in Liberia depend heavily on rainfall for agricultural activities, making access to reliable weather forecasts important for decisions about planting and protecting crops. Photo: World Bank

Adaptation finance was also a major concern at the civil society briefing.

“We will not let adaptation finance be traded off again,” said Daniel Rossell of the Talanoa Institute, referring to the commitment made at COP30 in Belém, Brazil, to triple adaptation finance.

Rossell questioned how countries could implement indicators under the Global Goal on Adaptation, an international framework for measuring progress in preparing for climate impacts, without the financial resources to act.

“How are developing countries supposed to implement indicators with a hundred metadata sheets of indicators and no means of implementation?” he asked.

The proposed Belém-Antalya Mechanism, intended to advance discussions on a just transition, is another area of disagreement. A just transition means moving towards a low-carbon economy while protecting workers and communities whose jobs and livelihoods may be affected.

“This is basically like being offered a seat at the table with no food, no plates, no cutlery, and very bad wine,” said Kuda Manjonjo of Power Shift Africa, criticizing the draft negotiating text for not providing enough practical support for meaningful participation. He warned that without resources and clear commitments, the proposed mechanism could become “an empty shell.”

Liberia is also following negotiations on carbon markets and climate finance. “Don’t tie adaptation around the sale of credit,” said Elijah Whapoe, who presented the country’s negotiating updates, warning against making adaptation support dependent on carbon-credit trading.

Whapoe outlined Liberia’s engagement with Article 6 of the Paris Agreement , which sets out ways countries can cooperate on climate action, including through the trading of emissions reductions and approaches that do not involve carbon credits. He said Liberia had not registered a non-market approach under Article 6.8, the provision that allows countries to cooperate on climate action without relying on carbon markets or trading carbon credits.

On the Climate Finance Work Programme , a two-year process for discussing how developed countries should provide climate finance to developing countries, he said Liberia was engaging through the Group of 77 and China, a coalition of developing countries, the African Group of Negotiators, which represents African countries, and the Least Developed Countries group, which represents the world’s poorest countries. Liberia wants the program to move forward without new language that could weaken its focus on developed countries’ financial obligations, he said.

As negotiations continue, Liberia and other climate-vulnerable countries are seeking an outcome that moves beyond political declarations and provides the resources needed to implement their climate plans.

“The conference is responsible to finance adaptation,” Whapoe said.

This story was produced as part of the COP31 Climate Change Media Partnership ,a journalism fellowship organized by Internews’ Earth Journalism Network, Informed Earth and the Stanley Center for Peace and Security.

World.title: Liberia: Despite US$50 Million Disbursement, IMF Warns Boakai Administration over ‘Macro-Critical’ Corruption, Weak Governance
World.content:
MONROVIA – Liberia’s economic recovery is increasingly presenting a complicated picture of progress and institutional vulnerability. On one hand, the administration of President Joseph Boakai has secured fresh financial support from the International Monetary Fund, recorded improvements in domestic revenue collection and maintained economic growth despite mounting international economic pressures.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

On the other hand, the same international institution providing the country with millions of dollars in additional financing has raised serious concerns about corruption, weak governance, inadequate institutional capacity and delays in implementing reforms intended to strengthen public accountability.



The contradiction is significant. While the latest IMF assessment has opened the door for approximately US$50 million in additional disbursements to Liberia, its accompanying country report delivers a sobering message about the country’s governance environment that economic growth alone cannot guarantee sustainable development when public institutions remain vulnerable to corruption, transparency is limited and accountability mechanisms struggle to perform their statutory responsibilities.

At the center of the assessment is the IMF’s characterization of systemic corruption and weak rule of law as “macro-critical” problems. The terminology is particularly important because it places corruption beyond the traditional understanding of an ethical or administrative failure. It identifies corruption as a direct threat to Liberia’s economic stability, investment environment, government revenue generation and the country’s ability to deliver inclusive development.

In practical terms, the Fund is warning that Liberia’s economic gains could remain fragile if the government fails to address institutional weaknesses that undermine confidence in public administration.

The IMF Executive Board completed the fourth review of Liberia’s Extended Credit Facility arrangement and the first review of its Resilience and Sustainability Facility on September 28, 2026. The decision unlocked SDR19.3 million, approximately US$26.2 million, under the ECF arrangement and SDR17.62 million, approximately US$23.96 million, under the RSF arrangement.



Combined, the two disbursements amount to approximately US$50.16 million.

The financial support is important for a country facing declining donor assistance, high infrastructure demands, external financing pressures and a narrow export base. It also demonstrates that Liberia has maintained sufficient progress in several areas of its economic programme to continue receiving support from the Fund.

However, the accompanying assessment makes clear that satisfying selected economic programme requirements is not the same as resolving the governance problems that have historically weakened Liberia’s public institutions.

The IMF’s concerns are particularly troubling because they come at a time when the Boakai administration has repeatedly presented governance reform, public-sector accountability and the fight against corruption as central pillars of its development agenda.

The government’s ARREST Agenda for Inclusive Development is intended to address longstanding challenges in infrastructure, agriculture, roads, education, sanitation and economic transformation. Yet, the success of those ambitions depends heavily on whether public resources are protected from misuse, government institutions operate transparently and officials entrusted with public responsibilities are held accountable. Without those conditions, increased revenue and international financial assistance could fail to produce the development outcomes expected by ordinary Liberians.

Corruption Becomes an Economic Threat

One of the most consequential findings in the IMF report concerns the country’s anti-corruption framework, particularly the declining compliance with asset-declaration requirements among public officials. According to the Fund, compliance declined by 19 percentage points compared with the previous year. The development represents a setback for a mechanism designed to help identify potential conflicts of interest, unexplained wealth and possible abuse of public office.

Asset declaration is one of the principal instruments through which governments establish accountability among officials entrusted with public resources. It allows the relevant authorities to examine whether the wealth and financial interests of public officials are consistent with their legitimate sources of income.

However, Liberia’s system continues to face legal and institutional obstacles. Under the existing arrangement, publication of public officials’ asset declarations requires court authorization. Proposed amendments intended to remove this requirement have been submitted to the Legislature but remain unapproved.

The IMF has urged the authorities to remove those legal barriers, strengthen verification procedures and establish effective enforcement mechanisms. The recommendation places responsibility on both the executive and legislative branches. Although the administration may express its commitment to transparency, meaningful reform requires the passage of legislation that gives accountability institutions the necessary authority to operate effectively.

The issue is particularly important because the LACC remains one of the principal institutions expected to investigate corruption and promote integrity in public service. Yet the IMF says the commission continues to operate under significant resource constraints, despite increased allocations to integrity institutions in the 2026 fiscal budget.

The Fund’s position is that the LACC must be fully operationalized, adequately funded and equipped to enforce accountability. This means providing the institution with sufficient financial resources, investigative personnel, technical equipment and operational independence to pursue allegations of corruption without unnecessary institutional obstacles. The concern raises a difficult question for the Boakai administration: how can the government expect an anti-corruption institution to deliver meaningful results when the international financial institution assessing its performance says it lacks the resources necessary to execute its mandate effectively?

The effectiveness of an anti-graft commission cannot be measured simply by the existence of its headquarters, the appointment of commissioners or the number of public statements issued against corruption. Its real performance must be reflected in credible investigations, verification of asset declarations, prosecution of substantiated cases and the recovery of public resources lost through corrupt practices. The IMF’s findings suggest that Liberia still has considerable work to do in this regard.

The commission’s own third-quarter 2026 report also provides an indication of the challenges confronting its operations. It recorded 237 officials as non-compliant with asset-declaration requirements at the end of the quarter and identified investigative and prosecutorial capacity as continuing institutional constraints.

Audit Findings and Unanswered Questions About Public Money

Beyond asset declarations, the IMF has identified weaknesses in the management and reconciliation of government revenue, raising additional questions about the transparency of public financial transactions. The report says recent audits identified discrepancies between revenues recorded in the Tax Administration System and amounts actually credited to consolidated revenue accounts.

The finding is significant because government revenue is expected to pass through transparent accounting and reconciliation procedures that allow authorities, auditors and citizens to determine how much money has been collected and where it has been deposited.

Any discrepancy between recorded collections and actual credits to government accounts requires prompt investigation and clarification. The IMF has consequently emphasized stronger reconciliation procedures and called for the publication of outstanding special audit reports, including the audit of historical domestic debt covering the period 1980 to 2024 and the audit of the National Social Security and Welfare Corporation.

The publication of these reports would allow the public to understand the findings, assess whether irregularities occurred and determine what corrective actions government institutions have taken. For Liberia, where public confidence in the management of national resources has repeatedly been undermined by allegations of corruption and financial mismanagement, the timely publication of audit findings is essential.

An audit that identifies irregularities but is never followed by corrective action risks becoming another administrative document with little practical impact. The IMF’s concerns extend to the Central Bank of Liberia, where implementation of recommendations arising from the General Auditing Commission’s compliance audit and the Kroll forensic audit has progressed more slowly than anticipated.

Although the Central Bank has started reconciling suspense accounts and strengthening oversight of financial guarantees, the Fund says outstanding safeguards recommendations must be accelerated. The objective is to bring the institution’s governance and internal-control framework fully into conformity with the Central Bank Act.

These recommendations are important because the Central Bank occupies a critical position in the country’s financial system. Its credibility influences monetary stability, confidence in the Liberian dollar, banking-sector performance and the country’s capacity to manage external economic pressures. Weak internal controls at such an institution could expose public resources to unnecessary risks and undermine confidence in the wider financial system.

The IMF’s assessment therefore suggests that governance reform must extend beyond ministries and agencies to include institutions responsible for monetary policy and financial regulation.

The US State Department Adds to Liberia’s Governance Concerns

The IMF’s warning is not the only recent international assessment drawing attention to corruption and institutional weaknesses in Liberia. A November 2026 assessment by the United States Department of State, contained in its 2026 Investment Climate Statement on Liberia, has similarly highlighted corruption, judicial inefficiencies, weak institutional capacity and limited transparency as significant obstacles to the country’s investment environment.

The report presents a mixed picture of Liberia’s economic prospects. It recognizes opportunities in mining, agriculture, energy, infrastructure and other sectors, but warns that persistent governance problems continue to undermine the country’s attractiveness to foreign investors.

Of particular concern is the State Department’s assessment that corruption remains one of the most significant obstacles confronting businesses operating in Liberia. The report says investors have raised concerns about unofficial payments, charges outside investment agreements and alleged extortion involving public officials. It also identifies weaknesses in public procurement, the legal and regulatory framework and the enforcement of existing laws.

The assessment further raises concerns about the judicial environment, including lengthy commercial disputes, difficulties enforcing court decisions and allegations of bribery involving court officials. The State Department’s report describes corruption as a

major impediment to democratic consolidation and economic growth, while identifying judicial delays and weak institutional capacity as continuing investment risks. The implications are particularly serious for a country seeking to attract foreign investment to finance infrastructure development, create employment and diversify its economy.

Investors generally require predictable regulations, transparent procurement procedures, reliable judicial protection and confidence that government agreements will be respected. When businesses believe that public contracts may be influenced by political connections, that unofficial payments are necessary to obtain government services or that commercial disputes may remain unresolved for years, investment decisions become more difficult.

Such conditions can increase the cost of doing business, discourage new investors and reduce the potential for employment creation. The State Department’s assessment therefore complements the IMF’s warning. While the IMF focuses on the relationship between corruption and macroeconomic stability, the American assessment highlights how similar institutional weaknesses affect the country’s ability to attract and retain investment.

The two assessments point toward a common conclusion that the country’s economic potential is substantial, but the credibility of its institutions remains a major obstacle to realizing that potential. It is also important to recognize that the State Department report acknowledges opportunities and reforms rather than portraying Liberia as an economy without prospects. Its concerns are directed at the institutional conditions under which those opportunities must be pursued.

For the Boakai administration, however, the timing of the assessment is uncomfortable. The government has repeatedly promised to restore public confidence, improve the investment climate and demonstrate that public officials will be held accountable for their actions.

The IMF’s latest assessment has therefore placed an important responsibility before the Boakai administration to ensure that the financial support Liberia continues to receive is matched by equally strong commitment to institutional reform. The US$50 million may strengthen the government’s immediate financial position, but it cannot independently resolve the governance weaknesses identified by the Fund.

The ultimate measure of the administration’s success will not be how much international financing it secures, but whether it can demonstrate that public money is protected, corruption is confronted, institutions are strengthened and economic growth produces visible benefits for ordinary Liberians.

World.title: Liberia: Judge Orders Gender Minister to Settle Rape Survivor’s School Fees by Nov. 30
World.content:
MONROVIA – More than two years after a 14-year-old girl was raped and made pregnant by a man who lived in her yard, the Liberian government has received an unusual warning from the bench: pay the survivor’s school fees, or face contempt of court.

By Willie N. Tokpah

Judge Wesseh Alphonsus Wesseh Sr., the assigned circuit judge of Criminal Court “E”, has rejected a request by the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection to put off paying the survivor’s school costs until the 2027 budget year. He gave the ministry until November 30 to pay the fees and file the receipts with the court. Criminal Court “E” is Liberia’s special court for sexual and gender-based violence.



The ruling puts new pressure on President Joseph Nyuma Boakai’s government to show that it protects vulnerable children. It also raises a hard question: how can the state convict a man of abusing a child and then fail to help that child rebuild her life?

The Court Rejects the Budget Excuse

The court sent its directive on November 17 through Clerk of Court Abraham Richards. It came after a conference between the judge and government officials about what the state still owes the survivor and her baby.

The meeting followed a November 11 summons, also signed by Richards, that ordered two officials to appear on November 16 at 10:00 a.m.: Acting Minister of Justice and Attorney General Betty M. Lamin-Blamo and Gender Minister Gbeme Horace-Kollie. They were told to explain how the government was supporting the survivor and her child.



At the conference, representatives of the Gender Ministry reportedly said the government’s 2026 budget year was nearly over. Liberia’s budget year now follows the calendar year. They asked for time to meet the court’s order through the 2027 national budget.

Judge Wesseh refused. According to accounts of the meeting, he said the girl’s education could not wait because the government’s budget year was ending. He reportedly called the matter personal and serious, and asked the officials whether they would accept the same treatment if the girl were their own daughter or relative.

The written directive says the ministry must file payment receipts with the clerk of Criminal Court “E” to prove it has paid. If it misses the deadline, it may be held in contempt. Minister Horace-Kollie could then face further proceedings, subject to due process.

The receipt requirement matters. It means the court will judge compliance by proof of payment, not by promises or administrative explanations. The contempt warning also turns a routine dispute over government spending into a possible clash between the judiciary and the executive.

A Girl, a Knife and a Life Interrupted

The case began in October 2024 in Jallah’s Town, a community in Montserrado County, which includes the capital, Monrovia.

According to the indictment, Victor Eze, then 35, sexually assaulted a 14-year-old girl who lived in the same yard. Prosecutors said he entered the room where she was sleeping, threatened her with a knife and raped her. She was injured and taken to JDJ Memorial Hospital for examination and treatment.

Eze was arrested on December 9, 2024, and charged with statutory rape under Section 14.70 of Liberia’s New Penal Law. Under Liberia’s 2005 rape law, rape of a child under 18 is a first-degree felony that can carry up to life in prison.

On June 11, 2025, Eze pleaded guilty. When the court questioned him about the plea, he admitted that the girl had given birth to a child as a result of the abuse. He said he was willing to support the mother and child. The court found that his plea was voluntary and that he understood the charge, and convicted him.

Gender Minister Gbeme Horace Kollie

On October 7, 2025, Judge Wesseh sentenced Eze to five years in prison, including the nine months he had already spent in pretrial detention. He must serve the remaining four years and three months in a Liberian prison.

The conviction held the offender to account. But the survivor’s ordeal did not end with the sentence. She is now a teenage mother, raising a child while trying to recover from the crime. She is reportedly still out of school, even though schools across Liberia have reopened.

Help That Fell Short

The question of support for the survivor and her child came up during the original trial. Court records mention US$50 paid through the Ministry of Justice’s Sexual and Gender-Based Violence Crimes Unit. The court also noted help from the Gender Ministry, including seed money for a small business and support through a program involving SOS Children’s Villages, an international child-welfare charity.

The new court order shows that this help has not covered her schooling. The issue is not whether the government did anything. It is whether what it did was enough, lasted long enough and met the court’s expectations and the child’s needs.

A small cash payment cannot replace an education. A small-business grant cannot replace schooling, counselling, healthcare and protection for a teenage mother and her baby. For a girl who was only 14 when she was attacked, school is more than a government benefit. It is her best chance to regain some normal life, become independent and avoid being trapped in poverty.

A Promise Put to the Test

The case is a test for the Boakai administration, which took office in January 2024. Boakai promised a government that would put human dignity, social protection and accountability first, and his administration has pledged to fight violence against women and children.

Sexual violence is a long-standing problem in Liberia, a West African nation of about 5.5 million people that is still rebuilding after civil wars that ended in 2003. Rape is among the most commonly reported serious crimes in the country, and many of the victims are children. In 2020, then-President George Manneh Weah declared rape a national emergency after a surge in reported cases.

The question now goes beyond whether Liberia can arrest, prosecute and jail offenders. It is whether the state keeps protecting the child after the sentence is handed down and public attention moves on.

Cllr. Betty Lamie Blamo

The Gender Ministry’s legal mandate is to protect and promote the welfare of women, children and vulnerable people. Yet here it has had to explain to a court why a rape survivor’s school fees have not been paid. The ministry says the budget year is almost over, and that may describe a real administrative problem. But it does not meet the girl’s immediate needs. The school calendar does not wait for the next budget, and neither does the state’s duty to a child whose life has been upended by sexual violence.

The Ministry of Justice, which took part in the earlier proceedings and was also summoned, is under scrutiny too. By summoning both ministries, Judge Wesseh signalled that he sees the survivor’s welfare as a shared government responsibility, not one that agencies can pass back and forth.

When the Executive Must Answer to the Judiciary

The order also raises a wider governance issue. Under Liberia’s constitution, the courts exercise judicial power, and the executive must obey lawful court orders. A ministry cannot treat a court directive as optional advice.

That gives the judge’s warning significance beyond this one case. It shows that the courts are willing to hold government agencies to account when their actions, or failure to act, harm vulnerable citizens. Contempt proceedings against a sitting cabinet minister would be a serious step, and any such case would have to follow proper legal procedure and give the minister due process.

November 30: A Deadline for the Government

The immediate obligation is clear: the fees must be paid by November 30, 2026, and the receipts filed with Criminal Court “E”.

But the government’s commitment to the survivor and her child must go further than a single court order. A five-year sentence may punish the offender, but it cannot send the survivor back to school or provide for her child. The state’s duty should be measured not only by how long the offender spends in prison, but by whether the survivor can return to class, get counselling and healthcare, and raise her child safely. That requires sustained government support.

For a girl whose childhood was cut short by sexual violence, justice cannot end with the conviction of the man who attacked her. A government that promises to protect its children cannot abandon them once the courtroom doors close.

World.title: Editorial: Stop Charging Liberians for a Scanner That Doesn’t Exist
World.content:
The gap costs traders and consumers money and leaves Liberia’s main seaport open to drug and arms smugglers. FPA urges the NPA, the LRA and the government to suspend scanning charges, publish a timeline, find a stopgap and make 24-hour operations real.

ON MONDAY, LIBERIA Revenue Authority Commissioner General Dorbor Jallah told the Senate there is “no cargo scanning that goes on at the Freeport at the moment” because the port “does not have a scanner in place.”

THAT SHOULD ALARM every Liberian who buys a bag of rice, a gallon of oil, or a tin of milk.



THE FREEPORT OF Monrovia is the country’s front door. Nearly everything Liberians eat, wear and build with passes through it. Yet the front door has no lock and no window. Customs officers cannot see inside the containers arriving every day. Meanwhile, importers say they are being billed for scanning that, by the government’s own account, is not happening.

A Fee for a Service That Isn’t Delivered

LIBERIA’S SMALL AND medium-sized importers are already stretched. Many bring in goods on bank loans. Every day a container sits at the port, interest piles up. On top of that come fees from the terminal operator, from MEDTECH and under the CTN/GTMS cargo-tracking system, charged before their goods arrive and before they are released.

IF ANY PART of those charges is for scanning, it is money paid for nothing. That is unfair to the trader, and the cost does not stop with the trader. It is passed on to the market woman, the taxi driver and the family in Paynesville or Ganta who pay more for the same goods. In a country where food inflation stands at 11.1 per cent, according to the Central Bank of Liberia, ordinary people cannot afford to subsidise a broken system.



A Security Gap We Cannot Ignore

THIS IS NOT only about money. A port without a scanner is an invitation. Liberia has made major cocaine seizures this year, and the country is struggling to shake the reputation that it is a transit point for international drug traffickers. Without scanners, customs and security officers must rely on paperwork, tip-offs and manual searches. That is slow for honest businesses and easy for smugglers to get around.

A COUNTRY SERIOUS about fighting drugs, arms trafficking and smuggling does not leave its main seaport blind.

The Warnings Were There

NATIONAL PORT AUTHORITY Managing Director Sekou Dukuly told senators that the World Bank warned Liberia in 2017 to expand its port infrastructure. Neighbouring countries listened, he said, and Liberia did not. He called the past six years “a complete catastrophe.”

WE AGREE THAT the crisis did not begin last month. But the public is not interested in assigning blame between administrations. Liberians want to know when it will be fixed. Dukuly urged lawmakers to take “politics and propaganda” out of the matter. The best way to do that is with clear facts and firm dates.

What Must Happen Now

WE URGE THE National Port Authority, the Liberia Revenue Authority and the Boakai administration to act on six points:

1. SUSPEND AND AUDIT scanning charges. Any fee linked to scanning should be suspended at once until a scanner is working. The LRA and NPA should publish what has been collected under that heading and say whether it will be refunded or credited to importers.

2. PUBLISH A TIMELINE. When will the new cargo facility be finished? When will the scanner from China arrive, be installed and be running? Liberians deserve dates, not “once we dedicate the facility.”

3. BE OPEN ABOUT the procurement. The public should know the cost of the scanner, the supplier and how the contract was awarded, in line with Liberia’s procurement law.

4. FIND A STOPGAP. Waiting months for a permanent facility is not acceptable. The government should explore leasing mobile scanners or seeking help from partners, as other ports in the region have done, to cover the gap.

5. MAKE 24-HOUR OPERATIONS real. Promises of round-the-clock customs and banking have been made before. The government should name a start date and get banks, customs, shipping lines and brokers working the same hours.

6. LEGISLATIVE FOLLOW-THROUGH. The Senate deserves credit for calling this hearing. It must now follow up with regular progress reports, so that this testimony does not end up as one more forgotten promise.

Restore Sanity at the Port

THE FREEPORT SHOULD be an engine of commerce. Today, for too many businesses, it is a place where money and time disappear. Traders are not asking for favours. They are asking for a port that works, fees that are fair, and a government that keeps its word.

THE SCANNER GAP was admitted in public, before the Senate. Now it must be fixed in public, with deadlines that Liberians can hold their leaders to. Until then, every day of delay is a tax on the poorest Liberians, and they have paid enough

World.title: Public workers urged to sensitise communities on government programmes
World.content:
Lusaka Province Minister, Obvious Mwaliteta, has called on public service workers in Rufunsa district to sensitize and educate the communities on the Government’s achievements in the implementation of developmental programmes and the Grow Zambia Agenda.

Speaking when he interacted with the workers in the district, Mr Mwaliteta says the government has done a lot in the last five years, in terms of debt restructuring, infrastructure development and social protection programmes which people need to understand for them to participate effectively in national development.

“You as public service workers have a responsibility to explain to the people government programmes being implemented so that they participate effectively in the Grow Zambia Agenda”, he said.

Mr Mwaliteta further called on the workers to desist from partisan politics, as time for politicking is gone and that it is time to work and develop the country.

The Provincial Minister said the Government remains committed to taking development to all parts of the country and he called on public service workers to support the national development agenda without engaging in partisan politics.

Mr Mwaliteta emphasized that public service workers had an important role to play in ensuring that Government programmes and policies were effectively implemented for the benefit of the people.

Meanwhile, the Provincial Minister expressed sadness at the slow pace Rufunsa was developing and challenged the Rufunsa Town Council to maximize the utilization of the Constituency Development Fund (CDF) to accelerate development in the district.

Mr Mwaliteta said it is unfortunate that Rufunsa town, which is along the Great East road has continued to appear underdeveloped despite the Government allocating resources through CDF to improve the living standards of local communities.

“You, as the Local Authority, have been given all the resources in human and capital and therefore, you must be proactive and plan for your town so that you attract investors”, said Mr Mwaliteta.

He called on the planners under the council to plan together with Ward Development Committees (WDCs) and implement sustainable projects that will make the town grow.

Mr Mwaliteta urged the local authority to be proactive in identifying development opportunities and opening up land to attract investors who could contribute to the district’s economic growth.

Meanwhile, Rufunsa District Commissioner, Richard Mabena, and Rufunsa Council Chairperson, Irene Chikatula, reaffirmed their commitment to working with local communities and other stakeholders to promote development in the district.

Mr Mabena and Ms Chikatula pledged to continue collaborating with the people to ensure that Government programmes were implemented and development initiatives translated into tangible benefits.

And Lusaka Province Permanent Secretary, Joe Kalusa, who accompanied the Minister, urged the public service workers to remain focused on their responsibilities and contribute to the effective delivery of public services.

World.title: Cash for work to benefit all- Mwiluzi Councillor
World.content:
Mwiluzi Ward Councillor, Patrick Chomba, has reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that Cash for Work benefits all.

Mr Chomba says to take advantage of the initiative, the ward plans to construct an office for the councilor in the ward.

Mr Chomba said the proposed office is an important infrastructure project that will not only benefit the current councilor but also serve future office barriers.

He noted that the facility will provide a neutral and accessible platform where residents can freely present their developmental concerns and engage with their elected representative on issues affecting their communities.

Mr Chomba has observed that having a permanent councilor’s office will strengthen community engagement and improve communication between residents and their local leadership.

He has since called on residents of Mwiluzi Ward to propose a suitable and neutral location where the office can be constructed, emphasising the importance of community involvement in identifying the site.

Mr Chomba further said his commitment to the Cash for Work initiative is aimed at ensuring that the programme translates into meaningful development and benefits for the people of Mwiluzi Ward.

World.title: ZAPD to issue disability cards in Chilanga District
World.content:
The Zambia Agency for Persons with Disabilities (ZAPD) in Chilanga district, will be conducting an exercise to issue disability cards to persons with disabilities.

Chilanga ZAPD Chairperson, Shadreck Kankwala, says disability cards are very important as they help the cardholders to access government social protection programmes.

Mr Kankwala said the cards also help persons with disabilities to support applications for assistive devices such as wheelchairs among other devices.

He noted that persons with disability are exempted from certain taxes upon producing the disability card when eligible.

“The disability card assists the individuals in applications for Social Cash Transfers, education bursaries, empowerment programmes, and act as official proof of disability’’, he stated.

Mr Kankwala points out that the cards also help the government to maintain accurate disability statistics for planning and service delivery.

The Chairperson explained that, the cards will be disbursed on Friday 20th November 2026, at Chilanga Primary School Library, on Saturday 21st November 2026 in Mwembeshi Ward at Machacha Ground, in Nakachenje Ward at the Mini Hospital and Kalundu Primary in Kalundu Ward.

He said other cards will be disbursed on Sunday 22nd November, 2026 at Apollo from 08:00 hours to 16:00 hours.

Mr Kankwala added that all persons with disabilities are encouraged to visit the designated centers on the dates and times indicated, with emphasis that the cards are free of charge.

World.title: Government hands over infrastructure at Malundu Community School
World.content:
Government has handed over school infrastructure worth K2.8 million to Malundu Community School in Chisamba district.

Previously, lessons were being conducted under a tree and in some cases neighboring churches.

And speaking during the handover ceremony, District Commissioner, Joel Mboyoma, who thanked Build It International for constructing the school, said the infrastructure will improve the learning environment at the school, and that learners will be taking lessons in a dignified environment.

Mr Mboyoma noted that the school did not have adequate infrastructure adding that some pupils would take lessons in a mud structure which he said was not conducive.

“These are not merely buildings. They are investments in human potential,” Mr Mboyoma said.

He called on the school management, parents and learners to take responsibility for maintaining the infrastructure so that it can benefit future generations.

Earlier, District Education Board Secretary, Florence Lubeya, said the new facilities will contribute to improved learning outcomes by providing learners with better classrooms, learning resources and appropriate sanitation.

Ms Lubeya said inadequate infrastructure had previously limited the school, with some learners having to travel long distances to continue their education.

“When children have safe classrooms, access to learning resources, appropriate sanitation facilities, and supportive learning environments, they are more likely to stay in school and achieve their full potential,” Ms Lubeya said.

Meanwhile, Build It International Board Chairperson, Lucie Kasanga, said the organisation was pleased to see the transformation of the school following the partnership between Build It International, Government and the community.

“Today, standing here together, we can see what partnership and community action can achieve,” Ms Kasanga said.

A Grade Six pupil at the school, Taonga Phiri, thanked Build It International for supporting the construction of the new classroom and ablution blocks.

Taonga said learners previously had to study under trees and faced challenges accessing sanitation facilities.

“As learners, we are humbled and excited to receive this new and beautiful classroom block and two ablution blocks. There was a time when we used to learn under trees, sitting on rough stones, while accessing sanitation facilities was also a challenge. Today, things have changed for the better,” Phiri said.

Malundu Community School, which started in 2003 with just 13 learners under early childhood education, now has more than 400 learners.

The school which has been constructed by Build It International includes three classrooms, a library, a staff room, a head teacher’s office and two ablution blocks.

World.title: NGO urges Journalists to verify stories
World.content:
A non-governmental organisation has urged Zambian journalists to remain professional in the digital media age and to stop posting unverified stories for the sake of gaining numbers on their social media pages.

The call was made during a one-day media training workshop on reintegration facilitated by the Reintegration Alliance for Formerly Incarcerated and Incarcerated Persons (RAFIIP) at Golden Peacock Hotel in Lusaka.

RAFIIP representative Charles Mafa reminded media personnel that speed and clicks must not come at the expense of accuracy, fairness and public trust.

Mr Mafa, who was also the facilitator, observed that most media houses are slowly moving away from issues of public interest and chasing anything that sparks public curiosity regardless of whether it is accurate or not.

He further urged participants to show responsibility in every story they publish by contextualising them.

“The media has a responsibility to shape society with a positive mindset by avoiding discriminatory and inaccurate stories,” Mr Mafa said.

Mr Mafa also challenged the media to play a frontline role in sensitising the community on the importance of reintegrating formerly incarcerated persons by using non-discriminatory terminologies when writing about them.

He noted with concern that many media houses have largely contributed to the failure by families and communities to accept formerly incarcerated persons and incarcerated persons due to the continued use of discriminatory words when describing them.

Mr Mafa pointed out some of the most common discriminatory words as ex-convict, prisoner, former inmate and junkies.

Reacting to the counsel, Information and Communication University Television (ICU TV) journalist Miriam Gamaani expressed appreciation to RAFIIP, saying the training workshop had been insightful.

She assured the facilitators that participants will take the knowledge learnt with high levels of seriousness.

The RAFIIP training workshop was organised to help the local media change the narrative and play a frontline role in the reintegration of persons in conflict with the law.

World.title: UTH conducts four kidney transplant operations
World.content:
The University Teaching Hospital (UTH) has performed four kidney transplant operations involving two donor-recipient pairs during its ongoing November transplant camp, as Zambia continues to strengthen local capacity in specialised medical services.

UTH Consultant Urologist and Lead Transplant Surgeon, Victor Mapulanga said the three-day camp is targeting six operations involving three donor-recipient pairs.

Dr Mapulanga said two pairs have already undergone the procedures, with the third pair scheduled for Friday.

He explained that each kidney transplant involves two operations, one to remove a kidney from the donor and another to transplant it into the recipient.

Dr Mapulanga said one of the successful procedures involved a 54-year-old father suffering from end-stage kidney disease who received a kidney from his 28-year-old son.

He said both the father and son are recovering well, adding that the transplanted kidney has already started functioning.

The second transplant involved a 43-year-old wife who donated a kidney to her 48-year-old husband, with both procedures successfully completed.

Dr Mapulanga explained that the programme conducts living-related donor kidney transplants, where a living person voluntarily donates a kidney to someone with whom they share a recognised relationship.

He clarified that the hospital does not keep kidneys in storage or source donors for patients, but instead requires patients to identify potential donors who subsequently undergo medical assessments.

Dr Mapulanga said spouses are also recognised as related donors, citing previous cases in which husbands and wives have donated kidneys to their partners.

He said the current camp is the fifth conducted under the local capacity-building programme, with the previous four camps recording two transplants each.

Dr Mapulanga disclosed that Zambia has so far conducted 10 kidney transplants under the local capacity-building programme over the past five camps, compared to 16 transplants recorded in the previous year.

He said the programme is a collaboration between the Ministry of Health, the Industrial Development Corporation (IDC) and the American College of Surgeons, which provides specialist surgeons to transfer skills to local medical personnel.

Dr Mapulanga said the initiative is expected to enable Zambian surgeons to independently conduct kidney transplant operations by mid-2027.

He explained that the programme is aimed at reducing the need to send patients to India for kidney transplant procedures, which previously required significant expenditure of public resources.

Dr Mapulanga said retaining the services locally will allow government resources to be used more efficiently while improving access to specialised healthcare for Zambians.

Meanwhile, National Coordinator for Kidney Diseases at UTH, Aggrey Mweemba said common causes of kidney failure in Zambia include high blood pressure, diabetes and HIV, as well as certain cancers, including cervical and prostate cancer.

He also warned against the prolonged and excessive use of some commonly available painkillers, such as Brufen and Diclofenac, saying they can contribute to kidney disease when abused.

Dr Mweemba further cautioned against the use of certain traditional herbal medicines, which could also damage the kidneys.

He said infections such as cholera and malaria could lead to kidney failure if they are not properly treated.

He urged members of the public to seek proper medical treatment for infections and avoid the misuse of medicines to protect their kidney health.

World.title: Ministries urged to fast-track Grow Zambia laws
World.content:
Government Ministries have been urged to work closely with the Ministry of Justice to ensure that legislation, contracts and agreements necessary for the implementation of the Grow Zambia Agenda are processed without delays.

Speaking during the handover ceremony at the Ministry of Justice in Lusaka, Minister of Justice Jack Mwiimbu called on all Ministries to collaborate with the Ministry of Justice to ensure that necessary legislation, contracts and agreements are put in place in good time.

Mr Mwiimbu further said the justice system is key to attracting tourists and investors, as security, law and order, as well as protection of investments are essential to economic development.

He also reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to upholding the rule of law and protecting citizens’ constitutional rights, including the right to petition Parliament, saying people should not be condemned for exercising their democratic rights.

Meanwhile, former Minister of Justice Princess Kasune said the Ministry had made progress in legal reforms and improving access to justice during her tenure.

She highlighted the access to Justice Programme and constitutional reforms as some of the notable achievements, while urging the Ministry to continue addressing outstanding legal and institutional matters.

World.title: Habeenzu urges youth to harness digital entrepreneurship
World.content:
Ministry of Technology and Science Permanent Secretary Brilliant Habeenzu has urged young people to embrace digital entrepreneurship as a means of creating employment and expanding Zambia’s economy.

Dr Habeenzu said the country’s expanding digital infrastructure, increased mobile and internet connectivity and the National Digital Economy Strategy present opportunities for young people to establish technology-driven businesses.

He said skills in information technology, creative digital media, e-commerce, financial technology applications and online platforms can enable young entrepreneurs to develop businesses capable of accessing markets beyond Zambia’s borders.

Speaking during the launch of Global Entrepreneurship Week 2026 at Evelyn Hone College in Lusaka, Dr Habeenzu said young people should not only aspire to secure employment but also become employers and exporters.

He said digital entrepreneurship has the potential to contribute to increased exports, improved trade balance, revenue generation and job creation.

Dr Habeenzu however, emphasised the need for a supportive entrepreneurial ecosystem, including access to finance, mentorship, equipment, markets and industry experience to help young innovators transform their ideas into viable businesses.

He has also called on businesses, financial institutions and development partners to support promising student innovations through technical expertise, product testing and business coaching.

Global Entrepreneurship Network (GEN) Zambia Director Edwin Zulu called for increased support towards young entrepreneurs to enable them to transform innovative ideas into viable businesses.

Mr Zulu said entrepreneurship plays a critical role in addressing unemployment, promoting innovation and creating opportunities for young people to contribute to national development.

Meanwhile, Evelyn Hone College Principal Charity Nyirongo said the institution is strategically positioned to nurture entrepreneurs through their training programmes in information technology, biomedical engineering, creative and digital media, hospitality, construction, fashion and design.

World.title: Chevrons seal series win in Sammons’ farewell Test
World.content:
ZIMBABWE beat Afghanistan by 57 runs in the final hour of the second Test in Sharjah today to clinch the two-match series 1-0, giving departing head coach Justin Sammons a winning send-off in his final match in charge.

Chasing a daunting 418 for victory, Afghanistan were bowled out for 360 with fewer than four overs of the minimum remaining. Veteran leg-spinner Graeme Cremer claimed the final wicket when Ziaur Rahman edged to captain Brian Bennett at second slip for a 14-ball duck.

World.title: MP warns of digital security threats
World.content:
HARARE, Nov. 17 (NewsDay Live) – Chivi Central legislator Exevia Moses Maoneke has raised alarm over Zimbabwe’s growing dependence on foreign-owned digital platforms, warning that disruptions to critical software services could cripple government operations and expose the country to serious national security threats.

Speaking in the National Assembly on Tuesday, Maoneke called for urgent investment in locally controlled digital infrastructure following a reported widespread disruption of Microsoft 365 services, which he said affected productivity across government departments, corporate offices and essential public institutions.

World.title: Women fight for safety and dignity in mining communities
World.content:
When her husband left for South Africa, life took a devastating turn for Mercy Nhando**.

“That was the last time my husband was in my life,” she says. Left to raise her children alone, she initially travelled from Mutare to the Chiadzwa diamond fields with other women to hawk maheu, soft drinks and buns.

World.title: Govt appeals for space to accommodate informal traders
World.content:
GOVERNMENT has appealed to local authorities and private property owners to open their vacant and underutilised buildings for use by informal traders.

Women Affairs, Community, Small and Medium Enterprises Development minister Monica Mutsvangwa made the call in Harare this Tuesday when she toured the Meikles Market which was burnt down by fire, leaving 69 traders stranded.

She urged councils to avail vacant buildings to her ministry and the Zimbabwe Women Microfinance Bank to expand access to affordable business premises.

World.title: Kenya: Kenya's 'World-Class' Stadium Gears Up for Historic Inauguration
World.content:
interview

Kenya is undertaking massive preparations as it gears up to co-host the 36th edition of the Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON 2027) alongside Uganda and Tanzania. This will mark the first time the tournament takes place in East Africa since Ethiopia hosted the 10th edition in 1976. Construction work is nearing completion on the 60,000-capacity Raila Odinga International Stadium (formerly known as Talanta Stadium). Ahead of its historic January 5 inauguration, the CEO of the AFCON 2027 Local Organising Committee, Tony Lungaho, told AllAfrica's Boakai Fofana that the occasion will bring two of Europe's most celebrated football clubs - FC Bayern Munich and Ajax Amsterdam - to Nairobi for a landmark clash.



Please give us an overview of what is expected to happen in January.

To understand January, it helps to look at how this idea started. After Kenya, Tanzania, and Uganda won the bid to host AFCON 2027 - and with the African Nations Championship (CHAN) coming first - I went on benchmarking trips to the CAF Champions League final and the AFCON final.

When I returned, I realized the capacity gap was too wide. It is unfair to ask a Local Organizing Committee (LOC) of nearly 400 people to execute a major tournament without prior hands-on experience. Since it is too expensive to fly 400 people abroad to observe major finals, we decided to bring that caliber of event home.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Second, we have built the most technically advanced stadium in Africa - the only venue on the continent combining a virtual offside line, a native VAR system, and goal-line technology. A stadium of that standard deserved an equally historic inauguration.

In January, for the first time in history, two UEFA Champions League-winning sides will clash on African soil. At first, clubs were hesitant because it had never been done in Africa before. By pulling this off, we are opening the door for the continent to experience top-tier global football right at its doorstep.

The first phase of tickets has already sold out. What does that say about anticipation in Kenya and the wider region?

It is complete vindication. People initially questioned our choice of teams, but African fans are discerning - when you deliver a superior product, they show up.

Selling out in eight minutes is practically unheard of. It proves our new ticketing system - which allows fans to select exact seats, understand their matchday experience, and pay across multiple financial platforms - works seamlessly. We have even sold tickets to fans in Colombia, Kazakhstan, Turkey, and Armenia. If we make it possible, the world will come to Africa.

Have you factored in affordability for ordinary fans in Kenya, Uganda, and Tanzania?

Absolutely. Tickets start at €15 to keep them as accessible as possible, while ensuring the event sustains itself through ticket sales and sponsorships without relying on government money.

To lower the barrier further, we introduced mobile-money installment plans, allowing fans to pay off a €15 ticket in €2 increments over seven months. Cost is usually the biggest obstacle keeping Africans from top-tier sports; this is a model that can be replicated across all 54 countries.

So you are using this match as a live test case for AFCON 2027?

Exactly. While we have partnered with international experts to ensure world-class execution, our own LOC staff are embedded directly into functional roles. All 400 committee members will gain real-time operational experience that we can refine ahead of 2027.

Beyond the match, building a stadium is one thing; making it financially viable is the true legacy. This venue will double as a premier concert and entertainment hub for our creative economy.

As head of the LOC, how are broader infrastructure preparations shaping up for AFCON?

Hosting AFCON relies on four pillars: competition venues, hospitality and healthcare, transport infrastructure, and the fans.

Kenya already has strong roads, airports, and hospitals. The missing piece was sports infrastructure. Talanta Stadium is 96% to 98% complete ahead of our November 30 handover. Meanwhile, Kasarani - which stood for 40 years and successfully hosted CHAN - now features an advanced Monaco-Bermudagrass hybrid pitch. Launching Talanta signals that Kenya is 100% ready to host the biggest football party Africa has ever seen.

What were your biggest takeaways from hosting CHAN, and what will you improve for AFCON?

Our biggest lesson was underestimating Kenyan enthusiasm. Even matches not featuring Kenya drew massive crowds; during the Morocco vs. Madagascar final, fans packed the stadium to capacity and even sang the Moroccan national anthem.

Close 

Going forward, we need tighter stadium crowd-flow controls, alongside more public fan zones and free-to-air broadcasts to absorb overflow demand. Aside from crowd management, CAF rated CHAN the most successful edition ever held.

What about the national team's readiness on the pitch?

As our Minister often says, we cannot build world-class stadiums just for other nations to shine in. We have heavily resourced the Harambee Stars, with a rigorous preparation program running through June next year. Any team facing Kenya won't just play 11 men—they will the millions of fans.

Finally, how are you leveraging this moment for grassroots football?

Kenya last hosted a multi-sport event of this scale 40 years ago during the 1987 All-Africa Games. Beyond upgrading six major stadiums to AFCON standards, we are building 29 community grounds - without using taxpayer money - to nurture young talent. Giving kids the chance to watch Africa's best players in accessible hometown venues will be the defining legacy of 2027.

With Kenya now visa-free for fellow Africans, we are inviting the continent and the world to join us for a once-in-a-generation experience.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - November 18, 2026
World.content:
press review

South Africa Reprimands Nigerian Envoy Femi Fani-Kayode Over Broadcast Dispute

South Africa has formally reprimanded Nigeria's new High Commissioner, Femi Fani-Kayode, following a public dispute with the Presidency over the broadcasting of his credentials ceremony. The Department of International Relations and Cooperation (DIRCO) summoned him, with Director-General Zane Dangor reminding him to raise diplomatic concerns through the relevant foreign ministries rather than directly with the president. Fani-Kayode had accused the Presidency of deliberately excluding his introduction and speech from an SABC livestream, a claim disputed by President Cyril Ramaphosa's spokesperson, Vincent Magwenya. The Presidency maintained that Ramaphosa had simply directed the commissioner to raise his concerns with the appropriate SABC official. DIRCO said diplomats are required under the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations to conduct official business through foreign ministries. The incident comes amid already strained relations between the two countries over allegations of xenophobic attacks and deaths of Nigerian nationals in South Africa.

Ugandan Politician Besigye's Wife Renews Calls for His Release Over Health Fears



The wife of detained Ugandan opposition leader Kizza Besigye, Winnie Byanyima, has renewed calls for his release, citing serious concerns about his deteriorating health and need for specialised medical treatment. Besigye was arrested in Kenya's capital, Nairobi. He was abducted and taken to Uganda, where he was first charged with treason before his case was transferred to the civilian justice system. Byanyima said that he is experiencing difficulties walking, speaking, and using his hands. His family remains concerned about inadequate medical care under military surveillance. She said that soldiers remain stationed inside and around the hospital room where he is being held, raising further concerns about his welfare. His defence team has also questioned his fitness to stand trial. They argued that his communication difficulties prevent him from properly participating in his defence. Four bail applications have reportedly been rejected, while another is awaiting a hearing date. His next court hearing is scheduled for 25 November.

UN Says Over 2,230 Civilians Killed in Sudan Conflict Since January

At least 2,230 civilians were killed in Sudan between January and October 2026, including more than 1,630 in drone strikes, according to the UN Human Rights Office. Its latest report highlights the growing use of drones by warring parties, with attacks targeting markets, hospitals, schools, fuel facilities and other essential infrastructure. The Kordofan region recorded more than two-thirds of verified civilian deaths. Attacks on electricity and fuel infrastructure have disrupted healthcare, water supplies and food production. During the first half of the year, the UN documented at least 39 drone strikes on markets, 20 attacks on civilian vehicles and 16 strikes on healthcare facilities. It warned that the actual death toll is likely considerably higher because its figures include only verified cases. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk said the violations could amount to war crimes and called for accountability and greater protection of civilians.

Guinea Jails 224 Over Illegal Gold Mining

A court in Guinea has sentenced 224 people, including 22 former regional administrators and 202 alleged illegal gold miners, over unauthorised mining activities in the northeastern Siguiri region. The former officials received two-year prison sentences. The miners were sentenced to three years for offences including environmental destruction, water pollution and illegal mining. Foreign nationals among those convicted were also banned from Guinea for 10 years. The sentences form part of a wider government crackdown aimed at protecting farmland, rivers and the environment from damage caused by illegal mining. The operation has triggered violent clashes between protesters and security forces, leaving 10 people dead and 13 injured. More than 1,200 artisanal miners have been arrested in November. Thousands have fled across the border into Mali, with many awaiting transportation back to their home countries, including Burkina Faso.

Ethiopia-Eritrea Fighting Reignites, Raising Fears of Wider War

Fighting has resumed along the Ethiopia-Eritrea border, raising fears of a wider conflict in the Horn of Africa as relations between the neighbours continue to deteriorate. Ethiopian government forces have pushed Tigrayan fighters to the Eritrean border, with reports of skirmishes and artillery fire near the contested town of Badme. Tensions have also been heightened by Ethiopia's repeated demands for access to the Red Sea, including references to Eritrea's Assab port. The town of Badme remains a sensitive territorial issue between the two countries, even with a peace agreement that awarded the town to Eritrea after their war from 1998-2000. Relations between Ethiopia and Sudan have deteriorated at the same time amid accusations of interference in each other's conflicts, including claims by Sudan that Ethiopia is backing Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, which Ethiopia and the United Arab Emirates deny. Analysts warn that proxy involvement could intensify, although direct military confrontation between Ethiopia and Sudan is considered less likely for now.

Close 

Mozambican Opposition Leader Venâncio Mondlane Goes on Trial Over Post-Election Unrest

Mozambican opposition leader Venâncio Mondlane has gone on trial at the Supreme Court over charges including terrorism-related offences, incitement and civil disobedience linked to deadly protests following the disputed 2024 elections. Mondlane, who denies wrongdoing, maintains that his calls for demonstrations were aimed at demanding electoral transparency after he challenged the victory of ruling Frelimo party candidate Daniel Chapo. Prosecutors accuse him of encouraging unrest that resulted in deaths, property damage and disruption of public services. He faces up to 24 years in prison if convicted of the most serious charge. The trial has prompted tight security in Maputo, with police urging citizens to remain calm and avoid actions that could threaten public order. Access to the proceedings has been restricted to selected media organisations, while live broadcasts have been banned over concerns about possible unrest. The case is widely viewed as a major test of Mozambique's political stability, nearly two years after the disputed elections triggered one of the country's deadliest post-election crises.

World.title: South Africa: ANC Postpones Media Briefing on Coalition Talks - South African News Briefs - November 18, 2026
World.content:
press review

ANC Postpones Media Briefing on Coalition Talks

The African National Congress (ANC) has postponed its scheduled media briefing on coalition negotiations, citing ongoing and extensive discussions, reports EWN. Party Secretary-General Fikile Mbalula is set to brief the media on progress at a revised date. The postponement comes after the ANC suffered major losses in the recent municipal elections. It lost its position as the largest party in Gauteng's three metros to the Democratic Alliance (DA).

Two Killed in Suspected Gang Shooting on Cape Flats



Two people have been killed and three others wounded in a suspected gang-related shooting in Seawinds, Lavender Hill, on Cape Town's Cape Flats, reports SABC News. The victims, two men in their thirties, were declared dead at the scene. A 53-year-old woman was among those injured. Police said that occupants of a vehicle drove up to the group and opened fire before fleeing. Police visibility has been increased in the area. Operation Prosper deployments are conducting crime prevention operations to restore calm.

Sport Minister Urges Athletes to Secure Own Sponsorships

Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie has urged athletes to secure individual sponsorships, reports EWN. He said that the government cannot afford to fully fund all sporting federations and their athletes. His comments follow Olympic swimmer Tatjana Smith's decision to withdraw from representing South Africa amid a sponsorship dispute with Swimming South Africa (SSA) over competing in national team sponsor Arena's apparel despite her personal Speedo sponsorship. McKenzie said federations should support athletes in securing individual deals rather than penalising them. He has demanded clarity on the sponsorship agreement while apologising to Arena for being caught up in the controversy.
