World.title: Africa: Climate Finance Needs Proof, not Promises
World.content:
opinion

In Gidan Dare, a farming community near the BUA Cement plant in northwest Nigeria, residents describe wells that once reached water at three or four metres now requiring seventy or more metres before anyone strikes anything.

They describe their mud houses cracking and collapsing under the vibration of heavy truck traffic. They talk about how, close to midnight, plant operations are loud enough to disturb their sleep. The International Finance Corporation (IFC) says it confirmed “broad community support” for the expansion during a site visit in August 2022. Yet none of the community leaders I spoke with recall being consulted before BUA expanded onto land their families had farmed for generations.

I lead Quest for Growth and Development Foundation in Nigeria, where I work with five communities around the plant, one of them resettled for the expansion. Their experience is a local face of the global climate problem that governments are debating at COP31. Projects like this one, financed by institutions such as IFC, rarely enter that conversation.

Once its new lines are running, this plant will emit about 4.1 million tonnes of COâ a year, 2.9 million of them from the expansion. IFC approved $210 million for that expansion and classifies it as Category A, which is its highest environmental and social risk tier. That raises a question for the World Bank’s Board of Executive Directors: do IFC’s climate promises actually mean what they claim?



IFC’s own file suggests not. It sets no reduction target and requires no independent verification of those figures, before approval or since.

What it does contain is a promise: IFC’s Climate Advisory arm “will support BUA integrate low-carbon solutions in the existing and new facilities, to further reduce its carbon footprint.” That leaves the core climate claim resting on future advisory work, rather than measurable commitments anyone outside the institution can check.

For the people living beside the plant, the same accountability gap remains. IFC’s record says they were consulted. They say otherwise. BUA says it supports its host communities through health care, scholarships, and donations. Those benefits matter, but they cannot substitute for consultation before a high-risk project is approved.

This is not a one-off failure at a single plant. It is what IFC’s published climate methodology permits for a project counted as aligned with the Paris Agreement. In practice, a promise is sufficient to earn the label. Verification is optional. For a high-risk cement plant expansion, in one of the hardest industrial sectors on earth to decarbonize, that gap is not a technicality.

It is the whole problem.

Cleaner cement is already financeable. For example, IFC has financed a calcined clay cement plant in Burkina Faso. For every cement investment, IFC should require a transparent alternatives analysis showing why lower-carbon production options are or are not feasible before approval.

None of this requires waiting for the outcome of the Independent Evaluation Group’s ongoing review of the World Bank Group’s Climate Change Action Plan, a review the World Bank’s own board requested this year, with no findings yet public. The evidence is already sitting in IFC’s own file on this project, in its own published methodology, and in what residents on the ground have reported for years.

IFC is rewriting its Sustainability Framework – the environmental and social rules for every project it funds – and a first draft is expected in the coming weeks. Executive Directors should insist on four changes that would close the gap that file exposes: Publish a measured emissions baseline before the board votes, rather than an advisory pledge to build one later. Require independent verification of climate and community consultation claims before a project is labelled climate-aligned. Make an independent audit against a credible pathway, such as the IEA Cement Roadmap, a condition of financing. And require a completed analysis of lower-carbon alternatives before approval.

Close 

I’m not asking the Executive Directors to take farmers in Nigeria at their word alone. I’m asking them to close these gaps in the Sustainability Framework revision.

Climate was barely discussed when the World Bank and its member governments gathered for their meetings this October. That is exactly the problem: when accountability lapses, IFC doesn’t absorb the cost. Families in communities like Gidan Dare do, and they have the least capacity to adapt.

The Board doesn’t need to wait for climate to return to the agenda. It needs a rule that makes the climate commitment binding and checkable, not a pledge to be resolved later. Climate finance should be able to prove what it promises.

World.title: Egypt: CPJ Urges Congress to Raise Press Freedom Violations With Egypt Foreign Minister
World.content:
On Tuesday, the Committee to Protect Journalists sent a letter to members of the U.S. Congress, urging lawmakers to raise Egypt's unprecedented decline in press freedom during Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty's visit to Washington, D.C. this week. The letter called on Congress to use all available diplomatic tools, including U.S. Foreign Military Financing (FMF), to press Egypt to end its criminalization of independent journalism.

In less than two months, Egyptian authorities arrested six journalists from the investigative platform Matsadaash -- who remain in detention on terrorism and false news charges -- and convicted Mada Masr Editor-in-Chief Lina Attalah of running the outlet without a license, fining her nearly US$54,000 and ordering the closure of the outlet. Attalah also faces a separate case stemming from Mada Masr's coverage of the war on Gaza, in which she was secretly sentenced in absentia to one year in prison. A hearing in that case is set for Wednesday, November 18, and her appeal in the closure case is set for November 25.

The crackdown coincided with the decision on October 1 by President Donald Trump to waive human rights conditions on $320 million in FMF for Egypt. Asked on November 10 about the crackdown, Secretary of State Marco Rubio described Egypt as a "reliable and good defense partner of the United States."

CPJ called on Congress to make clear that continued U.S. military aid is dependent on Egypt releasing the six Matsadaash journalists, reversing the closure of Mada Masr, ending the legal intimidation of Attalah, granting licenses to independent outlets and unblocking news websites, and amending Article 6 of Media Law No. 180 of 2018 so outlets can be established by notification rather than prior authorization.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Egypt remains one of the world's leading jailers of journalists, with 25 currently behind bars.

Read the full letter here.

World.title: Africa: World Governments Summit Sets Agenda for Latin America and Caribbean Talks
World.content:
press release

Mohammad Al Gergawi

Expanding cooperation, aligning visions and building global partnerships are essential to creating major opportunities and a more prosperous future

Víctor Bisonó

Hosting the Dialogue opens new opportunities for the Dominican Republic to strengthen international relations

Dialogue at a glance

10 heads of state and prime ministers to participate in the Dialogue

UAE government delegation led by Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan bin Mubarak Al Nahyan to participate in the Dialogue

More than 70 speakers and representatives from more than 30 countries

35 sessions and 15 high-level meetings and engagements to explore the future of government, the economy, investment and regional and international cooperation

More than 120 leading private-sector companies and institutions

Under the directives of His Highness Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, Vice President and Prime Minister of the UAE and Ruler of Dubai, the World Governments Summit Organization has announced the agenda for its Latin America and the Caribbean Dialogue. Organised in partnership with the Government of the Dominican Republic and the Center for Analysis for Public Policies (CAPP), the Dialogue will take place in Cap Cana on 20 and 21 November under the patronage and in the presence of His Excellency Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic.

The agenda features 35 sessions and 15 high-level meetings and engagements, with more than 70 speakers, representatives from more than 30 countries, and more than 120 private-sector companies and institutions. Sessions will focus on six themes: geoeconomics and strategic investment, tourism, culture and experience economies, international cooperation and regional integration, the future of government, logistics and global connectivity, and human capital and the future of work.

The Dialogue will bring together heads of state and government, ministers, leaders of international organisations and economic institutions, and representatives of major global companies. It will provide a platform to expand cooperation among governments, explore development and investment opportunities, and build partnerships that connect regional potential with global opportunities. The Dialogue will also help shape shared priorities for the future of the economy, development and government. Participants include H.E. Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic, H.E. José Raúl Mulino, President of the Republic of Panama, H.E. Rodrigo Paz Pereira, President of the Plurinational State of Bolivia, H.E. Nasry Asfura, President of the Republic of Honduras, the Hon. Philip Davis, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, the Hon. Dr. Natalio Wheatley, Premier of the British Virgin Islands, the Hon. Brigadier (Ret'd) Mark Phillips, Prime Minister of the Co-operative Republic of Guyana H.E. María José Pinto, Vice President of the Republic of Ecuador, and H.E. Félix Ulloa, Vice President of the Republic of El Salvador. They will be joined by H.E. Albert Ramdin, Secretary General of the Organization of American States (OAS), H.E. Shaikha Al Nuwais, Secretary General of UN Tourism, and H.E. Noemí Espinoza Madrid, Secretary General of the Association of Caribbean States (ACS).

The UAE ' s official delegation will be led by H.E. Sheikh Shakhboot bin Nahyan bin Mubarak Al Nahyan, Minister of State. It will include H.E. Noura AlKaabi, Minister of State at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, H.E. Mohammad Alhawi, Undersecretary at the Ministry of Investment, H.E. Dr. Alsaghira Alahbabi, Head of Mission, UAE Ambassador to the Republic of Paraguay and Director of the American Affairs Department at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Mohamed Yousef Al Sharhan, Managing Director of the World Governments Summit Organization, and other government officials.

The Dialogue's 35 sessions and 15 high-level meetings and engagements will bring together more than 70 speakers, representatives from more than 30 countries, and more than 120 private-sector companies and institutions. Its six themes cover geoeconomics and strategic investment, tourism, culture and experience economies, international cooperation and regional integration, the future of government, logistics and global connectivity, and human capital and the future of work.

The Dialogue builds on the World Governments Summit's role in convening governments, decision-makers, institutional leaders and experts. It connects expertise with policymaking and creates opportunities to share experience and develop partnerships. The initiative strengthens ties between the UAE and Latin America and the Caribbean and supports cooperation that can deliver lasting economic and development benefits.

Mohammad Al Gergawi highlights the Summit's role in helping governments respond to global change

H.E. Mohammad Abdullah Al Gergawi, Minister of Cabinet Affairs and Chairman of the World Governments Summit Organization, said strengthening dialogue and cooperation among governments was a strategic priority as countries respond to global shifts and work towards a more prosperous future. He added that shared priorities and effective cross-border partnerships were essential to seizing opportunities, addressing challenges and turning ambitions into tangible development outcomes that improve people's lives.

He said Latin America and the Caribbean had considerable economic, human and strategic potential, as well as promising opportunities to strengthen their role in the global economy. Dialogue with governments across the region would expand opportunities to share expertise, develop partnerships and identify new areas for integration and investment, supporting sustainable growth and prosperity.

He added that the World Governments Summit had established itself as a global platform that connects knowledge with decision-making and gives governments access to experience and expertise from around the world. This enables them to anticipate change, develop more innovative and efficient ways of working, and find practical solutions that improve quality of life.

Dominican Republic highlights opportunities to strengthen international ties

H.E. Víctor Bisonó, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic, said hosting the Dialogue would strengthen international relations and reinforce the country ' s position as an investment destination and a strategic gateway linking Latin America and the Caribbean with other regions.

He said the Dialogue offered an opportunity to build on the Dominican Republic's international engagement, deepen bilateral ties and explore new avenues for investment and development in the country and the region. Partnerships and stronger frameworks for cooperation would support economic growth and open up new opportunities.

Dialogue explores global opportunities and the future of international cooperation

The Dialogue will open with remarks by H.E. Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic, followed by a main address on behalf of the UAE Government and remarks by Mohamed Yousef Al Sharhan, Managing Director of the World Governments Summit Organization.

A presidential dialogue titled "Governments and the New Geography of Opportunity" will bring together H.E. Luis Abinader, President of the Dominican Republic, and H.E. José Raúl Mulino, President of the Republic of Panama. The discussion will examine how governments can use technology, trade and investment to shape new economic corridors, strengthen regional competitiveness and identify opportunities for growth and integration in the global economy.

The agenda includes a session titled "What Role Will Governments Play in Shaping the Next Tourism Destination?" Participants include the Hon. Dr. Natalio Wheatley, Premier of the British Virgin Islands, H.E. Harris Whitbeck, Director General of the Guatemalan Institute of Tourism (INGUAT), H.E. Shaikha Al Nuwais, Secretary General of UN Tourism, and Elena Martínez, Co-founder and CTO of SOS Biotech.

H.E. Albert Ramdin, Secretary General of the Organization of American States, will speak in "Threats to Peace: Ways to Mitigate and Resolve Them". The session will examine how diplomacy, preventive action and regional cooperation can help governments anticipate tensions and build lasting peace.

Artificial intelligence, investment and natural resources shape discussions on future economies

Sessions will examine the changes reshaping global economies, the opportunities created by technology, artificial intelligence, investment and innovation, and how countries can turn national assets and natural resources into lasting economic value.

"Global Insights: AI, Investment & New Economic Frontiers" will examine how AI, investment and connectivity are shaping the region's economy and the decisions facing its leaders. The session will feature the Hon. Philip Davis, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, H.E. José Ramón Icaza, Minister for Canal Affairs of the Republic of Panama, Senator the Hon. Jonathan W. D. Reid, Minister of Innovation, Industry, Science and Technology of Barbados, H.E. Noemí Espinoza Madrid, Secretary General of the Association of Caribbean States, and H.E. Mohammad Alhawi, Undersecretary at the UAE Ministry of Investment. They will be joined by Juan Sabater, Partner and Co-President of Valor Equity Partners, Alonso Aznar, Founder and CEO of Zaria Capital, and René Grullón Finet, Executive President of Grupo Popular.

World Governments Summit Luis Abinader with the participants of the dialogue in 2025 (archive)

Related sessions will explore how culture and local identity can become global exports, how technology can improve connectivity among islands and widen access to markets and services, and what lies ahead for aviation and logistics. They will also examine changes in capital flows and how governments can attract productive investment. "More Than an Island: A Conversation with Leaders of Small Island States" will bring together the Hon. Dr. Natalio Wheatley, Premier of the British Virgin Islands, and the Hon. Philip Davis, Prime Minister of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, to discuss how small island states can strengthen their role in the global economy.

"New Energy, New Economies: Where Should Governments Invest?" will examine how investment can support emerging industries and strengthen energy security. The session will feature H.E. Félix Ulloa, Vice President of the Republic of El Salvador, and Enrique Riquelme, Founder and Chairman of Cox Energy.

"From Natural Wealth to National Wealth" will explore how governments can turn natural resources into diversified economies, higher-value industries and lasting prosperity across generations. Participants include H.E. Rodrigo Paz Pereira, President of the Plurinational State of Bolivia, and the Hon. Brigadier (Ret'd) Mark Phillips, Prime Minister of the Co-operative Republic of Guyana.

Anticipating change and improving public services

The agenda places particular emphasis on how governments can prepare for rapid change. Sessions will examine ten trends expected to reshape government leadership, service delivery and the ability to create opportunities over the coming decade.

"Before Disaster Strikes: Are Governments Ready?" will examine how foresight, technology and partnerships can help governments anticipate emerging risks, protect essential services and strengthen national preparedness. "The Next National Advantage: Learning Faster" will explore how skills development and lifelong learning can prepare people and institutions for rapidly changing economies.

H.E. Hesham Amiri, Deputy Chief of Government Services at the UAE Prime Minister's Office, will speak in "What Does a Zero-Bureaucracy Government Look Like?" The session will showcase the UAE's Zero Government Bureaucracy model and its experience in streamlining procedures and delivering faster, more flexible and more efficient services.

Other sessions will examine how artificial intelligence can widen economic participation and improve public services, and how effective communication between governments and communities can strengthen trust and public participation.

UN Tourism regional dialogue to address air connectivity and economic integration

UN Tourism will convene a high-level regional dialogue titled "Air Connectivity in the Americas: Key to Competitiveness and Regional Integration". Ministers, airport and aviation leaders, and development partners will share policy experience, successful practices and recommendations for improving air connectivity, supporting regional integration and unlocking the economic potential of tourism. Discussions will address tourism's contribution to growth, investment, jobs and local and regional development, as well as its role in national development agendas. Participants will also discuss charges, taxes, innovative incentives and competitiveness.

The Association of Caribbean States will hold a high-level meeting titled "One Sea, Multiple Destinations: Connecting Destinations, Experiences and Opportunities" to explore ways to strengthen links between destinations and deepen regional cooperation.

Five Emirati-inspired majlises to foster exchange and shape shared priorities

The second day will feature five majlises inspired by Emirati traditions of dialogue. The roundtables will bring together government leaders, experts and institutional representatives to share experience and develop common perspectives on strategic issues and the future of development.

The majlises will cover government innovation, global connectivity and economic competitiveness, talent, skills and the future workforce, national resources and future prosperity, and artificial intelligence and the opportunities it opens.

Participants will examine how lessons from other governments can improve public services and institutional readiness, and how transport, trade and digital connectivity can strengthen competitiveness. The discussions will also cover the skills needed by emerging industries, how strategic resources can support long-term prosperity, and how countries can build AI capabilities and encourage innovation grounded in trust and accountability.

The facilitators include Abeer Tahlak, Director of the Mohammed Bin Rashid Centre for Government Innovation at the UAE Prime Minister's Office, Tim Kingston, Chairman and Head of Investment Banking for Latin America at Goldman Sachs, Steven Bertoni, Assistant Managing Editor at Forbes, Dr. Carlos Díaz-Rosillo, Founding Director of the Adam Smith Center for Economic Freedom, and Jason Marczak, Vice President and Senior Director of the Atlantic Council's Adrienne Arsht Latin America Center.

International discussions on the future of societies and the Global South

The programme includes a Global Insights session on regional cooperation and the future of societies. It will explore how partnerships, innovation and human potential can shape the region's future, with H.E. Félix Ulloa, Vice President of the Republic of El Salvador, and the Hon. Everly Paul Chet Greene, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Immigration of Antigua and Barbuda, alongside leaders and representatives of international institutions and companies.

H.E. Víctor Bisonó, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic, will open the second day. The programme includes "META RD 2036: The Future of Government", featuring H.E. José Ignacio Paliza, Minister of the Presidency of the Dominican Republic, and Celso Juan Marranzini, President of the National Council of Private Enterprise (CONEP) and Coordinator of the META RD 2036 Transversal Committee.

Sessions will also examine the future of aviation, global investment trends, shifts in energy markets and how government partnerships with the private sector can help build more diversified and competitive economies.

H.E. Noura AlKaabi, Minister of State of the UAE, the Hon. Frederick Mitchell, MP, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Commonwealth of The Bahamas, H.E. Víctor Bisonó, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Dominican Republic, and the Hon. Everly Paul Chet Greene, Minister of Foreign Affairs, Trade and Immigration of Antigua and Barbuda, will take part in " New Bridges, New Influence: The Future of Next Global South? " The session will examine the outlook, challenges and opportunities for countries of the Global South and their role in shaping international relations and future partnerships.

A partnership advancing regional and international cooperation

The inaugural Dialogue, organised by the World Governments Summit Organization and hosted by the Dominican Republic last year, marked a step forward in regional and international cooperation. It brought together representatives of 22 countries, 29 speakers and 59 leading companies and institutions across 14 sessions and 10 strategic engagements covering the future of government, economic transformation, tourism, innovation and regional cooperation.

At the inaugural edition, the World Governments Summit and the Government of the Dominican Republic signed a Memorandum of Understanding to strengthen cooperation, develop joint initiatives and establish a long-term platform for dialogue. The agreement supports closer partnerships between the UAE and Latin America and the Caribbean, and opens new opportunities for international cooperation and sustainable development.

World.title: South Africa: South Africa Must Close the Gaps in Corruption Referrals
World.content:
analysis

Thousands of referrals fall through the cracks of the country's many anti-corruption agencies. Better cooperation, tracking and follow-up are vital.

Between 2011 and August 2026, South Africa's Special Investigating Unit (SIU) made 5 944 criminal referrals to the National Prosecuting Authority (NPA). But only 570 registered police dockets, 91 court cases and 263 convictions in relation to these referrals were reported by the NPA to Parliament.

This does not mean thousands of referrals disappeared, as several may be consolidated into one docket; and not all provide sufficient evidence for prosecution. Parliament's concern was that the SIU, NPA and Directorate for Priority Crime Investigation (DPCI, or Hawks) could not provide a consistent, reconciled account of how individual referrals had progressed through the criminal justice system.



South Africa has numerous institutions with powers to investigate corruption, impose sanctions and pursue other forms of accountability. These include the SIU, NPA, Hawks, Financial Intelligence Centre, Auditor-General, Public Protector and financial regulators. Research from the Institute for Security Studies highlights that many depend on information or findings from other institutions to exercise their powers effectively.

The SIU's investigation into alleged corruption at the National Lotteries Commission (NLC) involving grants intended for community projects shows the difficulty in tracking a matter after it's referred. Between 2022 and 2024, 19 criminal referrals were made to the NPA. In May 2025, the SIU reported no recorded progress on 18 of these referrals. By March 2026, the NPA had consolidated the referrals into 16 matters, with two in court and 14 under investigation.

The NPA identified the Hawks' difficulties appointing forensic accountants as a major cause of delay. The Hawks later submitted dockets to prosecutors, but some were returned with requests for further investigation, as the Hawks explained in parliamentary proceedings.

Not every delay is avoidable. Evidence warranting an SIU referral may fall short of what is needed to prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Complex financial investigations take time, and prosecutorial decisions must remain independent.

But the NLC case exposed shortcomings in accounting for matters as they moved between institutions. Their status was revealed only through parliamentary scrutiny, when routine reporting should have done so.

Similar difficulties can arise regarding referrals for disciplinary action. The SIU's investigation into procurement corruption at Tembisa Hospital produced 116 disciplinary referrals concerning 13 officials. By September 2025, 108 had been delivered to the Gauteng Department of Health. As of October 2026, the SIU had not received feedback on the progress of its recommendations.

While this does not establish that the department failed to act, it shows how referring institutions can remain unaware of next steps.

The Tembisa investigation also raises questions about how findings from one investigation inform subsequent action. The SIU identified repeated purchases just below competitive tender thresholds. Earlier SIU investigations in the Gauteng Health Department had identified procurement governance weaknesses, some of which persisted in the Tembisa case. This shows the importance of sharing lessons across facilities and checking whether corrective measures have been implemented.

Existing legislation offers examples of how institutions can be required to account for their handling of referrals. Under the Public Audit Act and Material Irregularity Regulations, public bodies receiving referrals from the Auditor-General to investigate suspected irregularities must promptly acknowledge receipt, report on progress at intervals specified by the Auditor-General, explain delays and communicate outcomes.

The Independent Police Investigative Directorate Act goes further. Police commissioners must initiate disciplinary proceedings within 30 days of receiving recommendations from the Independent Police Investigative Directorate (IPID) and communicate outcomes. Failure to comply is a criminal offence.

Although their effectiveness is uncertain, these arrangements establish obligations to report on referrals without prescribing the final investigative or disciplinary outcome.

Similar reporting duties should be extended to other significant corruption referrals. Receiving institutions should be required to acknowledge referrals, explain decisions and report on progress, without compromising investigative or prosecutorial discretion.

Agreements alone have not resolved the problem. The SIU and NPA signed a memorandum of understanding in 2017, followed by another involving the Hawks and police in 2022. Yet the institutions still struggle to reconcile their figures.

Efforts to improve referral tracking are underway. The Presidency's SIU Referrals Coordination and Monitoring Mechanism monitors the implementation of SIU recommendations. Within this initiative, the Presidency, SIU and NPA worked with the State Information Technology Agency to develop a proof of concept for a Case Monitoring Mechanism to track SIU referrals to the NPA. In time, the system could also track disciplinary, administrative and regulatory recommendations.

While important, agreements and software systems are not sufficient to complete this work. Institutional leaders must ensure that staff record receipt, take responsibility for the next step, share relevant information, update case records and respond when deadlines are missed. Parliament should monitor whether the arrangements are implemented and whether overdue referrals receive attention.

The United Kingdom's counter-fraud standards offer useful guidance, recommending auditable records of referrals received, assessment decisions, reasons, milestones and outcomes. Such records would help institutions follow matters to their conclusion, even when several referrals are consolidated into one investigation or a case moves between institutions.

Close 

These improvements should also change how institutional performance is measured. Reporting should go beyond the number of investigations completed or referrals made to show how many referrals were acknowledged, assessed and concluded, how long this took and why matters remained outstanding.

South Africa's anti-corruption institutions have different mandates, and their independence must be respected. But this should not prevent them from accounting for how they handle matters referred by other bodies. Ultimately, accountability should not end where one institution's mandate stops.

For permission to re-publish ISS Today articles, please email us. In South Africa, News24 has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles. In Nigeria, Premium Times has exclusive rights to republish ISS Today articles.

Georgia Dorrington, Research Consultant, Justice and Violence Prevention, ISS

Martin Schönteich, ISS Consultant and former South African prosecutor

World.title: Central African Republic: Rights Defender in Central African Republic Dies
World.content:
press release

Remembering Nicolas Tiangaye, Who Fought for Constitutional Safeguards Until the End

Nicolas Tiangaye, a prominent Central African lawyer, human rights defender, and former prime minister died in Bangui on November 16, at the age of 70. One of the country's most respected rule of law advocates, his career spanned more than four decades.

Tiangaye first came into the spotlight as a young lawyer when he defended the former emperor, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, in 1986. Later he defended the future president, François Bozizé, when he was accused of plotting a coup.

For Tiangaye, the cardinal rule that all defendants must benefit from their right to a fair trial is one he lived by. By the early 1990s, Tiangaye was one of the leading Central African human rights advocates and served as the Bar Association president.



In 1996 he was the lead defense council for Jean-Paul Akayesu before the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. Human Rights Watch strongly advocated for the prosecution of Akayesu hailing his 1998 conviction as a historic international precedent. I once discussed the seminal conviction with Tiangaye and he reiterated that a good lawyer must be willing to defend clients and insist on due process, even in highly charged circumstances.

Throughout the 1990s and 2000s, he spoke out for judicial independence and democratic governance. This often put him at odds with the government. But threats, he said, came with the job.

He regularly ended up at the heart of national politics. Following Bozizé's successful coup, Tiangaye helped draft the 2004 Constitution. In January 2013, then-president Bozizé appointed Tiangaye prime minister amidst national turmoil. He remained in the position after Seleka seized Bangui and committed widespread abuses. Tiangaye despised the Seleka's crimes, he told me, and he resigned.

He returned to legal practice and his passion: defending the Constitution. He became an outspoken critic of President Faustin-Archange Touadéra's efforts to remove presidential term limits, insisting on constitutional safeguards and political pluralism.

His death is both a professional and personal loss for Human Rights Watch. More importantly, it occurs as independent voices and institutions remain under pressure in the Central African Republic. I spoke with him just last week about detained activists. I wish I asked how he would like to be remembered. I imagine he would have insisted that we not focus on the individual, but on his commitment to the rule of law and human rights--Tiangaye's ultimate legacy.

Close 

Lewis Mudge, Director, Central Africa

World.title: Lane Kiffin’s roster fight set the stage, Will Wade just threw a grenade in LSU-SEC war with RJ Luis
World.content:
The LSU Tigers officially escalated the legal battle with the SEC on Wednesday night when basketball coach Will Wade sent RJ Luis Jr. off the bench and into the game against Louisiana-Monroe.

Over the past five days, 19th Judicial District Court Judge William Jorden of Baton Rouge granted RJ Luis a preliminary injunction that allowed the LSU Tigers to roster the former professional athlete.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

This whole saga stems from the former St. John's player returning to college for another season, after already declaring for the draft following his final game at the collegiate level in March 2025. After signing a 2-way deal at the NBA level, Luis was seeking a return to college, and signed with LSU last spring.

Luis went undrafted in 2025, then ended up signing a 2-way contract with the Utah Jazz.

LSU LATEST BASKETBALL PROGRAM TO TAP INTO G LEAGUE RANKS, SIGNING FORMER PRO GUARD RJ LUIS JR

But, there have always been rules about former professional athletes coming back to college, though that did not stop Will Wade from recruiting RJ Luis to play basketball at LSU after the head coach returned to Baton Rouge.

And, for all of those that thought this was about college football, you were sorely mistaken.

"I'm gonna refer to our university statement from yesterday. I'll be happy to answer any questions on how he played. "Everybody we played tonight is eligible," Will Wade said postgame.

Will Wade's basketball team was always the play, not Lane Kiffin

Over the past three months, LSU had already been fighting the SEC and NCAA over its rules about athletes pursuing an additional year of eligibility based upon the new guidelines that were enacted around players having five years to play five seasons of competition.

This has led to the LSU athletic department having to make a decision on whether to roster two football players one day before the Tigers faced Clemson in Baton Rouge.

Ultimately, the Tigers' administration decided against officially adding the players to the roster.

LSU HOLDS OFF ON ADDING PLAYERS WITH NFL TIES AS SEC LAWSUIT LOOMS OVER PROGRAM, LANE KIFFIN

That did not stop the legal saga around both LSU and the SEC, after the conference was enjoined in a lawsuit filed by the football players in September that then led to commissioner Greg Sankey taking the stand inside a Baton Rouge courtroom.

Fast-forward two months, and the same situation has been playing out around the basketball court pertaining to RJ Luis.

"They [LSU] are hiding behind a judge, and I don't know why they think they won't ultimately find a way to punish them," one Power-four head basketball coach told OutKick. "They are actually going to fight the conference over one player and watch the world burn in the process?

"I guess they are really not worried about the fallout, because this makes the whole administration look petty. No matter how you feel about the SEC, it's obvious how they [LSU] feel about [Greg] Sankey and their counterparts within the conference."

SEC ACCUSES LSU OF LETTING LANE KIFFIN RUN WILD AS EXPULSION VOTE COMING THURSDAY IN EXPLOSIVE COURT FILING

After the same judge granted Luis an injunction against the SEC that would prohibit them from punishing LSU if it were to roster and play the basketball star this season, a war of legal words has led to a massive kerfuffle within the legal circles.

The SEC stated that it would not impose any type of fines or penalties against LSU after the injunction was granted, but they were clearly testing Will Wade and the Tigers administration on whether they would actually put RJ Luis into a game.

ATTORNEY COMPARES SEC COMMISSIONER GREG SANKEY TO ‘KIM JONG’ IN LSU-RJ LUIS ELIGIBILITY LAWSUIT

On Tuesday, the SEC released a statement that clearly let it be known that they did not agree with how LSU was interpreting a court order. The Tigers did not have to make the decision on actually putting RJ Luis on the court, which is where the main course of this argument starts.

"LSU's decision today to rely on its own interpretation of the Court's order to justify its actions is inconsistent with the expectations and responsibilities of [SEC membership]. This is a deeply concerning and disappointing development."

On Wednesday night, the top officially blew off the lid. During their game against UL-Monroe, and mid-way through the first half, Will Wade subbed in RJ Luis.

"He was eligible, and he played," Will Wade said following LSU's win.

The Tigers head coach did not discuss

If there ever was an official escalation to a war, this was it.

LSU decides to officially go to war with the SEC in Federal Court

Not only did LSU defy what the SEC President and Chancellors had voted on in the past three months, they were clearly jumping into the deep end of this very large pool of legal waters that will undoubtably set-off another chain of events that involve legal filings.

The conference wants to be able to enforce its own rules. LSU is using a court's order to waddle around the rules of rostering and playing a former professional athlete by using a Baton Rouge judge as the scapegoat.

INSIDE A LOUISIANA COURTROOM: SEC-LSU LEGAL CIRCUS PLAYED OUT LIKE A JOHN GRISHAM NOVEL IN STUNNING SHOWDOWN

In addition to the arguments made in a Louisiana court, the SEC had filed its own lawsuit against LSU on the same day Commissioner Greg Sankey took the stand in Baton Rouge.

In an Alabama federal court, the SEC sued LSU President Wade Rousse, athletic director Verge Ausberry and other Tiger officials for violating their first amendment rights pertaining to enforcing conference rules.

This has led to both sides exchanging legal jabs, with the latest coming on Wednesday, as the SEC was asking a judge to strike certain language used in a motion-to-dismiss filed by LSU. Legal counsel for the Tigers claimed that the SEC had brought forth "hallucinated" claims against defendants.

A judge ordered LSU lawyers to release a public apology through a press release, which Louisiana attorney general Liz Murrill told the court was not going to happen through her own filing.

In addition to the mess going on in an Alabama federal court, RJ Luis' attorney, Tony Clayton, filed a motion to hold the SEC in contempt of court that came in response to the conference's statement on Tuesday night.

"We want to hold [Sankey] and the SEC in contempt for the threat," Tony Clayton said. "Their lawyer sent us an email that they would not take any actions against LSU or threaten any actions. And then Sankey or an SEC official issued the threat about what they're going to do to LSU."

Now, ten minutes into a game against Louisiana-Monroe on Wednesday night, the LSU administration decided to pull the pin and throw the grenade.

ABC's "The View" co-host Whoopi Goldberg demanded that the incoming Democratic Congress impeach U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. after the country lost its measles elimination status Tuesday.

The panel on Wednesday's show discussed the Pan American Health Organization announcing that for the first time in 26 years, the U.S. lost its measles elimination status after more than 5,400 confirmed cases were reported this year.

The hosts largely blamed Kennedy for the outbreak, pointing to his past scrutiny of vaccines as a cause for the rise in cases, with Goldberg going as far as to hold him responsible for measles-related deaths.

RFK JR. BACKTRACKS ON TIMELINE FOR DETERMINING CAUSE OF AUTISM

"I’m just gonna say it: get his a-- out of there!" Goldberg said to a cheering audience. "Just impeach him! Impeach him! Impeach him. I don’t wanna say it, but I feel like he’s responsible for many people not making it. Get him gone, man!"

When co-host Joy Behar remarked that members of President Donald Trump's cabinet could still remain in office for two more years, Goldberg doubled down on Kennedy's impeachment.

"Start with this one!" Goldberg continued. "Start with this one, and then go to [Secretary of War Pete] Hegseth, and then go to the other ones, and get people in these positions who can actually do the damn job! We are tired of this! People are dying! Children are dying! Stop it! Impeach him!"

CHERYL HINES SAYS 'THE VIEW' HOSTS JUST WANTED TO 'GRILL' HER ABOUT RFK JR, DIDN'T TALK ABOUT NEW BOOK

In a comment to Fox News Digital, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster defended Kennedy and said that the Trump administration has repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, citing an ABC News interview with Trump from April 2025.

"President Trump and Secretary Kennedy have both stated that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles infections. CNN'S DANA BASH SPARS WITH RFK JR OVER VACCINE EFFICACY, DEMANDS HE 'LOOK INTO THE CAMERA' AND PUSH VACCINES

World.title: Fred Warner calls Mexico City NFL game 'super special' as Mexican roots take center stage
World.content:
This week’s NFL international schedule will feature a return trip to Mexico City.

The San Francisco 49ers last played in Mexico City in 2022, and this Sunday they will be back in Mexico's capital city for a Week 11 matchup with the Minnesota Vikings. The trip also has personal significance for linebacker Fred Warner, whose maternal grandfather was born in Mexico.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Warner’s grandfather died when Warner’s mother, Laura, was young, and Warner never had the opportunity to meet him. He has nevertheless spoken about his connection to Mexican culture, including the Spanish language he heard and spoke at home as a child.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Warner acknowledged the significance of Sunday night's game.

"Super special," he said after practice on Wednesday. "I remember that first time around, didn’t know what exactly what to expect, but I think that was my first time being out of the country and playing in a game of that magnitude."

Warner, the NFL's current leading tackler, took in a World Cup match at Estadio Azteca over the summer and recalled the electric environment.

"That was elite," Warner said. "Soccer, or football as they call it, the World Cup, representing your home country, that is a whole different animal. The NFL obviously is elite as well, but that was that was a once-in-a-lifetime experience."

NFL COMMISSIONER ROGER GOODELL CONFIRMS LEAGUE WANTS MULTIPLE TEAMS BASED OUTSIDE THE US: 'NO DOUBT'

San Francisco beat Arizona 38-10 in Mexico City on Nov. 21, 2022, and the team is following the same blueprint to prepare for Sunday night's game. After defeating the Dallas Cowboys last Sunday, the Niners flew to Colorado so they could practice at the Air Force Academy, where the 7,258-foot elevation is nearly equal to Mexico City, hoping to gain an advantage for the NFL’s final international game of 2026.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

49ers coach Kyle Shanahan recalled some of the stressful elements that came along with the 2022 Mexico City trip, including the bus carrying players getting lost on the way to the stadium.

"Usually our last bus of players gets three hours before the game, and they got lost somehow on the way to the stadium," coach Kyle Shanahan said. "They didn’t get there until an hour and 15 minutes before the game, and had like 12 starters on it. So that was somewhat stressful, but it didn’t affect us."

The 49ers enter Sunday at 8-1 and atop the NFC standings. The Minnesota Vikings acquired Kirk Cousins at last week's trade deadline, returning the veteran quarterback to the franchise where he spent six seasons.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: President Trump downplays panic over tech outages: ‘Nobody’s going to play games with us’
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

President Donald Trump sought to reassure Americans concerned about a series of technology disruptions over the past week, urging them to "relax" and saying no country would dare "play games" with U.S. digital infrastructure.

Trump’s remarks in China follow a slew of outages affecting the Federal Aviation Administration, Microsoft, major U.S. banks and other institutions, disrupting air travel and business operations and putting Americans on edge.

"Tell them to relax. Everything's good," the president told Fox News senior White House correspondent Jacqui Heinrich.

TIMELINE: AMERICA HITS A TECH WALL AS OUTAGES CRIPPLE EMAIL, GROUND FLIGHTS AND DISRUPT MAJOR BANKS

"I don't want to use specific names because they're treating me extremely well in China, and I have a lot of respect and a lot of relationships and a good relationship with President Xi. But if anybody did that to us, and we found out about it, they know what the repercussions would be with me," the commander in chief said on "The Ingraham Angle."

"Nobody's going to play games with us."

Trump, who said the outages were unrelated, warned that any bad actors should know better than to target U.S. technological infrastructure.

"They know they would be hit so hard," the president said.

RECENT SERVICE OUTAGES NOT STATE-SPONSORED ATTACKS, DNI JAY CLAYTON TESTIFIES

"These are individual events. ... I'll let you know if there's a problem."

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed Congress in part for the hours-long nationwide ground stop, arguing the system is outdated because the government has not provided the agency with sufficient funding to modernize its technology.

"They're putting in new equipment, and things happen when you put in new equipment," Trump said.

FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

"This is 50-year-old equipment, and it has to be changed. And it's gone down before, and we did the right thing. Nobody was injured. Nobody was hurt. No planes were bunking into each other," he continued.

Trump told Fox News that Duffy is doing "fantastic," standing behind the transportation chief over his handling of Friday’s nationwide ground stop.

He echoed Duffy’s concerns about the state of the system, saying that while the United States has money available, he believes it is better to wait for additional funding and pursue a complete overhaul rather than "piecemeal," patchwork renovations.

"We were given $12 million, but I said, 'Don't spend it until we can do the whole thing, the whole system. You don't want to do piecemeal,'" Trump said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We want to give out ... like the big, beautiful deal, one big, beautiful contract," he proposed. "We want to give out a contract to somebody that can coordinate everything."

The president touted his building background and said that with his plan, the United States will have the best air traffic control system in the world.

"I build very well. I've made a lot of money building things, always, and I know how to do this stuff," he said.

World.title: Ella Langley dominates CMA Awards with major wins as Taylor Swift makes stunning return to stage
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The 60th annual Country Music Association Awards took place live from Nashville’s Bridgestone Arena on Wednesday night.

Taylor Swift made her big return to the CMA Awards – after last attending in 2016. Her single, "I Knew It, I Knew You," is nominated for single of the year.

The singer took the stage to perform at the CMA Awards for the first time in 13 years, starting her performance with her nominated song, before transitioning into one of her classic hits, "Our Song."

Ella Langley dominated the awards ceremony, as her record-breaking hit, "Choosin’ Texas" won two awards, including single of the year and song of the year.

Langley also won music video of the year before the broadcast. "Choosin' Texas" was named as the music video of the year winner during Good Morning America Wednesday morning.

Later in the show, Langley got teary-eyed as she accepted the award for album of the year, for her album, "Dandelion," noting it took two years to make. She was speechless while accepting the award and received a standing ovation from the audience.

"I’m at a loss for words. I don’t know what to say," she said in her speech. "I love country music and I love what I do."

Her wins also resulted in two wins for Miranda Lambert, who is credited as a producer on the song.

Rising star Langley led the pack with 9 nominations, tying Lainey Wilson and Lambert's all-time record for the most nods by a female artist in a single year. Her win for single of the year left Swift going home empty-handed tonight.

Lambert also had a moment on stage with Kacey Musgraves, when the two sang their hit duet, "Horses and Divorces," from Musgraves' latest album, "Middle of Nowhere."

The song references the rumored feud between the two singers, with them patching things up earlier this year.

Brooks and Dunn won vocal duo of the year for the 17th time in a row at this year’s award show. In addition, the duo also received the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award, which was presented to them by Swift.

Prior to Swift handing them the award, Luke Bryan took to the stage alongside Brothers Osborne, HARDY, Marcus King, and Halestorm to pay tribute to the iconic duo.

Lady A introduced Tim McGraw to the stage to perform, "Don’t Take the Girl" for the first time on the CMA stage, as he is one of the Country Music Hall of Fame inductees this year. It was an intimate performance with the majority of the stage lights turned off save for a few spotlights behind him.

Wilson returned to host the event for the third consecutive time, her second solo. Wilson is also nominated for entertainer of the year, which she won in 2023 and 2025.

She also took to the stage during the show to perform her hit song, "Just A Woman."

Megan Moroney blew fans away while strumming on her pink guitar as she sang "Beautiful Things" into her pink microphone. During her performance, fans surrounding the stage held up pink roses, while everyone in the arena swayed to the beat as with their flashlights lighting up the crowd.

Tucker Wetmore got the crowd pumped with his performance of "Who Told You That," encouraging the crowd to get up and dance. While singing he enthusiastically played the piano which was surrounded by a circle of fire on the stage.

The show began with a tribute to Dolly Parton. Parton was one of the most decorated figures in CMA Awards history, earning 45 nominations and winning 10 trophies over her career, including entertainer of the year in 1978, two female vocalist of the year awards, and the Willie Nelson Lifetime Achievement Award in 2016.

Beyond her wins, she also helped define the telecast itself, famously co-hosting the ceremony in 1988 and returning in 2019 to co-host alongside Carrie Underwood and Reba McEntire.

Parton died on August 25, 2026, at age 80 in Nashville following a brief, private battle with cancer, roughly a year and a half after the passing of her husband of nearly 60 years, Carl Dean.

World.title: Alabama QB Keelon Russell's mother sues Marriott over twin's death, hotel counters with 911 audio
World.content:
April Moore, mother of Alabama quarterback Keelon Russell, is suing AC Hotel Tuscaloosa Downtown and Marriott International over the death of her daughter, Kierston Russell.

Details of the wrongful death suit surfaced ahead of a Dec. 7 hearing in Tuscaloosa County Circuit Court.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Russell has thrown for nearly 2,500 yards and 21 touchdowns this season. Off the field, his family is pursuing a jury trial over the events of June 3, 2025. Kierston, his 18-year-old twin sister, planned to enroll at Alabama alongside him.

Per defense filings, Moore and Keelon left their room around 7:20 p.m. after Kierston reported stomach pain and irregular sleep.

Moore returned, found Kierston unresponsive on the bathroom floor, called 911 at 9:55 p.m., and started CPR. Kierston died at DCH Regional Medical Center.

TWO MEN DIE AFTER SUSPECTED ELECTROCUTION AT HOTEL POOL AS RESCUE EFFORT INJURES OTHERS

Moore sued on June 15, 2026, accusing the hotel and Marriott of failing to train staff in CPR or provide a defibrillator. Her complaint states a worker knocked on the door during the emergency, forcing Moore to stop compressions to answer it, and offered no aid.

Plaintiff's attorney Derrick Mills said experts believe an AED would have saved Kierston's life, adding the hotel "literally frustrated April's efforts in trying to revive her daughter."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The defense disputes that account using timestamps.

In court filings, the defendants say 911 dispatchers never called the front desk, and staff responded only after a guest reported screaming. They contend 911 audio shows Moore never stopped CPR to open the door, requiring a worker to unlock it with a master key before EMTs began treatment within three minutes.

The defense also says 911 calls and bodycam photos place an AED in the room within three to five minutes, adding Alabama law did not require one. Defense counsel Rebecca Young declined comment.

FORMER CLEVELAND BROWNS WR DAVID BELL SEEKS $300M AFTER BOTCHED SURGERY ALLEGEDLY NEARLY KILLED HIM

To reach a jury under Alabama law, Moore must clear two hurdles: proving the hotel owed a duty beyond summoning paramedics, and proving its response cost Kierston her life.

Marriott and the hotel requested dismissal in October; Moore moved to seal records and filed a non-public response on Nov. 6, setting up a Dec. 7 showdown in court.

World.title: Bukele gets hero’s welcome from afar as thousands rally in Haiti after gang crackdown
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

Thousands of people in Haiti took to the streets Tuesday in a show of support for Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele deploying troops to the country to combat violent armed gangs.

The demonstration unfolded as Haiti's Minister of Justice and Public Security, Patrick Pélissier, prepared to travel to San Salvador to discuss anti-gang strategies and ongoing troop cooperation.

The president reflected on the moment in a post on X, sharing a video capturing a sea of people chanting, dancing and cheering in celebration.

"I never expected anything like this. I hear you loud and clear. I love you too. We will triumph. God will give us victory," Bukele said.

BUKELE WARNS HAITIAN GANG LEADERS THAT HIS FORCES WILL 'FINISH' THEM AS HE DID IN EL SALVADOR

According to Reuters, some demonstrators carried signs reading "Long live Bukele" and "Down with the gangs," while others voiced their support for the Salvadoran leader.

"Only a week of operation, we can see the path to change in Haiti. We say thank you to Bukele for all the help he gives us," demonstrator Claudy Mayas said.

Another demonstrator said Bukele was providing Haitians with the one thing they had been waiting years for.

"Four years ago, I could not go to Champs de Mars. I couldn't go to the south of Haiti," a demonstrator, also identified as Claude, said.

"We don’t ask much of the government. We don’t ask for jobs. We need only security."

ROBOT DOGS MOUNTED WITH RIFLES DEPLOYED IN ANTI-GANG STADIUM OPERATION IN HAITI

Just two weeks ago, Bukele backed an operation involving devastating airstrikes that destroyed the headquarters of 400 Mawozo, one of Haiti's most powerful criminal gangs. The home of its leader, Lanmò San Jou, was also targeted in the operation, Bukele previously said.

The direct military action marked a dramatic escalation in Haiti's fight against years of severe gang violence and insecurity.

Bukele joined the mission after four Salvadoran members of the U.N.-backed anti-gang force went missing in a suspected gang ambush near Port-au-Prince on Oct. 18. At the time, Bukele sent more than 2,000 troops to Haiti.

EL SALVADOR-BACKED AIR ASSAULT DESTROYS HAITI GANG HEADQUARTERS AMID SEARCH FOR MISSING TROOPS

While residents paraded through the streets in celebration, U.N. officials issued a statement Tuesday reminding leaders that anti-gang operations must prioritize civilian protection.

"Security forces must strictly limit the use of lethal force to situations where it is unavoidable to protect life from an imminent threat and as a last resort," the agency said.

According to the U.N., armed gangs control an estimated 80% to 90% of Haiti's capital and are expanding into surrounding regions.

World.title: Mayor of US city with largest Muslim population calls El-Sayed's election 'an American story'
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The mayor of the first Arab-majority city in the U.S., home to one of the largest Muslim populations per capita in the nation, told Fox News Digital Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed’s election to the U.S. Senate was "monumental."

"It was monumental, and it's [truly] an American story where the brightest and best of us was elevated to one of the highest offices in the world — a member of the United States Senate — and where the people of Michigan elected an individual regardless of the direction in which he prays, but rather based on the direction in which he wishes to lead," Dearborn, Michigan, Mayor Abdullah Hammoud told Fox News Digital.

"I think that is truly a beautifully American story."

NYC'S MAMDANI SAYS ABDUL EL-SAYED'S SENATE VICTORY IN MICHIGAN 'MEANS SO MUCH TO SO MANY'

Hammoud's comments followed El-Sayed’s Nov. 3 victory over former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in Michigan's high-stakes race to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. With the win, El-Sayed, a progressive Democrat and former Detroit health director, became the first Muslim American elected to the U.S. Senate.

In his victory speech in Detroit shortly after the race was called, El-Sayed took direct aim at the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC). The pro-Israel lobbying group and its affiliates poured roughly $30 million into the August Democratic primary to back U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens against El-Sayed, and he thanked the group for the chance to "beat you twice."

Celebrating his victory, El-Sayed also invoked the Arabic phrase "Alhamdulillah," which translates to "Praise be to God."

ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE

Throughout the campaign, El-Sayed faced repeated scrutiny over his rhetoric on Israel, concerns among some Jewish voters in Michigan and allegations of family ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, claims El-Sayed rejected. He also drew criticism from fellow Democrats over his campaign appearances alongside controversial far-left Twitch streamer Hasan Piker, who previously faced backlash over incendiary remarks regarding the Sept. 11 attacks and Israel.

Three days after his win, El-Sayed addressed the Arab America Foundation’s Connect Empowerment Summit in Chantilly, Virginia, just outside Washington, D.C., where he referred to Michigan as the "capital of Arab America."

"I know we’re here in D.C., which, of course, is the capital of the United States of America. But Michigan is the capital of Arab America," El-Sayed said.

During the speech, El-Sayed also pushed back against the attacks he faced on the campaign trail, saying opponents "wanted to make this a referendum on me and my name and my faith."

ASRA NOMANI: EL-SAYED GLIDES INTO ROLE AS ROCK STAR OF THE HARD LEFT'S RED-GREEN ALLIANCE

Hammoud, who became Dearborn’s first Arab American and Muslim mayor in 2022, explained to Fox News Digital what El-Sayed meant by calling Michigan the "capital of Arab America."

"I think he's just speaking to the idea that the largest concentration of Arab Americans happens to be in the city of Dearborn, just [as] you have so many other cities across America celebrating the unique demographic — sometimes the largest of X population residing within their city bounds — no different," Hammoud said.

World.title: House Democrats select Jeffries as leader, setting him up as the first Black speaker
World.content:
WASHINGTON — Rep. Hakeem Jeffries won House Democrats’ nomination for speaker Wednesday, putting him on track to be the first Black lawmaker elected to wield the gavel in January.

Jeffries was nominated in a closed-door, secret-ballot vote of 251-11, according to two sources in the room. It was a show of strength for Jeffries, who had faced grumbling from progressive members and activists calling for new and bolder leadership. But no challenger emerged.

Some of Jeffries’ allies had pushed for a vote by acclamation, which would not result in a tally. But Jeffries asked for a recorded vote to give his rank-and-file members an opportunity to voice their support or opposition — something he said the Democratic Caucus did when it returned Nancy Pelosi to the speaker’s office after the 2018 midterm elections amid calls for a new generation of leadership.

“The results of today’s election speak for themselves. We’re going to work hard throughout every corner of the caucus to deliver for the American people,” Jeffries told reporters when asked about the Democratic defectors. “Our job is to fight MAGA extremism, not each other — to fight MAGA extremism and to get big things done for the American people. And that is what we are going to accomplish together, beginning on Jan. 3rd.”

Jeffries after the vote Wednesday. Finn Gomez / Getty

After the vote, seven of the 11 Democrats who voted against Jeffries issued a joint statement explaining their position.

“Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues,” wrote Reps.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier, D-N.Y., Adam Hamawy, D-N.J., Frederick Haynes, D-Texas, Melat Kiros, D-Colo., Donavan McKinney, D-Mich., Chris Rabb, D-Pa., and Claire Valdez, D-N.Y.

“We have worked to secure commitments from Leader Jeffries in good-faith conversations. While we have seen meaningful progress, there is still work to be done to ensure that the direction our party takes this coming Congress reflects what our constituents are demanding of leadership,” they said. “Those conversations are ongoing. As such, our vote in caucus today was no.”

Jeffries was nominated by five colleagues representing the broad diversity of the Democratic Caucus: Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., Rep. Derek Tran, D-Calif., Rep. Mark Pocan, D-Wis., Rep.-elect Rebecca Bennett, D-N.J., and former Majority Whip Jim Clyburn, D-S.C., one of Jeffries’ political mentors.

“This is a very surreal moment for me,” Clyburn, a veteran of the Civil Rights Movement and former chair of the Black Caucus, told reporters before the vote.

Jeffries, a 56-year-old Brooklyn native, former attorney and former state lawmaker, is now poised to make history as the first Black speaker of the House.

He campaigned across the country in recent months and helped Democrats win what NBC News projects will be 259 seats — the largest majority in 35 years and well more than the 218 votes he will need to be elected speaker on the House floor on Jan. 3.

It means that Jeffries can afford roughly 40 Democratic defections that day and still be elected speaker. By contrast, in 2023, Republican Kevin McCarthy had a razor-thin 222-212 majority; he managed to win the speaker’s gavel on the 15th ballot.

Last week, House Republicans elected Judiciary Committee Chairman Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, over Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., to be minority leader in the next Congress.

Like the speaker race, the other major Democratic leadership races are also uncontested. Rep. Katherine Clark, D-Mass., was elected by her colleagues as majority leader, the No. 2 position. She will make history as the first woman in either chamber elected to that role.

Rep. Pete Aguilar, D-Calif., was elected majority whip, the No. 3 leader and party’s top vote counter. No Hispanic American lawmaker has ever climbed higher in the House.

Rep. Ted Lieu, another California Democrat, was elected as caucus chairman. He will make history as the first Asian American to hold that job.

And Rep. Joe Neguse, D-Colo., was elected assistant speaker.

The only significant contested leadership race is for vice chair of the Democratic Caucus, where Rep. Lauren Underwood, D-Ill., a member of the Black Caucus, defeated Rep. Sara Jacobs, D-Calif., a member of the Progressive Caucus.

Jeffries, a Pelosi protégé, had served as Democratic Caucus chairman before he was elevated to minority leader following House Democrats’ loss in the 2022 midterms.

He spent much of Tuesday holding meetings with the various factions of his massive new majority that he will need to unite to pass legislation on issues like affordability. He met separately with the leaders of the Congressional Progressive Caucus and the two moderate groups, the New Democrat Coalition and the Blue Dogs.

After Wednesday’s vote, Jeffries told reporters that Democrats will be laser-focused on affordability and lowering the cost of living when they take control of Congress.

“The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic, and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable,” said Jeffries, flanked by his top lieutenants, Clark and Aguilar.

“And we’re committed to delivering, in a meaningful way, the type of change that the American people deserve,” he said, “so that everyone in this country can live an affordable life, a comfortable life, and a good life.”

World.title: Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official over investigation of her political speech
World.content:
WASHINGTON — A Democratic senator repeatedly targeted by the Trump administration for potential prosecution due to her political remarks is firing back at a Trump-appointed Justice Department official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her rhetoric about congressional oversight.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is one of five Democratic members of Congress who have been the subject of letters that U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas Aaron Reitz has posted on social media. In one of the letters, which have come under scrutiny from legal experts, Reitz suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight potentially acting as a “deterrence message” to people considering joining the Trump administration could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.

“I made those statements consistent with my basic right to freedom of speech, a right that every American enjoys under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” Slotkin wrote Wednesday in a letter to Reitz obtained by NBC News. “In addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility.”

“The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts,” she wrote. “As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

Slotkin went on to say that Reitz’s “public threats” violated Justice Department policy, and that his decision to publicly post the letter rather than providing it to her, her attorney, or Senate legal counsel “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Reitz, 39, previously worked as chief of staff for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and became U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas over the summer after placing fourth in the Republican primary for Texas attorney general.

Reitz also posted letters on X to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass.; Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn.; Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif.,; and Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.

He told NBC News this week that he was “not interested in chilling free speech.”

Aaron Reitz, U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of Texas, on Capitol Hill last year. Chip Somodevilla / Getty

Slotkin and five other sitting Democratic lawmakers were separately targeted by the Trump administration earlier this year over a video they posted to social media that sought to remind members of the military and intelligence communities that they should not obey unlawful orders. Allies of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro tried to indict the six Democrats for their speech in that video, but federal grand jurors unanimously rejected the indictment attempt.

Slotkin’s attorney, Prett Bharara, had previously written a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche cautioning him against following President Donald Trump’s public instruction to look into Slotkin’s political speech, which he dubbed a “criminal act.”

Blanche has conceded that Slotkin’s words alone were “absolutely not a crime” and said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.”

Slotkin wrote in her letter that Reitz appeared to be “seeking attention” for himself and the Justice Department, or was “unaware” of basic constitutional rights.

“Given all of this, your threats are frivolous and a violation of your ethical duties as an attorney,” she wrote. “I reserve all rights to take appropriate actions in the future as it relates to this sham investigation.”

World.title: Anthropic is about to be worth more than $1 trillion. What that means for the rest of us.
World.content:
Leading AI lab Anthropic is expected to make the largest-ever public market debut when it starts trading on the Nasdaq stock exchange Thursday.

Founded in 2021 by brother and sister Dario and Daniela Amodei, both former employees of rival OpenAI, Anthropic and its main product, Claude, are seen as the gold standard of AI models, despite lacking the household-name cache of ChatGPT.

With a target market value of $1.5 trillion — larger than SpaceX’s record setting IPO just a few months ago — Anthropic’s public arrival will serve as more than just a measure of what Wall Street thinks the company is worth. It will be a test of current sentiment around AI itself at a pivotal moment for the industry.

For much of the past year, the AI investment wave has powered the stock market to new heights and sustained U.S. economic growth. But there are signs the wave may be starting to break.

“Investors have over recent weeks become increasingly concerned around the sustainability of the investment boom,” James McCann, senior economist for investment strategy at Edward Jones, said in a client note Wednesday ahead of Anthropic’s debut.

The market gains notched this spring and summer thanks to the AI boom have now largely been wiped out.

Fears of over-spending on infrastructure, rising debt loads, ballooning costs and uncertain demand have grown. At the same time, public opinion has turned against data centers and AI-skeptical Democrats won control of Congress earlier this month.

Then, the Jensen Huang scandal broke, creating a cloud of uncertainty over Nvidia, a company at the heart of the AI economy. The tech heavy Nasdaq was up 19% for the year recently. As of Wednesday, it’s higher by less than 5%.

“The leadership change at Nvidia meanwhile adds to short-term uncertainty around the sector, particularly given the important role this giant company has played in financially supporting a range of smaller technology firms in recent years,” said McCann.

“With the selloff in technology stocks continuing this week investors will be watching to see how well the Anthropic IPO is received.”

The offering priced Anthropic at $83 a share, above the company’s intended range, the company said late Wednesday.

There is little debate over how uniquely successful Anthropic has been. The latest edition of Claude, dubbed Fable, ranks No. 1 on Artificial Analysis’ leaderboard of top-performing large language models as it is able to handle complex computer engineering tasks.

And its Claude Code application is now used throughout the tech industry and by some accounts became the fastest-growing product in enterprise software history when it was released in Feb. 2025, hitting $1 billion in revenues within six months of launching.

In the first half of 2026, Anthropic saw total revenues of more than $16 billion. Samyukta Lakshmi / Bloomberg via Getty

Thursday’s IPO is also expected to mint a new crop of billionaires and multi-millionaires as Anthropic’s co-founders and early employees see their interest in the company turned into shares with a defined cash value.

Part of that will be fueled by a massive appetite for investing in the shares among mom-and-pop investors. According to Vanda Research, a markets consultancy, Anthropic could see approximately $250 million worth of buying among non-institutional or “retail” investors when it starts trading Thursday. That would be double the magnitude of interest following SpaceX’s IPO.

Other major winners will include Amazon, Google-parent Alphabet, Microsoft, and Nvidia, which will each own billions-worth of Anthropic shares.

Some observers see Anthropic’s debut as more of a major milestone than a make-or-break moment. In their view, there are plenty of other investments backstopping the AI boom.

“A strong IPO would help resurrect the AI trade, but it does not mean a weaker-than-expected IPO would bury that trade,” said Renée Friedman, global head of research at EXANTE, a Europe-based finance and technology group.

“There are significant commitments into the AI cycle by some of the world’s largest companies over a multi-year period. These are not going to just disappear,” he said.

In the first half of 2026, Anthropic saw total revenues of more than $16 billion. That compares with $41 million over the same period just three years ago. While Anthropic was technically operating at a loss to start the year, investors expect it to be profitable soon.

Those heady figures capture a tension at the heart of Anthropic’s IPO. In addition to being the leading AI lab, current and former Anthropic employees have also been some of the most vocal proponents of AI safety, giving voice to fears that, should the technology become too advanced, it could start to run amok.

“I think that without international coordination we will incur a risk of causing human extinction,” former Anthropic employee Jacob Coxon wrote of his concerns about AI shortly before resigning.

Yet some critics have said those concerns have proven no match for the seemingly unstoppable momentum of creating a company publicly valued at more than $1 trillion.

Dario Amodei has responded, arguing building safe AI and creating the world’s most advanced — and valuable — AI models are not necessarily mutually exclusive.

When a user criticized Anthropic for seeming to plunge ahead with its attempt to create “superhuman” AI despite the risks to humanity doing so, Amodei replied in an X post that “a list of things that Anthropic did in the past year that were pro-safety and commercially costly to us” would be much longer than a list of risks it posed to mankind.
