World.title: Trump and Xi speak at APEC summit ahead of rare joint meeting with Putin
World.content:
President Trump and his Chinese and Russian counterparts are in China for a summit and a set of rare face-to-face talks between the leaders of three of the world's most powerful countries.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Mr. Trump addressed members of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum in Shenzhen. Mr. Trump said the U.S. is committed to "growth and stability" in the Asia-Pacific region, and argued the American economy is "thriving like it has never thrived before." He also said the U.S. is negotiating "numerous trade agreements" and expects to sign some agreements with APEC members in the near future.

The president also vowed to block any "globalist regulation" of artificial intelligence.

"We do not want to do anything to destroy the tremendous potential of this technology," he said. "We have to watch it, we have to be careful, we have to cherish it. It's almost completely good, but it's got some bad elements, so we have to be very careful in managing those bad elements."

During Xi's remarks earlier in the session, the Chinese leader called on countries in the region to "look out for each other" and "expand our shared interests," including on free trade and economic growth.

Mr. Trump and Xi are scheduled to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin next.

The U.S. president has said he's planning to discuss denuclearization with the leaders of China and Russia — which, along with the United States, make up the world's three largest holders of nuclear weapons.

But a range of other global challenges and points of tension are lingering in the background.

President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping arrive for the plenary meeting at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 19, 2026. Ng Han Guan / POOL /AFP via Getty Images

The summit is taking place in the capital of the Chinese tech industry, a sector that has drawn intense scrutiny in recent weeks amid worries that advanced U.S. computer chips are surreptitiously reaching China. The scandal was sparked by allegations that now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a businesswoman and suspected Chinese intelligence asset, Alice Huang, whose company is accused of diverting Nvidia's coveted AI chips to China. Beijing has dismissed claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China."

Mr. Trump — an ally of Jensen Huang's — had previously told reporters he may bring up the businesswoman during his meetings in China, though he said, "I don't know that she is a spy." Her firm, Megaspeed, is under Justice Department investigation. It has denied wrongdoing.

Shortly after the concerns about Jensen Huang surfaced, the Trump administration issued a new rule aimed at curbing China and other countries' ability to remotely access advanced AI chips. China and the U.S. have also discussed broader AI policy issues in recent months, including setting up a communication channel to share information when AI systems go haywire.

Beyond AI, the U.S. and China have sought to stabilize their economic relationship over the last year, following a tit-for-tat trade war that sent tariffs above 100% in 2025. A tariff truce between the two countries is set to expire on Jan. 10 of next year.

President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping after leaders posed for a group photo during the summit on Nov. 19, 2026. Greg Baker / POOL /AFP via Getty Images

Iran is another contentious area, given China's status as one of the largest customers of Iranian oil, and Russia's ties with Iran.

The White House previously said the war in Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said he expected the issue to come up, calling it "my favorite subject."

Taiwan is another frequent discussion topic between the U.S. and China. During the U.S. president's visit to Beijing in the spring, Xi reportedly delivered a stern warning about the island, which he has long vowed to reintegrate with mainland China, floating potential "clashes and even conflicts" if the issue isn't "handled properly."

And Mr. Trump was expected to press Xi to release two detained Americans during his visit to China, CBS News has reported. Beijing has resisted repeated U.S. calls for their release.

World.content:
Cameron Logan Cox was honest with his employer when he recently submitted a request for paid time off.

"I literally just put GTA 6," the 34-year-old filmmaker and creative director at a music label in Kansas City told CBS News. He said his coworkers were already well aware that he'd be out of action when Grand Theft Auto 6 is officially released on Thursday.

"They all know I'm a huge gamer," he said. "We don't have anything too pressing happening, so it worked out nicely."

Cox is hardly alone. Other avid GTA fans told CBS News they've cleared their work schedules so they can dive headlong into Rockstar Games' latest, and long-awaited, installment in the hit franchise. According to data from payroll processor Gusto, PTO requests for the day of GTA 6's commercial release this week are up 9% compared with the two prior weeks.

In short, GTA 6 is as much a cultural happening as a video game. Analysts say the game, which took 13 years to make, is expected to be the largest entertainment release of all time.

"While it's common for people to plan time off around major entertainment releases and cultural events, the anticipation surrounding GTA 6 is on another level," Bart Spiegel, a partner at PwC who leads the consulting firm's global entertainment and media practice, said in an email. "It's the kind of cultural moment that could rival the Olympics in terms of the attention it commands, so there's certainly going to be an impact on workplaces."

Spoiler alert

One 27-year-old woman told CBS News that she submitted her PTO request back in March to be ready for this week's GTA launch. She knew she would want to start playing as soon as the game went live and to avoid online spoilers.

"I genuinely believe that this is one of, if not the biggest, gaming events in a lot of our lifetimes, and spoilers are going to spread so fast," said the Grays Harbor, Washington state, resident. "It's going to be nearly impossible to avoid them."

The woman, who works as a clerk for the U.S. Postal Service, has already pre-downloaded GTA 6 and plans to start playing at 9 p.m. PST on Wednesday.

"I'm probably just going to go throughout the whole night," she said.

Another player based in the U.K. told CBS News he is also trying to avoid spoilers. The 25-year-old is taking a long weekend beginning on Wednesday to "give [GTA 6] the attention it deserves."

The man, who works in tech finance and who requested anonymity because he's not authorized to speak to the media, set up his PlayStation account to appear as if he were in New Zealand — where the game is already live — so he could begin playing as soon as possible.

Gaming time off

Meanwhile, some companies are resigning themselves to the temporary brain drain and preemptively giving employees time off to focus on GTA.

Logitech, a California-based computer and electronics manufacturer, introduced a new perk for employees earlier this month: GTO (Gaming Time Off).

And in August, a U.S. Army unit in Georgia offered active-duty soldiers a four-day pass to play GTA 6 in exchange for reenlisting. The Third Infantry Division told CBS News that 43 of the 130 soldiers who were eligible selected this option as part of their reenlistment, along with other standard incentives.

While some U.S. employees may ditch work on Thursday, their absence from the office isn't expected to cause major economic disruptions, according to Victor Matheson, an economics professor at the College of the Holy Cross.

"Even if 5 million workers in the U.S. took the day off, the total U.S. labor force is 170 million people," he said in an email. "That's like 3% of the labor force."

So far, more than 17 million preorder copies of the game have been downloaded worldwide, according to Sensor Tower, a digital market intelligence company. Matheson expects the game to rack up more than 50 million users by year's end.

As for Cox, 27 years have passed since he first played Grand Theft Auto on an original PlayStation console owned by a relative. Yet the excitement is as fresh as ever.

"It feels like I'm a kid again," Cox told CBS News.

He'll be in good company when the game launches, as his son is also planning to stay home from school on Thursday and Friday. Cox agreed to let him take time off to celebrate his birthday, which falls on Friday.

"He has all of his schoolwork turned in. That was the condition," he told CBS News. "I was, like, as long as all your work's done, your grades are good, I'm fine with that."

World.title: Costco sees surge in panic buying after tech outages, report says
World.content:
Consumers are panic-buying at Costco, snapping up generators and other emergency-preparedness items in response to a recent string of technology outages, according to investment firm Mizuho Securities.

"Consumer anxiety following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco," Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a report.

Shoppers are "pantry-loading," while 21 of the retailer's 26 "high-ticket generators" were sold out online as of Sunday night, he added.

The recent outages, which blocked access to Microsoft apps, snarled flights nationwide and hindered banking activities at various times during the past week, are raising questions among Americans about a larger cybersecurity threat, CBS News chief correspondent Matt Gutman said on "CBS Mornings" on Wednesday.

The companies affected by the outages have said they were due to issues such as routine maintenance or upgrades, while the Federal Aviation Administration blamed its nationwide ground stop last week on a contractor updating its flight system.

"All of them have denied that cyberattacks are to blame," Gutman said. "Still, the system failures are fueling online speculation about a larger cyber threat."

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Wednesday that there's "zero evidence" that the recent outages in the U.S. are linked.

"The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we've seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated one from another," Rubio said during a news conference in the Philippines.

Costco didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The close timing of the outages highlights the country's increasing reliance on technology, John D'Arcy, a Temple University professor who researches cybersecurity and information technology failures, told CBS News Philadelphia.

"Our systems are so much more complex and so much more interconnected than they ever have been in the past, that when we just have one failure, the effects are much more dramatic," D'Arcy said.

The surge in panic buying could lift Costco's sales, Bellinger wrote. He raised his target price for the company's stock to $1,150 from $1,100. Other big-box stores, including Walmart and Sam's Club, could see similar "pantry-loading lifts," he added.

World.title: Musk says he's "not MAGA," feels "foolish" about midterm spending
World.content:
After opening his wallet to assist Republican candidates in the 2026 midterms, billionaire Elon Musk said Wednesday he feels "pretty foolish" about spending hundreds of millions of dollars.

The world's richest man — who served in President Trump's administration in 2025 — also argued he is "not MAGA" and described his political beliefs as "quite moderate" during an interview at The New York Times' DealBook Summit.

Musk donated vast sums of money to super PACs backing House and Senate Republicans. One of his largest investments was in Texas, where over $150 million of his fortune was transferred to a group supporting Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton.

Those bets largely did not pay off. Democrats won large majorities in the House and Senate, with Paxton losing to Democratic candidate James Talarico, who made Musk's support of his GOP opponent part of his pitch to voters. Democrats also won the Texas governor's office, a notable shift for the state where Musk has based many of SpaceX and Tesla's operations.

Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin his objective in the midterms was to help Republicans hold on to their Senate majority in order to prevent either party from controlling the presidency and both houses of Congress in 2029 — a goal he said "failed."

"Obviously, the Republicans were routed in this election, and … I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it. Or maybe it would have been much worse without that," the billionaire said, adding that "probably if I could rewind the clock, I would have spent less money."

Musk later said his goal was to preserve some "checks and balances," calling himself "ideologically quite moderate" and saying he doesn't have any "extreme political views."

Sorkin noted that Musk has made controversial statements on immigration and "MAGA stuff."

Musk responded: "I'm not MAGA. ... I'm not sure what MAGA means, but I don't think I'm, like, if it means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that. I think there are positives and negatives in both parties."

It's a change in tone for Musk, who has donned MAGA hats in the past, and joked at one 2024 Trump rally: "I'm not just MAGA, I'm dark MAGA." Musk spent hundreds of millions of dollars assisting the Trump campaign and other GOP candidates that year, and later led the Trump administration's cost-cutting Department of Government Efficiency. Musk and Mr. Trump had a brief falling-out last year, but Musk has appeared to maintain a close relationship with the president since then.

Musk also traveled to China this week for Mr. Trump's trip to the country.

Elon Musk joins President Trump during a campaign rally in Butler, Pennsylvania, on Oct. 5, 2024. JIM WATSON/AFP via Getty Images

Musk's alliance with Mr. Trump has drawn scrutiny from Democrats, who have vowed to aggressively investigate the Trump administration when they take the House and Senate next year. Musk is expected to be one focus of their oversight probes.

In Wednesday's interview, Musk said he is not worried that Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa could pose problems to his businesses, saying, "Based on everything I've heard about her, I think things will be fine in Texas with Gina as governor."

"The new governor, actually, I think, is going to be quite moderate," Musk said. "I don't think she's sort of a far-left governor."

He also said some Democrats' comments accusing him of illegality are "a little over the top," telling The Times, "There are definitely a few people grumpy about ... my funding in this past election."

"Hopefully in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison. Aspirationally, that should be how it works," he said.

Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona suggested he was unmoved by Musk's MAGA about-face.

"You are still getting a subpoena," Gallego wrote on X.

World.title: What to know about Trump's meeting with Xi in China
World.content:
Washington — President Trump is holding a high-stakes meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday, against the backdrop of a widening scandal over advanced U.S. chips reaching China and internal divisions within Mr. Trump's Cabinet about how to address it.

The bilateral meeting is taking place in Shenzhen, China, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, known as APEC. Mr. Trump embraced Xi when he arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday.

It's the third time the two world leaders are meeting face to face this year. The last time they met was in September, when Mr. Trump hosted Xi for a three-day summit at the White House. Mr. Trump is hosting Xi again for the G20 Leaders' Summit at Trump National Doral in Miami in December.

The Trump-Xi meeting will be followed by a meeting of Mr. Trump, Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Here's what Mr. Trump and Xi are likely to discuss.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and President Trump attend an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit dinner event in Shenzhen, China, on Nov. 18, 2026. Qilai Shen / Bloomberg via Getty Images

Jensen Huang, Alice Huang and Nvidia

Mr. Trump told reporters as he left for Asia that he may bring up Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. The Justice Department has been investigating Singapore-based Megaspeed for diverting semiconductor chips to China.

The president has cast doubts on assessments that Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset.

"I don't know that she is a spy," he said. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country, that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy. I don't know that she was a spy at all. I mean, I really don't."

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow for China and emerging technologies at the Council on Foreign Relations, said the scandal is much bigger than Jensen Huang and his alleged affairs.

"It's really kind of unfolded into a much bigger, longer-term scandal that involves the question of how many chips did China get, how porous were export controls, and how did the Commerce Department enforce them?" McGuire said on a phone briefing with reporters Wednesday. "Which I think is a much more important, longer-term strategic question for the United States, for the U.S.-China relationship than anything involving Jensen Huang's personal affairs."

China and chips

Shortly before the president left for Asia, the Trump administration announced new interim trade rules that will restrict Chinese AI companies from accessing advanced U.S. chips remotely.

The move comes after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent accused Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick of slow-walking restrictions on Megaspeed, revealing a rift between Bessent and Lutnick. Bessent told CNBC that Mr. Trump had indicated that China should not have access to the chips, but suggested that Lutnick was resisting. The president didn't take sides in the Bessent-Lutnick debate, telling reporters before he left for Asia that the men have "two different views" where "one wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China."

"One view is you don't want to insult China," Mr. Trump said Monday. "We have a very good relationship with China, and you don't want to insult them. And the other view is just go, you know, down and dirty and do what you have to do. Both can say either is wrong or right."

Ultimately, the Treasury Department and National Security Council, not the Commerce Department under Lutnick, wrote the new interim rule cutting off Chinese companies from remotely accessing the most advanced AI chips in data centers abroad, though the Commerce Department issued the rule.

"This is a very significant action that really cuts off a lot of the avenues that China is using to get AI computing power," McGuire said. "There was a digital forensic study that was done recently that showed that every single advanced Chinese model is actually trained with the most advanced American chips, so even though these chips have been banned to China, the controls have not been effective. They've probably had some impact but not that much."

The actions taken on Monday, however, will have a "really significant" effect on China's access to computing power, which "could materially widen the lead" between the U.S. and China on AI, McGuire said.

AI safety

Mr. Trump has shown no signs of wanting to slow the United States' AI advancement in the race against China. After a September summit between Mr. Trump and Xi, the U.S. and Chinese governments pledged to set up a communication channel to share information when AI goes off the rails.

But talking about wayward AI incidents after the fact isn't nearly enough, said Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow on technology with the Asia Society Policy Institute and a digital fellow with the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI.

Graylin will be interested to see if Mr. Trump and Xi can work past the negative news cycle, like the Jensen Huang scandal, to take more steps on AI safety collaboration by bringing together more technical experts for working-level discussions.

"I hope that we go beyond just having surface level discussion, and we start to actually create some enduring institutions around safety," Graylin said.

Taiwan

Before leaving for Asia, Mr. Trump was asked if he'll bring up Taiwan in his meeting with Xi.

"I'm sure he'll raise it," the president responded. "I won't have to raise it."

David Sacks, a senior fellow for Asia studies at the Council on Foreign Relations — not the former White House AI czar David Sacks — said he thinks that's right.

"I think that it's very clear that every time Xi sees Trump, they do a little check-in on Taiwan, and Xi Jinping raises his concerns on Taiwan and his expectations of how President Trump will handle Taiwan and cross-strait dynamics," Sacks told reporters on the Council on Foreign Relations call.

A $14 billion arms package to Taiwan is still pending on the president's desk, Sacks said. Earlier this year, the Navy said the arms sale had been put on "pause" to make sure the U.S. military had enough munitions for the Iran war. Sacks said there will be "more pressure from Congress in the coming months to move that arms package forward."

"And so, if President Trump is determined to resist that, you know he will need, you know — Xi Jinping will hope to kind of stiffen his spine and say, 'You're on the right track, and if you approve this arms package, you're going to send cross-strait relations reeling.'"

The Trump-Putin-Xi meeting

Lyle Goldstein, the director of Defense Priorities Asia, told CBS News he is actually optimistic about a Trump-Putin-Xi meeting. Goldstein said he doesn't think any "major results" will come out of the sit-down, but the discussions might bear fruit in a future U.S.-China-Russia meeting.

"I actually think it could allow for some, not for breakthroughs, but for some movement on major issues," Goldstein said. "And this is the first time ever that you have this trilateral format for Russia, China, and the U.S. So I would like to see this continue."

Mr. Trump said he has a range of topics to discuss with both Xi and Putin when they meet, including denuclearization.

"We're going to talk about denuclearization," Mr. Trump said. "Tough subject, because it's very hard for any of us to say we'll get rid of our nukes, right? Especially since you do have other countries."

They'll also discuss Iran, the U.S. president said. On Tuesday, Mr. Trump said Iran would have a major price to pay if it detonates a so-called dirty bomb, after CNN reported U.S. intelligence indicates Iran may be developing plans to set off such a device in the nation's capital.

The White House previously said Ukraine would not be a topic of discussion in the Trump-Xi-Putin meeting, since no Ukrainian representatives will be present. But on Monday, Mr. Trump said Ukraine will be a topic for the three leaders.

"We'll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine," he told reporters.

World.title: Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand
World.content:
Anthropic IPO raises record $81.3 billion on strong AI demand

toggle caption i Idrees Mohammed/AFP via Getty Images

The artificial intelligence company Anthropic said on Wednesday it sold more than 956 million shares at a price of $83 a piece in a record-breaking initial public offering that makes it one of the most valuable companies in the world.

The five-year-old AI powerhouse raised around $79.4 billion through the offering, exceeding the $75 billion IPO haul of Elon Musk's SpaceX earlier this year. Anthropic said in a statement that "certain stockholders" also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO, bringing the total haul to more than $81.3 billion.

Anthropic's shares will start trading publicly on Thursday on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT.

Sponsor Message

The listing was oversubscribed, despite coming at a time of growing concern about a possible AI bubble and volatility in tech stocks.

The number of shares sold and the price exceeded Anthropic's original expectations. The listing prospectus targeted a sale of 825 million shares at $70 to $78 per share.

Anthropic is a financial supporter of NPR.

World.title: The law releasing the Epstein files passed one year ago. What do his victims say?
World.content:
The law releasing the Epstein files passed one year ago. What do his victims say?

It's been a year since the House passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, forcing the Justice Department to release millions of files connected to the convicted sex offender. His victims speak out.

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Now we turn to an effort to shed light on the crimes of convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, an effort that, in some cases, revictimized the women he abused. It's been a year since a new law required the Justice Department to release millions of files related to the Epstein investigation. But when the files were made public last year, so were the names and even phone numbers of some of the women he targeted. NPR's Ava Berger spoke with two Epstein survivors and to the sister-in-law of one survivor who died by suicide.

ANNIE FARMER: My name's Annie Farmer. I was 16 years old when I was abused by Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

DANI BENSKY: My name is Dani Bensky, and I was 17 years old when I met Jeffrey Epstein.

AMANDA ROBERTS: My name is Amanda Roberts, and I am a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, and I am the sister-in-law of Virginia Roberts Giuffre, one of the most prominent survivors of Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell.

FARMER: There has been so much that's happened in the last 12 months and, really, in the lead-up, you know, to the passing of the legislation, as well - was very busy and very chaotic.

BENSKY: I keep thinking about that day. We sat in the gallery of the House, and we got to watch the votes come in. And it was so surreal to sit there and just watch the board and watch everything start to flip to yes. We went from that moment, and, you know, tears were streaming as we passed this new law.

ROBERTS: There was this feeling of we knew the pain that each other carried. And there was this moment of unity, and it was that feeling, that unity, that courage, together, that drove this entire year.

FARMER: The moment of joy that comes to mind for me from this year was actually the day that the files were released. I think that there - as more people in the public have become aware of both the extent of the crimes and also the amount of information that was gathered by the government about those crimes, there has been a sense of validation.

BENSKY: But then I did find my name in a memo pad. It certainly wasn't redacted, as it had my phone number in it. And we started to see that the perpetrators were really being protected, and we couldn't find perpetrators' names and predators' names, but we could certainly find a lot of victims' and survivors' names. And so that felt really awful.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

BENSKY: There are a thousand girls, more than a thousand girls and women that have been abused in those files. And so, yeah, you might be talking about some powerful people, but you're also talking about over a thousand lives that have been completely derailed.

ROBERTS: There is such an appetite for justice in this community, in our country right now that I believe if we just keep this momentum pushing forward, we will see real accountability for all abusers out there. And we can really see a societal shift that says it doesn't matter what power and position and money you have, we are all to be held accountable to the same laws and rules.

FARMER: I certainly hope that there's a future where I never have to speak the names Epstein and Maxwell. I think many, many survivors in this case are interested in their lives moving on and not having to look so much in the rearview mirror about, you know, what's happened here.

ROBERTS: If Virginia was here to see this, I would tell her that I'm so proud (crying) and that I wish that you would have held on just a little bit longer to see this. But I understand why she felt like she couldn't, because she had been failed by every single system in her life.

PFEIFFER: Virginia Roberts Giuffre was one of Epstein's most outspoken accusers. She died by suicide last year. That was Dani Bensky, Annie Farmer and Amanda Roberts speaking with NPR's Ava Berger on the one-year anniversary of the passage of the Epstein Files Transparency Act.

And if you or someone you know may be considering suicide or is in crisis, call or text 988 to reach the Suicide and Crisis Lifeline.

(SOUNDBITE OF MUSIC)

World.title: Why the Nvidia scandal is a national security issue
World.content:
Why the Nvidia scandal is a national security issue

The Nvidia scandal has spilled over into the Trump administration, which is now under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

For more than two weeks now, the tech world has been consumed by the rolling crisis around Nvidia. The company's cofounder and CEO, Jensen Huang, was pushed out after news reports of extramarital affairs that includes an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence agencies suspected of being a Chinese spy. The scandal has since spilled over into the Trump administration, and now it, too, is under intense scrutiny for how it allowed America's top AI chips to end up in China's hands. NPR's Ryan Lucas and Shannon Bond have been digging into this. Hey there.

SHANNON BOND, BYLINE: Hey there.

RYAN LUCAS, BYLINE: Hi, Scott.

DETROW: So the coverage so far has been about all the scandalous details of Huang's personal life, but this is a national security scandal. Tell us more about that.

LUCAS: Well, right. And China, of course, is a superpower. It has the economic and military might that puts it almost on equal footing with the United States, and China and the U.S., of course, are in a race to develop artificial intelligence. And AI has implications in all facets of life, including cybersecurity, on the military battlefield and technological development in the economy. So the trickle-down effects of this are enormous. And so protecting the current American technological lead in AI is seen is very much a national security issue.

BOND: And President Trump really sees this AI race with China as a binary win-lose situation. So here's how he described it back in September.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We're leading China in AI. We're the most sophisticated country in the world. And frankly, I want to keep it that way, because whoever wins AI wins.

BOND: And look, Nvidia makes these chips that are really crucial to AI development. And so Jensen Huang has long argued that American companies should, in fact, sell these chips to China so that Chinese AI development is reliant on U.S. AI hardware. That view is not universally shared, including in the government, but it's one that Huang has really successfully pushed during this second Trump administration.

DETROW: And this gets to an important factor here - the way that Huang's views have shaped administration policies.

LUCAS: Well, look, the Biden administration took a hard line on this. It severely restricted the sale of the most advanced American AI chips to China to try to protect the U.S. national security and the country's technological edge in AI. Trump came into office in January of 2025, and things changed. Jensen Huang was actively lobbying the administration to loosen the restrictions. And for the past 18 months or so, America's most advanced AI chips, Nvidia chips, have been flying out the door to America's biggest rival, to China. I spoke to Chris McGuire about this. He worked on the national security council on AI and export controls. I asked him why China would want Nvidia's most advanced chips. Here's what he said.

CHRIS MCGUIRE: These chips are the lifeblood of AI. They're the most important thing that you need for AI systems and AI development, and they're also the single biggest differentiator between the U.S. and China.

LUCAS: Now, China can't make these top-end chips themselves, but despite the national security concerns, McGuire says over the last 18 months, some $60 billion in AI chips have gone to Singapore, Malaysia and Thailand legally. But those three countries can't support that level of AI buildout on their own. So some of those chips are suspected of having been smuggled into China. McGuire says the rest are in data centers that are primarily being used by China's top tech companies to train their own AI to make those models better. Here's McGuire again.

MCGUIRE: The reason that this happened is that the Trump administration did not enforce the license requirement that would have applied to those countries, and it's just enabled a massive technology transfer out the door.

LUCAS: Now, McGuire said this is potentially the biggest transfer of export control technology to an adversary in U.S. history, which, of course, begs the question of why and how that was allowed to happen. And there's an argument that Jensen Huang's personal relationship with Trump played a role here.

DETROW: So what exactly did that relationship - that relationship between Trump and Huang - look like?

BOND: Yeah. I mean, his profile was not this high at the beginning of Trump's second term. For example, he was not one of the tech CEOs who attended the inauguration, but Huang really successfully launched this campaign of personal diplomacy. And, Scott, as an example of just how close he became to President Trump, back in September, Huang was on stage at a big tech conference, and he took a call from Trump on his personal cellphone.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

JENSEN HUANG: Mr. President, oh, yes, sir. I got to tell you something. I - if it wasn't because of you calling, I would - I'm on stage.

BOND: He went on to put Trump on speakerphone and lavishly praised his leadership on AI. And you can really see how he's cultivated this relationship and has helped him become one of the most influential voices shaping the administration's AI policy. And Huang and others who share these views have framed making China dependent on American AI chips as a way for the U.S. to stay ahead in this AI race, which as I said, Trump really cares about.

DETROW: So what actions has the administration taken that have benefited Nvidia?

LUCAS: Well, the Trump administration has lifted restrictions on two specific Nvidia chips to allow them to be sold directly to China. The Trump administration also secured a massive deal to give the United Arab Emirates access to Nvidia's most advanced chips, a deal worth billions of dollars, and it did so despite concerns that those chips could end up, again, in China.

Now, at the same time, I'm told that there was a recommendation in the summer of 2025 to impose an export license requirement to send AI chips to Malaysia and Thailand over the concerns that we have been talking about, but the Commerce Department sat on that. It didn't move forward. And so those chip sales - the chips that are at the very heart of the current scandal - those chip sales continued. And only this week, in response to this rolling scandal that we've seen, did the Commerce Department move to restrict those chip sales and close that loophole.

DETROW: OK. So the Commerce Department made that move. Huang is out at Nvidia. What comes next?

BOND: Well, Huang and Nvidia's top lawyer are set to answer questions from lawmakers on Capitol Hill. That'll start after Thanksgiving. Those lawmakers are going to have a lot of questions, you know, about this relationship, certainly, with the suspected Chinese spy, but also about these allegations, you know, that there may be ways in which they were evading export controls.

Now, I should note, this week, Nvidia's board said it had formed a committee to oversee the company's national security policies and its compliance with export controls. You know, that's going to be a live issue. And, of course, Scott, Democrats are now going to be in control of Congress. So I think there is going to be more to come in terms of scrutiny and questions for Jensen Huang, but also for these administration officials and the decisions they made and what some of the thought process behind that and who might have been influencing that.

DETROW: Yeah. That is NPR's Shannon Bond and Ryan Lucas. Thanks to both of you.

LUCAS: Thank you.

BOND: Thanks, Scott

World.title: Democrats nominate Jeffries for speaker, prep investigations into Trump's orbit
World.content:
Democrats nominate Jeffries for speaker, prep investigations into Trump's orbit

Democrats gave the official nod to Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Meanwhile, Democrats are ramping up their plans to investigate the Trump administration come January.

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Democrats have been busy today on Capitol Hill. House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries is one step closer to becoming the next speaker of the House after a vote behind closed doors this morning.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

HAKEEM JEFFRIES: The people of this country are demanding bold, dramatic and transformational change. The status quo is unacceptable.

PFEIFFER: And Democrats are previewing their investigation agenda for when they take over in January. NPR congressional correspondent Barbara Sprunt is at the Capitol and is with us on the line. Hi, Barbara.

BARBARA SPRUNT, BYLINE: Hello.

PFEIFFER: So it certainly appears that Hakeem Jeffries is the presumptive next speaker. But was this a unanimous vote?

SPRUNT: It was not. There was some grumbling from newly elected progressive members who had said that they wanted to see new leadership. But Jeffries did run unopposed. This was an overwhelming vote of support for him. The vote was 251-11, and this sets him up for January, which is when the full House will vote for speaker.

PFEIFFER: And on the Senate side, things are not looking as clear cut. The current minority leader is Chuck Schumer. He's being challenged by Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen. What are their respective arguments for why they should get the top Senate job?

SPRUNT: Well, some Schumer allies have been using a sports metaphor when talking about this. Like, if the manager brings a team to the World Series, why would they then fire him? You know, a lot of people see Schumer as instrumental in flipping nine Senate seats for Democrats, far beyond what many in the party even considered in their wildest dreams going into this election cycle. But Van Hollen argues voters made it clear that they want change, and he says that that extends to Democratic leadership. Progressives seem very excited about him, but zooming out, it was moderates and centrist Democrats who really opened up the map in big ways for Democrats this election cycle, particularly in the South. So there is this tension - right? - between the why switch horses midstream and the other side that says, well, the moment calls for shake-ups.

PFEIFFER: And what's the general view on whether Van Hollen actually is a candidate who represents change?

SPRUNT: Well, perhaps unsurprisingly, it depends on who you ask. You know, he calls himself an underdog. He's positioned himself as embracing the populist economic policies that really resonated with so many voters this cycle. And fairly early on, he joined calls to restrict arms sales to the Israeli government, which has certainly endeared him to a lot of progressives. He's been increasingly critical of the Democratic Party and the way that congressional leaders have historically approached the Trump administration. But others point out he's not really a generational-change candidate. He's 67 years old, about eight-ish years younger than Schumer. He represents a blue state. He's been in politics for decades. And in fact, he's already chaired both the House and Senate campaign committees, so he's not a new face.

PFEIFFER: Barbara, in terms of the Democrats' agenda, since the election, they have been saying that they will aggressively conduct oversight of the Trump administration. Did they address that at all today?

SPRUNT: They did, indeed. Congressman Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on oversight and the expected next chairman of the committee, sent a dozen letters to President Trump's allies and some family members telling them to hold on to their documents for upcoming investigations.

PFEIFFER: Ah, sounds like a target list of sorts.

SPRUNT: Exactly.

PFEIFFER: Who's on that list?

SPRUNT: Well, the president's two sons, his son-in-law, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, her adviser Corey Lewandowski, Vice President JD Vance. Those are just a few. Democrats' targets fall into four buckets broadly - alleged corruption within the Trump family, corporate corruption, misconduct in the Department of Homeland Security and what Democrats call the White House Epstein cover-up. Now, the White House has rejected those accusations of misconduct before and has warned Garcia that investigations could constitute a crime. That is something that legal experts push back on.

PFEIFFER: Sounds like months and maybe years of coverage for you coming up.

SPRUNT: (Laughter).

PFEIFFER: That's NPR's Barbara Sprunt. Thank you.

SPRUNT: Thank you.

World.title: After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives
World.content:
After Nepal's epic flood, they're restoring their community ... and their lives

toggle caption i Skanda Gautam/SOPA Images/LightRocket/via Getty Images

"I thought I wouldn't survive," says Januka Dhital.

Just minutes before that terrible thought, Dhital was busy preparing snacks. She ran a catering service out of her house in Uttargaya, Nepal, and was getting ready for an event later that day. Her work was interrupted by a man on a scooter, warning of a flood. She stepped outside to look.

"When I turned around, I saw darkness, dust and what looked like the entire hillside coming down," she says.

She grabbed her young son and hopped onto the back of the man's scooter. They raced to higher ground, eventually reaching safety. But she didn't know if her husband and daughter were safe, since they were at work and school when the waters came.

Sponsor Message

"It felt unbelievable"

After hours of waiting and searching, they were all reunited. Her husband was naked, covered in blood and badly injured, she says, but alive.

toggle caption i Family photo

"It felt unbelievable that our family had survived," says Dhital. But the wall of water and mud that descended from the mountains had obliterated their home, along with thousands of others. "We have lost everything. We have nothing now."

Dhital and her family are among the 100,000-some people whose lives have been upended by the devastating floods sparked by glacial melt, a phenomenon made worse by climate change . At least 1,500 have died, and more than 5,000 are still missing. Thousands are still living in temporary shelters or tents.

The flood damaged or destroyed seven health facilities, 23 schools, 10,000 toilets and 64 water systems, according to the United Nations. And there are early signs that malnutrition is spiking as winter approaches.

"The magnitude of devastation is unimaginable," says Shyam Pathak, a chief of health at UNICEF. The din of helicopters circling the wreckage looking for survivors has faded, he says. International attention and aid has fallen too, sources on the ground say, as the response turns to the arduous, but intimate work of helping these communities stitch their lives back together.

Sponsor Message

This disaster is somewhat unique, Pathak says, in that many of those doing the work are trying to rebuild their own lives at the same time. Dhital is one of them.

"I felt like I was losing my mind"

In the immediate aftermath of the flood, Dhital and her family moved into a holding center, one of a couple dozen that housed the displaced. They stayed there for about a month before moving into a relative's house. Those days were not easy.

"For almost a month, I felt like I was losing my mind," she says. "More than money, I am in great need of work."

She found that work through Helen Keller Intl , a nonprofit that's helping the response. After a short training program that included mental health support, she began helping her community rebuild. There's a lot to do.

"I go out into the community, we work with postpartum mothers, pregnant women and children under five," says Dhital. "This is the only thing keeping me going right now."

One of her jobs is screening for malnutrition among survivors.

Preliminary data suggest a notable increase. In Naukunda Gaunpalika, for instance, moderate acute malnutrition — a condition that can slow growth, weaken the immune system and become life threatening without treatment — appears to have gone up from 0.8% in June of this year to 8.7% in October, says Pooja Pandey Rana, who directs Hellen Keller's work in Nepal. These are likely conservative estimates too, she says.

"It's a big jump," says Pandey Rana, and likely driven by fallout from the flood.

In addition to losing homes, many families lost the gardens or local farms they relied on for nutritious food. "As a result, they have to depend on dried and packaged foods, such as instant noodles and biscuits," says Dhital. Poor sanitation and lack of clean drinking water is an issue too, she says. And many have lost their livelihoods, so they don't have money to pay for food.

Sponsor Message

Workers like Dhital are handing out supplies and cash to families in need. In some regions, that's a challenge.

Many of the communities along the flood's path were connected by bridges. More than 100 of them are now destroyed, according to the U.N. And for many living higher up the slopes, mountain roads were a lifeline that have now been severed.

"There still are places, especially in the upper north part of the impacted areas, which have been cut off by the flood," says Ayush Joshi, who works for the non-profit Save the Children in Nepal. "There is still a challenge to deliver food and life saving support to these areas."

"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction"

Pushmaya Tamang is a community aid worker trying to reach those areas. Often, she must cross the makeshift bridges hastily constructed to make up for the damage.

"The bridge shakes, making it difficult for elderly people to cross," she says. "It becomes dangerous when people try to cross the bridge from both directions at the same time. It almost overturns, making it extremely frightening."

toggle caption i Family photo

Such damaged infrastructure is a start reminder of what's been lost, she says. Tamang is from a village in Nuwakot that's essentially gone after the floods.

"Our hearts cannot bear to see the destruction," she says. "The village that was once full of colorful lights and life has now become gloomy and dark."

Tamang's heart is heavy with grief over the loss of her younger sister, too. Many of the families she helps in her work with Helen Keller are also grieving unimaginable loss, she says.

"When we visit other affected families, we do not even know what to say or how to talk to them," she says. "We do not have the words to comfort or console them."

Sponsor Message

Many survivors need significant mental health support, says Pathak of UNICEF, which is teaming up with other aid organizations to mobilize health workers who can provide counseling. Like Dhital and Tamang, many of them are trying to help rebuild their communities while dealing with their own trauma.

"A hallmark of this response is that the health workers, despite being the victim themselves, are back to the work," says Pathak. "This has helped a lot."

"Everything has been wiped out"

Winter poses distinct challenges for survivors.

Colder temperatures are threatening those who still live in temporary shelters or flimsy tents. "Winter in these areas is very harsh," says Joshi. "Exposure to cold, overcrowded living, poor ventilation in the tent, damp bedding and inadequate clothing can also increase health risk."

Responders are winterizing tents and getting families into safer shelters, says Joshi, in addition to providing food and medical care.

In the longer term, there's the question of rebuilding what was leveled.

"We still haven't really seen [plans] on where to rebuild, how many homes are needed, how do we fix the water systems, how do you rebuild the schools?" says Pandey Rana of Helen Keller. "Like everything has been wiped out."

Preliminary estimates put the cost of rebuilding at roughly $5 billion , a steep figure for the small nation. The U.N. Climate Fund, aimed at helping countries harmed by climate change , approved $20 million for recovery. Domestic and international donors have contributed over $100 million in additional funds, but it's still far short of what's needed.

For now, aid organizations are focused on the immediate needs of survivors. Tamang says the daily work helps keep her going amid so much loss.

"What else can I do," she says. "Life goes on, and we have to accept what nature has brought upon us."

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon
World.content:
Democratic Black women take over almost all state agencies in Georgia soon

In January, most of Georgia's state agencies will be headed by Black women who were all elected in the 2026 midterms.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Next year, Black women from the Democratic Party will be leading most government agencies in Georgia alongside the first ever Black woman elected governor anywhere in the U.S. DorMiya Vance with WABE reports on what the new leadership means for Black women.

DORMIYA VANCE, BYLINE: Georgia voters made it clear they wanted to see a change in who represents them next year.

MAUI BIGELOW: Every time there's a fire, y'all call Black women.

VANCE: Maui Bigelow (ph) cast her ballot in a south Atlanta suburb on Election Day. She said it was a pivotal moment to get more Black women into state government. That night, Democrats swept offices and celebrated historic wins. In Georgia, every state government office on the ballot went to Democrats. And Black women now hold eight of those 10 positions, including attorney general, secretary of state and, of course, governor.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

KEISHA LANCE BOTTOMS: Thank you, Georgia. I am honored to be your 84th governor.

VANCE: Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, a former mayor of Atlanta, beat Republican billionaire Rick Jackson, becoming the country's first-ever Black woman elected governor. She didn't emphasize her identity in her campaign. Still, voters were ready to give new candidates a chance, says Tammy Greer, a political scientist at Georgia State University.

TAMMY GREER: So the political environment happened. These women had the audacity to come forward. And they were able to get their message to translate across demographics.

VANCE: And when the state legislature convenes next year, Georgia will also have more Black women representatives. Greer says such prominence is new.

GREER: For so long, Black women have been in the background who have pushed others ahead of themselves while doing all the work.

VANCE: The governor is pretty powerful in Georgia. Bottoms can appoint and fill thousands of positions in state government. And she'll have a say over the state budget. Bottoms will have an ally leading the statehouse because Democrats won the majority there. Carolyn Hugley has been a state representative for over 30 years. She's nominated to become speaker of the House. She'd be Georgia's first Black woman in that role. She says this incoming class of Black women will be judged under a microscope.

CAROLYN HUGLEY: Sometimes people have unrealistic expectations of African American women in particular.

VANCE: She says she has dealt with prejudice and judgment throughout her career, including comments about her hairstyles and her clothes. And she expects harsh criticism ahead.

HUGLEY: That has always been a part of being a Black woman in America. And this is not new territory for me. I've been a Black woman for a long time.

VANCE: Hugley says, based on her experience, it's crucial that new leaders stay focused on their responsibilities as elected officials and not be distracted by any unreasonable backlash.

For NPR News, I'm DorMiya Vance in Atlanta.

(SOUNDBITE OF GLADYS KNIGHT AND THE PIPS SONG, "MIDNIGHT TRAIN TO GEORGIA")

World.title: As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit
World.content:
As overdose deaths fall, White House makes misleading claims about who deserves credit

toggle caption i Evan Vucci/AP

When the White House announced big improvements in the number of people dying from fatal drug overdoses earlier this week, officials pointed to hopeful new data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention showing U.S. drug deaths have plunged to their lowest level in roughly a decade, saving nearly 50,000 lives each year.

But leading drug policy researchers say the White House statement also made misleading claims about the timing and cause of the remarkable public health success when it said that gains occurred primarily over the last 18 months due to policies enacted under President Trump's leadership.

"The historic decline in drug overdose deaths demonstrates that America is unequivocally winning the fight against illicit drugs," White House Office of National Drug Control Policy director Sara Carter said in a statement.

Carter credited heightened border security under Trump and claims of success dismantling "narco-terrorist" organizations for the recovery. "Critically, this represents a an approximately 41.5% decrease in total drug overdose deaths compared to the peak under the previous administration," the statement said.

Sponsor Message

What the White House failed to disclose is that declines in overdose fatalities began much earlier, under the Biden administration, with most of the gains occurring before Trump returned to office.

"Since the spring of 2023, we have seen a steady decline in overdose deaths," said Vanda Felbab-Brown, a drug policy expert at the Brookings Institution. "The fact that it has been sustained is very important."

Fentanyl crisis on Biden's watch, then a pivot toward fewer deaths

According to CDC data, reductions in drug deaths began in 2023 and have continued steadily for at least 39 consecutive months — not 18 months as the ONDCP statement said. By the time Biden left office, fatal overdoses had already dropped by roughly one-third, an improvement described by addiction experts at the time as unprecedented.

Nabarun Dasgupta, a street drug researcher at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, was one of the first scientists to detect the stunning drop in overdose deaths. He said the trend toward fewer deaths began in some regions and among some demographic groups as early as 2021 and rapidly gained momentum nationwide.

"It was really the period early 2024 through spring 2025 where we were seeing the greatest rate of decline that we've ever seen," Dasgupta said.

Deaths from fentanyl smuggled into the U.S. from Mexico first began to rise in 2013 during President Obama's time in office and accelerated during Trump's first term. Fentanyl overdoses spiked sharply the first two years of Biden's presidency, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Despite progress, fentanyl remains the leading cause of drug deaths nationwide.

Sponsor Message

Dasgupta, Felbab-Brown and other and addiction experts credit the Biden administration for rolling out policy responses that included wider access to healthcare, making the opioid overdose medication naloxone more readily available, and negotiating a deal with China that disrupted the flow of industrial chemicals used to make fentanyl.

toggle caption i Doug Mills/Pool/The New York Times

The Biden team also scored significant drug interdiction wins against the Mexican cartels that smuggle fentanyl. "We have certainly been seeing over many years, going back to the Biden administration, important efforts to crack down against them," said Felbab-Brown.

Dasgupta and Felbab-Brown both said improvements in reducing drug mortality have continued under Trump. They said it's important to have an accurate timeline of the overdose crisis because researchers are still trying to understand why deaths involving fentanyl surged and why so many fewer people are now dying.

White House on Biden role in declines

NPR asked the White House about progress in the fentanyl fight under Biden. In an emailed statement, ONDCP director Carter, a former podcaster, journalist and Fox News contributor, blamed Biden for failing to secure the U.S.-Mexico border and for allowing drug deaths to surge in the first place.

"While drug overdose deaths eventually began to decline following the peak, the Biden Administration doesn't get to take credit for overseeing the highest drug overdose numbers in history, then bringing them down from their own failure," Carter said.

Responding to CDC data showing drug deaths began to plummet much earlier than stated the White House announcement, Carter said "this could be misinterpreted as progress on a graph, but it was not progress."

According to Carter, the Trump administration is now well-positioned to build on overdose death reductions made over the last three years, in part by maintaining border security and by continuing to "relentlessly attack" drug gangs.

"We are dismantling and eliminating the violent cartels and drug trafficking organizations through coordinated operations," she said.

Sponsor Message

But Felbab-Brown at Brookings said she doesn't share the Trump administration's confidence that there has been significant progress "dismantling and eliminating" narco-terrorist organizations.

"I cannot think of one narco-terrorist organization that has been dismantled," she said. "They all continue operating and they are all very strong. They all continue smuggling drugs."

Military experts have also questioned the effectiveness, and legality, of Trump's ongoing strikes against civilian boats in the Caribbean and eastern Pacific, described as smuggling vessels by the Pentagon.

Dasgupta, the addiction researcher at UNC, said he's also concerned about whether progress reducing drug deaths can be sustained next year as the Trump administration implements deep cuts to Medicaid passed by the Republican Congress.

The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cuts could mean as many as 10 million Americans losing access to health insurance coverage.

"Medicaid is the largest funder of addiction services in the United States," Dasgupta said. "Cutting Medicaid eligibility or making it harder to access forms of effective addiction treatment is guaranteed to leave people out in the cold."

World.title: Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story
World.content:
Karl Kani dressed hip-hop royalty for decades. Now he's telling his own story

toggle caption i Jason Koerner/Getty Images

Fashion designer Karl Kani believes hip-hop needed its own clothing brand, one that reflected the music, culture and style of the artists who were changing fashion in the 1990s.

"Hip-hop needed the clothing brand that fit that look, who was from the culture," Kani told NPR's A Martínez on Morning Edition. "And I felt like the marriage between Kani and hip-hop was, like, heaven-sent."

Kani, born Carl Williams, started designing clothing in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He was inspired by watching his father, a Haitian tailor, make matching linen suits to sell around the neighborhood.

Sponsor Message

At the time, hip-hop artists were already wearing names like Ralph Lauren, Tommy Hilfiger and Calvin Klein. But they weren't necessarily wearing the clothes as their designers intended. They favored oversized fits, mixed colors and created looks of their own.

Kani understood the appeal. He began making clothes as a self-taught designer in Brooklyn, New York, in the late 1980s. He helped turn that emerging streetwear style into a brand worn by some of hip-hop's biggest stars, including Tupac Shakur, Aaliyah and The Notorious B.I.G.

But the designer's ambitions extended beyond dressing famous musicians. He wanted to build an international fashion business that could last.

In his new memoir, Karl Kani: A Life By Design, Kani reflects on the creative instincts and business decisions that helped his brand survive long after the decade that made it famous.

Even his name reflects his ambitions. Kani, pronounced like "Can I?," came from the doubts he faced while building his business.

"Can I really come from the inner city and build a clothing brand?" he recalled asking himself. "I didn't know the answer to that question, but I knew if I call myself Kani, then every day I have to answer that question. Yes, I can."

After more than three decades in fashion, Kani also has some thoughts about what hasn't aged quite so gracefully: men in skinny jeans.

"I feel like a lot of guys kind of messed up when the skinny jeans phase came in," he said.

His advice? "Keep it simple, keep it slick and all black. You can never go wrong in all black."

In his conversation with NPR's A Martínez, Kani discusses his new memoir, the rise of his streetwear empire, hip-hop's influence on fashion and why skinny jeans aren't for everyone.

World.title: 'If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy,' Carney says of ongoing trade talks
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Wednesday that Canada is willing to sign a mutually beneficial deal with the Americans, but if U.S. President Donald Trump can't agree to those terms, then Ottawa will continue on its current trajectory: Aggressively diversifying away from the United States.

Speaking virtually to the Dealbook summit from China as he wound down his nine-day trade mission to Europe and Asia, Carney said Canada continues "to have a series of issues" when it comes to trade with the U.S.

While there has been some progress, "we're not there yet" on putting pen to paper on an agreement, Carney said.

Canada is trying to get the Trump administration to lift or reduce its punishing Section 232 tariffs on autos, steel, aluminum, softwood lumber and other products.

These tariffs have caused job losses and shuttered plants, imperilling what was once one of the closest bilateral relationships in the world.

Canada is also driving for Trump to lift the 50 per cent tariffs he levied on a grab bag of Canadian products, apparently retaliating for Canada's countermeasures on some U.S. goods that were imposed after the president first launched his trade war last year.

Carney met with Trump in China on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit — a conversation he described as "reasonably direct" but one that didn't produce a trade breakthrough.

With the prospect of a U.S. trade deal uncertain, Carney said Canada's talks with China have gone "exceptionally well" and are "very rational," and he has secured meaningful market access for Canadian commodities in return for allowing a relatively small number of Chinese EVs to be imported at lower tariff rates.

As part of his Asian tour, Carney also brokered two free trade deals in a single day with the Philippines and the 11-nation ASEAN bloc, which combined represent a $6-trillion market.

Canada is also on the cusp of a free trade deal with India within the next three months, Carney said.

WATCH | Carney brokers agreements with the Philippines, ASEAN: Carney brokers 2 free trade agreements with the Philippines, ASEAN | Duration closed caption 2:40 Prime Minister Mark Carney brokered two free trade agreements — slated to be signed next year — that will dramatically slash high tariffs on Canadian exports to the Philippines and the 11-member ASEAN bloc in a continued attempt to diversify trade away from the U.S.

Altogether, Canada currently has free trade access to economies with some two billion people, he said, and that number will soon reach three billion.

"We'd like to do a deal. If the U.S. doesn't want to do a deal, we're busy," Carney said.

Asked if the U.S. midterm results changed anything for Canada — the Democrats won both houses of U.S. Congress in a landslide — Carney said, "No, is the short answer."

Carney arrives at the Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport on Monday, ahead of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, China. (Pedro Pardo/Getty Images)

Carney said the only thing that will improve relations between the two countries is a U.S. reversal of anti-Canada trade actions that are designed to destroy key sectors of the economy.

"What will change views is policy decisions that are taken and that will stick," he said. "It will take action as opposed to intent."

But even then, Carney said the government doesn't want to slide into an old pattern of ever-deeper economic integration with the U.S.

Canada doesn't want to be "coerced" or "subjugated" by the U.S., or any other major power, anymore, he said.

The overarching goal of his trade policy — brokering associate membership with the European Union and thawing relations with China — is to secure Canada's long-term sovereignty, Carney said.

WATCH | Canada's ties with China not a 'top issue' for Trump, Carney says: Canada's ties with China not a 'top issue' for Trump, Carney says | Duration 2:00 Prime Minister Mark Carney, speaking from China on Nov. 18, said Canada and the U.S. have different types of trade relationships with Beijing, adding that in the 'hierarchy of issues' between Canada and the U.S., China is not 'the top issue at all.'

Asked about Trump's October assertion that the U.S. "holds all the cards" in its dealings with Canada, Carney was dismissive.

"Our cards are that everyone else in the world wants to deal with us," Carney said, relaying his commitment to double non-U.S. trade in 10 years.

"I'm not saying the transition is easy. It's not — there are challenges there."

Conservative MP Adam Chambers, the party's industry critic, meanwhile criticized Carney's decision to draw closer to China and pitch warmer relations with the Asian economic superpower as an alternative to securing a U.S. deal.

"If the prime minister thinks it's smart to play chicken with a U.S. administration that has a lot of leverage and harm it may choose to impose on Canada — the government should be very careful about doing that," he told reporters on Parliament Hill.

World.title: Cadets being told to stand down as Canada adds billions to defence
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian military has put a halt to most cadet training in various parts of the country because of ongoing budget restraint within the Department of National Defence.

The halt involves weekend training and participation in competitions and will last until the end of the fiscal year in March. Weekly parade nights, however, will continue at least for the time being.

Internal emails, obtained by CBC News, outline the decision and paint a picture of an organization struggling to manage the impact of the Defence Department's cuts to operations and support funding.

The Ottawa Citizen was the first to report on the restrictions involving the cadet program. The news was confirmed by a subsequent leak of emails to CBC News.

"Due to the current fiscal environment, all cadet activities are paused for the remainder of the current fiscal year, ending 31 March 2027, with the exception of weekly parade nights, which may continue at this time," said one leaked email quoting Lt.-Col. Raphael MacKenzie, who commands Ontario's Regional Cadet Support Unit (Central).

In a statement, the Defence Department said it is focused on operational readiness and acknowledged that funding for both the cadet and junior ranger programs is being reviewed.

"Adjustments to some planned activities will be required," said the statement, which noted funding for both programs had increased to an overall allocation of $265 million.

"We understand that this review may create uncertainty and concern among our cadets, junior Canadian rangers, families and communities. As responsible stewards of public funds, we must align our spending with available resources while making every effort to protect the activities and experiences that matter most to the young people who participate in these programs."

The statement said it's too soon "to determine the full extent of any changes or their impacts" going forward.

In mid-October, CBC News was the first to report on the department's internal belt-tightening, which is a knock-on effect from cuts mandated in previous federal budgets.

Department expected to find $459M in savings

The Defence Department has been given tens of billions of new funding by the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney. It has been told to focus that extra cash on priority areas, including the purchase of much-needed combat equipment.

At the same time, DND is subject to the demand for operations and maintenance reductions announced by the Trudeau government in 2023 and enacted in the 2024 federal budget.

Those reductions, according to the latest federal budget, are significant.

DND is expected to find $459 million in operational savings this fiscal year, and another $459 million next year.

Last week, CBC News reported on how a reserve unit in southwestern Ontario limited paid participation in Remembrance Day activities because of the budget restraint.

There are also unconfirmed reports of full-time reservists having their three-year contracts cancelled with less than 30 days' notice.

That runs contrary to the latest federal budget's departmental plans report, which downplayed the impact of the internal restraint.

"No job losses are anticipated as a result of these reductions," said the budget report, recently tabled in Parliament.

The department and the Canadian military remain in "a period of growth, supported by significant long-term defence investments that continue to strengthen operational readiness, capabilities and the civilian and military workforce needed to deliver them," the report said.

WATCH | Budget watchdog on defence spending: Defence will enter the 'top rank' of government spending: PBO | Duration closed caption 9:11 On Tuesday the Parliamentary Budget Office announced the government could spend as much as $163.6 billion by 2035 on the Canadian military. The fiscal watchdog added that the economic impact such a drastic increase in defence spending will have on federal finances and the Canadian economy is yet to be determined. Power & Politics speaks to Parliamentary Budget Officer Annette Ryan.

Conservative defence critic James Bezan said the reserves and cadets are bearing the brunt of the restraint and the budget chaos makes a mockery of the Liberal government's pledge to invest in defence.

"Mark Carney and the Liberals can't be talking out of both sides of their mouths, saying that they're investing in the armed forces and then cutting operations," Bezan said.

"That reduces our readiness. The Carney cuts are having real impacts on the day-to-day operations of the Canadian Armed Forces."

The restrictions on cadet activities took effect immediately in Ontario, while similar measures will come into force on Nov. 21 in British Columbia.

A separate email detailing the restraint in the B.C. region said that cadet leadership is trying to preserve activities that directly support the conduct of weekly training at corps and squadrons and that remains "our priority."

The commanding officer of the Pacific region plans to conduct town halls on Nov. 19 and Nov. 23 to further explain the decision.

"We recognize that this direction will come as a surprise to most and will be disappointing to cadets, families and your teams who have invested considerable time and effort in planning activities for the year ahead," said the second email, dated Nov. 16.

"We share that disappointment. These are not measures that would be taken if the resources were available to sustain the program as planned."

World.title: Judge orders Kinew government to disclose who excluded Tesla from Manitoba EV rebate program and why
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A Manitoba judge has taken the "exceptional and unusual" step of ordering the NDP government to disclose who made the decision to exclude Tesla Motors Canada from the province's electric vehicle rebate program — and explain why that decision was made.

In an order issued Nov. 13, Court of King's Bench Justice Elissa Neville gave Wab Kinew's government 10 days to produce "a complete record" of the decision-making process that disqualified anyone who purchased Tesla vehicles after March 19, 2025, from qualifying for Manitoba's EV rebates.

This means the NDP government has until Monday to explain the decision, which Tesla initially asked the court to overturn in May.

For the past six months, Tesla has argued the decision was unreasonable, untransparent and unfair because, the company contends, it's not clear who actually decided to exclude Tesla from the EV rebate program and whether that person was legally authorized to make that decision.

The government, in turn, has argued the exclusion can not be reviewed in court because it was a funding decision.

In her order, Neville said she can not make any determination without knowing who made the decision and said the NDP government has displayed "a baffling coyness" about the decision-making process.

"The disputed record filed with the court sheds no light whatsoever on the question of who made the Tesla exclusion decisions, how they made the decisions, why they made the decisions, and whether these decisions are reviewable," Neville wrote.

"The respondents' position, in effect, appears to be that the reviewability of the decision must be determined before they can identify the decision maker and produce the record."

The judge went on to note it is not routine for courts to order governments to disclose the rationale behind decisions.

"I acknowledge that compelling the respondents to file their record by way of an affidavit is an exceptional and unusual remedy," Neville wrote.

"That said, in the specific and unique circumstances of this case, where the respondents refuse to identify anyone as the decision maker, such an approach strikes me as the more practical and efficient means of ensuring that there is a clear and streamlined record before the court."

Rebates yanked on budget day 2025

Manitoba's EV rebate rolled out in 2024 but was retroactive to 2023. It entitled Manitobans buying a new electric vehicle or plug-in hybrid priced below $70,000 to a $4,000 rebate. Used and leased EVs qualified for a $2,500 or $1,000 rebate, respectively.

On provincial budget day in 2025, Finance Minister Adrien Sala said removing Tesla from the EV rebate was about "Trump-proofing our economy" and a "commitment to be elbows up." Chinese EVs were also excluded at the time.

Manitoba Finance Minister Adrien Sala speaks to reporters on March 20, 2025, when he unveiled a provincial budget that excluded Tesla from EV rebates. (Jaison Empson/CBC)

Tesla argued this exclusion ran counter to the stated purpose of the EV rebate program and also cost consumers $560,000.

During a court hearing in October, Tesla's legal counsel noted Premier Wab Kinew said in 2025 that Tesla CEO Elon Musk should "get Donald Trump to stop the tariffs, and then we can talk about the EV rebate."

In her order, Justice Neville noted "in the absence of a proper record, the applicant says it has only media reports and public remarks from Manitoba's Premier through which to glean the rationale for the Tesla exclusion decision.

The province, she noted, considered the EV rebate change to be a policy decision made under the government's spending power.

"The applicant is entitled to seek to challenge a decision affecting its interests. The respondents intend to argue in this case that the decision the applicant challenges is not reviewable because it is a policy decision," she wrote.

"I cannot make that determination without knowing who the decision-maker was. For some reason, the respondents are saying that it is for the court to make that determination, even though the respondents have neither taken a position nor provided the information necessary for me to do so."

A motion by the government to strike the Tesla application will be heard at the same time as the application, Neville said.

Tesla's Winnipeg legal counsel declined further comment.

The NDP government declined comment as well.

Traffic on the Crimean Bridge was temporarily suspended following an attack, Sergei Aksyonov, Crimea's Russian-installed governor, said on Telegram on Thursday, adding ​that an assessment of the ​damage was underway.

The attack was the third this ​week on the bridge connecting ⁠mainland ⁠Russia to ‌Crimea, which Russia annexed from Ukraine in 2014. It comes as a blow to President Vladimir ⁠Putin ahead of his meetings with U.S. and Chinese counterparts on Thursday.
