World.title: Trump’s Secretary of War Signs Military Pact with Delcy in Caracas
World.content:
Pete Hegseth: “January 3rd Was the Day of Venezuela’s Liberation”

US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth speaks at a press conference this Wednesday November 18 at the US Embassy in Caracas, Venezuela. Photo: EFE/ Miguel Gutierrez

Trump’s Secretary of War said Venezuela has gone from being “the most aggressive regional threat” to a cooperative partner.

By Efecto Cocuyo

HAVANA TIMES – US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth signed a military cooperation agreement on Wednesday, November 18, with the interim administration of Delcy Rodríguez during a previously unannounced visit to Miraflores Palace in Caracas. The meeting marks the highest-level visit by an official of Donald Trump’s administration to the country since the US military operation on January 3, which culminated in the capture of Nicolas Maduro.

According to reports from state media, Hegseth was received with honors after landing at Maiquetía Airport and holding meetings at the presidential palace with Defense Minister Gustavo Gonzalez Lopez and Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco.

A New Alliance and Historical References

In remarks broadcast on Venezuelan state television, the Pentagon chief said the two countries were resuming a defense alliance after more than two decades of interruption under the government of Hugo Chavez. According to Hegseth, the central objective of the agreement is to “ensure that the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors, narco-terrorists, or criminals, and that they are safe and protected within their sovereign borders.”

“We are signing a military alliance again after many years. We have the opportunity to fight terrorism and criminals who affect both countries,” the US official said. Hegseth also stated that they hope to “deepen our defense cooperation and partnership in ways that draw on the experience of the United States Armed Forces.”

During his remarks, Hegseth invoked the Monroe Doctrine and bilateral cooperation during World War II — including the joint protection of oil refineries against German submarines — describing them as precedents for “the natural military and strategic partnership between Venezuelans and US Americans.”

January 3rd and the Liberation

The visit comes more than ten months after the events of January 3, 2026. Following the official ceremonies at Miraflores, Hegseth spoke to reporters at the US Embassy in Caracas, where he emphasized the Trump administration’s three-phase plan for Venezuela and the renewed military agreement.

Hegseth said his country had resolved “a 27-year problem for the hemisphere” in Venezuela.

“Venezuela is better today than it was yesterday, and it will be better tomorrow than it is today,” he stated. He also described January 3 as “a day of liberation for Venezuela.”

Hegseth asserted Wednesday that, less than a year after the capture of Nicolas Maduro, Venezuela had gone from being “the most aggressive regional threat” to becoming “a cooperative security partner.”

“Venezuela has gone from being our most aggressive regional threat to becoming a cooperative security partner. In the process of rebuilding its Armed Forces alongside the United States, we are reestablishing our military alliance, which is natural and historic,” he said.

“All of this is thanks to close cooperation with President Delcy Rodriguez to stabilize Venezuela and rid it, once and for all, of narco-terrorists,” Hegseth continued.

He noted that the Department of War had brought Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, before the US justice system, which “put an end to the war that narco-terrorists had waged in Venezuela for decades against the US American and Venezuelan peoples.”

“We achieved this through the most sophisticated military operation in Latin American history, without a single United States casualty. The operation lasted just 48 minutes,” he said.

The result, he asserted, was “peace achieved through strength, by bringing narco-terrorists to justice and opening a new chapter for the United States, for Venezuela, for the Venezuelan Armed Forces, and for the entire Western Hemisphere.”

Hegseth said he was aware of the significance of the moment and noted that he was the first Secretary of War this century to set foot on Venezuelan soil.

“Just a year ago, my presence here, our presence here, would have been practically unimaginable. But this was possible for one simple reason: President Donald Trump had the courage to do what no previous president was willing to do: defend the United States through actions, not just words,” he said.

Interim Government Accepts the Agreement

For her part, Delcy Rodriguez expressed her administration’s interest in expanding training programs, equipment supplies, and access to new technologies for the Bolivarian National Armed Forces under the agreement.

The stop in Caracas is part of a regional tour by the US secretary, who is expected to continue on to Colombia — where he will deliver C-130 Hercules military transport aircraft — as well as Ecuador and possibly Honduras.

First published in Spanish by Efecto Cocuyo and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: A Letter from Havana Times
World.content:
18 years, seven days a week, from Cuba despite everything

Photo por Nester Nuñez

By Circles Robinson

Dear Readers,

In October we reached our 18th anniversary of nonstop daily reporting, commentary, diaries, and photography centered on Cuba, while also covering Nicaragua, Venezuela, and other Latin American countries.

Most of our contributing writers and photographers are in Cuba, documenting the extraordinarily difficult times they are living through. From Pinar del Río, Havana, Mayabeque, Matanzas, Camagüey, and Holguín they tell us of their days spent juggling scarcities of every kind. Yet these talented writers choose to take the time to be part of this online media project. In the coming weeks, some of them will tell you in their own words why.

The Havana Times family also includes others who help make the publication possible with their writing, editing, and technical support from Venezuela, Panama, Nicaragua, Brazil, Chile, Canada, Switzerland, Spain, and the United States.

We are not a large publication, with no salaried staff, but the reader survey we conducted in May, in which many of you participated, showed us that you have a high regard for the credibility of our work. That means a great deal to us. The results also told us that most of you feel Havana Times gives you a good picture of life on the ground in Cuba and a better understanding of the complexities of the country’s politics and the challenges it faces. That is exactly what our combined effort sets out to do.

I continue editing and publishing Havana Times out of a personal commitment to our writers and photographers as well as a love for both Cuba and Nicaragua, where I lived for many years. In this increasingly polarized world, I remain committed to a kind of journalism that emphasizes empathy and ethics while avoiding extremism.

I’m also happy to know that people from different countries who read Havana Times before traveling to Cuba have written to us after returning home to say the publication gave them an introduction to the country; this helped them better understand what they encountered and, thus, get more out of their trip. Many continue reading afterwards. Knowing that our work can serve readers in this way is deeply gratifying.

Our hope is to continue providing this service in the coming year and beyond. Later this month, we will launch our all-important annual reader fundraising campaign. If you also believe in the importance of independent journalism and care about the people and countries we cover, I hope to have your support.

Read more from Circles Robinson here on Havana Times.

World.title: Financing an Apartment in Brazil
World.content:
A condominium in Curitiba, Brazil

By Osmel Almaguer

HAVANA TIMES – I have a Cuban friend who managed to finance a place of his own through Brazil’s Minha Casa Minha Vida [“My house, my life”] Program. I remember writing about that while trying to explain the different ways an immigrant can purchase a property.

That was a more or less a year ago. My friend’s success inspired me to try it as well. He’s in the middle of his financing, which ends in 2028, and I just received an email offering us our own financing.

That doesn’t mean it’s going to work out. We’ve agreed to move forward with the process and learn more about the proposal, and now we’re waiting for a response from the real estate agency, to find out if there are any available units based on our ranking.

If the answer is yes, we’ll begin a series of in-person meetings with the real estate agency to work out the details before signing the contract.

First, they’d give us a full presentation of the project, including the projected construction timeline. After that, we’d discuss the contract details and payment terms.

We don’t yet know the total price of the apartment, but we do know that the condominium project is located in the Cajuru neighborhood, just a few minutes from downtown. I did some research, and it’s a residential area with excellent prospects for continued growth, so from a financial standpoint, it could be a good investment.

I’ve already mentioned that I firmly believe in this approach to managing our finances because, after all, if we spend our whole lives moving from one rental to another, we’ll never own a home of our own – but will still end up paying hundreds of thousands of Brazilian riais [note: 5.87 riais = $1 US].

Just to give an example, in the four years I’ve been in Brazil, I’ve already spent about 60,000 reais (approximately $12,000) on rent, which is equivalent to one-fifth of the value of a small apartment.

Minha Casa Minha Vida is a government program that subsidizes affordable housing for low-income families. Through this program, in combination with another program called Casa Curitibana, we could receive a subsidy of up to 30,000 reais ($6,000) to cover part of the down payment, with the remainder divided into monthly installments until the condo is completed.

A project of this kind raises several concerns. For example, having to pay the monthly loan installments alongside our current rent for two or three years. Construction interest accrues over the waiting period, causing the monthly down payment installments to rise from an initial 600 reais ($120) to as much as 2,000 reais ($400).

The size of the apartment is also a bit discouraging—only 34 square meters.

As an asylum seeker, I don’t have legal status that would allow me to finance an apartment; however, a driver’s license serves as legal identification, and it is possible to obtain one easily by paying between 1,500 and 2,000 reais (between $300 and $400).

For a family that lives paycheck to paycheck, all these expenses—even though they’re only possible thanks to programs like Minha Casa Minha Vida—mean it’s important to carefully calculate and manage every decision, because even the slightest slip-up could leave us in a bind.

Read more from the diary of Osmel Almaguer here on Havana Times.

World.title: International News Briefs for Wednesday, November 18, 2026
World.content:
HAVANA TIMES – We bring you some of the top international news stories compiled by Democracy Now on Wednesday, November 18, 2026.

NSA Claims “Temporary Degradation” Behind Outage of Classified Internal Network

Nov 18, 2026

The National Security Agency — the largest spy agency in the U.S. — says a “temporary degradation” is behind an outage of its classified internal network. The network, known as NSANet, has been down since at least early Tuesday morning, and some NSA staff have been unable to access their workplace systems, prompting the agency to stagger arrival times for personnel. U.S. officials tell CBS News that so far there is no evidence of a cyberattack.

Apple and Google Hit by Widespread Service Outages

Nov 18, 2026

Apple on Tuesday confirmed widespread service outages on many of its iPhone apps, including Apple Pay and iCloud. Meanwhile, thousands of Gmail users reported disruptions that Google later said were not related to any broad internal system interruptions. This comes amidst a series of other disruptions to air travel, banking and technology infrastructure, including a massive outage at Microsoft last week that disrupted communication for millions of people across at least 74 countries.

Nvidia’s Board of Directors Reportedly Not Considering Bringing Back Jensen Huang as CEO

Nov 18, 2026

Nvidia’s board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO. That’s despite Huang releasing a statement that he would be”honored to return as CEO.” Huang resigned from Nvidia, the company he founded, after 33 years as CEO, in light of his affair with Alice Huang, who is alleged to have contact with Chinese intelligence, as well as affairs with employees at Nvidia. This comes as Jensen Huang is expected to testify behind closed doors on December 1 before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, the Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party and the House Intelligence ​Committee.

Xi Personally Greets Trump on Tarmac in Shenzhen, Breaking Precedent

Nov 18, 2026

Chinese President Xi Jinping personally greeted President Trump on the tarmac when he landed in Shenzhen earlier today for the APEC summit, breaking precedent. After Trump stepped off Air Force One, he and Xi shook hands and hugged each other. The two leaders are set to hold a historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin Thursday on the sidelines of the summit.

Alaska’s Former Democratic Congressmember Peltola Defeats Incumbent GOP Senator Sullivan

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: X/MaryPeltola

In Alaska, former Democratic Congressmember Mary Peltola has defeated incumbent Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. Peltola becomes the first Indigenous woman from Alaska elected to the U.S. Senate. She won with 50.1% of the vote to Sullivan’s 45.8%. Her win brings the Democratic majority in the Senate to 56 seats. Peltola posted this message on social media after the race was called.

Sen.-elect Mary Peltola: “I’m so grateful you’ve put your trust in me, Alaska, and I’m ready to get to work. The future is full of opportunities for us to make Alaska a better place across the state. I’m looking forward to working hand in hand with all Alaskans over the next six years. Thank you again.”

Settlers Kill 72-Year-Old Palestinian Grandmother in the Occupied West Bank

Nov 18, 2026

In the occupied West Bank, Israeli settlers killed a 72-year-old Palestinian grandmother and wounded at least 10 others in an attack on the outskirts of Jericho. The woman was identified as Fadda Mohammed Fheidat. She was standing outside of her home when settlers began shooting at her and her family members, fatally striking Fheidat in the head. This is a witness.

Ahmed Aref: “We went outside the house after hearing the children shouting. Then everything escalated. The settlers started shooting. I was inside the house with the elderly woman. We went downstairs, and she was behind me. She stopped at this spot, and I walked past her. I looked back and thought she was still standing, but when I looked again, I found her lying on the ground with blood coming from her head. Look, her blood is here on the road.”

Israeli settlers have recently violently moved into Jericho, seizing several Palestinian homes.

In related news, the United Kingdom has sanctioned eight Israeli construction companies involved in building illegal Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, as well as a settler group blocking humanitarian aid to Gaza.

Meanwhile, Australia has imposed sanctions on three Israeli individuals and four Israeli organizations for their role in expanding illegal Israeli settlements and settler violence in the West Bank.

Guardian: IDF Uploaded 3.5 Million Photos of Palestinians to Amazon’s Platform

Nov 18, 2026

A new report by Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham in The Guardian shows that the Israeli military uploaded 3.5 million photos to Amazon’s Rekognition platform to assist in its facial recognition of Palestinians soon after the invasion of Gaza in 2023. Face recognition technology is routinely used at Israeli checkpoints in the occupied West Bank, and images captured at checkpoints have been used to surveil and target Palestinians.

Israeli Lawmakers Elect Matan Kahana as Speaker of Knesset in Blow to Netanyahu

Nov 18, 2026

In Israel, lawmakers have elected Matan Kahana, an ally of opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot, as speaker of the Knesset. It’s a major defeat for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose candidate lost the race for speaker. Kahana was backed by both Jewish-led opposition parties and Arab-led parties.

U.N. Warns Fighting Is Worsening Health Crisis in Taiz, Yemen

Nov 18, 2026

The U.N. warned Tuesday that fighting and road closures are worsening the health crisis in Yemen’s besieged city of Taiz, where water supplies meet just 8% of residents’ needs. Hospitals report thousands of cases of acute diarrhea, along with suspected dengue and cholera. This is a government employee in Taiz.

Mansour Mohammed: “We are in a situation, in a suffocating crisis, in a suffocating crisis. This siege has caused a suffocating crisis among all citizens. They can’t live, can’t get out and can’t get in. They sit silent inside and can’t earn a living.”

WaPo: Brazil Police Probes If MAGA Donor Group Linked to Vance Illegally Interfered in Brazil’s Presidential Election

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: Emily J. Higgins

The Washington Post reports Brazil’s Federal Police is investigating whether Rockbridge Network, a conservative donor group co-founded by Vice President JD Vance and Chris Buskirk, illegally interfered in the Brazilian presidential election in order to favor far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro. Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Flávio Dino ordered the investigation after the heated runoff between Bolsonaro and Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Dino cited allegations by a political activist named Renan Santos, who himself ran for president in the election and said he allegedly received messages from a Rockbridge intermediary searching for a conservative candidate that the MAGA donor group could back in the Brazilian presidential election. The probe also follows complaints by Lula’s Workers’ Party of possible U.S. interference. Flávio Bolsonaro fled to Florida last month after losing the election. He faces multiple criminal investigations back in Brazil.

AP: Immigrant Children Held in Cold, Sunless Rooms for Up to a Month

Nov 18, 2026

The Associated Press reports that immigrant children in the custody of Customs and Border Protection are being detained in cold, sunless rooms for up to a month at a time — far exceeding the legal limit of 72 hours. A legal motion filed by several advocacy groups also revealed immigrant parents held across CBP facilities in the Texas and California southern borderlands have reported widespread due process violations, including phone calls with lawyers that were restricted to less than five minutes. The parents have described being detained with their children in freezing rooms with cement floors while the lights are kept on day and night, making it hard for the children to sleep.

146,000 People Participate in Nationwide Protests in France

Nov 18, 2026

In France, about 146,000 people participated in peaceful protests across the country over the rising cost of living. High school and university students joined some private sector workers on Tuesday in the latest nationwide protests. This is a health worker.

Health worker: “We are paid a miserable amount. That’s one of our demands. We can no longer survive. I speak with my colleagues. It’s impossible to make ends meet at the end of the month. We can no longer do so, even though we have a salary. Our salaries as health workers is nearly minimum wage.”

Egyptian Writer Abdelrahman ElGendy Blocked from Entering the U.S.

Nov 18, 2026

Image Credit: Abdelrahman ElGendy

The Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy has been blocked from entering the U.S. and is unable to attend this year’s National Book Awards. He is a finalist for the nonfiction award for his book “Huna” about his time as a political prisoner in Egypt. ElGendy may also be ineligible for the prize since the National Book Awards rules require authors to be a U.S. citizen, a permanent U.S. resident or “maintain their primary, long-term home in the United States.” ElGendy currently lives in Europe, though he had lived in the U.S. for three years. He fled the U.S. last year fearing he would be arrested by ICE over his opposition to Israel’s war on Gaza and criticism of U.S. relations with Egypt.

Bahraini Human Rights Activist Nabeel Rajab Dies at 62

Nov 18, 2026

Bahraini human rights activist Nabeel Rajab died of a heart attack Tuesday in Turkey at the age of 62. Rajab led the Bahrain Center for Human Rights and became a leading voice of Bahrain’s 2011 pro-democracy uprising. He was jailed repeatedly, spending more than six years in prison. He was most recently arrested in 2016 for criticizing Bahrain’s role in the war on Yemen and was released in 2020. He later fled to Turkey fearing rearrest. Nabeel Rajab spoke to Democracy Now! back in 2014 about his role in pro-democracy protests in Bahrain.

Nabeel Rajab: “I urge American people to pressure the American government, through your member of parliament, through your congressman, to change the situation, to ask the American government not to support dictators.”

Read more news here on Havana Times.

World.title: Bedbug Epidemic in Sancti Spiritus, Cuba
World.content:
Forces the Provincial Court to close

Amidst cardboard, bags, household waste, and abandoned furniture, there appear mattresses that residents identify as infested. / 14ymedio

The infestation has spread to police stations, prisons, public buildings, and homes, while residents improvise remedies to prevent the insects from invading their houses.

Por Mercedes García (14ymedio)

HAVANA TIMES – “Don’t sit down, there are bedbugs.” The warning, given by a police investigator to a citizen who came to file a complaint, sums up an infestation spreading throughout the city of Sancti Spíritus, one that no longer distinguishes between neglected homes, spotless households, and government offices. The insects have found shelter in furniture, mattresses, and public spaces, while residents desperately search for ways to keep them from entering their homes.

Ramón, a self-employed businessman who recently experienced an attempted robbery at his business, has had to visit the First Police Unit several times to follow up on his complaint. Each time, he tells 14ymedio, the investigator has advised him to remain standing. According to his account, the infestation affects the lobby, the holding cells, and other areas where detainees, officers, and visitors come together.

“While I was outside the station waiting, I also heard that the mattresses in Nieves Morejón prison are just as badly infested,” Ramón adds. Two women waiting to be seen to were describing the situation involving a family member imprisoned at that facility. “The prisoners would rather sleep on the floor because the beds are crawling with bedbugs,” the man says.

The alarm has also reached the Provincial People’s Court, whose headquarters had to close because of a bedbug infestation. This would not be the first time. Employees and people familiar with the building’s operations say that services had previously been suspended because of the same problem, but a higher-level order forced them to resume without removing the affected furniture.

This time, they say, the insects were visible to people arriving to conduct business. Some visitors turned around as soon as they noticed them; others preferred to wait standing rather than risk carrying an unwanted passenger home in their clothing. Finally, a decision was made to close the premises again.

For residents on the block, the problem does not end behind the Court’s doors. They fear the insects will spread from one building to another and turn their homes into another source of infestation. “It’s not easy; you lose everything. A mattress costs more than $200, and that’s where you get your rest,” says one resident, who is also worried about clothing and other belongings that could be affected.

Household ingenuity is attempting to make up for the lack of solutions. Some people place cloths soaked in bleach near their entrances and keep their shoes inside plastic bags. One grandmother in the area has gone even further: she placed all four legs of her bed inside cans containing a little kerosene. “I can’t afford to buy a new mattress, so this is what I came up with,” she explains. These are desperate measures that do not guarantee the elimination of the insects and may introduce additional health and safety risks.

The problem is not limited to the city center. In the Garaita area, a heavily traveled road between the El Parque and Kilo 12 popular councils, piles of garbage have become part of the landscape. Soviet-inspired apartment buildings and prefabricated homes stand alongside one another, housing families with widely varying economic circumstances.

Among cardboard, plastic bags, household garbage, and abandoned furniture are mattresses that residents identify as infested. Their presence is especially concerning because rummaging through discarded items to recover usable belongings has become an everyday practice. A mattress thrown out onto the street can end up transferring the problem to another home.

Fighting bedbugs is also beyond the financial reach of many households. Specialized products are difficult to find, and many are imported from other countries at prohibitive prices for people earning government salaries. City residents also question the effectiveness of the cypermethrin fumigation treatments offered by sanitation services. They say they have to pay substantial amounts for these treatments without always obtaining results.

Bedbugs can appear even in carefully cleaned spaces. They are transported among personal belongings and hide in cracks, seams, and furniture. In Sancti Spíritus, however, the combination of persistent infestations, inadequate treatments, and economic hardship threatens to turn a household nuisance into a collective problem. While institutions close their doors and families improvise barriers, the insects continue finding places to settle.

Translated by Regina Anavy for Translating Cuba.

Read more from Cuba here on Havana Times.

World.title: IMF warns global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II
World.content:
IMF warns global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 03:51 UTC Full article

“The level of global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II. This requires urgent attention,” Georgieva said

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Thursday that global public debt will soon reach 100% of world gross domestic product, the highest level since World War II, and called for “urgent attention” to government finances.

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva warned on Thursday that global public debt will soon reach 100% of world gross domestic product, the highest level since World War II, and called for “urgent attention” to government finances.

“The level of global debt will soon reach 100% of GDP, the highest since World War II. This requires urgent attention,” Georgieva said at the plenary session of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

The warning comes amid a rebound in global inflation, which the IMF chief attributed both to the energy crisis caused by the war in the Middle East and to rising technology demand linked to the construction of artificial intelligence infrastructure. That rebound, she said, has led to tighter monetary policy through interest rate rises in many countries, making debt more expensive to service.

In the same speech, Georgieva highlighted that 2026 has been the first year in which artificial intelligence has had a tangible impact on global growth, and called on countries to prepare quickly for the changes it will bring.

World.title: IMF’s Georgieva at APEC: countries must “quickly prepare” for artificial intelligence
World.content:
IMF’s Georgieva at APEC: countries must “quickly prepare” for artificial intelligence

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 03:36 UTC Full article

“We are facing the fastest transformation in the history of humanity,” the Bulgarian economist said

International Monetary Fund (IMF) Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Thursday urged countries to “quickly prepare” their digital infrastructure, labour markets and workers for the rise of artificial intelligence, speaking at the plenary session of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

“We are facing the fastest transformation in the history of humanity,” the Bulgarian economist said. “Countries must quickly prepare their digital infrastructure, their labour markets and their workers for AI, and prevent risks, especially in ensuring financial stability and cybersecurity,” she added.

According to Georgieva, 2026 has been “the first year in which AI has had a tangible impact on global growth”, acting as a counterweight to the effect of the war in the Middle East on energy supplies. “While the energy crisis will eventually dissipate, AI is here to stay. It will be the most significant factor for competitiveness, productivity and growth in the medium term,” she said.

Artificial intelligence is among the priorities of the agenda promoted by China at the summit, alongside the defence of free trade and regional connectivity. The Shenzhen meeting culminates on Thursday with the first three-way encounter between the presidents of China, the United States and Russia.

World.title: US and Venezuela restore military cooperation with Hegseth’s surprise visit
World.content:
US and Venezuela restore military cooperation with Hegseth’s surprise visit

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 03:26 UTC Full article

Hegseth met acting President Delcy Rodríguez at the Miraflores Palace and signed the agreement with Venezuelan Defence Minister Gustavo González López

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth signed a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela in Caracas on Wednesday during an unannounced visit, the first by a Pentagon chief since the January 3 US military operation that removed Nicolás Maduro from power. The agreement restores cooperation that Hugo Chávez broke off in 2005.

Hegseth met acting President Delcy Rodríguez at the Miraflores Palace and signed the agreement with Venezuelan Defence Minister Gustavo González López. He said it includes joint training, strategic cooperation, intelligence sharing and the supply of defence equipment and capabilities, so that the Venezuelan people are “not threatened by foreign actors, narco-terrorists or criminals”. “In the process of rebuilding its armed forces alongside the United States, we are restoring our military alliance, which is natural and historic,” he said.

At a later event at the US embassy, Hegseth said Venezuela had gone from being “the most aggressive regional threat” to a “reliable partner”, and issued a warning to criminal groups: “To the narco-terrorists who have used this as a safe haven, your time is up. We will hunt you down, we will find you and we will kill you.”

Minister González López issued a statement, his first since taking office, setting limits on the agreement. The resumption of technical and military cooperation, he stressed, will be carried out in strict adherence to the Constitution and with full respect for “sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity, preserving the leadership, command and competence of the Bolivarian National Armed Forces”. The text notes that the new relations stem from the “harsh and painful events of January 3”. Rodríguez, who had just returned from a tour of Turkey, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, said Hegseth “has a great responsibility on his shoulders”.

According to El País, cooperation had already been working in practice for months. At least two operations on Venezuelan territory received US support in equipment and intelligence: a June attack on the hideout of the leader of the Tren de Aragua gang in Bolívar state and the drone destruction of a National Liberation Army (ELN) operations centre in Apure, both with doubts about the number and identity of those killed. After the June earthquakes in La Guaira and Caracas, some 2,000 US troops were deployed to help with the emergency.

In 2005 Venezuela replaced cooperation with Washington with Russia, Iran and China, which became its main arms suppliers. Hegseth continued his regional tour in Colombia and Ecuador, focused on security and the fight against drug trafficking.

World.title: Anthropic, maker of Claude, debuts on Nasdaq after the largest IPO in history
World.content:
Anthropic, maker of Claude, debuts on Nasdaq after the largest IPO in history

19th Thursday, November 2026 - 03:14 UTC Full article

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees led by siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, now chief executive and president, Anthropic has focused its growth on business customers

US artificial intelligence company Anthropic, maker of the Claude assistant, begins trading on Nasdaq on Thursday after pricing its initial public offering at US$83 a share, above the expected range, in what the US financial press describes as the largest offering in history. The deal values the company at around US$1.5 trillion.

Anthropic is selling 980 million shares, up from the 825 million initially planned, raising about US$81.3 billion, according to CNBC and CNN. The company had set a range of US$70 to US$78 a share, and demand reached almost seven times the shares on offer, according to Bloomberg. On top of that comes a private placement of US$26 billion in shares to major technology companies. The offering surpasses that of SpaceX, Elon Musk’s space company, which went public in June. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley are leading the deal, and the stock will trade under the ticker ANT.

Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees led by siblings Dario and Daniela Amodei, now chief executive and president, Anthropic has focused its growth on business customers. According to the prospectus cited by the press, its revenue rose from US$41 million in 2023 to US$386 million in 2024, US$4.6 billion in 2025 and US$16.3 billion in the first half of 2026 alone, and in the second quarter it posted its first operating profit, of US$974 million.

After the deal, Amazon and Google, which are at once suppliers, competitors and investors, will hold about 15% and 14% of the capital, respectively. The seven co-founders will retain shares giving them 50.1% of voting rights, although an independent body elects the majority of the board.

The IPO comes after weeks of sharp volatility in technology stocks, which fell heavily earlier this month, and is seen as a test of market confidence in artificial intelligence. In its prospectus, the company itself warns that the technology it develops could cause catastrophic harm, one of the risks it sets out for investors.

World.title: Xi and Putin reaffirm their alliance on the eve of the first three-way summit with Trump
World.content:
Xi and Putin reaffirm their alliance on the eve of the first three-way summit with Trump

18th Wednesday, November 2026 - 17:25 UTC Full article

Before the opening banquet, Trump and Putin greeted each other in Xi’s presence, their first encounter since the Alaska summit in August 2025.

Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin reaffirmed their strategic alliance in Shenzhen on Wednesday, hours before Xi personally greeted Donald Trump at the airport, on the eve of the first three-way meeting between the heads of state of China, Russia and the United States, to be held on Thursday on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

At their bilateral meeting, Xi described relations between the two countries as “as firm as a mountain in the face of any adversity or storm” and called for continued work towards a multipolar world order. “Coordination between Russia and China in foreign policy remains firm and produces good results. In a complex geopolitical situation, we continue to pursue constructive paths to forge a fairer multipolar world order,” Putin replied, referring to Europe’s “humiliating decline” and arguing that the sanctions imposed on Russia over the invasion of Ukraine have backfired.

Hours later, Xi went to the airport to greet Trump, an unprecedented gesture in his 14 years in power which, according to international media, had not occurred since Mao Zedong welcomed Soviet leader Nikita Khrushchev in 1959. “China is a country of courtesy with a long tradition of reciprocity,” Xi told him, according to the official Xinhua news agency, referring to the welcome Trump gave him in Washington in September. Before the opening banquet, Trump and Putin greeted each other in Xi’s presence, their first encounter since the Alaska summit in August 2025.

Opening the summit’s business forum, Xi warned that “unilateralism and protectionism are gaining strength” and called for global supply chains to be kept open. “Openness brings progress and isolation inevitably leads to backwardness,” he said.

According to China’s Foreign Ministry, Thursday’s three-way meeting will address how to “preserve world peace and promote strategic stability in relations between major powers”. Trump has said he wants to discuss reducing nuclear arsenals and, according to press reports, also the wars in Ukraine and Iran, although the White House had said Ukraine was not on the trilateral agenda. No agreements are expected.

Trade will also be on the table at the bilateral meeting between Xi and Trump. The tariff truce between the two countries expires on January 10, and China holds a dominant position in rare earths: in 2024 it mined about 60% of those used in magnets and accounted for 91% of their refining, according to the International Energy Agency. During his earlier stop in Manila, Trump promoted critical minerals agreements with Asian partners and approved arms sales to the Philippines worth more than US$5 billion.

World.title: Hamburg tribunal confirms it will deliver its Sea Lion order on November 28
World.content:
Hamburg tribunal confirms it will deliver its Sea Lion order on November 28

18th Wednesday, November 2026 - 14:21 UTC Full article

The tribunal’s statement makes final the date it had announced provisionally at the close of the hearings on November 10 and 11

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea has confirmed it will announce on Saturday, November 28, at noon Hamburg time — 8 a.m. in Montevideo and Buenos Aires — its decision on Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands. The order will be read at a public sitting by the tribunal’s president, Judge Maurice Kamga.

The tribunal’s statement makes final the date it had announced provisionally at the close of the hearings on November 10 and 11. The reading will be broadcast live on its website, where the text of the order will be published shortly afterwards.

In its final submissions, Argentina asked that the United Kingdom prevent new drilling for exploitation and the installation of production infrastructure in the North Falklands Basin, referred to in the Argentine filing as the North Malvinas Basin, in connection with Sea Lion; refrain from using information obtained during exploration to the detriment of Argentina’s rights; cease preventing Argentina from protecting the marine environment of the disputed areas; and refrain from measures that might aggravate the dispute, in particular the granting of new exploitation authorisations. The United Kingdom asked the tribunal to reject all the requests.

Sea Lion, operated by Israel’s Navitas Petroleum and Britain’s Rockhopper Exploration, is expected to begin drilling in January 2027.

World.title: Argentina’s lower house debates Falklands sovereignty bill today, with one chapter short of votes
World.content:
Argentina’s lower house debates Falklands sovereignty bill today, with one chapter short of votes

18th Wednesday, November 2026 - 03:46 UTC Full article

The bill, known as the Malvinas law, toughens sanctions for unauthorised exploration and exploitation of natural resources in the islands and their maritime areas

Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies debates the national sovereignty defence bill from noon on Wednesday, legislation that toughens sanctions for unauthorised resource exploitation in the Falklands. Javier Milei’s government is confident of passing it in general, but does not have the votes secured for the chapter on foreign interference, which requires a special majority.

The bill, known as the Malvinas law, toughens sanctions for unauthorised exploration and exploitation of natural resources in the islands and their maritime areas, reorganises defence and intelligence bodies and creates a National Security Council chaired by the head of state. It was cleared by committee on October 27, after the ruling party narrowed the sanctions to operators, licence holders and direct suppliers, in line with objections raised by the United States.

According to Ámbito, La Libertad Avanza is in talks with PRO, the Radical Civic Union, Argentina Federal and Provincias Unidas to resolve differences. The main obstacle is chapter 7, which introduces criminal offences related to foreign interference and electoral financing from abroad. Because it concerns electoral matters, that section requires 129 votes, a figure the ruling party has yet to secure.

The session also includes final approval of the reform of the Central Bank’s charter, which returns from the Senate with amendments, and approval of the free trade agreement between Mercosur and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) — Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland — signed in Rio de Janeiro in September 2025. It is the first of five sessions planned for the final two weeks of the ordinary session; the Chamber of Deputies will consider the 2027 budget on November 25.

The debate comes as the dispute over the islands escalates. Argentina on Tuesday rejected Princess Anne’s visit to the archipelago as a “provocation”, and the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea will announce on November 28 its decision on Argentina’s request to halt the Sea Lion oil project.

World.title: Argentina calls Princess Anne’s visit to the Falklands a “provocation”
World.content:
Argentina calls Princess Anne’s visit to the Falklands a “provocation”

18th Wednesday, November 2026 - 02:47 UTC Full article

According to the text, the visit “constitutes a provocation at a time when the United Kingdom is advancing in the illegal unilateral exploitation of hydrocarbons”

The Argentine government on Tuesday rejected the visit by Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, to the Falklands and South Georgia, calling it a “provocation” at a time when the United Kingdom, according to Buenos Aires, is advancing hydrocarbon exploitation in waters whose sovereignty Argentina claims. The Princess has been in the archipelago since November 9.

“The Argentine government rejects the official activities of Princess Anne, of the British Royal Household, in the Malvinas Islands and South Georgia, since they are carried out in the exercise of the illegal British occupation,” the Foreign Ministry said in a statement, which extends the rejection to the South Sandwich Islands and the surrounding maritime areas. According to the text, the visit “constitutes a provocation at a time when the United Kingdom is advancing in the illegal unilateral exploitation of hydrocarbons through the granting of illegitimate licences”.

The Foreign Ministry called on the United Kingdom to resume sovereignty negotiations in compliance with Resolution 2065 and other resolutions of the UN General Assembly and its Special Committee on Decolonisation. “It is time for the United Kingdom to comply with the mandate of the international community and put an end to the anachronistic colonial situation in those archipelagos, which are an integral part of the Argentine Republic,” it said. Argentina also protested against the Princess’s previous visit to the islands in 2022.

Princess Anne, travelling with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, is visiting as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation dedicated to protecting South Georgia’s heritage and environment. On November 10 she opened Stanley’s new National Sports Complex, an investment of about £5 million, and visited Cape Pembroke Lighthouse. In South Georgia she is due to unveil a memorial at a former whaling station, open the restored Stromness Managers’ Villa and visit Possession Bay, where navigator James Cook landed in 1775, as well as commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton. Buckingham Palace presented the trip, which runs until November 20, as a heritage and commemorative visit. At the time of writing, neither the British government nor the Falkland Islands Government had responded to the Argentine statement.

The visit coincides with a moment of tension in the dispute. The sports complex opened on the same day the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea began hearings in Hamburg on Argentina’s request to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the islands; the tribunal will announce its decision on November 28. Argentina is also in a diplomatic row with Chile over the Danstar, a vessel due to reopen the commercial route between Punta Arenas and the islands in December, and its Chamber of Deputies has yet to debate the sovereignty defence bill, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago.

World.title: Mexican environment groups are asking for more government regulation of data center development
World.content:
Environmental groups in the Bajío states of Jalisco and Querétaro are calling on the government to regulate data center development, citing concerns over energy and resource use in regions with already scarce water supplies.

Tech companies view Jalisco as an attractive region for development, given its reputation as a Latin American technology and innovation hub. However, advocacy groups have recently called on the government to address plans to build a thermoelectric plant to supply energy to data centers, which they say will harm the environment.

Un informe de la Universidad de Cambridge indicó que los centros de datos de Inteligencia Artificial generan un efecto de isla de calor, elevando la temperatura superficial del suelo en 2°C, detectable hasta 10 km a la redonda, con picos extremos de hasta 9,1°C. El impacto medioambiental de los centros de datos para Inteligencia Artificial podría afectar a más de 340 millones de personas en el corto plazo. Mientras las multinacionales contaminan masivamente y sin límites, a los trabajadores le dicen que se aprieten el cinturón y les prohíben ir al trabajo en su coche diésel en ciudad. — Daniel Mayakovski (@DaniMayakovski) June 29, 2026

In September, the Federal Electricity Commission (CFE) greenlighted the start of construction this year of the 480.5-megawatt Guadalajara Combined Cycle Power Plant, with operations expected to start in 2030.

Several organizations accused the Jalisco state government of modifying environmental impact and land-use planning documents to allow the project to proceed.

“The most worrying thing is that they chose such a fragile site,” Alan Carmona, a member of the Un Salto de Vida (A Leap for Life) collective, told the newspaper El Financiero.

The plant would be developed on 22.9 hectares within the Jalisco Logistics Center Industrial Park in the Ciénaga region, which lies within the Atotonilco Lagoon basin, an important ecological and cultural area. Data centers require large amounts of water for cooling, while the lagoon experiences an average annual deficit of about 2.3 million cubic meters, according to Mexico’s National Water Commission (Conagua).

“They will be using 24 liters per second,” Carmona said, adding that significant investment will be required to treat the dirty water.

Calling for data center regulation in Querétaro

In Querétaro, Eric Silva Hernández and Claudia Díaz Gayou, representatives from the Morena political party, submitted a proposal to the state Congress calling for the regulation of data centers, which would require companies to submit environmental and public health impact assessments before development can be approved.

The party members are working with the citizen collective Voceras de la Madre Tierra in calling for the development of a legal framework for data center development in Querétaro, which is home to over two-thirds of the country’s data centers, since the existing Environmental Code Law does not address this issue.

“We need transparency regarding the natural resources they will use… we need to know their water and electricity consumption,” Silva Hernández said. “There must [also] be a mandatory annual operating report for each facility, verifiable by the authorities.”

With reports from El Financiero and El Sol de México

World.title: Why was a Frida Kahlo painting pulled from auction at the last minute?
World.content:
Christie’s pulled a Frida Kahlo painting from a New York auction on Tuesday, hours before bidding was set to begin, after Mexican authorities asked the auction house to postpone the sale and document the work’s ownership history.

Kahlo painted “Congreso de los pueblos por la paz” (“Congress of the Peoples for Peace”) in October 1952 for a peace gathering in Vienna.

The work, which sold for US $2.66 million at Sotheby’s in 2020, was expected to fetch up to $3.5 million. The top price ever for an auctioned Kahlo work was US $54.7 million for her 1940 self portrait “El sueño (La cama).”

Christie’s told ARTnews this week it had agreed with the seller to withdraw “Congreso” for further research and hoped to offer it again. The Frida Kahlo Museum said Mexican authorities were investigating the work.

The advocacy group Defendamos la Colección Gelman (Let’s Defend the Gelman Collection) says the painting appears in an inventory that Kahlo’s husband, muralist Diego Rivera, compiled for the trust that oversees Casa Azul, her former home in Mexico City. The group contends the painting was removed from Casa Azul without authorization.

Mexico’s National Institute of Fine Arts and Literature initially said Kahlo donated the painting and that it left Mexico before a 1984 decree restricted the permanent export of her works still in the country.

The institute has since asked Christie’s for records to establish ownership history and clarify when the painting left Mexico.

The dispute comes as President Claudia Sheinbaum seeks to strengthen export restrictions on protected artworks amid controversy over the transfer of works from the Gelman Collection to Spain. That agreement covered 160 works, including 18 by Kahlo, that now fall under the management of Banco Santander.

The late Jacques Gelman, a leading producer in the Golden Age of Mexican Cinema and a business partner of comedian Cantinflas, began collecting modern Mexican art with his wife, Natasha, in the 1940s. In 2023, Mexico’s Zambrano family bought the privately held collection, which includes pieces by Kahlo, Rivera, Rufino Tamayo and María Izquierdo.

Mexican officials say the works sent to Spain are there temporarily.

Kahlo’s auction record of US $54.7 million in 2025 surpassed her previous mark of US $34.9 million paid in 2021 for “Diego y yo,” a self-portrait that shows Rivera on Kahlo’s forehead.

With reports from ARTnews, El País and Forbes Colombia

World.title: Travel+Leisure names 2 Mexican destinations to its 50 best places to visit in 2027
World.content:
The central state of Puebla and the resort city of Los Cabos at the tip of the Baja Peninsula have been included in the magazine Travel+Leisure’s 50 Best Places to Travel in 2027 — and for very different reasons.

Puebla was selected for its culinary offering, while Los Cabos, Baja California Sur, was included in the “For Nature Lovers” section. The magazine groups the destinations by type of experience, without assigning them a ranking.

Puebla and Los Cabos were the only Mexican destinations selected.

The recommendations come just weeks after another renowned travel publication, Britain’s CondéNast Traveller, featured Valle de Guadalupe, in Baja California, as one of the best places to travel to in North America and the Caribbean next year, highlighting the destination’s seafood and wine.

Here’s why Puebla and Los Cabos made T+L’s list:

Puebla

T+L praised the state of Puebla for its contributions to Mexican cuisine, including the staple dishes of chiles en nogada and mole.

It also highlighted a new development: the arrival in 2026 of the Michelin Guide, which recognized 14 restaurants, placing Puebla on the culinary global map.

“From acclaimed fine-dining establishments to family-run fondas, traditional markets, and generations-old kitchens, Puebla offers culinary excellence at every level,” Puebla’s Tourism Minister Carla López-Malo said.

The recent increase in international attention paid to Puebla has helped bring visibility to restaurants and kitchens throughout the state, beyond those recognized by Michelin. At Macuitl Molino, for example, chef and co-owner Gustavo Macuitl notes that his dining room is fuller these days, with lines that, in the past, were not typical outside of peak season.

Los Cabos

Although Los Cabos appears under the nature category, T+L focuses on the proliferation of luxury accommodations in what was once a fishing village and later a little-known getaway.

It begins its review with a new development in the hospitality sector: the arrival of the first Aman resort in Mexico, located in the East Cape. The complex features 18 casitas and, according to the magazine, a single night can cost as much as US $7,000.

Golf courses with big-name designers also stand out, with the magazine highlighting a new Ernie Els course at Oleada Golf Links; Old Lighthouse Golf & Ocean Club by Jack Nicklaus; and Tiger Woods’s third Los Cabos golf course, set to open at Diamante Cabo San Lucas next year.

Mexico News Daily

World.title: The MND Peso Index™ for November: At 18.67, MXN is 4.2% undervalued against USD
World.content:
THE MND PESO INDEX™

Tracking the exchange rate people actually experience MND Intelligence · Seventh edition Welcome to the seventh edition of the MND Peso Index™, part of the MND Intelligence™ suite of data products developed by Mexico News Daily. The MND Peso Index™ is a monthly purchasing power parity measure that assesses whether the Mexican peso is overvalued, undervalued or fairly valued against the US dollar by comparing the prices of a standardized basket of 20 goods and services in Mexico and Dallas, Texas. In November 2026, the index determined that the peso was undervalued against the dollar by 4.2%, an increase of 3.5 percentage points compared to a 0.7% undervaluation in October. This is just the second undervaluation assessment the MND Peso Index™ has yielded for the peso in seven editions. For a detailed explanation of the purpose of the MND Peso Index™, the makeup of the basket and more, please refer to the index article we published in June. You can read even more about the index in our introductory article published in early May. What did the MND Peso Index™ tell us in November 2026?

In November 2026, the MND Peso Index™ suggests that the USD:MXN exchange rate on the date we collected prices in various Mexican cities and in Dallas, Texas, undervalued the Mexican peso by 4.2%.

The Mexican and Dallas prices were collected on Nov. 10, 2026. The MND Peso Rate — the simple average of the 20 item-level implied exchange rates, rather than the rate produced by dividing the total Mexican basket cost by the total Dallas basket cost — came in at 17.89 pesos per dollar, compared with a Banxico FIX rate of 18.67 pesos per dollar on Nov. 10.

The gap between those two figures indicates that the peso — at a rate of 18.67 pesos to the US dollar — was undervalued by 4.2% on Nov. 10.

In the table above, you can see the Mexico and U.S. prices for all 20 goods and services in the basket, the total costs of the two baskets, the implied exchange rate for each item, the MND Peso Rate (i.e., the overall implied rate), the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected and the undervalued assessment for the peso.

Why did the peso’s ‘undervalued’ assessment increase between October and November?

For a second consecutive month, the MND Peso Rate (17.89) is lower than the Banxico FIX rate on the date prices were collected (18.67).

The gap between the two rates widened to 78 centavos in November from 13 centavos in October, an increase of 65 centavos. The widening is the reason why the undervaluation assessment for the peso increased to 4.2% from 0.7% last month.

The depreciation of the peso between Oct. 6 and Nov. 10 was the sole reason for the larger gap.

Based on Banxico’s FIX rate on the two dates, the peso depreciated 3.7% against the dollar over the period, with the USD:MXN exchange rate rising by 70 centavos to 18.67 pesos per dollar from 17.97 pesos per dollar on Oct. 6. Among the reasons why the peso depreciated between Oct. 6 and Nov. 10 was the narrower gap between the Bank of Mexico’s key interest rate (currently 6.25% after a 25-basis-point cut in early November) and that of the U.S. Federal Reserve (currently set at a 3.75%-4% target range after a 25-basis-point increase in mid-September).

The increase in the MND Peso Rate from 17.84 in October to 17.89 in November tempered the widening of its gap with the FIX rate by five centavos.

The slight variation in the MND Peso Rate is due to month-over-month changes in the implied rates for some individual goods and services. The implied rates that changed due to price fluctuations are highlighted in the table above.

7 months of the MND Peso Index™

Through the use of the MND Peso Index™, we have now determined that the peso was overvalued against the US dollar by 2.8% in late April, 4% in late May, 2.9% in late June, 2.4% in early August and 5.8% in early September. We subsequently determined that the peso was undervalued against the dollar by 0.7% in early October and 4.2% in early November.

The difference between this month’s undervaluation assessment for the peso and the highest overvaluation assessment — that in early September — is 10 percentage points. The peso was trading at 16.98 to the dollar when we determined September’s 5.8% overvaluation, whereas November’s 4.2% undervaluation assessment was calculated based on a USD:MXN rate of 18.67.

The higher exchange rate represents a 9% depreciation for the peso compared with the lower rate. The 10-percentage-point swing between September’s overvaluation assessment and November’s undervaluation assessment was almost entirely driven by the peso’s 9% depreciation against the US dollar.

So far in 2026, the peso has depreciated around 2.3% against the US dollar. It closed at 18.00 to the greenback on the final day of 2025, according to the Bank of Mexico, while the closing USD:MXN rate on Tuesday, Nov. 17 was 18.43. If the Banxico FIX rate was 18.43 when we collected the prices for the Mexican and Dallas baskets on Nov. 10, the undervaluation assessment for the peso would have been 2.9%.

World.title: El Jalapeño: Sheinbaum arrives at China summit after clearing standby for middle seat 46B, splitting UberX to hostel
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

SHENZHEN, China — Demonstrating an unwavering commitment to government austerity ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum arrived in southern China on Monday after flying standby in middle seat 46B, splitting an UberX to a youth hostel and eating tacos for dinner.

While previous Mexican administrations traveled abroad on a dedicated presidential Boeing 787 — sold to Tajikistan in 2023 — Sheinbaum’s travel office confirmed that standard commercial economy fares had been deemed insufficiently austere for a high-level diplomatic mission. Instead, the president arrived at Mexico City International Airport four hours before Saturday’s 12:35 a.m. departure of China Southern Airlines flight CZ8032, waiting near the gate podium with a single personal item, hoping to clear the standby list.

“She stood right behind a family of four and refreshed the airline app just like the rest of us,” said Rodrigo Méndez, a fellow passenger on the flight. “When the gate agent cleared her for 46B, she pumped her fist and asked if there was still overhead bin space near Row 14. There wasn’t.”

According to a statement from the National Palace, the middle seat — wedged between a sleeping software engineer and the rear galley — saved Mexican taxpayers about 7,000 pesos in seat-selection fees. During the flight’s scheduled 2 a.m. technical refueling stop in Tijuana, Sheinbaum declined to wait inside the airport’s VIP lounge, instead recording a video update for citizens from a plastic chair near Gate 9 while sharing a vending-machine bag of peanuts with Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard.

Upon touching down in Shenzhen at 11:30 a.m. Monday, Sheinbaum bypassed the traditional diplomatic motorcade of armored vehicles, opting instead for a shared rideshare that made two additional stops at a suburban logistics warehouse and a dental clinic before dropping the head of state at the Nanshan Backpacker Haven, where she secured a bottom bunk for the equivalent of 444 pesos a night.

“A true servant of the people does not require a diplomatic convoy, nor does she require a private bathroom,” Sheinbaum told reporters outside the hostel while waiting for a roommate to finish brushing his teeth. “True transformation begins when the executive branch negotiates quiet hours and air-conditioning settings with five strangers.”

Later that evening, rather than attending a formal state banquet, the president walked eight blocks to eat tacos at Tequila Coyote’s with Mexican citizens living in China, barely making it back to the hostel before the 11 p.m. door lock.

Presidential spokespeople noted that the trip successfully generated enough airline loyalty miles to cover a checked bag for next month’s G20 summit, provided the president qualifies for off-peak Tuesday departures.

World.title: Mexico-US trade talks ‘very far along,’ says Sheinbaum after meeting Trump
World.content:
Listen to this article

Trade was the main focus of a formal meeting between Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum and U.S. President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China, on Wednesday.

Sheinbaum and Trump — who are both in Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Leaders’ Meeting — met at The Langham Hotel in the southern Chinese city.

“We held a very good meeting with President Trump and his team,” Sheinbaum wrote on social media at around 6:30 a.m. Mexico City time.

“We continue to make progress on our shared agenda,” she added.

Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco accompanied Sheinbaum at her first formal face-to-face meeting with Trump.

The meeting took place as Mexico and the United States seek to resolve a range of trade differences that contributed to the U.S. government’s decision in July to not renew the USMCA free trade pact for an additional 16 years to 2042. Trump is particularly concerned about the United States’ large trade deficit with Mexico, while the Mexican government is pushing for a reduction of U.S. tariffs that currently apply to Mexican steel, aluminum and vehicles.

Bilateral trade negotiations are ‘very far along,’ says Sheinbaum

Speaking by video link from Shenzhen, Sheinbaum elaborated on her meeting with Trump during the government’s Wednesday morning press conference, which was led by Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez.

“The meeting lasted around 20 minutes and we mainly discussed the issue of trade agreements,” she said, noting that U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer were also present.

She said that Trump was informed about the progress that has been made in the bilateral trade talks that have taken place in the months since the U.S. government decided not to renew the USMCA.

“We can say that we’re very far along,” Sheinbaum said without offering any details on when a bilateral deal might be reached.

“It was a very good meeting, very pleasant. President Trump was in a very good mood,” she said.

“We agreed to meet again at the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago,” Sheinbaum added, referring to next month’s G20 Leaders’ Summit in Florida.

Ebrard, who leads Mexico’s trade negotiations with the U.S., said that 56 bilateral trade-related “technical meetings” have taken place. He also said that progress has been made in trade talks, but didn’t reveal whether the United States was prepared to cede ground on tariffs.

Standing next to Sheinbaum in Shenzhen, Ebrard described the relationship between the Mexican and U.S. presidents as “warm” and “respectful.”

Neither he nor Sheinbaum mentioned Trump’s recent tariff threat in their remarks on Wednesday morning. Last Thursday, the U.S. president threatened to double tariffs on Mexican goods if Mexico didn’t stop a migrant caravan that is currently heading north through the southern state of Chiapas.

As of midday Wednesday, neither Trump nor the U.S. government had publicly commented on the meeting with Sheinbaum. Trump arrived in Shenzhen shortly before the meeting took place.

Sheinbaum and Trump speak regularly by telephone and met at the FIFA men’s World Cup draw in Washington, D.C., last December and at the World Cup final in New Jersey in July. However, their meeting in Shenzhen was the first time they held formal in-person talks.

Beyond trade, there are several pressure points in the Mexico-U.S. relationship, including Sheinbaum’s allegation that the United States has interfered in Mexican affairs.

Outcome of bilateral trade negotiations is ‘critical’ for Mexican and US manufacturers, reports Reuters

Reuters reported on Wednesday that the outcome of the trade negotiations between Mexico and the United States is “critical for manufacturers on both sides of the border.”

“The two ‌countries ⁠are each other’s biggest trading partners and exchanged about [US] $779 billion in goods in the first nine months of this year, while supply chains in industries such as auto manufacturing routinely span the border,” reported the news agency, which noted that Mexico’s economy is “deeply intertwined” with that of the U.S.

A trade deal between Mexico and the United States — which both Sheinbaum and Trump said last month is “very close” — could make the U.S. government more willing to back a 16-year extension of the USMCA, although unresolved trade disputes between Washington and Ottawa could still stand in the way.

Beyond its large trade deficit with Mexico, other concerns for the United States include Mexico’s energy sector rules and its trade relationship with China. Trump has accused Mexico of being a transshipment hub for Chinese goods, a claim the Mexican government has denied.

Still, the Mexican government imposed new and higher tariffs on a wide range of imports from China at the start of 2026, a move seen, in part, as an effort to allay U.S. concerns.

Despite increased protectionism against Chinese goods, Mexico is seeking closer ties with China across a range of areas including science, technology, healthcare and clean energy. Sheinbaum, who met with Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen on Tuesday, has said that Mexico’s engagement with China shouldn’t affect its trade negotiations with the U.S.

Sheinbaum also held a bilateral meeting with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney in Shenzhen. Both expressed firm support for the renewal of the USMCA, which was negotiated and took effect during Trump’s first term as president.

Carney also met with Trump in Shenzhen on Wednesday. According to a statement from his office, the two leaders “discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create good jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada’s languages, culture and sovereignty.”

With reports from Reforma, EFE and Reuters

World.title: US and Mexico lose ‘measles-free’ status
World.content:
The Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) revoked Mexico’s status as a measles-free country, along with the United States and Bolivia, following at least 12 months of uninterrupted spread.

The decision comes a year after Canada lost its measles-free status in November 2025, becoming the first country in the Americas to lose the verification.

In Mexico, the outbreak assessed by PAHO began on Feb. 1, 2025, and reached one year of continuous transmission in February this year. Meanwhile, in the U.S., the outbreak began on Jan. 20, 2025, and reached the 12-month threshold earlier in January.

PAHO explained that loss of status does not mean that there are outbreaks throughout the entire territory of these countries, but rather that the virus is circulating nonstop in some areas.

In Mexico specifically, the northern state of Chihuahua was one of the main drivers of the upturn, as declining vaccination rates in the United States helped bring measles across the border.

Speaking at President Claudia Sheinbaum’s morning press conference on Tuesday, Rafael Valdez Vázquez, Undersecretary for Health Policies and Population Well-being, said that between 2025 and 2026, Mexico registered a cumulative total of 20,601 measles cases among a population of 133 million inhabitants.

He added that there are currently 14 active cases, following a sustained decline since the peak of infections in February, when 1,314 cases were reported.

To regain measles-free status, Valdés said the federal government has outlined an action plan comprising two stages.

The first stage aims to bring the measles outbreak to an end by the second half of 2027. To achieve this, it will strengthen vaccination efforts in areas where transmission persists, actively seek out new cases and maintain epidemiological surveillance in states that no longer report infections.

The next step will be to demonstrate that the country has gone at least 12 months without endemic transmission. With this evidence, Mexico intends to regain recognition from the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO) in 2028.

“The goal is to end the outbreak by 2027, and the next step, in 2028, is to move along the path toward having Mexico once again recognized as a measles-free country,” Valdés said.

Finally, he reported that twelve states have registered three months or more without a reported case, including Tamaulipas, Baja California Sur, Colima, Tlaxcala, Querétaro, Baja California, Sinaloa, Oaxaca, Hidalgo, Morelos, Michoacán and Sonora.

Meanwhile, México state, Mexico City, Chihuahua and Campeche have gone between one and three months without new infections.

With reports from The Associated Press and Infobae

Today’s mañanera underscored that there is frequent high-level engagement between Mexico and the United States on a range of issues. Rodríguez’s meeting with Johnson in Mexico City occurred as members of a large migrant caravan continue to walk through the southern state of Chiapas en route to Mexico City. Many of the migrants hope to eventually reach Mexico’s northern border and enter the United States.

Sheinbaum gives an update on her China trip

Flanked by Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard and Foreign Affairs Minister Roberto Velasco, Sheinbaum reported that she held a meeting on Wednesday morning with Vietnamese President Tô Lâm.

In a social media post, she wrote that the strength of the 51-year-old bilateral relationship was discussed at her meeting with the Vietnamese leader. “We expressed our interest in deepening the ties between both nations,” Sheinbaum added.

During her mañanera appearance, she also reported that she had visited a technologically advanced hospital in Shenzhen.

“We learnt about the use of artificial intelligence for health issues,” Sheinbaum said.

“We agreed to have a closer relationship with China on these issues,” she added.

Sheinbaum also said she attended a pre-APEC Leaders’ Meeting event.

On social media, she posted photos from the opening of the APEC Leaders’ Meeting. The photos include two in which she appears with Chinese President Xi Jinping and his wife Peng Liyuan. Sheinbaum also posted a group photo of APEC leaders, including Xi, Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Sheinbaum reports on ‘very good’ meeting with Trump

Sheinbaum noted that she also met on Wednesday with Trump.

“Marcelo and Roberto accompanied me to a meeting with President Trump,” she said, adding that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer were also present.

“It was a meeting of around 20 minutes and we mainly spoke about trade agreements,” Sheinbaum said.

She said that Trump was informed about the progress that has been made in bilateral trade talks.

“We can say we’ve made a lot of progress,” Sheinbaum said.

“It was a very good meeting, very pleasant. President Trump was in a very good mood,” she said.

“We agreed to meet again at the G20 meeting at Mar-a-Lago,” Sheinbaum added, referring to next month’s G20 Leaders’ Summit in Florida.

Rodríguez reports on migration-focused meeting with US ambassador

Rodríguez described her meeting with Ambassador Johnson on Tuesday as “cordial.”

“We reviewed progress in the bilateral cooperation to manage migration flows,” she said.

Rodríguez said that she and Johnson spoke about migrant caravans, adding that she reiterated the federal government’s public message. She and Sheinbaum have stressed that no migrant caravans have reached the northern border during Trump’s second term and explained that the government tries to persuade migrants to return to their countries of origin, in part by telling them how difficult it is to enter the United States.

Rodríguez said that she and Johnson also spoke about the need for cooperation between Mexico and the United States on development projects in countries migrants are leaving, especially Central American nations.

The Mexican government has long argued that tackling poverty and crime in migrants’ countries of origin is the best way to reduce irregular migration to the United States via Mexico.

Johnson wrote on social media on Tuesday that the “meeting with Mexican authorities reinforces the work we are advancing with the Government of Mexico to combat illegal migration and dismantle human smuggling networks.”

“We are delivering results and those results are saving lives, while helping ensure that migrant caravans do not reach the U.S.-Mexico border, as President @Claudiashein has emphasized,” he added.

World.title: Supreme Court Asked to End Venezuelan Shield
World.content:
File photo: the US Supreme Court building in Washington. Photo: Architect of the Capitol (public domain).

VENEZUELA · US IMMIGRATION

For hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans in the United States, the next 48 hours may decide whether they can work legally or face deportation. On Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to halt a lower-court order that would restore Temporary Protected Status (TPS), a program that shields migrants from deportation.

The emergency appeal is the latest turn in the Venezuela US tensions that now reach into American courtrooms. A California federal judge found it unlawful to end the protections, and an appeals-court pause on that ruling is set to expire Friday, Nov. 20.

Who: Hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans; about 600,000 have held the status, called TPS.

The numbers: Federal lawyers say 1,800 detainees would be freed and 332 deportation orders blocked.

What happens next: An appeals-court pause expires Friday, Nov. 20, 2026.

A court fight over work permits and deportation orders is now in the hands of the nine justices, and the clock runs out on Friday.

In plain English TPS is a US program that lets people from troubled countries stay and work legally for a set period. The government says Venezuela no longer qualifies, while the migrants and their lawyers say ending the program broke the law.

Why the Justice Department Went to the Justices

The Justice Department, the government’s legal arm, wants the Supreme Court to overturn a California federal judge’s finding that ending TPS for Venezuelans was unlawful. Federal attorneys told the court that reinstating the status would stop the administration from carrying out up to 332 deportation orders.

They said it would also force the government to provide work authorization, and they called the resulting harm “severe and immediate.”A ruling, or silence, before the pause expires on Friday, Nov. 20, will settle whether the detainees go free.

The sharpest number is the deadline. If the justices do not step in before Friday, the government says it could be required to free about 1,800 Venezuelans held in immigration detention.
