What the Migrants’ Lawyers Say

Emi MacLean, an attorney for the National TPS Alliance at the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU) of Northern California, a civil-rights group, said the administration has no basis for its request. The Alliance is the group of TPS holders that brought the case.

“The lower courts should be able to rule on this question, and they are taking it seriously and they’re moving expeditiously,” MacLean said. She accused the government of trying to “jump the line” to win Supreme Court backing for what she called illegal actions.

How Venezuelans Got Here

Venezuelans first received TPS in March 2021 under President Joe Biden, a Democrat. The program was expanded in September 2023, and about 600,000 Venezuelans have held the protections.

The Supreme Court let the administration strip those protections last year while the case was at an earlier stage. Work permits then stopped being valid, thousands of people faced deportation cases, and many were detained, deported or left on their own.

In October the Supreme Court also voided an earlier appeals-court ruling in the same fight. The pattern reaches well beyond Venezuela.

The administration has ended TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, and in June the Supreme Court allowed it to end protections for people from Haiti and Syria.

File photo: the Supreme Court building during facade restoration. Photo: Architect of the Capitol (public domain).

The Exceptions That Break the Pattern

The administration has not ended every program. In October it kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan.

For Venezuelans, the contrast matters. The justices have heard this case before and let the government end the protections while the lawsuit continued.

What It Means for US Readers

Employers who hired Venezuelans under TPS face the sharpest uncertainty, because work permits could switch on or off within days. Families and communities with Venezuelan neighbours are watching the same deadline.

The ruling will also show how far the administration can end humanitarian protections while challenges are still pending. Venezuelans in detention are the most immediate losers if the Court sides with the government, and the most immediate winners if it does not.

What Is Not Known

It is not known whether the Court will act before Friday, or whether it will ask the plaintiffs to respond first. The sources available to us do not give the exact time of the filing.

It is also unclear how many of the former TPS holders are still living in the United States. We found no statement from the Department of Homeland Security or the Venezuelan government.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is TPS?

Temporary Protected Status, created by Congress in 1990, lets people from countries hit by disaster or civil strife stay in the United States. It is granted in periods of up to 18 months and allows work.

What happens if the Supreme Court does nothing by Friday?

Federal attorneys say the government could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from immigration detention. Protections and work permits would return while the case continues.

Sources: US Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit (the federal appeals court for California), National TPS Alliance v. Mullin, No. 25-5724; Supreme Court of the United States; statements by the National TPS Alliance and the ACLU of Northern California.

World.title: Two Cuban Video Makers Face Trial Next Week
World.content:

Politics: Cuba

A court in eastern Cuba is due to try two video makers on Tuesday 24 November 2026, according to the wife of one of them, more than nine months after police arrested them. Ernesto Ricardo Medina and Kamil Zayas Pérez, founders of the social media channel El4tico, face charges that include propaganda against the constitutional order.

What Happened

Doris Santiesteban Batista, Medina’s wife, announced that the Provincial Court of Holguín has set the oral trial for 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday 24 November 2026. Holguín is both a city and a province in eastern Cuba.

Police detained Medina and Zayas in Holguín on Friday 6 February 2026 and seized computers, phones, cameras and other equipment. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an international press freedom group, said on 10 February that friends did not know where the men were or what they were charged with.

On 12 February the Holguín provincial prosecutor’s office confirmed provisional prison for both men, the Cuban form of pretrial detention. They have been in custody since their arrest.

By early October the prosecutor’s office had filed its provisional conclusions, the first formal statement of its case. The First Criminal Chamber of the Provincial Court received the filing and ordered an oral trial.

Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana. File photo. photo, 2016. Plaza de la Catedral in Old Havana. Photo: Yoeztudioz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons.

What Prosecutors Allege

According to the prosecution, the two men ran El4tico together from Friday 7 November 2025. It says they posted videos on social media.

Prosecutors say the videos criticised the Communist Party of Cuba and state institutions. They also allege that the videos urged members of the armed forces and the Interior Ministry, which runs Cuba’s police and security services, to disregard the established legal order.

The prosecution adds that the equipment was bought with remittances, money sent to Cuba from abroad. Its charges are propaganda against the constitutional order, defamation of institutions, organisations, heroes and martyrs, and incitement to commit crimes.

We could not open the Penal Code articles the prosecutor cites, so we give no article numbers. The prosecution’s filing is not published online, and its contents reach us through the families of the accused.

How the Channel Describes Itself and Its Reach

CPJ describes El4tico as a social media outlet in eastern Cuba whose founders make short, mocking videos about daily life and their frustration with the government. It quotes Yoani Sánchez, founder of an independent Cuban news site, as saying the channel has thousands of followers in a region where news is scarce.

Katherine Jacobsen, CPJ’s coordinator for the United States, Canada and the Caribbean, said Cuban authorities “should release them without delay and allow the free flow of information in the country.” CPJ said Cuban authorities did not answer its request for information in February.

Why It Matters

The alleged offences are speech and its funding, not violence, which makes the verdict a measure of how Cuban courts treat online criticism. For many residents of eastern Cuba, a local channel is one of few sources of local news, according to Sánchez, as cited by CPJ.

The remittance allegation reaches beyond the island, because it treats money sent to Cuba as part of a criminal file. More than nine months in custody before a first hearing is the baseline against which the sentence will be read.

Medina’s mother, Mileydis Medina Machín, has said the family expects a conviction. In her words, “perhaps the sentence will be reduced a little, but we have no doubt that they will be convicted.”

What to Watch

The one dated checkpoint we can name is the hearing at the Provincial Court of Holguín on Tuesday 24 November 2026 at 8:30 a.m. Cuba time, as given by Medina’s wife.

What Is Not Known

No court or government statement on the hearing has reached us, and the defence lawyers are not named in anything we found. It is also unknown whether the hearing will be open to the public and to relatives.

What It Means for You

If you send money to relatives in Cuba, this case shows that prosecutors can cite remittances in a criminal filing against someone else. If you travel to the island or follow it as an investor, it is a reminder that online criticism can carry a request of up to ten years in prison.

For wider context, see our Cuba news page. Related cases include a convicted influencer and police accusations against a Cuban journalist.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who are the El4tico creators on trial in Cuba?

Ernesto Ricardo Medina and Kamil Zayas Pérez founded El4tico, a social media video channel in eastern Cuba. Police detained them in Holguín on 6 February 2026.

What are the El4tico creators charged with?

Prosecutors charge propaganda against the constitutional order, defamation of institutions, organisations, heroes and martyrs, and incitement to commit crimes. They ask for eight years for Medina and ten for Zayas.

When is the El4tico trial?

Medina’s wife says the Provincial Court of Holguín set the oral trial for 8:30 a.m. on Tuesday 24 November 2026. We found no court statement confirming the time.

World.title: Colombia Presses Insurers on Quake Payouts
World.content:
File photo, 17 February 2022: the main square of Rivera, the Huila town near where the bus overturned (Photo: Cbl62, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons).

Economy: Colombia

Colombia’s financial regulator called on insurers on Wednesday 18 November 2026 to speed up damage valuations and claim payouts after the earthquake of 10 August. The regulator, the Superintendencia Financiera (Superfinanciera), is the state body that supervises banks and insurers.

By 6 November insurers had paid COP 1.43 trillion (Colombian pesos; about US$432 million), against 103,833 claims filed, at the official TRM of 3,309.55 pesos per dollar on 18 November. The TRM is the official daily market rate; for readers abroad, the total shows how much quake cover still awaits payment.

Key Facts What. Regulator wants faster payouts; insurers had paid COP 1.43 trillion (US$432 million) by 6 November; 103,833 claims were filed.

Numbers. At the 30 October cut-off, payouts were COP 1.26 trillion (US$381 million) on 102,923 claims.

What next. Insurers must pay within one month of a proven claim.

Power Index. Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in Colombia ranks 6th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 51.1 points (November 2026 edition).

Colombia’s insurance supervisor wants earthquake claims paid faster, and the latest tally shows about US$432 million paid while insurers have set aside far more.

What Happened

The Superfinanciera said on 18 November that insurers must pay within one month once a claim is proven, stop demanding unrelated documents, and drop delaying tactics, in Carta Circular 78. It warned that insurers could lose their licence for the affected line and that officials who tolerated breaches could be sanctioned.

Insurers have paid COP 1.43 trillion (about US$432 million) with 103,833 claims filed, a tally dated 6 November. The rate used, 3,309.55 pesos per dollar for 18 November, comes from the open data portal datos.gov.co.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Colombia ranks 6th of 14 with 51.1 points. Strongest pillar: military means (91); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (28). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (BB-); 26 homicides per 100,000; organised crime at 7.8 of 10. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The previous tally covered the period to 30 October, according to Fasecolda, Colombia’s insurers’ association. It showed COP 1.26 trillion (US$381 million at the same rate) paid on 102,923 claims.

Since then, payouts have risen by about COP 170 billion (US$51 million) and claims by about 910. These totals come from different reports, so the gap is only a guide.

The earthquake struck at 7:34 a.m. on Monday 10 August 2026 near San José del Palmar, in Colombia’s Chocó department. The Servicio Geológico Colombiano (SGC), the state geological survey, measured magnitude 7.4 at a depth of 103 kilometres.

Bogotá skyline, where the Superfinanciera has its headquarters. File photo.

The Big Picture

The Superfinanciera has pressed the sector before. On 13 August, three days after the quake, it issued Carta Circular 54 of 2026, reminding supervised firms to apply its Quejas Exprés (express complaints) procedure for disaster victims.

That circular is addressed to all supervised entities, not only insurers. It was issued three days after the quake.

Insurance reaches a minority of homes. Fasecolda, the insurers’ association, estimates that only 9.3% of Colombian homes had any home insurance in March 2026.

Gustavo Morales, Fasecolda’s president, said in August that many damaged buildings had no earthquake cover. We found no sourced figure that compares Colombia’s earthquake-insurance take-up with other Andean countries.

The SGC says the quake is the third-largest in Colombia’s history, according to its director, Julio Fierro Morales. That ranking is the survey’s own assessment.

Why It Matters

Reserves are the money insurers set aside for claims they expect to pay. Fasecolda’s report for 30 October put reserves at about COP 7.1 trillion (US$2.15 billion), so the COP 1.26 trillion paid by then was about 18%.

Payouts matter because owners cannot rebuild until an adjuster values the damage and the insurer pays. Reserves are largest in Valle del Cauca, the department around Cali, followed by Risaralda, where Pereira stands, according to Fasecolda.

For US readers with property, suppliers or staff in those cities, slow payouts can delay repairs and the reopening of businesses. Insurance is one stream of money among several, alongside Colombia’s earthquake fund and the cost of rebuilding.

What to Watch

We could not confirm dated checkpoints from an official calendar for the regulator’s next steps. Fasecolda issues numbered claim reports, with report 12 covering the period to 30 October, so its next tally will show whether payouts keep rising past COP 1.43 trillion (US$432 million).

What Is Not Known

We could not open the full text of Carta Circular 78 on the regulator’s website, so its wording rests on the published summary. The cut-off of the COP 1.43 trillion tally was 6 November.

No primary source we found gives the share of the total quake loss that was insured. That share therefore remains open.

What It Means for You

For investors, the payout pace is a gauge of how fast rebuilding money turns into spending around Cali and Pereira. For owners with business ties there, the first check is whether a policy covers earthquakes, since only 9.3% of homes had any home insurance in March 2026.

Claims keep arriving, with 553 new ones in the week to 30 October. Faster valuation, the step the regulator singled out, would show first in the claim tallies we follow in our Colombia news.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Colombia’s regulator demand on 18 November?

In Carta Circular 78 the Superfinanciera told insurers to pay within one month once a claim is proven and to stop demanding unnecessary documents. It warned that insurers could lose their licence for the affected line.

How much have insurers paid for the Colombia earthquake?

By 6 November insurers had paid COP 1.43 trillion (about US$432 million at the 18 November TRM of 3,309.55), with 103,833 claims filed. At Fasecolda’s 30 October cut-off the figure was COP 1.26 trillion.

How strong was the 10 August earthquake?

The Servicio Geológico Colombiano measured magnitude 7.4 at a depth of 103 kilometres near San José del Palmar, Chocó. It calls the quake the third-largest in Colombia’s history.

World.title: Ex-Vice President’s Prison Injury Disputed
World.content:
Politics: Ecuador

Ecuador’s prison agency, SNAI, said on Wednesday 18 November 2026 that former vice president Jorge Glas harmed himself on 11 November. His lawyer, Sonia Vera, had said the evening before that an officer and at least five soldiers beat him in the El Encuentro maximum-security prison.

The two accounts clash, and no independent medical examination has been published. For readers abroad, the dispute shows how Ecuador treats a high-profile prisoner who is protected by orders from the human rights bodies of the Americas.

Key Facts What. Lawyer Sonia Vera says soldiers beat ex-vice president Jorge Glas; prisons service SNAI says he harmed himself.

When. Lawyer’s video Tuesday 17 November; SNAI statement Wednesday 18 November 2026.

What next. A regional human rights court requires Ecuador to report on his health every three months.

Power Index. Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 in Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 37.2 points (November 2026 edition).

As of. 19 November 2026, 03:00 GMT.

A lawyer’s video and a prison agency’s statement give opposite accounts of what happened to a prisoner whose health a regional court is monitoring. Neither side has published its evidence.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

What Happened on 11 November

Vera published a video on the night of Tuesday 17 November with extracts of a video call with Glas. In it, Glas describes a beating on 11 November and shows bruises on his legs and back.

Vera said an officer who had already threatened Glas was involved. She said that officer and at least five soldiers then beat, kicked and dragged him while trying to handcuff him.

Latin America Power Index · November 2026 edition Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 with 37.2 points. Strongest pillar: military means (55); weakest: diplomatic & cultural influence (14). Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B); 51 homicides per 100,000. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

Glas also alleged a sexual assault by the officer, in the account Vera gave. We do not repeat the details, because they are the lawyer’s description of what her client told her.

Vera said Glas counted 37 bleeding wounds, and that state records list the incident as “self-harm”. On Wednesday 18 November, SNAI said a monitoring report for 11 November “reports self-harming conduct” by Glas.

SNAI said Glas had a scheduled medical appointment that day and showed a “presumed decompensation” during a general consultation. It said he received immediate care, according to prison health staff, has no complications that affect his current condition.

The National Court of Justice building in Quito. File photo. photo. The National Court of Justice in Quito, Ecuador, which handles extradition requests, July 2025. Photo: Ceancata, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on ecuador prisons Email address Follow

The Big Picture

Glas was vice president under former president Rafael Correa, who led Ecuador from 2007 to 2017. He has received three prison sentences, for bribery, criminal association and embezzlement.

On 30 June 2025 a panel of the National Court of Justice, Ecuador’s top criminal court, gave him 13 years for embezzlement in the Manabí reconstruction case. That ruling was first-instance, so an appeal can follow.

In April 2024 he was recaptured, when President Daniel Noboa ordered police into the Mexican embassy in Quito. Mexico had given him asylum there.

The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights, a body of the Organization of American States, has protected Glas with precautionary measures since 31 December 2019. In February 2025 it widened them to cover his health, and in July 2025 it asked the Inter-American Court of Human Rights to order binding measures.

On 17 October 2025 the Court ordered Ecuador to give Glas specialised medical care, family visits and contact with his lawyers and doctors. It refused therapeutic house arrest and a transfer to another prison.

The Court also asked for a report within 30 days. After that, Ecuador must report every three months.

Why It Matters

The Court’s provisional measures are binding on Ecuador under Article 63.2 of the American Convention on Human Rights, which covers cases of extreme gravity and urgency. That makes an injury in custody, with two conflicting records, a matter for the Court’s next quarterly review and not only for Ecuadorian prosecutors.

The government’s view is that its own medical and monitoring records show self-harm and no serious complication. The lawyer’s view is that the same records mislabel an assault, and each side rests on documents or testimony that the public has not seen.

What to Watch

We could not confirm a dated hearing, deadline or report for this case from an official calendar of the Court or the Commission. The Court’s order requires Ecuador to report on his health every three months.

What Is Not Known

No independent medical examination of Glas has been published, and we found no announcement of a prosecutor’s investigation into the alleged beating. We also found no statement from the armed forces, and the video has not been independently authenticated.

It is not known whether the Court or the Commission has been asked to act on the 11 November incident. SNAI has not published the monitoring report it cites.

What It Means for You

For investors, travellers and companies with staff in Ecuador, the case shows that prison conditions are now watched by an international court. That adds legal scrutiny to the government’s security drive, though it does not change Ecuador’s travel or market picture by itself.

Readers can compare the case with our earlier reports, the Ecuador Prison Riots Kill 8 on 22 October and the Ecuador Jails Luisa González on 23 October. Both belong to the wider story of Ecuador’s prisons and courts.

More: Ecuador news in English, every day from The Rio Times.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Ecuador say about Jorge Glas on 18 November?

Ecuador’s prison agency SNAI said a monitoring report for 11 November reports self-harming conduct by Glas. It said he received immediate care and has no complications affecting his condition.

What does Jorge Glas’s lawyer allege?

Lawyer Sonia Vera said an officer and at least five soldiers beat, kicked and dragged Glas in El Encuentro prison on 11 November. She published a video of him describing it on Tuesday 17 November 2026.

Why is Jorge Glas protected by international orders?

The Inter-American Commission has protected him since 2019, and the Inter-American Court ordered binding measures on 17 October 2025. They require medical care, family and lawyer contact, and reports from Ecuador every three months.

Sources: SNAI statement of 18 November 2026; lawyer Sonia Vera’s video of 17 November 2026; orders of the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights on Jorge Glas.

World.title: Argentina’s Milei Rules Out Peso Devaluation
World.content:
Politics: Argentina

Argentine President Javier Milei said on Wednesday 18 November 2026 that his government will not devalue the peso. He also ruled out a “plan platita”, a pre-election cash-injection plan, and said the budget balance will not be touched.

He spoke in a television interview, and the message matters to anyone holding Argentine bonds, shares or pesos. Annual inflation is still above 30%, so every currency promise gets close scrutiny (see our Argentina news coverage).

Key Facts What. Milei ruled out a peso devaluation and a “plan platita” stimulus ahead of the 2027 elections.

Numbers. Inflation was 33.1% in the 12 months to October; the peso closed at 1,559 per US$.

Prediction markets. Polymarket, a prediction market, gives 96.7% odds 2026 inflation ends at 30.0% to 34.9% (21:39 ET, 18 November 2026).

Milei used one interview to defend his budget discipline and exchange-rate policy against pressure to change course before the 2027 vote.

What Milei Said

In the interview, Milei said “No vamos a devaluar, es una tontería”, which means “We will not devalue, it is nonsense”. He added that calls for devaluation are calls for low wages.

Asked about Senator Patricia Bullrich, the leader of the governing bloc in the Senate, he said anyone who suggests a “plan platita” has a problem. He argued that a deficit would have to be financed with debt or printed money, and that printing causes inflation.

Alignment group: Closer to Washington. WatchRating below investment grade (B-); inflation of 42%; public debt at 80% of GDP. See the full index, the business lens and the data →

The Obelisco, a landmark of central Buenos Aires, at dusk. File photo.

Free download · Expat checklist Get the free checklist as PDF Moving to Argentina 2026: the step-by-step checklist. This guide condensed into 2 printable pages with tick boxes and the key official links. Email address Get the PDF Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

The Big Picture

Argentina’s central bank, the BCRA, runs a band system that was announced on 11 April 2025 and took effect on 14 April 2025 with a range of 1,000 to 1,400 pesos per US$. Inside the band the peso floats.

Since 1 January 2026 the band edges move each month with the national inflation figure from two months earlier. The peso closed at 1,559.25 per US$ on 18 November.

Because the edges follow inflation by formula, a government decision to devalue would mean changing the regime itself. Milei’s pledge therefore amounts to a promise not to change that regime.

INDEC, the national statistics office, reported that consumer prices rose 2.2% in October and 33.1% over 12 months, and 26.3% since December 2025. That is the latest official reading, published on 12 November 2026.

Milei said poverty fell from 57% when he took office to 32%, and that 12 million fewer Argentines are poor. INDEC’s latest survey, for the first half of 2026, puts poverty at 32.3% of people in the 31 urban areas it covers and extreme poverty at 7.5%.

What Prediction Markets Say

Polymarket, a crypto-based prediction platform, showed traders giving 96.7% odds that Argentina’s 2026 annual inflation ends between 30.0% and 34.9%, on about US$42,000 of volume in that bracket (US$105,000 across all brackets) at 21:39 ET on 18 November. That fits the 33.1% reading for October.

Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Why It Matters

A balanced budget and a floating peso inside a wide band are meant to anchor inflation expectations, and Milei says an election year will not change that. For bondholders the mechanism is simple: a deficit financed by debt or printed money would raise inflation and pressure the peso.

The baseline is demanding, because prices rose 2.2% in October and a stimulus would land on an economy still inflating fast. At 33.1% over 12 months, a policy slip would show up quickly in prices.

What to Watch

INDEC’s release calendar lists the November inflation report for Tuesday 15 December 2026. It is the next hard data point on prices.

What Is Not Known

The presidency has not published a transcript of the interview that we could find, so every statement attributed to Milei above is his own claim. His claim that 12 million fewer people are poor is not an INDEC figure.

What It Means for You

If you hold Argentine assets or plan to travel there, the useful numbers are the market rate, 1,559.25 pesos per US$ on 18 November, and the monthly inflation print. Those figures shape purchasing power.

Our earlier coverage of Argentina ruling out a peso devaluation and of the central bank rejecting stimulus gives the background. The next inflation report is due on 15 December.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did Milei say about devaluation?

Milei said on 18 November 2026 that Argentina will not devalue the peso, calling the idea nonsense. He also ruled out a “plan platita” and said the fiscal balance will not be touched.

What is the plan platita?

It is Argentine slang for a pre-election cash-injection plan that boosts spending. Milei said financing it would need debt or printed money, which causes inflation.

What is Argentina’s inflation rate?

INDEC reported that consumer prices rose 2.2% in October 2026 and 33.1% over 12 months. Accumulated inflation since December 2025 stands at 26.3%.

Sources: INDEC, Consumer Price Index, October 2026 (12 November 2026); INDEC, CPI release calendar; INDEC, Poverty and indigence in 31 urban areas, first half of 2026 (24 September 2026); BCRA, Exchange-rate band regime.

World.title: Fitch Sees Nigeria Rates Falling to 18.6%
World.content:
Another view of the NNPC Towers, the headquarters of Nigeria's state oil company in Abuja, in an undated photo. The photo does not show the IPO plan. Photo: Uncle Bash007 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Nigeria: Economy

Borrowing in Nigeria is set to get cheaper, but not quickly. Fitch Ratings, one of the three big global credit rating agencies, expects the country’s average policy rate to fall to 21.7% in 2027 and 18.6% in 2028.

Rio Times membership One dollar for your first month. All premium analysis. Enter your email and the link comes by mail. Privacy Send me the offer

Gaimin Nonyane, Fitch’s director of sovereigns, presented the forecast on Tuesday 17 November 2026 in its Nigeria: Sovereign Rating Review and Outlook presentation. The policy rate is the benchmark rate set by the Central Bank of Nigeria (CBN), and it steers what banks charge for loans and what the government pays on its debt.

For readers in the United States, the numbers matter to anyone who may hold Nigerian government bonds, priced in the naira (Nigeria’s currency), through a fund. They also show how fast Africa’s most populous country, where Fitch expects 4.3% growth in 2026, may loosen its money.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

Key Facts Who. Fitch Ratings, the credit rating agency, set out its Nigeria forecasts on Tuesday 17 November 2026.

What. Nigeria’s average policy rate to fall from 25.4% in 2026 to 21.7% in 2027 and 18.6% in 2028.

Why. Headline inflation, the overall price rise, is easing: 14.06% in October 2026, down from 14.63% in September.

Next. The central bank’s rate committee meets on Monday 23 and Tuesday 24 November 2026.

As of. 19 November 2026, 03:00 GMT.

Fitch expects borrowing costs in Nigeria to fall from 2027, yet they stay high: even at 18.6% the policy rate would sit well above inflation.

How Nigeria Got to This Point

The CBN kept its Monetary Policy Rate at 26.5% at its May and July 2026 meetings, then on 22 September 2026 its Monetary Policy Committee (MPC), the panel that sets the rate, reset it to 23%. In the same communique the committee set the standing facilities corridor, the band around the main rate within which banks borrow from and deposit with the central bank, at 0.5 points above and 3 points below the rate, which gives 23.5% for lending and 20% for deposits.

The CBN itself said this was an operational reset to make its rate signals work better, not a change in its policy stance. It said it is moving towards inflation targeting, which means publicly aiming for a set inflation level.

Inflation gives the committee room. The National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Nigeria’s official statistics agency, reported on Monday 16 November 2026 that headline inflation was 14.06% in October, against 14.63% in September, with food inflation at 19.13%.

Fitch raised its outlook on Nigeria to Positive and affirmed the rating at B in October, as we reported at the time (Fitch Lifts Nigeria Outlook on Reforms and Reserves). A Positive outlook means an upgrade is possible if reforms hold.

Aerial view of the business district of Abuja, the capital of Nigeria. (File photo)

Follow this story Get an email when there’s news on Nigeria Inflation Email address Follow

What Fitch Expects, Year by Year

Fitch’s table shows the annual average policy rate easing from 27.3% in 2025 to 25.4% in 2026, 21.7% in 2027 and 18.6% in 2028. Over three years that is a fall of 8.7 percentage points.

The agency ties the path to inflation. It sees inflation at the end of the year of 15.1% in 2026, 12.2% in 2027 and 10.9% in 2028, and inflation averaged over the year of 15.4% in 2026 and 13.1% in 2027.

Fitch blames sticky prices on high food, transport and utility costs and elevated inflation expectations, though it says easing services inflation, the rise in prices of services, should help. It expects ample liquidity in the banking system to keep monetary conditions tight for the rest of 2026, with moderate easing from 2027.

The CBN’s tight stance has cooled lending, Fitch noted. Credit growth, which peaked at about 95% in February 2024, had slowed to roughly 16% by the time of the presentation.

The cash reserve requirement, the share of deposits commercial banks must park at the central bank, stayed at 45%. On the wider economy, Fitch forecasts growth of 4.3% in both 2026 and 2027 and 4.2% in 2028.

It expects the budget deficit to widen to 3.6% of gross domestic product (GDP) in 2026, then narrow to 3.3% in 2027 and 3.1% in 2028.

Why It Matters: Rates Stay High Against Prices

The gap between the policy rate and inflation shows how tight policy remains. With the policy rate at 23% and October inflation at 14.06%, the gap is about 8.9 percentage points by our own arithmetic.

Fitch’s 2027 pair shows the same: a 21.7% policy rate against 13.1% average inflation leaves a gap of about 8.6 points. Such a gap can make borrowing in naira expensive for firms.

Falling policy rates generally lower what new loans cost, though what happens to yields on government bonds depends on the paper and on the naira. A slower fall keeps loans costly for Nigerian companies, while a faster one depends on inflation continuing to ease.

In Plain English

Policy rate: the central bank’s benchmark rate. It sets the tone for what banks pay and charge. B rating: a speculative-grade score, several steps below investment grade, which signals higher risk of default. Fitch Ratings: an agency that grades countries and companies on their ability to repay debt.

What to Watch Next

The CBN’s MPC holds its next meeting on Monday 23 and Tuesday 24 November 2026, according to the committee’s official statement (communique) of 22 September. That decision will show whether the committee leans towards the easing path that Fitch describes.

The NBS publishes November inflation next; we have not confirmed the release date. If the October slowdown continues, it would support Fitch’s assumption, and if prices re-accelerate, it would argue against it.

The Other Side of the Argument

The CBN did not describe its September move as the start of an easing cycle. The committee said the corridor reset did not change its stance, and that future decisions would remain data-dependent.

It also named risks that could slow any fall: prolonged Middle East tensions, which have pushed up global energy prices, and election-related spending at home. The committee also said that persistent geopolitical tensions could delay the normalisation of monetary policy worldwide.

What We Do Not Know

Fitch’s figures are forecasts, and we have the forecast table, not the full presentation. We could not confirm the assumptions behind the 2027 and 2028 averages.

The MPC’s November decision is not known, and neither is how much election-related spending the committee flagged will reach prices. Fitch’s forecast is an average over each year, so the rate on any single day will differ.

What It Means for You

If you hold Nigerian bonds or a fund with Nigerian exposure, Fitch’s forecast implies lower policy rates, and what that does to bond yields depends on the paper, inflation and the naira. This is a forecast and not advice, and the official rate decision on 24 November is the next hard data point.

If you do business in Nigeria or send money there, Fitch expects easing to be moderate, not sudden. Even in 2028, Fitch’s rate would still be well above its inflation forecast.

What does Fitch forecast for Nigeria’s interest rate?

Fitch Ratings projects an average policy rate of 25.4% in 2026, 21.7% in 2027 and 18.6% in 2028. The 2025 average was 27.3%.

What is Nigeria’s policy rate today?

The Central Bank of Nigeria reset its Monetary Policy Rate to 23% on 22 September 2026. Its next decision is due on 24 November 2026.

Why does Fitch expect rates to fall?

Fitch expects inflation to keep slowing, from an average of 15.4% in 2026 to 13.1% in 2027. It expects moderate easing from 2027, after tight conditions through the rest of 2026.

Is Fitch’s rate path a promise by the central bank?

No. It is Fitch’s forecast, and the central bank says future decisions will depend on data. The committee has also named Middle East tensions and election-related spending as risks to prices.

How does this affect people outside Nigeria?

Funds that hold naira government debt are sensitive to the central bank’s rate path. Yields on specific bonds depend on the paper and on the naira, so the policy rate alone does not settle them.

Merida, Yucatan. Health officials say the alert is confined to one closed lake in the north of the city (Photo: Eden, Janine and Jim, CC BY 2.0 via Wikimedia Commons)

A staff member of the Beta group of Mexico’s National Migration Institute (INM), a unit that protects migrants’ rights, says 122 undocumented Cubans were detained in the Yucatán Peninsula between January and November 2026. We could not find the figure in published INM statistics, so it rests on his account.

The checkpoints are on the Mérida–Campeche road near Halachó, and on the Mérida–Valladolid road under the Teya bridge, near Mérida. He called the pattern unusual: six detained on 3 November and four about a week later, with more groups of four soon after.

Who Lives in Yucatán Legally

The staffer cited census figures of nearly 12,000 legally resident migrants in Yucatán, though he did not name the census. Americans were the largest group with 2,954, followed by Cubans with 1,926, Venezuelans with 1,704 and Canadians with 372.

We could not check these numbers against a published census table. They are his figures, given in the same account as the detention count.

The Big Picture

He said Cubans without visas or documents cannot get formal jobs, which keeps them in informal work. He added that people deported by the United States are moving from Quintana Roo to Mérida, adding pressure on local services.

Detainees go to a provisional station in the state capital, where they start a process to regularise their stay, he said. The aim of that process is to give them papers, but he gave no outcome figures.

Why It Matters

Yucatán has a large American community, so a rise in detentions of Cubans touches the same cities where many of them live. The account also suggests that Mexico’s migration controls now reach the interior roads of the peninsula and not only its borders.

For Cubans, a detention in Mérida can be the first step toward regular papers in Mexico or toward removal. Without published outcome data, neither path can be measured.

What to Watch

Official migration statistics for November would show whether the 122 figure holds. We could not find a scheduled release date, so the date is not confirmed.

What Is Not Known

It is not known how many of the 122 were removed, how many were regularised and how many are still held. His suggestion that smugglers are involved is an assumption, not a finding.

We also could not confirm the Monday detentions or the November count with any second source. Both come from his account alone.

What It Means for You

Foreign residents and visitors in Yucatán with valid papers are not affected by these checkpoints. Document checks on roads between Mérida and its neighbours are a routine part of Mexican migration control.

The Cuban figures, if confirmed, would show how far migration from the island now reaches. They would also show that many Cubans stay in Mexico rather than moving on.

World.title: Noboa Blames Industry for Ecuador Power Cuts
World.content:
Houses on a residential street in Guayaquil, Ecuador's largest city, at night. File photo, July 2023. (Photo: Ceibos, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Ecuador · Energy

Ecuador’s President Daniel Noboa said on Wednesday 18 November 2026 that households will not face power cuts in the coming months, and he blamed companies for the cuts that still hit factories. He argues that large firms did not meet a rule to generate part of their own electricity.

What Noboa Said

In a radio interview reported on 18 November, Noboa said Ecuadorian families would not face electricity cuts in the coming months. He traced the interruptions that continue in the productive sector to industries that had not built their own generation.

He gave the same assurance on 26 October in another radio interview, when he said the government was weighing tax relief for companies that obeyed the disconnection rule. He also said fines for firms that did not comply were being considered.

How the Industrial Cuts Work

On 26 October Noboa said that industries without enough self-generation had 30% of their weekly hours cut. He added that industry had known for 18 months that it had to cover 30% of its consumption itself.

He said about 45% of industries had taken on that commitment. The idea, he argued, was to stop cuts from reaching homes.

Coca Codo Sinclair, Ecuador’s largest hydroelectric plant, in a file photo. Ecuador’s grid depends heavily on hydropower. Photo: amalavida.tv, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

The Big Picture

Ecuador depends heavily on hydroelectric dams, so dry spells cut output quickly and push the government to ration demand. From late September 2024 a severe drought forced rolling blackouts of up to 14 hours a day.

Noboa has repeated the promise of no household cuts several times, including on 5 October and 26 October 2026. The 2026 rationing has fallen on industry, which loses production days while homes keep their lights.

Why It Matters

For firms with plants in Ecuador, including US companies, grid access now depends on having their own generation. The government’s rule asks users to supply 30% of their power, and Noboa says the government may reward those that took it on.

For households the promise is politically valuable ahead of a vote. It also depends on rainfall and reservoir levels, which the president cannot control.

What to Watch

Ecuadorians elect mayors, prefects (the heads of provinces) and councillors on Sunday 29 November, according to the National Electoral Council. The campaign ends on 26 November, and a quiet period follows until the vote.

What Is Not Known

The government has not published how many firms remain disconnected or how many fines it has issued. It has also not detailed the size or timing of any tax relief.

Current reservoir levels and the cut schedule for the rest of November were not part of the interview. Without them, the pledge cannot be tested against the grid’s actual margin.

What It Means for You

Residents and visitors face no announced household cuts, while factories and large businesses may still see limits on supply. Investors in Ecuadorian industry should read the 30% self-generation rule as a cost of doing business there.

The promise is a political statement made during a campaign. The weather and the dams will decide whether it holds.
