World.title: Why Costa Ricans Head for Puriscal When the Rains Stop
World.content:
Ask a Costa Rican where to go on a Sunday in late November and there is a good chance the answer will be Puriscal. The city sits in the hills about an hour west of San José, close enough for a day trip and far enough to feel like the countryside most Ticos remember from childhood. For a few weeks between the end of the rains and Christmas, everything that makes the place worth the drive arrives at once.

Puriscal has never needed a beach or a volcano to draw visitors. What it offers is simpler: winding ridge roads, long views across the Central Valley, small farms, butcher shops with wood fires going and a pace of life that the capital lost long ago. This is the season when all of that is at its best.

The first reason is the weather. The National Meteorological Institute (IMN) forecast the dry season to settle over the Central Valley during the second week of November, and in Puriscal the change is easy to feel. Afternoon downpours give way to blue skies, and the trade winds that Costa Ricans call the Christmas winds begin to blow across the ridges.

Those winds matter here more than in most places. They clear the haze, cool the air and open up views that stay hidden behind cloud for much of the rainy season. On a clear December morning a visitor can stand on a ridge above Santiago de Puriscal and see the valley on one side and the hills falling away toward the Pacific on the other.

The timing also flatters the land. The rainy season has left the hills green, though in a drier-than-normal El Niño year the pastures may start turning gold sooner than usual. Back roads that turn to mud in the wet months are dry and passable again, which opens routes through villages that many visitors never reach.

The second reason is pork. Puriscal is known across the country as the home of the chicharrón, and families here have been raising pigs and curing meat for generations. People drive out from San José every weekend of the year for a plate of fried pork with yuca, tortillas and a squeeze of lime, but in the weeks before Christmas the habit becomes a pilgrimage.

The reason is the Feria del Chicharrón, the fair that has filled the center of Santiago de Puriscal in the early weeks of December for more than two decades. Vendors start frying before the morning mist has lifted, and by midday the smell of pork and woodsmoke has spread across the town. Past editions have added live music, craft stalls, carnival rides and a horse parade to the food.

The crowds are real and the fair has drawn more than 6,000 visitors to the canton in a single week, a large number for a town of this size. Last year it opened on the last weekend of November and ran through Dec. 8, and anyone planning a trip this year should check the dates with the organizers before setting out.

The calendar does the rest since the aguinaldo, the extra month of salary that Costa Rican workers receive at the end of the year, lands in December, and the school year ends around the same time. Families have a little more money and a lot more free time, and a drive to Puriscal costs far less than a weekend at the coast.

Pork is also the meat of the Costa Rican Christmas. It goes into the tamales that families make together in December and onto the table as roast leg on Christmas Eve. Plenty of visitors leave Puriscal with a cooler in the trunk, stocked by the same butchers their parents bought from.

There is more to do than eat. The canton lies where the dry forest of the Pacific slope meets the wetter forest of the highlands, and that mix draws birdwatchers, who find the trails easier going once the rains stop. Others come for the old tobacco country, the roadside stands selling fruit and local produce or simply the drive itself.

What Puriscal offers in these weeks is a version of Costa Rica that many people assume has disappeared. It has clean air, green hills, good food cooked over a fire and neighbors who still greet strangers in the street. Costa Ricans have always known where to find it, and this is the time of year they go.

World.title: Costa Rica Shifts UN Stance on Israel as Grynspan Leads Race for Top UN Job
World.content:
Costa Rica abstained today on four United Nations draft resolutions concerning Israel, the occupied Palestinian territories and Palestinian refugees, withholding support from measures it voted for at the same stage in November 2025. The votes took place in the General Assembly’s Fourth Committee, formally the Special Political and Decolonization Committee, which each year takes up texts on the UN agency for Palestinian refugees and on Israeli practices in territories occupied since 1967. All four passed by wide margins, and the committee’s recorded votes listed Costa Rica among the abstentions each time.

The first text backs the operations of the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees in the Near East (UNRWA), whose mandate the General Assembly has extended to June 30, 2029. It deplores Israeli laws restricting the agency and calls on Israel to respect its privileges and immunities. It passed 143 to 9, with 20 abstentions, with the United States and Israel among the votes against.

The second affirms Palestinian refugees’ rights to their property and the income it generates and passed 155 to 9 with 9 abstentions. The third reaffirms that Israel’s 1981 extension of its laws to the occupied Syrian Golan is illegal, passing 149 to 8 with 14 abstentions. The fourth declares Israeli settlements in the occupied Palestinian territory, including East Jerusalem, and in the Golan illegal, and calls for an immediate halt to settlement activity. It passed 143 to 11, with 17 abstentions.

Costa Rica supported all four in committee last year, when the tallies were broadly similar. Within the region, Panama and Ecuador abstained on three of this year’s four texts, while Argentina, Colombia and Paraguay voted against at least one. The change fits a wider pattern. On Nov. 11, in the Assembly’s Second Committee, Costa Rica abstained on a resolution asking Israel to compensate Lebanon for a 2006 oil spill, which it had backed in 2024 and 2025, and repeated its 2025 abstention on a text on Palestinian natural resources. Over the past week, Costa Rica has abstained on six Israel-related texts, five of which it supported a year earlier.

The shift did not begin with the current administration. In December 2025, under former President Rodrigo Chaves, Costa Rica voted for the settlements and Golan texts in committee, then abstained on both when they reached the full General Assembly, ending a record of support on settlements dating back at least a decade. What is new this week is that the abstentions now come at the first stage and extend to UNRWA and refugee property.

The votes are the clearest sign yet that President Laura Fernández, who took office May 8 as Chaves’s chosen successor, intends to carry that alignment further. Shortly after her inauguration, the office of Israeli President Isaac Herzog said she had told him she was willing to raise Costa Rica’s representation in Jerusalem to embassy level. The Foreign Ministry declined at the time to confirm or deny that account, saying any decision would be communicated through official channels.

Costa Rica’s embassy has been in Tel Aviv since 2006, when it was moved from Jerusalem in line with Security Council Resolution 478. The country signed a free trade agreement with Israel in December 2025, now before the Legislative Assembly, and opened a trade and innovation office in Jerusalem in March.

The government has not publicly explained Wednesday’s abstentions. Fernández’s foreign minister, career diplomat Ana Elena Pinto, took office Oct. 15 after the president dismissed Manuel Tovar.

The votes come in the middle of the most consequential diplomatic campaign Costa Rica has run in years. Rebeca Grynspan, the former vice president who heads UN Trade and Development, is the front-runner to succeed António Guterres as secretary-general when his term ends Dec. 31. In the Security Council’s eighth informal straw poll on Nov. 5, she received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, her strongest showing so far.

Her path still runs through the council’s five permanent members, any of which can veto her. Analysts have identified the United States and Russia as the main risks. Washington’s reservations have been linked to reports from her agency that criticized Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank, while Moscow’s have been tied to her disagreement with its justifications for suspending the Black Sea grain deal.

That leaves Costa Rica facing competing pressures. A voting record closer to Washington’s could ease concerns in the capital with the most leverage over the outcome. But the council’s choice must still be formally appointed by the 193-member General Assembly, where Arab and Muslim-majority states form a large bloc.

In May, Carlos Murillo, director of the University of Costa Rica’s development observatory, warned that Arab support for Grynspan could begin to erode if Costa Rica moved toward recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. No delegation has publicly linked its position on her candidacy to Costa Rica’s votes this week, and Grynspan, as an international civil servant, has no role in her country’s ballots.

The four committee texts now go to the full General Assembly for final adoption, typically in early December, the same stretch in which the Security Council is expected to try to settle on a recommendation for the next secretary-general. For a country that built its diplomatic identity on multilateralism and international law, the votes mark a clear change in direction. Whether that change carries a cost for Costa Rica, or for Grynspan, among its Arab and Latin American partners should become clearer within weeks.

World.title: Injured Puma Rescued on Route 32, Where Only 2 of 20 Promised Wildlife Bridges Had Been Built
World.content:
An adult puma in Costa Rica with broken legs was rescued Wednesday morning in Guápiles after it was apparently struck by a vehicle on Route 32, the main highway linking San José with the Caribbean port of Limón. Firefighters received the call at 6:25 a.m. They found the cat lying in front of a store window along the highway, about 150 meters (490 feet) west of the Pequeño Mundo store, keeping its distance from the people nearby.

Police cordoned off the area while a veterinarian from the National System of Conservation Areas (SINAC) traveled to the scene. Officers kept onlookers back because the animal, although calm, could attack if frightened. Staff from SINAC’s Tortuguero Conservation Area assessed the puma and sedated it in a controlled way so it could be handled safely. Rescuers then wrapped the sedated animal in a white cloth and placed it in a box for transport.

The puma was taken to Toucan Rescue Ranch for veterinary evaluation. An initial examination found fractures in its legs, and the animal was expected to be moved to the National University’s Small Animal and Wildlife Hospital in Heredia. Its current condition has not been reported. No driver or vehicle has been identified.

Elena Vargas, director of the Tortuguero Conservation Area, urged drivers to keep a prudent speed and stay alert to road conditions because wild animals can appear without warning. Driving at an appropriate speed gives motorists time to react, she said, and the loss of wildlife on the country’s roads is something that can be prevented.

Wild cats are among the most exposed. The Las Pumas Rescue Center and Sanctuary in Cañas counted 76 wild cats hit on Costa Rica’s roads in 2025: 54 ocelots, 12 jaguarundis, five pumas, four margays and one jaguar. Eighty-eight percent died at the scene. Across all species, researchers estimate that about four wild animals are killed on Costa Rican roads every hour.

Route 32 has long been one of the deadliest stretches. It crosses nine protected zones, including seven biological corridors and Braulio Carrillo National Park. Studies from about a decade ago estimated that more than 1,200 wild animals died along the highway each year. The highway’s widening was supposed to come with protection for wildlife. Its environmental permit calls for 31 underpasses and 20 canopy bridges.

In a report to the Constitutional Court last November, the National Roads Council (Conavi) said 29 of the underpasses had been built but only two of the 20 canopy bridges. Six more bridges were under construction and 12 were still pending. The court’s deadline for the work expired in 2024, and in May 2025 it rejected Conavi’s request for another extension. Conavi said it expected to finish the remaining bridges during 2026.

Even where crossings exist, they may not work for an animal like a puma. A study by Panthera Costa Rica, supported by the Inter-American Development Bank, monitored underpasses and canopy bridges on Routes 1 and 160 for six months. Pumas, collared peccaries, margays, jaguarundis and nine-banded armadillos were never recorded using the structures, even though they lived in the surrounding forest.

The same study documented at least 14 collisions with large animals such as tapirs, pumas and deer. Some of them sent people to the hospital and destroyed vehicles. The researchers concluded that crossings reduce roadkill only as part of a complete system. That system includes exclusion fencing to steer animals toward the crossings, regular maintenance and continuous monitoring.

A new law aims to make that the standard. The Law to Guarantee Wildlife Crossings in Infrastructure was published in the official gazette La Gaceta on Sept. 7. It requires wildlife crossings and other safe-passage measures wherever roads cut ecological connectivity. The law applies to new projects and to the rehabilitation, widening, improvement and maintenance of existing roads. It requires the Public Works and Transport Ministry, municipalities and SINAC to coordinate.

Anyone who comes across an injured wild animal on the road should not approach it or try to move it. Keep a safe distance and call the Environment Ministry at 1192 or the 911 emergency line so trained personnel can respond.

World.title: My Night of Scorpion Stings in Costa Rica
World.content:
I’ve been stung by scorpions a handful of times. It’s like a wasp sting but it hurts more, lasts longer, and makes your lips tingle. Once I picked up a palm frond in my front yard and got stung on the thumb. I never saw the culprit. Another time I was clearing some dried leaves with my hand in front of a camera trap and, again, got stung in the thumb.

One night, I caught two stings while sleeping in bed, the first in the very worst place a man could get stung and a second time on the hand during the removal process. I can’t talk about it in polite company, but it was horrendous. So that’s four times. Unfortunately, that total was going to increase.

I had to get up earlier than usual for work. Being the very responsible man that I am, I called it an early night. At 12:30am a scorpion stung me in my left forearm as I slept. I immediately knew what it was and jumped out of bed, ripping the sheet to the floor. I grabbed my cellphone, turned on the flashlight, and told my startled wife that I had just been stung.

I furiously tore through the bed, pillows, and sheets and looked around on the floor but there was no scorpion to be found. Unsure of where the little devil was, I grabbed a sheet and a pillow and headed for my son’s room. My wife, being the Costa Rica veteran that she is, never even got out of the bed and just rolled over and went back to sleep.

As I walked over to my son’s room, I considered that the pillow or sheet could be hiding the scorpion, so I ditched the sheet on a rocking chair, pulled the pillowcase off the pillow and gave it another thorough inspection. Nothing. I slid into my son’s bed with a throbbing arm and lips tingling. It was going to be rough trying to go back to sleep. The front porch light makes his room too bright and he’s a sleep-flopper. Like a doped-up ninja, he began unconsciously attacking me with his gentle kicks and chops.

After about an hour, I finally fell back to sleep. At 3:30 am a scorpion stung the back of my left knee. Again, I jumped up, ripped the blankets off the bed, and grabbed my phone for light. This time I found it. A big, fat, dark scorpion in the sheets. I flung it out of the bed with my phone, and it crashed into a hamper across the room. I grabbed a nearby juice cup, because my son eats and drinks in his room and never puts the dishes in the sink, and squished the scorpion. My son, being blessed with the sleep of the youth, never woke up.

Not knowing what to do, I headed back to my own bed so at least I’m safe from the sleep ninja. I got back into bed, and my wife gave a little arm tap because she loves me. As I laid in bed with a throbbing knee-pit and, once again, tingling lips, I could only think of three possibilities for what just happened.

One. The scorpion was on my clothing the whole time. This seems unlikely because I was rolling all over the place dealing with the boy’s nocturnal karate. If it was on me the whole time, it should have stung me much sooner.

Two. I just got stung by two different scorpions in two different beds in the span of one night. This seems nuts because what are the chances? The upshot of this scenario is that I am a heroic father who saved his 11-year-old son from getting stung in his sleep.

The third option is the most unsettling. Perhaps one devious scorpion stung me twice. That would entail the scorpion stinging me in my bed, then biding it’s time while I got into my son’s bed, got kicked, eventually fell asleep, and started blissfully dreaming about camera trapping crocodiles. Then it would have had to walk across the house, get into another bed, and sting me a second time. I don’t want to believe this one because I’m the nature guy. I can’t have nature attacking me like that.

It’s currently 4:47am. I never got back to sleep after the second sting. My arm hurts, my knee-pit hurts, and my lips are tingling. I still don’t know what happened.

At least I got a Tico Times article out of it.

About the Author

Vincent Losasso, founder of Guanacaste Wildlife Monitoring, is a biologist who works with camera traps throughout Costa Rica. Learn more about his projects on facebook or instagram.

World.title: Prosecutors Investigate Rodrigo Chaves Over Turrúcares Landfill Offer
World.content:
Costa Rica’s Attorney General’s Office has opened a criminal investigation into former president Rodrigo Chaves, now minister of the Presidency and of Finance, for alleged influence peddling linked to public works he offered an Alajuela community if local officials dropped their legal fight against a proposed landfill.

The Fiscalía General said it opened the case in response to published reports and a complaint it received. The office confirmed the investigation on Monday, Nov. 16. Prosecutors declined to provide further details, citing the confidentiality of the preparatory stage under Article 295 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The opening of a case does not mean that criminal responsibility has been established.

The investigation centers on a public meeting Chaves led on Nov. 4 at the high school in Turrúcares, a district of Alajuela. Several ministers, government officials, members of the Alajuela Municipal Council and community representatives attended.

At the meeting, Chaves presented a package of projects for the district, including a technical high school, a CEN-CINAI childcare center, care centers for older adults, sports facilities, and repairs to national routes 721 and 136 and their bridges. He made the investments conditional on the Municipal Council withdrawing lawsuits that seek to annul the land-use permits for a landfill planned at the Bajo Pita property in San Miguel de Turrúcares.

When Education Minister Leonardo Sánchez said staff would assess land for the technical school, Chaves instructed that the work not begin while the municipality’s lawsuits remained in place. The value of the package has been reported differently. Chaves announced works valued at about 6 billion colones (about $13.4 million). The Presidency has since cited a figure of about 100 million colones (about $223,000) in infrastructure projects.

The landfill would be built by Empresas Berthier EBI de Costa Rica, which the government has promoted as an environmental technology park. The Municipality of Alajuela granted the project’s land-use permits more than a decade ago but later moved to annul them through lesividad proceedings, arguing the project conflicts with the canton’s zoning plan.

Investors linked to the Canadian company Berthier EBI and to Bajo Pita S.A. then filed an arbitration claim against Costa Rica at the International Centre for Settlement of Investment Disputes (ICSID). Chaves told residents the state faces potential exposure of up to $150 million and that the municipality’s lawsuits weaken Costa Rica’s defense.

He also attached a deadline. Chaves said the offer would be withdrawn once the government had to pay for the country’s legal defense in the arbitration, a cost he estimated at 2 billion colones (about $4.5 million), with the process starting Dec. 2.

No signed agreement guaranteeing that the investors would withdraw the arbitration was presented at the meeting. Legal specialists Álvaro Sagot and Nicolás Boeglin have questioned Chaves’s reading of the case, arguing that the state has legal defenses available and that the claim may be time-barred.

Chaves has rejected accusations of extortion, saying his intervention was intended to warn of the economic consequences the country would face if it lost the international case. No response from Chaves to the opening of the criminal case had been published as of Wednesday morning.

Lawmakers from the National Liberation Party, the Social Christian Unity Party and the Broad Front accused Chaves of blackmail the day after the meeting. An opposition motion condemning his statements, filed Nov. 9, was rejected 31 to 24, with the ruling Pueblo Soberano party voting against it.

In Alajuela, the decision rests with the council. Council president Jorge Arturo Campos described the offer as a trade-off and said residents should take part in the decision, while Chaves rejected a popular consultation and said the council’s 11 members should decide. Two weeks after the meeting, Campos said the council had received no formal request to vote on the landfill and had nothing on its agenda. Turrúcares residents have protested at council sessions and want the court challenges kept in place.

Influence peddling carries a penalty of two to five years in prison under the Law Against Corruption and Illicit Enrichment in Public Service. Any prosecution would face an additional hurdle. As a minister, Chaves holds immunity from prosecution, meaning the Supreme Court’s full bench would first have to approve a request to lift it before the Legislative Assembly votes, where 38 votes, a two-thirds majority, are required.

A separate request by prosecutors to lift his immunity, in a case over alleged parallel financing of his 2022 presidential campaign, has been stalled for months by vacancies among substitute justices on the Constitutional Chamber. The dispute unfolds as the waste disposal capacity tightens. Olivier Álvarez, president of the Association of Chemical Engineers and Allied Professionals (CIQPA), said in remarks published Wednesday that three or four of Costa Rica’s seven active landfills are months, not years, from the end of their useful life, and that the Greater Metropolitan Area needs a new disposal site.

Álvarez said 55% to 60% of household waste is organic and roughly 20% could be recycled if kept clean, and he called for a model that recovers more material rather than one that depends on finding new places to bury garbage. Prosecutors have not said when the preliminary investigation might conclude.

World.title: Costa Rica Traffic Jams Doubled in a Year – Half the Roads Now Back Up
World.content:
If your drive across the Central Valley feels slower than it did a year ago, the numbers back you up. Traffic jams on Costa Rica’s roads doubled in intensity in 2025, and half of all road segments measured now back up at least once, according to the 2026 National Competitiveness Index.

The index, published Nov. 13 by the Council for the Promotion of Competitiveness (CPC), counted 117.6 jam reports for every 100-meter (328-foot) stretch of congested road. The year before, the figure was 57.4. The jam data comes from the State of the Nation Program, which draws on Waze reports shared through the Ministry of Public Works and Transport (MOPT). Of the road segments the index evaluated, 50.1% recorded at least one jam, the highest share since the series began.

The waits are getting longer, too. Drivers now lose an average of 207.4 seconds, or about three and a half minutes, on every congested 100-meter segment. CPC economist Andrés Fernández put it in starker terms. He said the average time drivers spend per kilometer (0.62 miles) of jammed road rose from about 30 minutes to about 35 in the latest edition.

Taken together, those figures pushed the index’s road connectivity score from 60.7 to 56.6 out of 100. The 4.1-point drop is the steepest since the series began in 2021. The worst-connected areas are mostly in and around the capital. San José, Escazú, Curridabat, Belén, Montes de Oca and Santo Domingo rank among the most congested, along with Corredores in the southern zone. The area of San José scored just 40.9 out of 100 on road connectivity.

The longest delays, however, turned up on the central Pacific coast. In Garabito, the area that includes Jacó, drivers lose up to 11.9 minutes for every 100 meters of congested road, the highest figure in the country. Heredia averages 5.9 minutes, while Sarchí has the shortest delays at about two minutes.

Fernández said congestion is heaviest in the Greater Metropolitan Area and on the approaches to the ports. Travel times to Puerto Caldera and to Daniel Oduber International Airport in Liberia both reached their highest levels in the index’s history. Over the past five years, 62 of the 82 areas lost ground on road connectivity, while 20 improved. Cartago, Vázquez de Coronado and San Isidro saw the sharpest declines, while Buenos Aires, Carrillo and Guatuso improved the most.

The smoothest traffic is found in Turrubares, Puriscal, Bagaces and Acosta. Congestion weighed on an otherwise improving national picture. Costa Rica’s overall competitiveness score rose 2.4 points to 58.6 out of 100, but the CPC identified worsening traffic and a 41.5% drop in real per-student investment in school infrastructure as the main factors limiting further gains.

For anyone who drives here, the index puts numbers to what the daily commute already suggests. Jams are more frequent, they cover more of the road network and they last longer than at any point on record.

World.title: Costa Rica Ties Worst Defeat in Its History With 7-0 Loss to Argentina
World.content:
Costa Rica’s national soccer team lost 7-0 to Argentina on Tuesday night in Córdoba. The result ties the worst defeat in the team’s history. The friendly at Estadio Mario Alberto Kempes, which kicked off at 5 p.m. Costa Rica time, was effectively over by halftime. Argentina led 4-0 at the break and scored three more after the restart. Costa Rica had less than a third of the possession and rarely reached the attacking third.

The score matches Costa Rica’s 7-0 loss to Spain at the 2022 World Cup in Qatar and a 7-0 defeat to Mexico in 1975. It is also the heaviest loss of Bryan Ruiz’s short time as head coach. Nico Paz opened the scoring in the eighth minute. Julián Álvarez doubled the lead in the 35th, Paz added his second three minutes later and Álvarez made it 4-0 just before halftime.

Franco Mastantuono replaced Paz at the break and scored in the 48th minute. Alexis Mac Allister made it 6-0 in the 78th after Costa Rica lost the ball deep in its own half. Mastantuono completed his brace two minutes from the end of regulation time.

Argentina finished as runner-up at this year’s World Cup and is playing without Lionel Messi, who has retired from international football. Lionel Scaloni’s side came into the match after a 2-1 loss to Uruguay in Buenos Aires four days earlier. Defenders Mariano Troilo and Aaron Anselmino made their senior debuts in the second half.

At his post-match news conference, Ruiz called it a very hard defeat that showed the gap between the two teams. He said the scoreline left little to add, that there was no justification for the performance and that he and his staff took responsibility. Ruiz said Argentina exposed his team in every part of the game and deserved the win. He admitted he made a mistake by having his side play out from the back. He also said he played some players out of their usual positions, including Andrey Soto, because he wanted to test him.

The coach said his staff will review every player in detail after the international window to decide who stays in the squad. He said he did not regret scheduling Ecuador and Argentina, because his players needed to see what competing at that level demands. In his view, Costa Rica is still far from it.

Tuesday’s loss ended a difficult trip to South America that began Friday with a 2-0 defeat to Ecuador in Quito. Ruiz called that performance very acceptable by comparison. Ruiz, a former national team captain, became interim coach on Sept. 28 after Argentine coach Fernando Batista was dismissed.

The Costa Rican Football Federation later named him permanent coach for the cycle leading to the 2030 World Cup. He also played in the 2022 defeat to Spain, coming off the bench with Costa Rica already 4-0 down. Midfielder Celso Borges started both matches.

Reaction at home was harsh. Commentators and sports pages across Costa Rica called the performance humiliating and questioned whether the team was ready for opponents of Argentina’s level. Costa Rica did not qualify for the 2026 World Cup, and Ruiz’s rebuild is aimed at 2030. Costa Rica has still never beaten Argentina, and Ruiz now has a long review ahead before the team plays again.

World.title: Costa Rica’s $9.8 Billion Banco Popular Has Had No Board Since July
World.content:
Banco Popular, Costa Rica’s fourth-largest financial institution by assets, has operated without a seated board of directors since July 31, and the banking regulator is now urging lawmakers to tighten the rules for who can sit on it. In a letter dated Oct. 9, Hazel Valverde, head of the General Superintendency of Financial Entities (Sugef), asked lawmakers to strengthen the legal requirements for the bank’s directors, including suitability, professional experience, technical knowledge, honorability and independence of judgment.

The regulator warned that governance weaknesses at systemically important institutions, a group that includes Banco Popular, Banco Nacional, Banco de Costa Rica and BAC, could affect the entire financial system. The stakes are large. Banco Popular reported 4.42 trillion colones (about $9.84 billion) in assets and 1.10 trillion colones (about $2.45 billion) in equity at the end of September. Dollar figures in this article use the Central Bank reference sell rate of 449.04 colones for Nov. 18, close to the record lows the dollar has hit this year.

Under the bank’s governing law, only the board can approve the annual budget and certain internal rules. The terms of all seven directors expired July 31, and the board had already stopped meeting after two members resigned on June 29 to join the boards of other state banks.

The bank’s internal audit office warned in August that management cannot take decisions reserved for the board. In September, the bank’s corporate general management cautioned that the 2027 budget, internal regulations and the external audit contract were at risk. The Comptroller General’s Office stated on Sept. 25 that budget approval is a power the board cannot delegate.

Sugef also recommended that lawmakers stagger the board’s terms. Today all seven seats run on four-year terms that expire at the same time. Banco Nacional and Banco de Costa Rica instead name directors to eight-year terms split across two administrations, three seats in one and four in the next. The regulator said that when every term ends at once, a bank can lose significant institutional knowledge and face long periods without a working board.

The government has moved to fill the gap. The Executive Decree allows the Governing Council to appoint, on an interim basis, the four directors and four alternates normally chosen by the bank’s Workers’ Assembly. Together with the three directors the Executive already names, that would complete the seven-member board.

The decree, signed by First Vice President Francisco Gamboa Soto, Minister of the Presidency Rodrigo Chaves Robles and Labor Minister Mercedes Flores Badilla, limits the government to candidates the Workers’ Assembly has already preselected. The assembly’s integration commission said last week that it had sent its shortlist to the presidential offices. As of early Wednesday, no appointments had been announced.

The leadership gap follows a turbulent stretch for the bank. On Sept. 11, Sugef lifted Banco Popular out of “financial irregularity,” a status tied to weaknesses in board governance, and placed it at normality level 3. In that resolution, the regulator rated the board’s suitability a 3 on a scale of 1 to 4, where 1 is best.

The bank’s numbers remain solid on paper. Conglomerate profit through September reached 26.4 billion colones (about $58.9 million), up roughly 47% from a year earlier, and capital adequacy stood near 22%, well above the 10% minimum. Loans sent to judicial collection, however, nearly doubled to 67.3 billion colones (about $149.9 million) from 34.1 billion colones (about $76 million).

Sugef’s letter responded to a legislative committee reviewing a bill that would fund non-contributory pensions with half of Banco Popular’s employer contribution, one of several proposals touching Costa Rica’s strained pension system. The regulator said board requirements should be examined as part of a broader review of the bank’s sustainability.

Banco Popular’s press office said the bank will respect the authorities’ decisions and that any changes will follow legal procedure. It described the interim appointment measure as relevant because it would allow a board to act on matters that cannot be decided today.

Banco Popular is one of the institutions many here use for savings, loans and currency exchange. How quickly the government seats an interim board will determine whether the bank can approve its 2027 budget on time, while the regulator’s proposals now sit with lawmakers already weighing a crowded economic agenda.

World.title: ‘I render aid’: Majestic Alley businessman denies harboring police officer after cop abandons post
World.content:
‘I render aid’: Majestic Alley businessman denies harboring police officer after cop abandons post

By Breaking Belize News Staff: Tyrone Kareem Staine, 46, pleaded not guilty to harboring a police officer on Wednesday, telling the Belize City Magistrate’s Court that he did not understand the charge and that the building where police found the constable was his shop, not his home.

Police allege that Staine knowingly allowed Police Constable Julian Gladden to stay inside the Pinks Alley building while Gladden was supposed to be on duty elsewhere. Staine, who appeared without an attorney, told the court he routinely gives people water and lets them shelter in his shop when it rains. “I render aid,” he said. The magistrate told him he could give his side at trial and that it was up to the prosecution to prove the charge.

As Breaking Belize News previously reported, a sergeant went looking for the overnight patrol after it stopped reporting its activity after 1 a.m. The sergeant said Gladden opened the door around 4:05 a.m. and stepped outside in uniform. The sergeant said he found two Belize Defence Force soldiers assigned to the same patrol sitting inside.

According to police, Staine told the sergeant that the officers were already inside when he found them and that he let them stay. After being cautioned, police say Staine told the sergeant, “I take care of the police. I look out for the citizens. It is not like I do it all the time.”

Police Staff Officer Assistant Superintendent Stacy Smith confirmed that Gladden faces internal disciplinary proceedings. She did not announce a criminal charge against him or say whether either soldier faced disciplinary action.

Staine met bail of $500 with one surety in the same amount. He is due back in court on February 4, 2027, when he is expected to receive disclosure.

World.title: St. Vincent & the Grenadines PM arrives in Belize for Garifuna Settlement Day celebrations
World.content:
St. Vincent & the Grenadines PM arrives in Belize for Garifuna Settlement Day celebrations

By Zoila Palma: Today, Dr. Godwin Friday, the Prime Minister of St. Vincent & the Grenadines arrived in Belize for an official visit.

He arrived at Philip Goldson International Airport, where Oscar Arnold, Chief Executive Officer of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Foreign Trade, welcomed him and his delegation.

Prime Minister Friday is a special guest of the Government of Belize who will participate in tomorrow’s Garifuna Settlement Day celebrations commemorating the arrival of the Garinagu in Belize.

The Prime Minister is scheduled to depart Belize on 20 November 2026.

World.title: Belize advances Inter-agency coordination for multi-hazard Early warning and disaster preparedness
World.content:
Belize advances Inter-agency coordination for multi-hazard Early warning and disaster preparedness

Belize is advancing efforts to strengthen its national disaster risk management capacity through improved environmental monitoring, early warning systems, technical cooperation, and inter-agency collaboration under the Belize Multi-Hazard Risk Management Capacity Building Project.

From November 5–10, 2026, a technical team from National Taiwan University (NTU), led by Associate Professor Hao-Che Ho, conducted technical assessments and consultations with key government agencies, including the National Hydrological Service (NHS), National Meteorological Service (NMS), National Emergency Management Organization (NEMO), Climate Change Department (CCD), and Forest Department (FD).

A key development was the assessment of a proposed wildfire monitoring site in Mountain Pine Ridge, which the NTU team, working with the Forest Department, confirmed as suitable. The planned solar-powered system will incorporate high-resolution cameras and environmental sensors to monitor conditions associated with wildfire risk. NTU will also support equipment installation and technical training in operation, maintenance, and data management.

Engagements with the National Meteorological Service advanced efforts to integrate approximately 80 meteorological monitoring stations into a unified network, strengthening information-sharing and support for Belize’s Early Warning System. With the National Hydrological Service, the team also reviewed data integration and reliability across monitoring stations in the Belize River Basin, including plans for a 360-degree camera at the Iguana Creek Flood Monitoring Station to support monitoring at Iguana Creek and Double Run.

Additional activities included an assessment of a proposed carbon sequestration monitoring pilot site in Corozal District, in collaboration with the Climate Change Department, Forest Department, and local partners. The assessment will inform future forest measurements, carbon stock monitoring, and technical capacity-building in carbon assessment methods.

Community preparedness also remains a priority. Following the initial disaster preparedness training in Dangriga on October 31, NEMO and the Taiwan Technical Mission (TTM) are conducting additional community training activities throughout November to strengthen local disaster awareness, preparedness, and emergency response capabilities.

The visit also featured an Inter-Ministerial Seminar and Annual Task Force Meeting, bringing together government agencies to address monitoring gaps, strengthen information-sharing and advance coordinated approaches to disaster preparedness and response. Associate Professor Ho shared Taiwan’s experience in multi-hazard early warning and disaster risk management.

The project is supported by the Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund (TaiwanICDF), coordinated by TTM, and implemented in collaboration with the Ministry of Sustainable Development and Climate Change (MSDCC) and the Ministry of Public Service, Disaster Risk Management and Enterprise (MPSDRME).

These efforts are strengthening the institutional collaboration and technical capacity needed to anticipate risks, improve early warning, and better protect Belize’s communities, livelihoods, and natural resources.

World.title: Belize receives 7 devices to help detect illegal refrigerant trade
World.content:
Belize receives 7 devices to help detect illegal refrigerant trade

By Zoila Palma: Belize is strengthening its efforts to combat the illegal trade of controlled refrigerants and protect the ozone layer through the implementation of its Hydrochlorofluorocarbon (HCFC) Phase-out Management Plan (HPMP).

The National Ozone Unit (NOU), through the Department of the Environment (DOE), recently received seven specialized refrigerant identifiers procured with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP).

The equipment will be provided to the Customs and Excise Department to assist officers in identifying refrigerants during inspections at ports of entry and detecting the potential illegal trade of controlled substances.

Before the official handover, the DOE will conduct capacity-building training for Customs Officers at all ports of entry to ensure they are equipped with the technical knowledge to operate the devices effectively. The initiative is expected to strengthen monitoring of refrigerant imports and improve enforcement against the illegal movement of controlled refrigerants.

The DOE said the initiative will also enhance collaboration among the department, UNDP and the Customs and Excise Department in implementing the HCFC Phase-out Management Plan and meeting Belize’s commitments under the Montreal Protocol, an international agreement aimed at protecting the ozone layer.

World.title: Grandson begs forgiveness after ‘grampa’ finds footage of him stealing $175; But jailed on separate bus-house burglary charge
World.content:
Grandson begs forgiveness after ‘grampa’ finds footage of him stealing $175; But jailed on separate bus-house burglary charge

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 28-year-old Crooked Tree man asked for forgiveness in court after admitting he stole $175 and a $400 cellphone from his grandfather. Deallin Andre Jones was fined for both thefts but was sent to the Belize Central Prison after he could not post bail on a separate charge of burglarizing a neighbor’s home.

Jones, who appeared without an attorney, pleaded guilty to two counts of theft. The magistrate fined him $1,000 for taking the cash and $3,000 for stealing the cellphone. Both fines are due by July 30, 2027.

As Breaking Belize News previously reported, Jones’ 75-year-old grandfather said he was checking security footage in November over a missing phone when he saw his grandson take cash from his bedroom on June 5. He told police that Jones had borrowed the phone, which belonged to his late wife, on September 28 and never returned it despite repeated requests.

In the separate burglary case, a 21-year-old woman told police she returned home on May 25 and saw Jones exit through the front door of the bus she had converted into a residence near Crooked Tree Junction. She said he ran when he saw her. The woman told police she had left the door unlocked and discovered that a $50 bill was missing from her purse.

Jones asked what sentence he might face and sought clarification about what constitutes burglary. The magistrate did not accept a guilty plea on that charge. The prosecution did not object to bail, which was set at $2,000 with one surety in the same amount or two sureties of $1,000 each. Jones was remanded after he could not meet those conditions.

World.title: Saldivar questions timing of Belmopan’s El Salvador Day, says PUP is frantic to hold its base
World.content:
Saldivar questions timing of Belmopan’s El Salvador Day, says PUP is frantic to hold its base

Former Belmopan area representative John Saldivar says the People’s United Party in Belmopan is “frantic” to hold on to its base, and he is questioning the timing of the City Council’s plan to celebrate the Salvadoran community.

In a written commentary, Saldivar argues that the PUP in Belmopan has relied heavily on the immigrant community for its election wins.

He claims that support in Belmopan Central proved short lived in the 2024 municipal and 2025 general elections. According to Saldivar, a UDP councillor candidate won in Belmopan Central and came within 246 votes of winning a seat overall.

The lesson, he says, is that the PUP needs strong support from its base on the periphery of the city to keep winning.

Saldivar alleges the party has abandoned those supporters. He claims they have lost access to pantry, land and jobs, and have been denied medical, school, flood and sports assistance.

On the council’s upcoming El Salvador Day, Saldivar says recognising the Salvadoran community’s contribution to Belmopan is “a worthy endeavor” and “well deserved.”

But he says there would be less resistance if the same council had not left St. George’s Caye Day off its official September programme two years ago. He adds that the council has not given official support or ceremonies for Garifuna Settlement Day.

“The timing however is very suspicious,” he wrote, suggesting the event is an attempt to pander to a base the party has neglected.

Saldivar also criticised area representative Oscar Mira, claiming he has focused more on himself and his family than on the people who elected him, and Mayor Pablo Cawich, whom he accuses of spending more time with “the society people than with the common people.”

He closed by pointing to the March 2027 municipal elections.

Saldivar is a former UDP minister and area representative, and the views expressed are his own. Mira, Cawich and the Belmopan City Council have not yet responded.

World.title: Where to eat in Belize for an authentic local dining experience
World.content:
Where to eat in Belize for an authentic local dining experience

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Visitors come to Belize for the reef, the rainforest and the ancient Maya sites. Many leave talking about the food.

For travellers and locals looking for an authentic dining experience in western Belize, Running W Restaurant at the San Ignacio Resort Hotel is one of the best known tables in Cayo.

The restaurant takes its name from Running W, the well known Belizean meat brand, and local beef is at the centre of its menu. Steaks are a signature, served alongside dishes that draw on Belizean, Maya and Mestizo cooking traditions.

That mix is what authentic dining in Belize looks like. The country’s food reflects its people, and Cayo’s kitchens bring together flavours from several cultures using ingredients grown and raised nearby.

The setting adds to the experience. Running W sits on the resort’s property on Buena Vista Street, a short walk from downtown San Ignacio, with terrace seating that looks out over the greenery of the Macal River valley.

The restaurant is open to the public, not only to hotel guests, and serves breakfast, lunch and dinner. That makes it a practical stop before or after a day of touring Xunantunich, Cahal Pech or the caves of Cayo.

Running W Restaurant is located at the San Ignacio Resort Hotel, 18 Buena Vista Street, San Ignacio. For reservations, email [email protected].

World.title: Universal Hardware announces EasyCare buy one get one free paint sale November 26 to 28
World.content:
Universal Hardware announces EasyCare buy one get one free paint sale November 26 to 28

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Universal Hardware will hold an EasyCare Premium Paint buy one get one free sale from November 26 to 28, 2026.

The sale will take place at both of its locations, in Spanish Lookout and Belize City.

Customers can choose interior or exterior paint in flat, satin or semi gloss finishes, with over 2,000 colours available.
