In Spanish Lookout, the store is on Center Avenue. Call 823-0254, WhatsApp 652-9933 or email [email protected].

World.title: ODPEM audit finds expired food, insect-infested supplies and millions in unaccounted donations
World.content:
Auditors inspecting warehouses holding Hurricane Melissa relief supplies found 359 boxes of crackers past their best-before dates, insects on the packaging of some consumables and 15 unopened containers that had not been recorded in the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM) inventory, exposing serious gaps in how the agency accounted for and safeguarded donated goods.

The findings are contained in an October 2026 compliance audit by the Auditor General’s Department, tabled in Parliament on Tuesday, which also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were not included in the donation schedules maintained by the Office of Disaster Preparedness and Emergency Management (ODPEM).

During a physical inspection of Warehouse 3 on June 18, 2026, auditors found that the 359 boxes of crackers had best-before dates ranging from March 4 to 10, 2026. Insects were also observed on the packaging of some consumable items, raising concerns about the conditions in which relief supplies were being stored.

The discovery came despite ODPEM having spent $450,000 on fumigation at the warehouse in May. The work was completed on May 14, but insects were still observed during the auditors’ inspection the following month.

The audit also revealed that concerns about pests at the facility had been raised months earlier. In an email dated March 23, 2026, ODPEM’s logistics manager informed the administrator that approximately 200 bags of rice at the warehouse were heavily infested with weevils.

The email warned that the infestation posed a significant risk to the condition of the remaining stock and could cause further deterioration if it was not addressed promptly.

However, auditors found that rice remained in storage about three months after the infestation had been reported. During their stock count, they recorded 20,400 packs of rice, contained in 204 bags, with each bag holding 100 packs.

The Auditor General said this pointed to weaknesses in storage conditions and the system used to ensure older supplies were distributed before newer ones, rather than being solely a question of whether the fumigation had worked.

Although ODPEM had arranged for the warehouse to be fumigated, the presence of insects during the June inspection raised questions about the effectiveness and lasting impact of the treatment. The auditor general recommended that the agency obtain an assessment to determine whether the affected items were suitable for consumption.

The inspection also exposed a basic problem with the agency’s record-keeping. ODPEM did not provide auditors with store records showing the quantities of goods that should have been in Warehouse 3. This meant the auditors could not compare what they physically counted with the supplies recorded as received since November 2025 or those distributed during the period under review.

The problems extended beyond the condition of goods in storage.

During a separate physical inspection at Warehouse 2 on September 4, 2026, auditors found 15 unopened containers and other items that had not been valued or entered into ODPEM’s records.

The audit also identified approximately $780 million in shipments that were absent from the donation schedules supplied by the agency. The value was based on the cost, insurance and freight figures that auditors could identify from the documents provided.

The auditor general said the discrepancies showed that ODPEM’s schedules did not provide a complete account of the donations received, limiting its ability to demonstrate that all shipments had been properly identified, recorded and valued.

The report recommended that ODPEM reconcile its customs clearance records against its donation schedules, identify and record the omitted shipments, and open, value and enter the 15 containers and other unrecorded items into its inventory.

The findings are particularly significant because similar problems had been raised in the Auditor General’s 2024 performance audit of ODPEM.

That earlier audit identified poor stock rotation, limited storage space and staff shortages, as well as unsuitable storage conditions that exposed relief supplies to mould, excessive humidity, water damage and pests. It also found that obsolete and damaged items were being stored alongside regular relief supplies.

ODPEM had informed the Auditor General in April 2024 that estimated losses of relief items amounted to $3.9 million.

In its response to the latest findings, ODPEM acknowledged the need to strengthen its procedures for receiving, issuing, counting and tracking stock, as well as managing expiry dates. The agency said the unprecedented scale and pace of the hurricane response had placed extraordinary pressure on its existing administrative systems.

It told auditors that it had begun improving warehouse records, revising receipt and issuing forms, updating inventory registers and introducing more regular inspections and stock checks.

In its September 2026 response, ODPEM also acknowledged that some of the weaknesses arose from gaps in staff knowledge and understanding of the requirements governing the management of public resources. It said it would provide targeted training, update procedures and strengthen supervisory checks.

The agency further said it had introduced periodic stock checks and the practice of distributing older supplies before newer ones.

The auditor general recommended that ODPEM establish stronger controls for monitoring the condition and expiry dates of relief supplies, carry out regular physical stock counts and ensure that every donation is supported by records showing what was received, stored and distributed.

Under the agreed targets, ODPEM was to have expiry procedures and a register in place by December 31, 2026, while the assessment of infested stock was due by November 30, 2026. The agency also committed to completing the reconciliation of shipments and recording the unopened containers by December 31, 2026.

The auditor general acknowledged the exceptional conditions under which ODPEM operated following the Category 5 hurricane, which struck Jamaica on October 28, 2025, but said the scale of the response made proper controls over donated resources even more important.

World.title: Reggae Boyz edged by Mexico in Nations League quarter-final
World.content:
Jamaica's defender #02 Miguel Freckleton reacts at the end of the Concacaf Nations League quarter-final second leg football match between Mexico and Jamaica at the BBVA stadium in Guadalupe, Nuevo Leon state, Mexico on November 17, 2026. (Photo: AFP)

Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz were edged by Mexico on away goals after losing 1-0 to El Tri in the quarterfinal return leg at the BBVA stadium in Monterey, Mexico on Tuesday.

A first half goal from Jesus Corona was the difference on the night, levelling the scores at 3-3 on aggregate, but the Mexicans won based on the two away goals they scored in Saturday’s first leg 3-2 loss.

Jamaica, ranked 66th in the world, spectacularly led the first leg tie 3-0 before Mexico rallied late at the National Stadium in Kingston to reduce the deficit.

In addition to being eliminated from the Concacaf Nations League, Jamaica will now have to attempt to qualify for the Gold Cup though the play-offs.

Tuesday’s win was the first for Mexico’s newly appointed coach Rafa Marquez in six games.

Jamaica had several chances in a frenetic first half, the best in the 25th minute when they caught Mexico on a break with goalkeeper Raul Rangel caught outside the 18-yard box. But, despite getting past the defender, Renaldo Cephas tripped up and was overtaken by a fast recovering defender.

At the other end, Jamaica managed to keep out Mexico which had made several changes to the team that started in Kingston. Goalkeeper Jahmali Waite made a brilliant save in the 13th minute, parrying a header from Roberto Alvarado for a corner.

However, the Boyz had no answer for a well struck left footer from Corona, starting for El Tri for the first time since 2022, from just on the edge of the 18-yard box into the low left hand corner of Waite’s goal in the 35th minute.

The second half failed to rise to the intensity of the first 45 minutes and, despite throwing a number of attacking players into the fray, Jamaica failed to get the goal that would have seen them create one of the biggest upsets in Concacaf football.

-Paul A Reid

World.title: SICK!
World.content:
.

DELAYED admission and treatment, late diagnosis, a lack of treatment, long waiting lists, and discourteous staff are among the 1,045 cases of patient complaints registered at hospitals across Jamaica’s four regional health authorities (RHAs) since July this year.

Just over 10 per cent of the complaints have been cleared up.

These are among the findings of a troubling review of Jamaica’s public health-care sector which was made public on Tuesday by Health and Wellness Minister Dr Christopher Tufton following a statement in the House of Representatives.

The conclusions are contained in a 50-page Ministry of Health and Wellness report, titled ‘Institutional Performance Review’.

Vowing to be open and transparent, Tufton ordered the review earlier this year. The minister had, during his contribution to the 2026/27 Sectoral Debate on May 12, committed to holding public health institutions to clear standards of governance, financial accountability and performance. He committed to report transparently, on progress and ensure that accountability is reflected in the experience of patients.

On June 19, the health ministry implemented the Accountability Framework (MAF) Scorecard, which rates 13 entities against 18 governance and accountability indicators, and the Client Care Connect (CCC), which managed 1,045 client feedback cases across the four RHAs within the first quarter of the current financial year.

Together, the two instruments answer two questions: Are the institutions well-run, and are they serving people well?

The review found that, in terms of access to service, patients typically complained about waiting lists, delayed admission and treatment, limited service availability, inadequate resources, limited service availability, difficulty obtaining appointments and specialist care.

Worryingly, in terms of quality of clinical care, patients complained about delayed diagnosis and treatment, patient management and clinical decision-making, as well as poor management of deteriorating and high-risk patients.

In terms of communication, patients were dissatisfied with inadequate explanations, poor information sharing, delayed responses to enquiries, and inappropriate verbal or non-verbal communication.

Unprofessional behaviour, poor customer service and lack of responsiveness also irked patients. Additionally, they were ticked off by what they perceived to be a lack of courtesy, disrespectful treatment, along with inadequate privacy considerations for them and their families.

According to the review, access to services was the leading category of complaints in every RHA, while quality of clinical care ranked second.

“Communication, professional conduct, and rights, respect and dignity were the other principal themes. Together, access, quality of care, professional conduct and rights, respect and dignity make up about 77 per cent of complaint references nationally,” the review stated.

It also noted that complaints, which make up the bulk of client feedback, are concentrated in a small number of hospitals. Five hospitals, roughly one-fifth of the public hospital network, generate 52.2 per cent of all cases; the top eight generate 64.1 per cent; and the top ten 69.1 per cent. It highlighted that Cornwall Regional Hospital and Kingston Public Hospital — being referral hospitals — naturally had most cases because they saw most patients.

In terms of service points, the accident and emergency departments, outpatient clinics, medical wards, surgical services and maternity services were the most frequently mentioned areas in all four RHAs for client complaints. “These are the highest-volume, highest-contact areas,” the review explained.

“Their recurrence across every region indicates that the issues are systemic, not isolated to individual facilities, and that improvements in patient flow, communication and responsiveness in these areas will have the greatest effect on client experience nationally,” it added.

The review also addressed why only 10.6 per cent or 111 of the 1,045 cases were closed during the quarter, pointing to explanations provided in reports at the regional level. Factors included: Delays in receiving investigation reports and responses from service areas; difficulty obtaining complete documentation and supporting records; high active caseloads and increasing demand for complaint management services; delays in implementing and verifying corrective actions; resource constraints affecting investigation and follow-up; and cases requiring multidisciplinary review before resolution.

“Delayed closure limits the ability to identify quality problems, conduct root-cause analysis, implement corrective action and prevent repeat complaints,” the report said.

It explained that closure performance is therefore treated in the report as a measure of management responsiveness, not merely of caseload.

The report also identified recurring quality problems that suggest systemic rather than individual causes. They include: Barriers to timely access; communication, engagement and navigation challenges; weaknesses in assessment, escalation and management of high-risk patients; deficiencies in clinical documentation and records; weak compliance with clinical and administrative standards; gaps in care coordination; inconsistent investigation and case management; weak monitoring of corrective actions; workforce capacity and oversight constraints; as well as data quality and reporting deficiencies.

According to the report, improvement initiatives were already under way. These include a structured review to strengthen investigation quality and organisational learning in addition to a review of complaints to strengthen patient safety and clinical governance.

Meanwhile, the health and wellness ministry has already piloted a family care presence programme in two hospitals to improve communication, family engagement and patient experience. It also has in place mental health consent and restraint reviews — a new policy guidance on patient rights, governance and accountability. The ministry also recently launched a channel for clients to submit feedback directly to RHAs.

World.title: Listed companies, foreign subsidiaries dominate Business Leader Award nominees
World.content:
Long-serving Observer Business Leader Selection Committee member Gassan Azan (right) shares a light moment with his best friend Gordon “Butch” Stewart at the Jamaica Observer Business Leader luncheon in 2012. The award programme has been renamed in Stewart’s honour and is set for December 13, 2026 at AC Hotel Kingston.

Publicly listed Jamaican companies and locally managed subsidiaries of overseas firms dominate the nomination list for the Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award that is currently under consideration.

There are 10 corporate nominees for the award which is seeking to identify and highlight the companies operating on Jamaican soil that provide the most wholesome and progressive environment for their workforce. Specifically, the theme of the award is ‘Business Leader: Employer of Choice’.

In an inauspicious outcome, no privately held Jamaican-owned organisation made it on the list of 10 nominees, a handful of genuine prospects for nomination having declined to participate in the programme.

The search for the list of potential nominees for this prestigious award had a disproportionately low representation among local private firms once the pool was reduced to the top 25 firms. These are the companies that had a real shot at being one of the 10 nominees. All 10 are survivors of a brutal culling process from a broad initial list of 60, then 40. They were further reduced to a group of 25. The members of this group were all considered potential nominees for the award, with 10 of them ultimately emerging as candidates to go forward.

They were selected after all 25 were asked to submit answers to a 42-question survey that was a deep dive into their industrial relations practices.

Of the 25 companies that were short-listed for the more rigorous probe, only five were privately held Jamaican enterprises. Four of the five declined to participate in the programme and so did not complete the questionnaire.

Only one publicly listed Jamaican firm declined, while three failed to meet the deadline for submitting their responses.

The questionnaires that were sent to the companies demanded significant executive time for completion under a compressed timeline. Some categories of local companies were specifically excluded from being considered for the award. Most notable is the Sandals/ATL Group which is owned by the Gordon “Butch” Stewart’s children, and whose nomination would, therefore, represent a profound conflict of interest. Companies owned by members of the Award Selection Committee were also ruled out for consideration. These are:

· Manpower and Maintenance Services Limited, owned by Audrey Hinchcliffe;

· MegaMart/Bashco Limited, owned by Gassan Azan;

· Paymaster Jamaica, owned by Ambassador Audrey Marks;

· Sterling Asset Management, owned by Charles Ross; and

· Tropical Tours Limited, owned by Fred Smith.

The other judge is Ian Neita, former managing director of Yellow (Pages) Limited.

Additionally, to qualify for consideration, companies were required to have a minimum of 300 full-time employees.

Workers at all 10 companies that have been nominated will be surveyed as part of the final evaluation process to determine the winner in December.

The Jamaica Observer will begin releasing the names of the nominees on Friday when the first of 10 stories will be published both online and in print.

The ‘Business Leader: Employer of Choice’ will be announced on Sunday, December 13, at a gala presentation and dinner at AC Hotel Kingston on Lady Musgrave Road.

The programme has been named in honour of Gordon “Butch” Stewart, the founder of the Sandals/ATL Group of which the Jamaica Observer is a subsidiary.

The first-ever Business Leader Award presentation was on December 11, 1996, two days outside of 30 years to the day when the 2026 award will be held.

The award is promoted by the Jamaica Observer whose name it carried for 30 years until the formal rebranding to the Gordon “Butch” Stewart Business Leader Award earlier this month.

World.title: Runkus’s faith rewarded with Grammy nom
World.content:
Runkus .

When Billboard named Runkus’s Supernova among its 50 Best Albums of the Year in June, the recognition offered an early indication of the heights the Portmore-born entertainer’s latest body of work could reach. Sharing the coveted list with projects from international heavyweights including Drake, Bruno Mars, Kehlani, and Jill Scott, the reggae artiste was already making an impression well beyond Jamaica’s shores.

“Straight out of Portmore, Jamaica, Runkus might have the best album from the Caribbean Diaspora this year,” the publication declared at the time.

Five months later, that early endorsement has been followed by an even bigger milestone, with Runkus earning a Grammy nomination for Best Reggae Album.

For the entertainer, however, the news was not entirely unexpected.

Having invested considerable time and effort into the project, he submitted it with confidence in what he had created, trusting that his faith would carry it the rest of the way.

“Nothing is promised in life ennuh, but I submitted knowing I had put out the best, and so I hoped for the best in return. I did the work and we know the Almighty say it’s faith and works, so we put in the work and we had the faith. It worked out,” he told the

Jamaica Observer. on Monday after the 2027 Grammy nominations were released.

While the nomination represents a first for Runkus as a solo artiste, it is not his first experience being associated with Grammy-recognised work. He has previously contributed to albums by fellow reggae artistes, but receiving the nod under his own name has brought a different level of satisfaction.

“This is my first nomination in the sense of a solo project. I have been a part of other projects before, contributed to records on Protoje and Jesse Royal’s albums in the past, but this one is my first nomination as Runkus, and it’s an overwhelming feeling of joy,” he said.

The entertainer, whose given name is Romario Bennett, added that he was particularly honoured to find himself among this year’s nominees, acknowledging the calibre of artistes and projects represented in the category.

Beyond the personal achievement, the nomination carries a much deeper significance for Runkus.

Supernova, he went on to say, was not created in isolation, but brought together contributions from several people he considers family, including his late father, veteran entertainer Determine, whose musical influence remains an important part of his journey.

“This is not just my first nomination, it’s also my dad’s as well. He is on the project. Also on the project is my uncle who is incarcerated, my 20-year-old brother, my bredren dem who I consider brothers, and so this project and the nomination is extra special. I earned this alongside family,” he said.

The opportunity to celebrate his father through the nomination is particularly poignant for Runkus, who believes Determine’s contribution to music cannot and will not be limited by accolades. He shared that, although his father’s name may not have been attached to the kind of international recognition now being afforded to

Supernova, he holds his musical accomplishments to the highest regard.

“My dad did exactly what the Almighty willed him to do. Even though there is no accolade attached to my dad’s name, he became one of the greatest artistes I have ever seen,” he said.

It is a sentiment that speaks to the broader meaning of legacy for Runkus, as it also provides an opportunity to acknowledge the people, experiences, and musical foundations that have helped shape him.

He was also keen to address some of the misconceptions surrounding the Grammy selection process, noting that the recognition is not simply a reflection of an artiste’s commercial popularity or record sales.

Runkus urged critics to pay greater attention to what the latest nominations represent for Jamaica’s music industry, instead of becoming caught up in debates about which artiste is more deserving or how many times an individual has been nominated.

“The Grammys is something people don’t understand. It’s peer-based and it’s not as easy as some would have it. It’s not about popularity; it’s not about sales,” he explained. “I believe people want to see people win and, ideally, new people. But what I would say is to pay close attention to this year’s nominees, because they’re all Jamaicans, and that in itself speaks volumes.

“So we can talk about who and how many times someone is nominated, or we can choose to focus on the fact that Jamaica is up,” he continued. “It’s Jamaica all the way, so more honour to all the nominees. I’m excited to keep making music, and I’m sure all the nominees feel that way.”

For Runkus, the nomination is also motivation to continue exploring his creativity. He said his approach to music remains rooted in consistently finding inspiration in the world around him and transforming his experiences into songs.

“If anyone knows me, it’s always work for me… So there’s definitely more work to be done. I’m a youth from Portmore, Jamaica, and we a do it big,” he declared.

Runkus is among six Jamaican artistes nominated in the Best Reggae Album category for the 69th annual Grammy Awards. Joining him are Buju Banton for Too Too Bad, Chronixx for Exile, Ziggy Marley for Brightside, Protoje for The Art of Acceptance, and Shaggy for Lottery.

The nominations represent another significant showing for Jamaica’s reggae fraternity, bringing together established Grammy winners, previous nominees, and a new generation of musical voices.

The winners will be announced on February 7, 2027.

World.title: SYGNUS COURTS LENDERS TO HIT US$1-BILLION TARGET
World.content:
(Photo: Dacx Productions)

SYGNUS Credit Investments Limited (SCI) expects to announce a second multilateral financing partnership within weeks and is in talks with two other development lenders, as it looks to secure a larger bank credit line to fund private-credit deals across the Caribbean.

Jason Morris, co-founder and chief investment officer of Sygnus Capital, told investors and analysts on SCI’s November 16 earnings call that the forthcoming partner would finance SCI directly. The company is still working towards term sheets with the two other institutions. Morris did not name the incoming lender or disclose the size and terms of the facility.

“We’ve cracked the glass ceiling, so to speak, by getting a partnership with IBD Invest, and as you’ll see, in hopefully days or weeks’ time, we have a second multilateral financing partner that will finance SCI directly,” Morris said.

SCI’s first multilateral partnership dates to June, when it agreed to guarantee an uncommitted revolving working capital facility of up to US$10 million from IDB Invest for Sygnus Investment Bahamas. SCI is also an anchor investor in the Bahamas vehicle, which provides financing against businesses’ receivables.

Morris said backing from several development lenders would expand the pool of capital SCI can invest and strengthen its case when it approaches banks.

“Once we have two, three, four multilaterals, which will increase SCI’s ability, our pool of capital, it will also increase SCI’s ability to perhaps, soon enough, get access to a credit line from a bank that wants to do business in the Caribbean,” Morris explained during the question and answer segment.

SCI wants to build up US$100 million in capital available for investment, preferably with a large share in revolving credit lines. That would give it room to draw funds as deals close and borrow again as it repays the lines. At September 30, the company held US$11.16 million in cash and short-term instruments available for investment, with about US$2.45 million in undrawn revolving credit lines. It received the equivalent of US$13 million from its Class J and Class K perpetual preference-share offer during the quarter and said it expected the remaining proceeds after quarter-end.

The continuous drive for funding comes as SCI aims to lift cumulative private-credit deployment across its platform to US$1 billion by June 2030. Morris said SCI and its Puerto Rico business, Acrecent Financial, had deployed more than US$683 million to date and that he would like to reach the target about a year early. He said the platform would need to originate and deploy at least US$100 million annually. At the time of the call, he put the platform’s portfolio at about US$332 million.

SCI financed US$4.11 million in new investment commitments in the September quarter, roughly in line with US$4.10 million a year earlier. Meanwhile, Acrecent deployed US$26.44 million over the same period, including deals originated in the previous quarter.

Morris noted that several SCI transactions had reached final documentation, with deployment likely to pick up later in the financial year.

Net profit attributable to SCI shareholders rose 14 per cent to US$3.62 million for the quarter, helped by higher net interest income, lower fair-value losses and stronger foreign exchange gains. Total investment income of the firm slipped 1.1 per cent to US$5.19 million, while net investment income fell 9.7 per cent as operating expenses rose.

World.title: PRO PUSH
World.content:
Shikiri Douglas (left) of Arnett Gardens FC tries to take a shot as Nickela Thomas of Los Perfectos FC closes in during the Jamaica Women’s Premier League (JWPL) first-leg semi-final match at JFF/Captain Horace Burrell Centre of Excellence on May 16, 2026. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WHILE the Jamaica Women’s Premier League (JWPL) is still in its early stages, Professional Women’s Football Jamaica Limited (PWFJL) Chairperson Christina Hudson believes it is making encouraging progress towards its goal of paying players in future seasons.



Prior to 2025, the women’s top flight was managed solely by the Jamaica Football Federation. However, that model changed with the establishment of the PWFJL, which is responsible for the league’s development, management and commercialisation.

The JWPL has secured record sponsorship over the past two seasons and has attracted further financial support ahead of the upcoming campaign including a US$100,000 ($15 million) grant from FIFA’s Women’s League Development Programme.

The PWFJL played a key role in developing the JFF’s five-year Women’s Football Strategic Plan, launched in June, which identified a fully professional league and player salaries as major objectives.

Hudson told the Jamaica Observer there’s still a long way to go, but that she believes the goal is within reach.

“I think that we are closer because the more costs that we are able to take on from the clubs, it frees them up to be able to put more towards their player development side of their business and that can include professional contracts,” she said.

“I think we’re not quite there yet. We’re still an amateur league; it will take baby steps. But each year that we are able to give back more to the clubs and help them be more financially stable, the closer it brings us to being able to have a league that is truly professional.”

The 12-team JWPL is set for its earliest start yet when the 2026/2027 season gets under way on December 5, with Hudson hoping to make that the norm in future years.

“December to May is supposed to be the correct time for the league,” she said. “Last year, we started late only because of Hurricane Melissa, so we had some delays on that front and the season was actually cut short from a six-month calendar to only three months and was pushed to the new year just because the clubs may not have been fully ready to go, especially the ones that were located in Montego Bay. So we’re actually reverting to the original planned calendar that begins in December and runs through to May for a full six months.”

JFF President Michael Ricketts told the

Observer this month that Hudson and her team at the PWFJL have been doing “extremely well” and have done “an excellent job in marketing and commercialising the premiership”.

While the PWFJL has overseen growth in financial support, attendance and viewership, Hudson says the organisation is focused on further development.

“[Planning] becomes easier in the sense that we know what to expect and we know there are certain things that have to get done off of our checklist that don’t change season to season,” she said. “However, we’re not trying to maintain the status quo. We’re trying to improve the product that we’re putting out year after year, so there is a bit of pressure on us to deliver more each season, more for our clubs, as well as more for the fans that we’re hoping to engage throughout the season.”

When the season kicks off in a few weeks, the Reggae Girlz could have already secured their place at a third-straight FIFA Women’s World Cup, once they beat Costa Rica in the Concacaf W Championship quarter-finals in Texas next week Friday.

Hudson believes that would provide a major boost to the JWPL’s success this season.

“I cannot wait for that to happen. I’m immensely proud of our Reggae Girlz and all that they have accomplished and I think for young players, seeing a pathway forward for themselves and seeing themselves in this Jamaican team will be very powerful in getting young girls interested in playing,” she said. “But I think it will also motivate our existing players to [realise] this is a level that they can truly reach if they keep working hard and getting seen by the right people.”

The 2026/27 season will have more on the line as the champions will be able to compete in next year’s Concacaf Champions Cup following all 12 clubs completing mandatory club licencing.

World.title: Fired up!
World.content:
There are more than 1,500 Church’s Texas Chicken locations in over 20 countries.

CHURCH’S Texas Chicken says it remains on track to open 10 restaurants in Jamaica in five years after its first two Kingston locations beat sales projections.

This was the update provided by Anthony Sabga-Aboud, director at Global Brands Limited, during the official opening of its second location at Parade Square, in downtown Kingston. Global Brands Group of Companies is the franchise holder for the Church’s brand in Trinidad & Tobago, St Lucia, St Kitts and Jamaica.

“So, we are on track to hit our goal of 10 locations in five years. This is our second location, and we are actively looking at other sites,” Sabga-Aboud explained on Monday.

The new downtown location saw the company invest more than US$1 million to transform the property at the corner of King Street and South Parade. The company then hired 70 new employees, while creating a space that meets the Church’s brand and improves disability access.

With the company securing two locations in under two years, the Trinidadian businessman noted that his team is in active discussion with several property owners about opening new stores next year.

“We’re very excited about this [Parade] location and we think it’s going to be an iconic location for us,” he said.

The Church’s brand returned to Jamaica in December 2025, nearly two decades after it last operated on the island. Global Brands made a similar investment in its first Jamaican location, at Mall Plaza on Constant Spring Road, where it hired 60 employees.

The re-entry to the Jamaican market broke several global records according to Watson George, the Global Brands executive responsible for the Church’s Texas Chicken brand. That Mall Plaza store broke metrics such as customer count, transaction count and even sales for the first-day opening of a new Church’s location. There are more than 1,500 Church’s locations in over 20 countries.

“In fact, that [Mall Plaza] opening in that market was the best opening globally,” George added.

The Parade Square location also broke a regional record as it’s now the largest Church’s restaurant in Latin America and the Caribbean. The available space on the property also gives the team more room to expand the operations as it adjusts to the downtown environment.

Although the company intends to expand across the island, focus will be placed on Kingston and St Andrew; Portmore and Spanish Town, St Catherine. Deandra Jones is the country manager for Church’s in Jamaica while Dane Swaby is the restaurant general manager for Mall Plaza location.

“We are proud to be part of downtown Kingston, proud to be creating jobs for Jamaicans and proud to bring that great taste. This is only the beginning of our Jamaican journey, and we think that the future is extremely bright,” George added in his remarks.

Aside from the new jobs created, George also pointed to the various suppliers and contractors who are benefiting from the continued expansion of the brand in Jamaica. Jamaica Broilers Group Limited, Wisynco Group Limited and Massy Gas Products Limited all supply each Church’s brand with various inputs needed to serve their customers. Massy Gas Products is a subsidiary of Trinidadian conglomerate Massy Holdings Limited.

The success of Church’s in Jamaica continues to reinforce Global Brands’ confidence in the Jamaican economy which was significantly impacted by Hurricane Melissa in October 2025. The positive reception from customers and speed to launch the second Church’s location reinforces the demand from the Jamaican public for different quick-service brands.

Global Brands currently operates several food brands such as Pizza Boys, Wok ‘n Roll, Rituals Sushi and Rituals Coffee House across the Caribbean. Rituals Coffee House operates at Village Plaza, adjacent to Mall Plaza.

“It’s been very, very positive. It’s a great country. A great economy. You know, we want to keep growing and keep being part of the community,” Sabga-Aboud reiterated.

Church’s Texas Chicken is currently owned by private equity firm High Bluff Capital, with the brand receiving an injection of capital by Golub Capital in July 2026. The company signed an agreement in April 2026 to open 600 or more restaurants in China over several years. Church’s Texas Chicken was founded in April 1952 by George W Church Sr.

World.title: Die Koalition der Wartenden: Europa blickt nach Shenzhen
World.content:
Share on LinkedIn

Share on WhatsApp

Share on X

Donald Trump, Xi Jinping und Wladimir Putin verhandeln in Shenzhen womöglich über die neue Weltordnung – und Europa guckt zu. Eine „Koalition der Willigen“ aus Dutzenden Staats- und Regierungschefs sucht gleichzeitig in Berlin nach einer Antwort auf die drohende Verschiebung und plant ein weiteres finanzielles Signal an Moskau, damit Putin den Ukraine-Krieg beendet. Darüber spricht Rixa Fürsen mit Hans von der Burchard.

Im 200-Sekunden-Interview warnt der CDU-Außenexperte Roderich Kiesewetter erneut vor den Folgen eines schnellen, von Washington diktierten Friedens. Er fordert, aus den Willigen nun Entschlossene zu machen.

Innenpolitisch liefert die schwarz-rote Koalition derweil ein seltsames Schauspiel ab. Nach einem achtstündigen Verhandlungsmarathon verkündet der Kanzler zwar eine Stromsteuersenkung, doch die Entlastung entpuppt sich als Tropfen auf den heißen Stein. Wie Merz nachts angeblich wutentbrannt den Raum verließ, was an dieser Erzählung dran ist und wieso das mühsam geschnürte Finanzpaket schon im nächsten Jahr wieder kollabieren könnte, erklärt Rasmus Buchsteiner.

Das Berlin Playbook als Podcast gibt es jeden Morgen ab 5 Uhr. Rixa Fürsen, Maximilian Stascheit und das POLITICO-Team liefern Politik zum Hören – kompakt, international, hintergründig.

World.title: EU lawmakers accuse Chinese officials of intimidation over Taiwan
World.content:
Taiwan has been politically separate from China since 1949, but Beijing views the island, home to 23 million people, as part of its territory and has long criticized Western governments for maintaining relations with Taipei — although the EU and its member countries do not recognize Taiwan as a separate country.

But MEPs allege they have faced more than just criticism for taking a pro-Taiwanese independence stance.

“I have never encountered such behavior from foreign diplomats,” said Engin Eroglu, a German liberal MEP who chairs the Parliament’s delegation to China. Eroglu said he had received “fierce” pushback from Beijing, without specifying what that entailed, and that he was troubled by Chinese officials’ actions toward other members of Parliament.

The Chinese mission to the EU did not reply to requests for comment for this article.

Markéta Gregorová, vice-chair of the China delegation — which manages relations between the European Parliament and China’s National People’s Congress — said she would ask Parliament President Roberta Metsola to bar Chinese officials from Parliament if Beijing doesn’t explain why she was stopped at the border during a recent visit.

Metsola, who helped broker the deal to lift sanctions and restart diplomatic engagements with China, has been in close contact with the MEPs concerned and “has conveyed our questions and concerns directly to the Chinese authorities,” her spokesperson, Juri Laas, said. “Diplomatic contacts are ongoing in an effort to ensure that further incidents can be avoided.”

World.title: Germany presses to make Ukraine aid Le Pen-proof
World.content:
Whereas passing the bloc’s next long-term budget — and the headroom plan Germany wants to attach to it — would require unanimous support among EU member countries, future decisions to raise money for Ukraine under the scheme would require only a qualified majority if Germany gets its way. That would make it harder for any single government to block EU support, according to an EU diplomat with knowledge of the discussions.

“In today’s geopolitical world, this [need for unanimity] doesn’t make sense,” the diplomat said.

The German proposal is likely to run into opposition from countries such as Hungary, Czechia and Slovakia — which have demanded opt-outs for Ukraine aid — and further complicate already tough negotiations over Europe’s seven-year budget ahead of a special EU summit set for Nov. 26-27.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and President of Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy attend a press conference at the Chancellery on November 3, 2026 in Berlin. | Pool photo by Filip Singer/Getty Images

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, however, is attempting to get his way on Ukraine aid by using the immense leverage his country derives from being the biggest contributor by far to the EU’s €2 trillion budget.

In a letter sent to European Council President António Costa earlier this month, Merz issued an ultimatum that made German support for the next budget contingent on the bloc’s agreeing to raise a further €45 billion for Ukraine for 2027, as well as a “financing perspective for Ukraine from 2028 onwards.”

In doing so, Merz was also implicitly threatening to cut German contributions to regional development funds that benefit Central European sceptics of Ukraine aid, should those countries attempt to block the headroom plan or opt out of aid for Kyiv.

World.title: How Burnham tapped the brakes on his big Brexit reset
World.content:
POLITICO spoke to more than 30 politicians, officials and campaigners in the U.K. and Brussels to ask the question: What is Andy Burnham’s grand strategy on Europe?

Andy Burnham stood up two months ago and promised a new national conversation on Brexit. The challenges were dawning on him before he even opened his mouth.

Britain’s prime minister — who heads to a long-awaited EU-U.K. summit Friday — has spent much of this week trying to calm a conversation about closer European ties that he started. He told his Labour Party in September that he would begin a public debate on long-term “options” for Britain’s future relationship with the EU around the time of the summit.





The PM and his aides now suggest he will do this in mid-December — if there are viable options at all — in comments widely interpreted as slowing his pace amid hesitation from members of his own Cabinet.

But it’s not the first time Burnham has had to temper his idealism on Europe. His September conference speech originally intended to go even further in his language on Europe, four people familiar with the discussions in Liverpool told POLITICO.

“There were various iterations [of the speech] knocking around with different language, some of which was stronger than what he delivered,” said one U.K. government official, granted anonymity like others quoted in this piece to speak frankly.

A person who speaks to No. 10 regularly added: “There was a very active debate about how far they should go. If you look back at the speech, the buildup to the Europe bit of it was quite a lot more emphatic than the dividend. A lot of us were sitting there thinking ‘and?’ … ‘and?’ … ‘and?’ … ‘oh.’”

Burnham’s allies insist the substance of his pitch has been consistent: that he will start a conversation on the future that could lead to him making a pitch to British voters in the next general election, due by 2029 — and it might go as far as pledging to rejoin the EU.

They argue that he has opened a conversation that no one before him dared to. “It has to be open-ended to work,” said a former Cabinet minister. “I am leading on Europe,” Burnham told MPs on Wednesday.





But the sight of the new prime minister adjusting his language in real time has led to suspicions among MPs and ministers that either he is watering down his ambition, figuring out his own position in real time — or both.

POLITICO spoke to more than 30 politicians, officials and campaigners in the U.K. and Brussels to ask the question: What is Burnham’s grand Brexit strategy?

Several of them responded by asking back: Does he have one at all?

Options by Christmas

Burnham’s first priority is to get through Friday’s summit, where he hopes to secure long-wrangled deals on food standards, carbon emissions trading and youth mobility, and work toward an assurance that Britain’s industries will not be cut off by Brussels’ Made in Europe scheme.

The trickier question is what happens after that. Burnham said on Tuesday that once he takes stock of the summit, he will “consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU” long-term.

The prime minister now intends to present these around the time of his largely domestic “10-year plan” — which is being lined up for publication on Dec. 17, two officials with knowledge of the conversation told POLITICO. It remains a movable feast and his team has not yet decided whether to present Europe options on the same day, or slightly earlier.

Burnham says he has not settled for or against any path, including rejoin, but in practice caution is the dominant theme. He said Tuesday that there is “no rush” and his team sought to stress that he will only press ahead if there is a domestic advantage.

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham arrives to address a press conference with the German chancellor in Berlin on Oct. 8, 2026. | Tobias Schwarz/AFP via Getty Images

A No. 10 official said: “The thing that’s most important to him is, how can our long-term relationship with the European Union help us with his domestic priorities? Whether that’s the cost of living, reindustrialization or growth in every postcode. He thinks that the best way to do that is in the context of the 10-year plan.” A second U.K. government official added: “It’s about showing something that’s tangible.”

The No. 10 official quoted earlier argued that this shift in position actually happened several weeks ago. Burnham wrote to his Cabinet on Oct. 28 saying merely that he would set out “next steps” on Britain’s EU relationship (rather than full-blown options) around the time of this week’s summit.

Burnham could speak about those “next steps” as soon as next week — “clearly there is an impetus for Andy to say more on this soon,” said the second U.K. government official quoted above — but even for those deep in Whitehall, the way ahead is unclear.





When Burnham does lay out options, officials suggest these may not go into granular detail — despite Westminster and the EU broadly knowing what is at stake after years of painful debate.

One minister in Burnham’s government said they expected him to focus in the near term on making “a pragmatic case” focused on GDP growth, which had a chance of appealing to more skeptical MPs and voters, rather than options per se.

“We’re still trying to get to a point where we know which options that we want to put forward to the British public,” said the second U.K. government official, arguing that whatever deal Burnham secures on Friday will give him the “right to be heard” on the future relationship.

“The big focus from everyone is just to get through the summit,” the official added. “All the questions of where you go after that haven’t fully been answered because we’re not yet there.”

The wrangling is “slightly painful” to watch, said Anand Menon, director of the U.K. in a Changing Europe think tank. “I think with every passing day, I become more skeptical about whether there’s a strategy.”

‘He’s always wanted to rejoin’

Some of this is down to Burnham’s personality. The new prime minister speaks his mind and talks off the cuff far more than his predecessor Keir Starmer.

This was his appeal to many Labour MPs, who see it as old-style leadership, but frustrates some officials who watch policies spring from Burnham’s turns of phrase. “The strategy will be whatever the PM decides when he wakes up in the morning,” grumbled one Labour official in government.





A U.K. official working on the upcoming reset summit said Burnham “makes it up as the questions come to him.” “If you can work out what his plan is, please let me know,” said one anti-rejoin Labour MP: “No one can work out if there’s some 4D chess or they’re just feeling as they go.”

Burnham played down his europhile tendencies in the June election for his seat of Makerfield, which backed Leave in the 2016 referendum. A week before becoming prime minister, he told Labour MPs it was not the time to re-run the Brexit vote.

He has never hidden his views though. Burnham co-authored an “epilogue to our grandchildren” in his 2024 book “Head North,” which expressed “hope that your generation will take us back into the EU.”

Like so many things for Burnham, there is a gut feeling. He has privately lamented the plight of musicians who find it harder to go on tour. “He’s got a Dutch wife whose surname is France,” said one campaigner who speaks regularly to the government. One person who has known him a long time added: “He’s always wanted to rejoin in his lifetime.”

The problem is many members of his Cabinet feel differently.

Burnham gives his first speech in front of No. 10 on July 20, 2026, after being asked by the king to form the next government. | Oli Scarff/AFP via Getty Images

Unlike Burnham, who spent the last decade as mayor of Greater Manchester, most of them bear the scars of Westminster’s Brexit wars.

Burnham held a meeting of his political Cabinet last Tuesday. His aides insist there was not a row, but some of his most powerful Cabinet ministers either have seats that backed Brexit, represent briefs that would be complicated by rejoin chatter or both — and many of their views are already on record.

Those appear to include Chancellor John Healey, Burnham’s top finance minister. Healey said last month that “we had a referendum, we’re out of the EU” and his role was to make the best of the economy.

They also include Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood and Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy, who one ally said previously had a “particular bugbear” about the Erasmus+ student exchange scheme, feeling that it helps few students in her working-class Wigan constituency. (An aide pointed to recent interviews in which Nandy backed the U.K.’s plan to rejoin Erasmus).





Housing Secretary Angela Rayner — a powerful ally of Burnham on the party’s “soft left” — voiced doubts about a second EU referendum when Starmer backed one in 2019, while Health Secretary Yvette Cooper, who represents a Leave-backing Yorkshire seat, argued in July this year that Europe’s future was about Ukraine, Norway and Turkey, not just the EU.

Business and Trade Secretary Jonathan Reynolds insisted last month that he agreed with the PM after telling POLITICO that re-litigating Brexit battles would cause “uncertainty” for business. Any push to rejoin the EU’s customs union would scupper trade deals, some of which Reynolds personally negotiated.

His business department is still quietly going about negotiating new trade deals which would be incompatible with rejoining a customs union with the EU. One official pointed out that talks with Turkey are ongoing while initial forays about another trade deal are due to start in the coming weeks.

Burnham holds his first Cabinet meeting at Downing Street on July 21, 2026. | Pool photo by Eddie Mulholland via Getty Images

One person who speaks regularly to the Cabinet said: “When they were the shadow Cabinet they could finish each other’s sentences. Now they see themselves as shop stewards for their departments.”

Menon added: “I get the sense that there are some members of the Cabinet who really do not want to reopen this debate. That’s the fight that will be going on at the moment — and I don’t know how Burnham plays that, to be honest. We’ve not got much experience of seeing Burnham see off disagreement within his own Cabinet.”

The first U.K. government official quoted in this piece predicted there would be points in the coming weeks where Burnham “temperature-checks the Cabinet” and “crowd-sources” from fellow ministers. “It’s not a ‘my way or the highway’ approach,” they said. Burnham told reporters last week: “We’ll take a decision as a Cabinet on what, if anything, comes next.”





A senior Labour official predicted that Cabinet ministers would fall in line as they do not want to upset Burnham’s momentum, since Labour is six points ahead of Nigel Farage’s right-wing Reform UK in POLITICO’s Poll of Polls. “People know we have just had a chance to do the most incredible mid-air refuelling job,” the official said.

That doesn’t guarantee that Burnham’s ministers know his mind. One Cabinet minister laughed when asked if they knew the Europe strategy: “They don’t tell me anything!”

EU says: tell us when you’re ready

All this hard thinking sets up a culture clash with the EU, where officials’ view of Britain is “when you’ve got an ask, come and ask,” said Menon.

One EU diplomat told POLITICO: “On the next steps, it should be about the U.K. first assessing its options and then engaging with the EU, rather than the other way around.”

Burnham met European leaders at the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week. The No. 10 official quoted above suggested the PM has told his counterparts he needs to get a good deal at the summit because if not, it will be harder to win over the British public in future talks.

Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen in Dublin on Nov. 12, 2026. | Pool photo by Stefan Rousseau via Getty Images

It is a message reminiscent of David Cameron, Theresa May and Boris Johnson before him. Like his predecessors, Burnham is trying to win better treatment from a technocratic Brussels machine — a tough job for Hamish Falconer, the ex-diplomat who once negotiated with the Taliban and is now European relations minister.

One person who was in a recent meeting with Falconer said: “I sat in a meeting with Hamish where he was saying, I’m pretty sure with geopolitics and my negotiating prowess, the EU will give us a special deal on the single market.” (A U.K. official said they did not recognize this characterization.) The same person said each administration had thought they could forge a better relationship with Brussels than the one that came before, and “I’m worried that Burnham is falling into that same trap.”

An official who worked on Brexit issues under Starmer added: “Politicians always unfortunately have a strong lack of realpolitik in this space. No matter what pathway the U.K. decides to take, the EU will get what it wants.”





Personality plays a part too. When Burnham met European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen on the same day as U.S. President Donald Trump at the U.N. General Assembly, the stark difference in character did not go unnoticed. While British officials respect Von der Leyen’s precise, calm style, Trump’s approach was far more like Burnham’s — conversational, anecdotal and gliding over the hard policy details.

After Burnham’s September speech, confused officials from EU member countries tried to decode his pledge to lay out options “around” the EU-U.K. summit. Some complained privately that the PM should’ve been clearer that the summit was about technical talks that began under Starmer, and talks about the world beyond that could only begin afterwards.

Sandro Gozi, an MEP for French President Emmanuel Macron’s Renaissance party, said he agreed with Burnham that “Brexit has been a disaster,” but added: “I hope that [he] will be bolder and more specific.”

France’s President Emmanuel Macron hugs Burnham next to their wives on Sept. 3, 2026. | Ludovic Marin/AFP via Getty Images

The good news for Burnham is that it is in the EU’s geostrategic interests for new members to want to join.

An EU official said Brussels would not treat the U.K. like most candidate countries because its past membership means it is still fairly aligned with EU law, and “it is frankly just a more developed country with the rule of law, which some other candidates are not.” Another EU official said: “His willingness to be open about the different options and the trade-offs has been noticed. That hasn’t always been the case in the U.K.”

But the U.K. official working on the summit quoted above said the EU did not need another distraction while eyeing the far-right’s rise in France and Germany. “The EU are at their wits’ end with us,” they said. “Showing up and saying ‘can we once again have something else, but we’re not sure what, for nothing’ is going down like a bucket of cold sick.”

A Brentry referendum?

No. 10 officials stress that Burnham has not made up his mind and his political operation hold their cards close. Much of the work on Brexit is being done by his chief of staff James Purnell — who one long-time associate said backs rejoining the EU in private — and Political Secretary Hayden Munro.

In that vacuum, the focus among many MPs is settling on the most extreme choice in Burnham’s arsenal — reversing Brexit.

Supporters, including the former Starmer Cabinet ministers David Lammy and Peter Kyle, and the Institute for Public Policy Research think tank that is influential in Labour circles, believe rejoining is the the most viable option to secure much closer ties beyond this point.





Yet despite Burnham’s personal support for rejoining, he has said very little recently about whether he would push for it or how it would happen.

Downing Street officials have not even confirmed if they would make a second referendum a precondition of rejoining, rather than trying to do so based on an election mandate alone — which would outrage anti-EU campaigners. (The No. 10 official quoted above said: “We’re just not going there at the moment.”)

London mayor Sadiq Khan has indicated he would support rejoining based solely on an election mandate. Khan told POLITICO: “I think at the general election, we should have in our manifesto that if you vote Labour and Labour wins, we will rejoin the EU.”

Former Starmer ministers Peter Kyle and David Lammy, by contrast, both said on Wednesday that Burnham should promise a second referendum on rejoining.

Plenty of Labour MPs in “red wall” seats — Brexit-backing areas of the Midlands and northern England — don’t want to touch the debate at all. Northumberland MP David Smith said the party should “respect the democratic decision” of a decade ago, while Grimsby MP Melanie Onn declared: “I don’t think we should be having another referendum.”

A photo provided by campaign group Led By Donkeys, showing their action at a field in Castle Eaton on June 23, 2026. | Led By Donkeys via Getty Images

And that’s if Burnham even wants to follow through. The senior Labour official quoted earlier in this story predicted the PM’s enthusiasm for rejoining could wane if Marine Le Pen won the French presidency and pulled the bloc’s axis of power toward the far right. “In private Andy is incredibly passionate but there’s no cunning plan — he is pragmatic,” they said.

Other MPs and think tanks are putting forward alternative options between membership and the status quo, such as a “Swiss-style” deal that has free movement of people — anathema to some Labour MPs — but not membership of the customs union.

Alain Berset, former Swiss president and current secretary general of the Council of Europe said: “Switzerland’s experience shows that you can have a close and constructive relationship … what matters is dialogue, cooperation and finding practical solutions.”

But the rejoin argument has the most cut-through. Of 2,000 Brits polled by the Labour-friendly Good Growth Foundation think tank, 44% said they believed Labour wants to rejoin the EU. Only 23% of them thought Labour wants a closer relationship without rejoining.





EU officials are making clear it will be “all or nothing,” argued Menon: “We’re going to face a decision, which is we either go single market and customs union membership or we stay where we are. Once you start thinking seriously about Finland, Norway or Switzerland [which all have complex deals without full membership], you realize they’re awful. So the debate very quickly becomes binary between rejoin or stay put.”

Smith disagreed: “Many people around this debate are steeped in law, but politics is also about the art of the possible. The people who tell us we can’t join the EU are often the same people who said we’d never get the deals being negotiated at the summit this week.”

Burnham’s ‘bloc efficiency’

Downing Street has been buoyed by polling that suggests the cost of living — rather than immigration — is now the main priority for many voters, and opposition to Brexit has risen. “If you look at the polling now, it has changed since 2016 and it’s changed in all parts of the U.K.,” Burnham said Wednesday.

That could in turn give Burnham a boost in the next general election — where he is fighting a five- or six-party battle and has only one large viable coalition partner: the pro-EU Liberal Democrats. Several people around Burnham said they believe he is thinking about the Europe debate in terms of electoral politics.

Steve Akehurst, the director of the research firm Persuasion UK, said “bloc efficiency” is a key consideration. “If you need to build a coalition that unites the left, but also can then bring over some soft Tory voters, you quite quickly get to Europe — especially once you assume most of the Labour to Reform vote are not coming back.”

But several people working with No. 10 told POLITICO there is nervousness inside Downing Street about polling that appears to show support for rejoining the EU.

Backing for rejoin “will all hinge on the wording,” said one person running polls. Wary Labour officials have noted that support appears to fall if voters think Britain would use the euro or pay into the EU budget. And they have discussed polling by the research organization More in Common on how support for rejoin falls when the question is about “removing limits on immigration,” rather than “freedom of movement”.

Akehurst said support for rejoin is “soft” because the idea has high sympathy but low salience. “Most people are just not thinking about this subject right now,” he said. “The basic winning argument against [it] is, ‘can we really be fucked with this?’”





Akehurst added: “The big unknown unknown is, what does it do to the other side’s bloc efficiency? It might fire up the Labour vote and the progressive vote, but does it unite the right against them in red wall seats? Do people suddenly become willing to vote Reform just to stop Labour?”

Reform is raring for a fight; Farage has already called Burnham’s Europe push the “ biggest boost in my career.” It is more difficult for the center-right Conservative Party, which opposes rejoining but sees limited political capital in devoting energy to the debate.

Robert Hayward, a polling analyst and Conservative peer, said party leader Kemi Badenoch “is keen to avoid a prolonged Brexit debate because it risks rejuvenating Reform.” Ironically, given Burnham has restarted the debate, Hayward argued the same argument applies to Labour. “Both legacy parties will adopt a policy of ‘don’t scare the children.’”

Protesters demand rejoining the EU in central London on Oct. 14, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images

The former Conservative aide Oliver Lewis rejoined frontline politics at the weekend to set up a new anti-rejoin group, “Stay Out.” Both he and the government have the same argument: that Burnham wants to tear things up. “People don’t think the status quo is good enough,” argued the No. 10 official quoted earlier. “Stay Out are the status quo campaign.” Lewis accused Burnham of “gaslighting” the British public with ever-shifting positions on Europe.

The Lib Dems have the opposite risk: not appearing europhile enough. The party currently has a “four-stage plan” that places rejoin only in step four. Senior officials believe that Burnham has allowed the conversation to run away from him and it needs careful pacing to win over the public.

But one campaigner who works with the party claimed “I think they will move” to a full-throated rejoin policy. “I think they’re realizing one can’t be half-pregnant. They’re all quite worried they are about to be leapfrogged by Labour.”

Starmer’s No. 10 discussed dropping ‘red lines’

Even senior Labour officials can’t agree over what drives Burnham the most to reopen old wounds on Brexit.

But growth is the reason for closer EU ties that Burnham talks about the most in Downing Street, the No. 10 official quoted earlier in this story argued. The PM has said this week’s deal with the EU could raise U.K. GDP by 0.4%. Last week he told Cabinet ministers that closer ties with the EU were the most impactful lever he could pull to boost growth, the same official said.

The geopolitical context has changed since 2016, too, with a protectionist U.S. and China encroaching on Europe’s turf in areas such as car manufacturing.

Starmer’s No. 10 noticed that too, despite the “red lines” — not rejoining the single market or customs union before the next election — on which he won in 2024.





Two former senior officials in Starmer’s Downing Street said that by the time he left, there were internal conversations about dropping the red lines at the next election.

One of the two ex-officials said: “It was certainly not the working assumption we would have the same red lines going into a subsequent election.” The other said that in the context of global conflict including Iran, “there was a view in No. 10 that we would need a discussion with the public about whether the red lines were still in the right place — and that this would happen pre-election, not as part of the manifesto.”

The seeds of this conversation were in 2025, when Falconer’s predecessor Nick Thomas-Symonds gave a speech pointing to closer European ties — and No. 10 strategists were surprised at the lack of outrage from opposition parties. They believed Westminster’s omerta around Brexit was coming to an end.

Starmer got personally involved and would digest negotiations in person with Thomas-Symonds at the British residence in Brussels, with a whisky in front of an open fire. (“Keir was very adept at lighting the fire,” Thomas-Symonds said.)

Keir Starmer, then-Britain’s PM, and Burnham meet with schoolchildren in Ashton-under-Lyne, on Apr. 13, 2026. | Pool photo by Paul Ellis via Getty Images

This has left a bad taste in the mouth of some former Starmer aides — who believe Burnham has simply put a shiny gloss on the direction of travel that they created, first by rebuilding the basics of the European relationship and then by pushing for “iterative” deals, each year building on the last.

The second ex-Starmer official hailed the appointment of Ben Nunn — a political aide who was once one of Starmer’s closest allies — to Burnham’s No. 10 to work on the EU relationship, arguing it showed a consistent approach across two prime ministers. There is “no change in substance” and “this is a consistency of approach in every form, except for floating rejoin post-election,” they said.

Burnham’s allies, of course, would argue that the mere mention of rejoining shows a huge difference — that Burnham is talking more favorably about the EU than Starmer ever dared.

The question will be whether he follows through on his most radical options; a prospect that plenty in his party still doubt, especially when he will also face Cabinet resistance on other bold prospects such as electoral reform.





One Labour MP compared Burnham’s big pitch to one of the first acts by former Prime Minister Tony Blair. In 1997 Blair asked the Labour grandee Roy Jenkins — a former president of the European Commission, no less — to investigate whether the voting system should be changed. It did not.

One government minister said they doubted that Burnham will even present detailed options for the U.K.-EU relationship before the next election, despite his promise to spell out the choice in December. “It would be such a distraction,” said the minister quoted earlier in this piece. “We’re Perfidious Albion — we’re neither one nor the other, not fully out, not fully in.”

“The logic is to go for membership,” said Menon, “but I think the more the practical problems of that become more apparent, the more if I were prime minister, I would get scared off.”

Menon added: “I genuinely don’t know whether he’s going to follow through.”

Additional reporting from Charlie Cooper, who interviewed Sadiq Khan, and Caroline Hug, who interviewed Alain Berset.

World.title: Inside Ukraine’s Coalition of the Wobbling
World.content:
Macron and Merz are weakened at home and Burnham is untested abroad. Can they help Ukraine — and Europe — stand up to Putin, Trump and Xi?

When Vladimir Putin posed for the cameras with U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping, it marked a rare moment of international acclaim for Russia’s ruler since he ordered the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

By contrast, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will on Thursday find himself among a motley assembly of small and medium-seized countries, convened by two weak European leaders and a rookie without a mandate.

The so-called Coalition of the Willing, an alliance of more than 35 nations supporting Kyiv, will gather in Berlin to try to work out how to help Zelenskyy steer his nation through another winter of brutal Russian bombardment and freezing temperatures.





But some diplomats and officials among Ukraine’s allies worry that this group has suffered a lack of leadership and faltering momentum in recent months, and could be consigned to irrelevance by any deal Trump concocts with Putin.

Four European government officials told POLITICO that the political authority of the coalition’s co-chairs — France, Germany and the U.K. — is crucial for Ukraine’s success but also weaker than it has been in years. “The leadership is wobbly in France and Germany,” said one European official, who like others quoted in this story was granted anonymity to speak candidly. “In the U.K., [new prime minister] Andy Burnham seems to be quite solid on Ukraine but he’s still finding his way, so we are waiting.”

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz barely clung onto his job this fall after a surge in support for far-right populists led to what he admitted was electoral “disaster” for his center-right Christian Democrats. Emmanuel Macron, the French president, is historically unpopular and faces a wipeout for his centrist allies amid a wave of support for another far-right leader, Marine Le Pen, at next year’s presidential election.

Only Burnham has a solid majority backing him in parliament — but he has generally sought to focus on domestic policy since taking over from Keir Starmer in July without winning a general election, and remains relatively untested on the world stage.

The crisis coalition

The Coalition of the Willing began life on March 2, 2025, a few days after Trump and his vice-president JD Vance unleashed a torrent of criticism at Zelenskyy in the Oval Office, for allegedly not being grateful enough to the U.S. for its support.

In the ornate surroundings of Lancaster House in London, which served as a filming location for Netflix series The Crown, Starmer told gathering of 18 leaders he would put British “boots on the ground and planes in the air” if necessary to secure any peace deal that emerged for Ukraine. Macron made similar military commitments.





In the year or so that followed, the number of countries in the grouping doubled and Merz formally came aboard as a co-chair of the format.

When Trump seemed on the brink of trying to force Ukraine to accept what Europeans regarded as a toxic peace plan a year ago, the coalition became a critical bulwark in Zelenskyy’s defenses, one EU diplomat said.

It meant Ukraine’s backers had concrete evidence to show Trump that Europeans were willing to put their own soldiers, equipment and money on the line to guarantee a peace deal. The hope was that this would mean any settlement would be fair.

The participants at the summit of the Coalition of the Willing on Jan. 6, 2026 in Paris. | Pool photo by Ludovic Marin via Getty Images

But momentum on peace talks and meetings of the coalition faded and dwindled after the U.S. and Israel launched into a war with Iran in the spring. Thursday’s gathering will be the coalition’s first leaders’ meeting since August.

It coincides with the coalition’s first military exercise, held in Poland, where thousands of troops are currently rehearsing how they would maintain any potential peace in Ukraine, despite that prospect still remaining out of reach.

Britain’s new kid

Burnham is a relative newcomer to the world stage, and was not expected to make foreign policy a central plank of his premiership in the way Starmer did.

He confounded that expectation to some extent by holding a flurry of meetings with world leaders upon gaining the keys to No. 10 and reopening a highly fractious debate on the future of the U.K.’s relationship with the EU.





Nonetheless, some close observers argue upheaval at the top of government inevitably meant a setback in the highest level of diplomacy. Ed Arnold of the British Foreign Policy Group said “momentum has been lost through a change of PM,” while one U.K. minister noted this was also true for the U.K.’s new defense secretary, Wes Streeting.

A British official strongly denied Burnham would have any less energy for the coalition format or for supporting Ukraine than his predecessor. He is “really focused” on sustaining British backing for Ukraine, the official said, pointing to recently announced sanctions and assistance in developing long-range missiles. “The importance of the coalition of the willing is not receding in any way,” the official added.

Burnham himself sought to dissolve the distinction between foreign and domestic policy, saying in a speech on Monday: “The world is so interconnected now that it is impossible to disentangle decisions taken in Moscow with what happens on the ground in [his constituency seat] Makerfield.”

Trump’s peace drive

The revival of the coalition leaders’ engagement comes amid a renewed push from Trump to get a peace deal agreed.

The chief objectives of the meeting on Thursday are to develop plans for robust and legally binding security guarantees for Ukraine, including a multinational military force to safeguard a ceasefire; to commit additional funding for Kyiv’s war effort over the next year; to provide military support — especially air defenses against jet-powered drones, and long range strike capabilities; and to coordinate views on the ongoing peace negotiations mediated by Trump’s team.

On Wednesday, the European Commission proposed a loan of €45 billion in extra financial support for Ukraine for 2027. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was looking for more contributions from countries outside the EU, adding: “We will discuss the proposal also with our partners in the coalition of the willing.”





Another question preoccupying officials and diplomats as they prepared for the Berlin meeting was whether Trump will support Putin’s demands for reshaping European security and NATO’s role on the continent as part of the Ukraine peace process.

Many European governments already worry about the U.S. pulling troops out of Europe and some fear Trump’s criticism of NATO members has weakened the alliance’s ability to deter Russian aggression.

Yalta fears

With these concerns in mind, officials in Brussels and European capitals were keeping a close eye on the meetings between Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, southeastern China.

“The danger for Ukraine is that Trump uses this summit [in China] to try to advance his notion of peace, including giving Russia territory it has not managed to seize by force,” said Bronwen Maddox, director of the Chatham House think-tank in London. “Ukraine will be able to hold out, but only with European help.”

A meeting of tmeeting of the Coalition of the Willing on Aug. 24, 2026 in Kyiv. Merz and Macron participated remotely. | Pool photo by Henry Nicholls via Getty Images

A German official said the outcome of the Ukraine war is expected to shape Europe’s security architecture for years to come, and this will also form part of the discussion in the group on Thursday. A French official said far from acceding to Putin’s demands, Paris wanted Ukraine to join an expanded NATO.

In Kyiv, Zelenskyy’s government is desperate for as much support as possible from its backers, particularly when it comes to F-16 fighter jets, air defenses and money. But the Ukrainians also appreciate that, with the transatlantic alliance now fractured thanks to Trump’s policies over the past two years, an imperfect group such as the Coalition of the Willing is better than nothing and may be as good as it gets.





“They are doing a lot for Ukraine in terms of their capabilities,” one senior Ukrainian official told POLITICO. “Burnham is a great guy, he makes a lot of right moves. We are very happy to work with him. Merz and Macron are doing everything they can too. In terms of support Germany is the leader. France is a strong ally.”

And the real test of the coalition, the Ukrainian official said, may only come when the war ends and someone has to send troops in to protect the peace.

Veronika Melkozerova, Hans von der Burchard, Sérène Nourrisson, Bjarke Smith-Meyer, James Angelos, Victor Jack and Nicholas Vinocur contributed to this report.

World.title: Europe argued over who would talk to Russia. Agreeing what to say is even tougher.
World.content:
Europe was largely left out of talks between Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. in Abu Dhabi last week, but the Kremlin and the White House signaled that wouldn’t be the case at future meetings. After days of disagreement, EU leaders settled on a team made up of officials from four major countries ― France, Germany, Italy and Poland ― plus the U.K. and top representatives from NATO and the European Commission and Council.

Now, “the focus must shift from the ‘who’ to the ‘what’,” Austrian Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger said.

In a 15-point paper shared ahead of a foreign ministers’ meeting on Monday, Austria spelled out what some of those confidence-building measures could be: proposing limited or partial ceasefires to pave the way for a wider truce, for instance, or offering to set up an international forum to monitor any peace agreement.

Austria’s Foreign Minister Beate Meinl-Reisinger speaks during the 81st United Nations General Assembly at UN headquarters in New York on September 24, 2026. | Leonardo Munoz/AFP via Getty Images

The proposal amounts to “an offer to all 27 [EU countries] to work towards a common position,” Meinl-Reisinger said.

Norway, which isn’t part of Europe’s negotiating team but had direct contacts with Russia, is also floating ideas to lower tensions. Ukraine’s backers should look back to the Cold War for examples of how Russia and the West managed extreme tensions, specifically the 1975 “Helsinki Accords” which laid out principles for state-to-state relations, Foreign Minister Barth Eide said.
