“NATO deployments in NATO countries, for instance, is not a question to discuss with Russia” but Cold War deals on arms limitation “must be relevant in the post-war scenario.”

World.title: 5 key places that signal where Spain’s election is heading
World.content:
We analyzed the results of every congressional election in the country’s history to find the battlegrounds you need to know about.

In Spain’s election this month, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez risks losing the only province that his Socialist Party has held since the fall of fascist General Francisco Franco.

That is just one of the multiple historic changes to Spain’s electoral map that pollsters are forecasting ahead of the Nov. 29 snap election.

The center-right People’s Party is leading in the polls, with the far-right Vox party set to take third place with enough votes to help the conservatives govern as a coalition. Sánchez’s Socialists are trailing in second place, and fragmentation among smaller left-wing parties is greatly reducing his chances of securing a coalition.

From vanishing heartlands to bellwether villages and regional rivalries with national impact, here are the five places to watch on election night.





1. Seville, Andalusia

The Socialist Party’s traditional heartlands are in Andalusia, which contributes the most seats of any region to congress thanks to its large population. The region is home to Seville — the only province the Socialists have won in every election since the return of democracy in 1977, after Franco’s death in 1975.

Sánchez opted to kick off his campaign in the southern city, in a clear bid to retain and regain ground, even as support for his party has dwindled in recent years due in part to a series of scandals.

In the last general election, the Socialists won 37% of the vote in Seville, with the PP trailing just over 3 percentage points behind — a far cry from their strong performance in the 1980s and 1990s, when the party took homeover halfof the province’s votes on average in each congressional election.

Yet polling suggests the PP could win Seville in next week’s vote, which would be a historically bad night for the Socialists.





2. La Cañada de Verich, Aragón

The northeastern region of Aragón has voted for the same party that ends up winning the entire election every year since 1977, giving it a reputation as Spain’s “Ohio.”

Aragón’s three provinces — Huesca, Zaragoza and Teruel — have been described as a microcosm of the country at large: Zaragoza is a key urban center, while rural parts of Huesca and Teruel are similar to other sparsely populated parts of the country often referred to as España vaciada (“Emptied Spain”).

Within Aragón, a handful of tiny municipalities have consistently mirrored national results: In 2023, the 63 voters in La Cañada de Verich presciently voted for the national winners — the 14th time in a row the community has done so.

Aragón is currently slated to vote for the PP on Nov. 29, in line with pollsters’ projections that the party will win the most votes at the national level.

The region is worth watching for two reasons: It can provide an early indication of the national result on election night, or, if it ultimately diverges from the national picture, it will be a big blow to its bellwether status.





3. Biscay, Basque Country

The regional politics and distinct cultural identity of the Basque Country are taking center stage in this election as left-wing nationalist party EH Bildu hopes to clinch its first region-wide victory.

Several of the party’s members were previously linked to the Basque militant separatist group ETA, but over the past decade it has transitioned into a classic European Green party. ETA was responsible for the deaths of more than 800 people before it disbanded in 2018.

EH Bildu has seen significant success since entering general elections in 2015, with its share of the Basque vote rising from 15% to 24% in 2023.

Polls currently suggest that EH Bildu will win the most seats in Biscay — which would be a seismic blow to the center-right Basque National Party that has won the most votes in the region in most of the country’s elections.

A win for EH Bildu in this national election would symbolize its successful transition into mainstream politics and would set the stage for conflict with a PP-Vox coalition.





4. Barcelona, Catalonia

Separatist Catalonia on the northeast tip of Spain elects the second-highest number of lawmakers to Congress, many of whom end up playing the role of “kingmakers” as national parties try to form governments.

A wide variety of parties compete in Catalonia, with the issue of independence and traditional left–right ideological divides playing a large role in vote choice. Results can vary massively: None of the four provinces in Catalonia have voted for the same party in each election since 1997.

In this vote, Sánchez’s slim chances of forming a coalition will depend heavily on the fate of the Republican Left of Catalonia, or ERC.

On the other end of the spectrum, a new anti-migration party called the Catalan Alliance is drawing right-wing voters. While it has chosen not to run, some view Vox’s more moderate tone on Catalonia as a sign of the party’s hope to draw some of the Alliance’s would-be voters.

According to El País’ analysis, Barcelona has the most seats, second only to Madrid, that are still up for grabs in the country. Which parties snatch those up will be important to coalition calculations following the election.





5. Murcia and beyond

Far-right Vox is hoping to make its governmental debut after this election, having won its first seat in parliament in 2019. In the same year, the party won the largest share of the vote in the coastal province of Murcia, which is now considered its early heartland.

Vox’s success in this election won’t necessarily be driven by winning provinces outright, but instead by increasing its vote share across the country to win as many seats as possible and improve its standing in coalition negotiations.

Polls suggest that Murcia will be dominated by the PP and Vox, which could together claim eight of the 10 seats on offer. Across the entire country, Vox is projected to win 18% of the vote.

World.title: EPP moves to suspend Serbia’s former ruling party
World.content:
Aleksandar Vučić speaks during a pre-election rally of his Serbian Progressive Party in Belgrade on March 24, 2017. | Andrej Isakovic/AFP via Getty Images

SNS will have 12 months to deliver on the EPP’s demands, or face expulsion.

The center-right European People’s Party leadership decided Wednesday to suspend the Serbian Progressive Party, the political home of former Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić.

The move comes after the Serbian party, also known as SNS, lost the October 2026 general elections, ousting Vučić, its de facto leader and the country’s president for nine years.

The decision, seen by POLITICO, will need ratification by the EPP’s Political Assembly on Dec. 7-8. After that, the SNS, which has associate member status because Serbia is not an EU country, will have one year to deliver the reforms demanded by the political family. If it does not meet the demands by then, it risks expulsion from the group, as reported earlier in POLITICO’s European Parliament Insider WhatsApp channel.

World.title: Alleged Russian agent arrested for spying on Silicon Valley tech firm
World.content:
A Russian national has been arrested in California on suspicion of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defence company that provided support to Ukraine, US officials said on Wednesday.

 

Igor D'iu faces charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, operating as a foreign agent without notifying US authorities, stalking and fraud.

"Igor D'iu was allegedly recruited, directed, and funded by the Russian government to stalk employees of a major US technology company," Roman Rozhavsky, assistant director of the FBI's Counterintelligence and Espionage Division, said in a statement.

Rozhavsky said D'iu used "physical surveillance, electronic tracking devices, and fraudulent identities to gather intelligence."

US Attorney Craig Missakian said the company was targeted because of its "assistance to Ukraine in its war with Russia."

"We will not tolerate any efforts -- by foreign governments or otherwise -- to turn Silicon Valley into a base for foreign intelligence operations," Missakian said.

What does the indictment say?

According to the indictment, D'iu travelled from Turkey to Mexico in June 2026 before being smuggled into the United States, where he allegedly communicated with his Russia-based co-conspirators via Telegram.

They allegedly instructed him to gather information on company employees and visit a coffee shop near its Palo Alto office to "photograph their laptop screens while they worked."

FBI agents found $18,000 (€15,500) in cash, a fake US passport under the name "Hugo Landry Johns" and two Russian passports during an October raid on D'iu's home in East Palo Alto, according to the Justice Department.

If convicted, D'iu faces up to 10 years in prison for acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the US attorney general, five years for conspiracy, five years for stalking and one year for fraud.

He is scheduled to appear in federal court on 24 November.

World.title: Bukele confirms airstrike on Haitian gang leader Jeff's luxury mansion
World.content:
The president of El Salvador, Nayib Bukele, confirmed on Wednesday that his forces had attacked and destroyed the luxurious mansion of one of the main leaders of Haiti's criminal gangs, known as "Jeff" Larose. For now, it is not clear whether the leader was killed in the strike or whether he was even in the house when it was bombed.

 

Bukele posted a video on the social network X showing images of Jeff posing in front of his mansion, followed by Salvadoran helicopters that approach the building and open fire. The footage shows several columns of smoke rising above the property.

"My gift to the Haitian people on the anniversary of the Battle of Vertières," the president wrote, referring to the 1803 battle that helped secure Haiti's independence from France and make it the world's first black republic.

Thousands of Haitians took to the streets of Port-au-Prince for the second day in a row to celebrate the operation and chant the Salvadoran president's name. "Jeff is a criminal and I hope he is dead. We asked for help and Bukele answered us," said Mario Jean-Pierre, a 45-year-old vendor.

Jeff Larose, also known as Jeff Canaan, Jeff Gwo Lwa or Taliban, leads a gang that has controlled the community of Canaan, north of Port-au-Prince, for years. According to Haiti expert Diego Da Rin of the International Crisis Group, speaking to AP, it is one of the country's most structured criminal organisations and one with the greatest territorial control.

Related Haiti formalises security pact with El Salvador as thousands march in support of Bukele

The strike comes after Salvadoran forces also attacked the residence of Wilson Joseph, leader of the 400 Mawozo gang, on 8 November. The two leaders were allies and are considered two of the main criminal bosses in the capital.

Salvadoran deployment endangers civilians

Bukele deployed about 2,500 troops to Haiti last month, after four Salvadoran soldiers were attacked on 18 October in gang-controlled territory and went missing.

The use of helicopters and explosive drones has made it possible to step up operations against criminal organisations, but it has also increased the risk to the civilian population.

Experts warn that one of the main challenges remains keeping control of the territories that have been retaken and preventing the gangs from taking reprisals against residents.

World.title: Data watchdog probes massive Deutsche Bank leak of 15M files
World.content:
Following the massive data breach that leaked over 15 million internal records, the office of the commissioner for data protection in Hesse has said on Wednesday that it has launched a probe into Deutsche Bank.

 

Alexander Rossnagel, the data protection commissioner, said he will check whether the bank had appropriate data protection measures and if the leak was reported in a timely fashion.

"I am investigating whether Deutsche Bank promptly notified the affected individuals," Rossnagel said.

Whistleblowers leaked internal documents to a group of international media, revealing that the bank had reportedly ignored repeated internal warnings about money laundering, corruption or sanctions violations.

Among the bank's clients are Russian oligarchs, US President Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Deutsche Bank CEO admits errors

"When you look at the events today, you naturally question whether something could have been done differently," CEO of Deutsche Bank, Christian Sewing, told German newspaper Handelsblatt.

"Looking back, you can always say that at a certain point in time you might have been able to prioritise differently," Sewing told Handelsblatt.

When asked whether he took internal warnings seriously, Sewing refuted: "During the customer review, I asked whether a private customer needs the same complex process as a large company with 300 subsidiaries," Handelsblatt reports.

"That doesn't mean I wanted to put risks aside."

A blow to Deutsche Bank's reputation

Although Deutsche Bank said the matters "date back many years" and that it had reinforced its controls, the leak has dealt consequential damage to the bank's reputation, sending its share down.

The bank claims it proactively informed the appropriate authorities about the leak and that testing found no account information, login credentials or payment data were accessed.

While the probe won't investigate the documents, it will assess the technical and organisational measures put in place to judge if they were appropriate.

World.title: US Defence Secretary announces military cooperation in surprise Caracas visit
World.content:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced a military cooperation agreement with Venezuela on Wednesday, state TV reported, during an unexpected visit to Caracas.

 

Hegseth was received by Venezuela's interim leader, Delcy Rodríguez, in the capital ahead of a planned visit to Colombia later Wednesday.

"We see this as a renewal of our defence partnership and an opportunity for our two great armed forces to work together," Hegseth said, according to footage broadcast by VTV, Venezuela's state television channel.

The trip, which had not been publicly announced by the Pentagon, marks another step in the rapprochement between Washington and Caracas following the capture in January of Nicolás Maduro.

US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth, right, meets Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodríguez at Miraflores Palace in Caracas, Venezuela, on Wednesday, 18 November 2026. (Miraflores presidential press office, via AP)

What does the agreement include?

The cooperation agreement announced by Hegseth and Rodríguez provides for the resumption of technical and military cooperation between Washington and Caracas, which had been suspended for years amid deteriorating diplomatic relations between the two countries.

According to the Venezuelan leader, one of the main objectives is to strengthen the training of Venezuelan armed forces personnel through joint training and cooperation programmes. Rodríguez said the initiative would help improve the military's preparedness to respond to shared threats.

The agreement also aims to improve the operational equipment available to Venezuelan forces and provide access to new technologies. So far, neither government has provided details on the timeline for implementing the agreement, the resources to be allocated or the specific mechanisms through which cooperation will take place.

Washington and Caracas strengthen ties

Rodríguez took power after Maduro was captured, although her continued leadership of the country remains shrouded in uncertainty. Her interim mandate expired in July and there is still no announced date for the next presidential election.

The rapprochement between Washington and Caracas has also been marked by agreements over Venezuelan oil and by the United States' strategy against drug trafficking in the Caribbean and the Pacific, which has caused the deaths of at least 240 people since September 2025 in attacks on vessels suspected of carrying drugs.

Hegseth's visit is part of efforts by Donald Trump's administration to expand its influence in Venezuela. The defence secretary is the third member of Trump's cabinet to travel to the country this year, following trips by the interior and energy secretaries, focused on Venezuela's oil and mineral resources.

World.title: Europe Tonight: former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves speaks on the future of the global order
World.content:
US President Donald Trump has arrived in China ahead of historic trilateral talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

 

The meeting is being compared to the 1945 Yalta Conference, which helped shape post-war global power and spheres of influence.

Presenter Mard Gwyn Jones speaks live with former Estonian President Toomas Hendrik Ilves to discuss what the summit could mean for Europe and the future of the global order.

World.title: Germany’s Digitalisation Minister Wildberger discusses Europe's AI race with the US and China
World.content:
Watch on Europe Tonight, Germany’s Digitalisation Minister, Karsten Wildberger, speaking on the importance of Europe catching up with China and the US in the AI race.

 

Wildberger also says that France and Germany are aligned on how to strengthen Europe’s homegrown tech industry, despite taking different approaches.

Don't forget to watch Europe Tonight from Monday to Friday, the show where we break down the news of the day for you with top analysts and guests.

World.title: Are migrant return hubs in Rwanda an effective solution or a dangerous precedent?
World.content:
This week, five EU countries announced the first-ever return hub for migrants in Rwanda. Denmark, Austria, Germany, the Netherlands and Greece unveiled the pilot project during the Vienna Migration Conference.

 

While supporters argue that a credible migration system needs effective returns and better control of irregular arrivals, critics, however, warn that outsourcing migration management could weaken access to asylum and leave vulnerable people without legal protection.

In this edition of The Ring from the European Parliament in Brussels, anchor Maria Tadeo is joined by German MEP Lena Düpont from the European People's Party (EPP) and her Polish counterpart Robert Biedroń from the Socialists & Democrats (S&D).

Is Europe striking the right balance between security and human dignity, or moving towards a more restrictive approach? Are return hubs part of the solution?

This episode of The Ring is produced by Luis Albertos and Amaia Echevarria, and edited by Vassilis Glynos.

You can watch the debate in the player above.

World.title: Faster electrification is essential for Europe to escape fossil fuel shocks, Jørgensen warns
World.content:
Energy Commissioner Dan Jørgensen welcomed the recent deal struck by EU lawmakers on permits for energy infrastructure and clean power, describing it as a major win towards integrating more renewable electricity into Europe's energy system and allowing consumers to switch from gas and oil to electricity.

 

Speaking to Euronews' Europe Tonight, Jørgensen explained that getting those permits can take five years or even a decade, making lengthy approval processes one of the biggest hurdles to electrification.

The deal struck on Wednesday between the EU co-legislators, the European Parliament and the European Council, seeks to bring those permitsdown to just six months for most projects, a significant push intended to unlock investment and help electricity networks keep pace with growing demand.

"This is about making sure that we have the infrastructure to actually electrify our societies, to get the renewable energy into our systems so that we can drive our cars on electricity, we can have heat pumps and so forth," Jørgensen said.

Critics argue that faster permits do not automatically mean cheaper electricity, citing the lack of investment in infrastructure and the fact that network expansion will still have to be paid for.

EU countries are currently discussing the proposal, which has raised some divergences. Sweden pushed back hard, arguing Brussels would redirect money paid by Swedish power consumers and grid operators to fund electricity grids elsewhere in Europe instead of benefiting Stockholm.

Hailing electrification as a new climate doctrine, the Commissioner argued that expanding renewables, improving energy efficiency and connecting national electricity markets would help bring down energy costs.

"The main way of bringing down prices is to deploy more renewables, because renewables are cheaper than the fossil alternative," he said.

Europe has saved more than €30 billion annually through cross-border electricity connections, Jørgensen added, arguing that the potential for further savings remains much greater.

MEP Niels Fuglsang (S&D/Denmark), leading the file in the Parliament, described the deal to speed up the granting of permits as a "very important step".

The Danish lawmaker said the agreement will allow for faster rollout of renewables and grid infrastructure, to the benefit of our citizens, to mitigate climate change and to boost the EU's competitiveness.

A difficult winter exposes Europe's fossil fuel vulnerability

Despite the celebrations in Brussels over the agreement on permits, the Commission's longer-term electrification strategy is unfolding against an immediate energy security challenge. The deal struck on Wednesday won't alleviate energy prices in the short term.

With tensions in the Middle East threatening supplies and markets, the energy Commissioner warned that Europeans should not expect energy prices to return quickly to normal, even if the geopolitical situation stabilises.

"We don't even know if they will come down. What we do know is that it's a very unstable winter that we are going into (...) We also know that even if there's a normalisation of the situation, it'll take months for the prices to normalise," Jørgensen added.

The warning suggests Brussels is preparing for another winter in which households and businesses could face sustained pressure from energy costs, reinforcing the political argument for reducing dependence on imported oil and gas.

The Commissioner urged consumers to switch from gas and oil boilers to heat pumps, replace combustion-engine cars with electric vehicles and improve home insulation.

"We probably have to prepare, or not probably. We unfortunately, for sure, have to prepare for a difficult winter," Jørgensen said.

World.title: Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Russian official says
World.content:
The Crimean Bridge has been attacked again, Crimea's Russian-installed governor said. The attack comes as Vladimir Putin prepares to sit down with Donald Trump and Xi Jinping for joint talks in China.

The Crimean Bridge was attacked for a third time this week, a Russian official said on Thursday.

Traffic had been temporarily suspended, according to Crimea's Russian-installed governor.

"The damage is currently being assessed," Sergei Aksyonov, the governor, said on Telegram, adding that emergency services were at the scene.

The bridge, which supports a four-lane roadway and a railroad, is the only bridge linking mainland Russia with occupied Crimea.

Crimean Bridge attacked for a third time this week

This is the third Ukrainian attack this week targeting the strategic bridge that is a key symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

The bridge has played a key role in supplying Russian troops in occupied parts of southern Ukraine since the 2022 Russian invasion, making it a key target for Kyiv.

Steel arch of bridge collapses after Ukrainian drone strikes earlier this week

On Tuesday, Ukraine carried out a major attack on the bridge using missiles and drones, destroying the steel arch of the 19-kilometer-long road section of the crossing.

Ukraine's SBU security service had said that the "road span beneath it (the arch) has been completely destroyed."

The latest attack appears to have impacted rail traffic on the bridge, according to German press agency DPA.

The Ukrainian attack came just hours before an unprecedented meeting scheduled between Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit.

World.title: Ukraine's allies gather in Berlin for 'Coalition of the Willing' summit
World.content:
The UK pledged to provide Ukraine with long-range cruise missiles capable of reaching areas in Russia beyond the front lines.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham is expected to make that announcement at the "Coalition of the Willing" summit in Berlin.

The drones are a part of the support package for Kyiv worth £260 million pounds ($338 million, €311 million) ahead of the winter.

"Plunging millions of Ukrainians into the freezing cold and starving them of heat and warmth won’t see Putin win this war, it will only cement our resolve to support Ukraine," Burnham said, adding that he is "determined" to help Ukraine defend itself.

According to Burnham, Ukraine's backers are "as united as ever" to secure an end to the war with Russia.

World.title: Almost 1 in 4 children live in conflict zones — report
World.content:
Denial of humanitarian access, abductions and sexual violence are among several violations against children that have increased dramtically over the past year, according to a new report by Save the Children.

A record number of children were living in a conflict zone in 2025, Save the Children findings revealed on Thursday.

In the latest report in the "Stop the War on Children" series, the humantarian group said 589 million children worldwide lived in conflict zones. That's the highest number since records began in 1990, and more than double the total in the mid-1990s.

"For millions of children, fear, violence and displacement are part of every day life," said Save the Children Germany CEO Florian Westphal.

He said this needed to be a "wake-up call" for the international community.

Where children are living in conflict zones

Around two in five children in both Africa and the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025, the report found. Africa, alone, accounted for 44% of all children living in conflict zones worldwide.

In terms of regional proportions, 40.2% of children in the Middle East were living in conflict zones in 2025. That represented roughly two in five children across the region, and a particularly steep rise in the number of children affected. The figure jumped by nearly 29% from 52 million in 2024 to 67 million last year.

Palestinians in the Gaza Strip depend on humanitarian aid Image: Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu/picture alliance

Children's exposure to conflict in Africa has more than tripled over the past 15 years, with the share of children living in conflict zones rising from 12% in 2010 to 39% in 2025.

Grave violations against children in armed conflict zones increase

The report highlighted the dramatic increase in the denial of humanitarian access.

A total of 8,322 verified incidents of denying access to humanitarian aid to children were recorded in 2025, a 16-fold rise over the past decade. The figure was 509 in 2015, and only eight incidents were reported when the United Nations (UN) established the Monitoring and Reporting Mechanism (MRM) in 2005.

The Palestinian Territories accounted for the vast majority of cases, with 5,946 incidents, or more than 70% of all verified cases globally.

"No grave violation has increased as dramatically or changed the overall pattern of verified violations as much as the denial of humanitarian access," the study noted.

According to the report, denial of humanitarian access rose from around 2% of all verified grave violations against children in 2015 to more than 21% in 2025, becoming the second-most frequently recorded violation after the killing and maiming of children.

Palestinians rush to collect humanitarian aid airdropped by parachutes in the Gaza Strip, August 2025 Image: Abdel Kareem Hana/AP Photo/picture alliance

Grave violations as laid out in the MRM also include the recruitment of children by armed forces, sexual violence, abduction and attacks on schools and hospitals.

Where violations against children were concentrated

The study found that, overall, 38,967 grave violations against children were verified by the UN.

This was the second-highest annual total since the MRM was established, surpassed only by the record 41,763 violations documented in 2024.

More than half of these took place in just three areas: the Palestinian Territories, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Nigeria. The Palestinian Territories alone accounted for 12,449 verified violations, nearly one-third of all cases.

As well as the denial of humanitarian access, violations in 2025 included:

14,224 children killed or maimed in conflicts in 2025

A record 5,128 child abductions

1,787 cases of sexual violence, a 71% increase in the past decade

A fifth straight year of increased attacks on schools and hospitals, at 2,930 cases

Strike on Iran school: Did US commit a war crime? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Palestinian Territories recorded the highest number of attacks on schools or hospitals, with 837 incidents, followed by Ukraine with 643. Together, the two accounted for more than half of all reported cases worldwide.

The sharpest rises in sexual violence incidents were recorded in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), where cases jumped from 358 in 2024 to 592 in 2025, and Sudan, which saw an increase from 74 to 193. Around 86% of all cases were documented in African conflict zones.

"Children have the right to live free from violence. Changing the odds requires political choices that put children’s safety first, and a sustained commitment to stop the war on children," the NGO said.

World.title: Grand Theft Auto VI released as gamers rejoice globally
World.content:
After 13 years of waiting, fans around the world will get to play the latest installment in the blockbuster video game series. In focus: A tale of crime and violence in a fictionalized version of Miami.

Grand Theft Auto VI will be officially launched Thursday, ending a 13-year wait for one of the most anticipated games ever.

The game will become playable at midnight local time (CET) on a wide range of platforms, including PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X, meaning gamers in Asia will get to play the game ahead of users in the US and Europe.

In New Zealand, one of the first countries worldwide where the game became available, the release prompted internet providers to prepare for a spike in internet usage at midnight.

This comes due to the game's size of 212 gigabytes, more than a quarter of the average New Zealand household's usage in a month.

Rockstar Games, the company behind the GTA franchise, faces high expectation after 13 years of anticipation, with previous versions having become commercial and cultural hits around the world.

GTA games sold 470 million units worldwide, and the fifth installment generated $1 billion in retail sales in just three days after its release in 2013.

Jason and Lucia's experiences are at the center of GTA VI Image: Rockstar Games

GTA's global success

Take-Two Interactive, Rockstar Games' parent company, saw its shares rise by more than eight percent the day before the game's release.

The game takes place in Vice City, a fictional version of Miami.

It follows Lucia Caminos and Jason Duval, a couple drawn into criminal networks while trying to secure a better life. GTA games are often criticized for including excessive violence and for glorifying crimes and drug use.

Lucia, a former prisoner, and Jason, an ex-military man, experience a series of criminal jobs that go wrong in the drug-trafficking world of Leonida, a fictional state based on Florida.

According to Rockstar, Leonida is the company's most detailed open world so far, extending beyond Vice City into smaller communities and nightlife hotspots inspired by locations in South Florida.

Music has been an intrinsic part of the GTA experience, and the latest game is expected to feature a soundtrack including artists like Tame Impala and SZA.

World.title: What the Crimean bridge attack means for Russia
World.content:
Ukraine's latest strike on the Kerch Bridge has disrupted a key transport link between Russia and Crimea. Beyond the damage, the attack could have serious consequences for Russian military logistics and Putin's prestige.

It had been a year and a half since Ukraine last attacked the 19-kilometer-long Kerch Bridge connecting Russian-annexed Crimea with Russia's Krasnodar region.

Now, Ukraine has struck again. The attack during the night of November 17 caused the highway section of the bridge to collapse into the sea. As a result, shipping traffic between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov has also been disrupted.

Russia's ministry of transport announced a "temporary suspension" of road and rail traffic on the bridge, though later, rail services were resumed. Russian authorities have launched a criminal investigation into what they are calling a "terrorist attack." It was only after this announcement that the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) confirmed the attack.

The Kerch Strait bridge is considered one of Russian President Vladimir Putin's most prestigious projects. Its construction began after Russia's 2014 annexation of the Ukrainian Crimea peninsula, an act considered illegal under international law. The Kerch Bridge was completed four years later.

It has been targeted by Ukraine on several occasions since Russia's 2022 full-scale invasion. The most well-known strike occurred in October 2022, when an explosives-laden truck detonated on the bridge, causing extensive damage and several months of traffic restrictions. The most recent attack took place in June 2025, when the SBU reported that an underwater support structure was blown up.

A long time in the making

The latest Ukrainian operation lasted about a month, and consisted of seven distinct phases. "First, the SBU and armed forces systematically neutralized the enemy's air defense system. After that, the direct attack on the bridge began," says the SBU Telegram channel.

Some Russian military bloggers claim that the attack was carried out with the support of Ukraine's Western allies, or at least using their equipment and weapons.

Russian President Vladimir Putin (center) personally oversaw the bridge's construction Image: YURI KOCHETKOV/AFP

Ukraine has not confirmed this. It has instead pointed out that various Ukrainian-made weapons were used in the attack, ranging from a variety of drones, to FP-5 Flamingo and R-360 Neptun missiles. British daily The Times has cited Ukrainian military sources, saying that Ukraine attacked the bridge without the support of SpaceX's satellite network system Starlink. There has been no confirmation of this so far.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, meanwhile, described the strike as a response to Russian attacks: "Russia is attacking our infrastructure every day, particularly bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region." He said "we are rebuilding our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that the war always returns to where it began."

Ukraine hits strategic Russian bridge to Crimea To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The impact on shipping

After the attack, pictures and videos of the bridge were shared on social media. The Krimskij Veter Telegram channel has highlighted damage to the railroad link and questioned why Russian authorities have opted to resume train services.

The Kerch Strait shipping channel is also completely blocked by debris. "This brings road traffic to a standstill, but also shipping between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov," the channel writes.

Indeed, the Kerch Strait navigational channel is merely 120 meters wide, writes Mychajlo Hontschar of the Ukrainian Center for Global Studies "Strategy XXI" on Facebook. "The strait is shallow, only three to five meters deep."

As early as the 19th century, the seabed was dredged to allow heavier ships to pass from the Black Sea to the Sea of Azov and vice versa. "Now, Vladimir Putin's bridge-building efforts have brought shipping to an indefinite standstill," Hontschar said.

Not only will river-sea vessels no longer be able to leave the waters of the Sea of Azov, the Don, and the Volga, but boats and small ships from the Black Sea fleet and the Caspian flotilla based in Novorossiysk will also be unable to do so.

The military consequences

Many pro-Kremlin Telegram channels have been quick to claim that the bridge does not play an important role in the Russian army's logistics or in supplying Crimea.

The Dva Mayora (Two Majors) channel quotes the "Deputy President of the Republic of Crimea," Olga Kurlayeva, who described the bridge as a "purely civilian structure."

Ukrainian military experts interviewed by DW, on the other hand, point to the systematic disruption of Russian logistics. These efforts also included regular attacks on the R-80 highway leading through Russian-occupied territories of the Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson regions.

Russia cannot replace the Kerch Bridge with any other land connection, says Oleksandr Kovalenko, a Ukrainian military expert with the Information Resistance Group that seeks to counter disinformation. He expects the damaged bridge will cause supply problems for the Russian armed forces: "If there is a resource shortage during attacks or in defense, then either the attacks or the defense will fail."

The bridge's road-traffic arch has collapsed into the sea Image: Ukrainian Security Service/AFP

That is why he does not rule out a decline in attacks from occupied Crimea on the rest of Ukraine. "There are many launch pads for kamikaze drones in Crimea — in the Hvardijsk area, at Cape Chauda and in Balaklava," Kovalenko told DW. "From there, many drones are launched toward Odesa, Mykolaiv, and the right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. They also fly over Crimea en route toward Ukraine. Then there are attacks using Iskander-M ballistic missiles, as well as Zircon and Oniks missiles, guided missiles, and glide bombs. And while they don't originate in Crimea, they are brought over via the Kerch Bridge."

A bad look for Putin

Kovalenko says the bridge strike has dealt a serious blow to Vladimir Putin's standing. It comes at a sensitive time as Putin is about to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, China.

Memes and witty comments about the bridge abound on X. Meanwhile, the Russian president's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov has promised to rebuild the bridge and assured that it will be "even better than before."

Andrii Korezkyj of the Kyiv University of Transportation, however, says this is not likely to happen anytime soon. "All in all, I would estimate that it would take between one and a half and three years [to rebuild]," Korezkyj told DW, adding, "I don't think they'll let the Russians build another [bridge] arch like that near the Ukrainian border without interference."

Pro-Russian commentators, known as Z-bloggers, agree with this view. "Unlike in 2022 and 2023, the Ukrainian armed forces are now able to launch strikes against floating cranes and repair teams."

"Even installing a pre-assembled arch under these conditions would constitute a challenging task," writes the pro-Kremlin Rybar Telegram channel.

This article was translated from German.

World.title: US Pentagon chief Hegseth signs military deal in Venezuela
World.content:
On a visit to Caracas, Pete Hegseth signed a deal that signifies the "reestablishment of our defense partnership." US-Venezuela ties were strained for years until US troops ousted ex-President Nicolas Maduro in January.

US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth visited Venezuela on Wednesday, met with the country's interim authorities and also signed a military cooperation deal with the Latin American country.

What do we know so far about Hegseth's trip?

The Pentagon did not release any information on Hegseth's trip or confirm the visit, although it was broadcast on Venezuelan state media.

The visit comes after US forces in January ousted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and took him along with his wife to New York to face drug trafficking charges. Since then, US President Donald Trump has backed acting President Delcy Rodriguez to lead the country.

Hegseth also met with new Venezuelan Foreign Minister Oliver Blanco, who had belonged to a party opposing Maduro Image: Miraflores Palace/Handout/REUTERS

Both Rodriguez and Hegseth touted the new military agreement between the two countries at the presidential palace in Caracas.

Rodriguez said the deal would strengthen training for the Venezuelan military while facilitating access to new technologies. She said this would allow the two nations to "face common threats."

Hegseth said the US sees the deal "as a reestablishment of our defense partnership and the opportunity to work together between our two great militaries."

The agreement includes intelligence sharing between the two nations in addition to joint training.

The Pentagon chief said the US seeks "to ensure the Venezuelan people are not threatened by foreign actors or narco-terrorists or criminals and that they are safe and secure inside sovereign borders."

Hegseth said Wednesday that since Maduro's ouster, Venezuela "has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner."

How have US-Venezuela relations changed?

US-Venezuela relations were strained under Maduro, who had taken office in 2013. In 2019, Maduro cut off Venezuela's formal diplomatic relations with the US after Trump's first administration recognized Venezuelan opposition leader Juan Guaido as the country's interim president.

Is the US looting Venezuela? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

After the ouster of Maduro, the Trump administration urged Venezuela to comply with demands such as US access to the Venezuelan oil market. Trump had threatened Rodriguez, who was Venezuela's vice president, with a "fate worse than Maduro" if she didn't cooperate with Washington.

Trump has later praised Rodriguez as a "terrific person" who is doing a "great job."

Under Rodriguez, Venezuela has released political prisoners and facilitated the shipments of oil to the US, with the US then controlling the proceeds and returning the money under an energy deal. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio has been overseeing Venezuela's transition and is in close contact with Rodriguez.

Elections after Maduro's ouster are expected at some point in Venezuela, but with Rodriguez's government acting favorably towards the US, it's unclear whether they would happen anytime soon. Nobel Prize winner and opposition leader Maria Corina Machado recently urged elections after arriving in Venezuela.

World.title: Would Ukraine trade land for NATO membership or protection?
World.content:
The US is exploring whether Ukraine would cede parts of Donetsk province still under its control in return for NATO membership or protection. Experts warn the idea is risky.

The US has asked Ukraine whether it would be willing to cede Donetsk province to Russia in return for NATO membership. Together, Donetsk and Luhansk constitute the so-called Donbas region. Russia currently controls most of Luhansk province, and large swathes of Donetsk, though Ukraine continues holding a number of major cities there, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.

So far, no concrete proposal had been put forward, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. He said he would publicly discuss the matter once the US and NATO member states had agreed on the plan, stressing that he could not make any such decision "on his own." Zelenskyy also said any potential agreement would go ahead "without recognizing Russia's occupation of these territories."

The Ukrainian leader said the US was talking about guarantees similar to those enshrined in Articles 4 and 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty, though did not envision US troops on Ukrainian soil. Article 4 provides for consultations among member states in the event of imminent threats, while Article 5 stipulates that an attack on one state is considered an attack on all. The US, however, has said it pictures bilateral guarantees for Ukraine similar to those established with Israel and certain Middle Eastern countries.

Russia has yet to comment on these proposals, with President Putin's spokesperson Dmitry Peskov stating that "we maintain our position that, in the interest of the peace process, it is not appropriate to disclose details of the talks between us and the Americans."

US special envoy Steve Witkoff and President Donald Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner recently met Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky (right) in Dublin Image: Paul Faith/AFP

Budapest Memorandum 2.0?

Experts interviewed by DW are skeptical of the land-for-security-guarantees idea, objecting that the US cannot uphold such an arrangement on its own.

"It seems to me that this is what happens to normal diplomacy when it's been run by real estate agents who are used to selling people something that doesn't really exist," Oleksandr Kraiev of the North America-Israel Research Program at Ukraine's Ukrainian Prism think tank tells DW. He says that at least half of NATO's member states have reservations about Ukraine's accession.

"We'll just end up with a second Budapest Memorandum, it'll just carry a different name," Kraiev told DW. The original 1994 Budapest Memorandum stipulated that Russia, the US and UK respect Ukraine's independence and sovereignty in its existing borders and refrain from the threat or use of force to change its territorial integrity. Ukraine in return committed to giving up all nuclear weapons.

The Budapest Memorandum, however, did not contain any commitment by the UK or US to defend Ukraine in the event of an attack.

A dangerous precedent

Most experts interviewed by DW are critical of the idea of holding a referendum to let ordinary Ukrainians decide whether their country should hand over full control of Donetsk province in exchange for NATO membership.

This is because ceding territory would not only violate Ukraine's constitution and harm its national interests, but would also undermine a world order "in which borders cannot be redrawn by force," Oleksandr Khara of Ukraine's Centre for Defence Strategies told DW. "It doesn't matter whether the citizens of Ukraine vote for or against such a proposal," Khara said, adding that any such referendum would set "a very dangerous precedent."

A survey by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology (KISS) conducted between October 8 and 16 found that 61% of respondents categorically reject withdrawing troops from Ukrainian-controlled parts of the Donbas, such as cities like Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, even in exchange for US and European security guarantees. 35% of respondents said they would begrudgingly accept a land-for-security deal.

Donbas dilemma: Why Russia and Ukraine won't let go To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What are the alternatives?

Defense analyst Khara doubts a bilateral agreement between Ukraine and the US, akin to those established between the US and Israel, would guarantee Kyiv any more support than it presently receives.

"This concerns financial support, joint weapons production and development, and the training of Ukrainian troops — everything that falls below the threshold of collective security," Khara told DW. "It is good that these commitments — security agreements, political declarations, and the allocation of funds in the budgets of the countries supporting us — are set out in writing, at least for the next five years." Yet to prevent another war, Khara believes that ideally, Ukraine needs "a nuclear shield," specifically, a "strategic one from the US" and a "tactical one from Europe."

Ukrainian experts already floated to the idea of an alternative security arrangement to NATO members in December 2023, says Sergiy Solodkyy of Ukraine's New Europe research center. The arrangement would see Ukraine join the alliance within its internationally recognized borders, though specific protocols would stipulate that only territories under Kyiv's control would be defended.

This arrangement could be modeled on the German case, where West Germany became a member of NATO first, while East Germany joined the alliance only after German reunification.

West Germany never gave up on reunification, Solodkyy told DW. "That means we, too, should not give up on our territory or recognize the border." That is why he says the land-for-security deal proposed to Ukraine is unacceptable.

"This is a trap that Russia and the US negotiators are trying to lure the Ukrainian side into," Solodkyy told DW.

This article was translated from German

World.title: Israel launches new ground operation in Gaza
World.content:
Israel has said its military is targeting Hamas infrastructure in central Gaza and urged civilians to avoid the area. The fight is unfolding against the backdrop of a dire food and shelter situation for Palestinians.

Israel says its military is involved in operations on Wednesday in central Gaza in an effort to dislodge Hamas militants.

France's AFP news agency reported "intense Israeli artillery shelling amid ongoing gunfire and airstrikes."

A statement from the Israeli military (IDF) said, "The IDF launched a precise operation within Gaza earlier today west of the Yellow Line to remove a threat posed to IDF troops operating in the Gaza Strip."

The Yellow Line in Gaza was established in an October 2025 ceasefire between Israel and Hamas, and separates Israeli and Hamas-controlled territory.

On Wednesday, COGAT, an Israeli military body responsible for civilian matters in the Palestinian territories warned international aid agencies and Palestinian civilians to avoid areas near the Al-Bureij and Nuseirat refugee camps and Gaza's main thoroughfare, the Salah al-Din road.

Has the war in Gaza weakened Israel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why are the IDF and Hamas still fighting?

Palestinian medics told Reuters news agency that one person had been killed in an Israeli airstrike in central Gaza and that two more had been killed in separate incidents unfolding in Deir al-Balah and Gaza City.

Hamas — which is listed as a terrorist organization by Israel, the US, Germany, the EU and others — blasted the Israeli operation, calling it "a flagrant violation of the ceasefire agreement and confirmation that the occupation has reneged on its obligations."

Israel's military countered that it was reacting to Hamas ceasefire violations and the group's attempts to rearm.

The October 2025 ceasefire halted major operations, but both sides have continued to carry out limited attacks. Gaza health authorities report at least 1,600 Palestinian deaths and Israel reports the loss of fewer than 10 soldiers since the ceasefire went into effect.

In all, Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed inside Gaza during Israel's retaliation for Hamas' October 7, 2023, assault — which killed roughly 1,200 Israelis, most of whom were civilians.

Israelis demand accountability for October 7 To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

How dire is the situation for Palestinian civilians in Gaza?

Beyond the threat of violent gunfire and airstrikes, civilians in Gaza continue to face ongoing food insecurity and lack of adequate shelter as winter approaches.

On Tuesday, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) and the UN's World Food Programme (WFP) warned that funding shortfalls and access restrictions put untold numbers of Palestinian lives at risk.

Currently, more than 1.7 million Gazans are displaced, with IOM and WFP saying 1.4 million face acute hunger and 1.98 million require shelter assistance.

With Gaza's infrastructure decimated by years of Hamas mismanagement and pounding Israeli attacks, more than 80% of Palestinians are unemployed, meaning they cannot afford food and have been forced to burn garbage to try to keep warm.

"Families in Gaza are facing their first sleepless nights of a very long winter ahead," said WFP Palestine Country Director Shaun Hughes. "Unless we get immediate support to scale up the humanitarian response, we risk this becoming not only a shelter crisis but also a deeper food security crisis."

World.title: Feijóo abre la puerta a una “derogación total” de la ley de la eutanasia
World.content:
El Partido Popular es contrario a la ley de la eutanasia aprobada por el Gobierno de coalición de PSOE y Podemos. El PP votó en contra en el Congreso de los Diputados durante su tramitación, cuyo debate final se celebró en marzo de 2021. Durante las últimas semanas, y ante las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre, Alberto Núñez Feijóo ya había adelantado que modificará la norma si es investido presidente del Gobierno tras las urnas. Finalmente, en una entrevista publicada este miércoles, el candidato popular abre la puerta a que el cambio legislativo se lleve a cabo con una derogación total del texto.

“¿Nosotros estamos de acuerdo con la ley de la eutanasia? No. ¿Queremos modificar la ley de la eutanasia? Sí. ¿Esa modificación puede ser una derogación total o parcial? Por supuesto”, aclara el líder del PP en una entrevista ofrecida en el podcast El sentido de la birra, difundida este miércoles en YouTube y cuya grabación se produjo el viernes pasado, durante el primer día de campaña. El programa electoral del Partido Popular para el 29-N propone la aprobación de una “ley nacional de cuidados paliativos” para armonizar las normativas autonómicas sobre la materia, y “con el fin de que nadie se vea empujado a la aceleración de la muerte por falta de alternativas ni tenga que afrontarla en soledad”, explica el texto en su apartado 226. Sin embargo, el programa no menciona la vigente ley de eutanasia ni qué pasará con esa norma en caso de que el jefe de los populares llegue a La Moncloa.

En el El sentido de la birra, ante el youtuber Ricardo Moya, Feijóo clarifica que sí está sobre la mesa la posibilidad de que su futuro Gobierno derogue por completo la norma sancionada en 2021, que fue recurrida por el PP de Pablo Casado ante el Tribunal Constitucional en junio de aquel año y avalada por el órgano de garantías en marzo de 2023. “Nosotros, junto con la regulación de la muerte digna, tenemos que garantizar la vida digna y tenemos que garantizar todo un sistema de cuidados paliativos que en este momento en muchos sitios en España no están desplegados y tenemos que asesorar bien a una persona que aparentemente toma la decisión de poner fin a su vida”, añade el líder del Partido Popular, que vuelve a traer a colación el mediático caso de la joven Noelia Castillo.

El PP también rechaza la ley trans, que Feijóo califica de “disparate” y cuya modificación también se incorpora en su programa electoral. “Revisaremos las normas que hayan generado inseguridad jurídica en nombre de la igualdad, como la Ley Trans, y eliminaremos la libre autodeterminación registral del sexo, para reforzar la seguridad jurídica y proteger a los menores. Garantizaremos que el sexo biológico sea el criterio para las categorías deportivas femeninas”, indica el apartado 115. Y en ello se reafirma Feijóo: “En el ámbito del deporte y en el ámbito de las federaciones deportivas, esto de que un señor pueda formar parte de una selección femenina...”.

Por otro lado, Feijóo insiste en que la receta del PP para aliviar el problema de la vivienda es construir más inmuebles. “El problema no se soluciona con decretos, se soluciona con ladrillo”, alega el líder del PP, que carga contra las medidas del Gobierno por considerarlas propias de una “legislación ideológica”. “Hay que construir un millón”, reitera, y apunta a que serán “las empresas, las coperativas” las que pongan en marcha los proyectos de edificación. Para favorecer esa construcción, su programa ofrece: ley antiokupación, que los Ayuntamientos otorgen licencias de construcción con máximo de 90 días y tanto rebajas como prorrateo de impuestos para quienes adquieran una casa. También pedirán flexibilidad a los bancos a la hora de otorgar créditos. Sobre la escasez de mano de obra en el sector, Feijóo sostiene que hay que “recuperar” a los albañiles que se marcharon por la caída de la construcción. Y además quiere a inmigrantes con contratos de obra en origen. “Todas las personas que entren con permiso de trabajo tienen que tener un permiso de residencia en nuestro país, aparecerá mano de obra, si viene un albañil peruan tendrá permiso de residencia. Es un círculo virtuoso”.

“Al PP se le ha juzgado judicialmente y políticamente”

Al margen de la entrevista, el líder del PP ha despejado el resto de su agenda de este miércoles y de este jueves para centrarse en la preparación del cara a cara con Pedro Sánchez de mañana. No tiene más actos ni comparecencias. “Feijóo está tranquilo, pero con ganas de poner al presidente del Gobierno frente al espejo de su incompetencia. Y combinará moderación y sentido de Estado con un examen exigente a la gestión de alguien que debería llevar fuera ya muchos años de la Presidencia del Gobierno”, señalan fuentes de su Gabinete en un comunicado. Génova también carga contra el candidato del PSOE por su entrevista en la revista Lecturas. “Pedro Sánchez lleva a la portada de Lecturas y al atril de sus mítines al elemento que más le alejaba de su masa electoral”, sentencian después de haber encargado, hace un año, una encuesta sobre la repercusión en el electorado de los procesos judiciales que rodean al secretario general de los socialistas.

En el podcast de El sentido de la birra, el líder del PP recuerda sus orígenes en Os Peares (Ourense), de niño, y su licenciatura en Derecho. También rememora que se planteó prepararse las oposiciones de judicatura, pero que lo descartó porque quería independizarse en menos tiempo y se decantó por otras a letrado de la Xunta. Se afilió al PP ya en el 2000. Feijóo recuerda también que votó al PSOE de Felipe González en las elecciones generales tras el golpe de Estado del 23-F. “Felipe era el cambio, la consolidación de la democracia, si gobernaba Felipe, si gobernaba el PSOE, el golpe de Estado no se iba a volver a producir”, cuenta el líder del PP sobre por qué se decantó por los socialistas.

Feijóo se ha defendido además de los casos de corrupción que afectaron a su partido y que fueron sentenciados. “Aquí, cada uno tiene su propia historia, ahora, de lo que ha pasado, cada uno tiene que aprender. Llevo cuatro años dirigiendo mi partido, a mí que se me juzgue. No acepto que nadie meta la mano en la caja. Al PP se le ha juzgado judicialmente y políticamente”, ha dicho en referencia a la Gürtel y a la moción de censura de 2018. “Los errores del pasado los asumimos”.

Por último, Feijóo no descarta del todo que Carlos Mazón siga en política tras las elecciones autonómicas de mayo del año que viene, cuando perderá su escaño como diputado valenciano. “El señor Mazón no es candidato a la presidencia de la Generalitat”, responde el líder del PP a Ricardo Moya en El podcast de la birra. “El señor Mazón es diputado en la Cámara. Ha cesado de sus responsabilidades de presidente de la Generalitat y, por tanto, en la siguiente legislatura veremos a ver lo que ocurre”, ha remachado el líder del PP. “Una dana no es una falta de mantenimiento y conservación, es un efecto meteorológico”, ha continuado Feijóo para cargar en su lugar contra el Gobierno central por los accidentes de trenes de Adamuz y Urda.

El jefe de la oposición compara además lo vivido en la Comunidad de Valenciana con lo sufrido en Letur (Castilla-La Mancha), para sostener que los efectos fueron similares, solo que el municipio albaceteño es más pequeño y por eso, ha dicho, el número de muertos —7— no fue tan elevado como en Valencia. “¿Qué censo tiene Letur? ¿Y cuántos muertos ha habido? Coge el porcentaje. Y el señor Page tenía la información que le daba la AEMET. No tenía más. Es que si no tienes más información y no tienes más competencias, tú ejecutas de acuerdo con tu información y competencias. Y el señor Mazón no tenía esa información y no tenía esas competencias”.

World.title: El PP consolida su posición frente a Vox
World.content:
El sexto ‘tracking’ de 40dB. apunta a que el flujo de votos entre bloques solo funciona hacia la derecha

Día a día, la primera fase de la campaña va consolidando una tendencia en el bloque de la derecha: el PP se recupera a costa de Vox. De tal modo que la última entrega del tracking, el sondeo continuo, de 40dB. para EL PAÍS y la Cadena SER da oxígeno al partido de Alberto Núñez Feijóo en su pugna con el PSOE por la primera plaza.

El dato más elocuente de la encuesta proviene del freno a las fugas del PP hacia la extrema derecha. Hace una semana, la encuesta diaria -con una muestra de 2.000 entrevistados y un margen de error del 2%- apuntaba a que los populares podrían perder hasta un 20% de su electorado en favor de Vox. La última entrega lo reduce al 13,5%, lo que implicaría para el partido de Santiago Abascal un descenso de punto y medio en su estimación de voto desde el comienzo de la campaña. Aun así las desafecciones populares hacia la extrema derecha siguen marcando niveles considerables, de hasta 1,2 millones de sufragios, según los cálculos de la encuesta.

De esos votos a la fuga, el PP recuperaría algo más de la mitad gracias al electorado más moderado del PSOE que parece dispuesto a pasarse al PP. Los socialistas, a su vez, lo compensarían con el bocado que pueden dar a las formaciones a su izquierda. A las de ámbito estatal, porque las territoriales aparecen todas al alza.

El balance de esos flujos de votantes es claramente favorable a la derecha. Teniendo en cuenta que incluso Vox pica un poco entre los que apoyaron a Sánchez en 2023, el bloque derechista tendría una ganancia neta de 800.000 votos. La encuesta no advierte fugas relevantes en sentido contrario, del PP y Vox hacia la izquierda.

Descargables

A continuación, puede acceder a enlaces de descarga con los cuestionarios usados, la documentación del sondeo y las matrices con todas las respuestas en varios formatos (hoja de cálculo, dta y sav), entre otros documentos.

World.title: El mapa del voto táctico para que el último escaño por provincia se lo lleve la derecha o la izquierda: ¿qué dicen las encuestas?
World.content:
El modelo de EL PAÍS dice que hay 42 escaños en el aire. Consulta a qué partido le sirve más tu voto

Las encuestas tratan de predecir los votos del próximo 29-N, pero el modelo electoral que publicamos en EL PAÍS desde hace una década va más allá: estima el voto y los escaños en cada provincia, y les asigna probabilidades. A continuación mostramos sus pronósticos en cada territorio, con las encuestas publicadas hasta el 16 de noviembre.

En el interactivo puedes ver los escaños seguros (99% de opciones), probables (75%-99%) y en juego (25%-75%) de cada partido. En total hay 168 seguros, 140 probables y 89 en juego (suman más de 350 porque varios partidos se disputan los escaños). También puedes elegir una provincia y ver nuestra estimación allí.

Las provincias con más escaños en juego son las más grandes, Madrid (con 10) y Barcelona (con nueve). Pero hay pulsos muy reñidos en algunas provincias pequeñas. En Lleida, que reparte cuatro diputados, cinco partidos se disputan los dos últimos: Junts, PP, PSOE, ERC y Vox.

El voto táctico: ¿qué voto ayuda a tu bloque?

Muchas personas votan para maximizar las opciones de un gobierno de izquierdas o de derechas. Quizás tienen un partido favorito, pero se hacen otra pregunta: ¿a qué partido de su bloque le sirve más su voto? Es lo que se llama voto táctico o estratégico. La respuesta cambia en cada provincia: por el método D’Hondt, un voto al PP y otro a Vox no valen lo mismo en escaños, porque uno de los dos suele estar más cerca de ganar el último diputado. Y lo mismo pasa con PSOE, Frente Amplio o BNG.

¿Cuál es el voto táctico en tu provincia? Puedes verlo en el mapa. Primero elige un bloque. Entonces el mapa mostrará, para cada provincia, el partido de ese espectro que tiene más probabilidades de ganar (o salvar) un escaño para su bloque.

Para un votante de derecha, existe voto táctico en 38 provincias. Hay 21 donde le conviene votar al PP (probablemente) y 17 donde le conviene hacerlo por Vox. A veces la diferencia es grande: en Gipuzkoa, Lugo y Ourense, un voto a Vox casi nunca decide un escaño, mientras que el PP se disputa el último con Bildu o el BNG. En Álava o Melilla, un voto al PP vale más de cinco veces lo que uno a Vox. Pero hay territorios donde un votante indiferente entre PP y Vox maximiza sus opciones eligiendo al partido de extrema derecha. Es lo que pasa en La Rioja, por ejemplo.

En la izquierda, el voto táctico favorece casi siempre el PSOE. En 23 provincias es el único del bloque que mueve escaños en nuestras simulaciones, porque los Frentes y Podemos tienen números débiles en los sondeos. Hay excepciones en territorios con fuerzas locales: por ejemplo, en Lugo y Ourense parece que un voto al BNG es mejor para los intereses del bloque. Y ocurre algo parecido con Adelante Andalucía en Córdoba y con la Unidad del Pueblo Canario en Santa Cruz de Tenerife.

En las provincias grandes, en cambio, el voto táctico apenas existe. En Madrid, Barcelona, Valencia o Sevilla da casi igual votar a un partido u otro del bloque: las fuerzas principales tienen todas opciones de lograr representación.

Nuestra simulación también muestra otra cosa: mover un escaño es mucho más barato en las provincias más pequeñas. La probabilidad de que justo tu papeleta sea la decisiva es siempre minúscula (un voto cualquiera tiene una posibilidad entre 116.000 de decidir un escaño). Pero no es siempre igual de minúscula. En Lleida un voto al PP pesa casi seis veces más que la media: una posibilidad entre 20.000. Y en Ávila o La Rioja, uno al PSOE pesa unas cinco veces más. En el otro extremo, un voto al PP o a Vox en Madrid vale la mitad de lo normal, en parte porque allí cada escaño cuesta más votos: hay unos 94.000 votantes por diputado, frente a 25.000 en Soria.

Una advertencia: esto no es una recomendación de voto. Es la aritmética de los escaños según las encuestas de hoy, que todavía pueden moverse y que son siempre una aproximación. Además, el voto táctico solo mide la probabilidad de mover un escaño, pero un voto puede tener utilidad para apoyar unas ideas o una formación incluso cuando no se traduzca en asiento del Congreso.

¿Cómo funciona el modelo?

El modelo parte de nuestro promedio de sondeos, lo proyecta a cada provincia con su historia y microdatos del CIS, y le añade la incertidumbre de las encuestas en el pasado. Después simulamos las elecciones 20.000 veces y contamos cuántas veces gana cada partido cada escaño. Así podemos clasificarlos en tres grupos: seguros, probables y en juego.

El siguiente gráfico muestra qué significan estas probabilidades. Puedes simular las elecciones una, dos, tres o cien veces para hacerte una idea intuitiva de cuántas veces se gana un escaño de cada tipo.

El modelo es sólido. Cada pieza la hemos puesto a prueba con otras elecciones generales. Por ejemplo, hemos probado varias formas de repartir el voto entre provincias, siguiendo técnicas habituales, y nos quedamos con la más precisa en votos y escaños.

El modelo es cauteloso. Y lo es por diseño: predecir cada provincia es difícil porque las encuestas pierden precisión a escala provincial. Un sondeo de 2.000 o 5.000 entrevistas no basta para estimar directamente el voto de Soria, Pontevedra o Castellón. Por eso no lo intentamos: lo que hacemos es usar el voto histórico de cada partido en cada provincia y lo que dicen en cada comunidad los microdatos del CIS, que acumulan decenas de miles de entrevistas. Además, las fuerzas locales no siempre salen en las encuestas y pueden sorprender al final: Teruel Existe gana escaño en una de cada cinco simulaciones. Y pasa algo similar con partidos pequeños en las provincias grandes: Podemos consigue un diputado por Madrid en el 60% de las simulaciones, y SALF, en el 24%. Si detectas cualquier omisión, escríbenos.

Y el modelo es confiable. Estas predicciones las hemos hecho muchas veces. Por eso sabemos que el modelo funciona y está bien calibrado. En 2023 dimos 189 escaños como seguros y se cumplieron todos, igual que en las dos elecciones de 2019 (156 y 153). Los que dimos como probables se cumplieron el 94% de las veces (365 de 388), en la parte alta del 75%-99% que prometíamos. Los errores de cada provincia se compensan en parte al sumarlos, así que el total es más fiable que cada provincia por separado. El modelo también acierta en el total nacional: en las generales de 2016 a 2023, los escaños de cada partido grande cayeron dentro de nuestra horquilla del 80% en 19 de 20 casos, más de lo prometido: es la cautela de la que hablábamos.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate el nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

Metodología

Las predicciones las produce un modelo estadístico basado en sondeos y en su precisión histórica. Es una versión renovada del que hemos usado en unas 40 elecciones desde 2016: en Andalucía, Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, las europeas, las generales de abril y noviembre de 2019 y de 2023, y otras en México, Francia o el Reino Unido.

Funciona en cuatro pasos. 1) Un promedio de encuestas que pondera cada sondeo por su tamaño, su fecha y la precisión histórica de su encuestadora, según nuestro comparador. 2) Una proyección del voto a cada provincia con un modelo logístico, que parte de las generales de 2023 —y, para los partidos nuevos o que ahora concurren por separado, de las europeas de 2024 y las andaluzas de 2026— y se alimenta también con microdatos del CIS de cada comunidad. 3) La incertidumbre de las encuestas, calibrada con los errores de 44 elecciones en España desde 1986 y con una base internacional de miles de sondeos, según el tamaño de cada partido y los días que faltan para votar. Usamos distribuciones t de Student, con colas más anchas que una normal, y errores correlacionados entre partidos. Esos errores tienen una parte común a toda España, porque las encuestas suelen fallar en la misma dirección en todas partes, y otra propia de cada provincia. 4) 20.000 simulaciones de las elecciones, repartiendo los escaños según D’Hondt con barrera del 3% en cada circunscripción.

Un escaño es seguro si un partido lo gana en más del 99% de las simulaciones; probable, entre el 75% y el 99%, y en juego, entre el 25% y el 75%. En nuestras pruebas con las generales de 2016 a 2023, esas probabilidades están muy bien afinadas: los escaños en juego se cumplieron 202 veces, frente a las 195 que predecía el modelo.

Para calcular el voto táctico usamos las mismas 20.000 simulaciones. En cada una añadimos (o quitamos) un puñado de votos a cada partido en cada provincia, y miramos si su bloque gana (o pierde) un escaño. Solo contamos cuando el escaño cambia de bloque. El resultado es la probabilidad de que un voto decida un asiento para su bloque ideológico. Los bloques son derecha (PP, Vox y SALF), e izquierda (PSOE, Frente Amplio, Podemos, ERC, EH Bildu, BNG y Adelante Andalucía). PNV, Junts y CC quedan fuera.

En los gráficos nacionales agrupamos como Izquierdas a Frente Amplio, Podemos y las coaliciones Compromís-Front Valencià, Unidad del Pueblo Canario y Ara Més-Front Ampli; en cada provincia aparecen por separado.

Si quieres seguir todas las encuestas del 29-N, apúntate al nuevo pódcast de Kiko Llaneras, en Spotify, YouTube, Apple Podcasts o iVoox.

World.title: El Congreso aprueba siete decretos sociales con un amplísimo respaldo pero entre críticas de campaña
World.content:
La Diputación Permanente del Congreso ha convalidado este miércoles con una amplísima mayoría, que en algún caso ha llegado a la unanimidad, siete decretos ley aprobados por el Gobierno de coalición con una catarata de medidas de contenido social que abarcan desde ayudas para reparar la situación sufrida en Ceuta con la avalancha de inmigrantes del verano, otras para paliar los daños de la dana Adam, mejoras en la Seguridad Social, reforzamiento de la red ferroviaria tras los últimos accidentes, reparación de las víctimas del siniestro en Urda, más protección para las familias numerosas y monomarentales y la reestructuración casi total del sistema de dependencia en España. Esos decretos forman parte de los aprobados en el último mes en el Consejo de Ministros en lo que se conoce como los martes sociales y que han sido cuestionados y criticados por la oposición como una estrategia dirigida a incidir en la campaña electoral del 29 de noviembre. La izquierda más allá del PSOE los ha considerado tardíos.

Seis de esos siete decretos han concitado un amplio apoyo de casi todos los parlamentarios representados en la Diputación Permanente (63), menos los seis del partido ultra Vox, que solo se ha apuntado a la unanimidad del voto a favor en el que contempla las reparaciones a las víctimas del accidente del AVE en Urda. La Diputación Permanente es el órgano que funciona en el Congreso para estos periodos especiales con las Cortes disueltas. El debate ha durado siete horas y ha estado totalmente contaminado de discursos propios de mítines electorales. Habrá más sesiones similares porque el Gobierno del PSOE y Sumar tienen previsto aprobar y derivar a la Diputación Permanente más decretos en esta línea incluso tras las elecciones.

El ministro de Política Territorial y Memoria Democrática, Ángel Víctor Torres, ha aprovechado su doble función de comisionado sobre la crisis en Ceuta para ofrecer el último balance sobre la situación en la ciudad autónoma. Torres indicó así que en estos momentos quedan en Ceuta 5.037 personas atendidas con recursos del Estado (532 menores), 3.156 menores por parte del Gobierno local, ya no existe rastro levantado de ningún asentamiento de chabolas, tampoco estructuras con ese cometido en el puerto y han vuelto a Marruecos desde la avalancha un total de 16.475 inmigrantes. El Gobierno ha empezado este miércoles a desplegar el nuevo espigón alargado a 150 metros en la zona del Tarajal y ha derivado a la ciudad una inversión de 45,3 millones de euros.

Torres expuso sus datos y ese esfuerzo, y no entró en ningún debate, pese a que recibió duras críticas de la gestión realizada. La portavoz de Podemos, Ione Belarra, y luego la de Sumar, Aina Vidal, lamentaron la falta de investigación de algunas agresiones y hasta torturas denunciadas sobre miembros de las fuerzas armadas. El representante de Vox, José María Sánchez, abundó en las quejas que más tarde repitieron todos los portavoces de esa formación: que el Gobierno abusa de la Diputación Permanente para hacer mítines. Sánchez, además, ya no habla de “invasión” para definir lo ocurrido en Ceuta y sostiene que es un “casus belli”, es decir un motivo para declarar la guerra de libro.

La líder de Podemos, Ione Belarra, interviene durante la reunión de la Diputación Permanente del Congreso, este miércoles. Chema Moya (EFE)

La diputada melillense del PP, Sofía Acedo, machacó sobre el mismo discurso que ha reiterado estos meses sobre el abandono a Ceuta, las agresiones sexuales y la falta de normalidad en la ciudad. Esa diputada del PP, y todas las demás que intervinieron durante la larga sesión, acabó su alocución aventurando la inminente victoria electoral de su líder y su llegada a La Moncloa para gobernar y cambiarlo todo a mejor.

Para defender el segundo decreto con actuaciones para paliar los daños de la dana Adam sobre la cornisa mediterránea los pasados 17 y 19 de octubre, el ministro Torres aludió a que eran medidas “lógicas y sensatas”. Esa apelación no impidió que Mikel Legarda, de PNV, Teresa Jordá, de ERC, Alberto Ibáñez, de Compromís, expresaran sus reparos a que pudieran ser también tardías, cortas o recentralizadoras. El PSOE apeló ahí a la necesidad de un pacto de Estado ante la emergencia climática y el PP reclamó que esas promesas se ejecuten.

La ministra de Inclusión Social y portavoz, Elma Saiz, argumentó sus razones para el decreto que cambia aspectos clave de mayor y mejor protección en la Seguridad Social, con más patologías y la prestación para la etapa de la menopausia. Los partidos de izquierda defendieron esa necesidad del tercer pilar social, Vox solo observó fines partidistas y el PP insistió en la falta de urgencia para proponer ahora fuera del Pacto de Toledo tanto decreto dispar (con nueve cambios normativos) en estos momentos políticos.

El vicepresidente primero, Carlos Cuerpo, defendió ahora también como ministro de Transportes los dos decretos relacionados con la seguridad ferroviaria y las ayudas a las víctimas del siniestro en Urda. Las posiciones se repitieron y en ese punto entró el portavoz de Junts, Josep Maria Cruxet, para recuperar todas las demandas recurrentes de su formación sobre la discriminación a Cataluña. La secretaria general del grupo popular, Macarena Montesinos, tuvo que admitir ahí que algunas acciones planteadas estaban “bien dirigidas en parte”, pero para acribillar los mensajes del argumentario popular sobre que el Gobierno de la corrupción de Ábalos, Cerdán, las prostitutas, el falcón y los muertos de los accidentes.

El ministro de de Política Territorial y Memoria Democrática, Ángel Víctor Torres, a su llegada a la reunión de la Diputación Permanente del Congreso, este miércoles. Chema Moya (EFE)

Los dos últimos decretos los razonó el ministro de Asuntos Sociales, Pablo Bustinduy, para argumentar que las mayores protecciones previstas para las familias numerosas y las monomarentales (80% madres sin pareja a cargo de hijos) deberían ser algo a estas alturas de consenso totalmente transversal porque benefician a 770.000 personas directamente. A Vox le pareció una iniciativa muy contaminada ideológicamente y sin negociar. La diputada abulense del PP, Patricia Rodríguez, la descalificó como “chapuza” y usó su tiempo para despedirse del Parlamento, porque no repite. Bustinduy, en contra de la tónica general de otros ministros, sí quiso ahí entrar al debate cuerpo a cuerpo y le refrescó a la portavoz de Vox que entre las ayudas contempladas estaba el bono eléctrico para las familias numerosas, que Vox ha tildado hasta hace poco como “las paguitas” a suprimir y que en estos días se ha conocido por una información de Infolibre que disfruta la pareja y los cinco hijos del propio Santiago Abascal.
