World.title: Surge in software patches likely behind recent tech outages; bank regulators on alert
World.content:
The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software

Recent disruptions to the way people work, access bank accounts, and travel are likely linked to corporate efforts to rapidly patch newly discovered software vulnerabilities in the AI age, experts said.

US government officials have sought to reassure the public that the tech outages are not related, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio telling reporters in Manila this week that company patches — software and operating system updates intended to fix security vulnerabilities — are, at times, “creating short-term disruption in the way the system works.”

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton also told a House of Representatives Homeland Security Committee hearing on worldwide threats on Wednesday, November 18, that there is so far no indication that the tech outages are related.

That said, disruptions to services at JPMorgan Chase on Monday that also affected other banks drew immediate attention from US banking regulators, who have contacted lenders to ensure incidents are contained and not linked to a cyberattack, two people familiar with the matter said.

One of the people said that Treasury officials also were making inquiries.

The advent of easily accessible AI tools and large language models has supercharged the discovery of vulnerabilities in software. Microsoft this month has addressed more than 1,200 software vulnerabilities, nearly 20 times higher than in the same month a year ago, according to cybersecurity firm Qualys.

“AI has made finding critical vulnerabilities fast and cheap, and the number of flaws that demand immediate patching has grown with it,” said Yuval Itzchakov, CTO and co-founder of autonomous offensive security company A Security.

“Emergency patches go into core infrastructure within hours, often without the full testing cycle, and they are intrusive by design: they change runtimes, kernels and network components that everything else depends on. That speed and scale of change is itself a source of failure,” Itzchakov said.

Josh Bressers, director of coordinated vulnerability disclosure at cybersecurity firm VulnCheck, said that in 2026 there have been 100,000 publicly disclosed vulnerabilities, tracked by industry as Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, or CVEs. Of those, Bressers said, 1,363 were known to have been exploited in the real world.

Bank regulator plans deep dive into issue

Within the banking sector, at least one major bank was rushing to address a wave of recent patches and there is a lot of work needed, a person at the bank said.

After the outage at JPMorgan Chase, lenders received inquiries from the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), according to a separate person, who added that the US banking regulator was trying to assess the impact and wanted to know about communication to customers.

The Treasury and the OCC were calling banks minutes after the incident was reported to check that the issue was contained and it was not a cyber-related incident, a third person said.

The banks were asked to communicate to the customers that they should not panic and that everything was under control, that person said.

The OCC is also going to do a deep dive into the issue and check that everything the regulator was told is correct and that there are no other shortcomings, the person added.

All sources spoke on condition of anonymity.

OCC head Jonathan Gould told an industry event on Tuesday that the JPMorgan outage was “an isolated incident”.

“The OCC, as you would expect, was very involved identifying the issue, talking to the bank in question and talking to the other banks that were affected,” he said.

The US Treasury did not respond to a request seeking comment.

Ronald Gestiehr, director of wealth management at Luttner Financial, said technology has made banking “incredibly convenient, and while occasional outages can be frustrating, I don’t believe the outages will have a significant impact on consumer confidence or change how most people manage their money.”

“Financial institutions have invested heavily in technology and security, and, unfortunately, occasional disruptions will happen,” Gestiehr said. “What matters most is how quickly those issues are identified, resolved and communicated to customers.” – Rappler.com

World.title: FACT CHECK: Trump did not call an ABS-CBN reporter ‘stupid’
World.content:
In the video, the person US President Donald Trump addressed as ‘stupid’ was a reporter from ABC News, not ABS-CBN News

Claim: US President Donald Trump called a reporter from ABS-CBN News “stupid.”

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The claim was made in a video posted by Facebook user Herson Capino on November 16. Though the reaction count was hidden, the post reached over 3,700 comments and 4,700 shares as of writing.

The video shows Trump entertaining questions from the media. After one reporter spoke to Trump, he asked: “Are you a stupid person?”

Trump then asked the reporter which news organization they were working for. He doubled down, again called the reporter “stupid” and added that their network is the “worst of all.”

Text overlaid on the video reads, “Isang reporter ng ABS-CBN tinawag ni President Donald Trump na ‘Are you stupid’.”

(President Donald Trump asked a reporter from ABS-CBN, ‘Are you stupid?’)

Several users have reposted the video, with some leaving comments saying the supposed ABS-CBN reporter was humiliated by the exchange.

The facts: Trump did not call an ABS-CBN reporter stupid. The US president was talking to a reporter from an American TV network, ABC News.

According to a fact-check by ABS-CBN News, the Facebook reel misrepresents an October 21, 2026 video, in which a reporter asked Trump whether the US waived sanctions on Russia in exchange for the release of Stephen Hubbard, an American jailed in Russia for allegedly fighting for Ukraine.

In the original clip, the reporter can be heard answering “ABC News” when asked to identify their news organization.

The misleading reels merely added overlaid text falsely claiming that Trump was speaking to a reporter from ABS-CBN.

Trump in PH: The posts circulated on social media as Trump arrived in Manila on November 17 for a state visit and to participate in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)-US Special Summit, as well as the Quadrilateral Security Dialogue leaders’ summit. (READ: Marcos rolls out red carpet for Trump state visit)

Following his bilateral meeting with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., Trump said on November 18 that the US and the Philippines secured a trade deal — the “biggest deal” so far between the two countries. However, he gave no details about the deal. Marcos’ office later said both sides reached an understanding on areas of economic cooperation.

The US president then headed to China for a summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin, focusing on issues like nuclear weapons, trade, and tensions over Ukraine and Iran.

Debunked: Rappler has debunked false claims about Trump:

– Lourence Angelo Marcellana/Rappler.com

Keep us aware of suspicious Facebook pages, groups, accounts, websites, articles, or photos in your network by contacting us at factcheck@rappler.com. Let us battle disinformation one Fact Check at a time.

World.title: Navigating Our Future Together Means Leaving No One Behind
World.content:
Hindi matatawag na tunay na pag-unlad ang anumang pagsulong na nakakamit kapalit ng karapatan at kapakanan ng mamamayan.

The right of our Filipino people to speak, to assemble, and to disagree are not negotiable; it is a right enshrined in the Constitution and a necessary foundation of a truly just society. One that serves all citizens, and not just a select few.

As the Philippines hosts the 49th ASEAN Summit and welcomes United States President Donald Trump, we keep in mind that every Filipino voice must be respected and protected. We call on the authorities to honor the due process and protect fundamental civil liberties in light of what happened November 15—students and advocates and members of the press were arrested and scattered all over Metro Manila and Cebu.

From university campuses to the streets, these are our people—those who voiced concerns for the marginalized groups fearing for their lands and livelihoods, and who spoke out against Trump’s visit and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. However, they were met not with answers, but with force from those who swore to protect the Filipino people, even detaining student journalists and effectively preventing the youth from doing what a free press was always meant to do.

But worries about Pax Silica go beyond political differences. Indigenous communities have cautioned about possible displacement of their populations, expropriation of ancestral lands and the environmental fallout that can come from large-scale industrial development. These are not minor considerations that can simply be dismissed in the name of modernization.

We still value those things, but we have to look closer: is this really progress, or are we just enforcing compliance? How easy it is to frame all this in the name of respect and decorum, for innovation and advancement.

Our people are being forced into a false choice between innovation and justice. But progress must be collective, not selective. Progress is not progress if it leaves people behind. Development is not sustainable if it destroys the very communities, cultures, and ecosystems it is supposed to serve.

And yet, this is the exact type of development our government is pushing. As an organization that advocates for the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals, we believe development must be inclusive, equitable, and sustainable.

While the Philippines signed the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals in 2015, the government continues to be selective in which goals it honors, overlooking that human rights and sustainable development are indivisible. The SDGs call for strong institutions, climate action, reduced inequalities, and the protection of life on land. These commitments mean little if the very people advocating for these causes face intimidation for making their stances heard.

At the same time, this year’s ASEAN theme, ‘Navigating Our Future, Together,’ emphasizes collective action and shared progress. Moving forward together requires ensuring that no community is excluded, no voice is disregarded, and no one is left behind. Solidarity must extend beyond international commitments and be reflected in how people are protected at home, starting with the very institutions tasked with keeping them safe.

The Philippine National Police and other law enforcement institutions must remain accountable to the public and uphold their fundamental mandate to serve and protect. Their actions must reflect respect for human rights and due process, regardless of the affiliations or causes of those exercising their rights.

The protection of Indigenous Peoples, the dignity of ordinary Filipinos, and the right to peaceful expression must remain central to any commitment to democracy and sustainable development.

Hindi matatawag na tunay na pag-unlad ang anumang pagsulong na nakakamit kapalit ng karapatan at kapakanan ng mamamayan. Hindi rin tunay na pagkakaisa kung ang mga tinig ng mga katutubo at ordinaryong Pilipinong ipinaglalaban ang kanilang mga karapatan ay binabalewala o hindi pinakikinggan. Ang kinabukasan ng bansa ay hindi dapat pinagpapasiyahan nang hindi kinikilala ang karapatan ng sambayanan na magkaroon ng tinig at makilahok sa mga desisyong direktang nakaaapekto sa kanilang buhay at kinabukasan.

World.title: Alagang Ayala advances social infrastructure to power nation-building and business growth
World.content:
Ayala chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala shares he believes the three pillars for countries to move forward are education, health, and livelihood

Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Ayala Corporation and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Ayala Corporation is putting greater focus on social infrastructure, bringing together platforms in healthcare, education, community development, and sustainability to support human capital while strengthening its presence in sectors with strong, sustained demand. The move underscores a push to scale essential services and aligns business growth with evolving needs in human capital and access.

Ayala chairman Jaime Augusto Zobel de Ayala framed the role of the private sector during the recent InvestPH 2026 panel organized by the Philippine Stock Exchange, saying public-private partnerships can broaden private participation and allow government to direct more resources to education and health.

“If you look at how countries move forward, there are three basic pillars. Number one is education, for the future. Number two is making sure citizens are healthy. Number three is ensuring that they earn an income,” Zobel de Ayala said.

That perspective is now being brought together under Alagang Ayala, the Ayala Group’s social infrastructure platform. Ayala believes that by aligning business capabilities with community needs, social infrastructure can create shared value that expands opportunity and advances inclusive progress.



“While continued investment in physical infrastructure is important, we must invest just as intentionally in the social foundations that make thriving possible. Alagang Ayala reflects our conviction that infrastructure must also build people—and, in turn, help build a stronger and more prosperous nation,” said Ayala Corporation chief social infrastructure officer Paolo F. Borromeo.



Ayala’s healthcare platform, AC Health, was established in 2015 with a vision to help transform health for every Filipino.

Today, AC Health has touched the lives of more than 6.5 million Filipinos through its network of seven hospitals, 18 multispecialty centers, over 350 corporate clinics, and nearly 900 pharmacies under Generika Drugstore and St. Joseph Drug. Its integrated healthcare ecosystem also includes pharmaceutical importation and distribution businesses, IE Medica and MedEthix, which strengthen its portfolio of trusted healthcare products.

AC Health’s integrated ecosystem gives Ayala a presence across different points of care – from medicines and consultations to hospital services and specialized treatment – enabling Ayala to address the growing demand for quality and affordable healthcare across the Philippines.

Education is another major component, with iPeople serving as the group’s platform for quality and workforce-relevant learning. A joint venture with the Yuchengco Group’s House of Investments, iPeople includes Mapúa University, Mapúa Malayan Colleges, National Teachers College, APEC Schools and the University of Nueva Caceres.

Mapúa’s expanded partnership with Arizona State University gives students access to globally benchmarked content, international pathways, AI-enabled education, and online learning options, supporting skills for a technology-driven economy.

National Teachers College, founded in 1928, was the country’s first higher education institution to offer collegiate programs dedicated to teacher education and is among the Philippines’ top producers of teachers and school administrators.

Ayala Foundation supports public education through its CENTEX programs. In San Marcelino, Zambales, its CENTEX Digital Education pilot reached more than 1,600 Grades 4 to 6 learners in nine public elementary schools. After 12 weeks, average math scores rose from 27 percent to 56 percent. The program is being expanded by DepEd Zambales to 60 schools, with at least 22,500 learners expected to benefit. The Foundation is also expanding its CENTEX Early Grades program, working with local governments, schools, and child development centers to strengthen teaching practices, engage parents, and improve learning outcomes for children ages 3-5 years old.

Across its community development programs, the Foundation helps communities build sustainable livelihoods and increase household incomes through integrated, place-based initiatives that improve access to education, health, financial inclusion, and basic services. It also mobilizes volunteers through its public volunteer platform, engaging more than 4,300 individuals who contributed over 129,000 volunteer hours in 2026 alone.

Ayala’s sustainability and mobility platforms add another layer. Through ACEN’s solar, wind, and geothermal projects, the Ayala Group supports access to clean, reliable, and affordable forms of renewable energy. ACEN currently has more than seven gigawatts of attributable renewable energy capacity. Borromeo cited Makati City’s shift to renewable electricity through ACEN as one example of cleaner energy addressing energy security and costs.

Meanwhile, ACMobility is a prime mover in electrifying mobility in the country, building an electric vehicle ecosystem that includes EV distribution and charging infrastructure nationwide. Through this growing ecosystem, ACMobility is helping institutions and consumers alike transition to cleaner, more future-ready transport solutions. An example is Valenzuela City’s shift of its police patrol fleet to electric vehicles which can help reduce emissions and lower operating costs as it serves the community.

For Ayala, the measure of Alagang Ayala will depend on how these platforms improve access, affordability, resilience, and outcomes as they are scaled, while supporting businesses in areas important to national development. – Rappler.com

World.title: Anti-Pax Silica protesters released after 3 days in detention
World.content:
The protesters had been detained at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig for more than 70 hours without charges being filed within the prescribed period, raising allegations of illegal detention

MANILA, Philippines – After three days in detention, 236 people arrested during a protest against the US-led Pax Silica initiative in Muntinlupa City were released on Wednesday evening, November 18.

In a resolution issued earlier the same day, the Muntinlupa City Prosecutor’s Office ordered their release pending further investigation into complaints of illegal assembly, disobedience, and grave coercion. Prosecutors dismissed the complaints of malicious mischief and alarms and scandals for lack of evidence.

The protesters had been detained at Camp Bagong Diwa in Taguig City for more than 70 hours without charges being filed within the prescribed period, raising allegations of illegal detention.

Most of those arrested were protesters from Southern Tagalog. Among them were campus journalists and students, including minors who were arrested and brought to Bahay Pag-asa Tunasan, Muntinlupa.

The arrests drew condemnation from lawmakers and various groups.

They were arrested during a protest on Sunday, November 15, the opening day of the 49th ASEAN Summit. The demonstrators opposed the US-led Pax Silica initiative and the visit of US President Donald Trump to the Philippines.

Their release came just hours after Trump left the country for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation Leaders Meeting in Shenzhen, China, which will also be attended by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr..

At a press conference in Malacañang with Trump, Marcos said there was no signing of a Pax Silica agreement during the US President’s visit to the Philippines.

Department of Trade and Industry Undersecretary Ceferino Rodolfo earlier said the Pax Silica deal would be signed before the year ends.

Pax Silica is a US-led initiative that seeks to secure supply chains for critical minerals and semiconductors through partnerships with other countries.

Activists have warned that Pax Silica could put indigenous communities and farming areas at risk, particularly amid growing demand for minerals used in advanced technologies.

– Rappler.com

World.title: Meet Jewel Encarnacion, Choco Mucho’s hidden gem in PVL title pursuit
World.content:
Already in her third pro league team in three years, former UP star Jewel Encarnacion finally shines in the PVL as an important role player with the Choco Mucho Flying Titans

MANILA, Philippines – Last November 12, the Choco Mucho Flying Titans erupted in joy as they downed their “big sisters” Creamline Cool Smashers in a thrilling five-set marquee matchup of the 2026 PVL All-Filipino Conference Siklab Series at the packed Araneta Coliseum.

The jubilation was justified on all fronts, as in the history of this moneymaking, crowd-drawing rivalry, the two-time silver medalist Choco Mucho has only beaten the 11-time champion Creamline twice in 21 meetings dating back to the Flying Titans’ inception in 2019.

Though the historic win certainly meant a lot to every Choco Mucho player who helped forge the late escape, none took the win more emotionally than Jewel Encarnacion, who was later seen in tears as she was interviewed on-court as the Player of the Game.

Play Video

For stars of the Rebisco-owned teams like Sisi Rondina-Rosales, Eya Laure, Jema Galanza, and Alyssa Valdez, game-based awards like this come as second nature. But for unheralded role players like Encarnacion, each recognition counts for a whole lot more.

“I cried because this is the first time I was named Player of the Game in my PVL career,” the former UP star told reporters in Filipino. “It was made all the sweeter because we got the win, we won against our sister team, and that this is a champion team.”

Though 10 points and 9 excellent receptions are modest numbers in a pro league setting, Encarnacion’s efforts shone especially bright as she helped Choco Mucho most in the closeout fifth set, when Laure was unable to be at her best due to a noticeable back issue.

It was a textbook “next-man-up” call successfully answered, and at a time when PVL roster spots are hard to come by due to multiple team disbandments in recent years, role players like Encarnacion would certainly love to hold onto any recognition that comes their way.

“I’m not trying to think that I have to fill a big role, because that’s just added pressure,” she continued. “I’m just telling myself that I have to just do what I do and perform. I just have to show my strengths and minimize my weaknesses. It’s just filling in for one another. Teamwork.”

Fighting for home

Already a journeywoman in just her third year, Encarnacion was one of many unintended casualties of the Cignal Super Spikers going on leave last year, shortly after she signed as a free agent following the expiration of her rookie contract with the Galeries Tower Highrisers.

Though she was soon able to latch on with Choco Mucho, she then had to fight for her spot in Dante Alinsunurin’s loaded spiker rotation that already included established outside hitters like Rondina-Rosales, Laure, captain Des Cheng, fellow UP alumna Isa Molde, and Mean Mendrez.

Also loaded with opposite wingers Kat Tolentino, Caitlin Viray, Dindin Manabat, and Ayesha Juegos, Choco Mucho is just another PVL team burdened and spoiled for choice when it comes to fixing rosters game by game like Creamline, Nxled, and other contenders.

At this point, however, Encarnacion is just content on letting the chips fall where they may, as she focuses on contributing, more than surviving, for a team that still welcomed her with open arms despite barely having room to let her in.

“From the first day, I already embraced Choco Mucho the way they embraced me — from my Rebisco family to my teammates, they all embraced me,” she said. “So I just really try my best to give back to their community.

“Everyone’s heart for one another is in the right place, and I’m overjoyed to be a part of all this.” – Rappler.com

World.title: Duterte trial: Witness says Cabrera’s 2-week financial report possible
World.content:
Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente of AML Consulting PH takes his oath before testifying on fundamental legal concepts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act during the 44th day of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at the Senate in Pasay City on Thursday, November 19, 2026. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — The witness presented by Vice President Sara Duterte’s defense team in her impeachment trial admitted that preparing a financial report on questionable transactions in just two weeks, as the prosecution’s witness did, is possible but difficult.

The admission came during Thursday’s resumption of the trial, when defense counsel Mark Vinluan asked former Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) investigator Reinel dela Fuente whether an “extensive financial investigation” could be completed in just two weeks.

Before posing the question, Vinluan had asked dela Fuente about his credentials and work at the agency.

Article continues after this 

“I would just like to ask very quickly, can you do an extensive financial investigation in two weeks?” Vinluan asked.

“Two weeks? That’s possible, but it’s hard, if we’re being very realistic. Doable, but it’s extremely hard,” dela Fuente replied.

“Alright, we’ll leave it at that because the other so-called experts said they did it in two weeks only,” Vinluan said.

Prosecution witness and financial forensic analyst Atty. Alexander Cabrera previously told the Senate Impeachment Court that he prepared the report on Duterte’s questionable transactions in two weeks.

Cabrera claimed that Duterte had over P817 million in unexplained wealth, or assets that the vice president did not declare in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN).

Article continues after this 

READ: Analyst: VP Duterte didn’t declare P207-M cash, total assets reach P817M

Last October 12, Cabrera was questioned by Senator-judge Robin Padilla about why he had repeatedly described his report as rushed, given the magnitude of the allegations covered in the analysis.

Article continues after this 

Cabrera assured Padilla that he could produce a competent report despite the limited time, saying that while everything a financial analytics company does is rushed, that does not mean its output is not credible.

Padilla then questioned why Cabrera seemed to change his tone: He initially said the report was rushed but later maintained that it had been done properly. Cabrera said both could be true at the same time.

READ: Cabrera tells Padilla: We can do a good job even if we’re in a hurry

The prosecution considers Cabrera’s testimony important, especially after the panel decided to drop all charges against Duterte except for Article II, which deals with unexplained wealth and the non-declaration of assets in her SALN.

At one point, Cabrera said Duterte had exhibited “unusual banking behavior” in 2025, which included a meal at Ginza Inakaya Tokyo in Japan worth P200,007.29, with a transaction date of March 19, 2025; two transactions at the Nike store in a Davao City mall worth P93,750.00 and P205,392.00 on December 27, 2025; and another transaction at a Nike store in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, worth P256,882.50.

Two transactions were recorded at a Don Quijote outlet in Shibuya, one of Tokyo’s main business and entertainment hotspots. One was worth P62,900.95 and the other P65,877.64, both on December 8, 2025.

READ: From Donki to Nike: Analyst says VP had ‘unusual’ purchases in 2025

The other Don Quijote outlet where Duterte made a transaction was in Naka Ward, Aichi Prefecture. The transaction, which took place on July 20, 2025, was worth P111,109.24.

It was eventually revealed that the card belonged to Duterte’s husband, lawyer Manases Carpio.

During its turn to present witnesses, the defense called lawyer Anel Antero to testify that the P200,000 dinner in Tokyo was for 11 individuals. He said he was among those who eventually reimbursed Carpio.

World.title: Prosecution, defense in Sara Duterte trial bicker over ‘expert’ witness
World.content:
Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente of AML Consulting PH takes his oath before testifying on fundamental legal concepts under the Anti-Money Laundering Act during Day 44 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte at the Senate in Pasay City on Thursday, November 19, 2026. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Prosecution and defense counsels in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on Thursday bickered over an “expert” witness called to testify on supposed money laundering allegations against the vice president.

According to defense counsel Mark Vinluan, their witness, Atty. Rainer Dela Fuente, could enlighten the impeachment court on fundamental legal concepts related to the Anti-Money Laundering Act through his knowledge and experience as a certified public accountant, lawyer and anti-money laundering compliance practitioner.

The witness’ testimony would also prove that the findings of Duterte’s alleged unexplained wealth were “erroneous, malicious, and without merit,” Vinluan added.

Article continues after this 

READ: Analyst: VP Sara didn’t declare P817-million wealth

When Vinluan proceeded to qualify the witness as an expert, House prosecutor Chel Diokno objected.

“I’m very sorry to interrupt the defense and the witness. But may I know the relevance of this line of questioning?” Diokno asked.

“The witness apparently is delivering his credentials on anti-money laundering, but the respondent in this case is not being charged with any money laundering crimes. The issues before this court are all centered on unexplained wealth, non-declaration of SALN (statement of assets, liabilities and net worth), and participation in business. And I haven’t heard anything from this witness that would qualify him on those matters,” he said.

Vinluan claimed that the articles of impeachment contained allegations “pertaining to money laundering and other related matters.”

Article continues after this 

“In fact, Your Honor, they presented an AMLC (Anti-Money Laundering Council) witness and they made interpretations on the data as well. They also presented their own witness, Your Honor. So it is our position that, Your Honor, that we also have the prerogative to present our own expert on the matter,” he said.

Diokno refuted this, saying there was not a single word in the articles of impeachment lodged against Duterte that referred to the respondent committing any crime under money laundering.

Article continues after this 

When Vinluan said he would show it to the court later, the prosecutor challenged him to point to the specific allegation in the articles of impeachment.

“Because an allegation like that is too serious to let pass,” Diokno said. “I hope that I will count you to it, counsel, that you will show it at the point you decide to.”

Presiding Officer and Sen. Francis Escudero intervened, explaining that qualifying the witness as an expert only meant that he could give his opinion.

“Not that it’s gospel truth, not that it’s the truth, not that it’s accurate, not that it’s correct, but only to allow the witness to give his opinion if he is qualified as an expert witness,” Escudero said.

“He will be testifying to giving his opinion on documents identified, AMLC documents identified, presented, offered, and allowed by this court,” the presiding officer added.

But Diokno stood pat, refusing to stipulate to the defense’s bid to qualify the witness as an expert on the AMLC documents previously presented before the court.

Later in the proceedings, the counsel for the defense pointed to a portion in the articles of impeachment where “money laundering” was mentioned.

Vinluan said page 4 of the articles of impeachment reads: “Relevantly, the investigation reports from the AMLC on respondent and her spouse indicate that the bank transactions involving their bank accounts may have been involved in predicate offenses of money laundering.”

While he said the prosecution was accusing Duterte of accumulating more than P800 million in explained wealth, the defense lawyer noted that the articles of impeachment merely indicated “may have been involved in predicate offenses.”

“My question is this. Based on your knowledge and experience as a financial investigator, how important is it to be certain with accusations of unlawful activity and or money laundering?” Vinluan asked the witness.

Diokno objected even before the witness could answer the question.

“The question is misleading. The quoted portion ‘may have been involved in predicate offenses’—it’s not part of the substantive charges that are pending before this court,” the prosecutor said.

He pointed out that the main issues brought before the court were Duterte’s unexplained wealth, failure to declare all her assets in her SALNs, and continued participation in business.

World.title: Sandiganbayan tags Zaldy Co’s 3 co-accused as fugitives
World.content:
Facade of the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City. INQUIRER PHOTO

MANILA, Philippines — The Sandiganbayan Fifth Division has declared three co-accused of former lawmaker Zaldy Co as fugitives and ordered their passports canceled.

In a resolution promulgated on Nov. 10, the court granted the prosecution’s motion to declare Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) material engineer Timojen Sacar and Sunwest board members Anthony Ngo and Consuelo Aldon fugitives.

The prosecution also invoked Republic Act No. 11983, or the New Philippine Passport Act, which authorizes the Department of Foreign Affairs to cancel passports upon court orders.

Article continues after this 

READ: Accused in flood works mess missing; ‘manhunt’ on

“ACCORDINGLY, premises considered, the prosecution’s Ex-Parte Motion to Declare as Fugitives from Justice Accused Timojen A. Sacar, Anthony L. Ngo and Consuelo D. Aldon and to Order the Cancellation of Passports is GRANTED. Accused Timojen A. Sacar, Anthony L. Ngo and Consuelo D. Aldon are DECLARED FUGITIVES FROM JUSTICE,” the resolution, penned by Associate Justice Zaldy Trespeses, read.

The court noted that the three co-accused remained at large despite the issuance of arrest warrants against them in November 2025. The warrants were issued in connection with the graft case involving an alleged substandard P289.5-million flood control project in Oriental Mindoro.

The court also said the co-accused were aware of the criminal proceedings and the arrest warrants issued against them, given the high-profile nature of the case.

“Thus, by staying beyond the reach of law enforcement while fully aware of pending warrants of arrest confirms accused’s deliberate intent to evade judicial process. By choosing to remain at large for nearly a year, accused Sacar, Ngo, and Aldon have rendered themselves fugitives from justice,” it added.

Article continues after this 

READ: Witness: Zaldy Co’s alleged kickbacks have acknowledgement receipts

The court also said that canceling their passports “is an essential remedy to address the flight risk posed by individuals facing criminal charges, thereby safeguarding the administration of criminal justice.”

Article continues after this 

It noted that the order would prevent them from leaving the country to evade the judicial process. /mcm

World.title: Myanmar Regime Chief to Review Relations With ASEAN After Manila Snub
World.content:
Myanmar coup leader-turned-president Min Aung Hlaing said on Wednesday his regime will review its relations with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in response to statements issued by the bloc at its recent summit in the Philippines.

In a three-hour speech to the military-dominated parliament in Naypyitaw, the regime chief decried the “unreasonable” position on Myanmar taken by the bloc, whose leaders met in Manila this week.

“During the ASEAN Summit held in recent days, we saw unreasonable statements… I would like to say that we have also decided to review how we will proceed with our future relations with ASEAN,” he said.

At the 49th regional summit in the Philippine capital, ASEAN leaders agreed to extend a ban on Myanmar regime leaders attending the bloc’s summit meetings, citing “insufficient progress” in implementing its Five-Point Consensus (5PC) peace plan.

In a statement, the leaders reaffirmed that the consensus remains the bloc’s main reference for addressing Myanmar’s political crisis, while agreeing to continue engagement with the country. Myanmar was represented at the summit only by a non-political representative, Han Win Aung, director-general of the regime’s ASEAN Affairs Department.

ASEAN adopted the 5PC in April 2021, calling for an immediate end to violence and dialogue among all parties. However, the regime failed to implement the agreement and subsequently rejected it.

On Wednesday, Min Aung Hlaing again claimed that he had never agreed to the consensus and accused ASEAN of selectively abandoning its longstanding principle of non-interference in the internal affairs of member states.

He argued that ASEAN’s position did not represent the views of all its members, but was instead driven by the prejudices of three countries, which he did not identify.

He further accused the bloc of applying pressure exclusively on Myanmar despite political crises, election disputes and public protests in other member states.

“No other ASEAN member state has faced such political pressure or been subjected to attempts to discredit it. We see these actions being directed specifically at Myanmar,” he argued.

Since assuming the presidency, Min Aung Hlaing has visited several ASEAN member states in an apparent effort to restore Myanmar’s standing within the regional bloc. The diplomatic push failed to win him admittance to the latest summit, however.

The regime chief claimed the visits showed that some ASEAN member states wanted to restore normal relations with Myanmar.

“We have visited neighboring countries, including Laos, Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia and Malaysia. During these visits, the leaders of these countries openly expressed their desire for Myanmar to have normal relations within ASEAN. Some told us they wanted to see us at ASEAN meetings. Some spoke to us privately in a friendly manner, while others raised the matter during meetings. This shows that the position being pursued within ASEAN does not represent the wishes of all member states,” he said.

According to AFP, Min Aung Hlaing also told Parliament that talks were ongoing with the U.S., which shunned his country after the 2021 putsch but is now eyeing its rare earth resources.

“Now, we have discussions with our adversary, great power the United States, which has been constantly having issues with us,” the former general said.

“There is a certain level of engagement anyway. However, it has not yet been fully finalized. Relations and discussions are ongoing.”

Citing media reports, AFP said US Assistant Secretary of State for Intelligence and Research Michael Vance joined talks with Min Aung Hlaing in Naypyitaw in September, in the highest-level publicly reported contact between the two countries since the coup.

The discussions reportedly focused on securing the release of a US businessman detained in Myanmar.

According to Khin Ohmar, a prominent Myanmar democracy activist and founder of the Progressive Voice human rights organization, ASEAN said it would consider gradually restoring Myanmar’s political representation only when there is real, concrete progress on the 5PC. “If holding this criminal military junta, which has broken its promises for five years, bombed villages, schools and hospitals, blocked aid, and kept more than 15,000 political prisoners in detention, to this minimum standard is unreasonable, then nothing is reasonable,” she said.

Describing the junta as “brazen,” she accused it of complaining about the consequences of its own crimes. “The one who tried to seize the people’s power by force, who is bombing the people, who is turning international aid meant for the people into a weapon, saying ASEAN is unreasonable is laughable. ASEAN does not need reviewing. It is the junta that needs reviewing. Stop the attacks. Release all political prisoners. Let aid reach the people without discrimination,” she said.

She added that the junta is not Myanmar’s government and therefore has no role in reviewing the relationship with ASEAN on behalf of the state or the Myanmar people.

Thinzar Shunlei Yi, a Myanmar democracy and human rights activist, urged ASEAN to continue to put strategic pressure on the junta and not to “play its game.”

Myanmar joined ASEAN in 1997.

World.title: ASEAN Leaders Accused of Enabling Myanmar Regime Atrocities
World.content:
Rights group Justice for Myanmar (JFM) has accused ASEAN leaders meeting in Manila of maintaining a status quo that enables Myanmar’s military regime to wage a terror campaign against civilians with impunity.

The bloc is aiding the regime’s war crimes through military engagement and a business-as-usual approach, JFM said on Tuesday as the 49th ASEAN Summit wrapped up.

While putschist president Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership remain barred from ASEAN summits over their failure to implement the bloc’s Five-Point Consensus (5PC), JFM noted that regime personnel still participate in regional meetings, defense training and military exercises. Participants include regime army, navy and police officers who are directly responsible for perpetrating war crimes under the guise of “counter-terrorism,” it added.

In September, JFM reported that regime officials have been invited to an upcoming ASEAN Regional Forum workshop on countering drone warfare, warning that the move risked technology and knowledge transfer to a military that routinely bombs civilians, schools, and hospitals.

“The Myanmar junta is a criminal cartel that should be held accountable for its international crimes, not allowed to join meetings, training, and workshops,” JFM spokesperson Yadanar Maung told The Irrawaddy.

Regional cooperation only emboldens the regime to commit war crimes and crimes against humanity, she added.

Although barred from the Manila summit, regime Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin attended the 27th ASEAN Chiefs of Army Multilateral Meeting (ACAMM) in Malaysia on Tuesday.

JFM stated ASEAN’s 5PC peace plan has served as a diplomatic smokescreen while member countries and businesses continue to supply the regime with funds, weapons, and aviation fuel. It accused Thailand’s state-owned PTT energy conglomerate and Vietnam’s Viettel of bankrolling the military regime through natural gas imports and a telecoms partnership respectively.

Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand also permit domestic companies to broker sales of arms, equipment and aviation fuel to the regime, bypassing international sanctions, JFM noted, urging ASEAN to stop enabling the war crimes of a “criminal regime.”

Prominent human rights activist Thinzar Shunlei Yi said the 5PC had failed to curb civilian atrocities in Myanmar.

“They [ASEAN] must recognize that penalties imposed on the junta in 2021 were weak in their impact, which is why the violations continue,” she commented, calling for broader and more severe sanctions against the regime.

The Myanmar Defense & Security Institute (MDSI), a research institute founded by military defectors, reports the regime conducted 161 airstrikes in October alone, killing 145 civilians and injuring 316 others.

World.title: Regime’s Air War in Arakan: Territorial Losses and the Growing Civilian Toll
World.content:
Myanmar’s military has lost control of much of Arakan (Rakhine) State, but it retains the power to inflict devastating destruction from the air.

Across the western state, the dangers of war extend far beyond the front lines. Airstrikes have devastated markets, damaged medical facilities, struck displacement camps and disrupted vital transport routes, leaving civilians to bear the consequences of a conflict that shows little sign of ending.

These attacks raise a troubling question: As Myanmar’s military loses territory to the Arakan Army (AA), is airpower becoming a means not only of pursuing military objectives, but also of undermining civilian life in areas beyond its control?

The question matters because the consequences extend far beyond immediate casualties. They threaten livelihoods, essential services and the ability of communities to recover from years of conflict.

Losing territory, retaining the power to strike

Since fighting resumed in November 2023, the AA, an ethnic armed organization seeking greater autonomy for Arakan, has captured most of the state from Myanmar’s military.

These losses have weakened the military’s ground positions, administrative authority and political influence. Yet losing territory does not mean losing the ability to wage war.

The military continues to use aircraft, naval firepower and long-range artillery to attack areas it can no longer effectively control on the ground.

As efforts to regain territory become increasingly difficult, airpower allows the military to exert pressure without maintaining a physical presence.

This creates a fundamental distinction between territorial control and destructive capability.

The military may no longer govern much of Arakan, but it retains the ability to make civilian life extraordinarily difficult.

For communities living under the threat of bombardment, changes in territorial control have not necessarily brought greater security.

Markets and hospitals: the wider cost of airstrikes

One of the deadliest reported attacks occurred on September 28, when military airstrikes hit the area around India Market and Kissapanadi Bridge in Kyauktaw.

According to Development Media Group (DMG), at least 50 civilians were killed and 58 injured. The United Nations cited similar reported figures, while independent investigators confirmed evidence of an airstrike and extensive damage but could not verify the full casualty toll.

The attack illustrates how aerial bombardment can devastate communities beyond the immediate loss of life.

Markets are essential to local economies. They support traders, transport workers, small businesses and families dependent on daily commerce.

When a marketplace is destroyed, livelihoods disappear, supply chains are disrupted and access to food and other necessities becomes more difficult.

In Arakan, where years of fighting and restrictions on movement have already undermined trade and driven up living costs, such destruction deepens an existing humanitarian crisis.

Healthcare facilities have also suffered.

On November 1, an airstrike damaged a temporary maternity ward in Mrauk-U. Five people, including a newborn baby, were reportedly killed. The incident was documented by Reuters and condemned by Médecins Sans Frontières (Doctors Without Borders).

The consequences extend beyond those directly affected.

When hospitals and clinics become unsafe, pregnant women may delay essential care, patients may avoid treatment, and already overstretched healthcare services may struggle to continue operating.

In a region facing serious shortages of medicines, medical personnel and equipment, the loss of even one functioning clinic can endanger many more lives.

The destruction of markets and medical facilities therefore cannot be measured solely by casualty figures. Its longer-term effects on livelihoods, public health and community survival must also be considered.

Nowhere safe for the displaced

The dangers are especially severe for people who have already fled their homes.

On November 13, a military airstrike hit the Byarla camp for internally displaced persons in Ponnagyun Township, killing 12 people, including children, and injuring 18 others, according to local rescue workers and witnesses.

The same camp had reportedly been bombed in October, killing six displaced people.

These incidents expose the extreme vulnerability of communities displaced by war.

Families who flee their homes often arrive at displacement camps with few possessions, limited access to food and healthcare, and little prospect of returning home.

When those places of refuge are also attacked, displacement becomes an ongoing struggle for survival rather than a temporary escape from danger.

Beyond the immediate casualties, repeated attacks can destroy shelters, interrupt humanitarian assistance and inflict lasting psychological trauma.

They also place additional pressure on local authorities and humanitarian organizations already operating with limited resources.

Damaged bridges, isolated communities

Roads and bridges have also been affected by military attacks.

In early November, airstrikes damaged transport infrastructure in Kyauktaw Township. Further attacks affecting bridges elsewhere in Arakan were reported later in the month by local sources and the AA.

Bridges may serve military purposes, but they are also essential to civilian life.

They connect farmers to markets, patients to hospitals, and communities to food, medicines and humanitarian assistance.

Their destruction can isolate entire communities, increase transport costs and further restrict access to essential services.

Under international humanitarian law, a bridge may constitute a legitimate military objective under certain circumstances. However, attacks must still comply with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precautions to protect civilians.

The central questions are whether a particular structure was a military objective, what military advantage was anticipated, and whether foreseeable civilian harm was excessive in relation to that advantage.

Not every attack on infrastructure is automatically unlawful. But a claimed military purpose does not justify unlimited civilian suffering.

A strategy of destabilization?

Taken together, attacks affecting markets, hospitals, displacement camps and transport networks have consequences extending far beyond the immediate battlefield.

Destroyed markets weaken local commerce. Damaged medical facilities undermine healthcare. Disrupted transport routes restrict the movement of people and supplies. Attacks on displacement camps increase humanitarian needs.

Collectively, these effects can make AA-controlled territories more difficult to administer.

The AA must devote scarce resources to emergency relief, infrastructure repairs, medical assistance and the restoration of essential services, even as it continues military operations.

This raises the possibility that Myanmar’s military views airpower as a means of weakening the AA’s ability to govern territories it has captured.

Unable to regain control on the ground, the military may seek to impose economic, humanitarian and administrative costs from the air.

Myanmar’s military authorities have maintained that their operations target armed opponents and have rejected allegations that they deliberately attack civilians. However, the scale and repeated nature of civilian harm demand closer scrutiny.

The consequences of an attack do not, by themselves, establish its intended purpose.

Determining whether civilian infrastructure is being deliberately targeted as part of a broader strategy requires credible evidence concerning military orders, target selection and operational decisions.

Even without establishing a single overarching strategy, the repeated devastation of civilian communities raises serious questions about the military’s conduct of hostilities.

Civilian protection and accountability

International humanitarian law requires all parties to armed conflict to distinguish between civilians and combatants, and between civilian objects and military objectives.

It prohibits intentionally directing attacks against civilians, indiscriminate attacks, and attacks expected to cause excessive civilian harm in relation to the concrete and direct military advantage anticipated.

Attacks affecting hospitals, schools, displacement camps and populated areas therefore warrant credible, independent investigation.

Whether particular incidents constitute war crimes must be established through evidence and applicable legal standards.

Nevertheless, repeated civilian deaths cannot simply be dismissed as an inevitable consequence of war.

Accurate documentation by independent journalists, humanitarian organizations and investigators is essential to establishing what happened and preserving evidence for future accountability.

These legal obligations apply to every party to the conflict, including Myanmar’s military and the AA.

The AA’s responsibilities beyond military victory

As the AA consolidates control over much of Arakan, its responsibilities extend beyond military success.

Capturing territory does not automatically guarantee the safety and welfare of the population.

The AA must increasingly address civilian protection, early-warning systems, emergency shelters, healthcare access and assistance for displaced communities.

It must also take feasible precautions to reduce risks to civilians in areas under its control.

These responsibilities are particularly demanding in a region facing continued aerial attacks, economic disruption and limited humanitarian access.

Ultimately, the credibility of any governing authority depends not only on the territory it controls but also on its ability to protect civilians and provide essential services.

Military victories alone cannot establish effective governance.

The real test beyond the battlefield

Arakan’s war has exposed a widening gap between territorial control and civilian security.

The AA controls much of the state, yet it cannot fully prevent airstrikes against communities under its authority.

Meanwhile, Myanmar’s military retains the capacity to destroy infrastructure and disrupt civilian life, even where its administrative control has collapsed.

But destruction cannot restore political legitimacy. Nor can the fear created by aerial bombardment be mistaken for genuine public support.

The future of Arakan will not be determined solely by the number of townships controlled by either side.

It will also depend on whether children can safely attend school, patients can reach hospitals, traders can rebuild their livelihoods, and displaced families can eventually return home.

Myanmar’s military may have lost much of Arakan, but it retains the power to destroy. Yet the ability to destroy is not the ability to govern, and civilian fear is no substitute for political legitimacy.

The ultimate measure of the conflict will lie not only in military victories or territorial gains, but in whether the lives, security and fundamental rights of civilians can be protected.

Aung Marm Oo is the editor-in-chief and executive director of Development Media Group, a news agency based in Arakan. He faces charges under Myanmar’s Unlawful Associations Act and has been in hiding since May 2019.

World.title: Regime Blames Thailand for Border Scam Hubs While Shielding Militia Allies
World.content:
The Myanmar military regime has again attempted to shift the blame to Thailand for online scam operations along the border, with Deputy Commander-in-Chief Kyaw Swar Lin calling on Bangkok to do more to cut off essential supplies to scam syndicates operating in Karen State.

During talks with Pana Claewplodtook, commander-in-chief of the Royal Thai Army, on the sidelines of the 27th ASEAN Chiefs of Army Multilateral Meeting in Malaysia on Monday, Kyaw Swar Lin said Thailand should cooperate in blocking the flow of food supplies, fuel, electricity and telecommunications services used by scam syndicates operating along the border, according to regime media.

The regime said the meeting also covered military-to-military cooperation, border security and efforts to combat narcotics trafficking and illegal cross-border trade.

The junta has repeatedly sought to blame Thailand for the flourishing online scam industry centered on Myawaddy and Shwe Kokko on the Thai-Myanmar frontier. Since early 2025, regime officials have argued that scam compounds rely on electricity, internet connections and other logistical support originating from the Thai side of the border.

Kyaw Swar Lin also told the Thai army chief that scam syndicates were operating under the protection of certain insurgent groups, as he sought to distance the Myanmar military from notorious scam hubs. He did not mention, however, that the organizations he blamed are aligned with the Myanmar military.

Among the most notorious figures linked to the industry is Border Guard Force commander Colonel Saw Chit Thu, whose forces control Shwe Kokko and who has been sanctioned by the U.S. over his alleged involvement in online scams.

International pressure on scam networks along the Thai-Myanmar border has intensified since last year. The United States and China have both pushed for tougher action against syndicates operating in Karen State. The FBI is collaborating with the Royal Thai Police to crack down on the scam industry on the border, including Chinese transnational criminal organizations, which, according to U.S. officials, defraud Americans of US$10 billion annually from scam centers based in Myanmar, Laos and Cambodia.

Political analyst Htin Kyaw Aye said the regime was trying to distance itself from online scam operations as both Washington and Beijing view the issue as a top priority.

“Given that these major powers are treating the issue with such concern, it is hardly surprising that the military regime is scrambling to deny any involvement and distance itself from the problem.”

The U.S. Embassy in Yangon on Monday again shared a reward offer of up to US$10 million for information leading to the recovery of assets linked to the Tai Chang scam network operating in areas controlled by the junta-aligned Democratic Karen Benevolent Army. The same day, Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia, arrived in Bangkok to discuss joint efforts against transnational scam networks.

Earlier this month, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi told the Myanmar regime to prevent a “resurgence of chaos” in Myawaddy, months after Beijing hailed the “success” of a trilateral mechanism involving Bangkok and Naypyitaw launched in March 2025 to fight scam compounds in the border town.

While the regime portrays the fight against online scams as a national priority, the industry has spread far beyond the borderlands. Recent crackdowns have uncovered scam operations in Yangon and Mandalay, reinforcing findings that syndicates have established permanent footholds in Myanmar’s major cities while continuing to operate from militia-controlled enclaves along the Chinese and Thai borders.

In October, Kyaw Swar Lin warned senior army officers to steer clear of fraud, online gambling and narcotics.

“It is common knowledge that various levels of the regime have been involved and benefited from online scam operations and the drug trade, and are implicated in those activities,” said Htin Kyaw Aye.

Former regime spokesman Major General Zaw Min Tun previously acknowledged that senior officials from regional and state governments had been implicated in online scam operations and that major disciplinary action had been required against some of those involved.

World.title: Regime Minister Turns to Migrant Workers in Malaysia to Plug Foreign Currency Gap
World.content:
Regime Labor Minister Maung Myint, admitted while talking to Myanmar workers in Malaysia last week that the junta is increasingly relying on migrant workers to bring in foreign currency as sanctions and declining export earnings squeeze its finances.

“The world sanctions us,” Maung Myint said during his visit to the country. He also claimed that one of the reasons for the decline in Myanmar’s international revenue was that the regime had deliberately “reduced” exports of natural resources.

Following the 2021 coup, Western countries and blocs including the U.S., the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada imposed targeted economic sanctions on senior Myanmar regime officials, including coup leader Min Aung Hlaing, as well as state enterprises and military-controlled banks.

The sanctions remain in place, leaving some foreign development assistance programs suspended and interrupting international banking transfers, fueling the country’s foreign currency shortage and exacerbating an economic crisis caused by the regime’s mismanagement.

While Maung Myint claimed the regime had deliberately reduced natural-resource exports for environmental reasons, a World Bank report suggests that natural gas exports to Thailand and China—one of Myanmar’s major sources of foreign income—dropped by US$200 million in 2025-26 due to “reduced output” from existing offshore operations.

As international sanctions began to bite, the regime imposed remittance rules and enforced tax laws targeting overseas workers in 2023, aiming to extract funds from them. Foreign remittance value reached US$5.6 billion in 2025, and Maung Myint is hoping to match that figure this year.

“We’re trying to cover the shrinking income with remittances from workers,” he said in a video posted on his TikTok channel on Sunday.

He added that the rules and restrictions targeting migrant workers would be only temporary, claiming that potential increases in revenue from rare earths and a major deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea would eliminate the need for them.

However, he cautioned that rare earth sites “are not under the government’s control,” and are a “prospect” for foreign revenue once the regime gains control of them.

The majority of Myanmar’s approximately 600 rare-earth mining sites are concentrated on the China-Myanmar border in Kachin State under the control of the Kachin Independence Army. The rest also lie beyond the Myanmar regime’s control in eastern Shan State, in territory run by armed groups over which China exerts a great influence, including the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Its lack of control over these deposits deprives the regime of billions of dollars in potential revenue, as global powers like the U.S. and India court it for access to the critical minerals.

He said the deep-water drilling project in the Andaman Sea’s Block M-15 could earn $400-500 billion. According to the World Bank report, the project could produce up to 94.6 trillion cubic feet of usable gas “if confirmed”, but its output “is not expected soon.”

Maung Myint last week turned his focus to Malaysia, which hosts the second-largest population of Myanmar migrant workers, after his efforts to extract more foreign currency met with resistance from migrant workers in Thailand.

Since being appointed labor minister in October, he has been pushing hard for workers to comply with the new remittance and tax rules, particularly the Certification of Identity (CI) process.

The push sparked widespread boycotts in Thailand, where only 15,000 of nearly 750,000 undocumented Myanmar workers applied for the CI. Workers refused to apply for fear of funding the military’s war on civilians and exposing themselves to military conscription.

In Malaysia, he used flattery, calling workers national “heroes” and comparing them to soldiers who “sacrifice their time with families to serve the country.”

World.title: All Quiet in Northern Shan—and for Good Reason
World.content:
For several months, speculation has swirled over whether northern Shan State could see a return of resistance offensives on the scale of Operation 1027. But what is the likelihood of a resurgence of fighting?

The speculation appears to stem from signs of friction between Beijing and Myanmar’s military regime over how the ethnic armed organizations are to be managed, as well as the regime’s recent efforts to restore ties with the U.S. and Japan.

Yet the differences between China and the military regime are not fundamental—they do not amount to a strategic or ideological split.

China has not abandoned its long-held view that the military is a central pillar in maintaining stability in Myanmar. What has changed is Beijing’s growing recognition that the crisis cannot be managed through the military alone.

The fact that Beijing now acknowledges other forces has become a source of discomfort for the regime. But that is not a policy shift, only a tactical adjustment in how China seeks to implement its existing policy.

Beijing’s position on border stability remains unchanged. China does not want to see a return of armed conflicts to northern Shan, which shares a 200-km stretch of border with Yunnan.

All the rare-earth mines and other major investments operating in areas controlled by Myanmar National Democratic Alliance Army (MNDAA) and Ta’ang National Liberation Army (TNLA) in northern Shan involve Chinese capital. Given the technical requirements involved in rare-earth extraction, the companies operating these projects are more likely to be state-linked Chinese enterprises than private firms. The Chinese government is unlikely to allow such investments to be jeopardized.

One point of frustration for China has been the regime’s handling of border trade. Naypyitaw frequently claims that cross-border trade was disrupted by ethnic armed organizations (EAOs) that now control the major border trade routes. Yet Beijing is well aware that the military has also restricted border trade with Thailand, even though it fully controls the trade corridor there. From China’s perspective, regime policy puts up more barriers to trade than the MNDAA or TNLA.

Estimated at US$6 billion annually, that business is relatively small compared with the scale of the Chinese economy. The more pressing concern for Beijing has been online scam operations. Since the MNDAA and TNLA established control over large parts of the border, scam syndicates targeting Chinese citizens have been brought under much tighter control. The central military regime, by contrast, failed for years to address the problem.

Chinese policymakers may therefore calculate that restoring central military control across northern Shan could revive the criminal networks Beijing has made considerable effort suppressing. The financial and political costs of that scenario would surely outweigh the benefits of expanded border trade.

The EAOs themselves have little incentive to launch new offensives. The MNDAA and TNLA now control substantially more territory than before Operation 1027, and arguably more than they had dared to dream of. Having achieved those objectives, neither group has a pressing need to expend additional force.

Beijing may have a similar view and is therefore likely to restrain them from fighting the regime again. That means there is virtually no prospect of the MNDAA or TNLA initiating hostilities. The only realistic scenario under which fighting might resume would be if the military regime attacks first.

For its part, Naypyitaw expects China to pressure EAOs to return all the territories in northern Shan State to it. That is how the regime recovered the northern Shan capital of Lashio. Chinese Special Envoy Deng Xijun’s recent proposal of “high-level autonomy” for ethnic forces was therefore a bitter pill for the regime to swallow. And soon after Deng made the proposal, the regime dispatched reconnaissance planes to northern Shan.

Having survived the military disasters of 2023 and 2024 in large part because of Chinese intervention, the military’s top brass is now dreaming of eventually reclaiming all lost territory by force. Such thinking is hardly surprising for an institution that seized power by forced and continues to view military means as the answer to political problems.

But here dreams and reality collide. Before Operation 1027, the Northeastern Command was backed by roughly 20 infantry and light infantry battalions, in addition to artillery, logistics and support units. It was further reinforced by as many as seven or eight division-sized formations rotated through the theater.

That force no longer exists. Now only about 10 infantry and light infantry battalions remain under Northeastern Command, dispersed across Muse, Tangyan and Mongyai. The military now fields only a single major combat formation across the region, spread among Nantlan, Kyaukme, Hsipaw and Nawnghkio, while smaller units are deployed in Mongmit and Mogoke.

Indeed, since the ceasefire with the MNDAA and TNLA, the regime has moved an estimated seven division-sized formations out of northern Shan State to active fronts in Rakhine, Chin, Magwe, Sagaing and Mandalay.

That mean it simply does not have the strength to maintain more than a presence in northern Shan and hold existing positions. The convoys that are regularly observed traveling between Taunggyi, Kho Lam, Mong Nawng, Mongyai and Tangyan do not represent substantial reinforcements: they mainly transport batches of new recruits to and from military training facilities.

The military’s ability to sustain operations elsewhere, then, depends heavily on the fact that northern Shan remains relatively quiet. To reopen that front, it would first have to withdraw troops from other battlefields, which would risk repeating the overstretch that contributed to the military’s earlier defeats.

In essence, the regime would be creating a new battlefield at a time when it can barely manage the existing ones.

No matter how much it resents the loss of northern Shan’s borders, there is nothing it can do about it. In addition, any attempt to violate the Beijing-brokered ceasefire could invite retaliation from China itself. Unlike Thailand, which has repeatedly shown restraint when fighting spills across its border, Beijing is unlikely to tolerate renewed instability along a frontier it regards as strategically vital.

In other words, the regime would be digging its own grave.

Moe Set Nyein Chan is a military analyst

World.title: Dozens of Civilians Killed in Myanmar Regime Strikes as ASEAN Leaders Meet
World.content:
The Myanmar regime has continued bombing civilian targets nationwide after its leaders were barred from attending the ongoing 49th ASEAN Summit for rejecting the bloc’s peace plan.

Rakhine State has borne the brunt of attacks, which have killed over a dozen civilians in the past week as the ethnic Arkan Army (AA) pushes to seize the state capital, Sittwe, and Kyaukphyu, home to China-backed mega projects.

Junta warplanes pounded residential areas in the AA-held town of Kyauktaw on Monday night, but casualty figures were unclear as of press time. The strike followed an Oct. 28 attack on the town’s busy market that killed 50 civilians including children and wounded 60, drawing international condemnation.

The AA also reported another deadly strike on a displacement camp in Ponnagyun Township on Friday evening. Twelve people were killed and 18 injured as blasts ripped through the Byar La shelter for war-displaced civilians. The attack came just weeks after two regime fighter jets bombed the same IDP camp, killing eight civilians and destroying homes and shops on October 4.

The airstrikes continued Sunday as ASEAN leaders gathered for their summit in Manila, with Myanmar’s crisis topping the agenda.

Blasts destroyed bridges in the Rakhine townships of Minbya and Ramree, according to the AA. The attacks followed a Nov. 1 airstrike on a Kyauktaw bridge that killed seven commuters and injured seven others.

Meanwhile, the regime’s Taung Maw Oo naval base used drones and artillery to destroy around 60 homes Kyaukphyu’s Sane town at the weekend, months after it was abandoned by civilians.

Former army captain Zin Yaw, who defected following the 2021 coup, said the regime is targeting bridges to cut supply lines of the AA, which is pushing to seize the regime’s last remaining toeholds in Rakhine.

“The regime has failed to meet its military objectives, so it is now attempting to destroy the enemy’s administrative and supply chains,” he said.

Wai Hun Aung, a prominent Rakhine writer and relief worker, said regime forces are destroying bridges to slow the AA’s advance.

The AA has seized 14 out of Rakhine’s 17 townships plus Paletwa Township in neighboring Chin State since launching a major offensive in November 2023.

The ethnic army has also expanded offensives across the border into Magwe, Bago and Ayeyarwady regions.

World.title: UN Chief Backs Engagement With Myanmar But ‘Violence Needs to Stop’
World.content:
MANILA—UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres expressed support Monday for fresh diplomatic efforts to engage with Myanmar’s post-coup government, but said that “violence needs to stop.”

Guterres made the remarks in Manila, where leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) agreed Sunday to pursue a “calibrated engagement” with the war-torn country.

Myanmar has been excluded from high-level ASEAN meetings since a military junta seized power in a coup in 2021, but the regional bloc is seeking a path towards normalizing diplomatic relations.

“We have never opposed the idea that it is always necessary to engage with whoever is involved in a conflict,” Guterres told a press conference on the sidelines of the ASEAN summit.

While “engagement is not appeasement,” Guterres said the “intolerable violations of human rights in Myanmar” must end.

“Violence needs to stop, humanitarian access needs to be granted, and all those arbitrarily detained must be immediately released,” Guterres said.

“And these are the conditions that could allow for what everybody should will [to happen], which is that Myanmar will find a way to move… to a true democratic situation.”

Thailand has been leading efforts to normalize relations with Myanmar since coup leader Min Aung Hlaing was installed as civilian president this year following elections dismissed by monitors as a charade.

Bangkok has called for a “calibrated engagement” in an effort to implement ASEAN’s long-languishing five-point plan to end the war between the military and a coalition of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic minority armed groups.

ASEAN leaders adopted that language on Sunday in calling for the pursuit of “a calibrated engagement with Myanmar through a phased and progress-based approach,” according to the joint statement.

Guterres’s remarks came as the UN’s International Court of Justice prepares to rule on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalized Muslim Rohingya minority.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Oil and Coal Output Rises as Gas and Copper Production Falls, Eni Reports
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan posted growth in oil and coal production in 2025, while natural gas and copper output declined, revealing contrasting trends across the country’s energy and mineral industries, according to Italian energy company Eni’s World Energy Review 2026.

The report, released on Nov. 2, examines global energy production, consumption and trade, as well as developments in critical minerals and renewable energy.

Kazakhstan’s oil production, including crude and unconventional oil and natural gas liquids, increased 11.8% to 2.098 million barrels per day in 2025, up from 1.876 million barrels per day a year earlier.

The country remained Central Asia’s largest oil producer, accounting for approximately 88% of the region’s combined output. Turkmenistan followed with 200,000 barrels per day, while Uzbekistan produced 81,000 barrels per day.

The increase preceded a sharp contraction in global oil demand in 2026. According to the International Energy Agency’s (IEA) November Oil Market Report, worldwide oil consumption is projected to fall by 2.7 million barrels per day this year to 102.3 million barrels per day, amid supply disruptions and elevated fuel prices.

The IEA expects demand to rebound by two million barrels per day in 2027, with liquefied petroleum gas, ethane and naphtha accounting for approximately 80% of the increase as supply chains normalize.

The agency also said the global oil market shows “tentative signs of rebalancing.” Global oil supplies have for the first time exceeded demand since the war in Iran.

Coal

Coal production in Kazakhstan also increased, rising 6.7% to 106 million tons, compared with 99 million tons in 2024. Kazakhstan ranked ninth among the world’s largest coal producers and recorded the fastest annual growth among the top 10.

The increase contrasted with a marginal decline in global coal production, which fell 0.1% to 8.825 billion tons in 2025. China remained the world’s largest coal producer, accounting for more than half of global output.

Natural gas

Natural gas production followed a different path, falling 6.1% to 28.21 billion cubic meters in 2025, down from 30.04 billion cubic meters in 2024. Kazakhstan remained the third-largest natural gas producer in Central Asia, behind Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

According to the report, Turkmenistan produced 72.48 billion cubic meters, a decline of 1.4%, while Uzbekistan increased production by 2.4% to 40.16 billion cubic meters.

Copper production

The report also highlighted Kazakhstan’s position in global mineral production. Kazakhstan produced an estimated 710,000 metric tons of mined copper in 2025, down from 724,000 metric tons in 2024 and 740,000 metric tons in 2023.

The country accounted for approximately 3.1% of global copper production, placing it among the world’s 10 largest producers. The decline comes as global copper mine production reached 23.01 million metric tons in 2025.

Copper is an important material for electricity networks, renewable energy technologies and industrial manufacturing, making its production increasingly significant to global energy supply chains.

According to the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), global demand for the metal is projected to increase by more than 40% by 2040, driven by the expansion of renewable energy, electricity grids, electric vehicles and digital infrastructure.

Profound transformation

The findings come against a backdrop of growing global energy demand. According to Eni, worldwide energy consumption rose by just over 1% to approximately 15.7 billion tons of oil equivalent in 2025, while oil, natural gas and coal continued to account for around 80% of the global primary energy mix.

Eni said the report reflects an “energy system undergoing profound transformation.” This transformation is fueled by rising energy demand stemming from AI and data centers, renewable energy development, and the “continued essential role of conventional energy sources in ensuring security, continuity and affordability.”

Beyond fossil fuels, Kazakhstan also maintained a leading position in the region in terms of wind power capacity. According to Eni, the country’s installed wind power capacity reached 1,909 megawatts in 2025, compared with 1,652 megawatts in Uzbekistan. Kazakhstan recorded a 25.6% increase in wind power capacity.

Financial analyst Andrey Chebotarev, founder of FINANCE.kz Telegram channel, said the findings underscore Kazakhstan’s dominant position in Central Asia’s energy sector but also highlight the importance of using revenue from traditional energy resources to develop other industries.

He emphasized that Kazakhstan’s leadership in oil and coal production provides an important economic advantage, but maintaining that position should not become an end in itself.

World.title: Four Kazakh Boxers Reach No. 1 in World Boxing Ranking
World.content:
