World.title: Part of Crimean Bridge collapses into sea: what damage to one of Kremlin’s key propaganda symbols means
World.content:
On 17 November 2026, the Crimean Bridge, which spans the Kerch Strait, was severely damaged in another Ukrainian attack. Video footage and photographs circulating online appear to show a large metal arch and a section of the road deck collapsing into the sea. Both road and rail traffic across the bridge have been suspended.

The attack is particularly significant because the Crimean Bridge is a vital land corridor linking the Crimean Peninsula, which Russia annexed in 2014, with Russian territory. Moscow has also used the bridge to supply its military forces.

For years, the Crimean Bridge was regarded as one of Vladimir Putin’s largest infrastructure projects and a symbol of Russian control over Crimea. Its damage creates several problems at once: it complicates Russian military logistics, increases the cost of supplying Crimea and shows how difficult it is for Moscow to secure one of its most heavily protected strategic assets.

It is important to note that the collapse on 17 November was preceded by an attack on 16 November, which also reportedly damaged the bridge’s structure. This means the bridge has been hit in a series of successive strikes rather than in a single isolated incident.

According to Anton Herashchenko, an adviser to Ukraine’s interior minister, the attack involved a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile. Russian authorities confirmed the attack and the suspension of traffic across the bridge, but have yet to issue an official statement about its collapse.

The Russian outlet Agentstvo reports that federal television channels did not mention the attack on the Crimean Bridge in their morning news bulletins. Instead, they covered strikes on several bridges in Kyiv and other parts of Ukraine.

The collapsed Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

What does the collapse of the bridge arch mean from an engineering perspective?

To understand the scale of the damage to the Kerch Bridge, it is important to know how it is constructed.

The bridge is approximately 19 kilometres long and consists of two independent parallel structures: one carries road traffic and the other railway traffic.

Both structures rest on concrete supports. However, the navigable section of the Kerch Strait features large metal arch structures that support the corresponding spans and provide sufficient clearance for ships to pass underneath.

According to reports published on 17 November, a roughly 227-metre-long arch of the road bridge collapsed into the sea, along with the section of road deck connected to it. The adjacent railway arch was also damaged but has not collapsed.

Why does this matter?

The arch is not a decorative feature of the bridge but a key load-bearing element. Its damage means that the load in the affected section can no longer be safely distributed.

This creates several technical problems:

Damage to the load-bearing structure: After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles.

After the arch collapses, the affected section of the bridge can no longer support the weight of cars and heavy vehicles. Risk of damage to adjacent elements: The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans.

The failure of one major structural component can place additional stress on neighbouring supports and spans. Safety of the railway infrastructure: The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure.

The road and railway sections are separate structures, but they form part of the same transport corridor. Suspending rail traffic until the damage has been assessed is therefore a logical safety measure. Possible disruption to shipping: Debris from the collapsed structure could also obstruct the shipping channel used by vessels.

It is important to stress that the collapse of the arch does not mean the entire 19-kilometre bridge has been destroyed. However, one of its most important sections has been damaged. Restoring traffic will require a detailed structural assessment, the removal of debris and the necessary engineering and repair work.

Rebuilding such a large load-bearing element is a far more complex, time-consuming and costly process.

What does the collapse of the Kerch Bridge mean symbolically?

For Russia, the bridge is one of the most visible political symbols of the annexation of Crimea.

When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, one of Moscow’s main challenges was establishing a land link between the peninsula and Russian territory, as the Kerch Strait separates Crimea from Russia’s Krasnodar Krai. By building the bridge, the Kremlin overcame this geographical barrier.

Vladimir Putin personally championed the project. In May 2018, he drove a lorry across the bridge and officially opened its road section. The event was broadcast on Russian state television and became an important part of the Kremlin’s propaganda narrative.

For Moscow, the bridge carried several key messages:

Consolidation of the annexation of Crimea: The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory.

The bridge served as a demonstration of Russia’s integration of the peninsula into its own territory. Putin’s political project: Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities.

Its construction was presented as a personal achievement of the president and a showcase of Russia’s engineering capabilities. Demonstration of Russian control: The bridge signalled that Moscow intended to maintain a long-term presence in Crimea and had no plans to return the peninsula to Ukraine.

Russia decided to build the bridge in 2014, following its annexation of Crimea. Construction began in 2016. The road section opened on 15 May 2018, while rail traffic began in December 2019.

The bridge is considered one of the longest in Europe. Its construction cost around 228 billion roubles (approximately $3.5–3.8 billion at the exchange rate at the time).

The project involved extensive engineering work. The structure includes supports on both land and underwater, while specially designed high arches allow ships to pass through the navigable section of the strait.

After the first explosion in 2022, the damage to the bridge was seen in Ukraine as an important moral and symbolic victory. At the time, Al Jazeera reported that the attack had heightened the perception of Russia’s vulnerability.

Crimean (Kerch) Bridge

How many times has Ukraine attacked the Kerch Bridge before?

Before the attack on 17 November 2026, Ukraine had carried out three major successful operations against the Kerch Bridge. Ukrainian officials subsequently confirmed or acknowledged responsibility for them.

The strike on 16 November 2026, which directly preceded the attack on 17 November, should also be treated as a separate incident.

8 October 2022: First major explosion

A lorry travelling across the bridge exploded, damaging several road spans and causing some of them to collapse. The blast also set fuel tankers on a passing railway train on fire. Four people were killed.

Ukraine subsequently acknowledged its involvement in the attack. Repairs to the damaged sections took several months.

Damage to the Kerch Bridge on 8 October 2022

17 July 2023: Sea drone attack

Ukraine attacked the bridge using Sea Baby naval drones. The road section sustained damage, and one of its spans collapsed. Two civilians were killed in the attack, and their child was injured.

Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), later confirmed that Ukrainian forces had carried out the operation.

Sea drone attack on the Kerch Bridge in 2023

3 June 2025: Underwater explosion

Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU) detonated explosive devices near the bridge’s underwater supports. According to the Ukrainian side, the blast had an estimated force of 1,100 kilograms of TNT.

The SBU said the operation had been in preparation for several months and that the bridge’s supports had sustained significant damage. The agency claimed that the structure had been left in a critical condition.

Underwater explosion on the Kerch Bridge in 2025

16 November 2026: Another strike

The Ukrainian drone attack damaged the bridge’s structure. Russian authorities initially described the damage as minor, but traffic across the bridge was temporarily suspended and later partially restored.

16 November 2026: Another strike on the Kerch Bridge

What did Russia use the Kerch Bridge for?

For Russia, the bridge was not just a transport link for Crimea’s population. It was also one of the key logistical routes used in its war against Ukraine.

Military role

After Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, the bridge acquired particular strategic importance. It allowed Russia to transport military supplies from its territory to Crimea and then onwards to the occupied regions of southern Ukraine.

These supplies included:

military equipment and armoured vehicles;

ammunition and weapons;

fuel and other military supplies;

military personnel and logistical resources.

The bridge allowed Russian forces to move military supplies relatively quickly from Russian territory to Crimea and then distribute them towards the front line in southern Ukraine.

In March 2024, Vasyl Maliuk, head of Ukraine’s Security Service (SBU), said Russia had significantly reduced its use of the bridge to transport military equipment following Ukrainian strikes.

According to Maliuk, 42–46 trains carrying weapons and ammunition crossed the bridge every day before the attacks. After the strikes, that number fell to four or five.

Civilian and economic role

The bridge is also an important transport route for Crimea’s residents and tourists.

It was used to deliver:

food;

fuel;

consumer goods;

construction materials;

various industrial products.

The bridge also carried passenger trains and cars travelling between Russia and Crimea.

A prolonged disruption would therefore affect not only military supplies but also everyday economic life in Crimea, the cost of delivering goods and the tourism industry.

The collapsed section of the Kerch Bridge

What alternatives does Russia have?

Disabling the Kerch Bridge does not mean that Russia will lose the ability to supply Crimea altogether.

Moscow can use the land corridor through the occupied parts of southern Ukraine. It links Russia’s Rostov region with the occupied territories of Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions, and Crimea.

However, this route has several drawbacks. It is significantly longer, runs close to active combat zones and is itself vulnerable to Ukrainian strikes.

Russia could also use the ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait, but it would not be able to fully replace the bridge’s capacity.

Disabling the Kerch Bridge therefore represents a serious logistical blow to Russia, even if Moscow continues to supply Crimea via alternative routes.

Why is this attack significant?

From a military perspective, Russia is losing – at least temporarily – one of its most important transport corridors, which it used to supply its forces in Crimea and southern Ukraine.

From an economic perspective, a prolonged closure of the bridge will increase the cost of supplying Crimea and put additional pressure on alternative transport routes.

From a political perspective, it is another blow to Putin’s project, which has become a symbol of Russia’s annexation of Crimea.

It is also particularly significant that the bridge was considered one of Russia’s most heavily protected strategic assets. It was guarded by air defence systems, maritime barriers and other security measures. Yet Ukraine has managed to strike it repeatedly.

However, the ultimate strategic impact will depend on how long the bridge remains out of service, how severe the damage is to its supports and the adjacent railway structure, and how quickly Russia can increase the capacity of alternative routes.

One thing is clear: the Kerch Bridge is one of the most important symbols Putin has created since the annexation of Crimea. Its repeated damage sends Moscow a clear message: in its war against Ukraine, no infrastructure asset is safe or beyond reach.

World.title: EU foreign policy chief: ‘Syria must withdraw recognition of occupied territories in Georgia and Ukraine’
World.content:
EU foreign ministers have called for closer relations with Syria. However, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said that any association agreement with Syria should include a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine, alongside commitments to protect human rights.

Kallas made the remarks at a press conference following a meeting of EU foreign ministers.

According to Kallas, EU member states agreed that maintaining relations with Syria was important. Without EU engagement, other actors would fill the existing political and diplomatic vacuum in the country.

Kallas said the EU was considering signing an association agreement, negotiations on which began in 2008. The agreement would provide a common framework for cooperation between the two sides. At the same time, the EU would begin work on a new mandate to modernise the agreement.

“The question now was the status of the agreement. Negotiations on it took place in 2008, quite a long time ago. So the question arose as to whether we should make changes to it.

“The EU works in such a way that decision-making takes time. That is why the compromise would be to sign the 2008 association agreement. This would give us a framework within which we could work on all the issues that matter to both sides. At the same time, together with the Council, we will begin work on developing a new mandate for a modernised agreement,” Kallas said.

Kaja Kallas

Kallas said EU foreign ministers had called for several key issues to be addressed in the agreement. These include clear conditions on human rights protection and a commitment not to recognise the occupied territories of Georgia and Ukraine.

She explained that the issue concerned the territories whose independence was recognised by Bashar al-Assad’s regime.

“We are now working in technical groups on the details, both technical and legal, but we are making progress,” the EU foreign policy chief said.

At the press conference, Kallas also commented on the architecture of European security. She said that Russia had been a party to several international agreements that laid the foundations for European security. However, the main problem was not the existence of these documents, but Moscow’s failure to honour its commitments.

In this context, Kallas cited the Helsinki Final Act, the Paris Agreement and the Budapest Memorandum.

“The problem is not with the agreements themselves, nor with Ukraine’s position on this issue. The problem is that Russia violates these agreements and fails to comply with their terms. So the main question is: how can we restore the European security architecture?” Kaja Kallas said.

Background

On 29 May 2018, the regime of former Syrian President Bashar al-Assad recognised the independence of Georgia’s occupied regions of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region (South Ossetia). Tbilisi responded by severing diplomatic relations with Damascus. The EU condemned the decision on the same day, saying it violated international law and the principles of Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Assad’s decision followed Russia’s military intervention in the Syrian civil war. Moscow was one of the main supporters of Assad’s government, and Damascus’s move was seen as serving the Kremlin’s interests.

In June 2022, Syria also recognised the independence of Ukraine’s occupied territories of Donetsk and Luhansk. Ukraine responded by severing diplomatic relations with Syria.

Assad’s regime fell in December 2024, and a new government took power in Syria. Against this backdrop, Tbilisi called on Damascus to withdraw its recognition of Abkhazia and the Tskhinvali region.

Ukraine restored diplomatic relations with Syria in September 2025. The association agreement now under consideration by the EU could therefore mark a new stage in relations with Syria. However, the territorial integrity of Georgia and Ukraine remains one of the key conditions in this process.

World.title: Old links on Aliyev’s X account redirected users to opposition videos: cyberattack or global vulnerability?
World.content:
Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

On 15 November, links in some old posts on President Ilham Aliyev’s account on X redirected users to videos featuring opposition politicians and bloggers, as well as footage of protests. Most of the posts dated from 2010–2011. The links led to videos featuring Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, and bloggers Mehman Huseynov and Gabil Mammadov.

The posts themselves remained unchanged, but the links they contained began directing users to different pages. The altered links remained accessible for several hours, and users shared the posts across social media.

That evening, the Azerbaijani president’s press service issued a statement:

“Cyberattacks are currently targeting the social media accounts of Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev. Relevant agencies are taking the necessary measures to prevent these attacks and investigate the incident.”

The statement did not specify which platforms had come under attack, how the attacks were carried out or who was behind them.

Similar incidents affected the accounts of several prominent politicians, government agencies and companies around the world on the same day. This raises the question:

Were the president’s accounts actually hacked, or was the incident the result of a global vulnerability that affected numerous accounts, including those of Donald Trump and McDonald’s?

Trump, Gates and Burger King among those affected by similar incidents

According to a CNN investigation published on 15 November, links in old posts by politicians, government agencies and companies on X began redirecting users to unrelated videos, images and websites over the weekend.

The largest number of such cases involved the personal account of US President Donald Trump. Links in at least 12 of his posts began directing users to other websites. Similar changes affected posts by Bill Gates dating from 2010 and former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau from 2011.

A link in a 2011 Burger King post listing the locations of its restaurants redirected users to a page listing Nazi concentration camps. A link in one of McDonald’s posts led to a page about the 11 September attacks. Similar cases also affected posts by the FBI, the US Department of Defence and former Vice-President Mike Pence.

All the links had been shortened using Bitly, a service that turns long web addresses into shorter ones. The service was widely used on Twitter, now known as X, between 2009 and 2014. According to CNN, Bitly links do not expire, and users with paid subscriptions can change the addresses to which they redirect.

Bitly said it had identified “an issue that allowed malicious actors to reuse some old, inactive links”. The company said it had suspended the accounts used to change the links and deactivated the links themselves. However, Bitly did not say who was behind the activity.

No password required

An attack of this kind does not require access to an account password. The original post remains unchanged; only the destination address of the shortened link changes. As a result, someone clicking a link in a post published by the president 15 years ago ends up on a completely different page.

IT expert Osman Gunduz also believes that the problem stems not from hacked accounts but from a security vulnerability in Bitly’s system. He recommended that government agencies and other organisations check their old links, deactivate potentially dangerous ones and use their own domains wherever possible.

Ari Lightman, a professor of digital media at Carnegie Mellon University, told CNN that many old accounts remain inadequately monitored. He described the situation as “problematic”.

Government agencies have not yet confirmed that the incident involving the president’s account was linked to a Bitly vulnerability. The president’s press service has issued no further statements on the matter.

Who appears in the videos?

The videos feature some of the most vocal critics of the Azerbaijani authorities.

Ali Karimli, chairman of the Azerbaijan Popular Front Party, has been under arrest since November 2025. Authorities accuse him of actions aimed at violently seizing power. Karimli rejects the charges, calling them fabricated and politically motivated. The investigation ended in October. If convicted, he faces a prison sentence of 12 years to life. On 12 November, he received the Magnitsky Human Rights Award in London.

Blogger Mehman Huseynov was sentenced to two years in prison in 2017 on defamation charges. He was released in March 2019. Following the incident, Huseynov sarcastically “thanked” the president on Facebook for sharing a video featuring him: “Thank you, Mr President!”

Blogger Gabil Mammadov, who lives abroad, has been convicted in absentia in Azerbaijan. The Baku Court of Serious Crimes sentenced him to 16 years in prison.

What does “cyberattack” mean?

In the past two months, the Azerbaijani authorities have reported cyberattacks for the second time. On 13 October, more than 100 government websites came under attack. At the time, the State Service for Special Communication and Information Security said when the attack began, which systems it targeted and that its impact had been limited. The agency blamed an unnamed “foreign hacker group”. However, the pro-Iranian group 313 Team, which is believed to operate in Iraq, claimed responsibility. Its members said they had acted in protest against the ban on wearing hijabs in schools.

The statement about the attack on the president’s accounts, however, provided no similar details.

Previous cyberattacks on social media accounts in Azerbaijan have mainly targeted independent media outlets. According to the Committee to Protect Journalists, an international press freedom organisation, almost all Azerbaijani-language posts disappeared from Meydan TV’s Facebook page in June 2020. In August this year, eight independent Azerbaijani media outlets operating in exile issued a joint statement. They said a series of coordinated copyright infringement complaints had led to the suspension of several of their Facebook and Instagram accounts.

This time, the incident affected the president’s own account. It remains unclear who changed the links and why they chose opposition videos as the new destinations. Bitly has not disclosed who owned the accounts it suspended.

Interference with Ilham Aliyev’s X account

World.title: Azerbaijan rejects France's criticism of normalization process with Armenia
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Azerbaijan has rejected recent statements by French officials concerning the normalization process between Baku and Yerevan, accusing France of taking a one-sided approach and relying on politically motivated narratives.

"Such a selective approach, one-sided assessments and continued reliance on politically motivated narratives by France do not contribute to advancing the peace agenda in the region," Azerbaijani Foreign Ministry spokesperson Aykhan Hajizada said in a commentary.

Addressing France's criticism of Azerbaijan's anti-terror measures in September 2023, Hajizada said the operation was aimed at ending the illegal military presence and activities of the Armenian armed forces and affiliated structures in Azerbaijan's sovereign territories, restoring constitutional order and ensuring the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity.

He described attempts to portray the measures as violations of international law, while overlooking decades of occupation, ethnic cleansing and violations of the rights of hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis, as unacceptable.

Hajizada also rejected France's characterization of individuals facing or having faced judicial proceedings in Azerbaijan as "arbitrarily detained." He said those held accountable were accused or convicted of serious crimes, including war crimes, crimes against humanity and terrorism, and that their cases were handled under Azerbaijani law and applicable international obligations.

"Any external attempts to demand the release of individuals convicted of serious war crimes are incompatible with the principle of the rule of law," he said.

The spokesperson further dismissed allegations of the destruction or deliberate alteration of cultural and religious heritage in Azerbaijan's liberated territories, saying that the protection and restoration of heritage sites remained among the country's priorities. He also drew attention to the destruction and appropriation of Azerbaijani cultural and religious heritage during Armenia's decades-long occupation, including mosques, cemeteries and historical monuments.

Hajizada said the rights of hundreds of thousands of Azerbaijanis forcibly displaced from their homes in Armenia and the formerly occupied territories of Azerbaijan, including their right to safe and dignified return, should receive equal attention.

He also criticized France's own human rights and governance record, referring to concerns over the use of force by law enforcement authorities against demonstrators, including minors, as well as investigations into alleged police misconduct. He also cited judicial proceedings and corruption investigations involving French political figures as grounds for questions about transparency and public accountability.

Hajizada called on the French Government to abandon what he described as a biased approach and refrain from interfering in Azerbaijan's internal affairs.

World.title: High production costs at heart of Iran's inflation, economist says (Exclusive)
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. The problem of inflation in Iran, and its root cause, stems from the supply side, specifically from production costs, an Iranian economist and a faculty member at Shahid Chamran University in Iran, Seyyed Morteza Afghah, told Trend in an exclusive interview.

"However, from an economic perspective, the root of the inflation problem in Iran is generally considered to be demand-driven. This is attributed to high levels of liquidity, specifically, the fact that the growth rate of liquidity exceeds the growth rate of domestic production," he noted.

The expert said that, in economics, inflation is typically linked to a situation where the growth rate of liquidity outpaces that of domestic production. For this reason, in the period following the Iran-Iraq War, economists, particularly proponents of a free-market, liberal economic approach, have consistently argued that liquidity levels are too high and that the government must reduce liquidity to curb inflation. On this basis, economists globally who emphasize the role of money supply in inflation also maintain that liquidity contributes to rising inflation.

Afghah added that while proponents of a liberal, free-market economy argue that high liquidity drives inflation, many small and medium-sized manufacturing enterprises report suffering from a lack of liquidity. This issue hasn’t received much attention to date, highlighting a discrepancy between the views of economists and the reality of the actual economy, a persistent problem that remains present today.

"Even now, despite claims that liquidity is high, the primary challenge, or at least one of the foremost challenges, facing Iran’s manufacturing sector, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, is a lack of liquidity," he remarked.

Afghah pointed out that the cost of production in Iran is extremely high, a situation stemming largely from domestic issues. This is linked to significant flawed policies, a lack of policy stability, and instability in management. Inadequate management and the frequent turnover of executives further exacerbate the problem.

The expert said that the enactment of laws related to the production sector, characterized by a dizzying number of regulations, some of which are even contradictory, has further exacerbated the problem. This combination of systemic shortcomings and an inefficient bureaucracy acts as a barrier to production and development. Collectively, these factors have resulted in high production costs in Iran.

According to him, a product that costs "N" to manufacture in Iran could be produced in another country, under competent and stable management, at a cost of "N-1," while maintaining the same level of quality.

"Therefore, in my view, the primary driver of inflation in Iran is not merely an excess of liquidity; rather, it stems from deficiencies in management and the implementation of policies," he noted.

Afghah added that the lack of legal stability within the economic sector, the incompetence and frequent turnover of managers, and an inefficient bureaucracy are all contributing to inflation in the country. Furthermore, another issue driving up production costs is the sector's heavy reliance on foreign currency. Since 80% of the country's imports consist of intermediate goods, or products used in the production of other goods, any increase in the value of foreign currency against the Iranian currency leads to a rise in the cost of domestic production.

"Ultimately, there are two primary reasons for high inflation in Iran: first, a lack of legal stability and an inefficient bureaucracy; and second, the rising value of foreign currency against the Iranian currency. To address these issues, several steps must be taken: officials, whether elected or appointed, must possess sufficient expertise in their respective fields, and there must be stability in foreign currency-related revenues, ensuring that inflation from imported goods is not passed on to domestic production," he noted.

According to him, it is clear that no country can produce every product it needs domestically using only its own resources and labor force. Therefore, countries meet their needs through trade with other countries.

Afghah expressed hope that the economic blockade and the restrictions on imports and exports currently facing Iran will prove to be temporary. Otherwise, if the war doesn’t end, sanctions against Iran aren’t lifted, and regional tensions don’t subside, there is no solution. This is because Iran lacks both the reserves to cover all its product requirements and the capacity to manufacture them domestically. The raw materials for many goods produced in Iran are imported.

In conclusion, the expert expressed hope that if the war and the blockade end, the country will return to a normal state, with prosperity increasing through both domestic production and trade relations with other countries.

World.title: Kazakhstan's coal production falls 1.6% to 93.38M tons in January-October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Kazakhstan produced 93.38 million tons of coal, including lignite and coal concentrate, in January-October 2026, down 1.6% from 94.94 million tons in the same period last year, according to Trend's calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics.

In October 2026, coal production totaled 10.97 million tons, up 12.9% from 9.72 million tons in September and 0.3% from 10.94 million tons in October 2025.

In monetary terms, output in the coal mining sector, which comprises 19 operating enterprises and production facilities, reached 748.23 billion tenge ($1.68 billion) in January-October 2026, an increase of 5.3% year-on-year.

In October, the sector's output amounted to 80.23 billion tenge ($180.54 million), up 1.16% from 79.31 billion tenge ($178.46 million) in September. The industrial production index stood at 108% compared to September and 93.7% compared to October 2025.

Coal mining output accounted for 2.71% of Kazakhstan's total mining and quarrying output, which amounted to 27.605 trillion tenge ($62.12 billion), and 1.28% of the country's total industrial output of 58.52 trillion tenge ($131.68 billion) in January-October 2026.

According to the Eni World Energy Review 2026, Kazakhstan ranked ninth among the world's top 10 coal-producing countries in 2025, with output reaching 106 million tons (Mton), up 6.7% year-on-year. Kazakhstan's coal production recorded a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 2.6% over the 2015–2025 period.

The currency conversions are based on the official exchange rate of $1 = 444.4 tenge as of November 17, 2026.

World.title: Another group of former IDPs relocated to Jabrayil and Zangilan districts
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Another group of former internally displaced persons (IDPs) was sent to Azerbaijan’s Jabrayil and Zangilan districts.

On November 19, the group was sent to Soltanli village in Jabrayil district, and Jahangirbeyli village in Zangilan district.

The recent families are former internally displaced persons who had been temporarily housed in various regions of the republic, primarily in dormitories, sanatoriums, and administrative buildings.

At this stage, 16 families (80 people) to Soltanli, and 19 families (75 people) to Jahangirbayli.

World.title: Trump says he seeks swift resolution to conflict with Iran
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. US President Donald Trump has expressed his intention to achieve a swift resolution to the conflict with Iran.

The American leader made the remarks while answering questions from journalists.

"Yes, I will solve this problem. Yes, soon. One way or another, we will resolve it. They want to make a deal, but we need a long-term agreement," Trump said.

He was responding to a journalist's question about whether Washington intends to keep American troops in the region until an agreement is reached with Tehran.

Trump also stressed that he seeks to secure an agreement that would remain in force even if the country were led by a "bad and weak" president.

World.title: Kazakhstan's gold-bearing ore output rises 12.4% in January-October
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Kazakhstan produced 34.58 million tons of gold-bearing ore in January-October 2026, up 12.4% from 30.77 million tons in the same period last year, according to Trend's calculations based on data from the Bureau of National Statistics.

In October 2026, gold-bearing ore production totaled 4.05 million tons, up 13.7% from 3.56 million tons in September and 22.36% compared to 3.31 million tons in October 2025.

Meanwhile, gold-bearing concentrate production amounted to 221,100 tons in January-October 2026, down 18% from 269,600 tons in the same period of 2025.

In October, concentrate output totaled 23,300 tons, down 12.1% from 26,500 tons in September and 5.7% from 24,700 tons in October 2025.

Overall, output in the metal ore mining sector, comprising 70 enterprises and production facilities, amounted to 6.427 trillion tenge ($14.46 billion) in January-October 2026, with the physical volume of production increasing by 1.7% year-on-year.

Metal ore mining accounted for 23.28% of Kazakhstan's total mining and quarrying output, which amounted to 27.605 trillion tenge ($62.12 billion), and 10.98% of the country's total industrial output of 58.52 trillion tenge ($131.68 billion) during the reporting period.

The currency conversions are based on the official exchange rate of $1 = 444.4 tenge as of November 17, 2026.

World.title: Repsol’s Q3 upstream production rises 4.2% to 574,000 boe/d
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. Repsol’s upstream production rose 4.2% year on year to 574,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (kboe/d) in the third quarter of 2026, the company said. Upstream adjusted net income was €415 million, 93% above a year earlier.

Trend’s calculations based on company data show that the total is 16 kboe/d (2.9%) above the second quarter’s 558 kboe/d and 23 kboe/d above 551 kboe/d a year earlier. Liquids rose 2.6% to 199 kboe/d and gas 3.0% to 2,106 million scf/d on the quarter. Nine-month production was 557 kboe/d, up 1.5%.

The US Pikka project averaged 10,000 net barrels per day, about 1.7% of total output and equal to 43% of the year-on-year increase. Gross production reached 69,000 barrels per day at the end of September, 86% of the 80,000 plateau target.

Consolidated liquids rose 13.1% on the quarter to 138 kboe/d, while equity affiliates’ liquids fell 15.3% to 61 kboe/d and their gas rose 3.7% to 891 million scf/d.

Realized crude was $89.3 per barrel, down 9.3% on the second quarter’s $98.5 and up 36.3% on the year. Realized gas was $4.8 per thousand scf, up 26.3% and 45.5%. NBP averaged $18.4 per MBtu, up 12.2% and 70.4%.

Operating income was €707 million, up 26.3% on the quarter and 80.4% on the year. Higher prices added €380 million and volumes €178 million, against costs of €100 million, amortization of €53 million and royalties of €30 million, while income tax rose €123 million. Prices and volumes thus account for 68% and 32% of the €558 million of gains.

Capex fell 74.5% to €98 million from €384 million, while cash flow from operations fell 29.5% to €693 million and was up 37.5% on the year.

World.title: First trilateral meeting between Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping scheduled for November 19
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 19. The first trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping is scheduled to take place on November 19 at approximately 10:30 a.m. Baku time.

The talks will be held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in the Chinese city of Shenzhen.

Delegations from all three countries will participate in the meeting, and their composition has already been agreed upon. Meanwhile, work on a draft joint communiqué is still underway.

The duration of the meeting will be determined by the three heads of state themselves.

The talks are expected to take place at the Chinese president's state residence.

World.title: Economists warn Australia is showing the hallmarks of recession
World.content:
As Christmas presents go, it's probably a dead heat with a lump of coal.

But mortgage holders may at least take some comfort that the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) seemingly relentless campaign to make them poorer is over for this year, and possibly the next.

Financial markets have removed all bets of another pre-Christmas rate rise when the reserve board concludes its final meeting of 2026 on December 8.

After a gloomy jobs report, markets are now tipping Christmas 2027 will see interest rates at least one rate cut lower, and maybe two.

Grim outlook for job hunters

A lot can change between now and then, of course.

Any joy at a rates reprieve comes at the expense of the growing proportion of Australia's 15.5 million-strong labour force who are finding themselves without a seat in the game of musical chairs that is our jobs market.

For the first time since COVID, more than 750,000 Australians who were available and actively looking for work in October were unable to find it.

And that's before the impact of the RBA's latest rate hike this month.

The bank's latest forecasts tipped the official jobless rate to rise to 5.1 per cent by next Christmas. Well, in one leap, October's 0.2 percentage point rise in the jobless rate to 4.9 per cent gets us halfway there already.

Recession alarm bells ringing

Economists are now sounding the alarm about an increasing chance the RBA's campaign to cool inflationary pressures could tip the Australian economy into recession.

"Recession is clearly a concern," HSBC chief economist Paul Bloxham said.

Indeed, there is a chance we are already in one, according to Betashares chief economist David Bassanese: "Consecutive large employment declines might suggest the economy already has one foot in recession."

If it quacks like a recession…

There are many different definitions of a recession.

In Australia, we tend to speak of two consecutive three-month periods in which economic output contracts (you might hear people saying "two quarters of negative GDP growth" but that's just a fancy way of saying the same thing).

The unemployment rate has ticked up more than expected. (Reuters: Brian Snyder)

In the US, the National Bureau of Economic Research, which officially dates American recessions, defines them more loosely as "a significant decline in economic activity that is spread across the economy and that lasts more than a few months".

Are there alternatives to interest rate hikes? Mortgage holders reeling from five interest rate hikes this year are questioning whether there are other ways of controlling inflation.

A shrinking economy, of course, means fewer job opportunities.

So some economists prefer to say a recession is when the jobless rate rises by one percentage point.

Against that yardstick, Australia's jobless rate has now climbed 0.8 percentage points since its Christmas 2025 level of 4.1 per cent.

Which just about passes the "duck test". Namely, if it looks like a recession, swims like a recession and quacks like a recession, then it probably is a recession.

Loading

RBA to take stock

RBA governor Michele Bullock is adamant it is not the bank's intention to deliberately drive the economy into recession.

But even if we avoid the technical definition of recession, Bullock has already conceded interest rate hikes will make this a tough Christmas for many.

"It is going to make people feel like it's a recession because they feel poorer. Their spending can't grow very quickly, because their incomes aren't growing very quickly," she said.

The RBA is now expected to use its Christmas break to take stock of the impact of its five rate hikes this year.

But amid continued global disruptions, elevated oil prices and a falling Aussie dollar — which adds to domestic inflation — the path ahead for interest rates in 2027 is anyone's bet.

World.title: Live: Trump, Xi and Putin to meet for the first time in China
World.content:
While the bilateral meeting between Xi and Trump seems to be an afterthought for many, it could actually be more important than the trilateral with Putin.

"I think the trilateral meeting will be a lot of pomp and photographs, but not much outcome, whereas the US-China one could actually be significant," said Nick Bisley, a professor of international relations at La Trobe University.

He said the bilateral meeting — Xi and Trump's third this year with one more expected next month — could touch on key topics such as Taiwan and artificial intelligence — even former Nvidia chief Jensen Huang.

Xi Jinping was hosted at the White House by Donald Trump in September. (Reuters: Evelyn Hockstein)

Professor Bisley said his guess was that because the landscape was so unsettled the outcome would likely just be an anodyne statement about AI being an important technology that needs to be regulated.

"But what's the tone and tenor of that relationship? Can the stability of the relationship that was established earlier be continued? Does it get frosty? Does Trump revert to his more hawkish position on China? And that's all a bit up for grabs," he said.

"You can overrate how important these bilateral meetings are, but both the US and China have highly personalised political systems at the moment — so seeing how those two get along and what they achieve or not will be pretty important to watch."

World.title: Cheap Chinese EVs are causing havoc on the Australian used car market
World.content:
More used cars are for sale; they are selling for less, and petrol cars are losing value fastest.

These are insights from the latest industry data showing the impact of low-cost Chinese EVs on a second-hand car market dominated by petrol and diesel vehicle sales.

Dealerships are struggling to shift stock and say conditions are the "worst ever".

Some in the industry believe the value of used fossil fuel vehicles will continue to decline as EVs get cheaper and buyers look to save on fuel.

So, what does this mean for the value of your car?

And what vehicle types are likely to see the sharpest declines?

The year that reshaped the car market

Although new-car sales get the most attention, most Australians buy their cars on the second-hand market.

In 2026, changes in the new-car market rippled through auction houses, dealerships and online marketplaces that shift over 2 million used cars every year.

The war in Iran and high fuel prices, along with an influx of low-cost, heavily discounted Chinese brands, drove a surge in new EV sales.

Many of today's top-selling brands were unheard of a few years ago.

As EV uptake increased, used petrol and diesel vehicles flooded the second-hand market.

Low-cost new cars also put pressure on used car prices.

New Chinese SUVs were advertised for the typical asking price of a three-year-old Toyota Rav4, Steven Bragg, a motor industry adviser at Pitcher Partners, told the ABC.

"The Chinese SUV probably has better tech, better specs, and a new car warranty of eight years," he said.

He said dealerships found themselves stuck with stock that was rapidly losing value.

"It's the hardest conditions they've been through," Mr Bragg said.

"Even the GFC was better than this."

The Australian Automotive Dealers Association (AADA) wants to stop new brands entering the market.

"It's becoming more difficult to value some vehicles on the used car market because such is the rate of change," AADA chief executive James Voortman said.

Australians prefer to buy their cars second-hand, making the used-car market about twice the size of the new-car one. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Used cars always depreciate, but now some models are losing value faster than before.

Petrol cars (excluding hybrids and plug-in hybrids) lost five times more value in 2026 than in the previous year, according to data from the analytics platform AutoGrab.

Diesels lost about twice as much value in 2026 as hybrids and battery-electric vehicles, with SUVs faring worse than utes and four-wheel drives designed for heavy towing, data from online used car dealership Carma shows.

Some say this is the market correcting itself after used cars became overpriced during the pandemic.

But others argue these falls are a sign of big changes to come.

Will the value of used petrol and diesel cars keep falling this fast?

This is the big question, and there are many conflicting opinions.

Variables affecting depreciation rates include fuel prices and electric alternatives, inflation, and broader cost-of-living pressures.

"Most of the key industry data sources say it's likely used car prices will continue to fall for the foreseeable future," Mike Costello, an industry analyst at Cox Automotive, told the ABC.

He said demand for used diesel utes and large four-wheel drives should remain robust while there are few EV equivalents.

But other vehicle types "will probably fare differently".

" Selling a diesel mid-sized SUV in 2029 is going to be a potential challenge … These are uncharted waters that we are swimming towards. "

The EV industry's peak body, the EV Council, made a similar prediction.

"Demand for certain vehicle segments is going to evaporate and may evaporate quicker than people expect," EVC head of policy Aman Gaur said.

"I would just urge people who are buying petrol cars to be cautious about what the future demand might be, given the demand for petrol cars is decreasing, and the demand for electric cars is increasing."

Market segments already well served by EVs include hatchbacks, sedans and mid-size SUVs. (ABC News: John Gunn)

Sales of new petrol cars (excluding hybrids) have almost halved over six years.

But Fleet News director Marc Sibbald dismissed the idea Australians would flock to EVs.

"In five years time we'll still be struggling with charging infrastructure," Mr Sibbald said.

"There'll still be non-believers. There's my neighbour who thinks BYD is spying on them, the guys I drink with at the pub who think EVs are going to catch on fire."

EVs hit mainstream Electric cars have become mainstream in the past decade, making up one in four new car sales.

He advises fleet managers that petrol and diesel cars will depreciate at the long-term average rate.

Brendon Green, a general manager at Pickles Auctions, said fossil fuel vehicle resale values would not collapse.

"We anticipate a gradual shift in resale values rather than a dramatic decline, with the extent of any price movements varying across vehicle segments."

What about used EVs?

Used EVs tend to depreciate much faster than used fossil fuel cars, losing about half their value over three years.

The spike in EV demand in March meant they temporarily gained value, but industry data shows they are now losing value again.

But depreciation rates are hard to predict.

Cox Automotive's Mr Costello expected EVs would hold their value better as fears about severe battery degradation proved unfounded.

"We're seeing cars with 90–95 per cent of battery health remaining entering the second-hand market," he said.

Will new EVs keep getting cheaper?

The influx of low-cost Chinese brands in 2026 was the result of a combination of events that may not be repeated, Carma chief executive Lachlan MacGregor said.

Chinese domestic sales slumped, causing manufacturers to expand overseas just as the United States, Europe and Canada banned or limited vehicle imports.

"We've had the fierce forces of competition like no other market has had," he said.

Manufacturers cannot sell the cars any cheaper.

" I wouldn't say that I would forecast that EVs become cheaper again. In fact, with incentives rolling off, maybe they go up in price. "

The price of EVs in five years will depend largely on battery prices, which in turn depend on research outcomes and manufacturing advances that are hard to predict.

Another variable is what models manufacturers make available in Australia.

Small EVs with limited range are being sold in China for less than $10,000.

Mr Bragg said a car like this in the Australian market could collapse the value of used hatchbacks, but only if buyers thought it was as good as petrol models.

"If it's a Corolla-level-good vehicle for a great price, then 100 per cent it would impact the market."

While the future was uncertain, he said one thing was clear.

"It's never been a better time to buy a car."

World.title: Humble Ash Barty inducted into hall of fame
World.content:
Ash Barty has never been one to trumpet her achievements, so perhaps it was no surprise her election to the International Tennis Hall of Fame (ITHF) left the Australian delighted but wondering whether she truly belonged among the game's greats.

The three-time grand slam singles champion and former world number one will be formally inducted at a ceremony in Newport, Rhode Island, next August and take her place among luminaries including Roger Federer, Billie ‌Jean King and Margaret Court.

Nearly five years on from retirement but still only 30, Barty was touched to have personal messages of congratulations from nearly 20 Hall of Famers, including Federer and Martina Navratilova, as ITHF co-presidents Kim Clijsters and Patrick McEnroe gave her the news in a surprise call.

"I feel very, very ‌humbled and grateful. And to be honest, I've got a little bit of impostor syndrome, where I feel I don't quite belong," she told Reuters in a call from her home base in Queensland.

"The Hall of Fame is ‌for the absolute legends of our game, and I'm not sure I'm quite there."

Ash Barty won Wimbledon in 2021, the third Australian woman to do so after Margaret Court and Evonne Goolagong Cawley. (Getty: Clive Brunskill)

Few of her compatriots ‌would share that assessment of Barty, whose triumph at the 2022 Australian Open ended a 44-year wait for a homegrown women's singles champion.

The all-court player won grand slams on three different surfaces, claiming the 2019 French Open title and 2021 Wimbledon crown, and spent 114 consecutive weeks with the number one ranking.

Barty is the 35th Australian player, male or female, to be inducted into the Hall of Fame.

She will be inducted along with Japan's four-time Paralympic gold medallist and 50-time major ‌champion Shingo Kunieda, who was elected in the wheelchair tennis category.

Barty said her honour belonged as much to the team that accompanied her on her roller-coaster tennis journey, which included struggles with depression, a nearly two-year break from the game and a fascinating diversion as a professional cricketer.

"I'm probably most excited to tell my team because it ‌feels like it's as much for me ‌as it is for them," said Barty, now a mother to two small children.

Her retirement from tennis at 25, barely two months on from her Melbourne ‌Park triumph, has long fuelled speculation of whether she might one day come back.

Ash Barty (right) and Evonne Goolagong Cawley (left) are two of the eight Australian women to be inducted into the ITHF. (Getty Images: James D. Morgan)

The Hall of Fame includes players who balanced motherhood with grand slam glory in Court, Clijsters and Barty's mentor, Evonne Goolagong Cawley.

But a happy Barty said she had ‌no intention of joining them, being content and focused on family.

Asked whether her position had hardened from "never say never" to simply "never", she replied: "No, mate, it was always never."

And there were no regrets about retiring young.

"No, no, no, not one."

Barty had little to say about Serena Williams's return to tennis at the age of 44 and the American's motivation of having her kids see her play.

"My kids don't even know that I played tennis, and I'm sure that at the induction next year they'll wonder what's going on," she said.

"I'm deep in the trenches with my two little ones at the moment, and I ‌absolutely love it."

Barty will join ‌Goolagong Cawley as the second Indigenous Australian in the Hall of Fame, and hopes more will follow.

"I think if you can provide the opportunity and the platform for them to learn and grow, then hopefully, maybe one day, there's another young boy or girl being inducted into the Hall of Fame," she said.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.

World.title: Little penguin comeback on NSW far south coast threatened by fox attacks
World.content:
An attempt to reintroduce little penguins to the NSW far south coast is under threat, with foxes killing multiple birds over the past two years.

Bega Valley Shire Council confirmed that a little penguin died from canine predation on Monday, with testing revealing that foxes were the likely culprit.

The attack is the latest setback for a colony that conservationists have spent years trying to rebuild after little penguins disappeared from the mainland NSW far south coast three decades ago.

Friends of Little Penguins Eden chairperson Wendy Noble said there were at least eight birds with four nests across the colony around Eden.

She said the latest fatality had been devastating.

"It's a real blow because we're working really hard to protect this colony that's trying to come back to Eden," she said.

" It's senseless, and a waste of the penguins trying to come in and produce another generation. "

Birds locally extinct for 30 years

Little penguins had been recorded in Eden since the 1930s, but the population became locally extinct in the 1990s due to a combination of storms and predators.

In 2020, scientists and conservationists reintroduced the birds to a fenced site at Wheel Cove near Eagles Claw Nature Reserve using an audio system that projected mating sounds.

Two pairs were spotted breeding at Wheel Cove near the Eagles Claw Nature Reserve last year. (Supplied: Julianne Noble)

The colony grew to at least 12 birds, and in October 2023 the first penguin chick was born in Eden for the first time in 30 years.

But some birds began nesting at nearby Shelly Beach, where there was no predator-proof fencing.

Since then, five little penguins have been killed in suspected fox attacks at the site, with two adults killed in 2025 and a fledging and an adult killed in 2024.

Monday's attack comes just weeks after a juvenile fox was captured by wildlife cameras lurking near the nesting area.

Monitoring stations at the nesting site captured a juvenile fox lurking nearby in October. (Supplied: Little Penguins of Eden)

Using the cameras, Ms Noble said she had identified one nest at Shelly Beach this year, compared to five nests spotted last year.

"There could only be one nest this year because of the impact of the foxes," she said.

" The fox really has a huge impact. They could go into a colony and kill every bird in one single night. "

Evolved without predators

Seabird ecologist Nicholas Carlisle, who has been involved in the recovery effort, said predators like foxes were the biggest threat to the colony's survival due to how the birds evolved.

Nicolas Carlisle says the attack is "heartbreaking." (ABC News: Toby Hemmings)

"They've evolved without predators because they're mostly breeding on offshore islands," he said.

" They're not the smartest card in the deck and they choose sites purely because they look like good places to breed and are not necessarily well protected. "

These little penguins were spotted at Eden last year. (Supplied: Friends of Little Penguins Eden group)

Eden is one of only two mainland locations in New South Wales where little penguins live. The other colony is at Manly in Sydney.

Other colonies survive on offshore islands, including Baranguba Montague Island, Snapper Island and Gabo Island.

A fence to protect the colony

The latest attack has prompted Bega Valley Shire Council to begin targeted fox-control operations after previous attempts at non-lethal trapping failed.

The Friends of Little Penguins Eden group has been working with the council to install a fence around the rock wall at the vulnerable Shelly Beach nests.

It is hoped a proposed fence at the Shelly Beach nesting site will help protect the species. (Supplied: Phillip Island Nature Parks)

In a statement, the council said it was working with the Port Authority of NSW to install the fence, with a Crown land licence application under assessment.

Mr Carlisle said he hoped a fence would help.

"We've all been holding our breath since the fox turned up on camera and hoping that the control measures that have been put in place are successful," he said.

World.title: Teen accused of Parliament House hoax threats faces terrorism charges
World.content:
A teenager accused of making hoax threats against Australia's Parliament House has also been charged with terrorism-related offences after federal police allegedly found racist extremist material at an Armidale home.

Australian Federal Police (AFP) also allegedly seized materials used to make improvised explosives.

A 63-year-old man from Armidale has also been charged with weapons offences as a result of the investigation.

The charges follow an investigation into a series of alleged threats against prominent buildings and facilities, including Parliament House and Melbourne Airport, in October.

The threatening calls were allegedly made from a payphone in the Armidale area on October 28 and 29.

According to the AFP, on October 29, New South Wales Police issued a move-on order to a young person near a payphone in Armidale after a report of suspicious activity.

The AFP's National Security Investigations team (NSI) later searched a home in Armidale on November 18, where they found several weapons, including gel blasters and ammunition, imitation firearms, knives, a crossbow, as well as multiple electronic devices

Australian Federal Police allegedly seized weapons including imitation firearms from a home in Armidale, (Supplied: AFP.)

It is alleged several of the items seized in the search could be used to create improvised explosives, and some of the electronic devices contained violent extremist material.

The NSI also allegedly found a series of handwritten notes in support of nationalist and racist extremist ideology.

Australian Federal Police allegedly seized weapons including gel blasters and gel blaster ammunition after searching a home in Armidale. (Supplied: AFP)

The teen is expected to appear before the Children's Court today.

He is facing four counts of using a carriage service for a hoax threat, one count of possessing or controlling violent extremist material obtained or accessed using a carriage service, and two counts of unauthorised possession or use of pistols or prohibited firearms.

He is also charged with collecting or making documents likely to facilitate terrorist acts and one count of possessing things connected with a terrorist act.

The 63-year-old has been charged with 11 weapons-related offences, including nine counts of unauthorised possession or use of pistols or prohibited firearms, one count of unauthorised possession or use of a prohibited weapon and one count of supply, acquisition and possession of ammunition.

He faced court and was refused bail.

World.title: One Nation candidate's migrant welfare graph completely wrong, researcher says
World.content:
A leading researcher has rubbished a graph posted by New South Wales One Nation upper house candidate Katherine Deves that depicts high rates of welfare use among some migrant groups.

Peter Whiteford, the director of the Social Policy Institute at the Australian National University, told 702 ABC Sydney Mornings the graph was "very misleading" and its figures were "completely wrong".

Ms Deves, a lawyer and anti-transgender activist, ran unsuccessfully as a Liberal Party candidate for the seat of Warringah in the 2022 federal election, before leaving the party to join One Nation earlier this year.

She was announced as One Nation's candidate for the NSW Legislative Council on Sunday.

In an interview with Hamish Macdonald on 702 ABC Sydney Mornings yesterday, Ms Deves claimed a high rate of migrants receiving welfare payments was a reason to drastically reduce migration to Australia.

"When you look at some of the cohorts of people that have come from overseas, some of them are — up to a quarter of them are — on welfare compared to the Australian … I believe that they're Middle Eastern communities and it's up to 24 per cent," she said.

"We have concerns for the pressure being put on the NDIS, on health, education, on housing."

One Nation later said the source of the claim was a graph, which Ms Deves posted on her social media. It shows working-age welfare rates in Australia by country of birth, excluding the aged pension.

According to the graph, the highest rates of welfare recipients in Australia are people born in Sudan, Iraq and Syria.

It cites Department of Social Services and Bureau of Statistics longitudinal data sets as its source. However, it does not explain the methodology used to determine the figures shown in the graph.

Professor Whiteford said that most of the numbers in the chart were "puzzling to say the least".

"It is wildly off," he said.

" The numbers are completely wrong, as far as I am concerned. "

Professor Whiteford said people born in countries such as Iraq, Syria and Afghanistan have high rates of social security payments because many arrived in Australia as refugees and have immediate access to the welfare system.

He also said migrants from countries such as India and China have lower rates of social security payments than the Australian-born population.

During the interview, Ms Deves also threw her support behind fellow NSW One Nation candidate Stuart Bonds, who told an anti-immigration rally earlier this month that white Australians were being "demographically replaced".

Those comments were widely condemned for being an apparent reference to the "great replacement theory", a far-right conspiracy theory that claims white populations in Western countries are being deliberately replaced by immigrants from ethnic minorities.

"This is not a conspiracy theory, Hamish," Ms Deves said.

"We have a third of people currently in Australia who were born overseas. We have over half of Australians where they have one parent born overseas.

"So we are having mass, rapid, uncontrolled immigration in this country, the likes of which have never been seen before."

Chris Minns says Katherine Deves's comments are "not the kind of politics we need". (ABC News)

New South Wales Premier Chris Minns said Ms Deves's comments were "horrifying".

"Middle Eastern Australians or anyone who's come here have contributed a lot to New South Wales," he told reporters yesterday.

"They've started families, they've built businesses, they've joined communities. They're proud Australians.

"To see someone who isn't even elected decide that she's going to demonise them in order to get herself elected to the New South Wales parliament, I think it's not the kind of politics we need in Australia."

Ms Deves was contacted for comment.

World.title: Hippo who ate hat under round-the-clock medical watch at US zoo
World.content:
Fiona the hippo captivated hearts around the world when she was born six weeks premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017.

Severely underweight and unable to walk, the feeble baby had doctors from a children's hospital to thank for saving her life.

Now, nine years later, she's in survival mode again.

Fiona, who was named after the Shrek character, has been under 24-hour medical care for about nine days after ingesting a hat accidentally tossed into her habitat by a visitor.

A child had thrown a knitted cap into the air when a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area's viewing window, Cincinnati Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told US media.

Seemingly unharmed initially, the beloved hippo has been under constant medical supervision after staff began to notice her appetite reducing.

She underwent a colonoscopy earlier in the week, but her specialist care team are hoping a new approach can help her pass the foreign object.

Zoo hoping to shake it loose

Zoo officials borrowed a vibration plate from a nearby horse farm and have encouraged Fiona to stand on it several times throughout the day.

"The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass," the zoo said in a statement.

Fiona has been under constant medical surveillance for nine days. (Supplied: Cincinnati Zoo & Botanical Garden)

Surgery has been ruled out on advice from experts who said that was not an option for fully grown hippos.

"Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," zookeeper Mike Wenninger said.

Fiona is now being monitored around the clock as staff employ whatever measures they can to help her pass the hat, including keeping her hydrated, giving her pain meds and feeding her her favourite foods.

"Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked," the zoo said.

"And they were happy to see her respond."

An ultrasound performed on Wednesday, local time, has zoo staff optimistic the hat was beginning to pass through Fiona's small intestine.

Dr Wenninger said she was "large enough that a smallish hat should be passing through".

"At this point what we can do is supportive care … support her through passing it," he said.

"She's getting 24-hour care and attention and we will regroup tomorrow to see how things are going, and may need another procedure in the future."

The zoo said staff were rooting for Fiona and hoped she would be as "strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life".

Fiona the hippo has achieved a cult online following since her traumatic birth. (AP: John Minchillo)

When she was born, Fiona weighed 13 kilograms and became the smallest hippo known to survive premature birth.

Birth weights at the time ranged between 25 and 54kg for the popular zoo species, which can grow to become extremely aggressive.

A Washington man wrote in The Guardian how he was disembowelled by a hippo protecting her young while on a honeymoon safari in Africa last year.

Life has been far more peaceful for Fiona.

Her first steps in front of cameras, nearly two weeks after birth, took social media by storm, effectively establishing her celebrity status. She earned her name due to her ears' resemblance to those of Princess Fiona from Shrek.

Just eight months earlier, Cincinnati Zoo stole global headlines for entirely different reasons when the 17-year-old gorilla named Harambe was fatally shot by zoo officials after dragging a three-year-old boy who had climbed into his enclosure.

ABC/AP

World.title: ‘At a crossroads’: Business leader says ‘vicious slur’ against Jews must not be normalised
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAntisemitism ‘At a crossroads’: Business leader says ‘vicious slur’ against Jews must not be normalised Matthew Knott November 19, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of Australia’s leading businessmen, Steven Lowy, has called for the nation to seize an opportunity to push anti-Jewish hate to the fringes of society when Virginia Bell delivers the final royal commission report into antisemitism, as he insists Jewish Australians must not be excluded or harassed for being supporters of Israel. Lowy, the former co-chief executive of Westfield Corporation, said universities, arts organisations and businesses must take tackling antisemitism as seriously as discrimination against Indigenous Australians, Muslim Australians or women to receive public funding. “I fear that Australian society is at a historic crossroads,” Lowy told a conference organised by the Jerusalem Post newspaper in Sydney on Thursday. “The royal commission now has the nation’s attention, and the world is watching.” Businessman Steven Lowy said antisemitism must be taken as seriously as prejudice against other minority groups. AAPIMAGE



Bell will hand down her final report on December 18, four days after the first anniversary of the Bondi attack which killed 15 people in the nation’s worst terror attack. Lowy said tackling antisemitism will require difficult decisions by private and public institutions. “Who receives public funding? Who gets a grant, a platform, or a seat at the table?” he asked. “Are codes of conduct enforced or quietly set aside when enforcement is awkward? “Ministers, vice chancellors, arts boards, chief executives and councils make those decisions every week. Each one sends a signal about what this country will tolerate.



“The principle is simple: public money should not support people or organisations who promote hatred against any group of Australians.” Lowy, who has previously spoken about the online attacks faced by his family, added that ordinary Australians such as teachers, nurses, tradies and small business owners will have the most important role in ensuring that antisemitism does not become normalised. University of Sydney chancellor and former Telstra chief executive David Thodey agreed with Lowy, telling the conference: “I worry about Australia. This is not what we stand for. We are about inclusion. We are not about antisemitism, and I just find it abhorrent.” The conference venue was heavily protected by armed police guards, but there was no sign of protest activity. Lowy said he believed the rise of antisemitism following the October 7 attacks in Israel, when 1200 people were killed, can be partly explained by a “willful corruption” of words such as genocide, colonisation, apartheid and Zionism “to turn a complex conflict into a license to demonise Jews”.



The word Zionist in particular, he said, “has been twisted and distorted beyond all reality” and “has become weaponised as a vicious slur”. “This brand of antisemitism reflects the hardest prejudice to confront. This is the prejudice that believes itself virtuous, that excluding Jews or denying Jewish self-determination as a stand against racism is somehow a moral and correct thing to be doing,” he said. Lowy argued in his speech that you “cannot separate support for Zionism or the right of Israel to exist from the Jewish people generally”. “I am a proud Jew, and I am a proud Zionist, and the vast majority of Jewish Australians feel responsible for ensuring that Israel continues to exist,” he said. “When an institution says Zionists are not welcome on a panel at a music, art, or literary festival, or in a workplace, Jewish Australians overwhelmingly and understandably interpret that as Jews not being welcome.” Lowy’s stance differs from groups such as the progressive Jewish Council of Australia and non-Zionist Jews, who argue that Jewish identity and support for Israel’s existence should not be conflated.



Related Article Opinion

Antisemitism The abomination on Bondi Beach is a failure that extends beyond any politician or party Steven Lowy Businessman and philanthropist Lowy said Zionism simply describes a “belief in the right of self-determination of the Jewish people in the historic, spiritual, religious, and physical homeland, Israel”. “Zionism does not necessitate any views about borders of Israel, settlements, the legal status of Jerusalem or Palestinian statehood,” he said. Israel’s global standing has plummeted since the war in Gaza began in 2023, with Pew Research polling released in June showing 79 per cent of Australians now hold an unfavorable view of Israel. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the war began according to the Gazan health ministry, a figure that includes Hamas combatants.



Israel has been accused of genocide at the International Court of Justice and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been charged with war crimes by the International Criminal Court. Related Article Updated

Israeli-Palestinian conflict Australia sanctions Israeli settlers, construction company Lowy said he supported a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and that he believed a new government in Israel not led by Netanyahu could help improve relations between Israel and Australia and reduce divisions within Israeli society. “Personalities do matter,” he told this masthead on the sidelines of the conference. He said he opposed the sanctions on Israeli settlers and settler organisations Foreign Minister Penny Wong announced this week, arguing they would damage the Australia-Israel relationship but have no practical impact on settlement building in the West Bank.



“It is in Australia’s interest to have close ties to Israel,” Lowy said, pointing to co-operation between spy agencies ASIO and Mossad on national security as well as technological and business links.
