World.title: The new Parks and Recreation? Inside Amy Poehler’s long-awaited return to TV
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Amy Poehler called Parks and Recreation co-creator Mike Schur and said she had a new idea for a show and wanted to act again, he said yes before he even knew what it was. “It kind of didn’t matter,” he says, speaking to me before the premiere of their new comedy-mystery, Dig, Poehler’s first major TV series in more than a decade. “This is going to sound corny, but the magic [that turned Parks and Recreation into a phenomenon] is Amy. The experience of working with her on that show and creating the character of Leslie Knope was so fun and so formative for me. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘What the hell have I done?’: The crisis that inspired Nazeem Hussain’s new comedy “Especially at this point in our careers and in our lives, the people you do things with matter as much or more than what those things are.” It’s a line that sounds almost exactly like one Leslie uttered to her colleagues in the Parks and Rec finale, co-written by Schur and Poehler 11 years ago: “Teddy Roosevelt once said far and away the best prize that life has to offer is the chance to work hard at work worth doing. I would add that what makes work worth doing is getting to do it with people that you love.” The sentiment isn’t a world away from Poehler’s new character either – another hard-working and often idealistic woman who finds strength in female friendship, this time an archaeologist gearing up to take over the dig site she’s been working on for years in Greece. Although Elise (Poehler) is someone who’s had her spirit broken more than Pawnee’s perkiest public servant. Loading



Amy Poehler (third from right) in the 2015 finale of Parks and Recreation. Divorced and well accustomed to disappointment, this talented archaeologist has been toiling in a “dying field” without the credit she deserves when she comes across an impressive find that could change everything. Unfortunately, Elise is quickly confronted with the reality that good work alone is rarely enough to get ahead. It’s a less hopeful vision of the world than the one Parks and Recreation, the definitive show of the Obama era, gave us – but it’s much more resonant for 2026. Editor's pick Streaming How do you follow-up Adolescence? Stephen Graham went full psycho “As she’s dreaming about taking over a dig, moving up in the world, she starts having to dip her toes into the worlds of [fundraising and glad-handing] and encountering a lot of deeply unpleasant people,” Schur says. Her haughty boss Neville, played by Hugh Laurie, who studied archaeology in his uni days while getting into comedy with the Cambridge Footlights, is great at it. “He loves holding court, orating and basking in the glow of the admiration of the people who surround him,” Schur says of the character. But even he is challenged through the series – especially by the rise of a new guard, including the vacuous heir of a benefactor who cares less about the excavation and discovery of ancient human history and more about dancing on boats and innovation in T-shirt design. “There are two ways to try to make your way in the world: one of them is through stuff that doesn’t really matter, and one of them is through stuff that does matter,” Schur says. “The hard fact is, the people who do the glad-handing and the superficial stuff often are the ones who are getting ahead.” Fina Strazza as Patty, Antonia Thomas as Clare and Geraldine Viswanathan as Dylan in new comedy Dig. Colleen Hayes/Peacock



Based on Kate Myers’ 2023 novel Excavations, the series is both a mystery and an ensemble comedy. It kicks off with a White Lotus-style flash forward in the first episode, with Poehler’s character advising her young cohorts to “tell the right story for the rest of their lives” before biting, kicking and shooting each other – and much of the series is dedicated to what inspired that chaos. Adding that element of mystery is an increasingly common tactic to keep audiences bingeing. But the pleasure of Dig, like the other workplace comedies Schur has worked on, including Parks and Recreation and Brooklyn Nine-Nine, is in its quirky character dynamics. Related Article Streaming Hollywood can’t get enough of this Aussie star. Why is she overlooked at home? Elise isn’t down in the dirt on her own. She’s joined by Dylan (Australia’s Geraldine Viswanathan), a flighty twenty-something who has returned to the site to make amends; Clare (Antonia Thomas, Lovesick), a well-to-do lab tech in her 30s who she’s had beef with for years; and Patty (Fina Strazza, Paper Girls), a dweeby but knowledgeable young assistant overwhelmed on her first dig. “Each of these characters has their strengths and weaknesses,” Viswanathan says. “They take [cues] from each other and grow stronger that way. Dylan’s strength is her fearlessness. She’s down to try anything. And I think she helps embolden Elise, Amy’s character. “I feel like my generation is like, ‘Get it, girl!’ And she’s like, ‘Well, you have to earn it, and you need to do it right.’” Loading



With such a broad range of ages in the main cast, there are plenty of intergenerational gags throughout. Elise, Gen X through and through, is dismayed Dylan has never heard of Pretty Woman and thinks Watergate is a book. But the relationships between her and all the younger women are never condescending or shallow – a fact that reflects Poehler’s respect for younger talent off-screen, too. Viswanathan met Poehler (who is also a creator and executive producer of the series) well before she was hand-picked for the role. Poehler’s production company, Paper Kite, which developed Broad City from a low-budget web series into a hit sitcom in the early 2010s, asked for a meeting with the rising star a while back. “They just wanted to meet me and see what’s up,” she says. “I think Paper Kite keeps their finger on the pulse, especially around women in comedy.” Geraldine Viswanathan as Dylan, Fina Strazza as Patty. Colleen Hayes/Peacock It was a surreal moment for the now 31-year-old, who started doing stand-up at the student bar at the University of Sydney and sketches with local group Freudian Nip (Jenna Owens and Vic Zerbst) before her Hollywood breakthrough in the 2018 sex comedy Blockers. Though now well established on screen – with Thunderbolts last year, she even has a Marvel movie under her belt – working with Poehler is a bucket-list item. “Amy has been on my Mount Rushmore of comedy heroes since I could remember,” she says. “I was such a comedy nerd growing up with Parks and Rec and SNL. She, Tina [Fey] and Mindy [Kaling] were my heroes. I have a really embarrassing Instagram post that’s archived from 2012 of their books, and it’s like ‘#church’. I was studying them. I just wanted to be them so badly.”

World.title: ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Wall Street is about to mint thousands of instant millionaires
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Wall Street is about to mint thousands of instant millionaires Sabrina Valle November 19, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Anthropic’s initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history. The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world’s most valuable companies. Siblings and Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei. Bloomberg The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely. Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least $US100 million ($150 million) in equity after the initial public offering. Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $US83 per share, above its targeted range of $US70 to $US78, giving it a value of around $US1.5 trillion.



Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least $US1 million of pre-tax vested equity at a $US1.35 trillion valuation. Related Article Wall Street How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals. But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast. Anthropic option-holders were sitting on $US119 billion of paper gains as of September 30, at a weighted average exercise price of $US2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About $US73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately. Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates.



“The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for,” Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. “It doesn’t get better than this.” In a letter to potential shareholders, Anthropic’s co-founders said that AI and Anthropic “represents one of the greatest economic opportunities in history”. Bloomberg Equity at entry level Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago — even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than $US1.



Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows. Related Article Opinion

AI Nvidia’s result is gobsmacking, but a sideshow to its CEO spy scandal Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade. “Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO,” Benson said, referring to Anthropic. Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings.



Early hires reap rewards Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5300 employees as of September 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool. Wall Street is bracing for the Anthropic IPO. Bloomberg A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic’s stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers. The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of $US140,000 to $US190,000.



The posting added that equity would be “a major component of the total compensation” beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay. Related Article AI Australia’s largest media companies to unite against AI giants That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of $US1.30 per share. “And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organisation chart do quite well in IPO,” said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra. Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a $US1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly $US1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes.



Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead. After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said. World.title: ‘Crisis moment’: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous people in Brazilian rainforest
World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaBrazil ‘Crisis moment’: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous people in Brazilian rainforest Steven Grattan November 19, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Bogota, Colombia: A rare encounter between Indigenous people living in isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest and members of a neighbouring community has prompted government protections amid concerns about the group’s health and threats to its forest home. The encounter began earlier this week near a government access control post and the Guajajara Indigenous village of Tawari in the north-eastern state of Maranhao, according to a statement from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples. An uncontacted Awa man and others filmed in the Brazilian Amazon in November. Guajajara, Survival International The ministry said about 20 members of the isolated Awa people had been sighted approaching the area in the Arariboia Indigenous Territory, but cautioned that information remained preliminary as authorities assessed the situation. The encounter has raised concerns about why members of a group that has spent decades hunting, fishing and gathering food while avoiding outsiders would suddenly approach a neighbouring community, particularly as illegal logging, hunting and other intrusions threaten their forest territory.



Sarah Shenker, head of Survival Brasil, part of Survival International, an organisation that advocates for Indigenous peoples’ rights, called the encounter “a crisis moment, really, and a wake-up call”, urging Brazilian authorities to crack down on illegal intrusions into Awa territory. She said the images of the encounter could help reinforce the existence of isolated Indigenous groups, whose presence was sometimes disputed by those seeking access to their lands. But she warned that the circumstances surrounding the encounter were troubling. A still from footage of the Awa people who approached a neighbouring Indigenous community. Guajajara, Survival International Footage recorded by members of the neighbouring Guajajara Indigenous community and shared by Survival International shows Awa adults and children gathered amid dense vegetation, some carrying bows and arrows and wearing feathered headdresses and necklaces. The reason for the group’s approach remains unclear, but Survival International says the Awa apparently approached a government team, asked for yams and took them back into the forest.



The Arariboia territory had faced decades of pressure from illegal intruders, Shenker said, leaving isolated communities increasingly vulnerable as surrounding forests had been cleared. The Brazilian government said the Awa group was already registered in the official database of isolated Indigenous peoples and was monitored by a protection team from Funai, the federal Indigenous affairs agency. Funai personnel and Indigenous health workers were in the area, and authorities had activated an emergency co-ordination mechanism to assess potential contact situations and health risks. Survival International has previously estimated that about 100 Awa remain uncontacted, although that is not necessarily a current population count; other Awa live in settled villages and maintain contact with outsiders. One of the most immediate concerns is the risk of disease. Indigenous peoples living in isolation can be particularly vulnerable to infectious illnesses because of their limited previous exposure to pathogens common in the wider population.



The ministry stressed that its policy was not to encourage contact but to protect the Awa’s right to remain isolated and determine for themselves whether to establish relations with outsiders. It also cautioned that a brief encounter did not necessarily mean a group had abandoned its isolation or chosen to establish permanent contact. Related Article Analysis

Paris Agreement What Lula’s win in Brazil means for the Amazon and the warming world The Arariboia territory is also home to the Guajajara people, whose Indigenous forest guardians have spent years monitoring their lands and confronting illegal intrusions. Shenker said those efforts had led to violence against the community, including killings of some community members, while responsibility for protecting the territory ultimately rested with the Brazilian government. “The only way that they will survive is if intruders are kept out of their forest once and for all,” she said. Despite the attention generated by the rare images, Shenker said she would rather the Awa had remained out of sight, living undisturbed in their forest. “We would rather not have images and not have video footage of the uncontacted Awa when that means that they are living in the way that they choose in their forest, able to get on with their lives, hunting, fishing, gathering,” she said.

World.title: A matter of ‘faith’: Speaker admits no one checking WA’s MP declarations
World.content:
PoliticsWAWA Parliament A matter of ‘faith’: Speaker admits no one checking WA’s MP declarations Hamish Hastie November 19, 2026 — 3:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Parliamentary speaker Stephen Price has admitted no one checks the veracity of members’ disclosures, but said it was something that should be “looked at”. The extraordinary admission came as beleaguered Riverton MP Jagadish “Dr Jags” Krishnan confirmed to this masthead he sought external legal advice, after conferring with the clerk of parliament, because of his “financial arrangements”. Riverton MP Jagadish Krishnan, AKA “Dr Jags”. Hamish Hastie WA Parliament’s declaration rules have come under the spotlight in the past fortnight after questions emerged over whether Krishnan had met his obligations, despite not declaring several loans he secured over the past few years. This masthead revealed Krishnan, who co-owns a large network of GP clinics, has several alleged debts and legal demands for money owed totalling nearly $4 million.



Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas used parliamentary privilege on Tuesday to suggest the total figure Krishnan owed was close to $15 million. Labor defeated a motion by the opposition on Tuesday to send Krishnan’s financial affairs and declarations to the powerful Procedures and Privileges Committee, and Premier Roger Cook has deflected further questions to parliament’s presiding officers – of which Price is one. Speaker Stephen Price’s press conference Journalist: Is it your job to ensure that annual returns are accurate? Speaker Stephen Price: No, it’s not. J: So, whose job is it, and what’s the point of those declarations? SP: That’s actually a good question. J: Do you know the answer? SP: I don’t know whose responsibility it is. The clerk is the registrar who collects and holds the record. J: Is public confidence in politicians’ annual returns undermined if there’s an open question whether they’re accurate? SP: Everyone has the same responsibility to ensure that financial returns are as accurate as required under the appropriate legislation. J: But how do we know that responsibility is actually being discharged properly? How does the public know that? SP: That’s a good question. I don’t know the answer. J: Was the premier wrong in to suggest that it was up to presiding officers to deal with this? SP: Look, it’s not our responsibility, but most people think it is. Speaking outside Parliament on Thursday, Price said he had not been asked to check Krishnan’s declarations. He said it was not his job to ensure MP declarations, known as annual returns, were accurate and was asked in response whose job it was to ensure this and what the point of those declarations were.



“That’s actually a good question,” he said. Related Article Updated

WA Parliament Zempilas accuses WA Labor MP of owing as much as $15 million in heated debate When asked whether he knew the answer he replied: “I don’t know whose responsibility it is. The clerk is the registrar who collects and holds the record.” When asked by journalists whether he said the situation was “farcical”, Price said he wouldn’t use those terms. “It has highlighted that we need to have a look at it,” he said.



Declarations are required by the Members of Parliament (Financial Interests) Act 1992, which requires MPs to disclose things including debts, gifts and contributions to travel. Krishnan’s annual return currently only notes a loan with Commonwealth Bank. Stephen Price’s press conference (continued) Journalist: The government of the day needs to take the lead, don’t they? Speaker Stephen Price: I’m not sure. As I said, we have to ... I have to have a look at it. J: I don’t mean any disrespect here, Speaker, but you’re very vague. SP: I don’t have the answers that you want. J: Doesn’t someone need to be able to answer these questions? SP: Now that has come up, yes. On multiple occasions, Krishnan said he was adamant he had met his obligations, citing legal advice he has received. He revealed to this masthead he sought that legal advice because of advice he received from parliament officers.



“After my re-election as the Member for Riverton at the last election, I sought advice from the Clerk of the Legislative Assembly, to ensure my declarations were correct,” he said. “The Clerk advised that given my financial arrangements I should seek further legal opinion. “As I have said previously, that advice provided last year has confirmed my disclosures are correct. Given it is a privileged legal opinion, it will not be released.” But the privilege over legal advice only operates in litigation. Privilege can also be waived by the person’s conduct, such as disclosing the substance of the advice. Zempilas acknowledged there was an element of “faith” in declarations, but threw his support behind an inquiry of some kind into MP disclosures.



“The reason the declarations exist are, for example, if I owe money to that person over there, and there’s a matter surrounding that person over there in parliament, and I’m advocating for them or in support of them, people can see that I might be taking a position because actually I owe that person money,” he said. “In its simple form, that’s what these declarations are about. But if it is impossible to be able to substantiate them, or nobody is in effect policing them, what is the point of them?” WA Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas. Trevor Collens Zempilas then turned the blowtorch on the government for voting down his effort to send Krishnan to the Procedures and Privileges Committee. “The very different issue here is there have been legitimate questions asked in the Parliament of Western Australia through the proper forums and techniques about the member for Riverton’s declarations,” he said.



“When given the opportunity to refer that on to the Privileges and Procedures Committee, the one body within our parliament that can look at these things, the government said no. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament WA Police receive complaints about embattled Labor MP’s alleged debts “That’s because they’re running a protection racket around their member for Riverton, and that is unacceptable. “I don’t know if it passes Labor’s tests. It doesn’t pass the pub test.” Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti again defended Krishnan and said the opposition did not bring any evidence to parliament to suggest he had not met his obligations.



Saffioti suggested all of Krishnan’s loans were related to his companies, and said all MPs were held to account by media and the opposition. “It’s been a system that has existed, and as I’ve said, when people haven’t told the truth, that’s normally found out,” she said. Saffioti said if the presiding officers wanted to look at disclosures she would be “very happy to support that”.

World.title: One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalInterest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes Shane Wright November 19, 2026 — 3:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. It was only a fortnight ago that Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock declared “we don’t see the economy cracking at this point”. Explaining the RBA’s 6-3 decision to deliver a fifth quarter percentage point rate rise in nine months, Bullock said the unemployment rate was “still relatively low” with the country enjoying jobs growth. RBA governor Michele Bullock said the bank thought the labour market was a bit tight. Renee Nowytarger In fact, she argued, “We think that the labour market’s a little bit tight.” After Thursday’s jobs report, that argument – about the strength of the jobs market and the overall economy – has to be revisited.



After the country lost 36,400 jobs in September, the bureau of statistics revealed a further 43,600 positions disappeared in October. It was the worst back-to-back result since 2021 during the pandemic. As Betashares chief economist David Bassanese noted, back-to-back monthly drops in employment seems to suggest “the economy has one foot in recession”. It’s not as if the RBA had not been warned that its aggressive tightening of monetary policy this year might have unwanted economic consequences. The minutes of its November meeting noted the pushback from the three people who voted against the increase. They were worried that, with four rate rises already working their way through the economy, including one inflicted on the country at the end of September, it was too early to tighten the monetary policy screws further. The slowdown in the property market, they said, might reduce economic activity more than expected which, in turn, would feed into employment growth. They were also not persuaded by the argument by the bank’s staff that the labour market was a little tight.



Related Article Employment Unemployment hits five-year high as RBA squeezes jobs market “These members expressed their concern that the economy might be near the point of entering a materially sharper downturn and pointed to the costs in terms of unemployment,” those minutes showed. The Reserve first lifted rates this year on February 4. On that day, unemployment was 4.1 per cent. Over the previous eight months, the country had added 155,000 jobs and the total number of unemployed was up by just 1100. In the eight months since that February rate rise, the number of unemployed has climbed by 91,700 while total jobs growth has slowed to just 20,500. Since that February decision, US President Donald Trump launched his ill-fated war against Iran while the AI construction boom – something that surprised the Reserve if its forecasts are anything to go by – has accelerated and deepened.



Inflation was too high in February and justified the bank’s move that month and the subsequent rate rises in March and May. But, as Bullock and the bank often remind the public, changes in interest rates take up to 12 months to work their way through the economy. That means those rate rises in the first half of the year have yet to fully work their anti-inflation magic. That doesn’t include the impact of the turmoil in the property market caused in part by the rate rises and the federal government’s overhaul of negative gearing and capital gains tax. Unsurprisingly, NSW, the state with the most expensive and disconnected-from-reality property market in the country, has suffered the biggest jobs hit. Since February, it has shed more than 31,000 workers. That’s occurred before the September 30 and November 4 rate rises have even begun to hit the economy.



Bullock and her team may soon be hearing a cracking noise outside their windows. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Crown prosecutor delivers closing address ahead of jury deliberations
World.content:
Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, shows the jury a draft of a long message Lamarre-Condon sent to Baird in November 2023.

In the message, the accused falsely denied blocking a man on Baird’s phone and posting a story on Instagram to give the mistaken impression that Baird had sent him flowers. Lamarre-Condon told the court that he later admitted both of these things to Baird.

This is an extract of the message.

Jesse, I’m literally sitting here in tears trying to piece this all together. Firstly I want to validate how you would be feeling. You feel as if I possibly blocked someone on your Instagram, as I was with you this morning, which would be a massive betrayal of your trust and I hear, understand and see why you would have thought that, being as we were just together. I 100% agree it doesn’t go in my favour/look good for due to the timing and if I was in your situation, I would see why you may have those thoughts/suspicions based on that ...

There is no excuse to violate someone’s privacy and do that period!

I’m still so confused about the flower situation and why that got brought up/or is an issue,or how it even relates to this? You’re in my close friends, why didn’t you just reply to the story instead of taking a screenshot then sending it to me today? You mentioned that a few examples have been brought to your attention and I will happily own anything I’ve done wrong and will be honest about those things.

You know me Jesse, the real Beau, I’ve never done anything “crazy” with/to you and I’ve always been proud the way we could communicate openly and honestly with one another as grown adults, who have a lot of respect for one another. You know I always believe in taking the high road and not doing “petty” things to people … and this shit is simply out of character for me because I would never even have the thought to want to do anything to betray your trust or think of doing this.

World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Grima hoping stars align again with long-shot chance in rich race Craig Kerry November 19, 2026 — 3:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A lightweight, Chris Waller-trained long-shot in a rich race from a wide gate. It’s a familiar and memorable scenario for champion Sydney apprentice Siena Grima. Only this time, Grima will not be on God’s Window. Siena Grima salutes on God’s Window in the Epsom Handicap. Getty Images With her first group 1 ride, Grima scored a dream victory in the $1.5 million Epsom Handicap (1600m) with $26 hope God’s Window last month at Randwick.



On Saturday at Kembla, premier jockey James McDonald takes over on God’s Window in the $1 million The Gong (1600m), where the six-year-old was a $6 chance from gate nine. “When the best jockey in the world wants to jump on, you can’t really say no, can you?” Grima said. The 24-year-old, though, still has a job to do for her boss, Waller, who has four in the race. She rides Osipenko, a $34 chance, from gate 13. The seven-year-old, which has just 53 kilograms, has been less than two lengths away at his past two runs, in the Filante Handicap (1600m) and listed Ladies Day Cup (1500m). “I’ve been happy with him,” said Grima, who has ridden Osipenko in a trial only.



“I’ve done a little bit of his work recently and I think a lightweight will bring him into it and if it all goes to plan, I think he’ll be well enough in the finish. “He always tries hard and he’s an older horse so he knows how to get the job done.” Grima also rides for Waller in the third race, where she takes two kilograms off topweight Medatsu ($12). The pair were fifth last start in a benchmark 78 handicap over 2400m and drop to 2000m in the same grade on Saturday. “He’s always there, but he’s very one pace,” she said. “If he wants to do it, he will, but he’s pretty smart. He carries a big weight, which always makes things harder.”



Grima was happy to stick with Jason Coyle-trained Lulumon ($34) in the sixth, a 1000m benchmark 78 handicap after taking her to second place at her past two starts. She believed Danny Williams-trained Chemtrail ($31) would also run well in the final race after they finished third last time out. “I’ve been looking forward to getting back on her,” she said. “She just can’t really seem to draw a gate, but she’s really tough. I think a bit of give in the ground will help her out, and I think the freshen up will do her well. “It’s good. I’ve got a lot of rides. Chemtrail last start was super and he carries the lightweight again and I don’t think he’s drawn terribly. If he runs up to last start, he’ll be really, really good.” Grima has been among the grieving friends of 22-year-old Scone apprentice Izzy Neale, who died following a race fall at Warren on November 8. A celebration of Neale’s life will be held on Wednesday at Merriwa Showground from 12pm.



Last Saturday at Newcastle, Grima was an emotional winner aboard Ertijaaj of the Izzy’s Gift race, held to honour Neale and her organ donation. Siena Grima winning on Ertijaaj at Newcastle last week. Getty Images “Saturday was still pretty raw, and then winning her race, I was a bit upset,” she said. “But I’m just pushing through and trying to ride as best as I can because she died doing what she loved, and I get to do it every day, which I’m very blessed to do.”

World.title: ‘At a crossroads’: Business leader says ‘vicious slur’ against Jews must not be normalised
World.content:
PoliticsFederalAntisemitism ‘At a crossroads’: Business leader says ‘vicious slur’ against Jews must not be normalised Matthew Knott November 19, 2026 — 3:48pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

One of Australia’s leading businessmen, Steven Lowy, has called for the nation to seize an opportunity to push anti-Jewish hate to the fringes of society when Virginia Bell delivers the final royal commission report into antisemitism, as he insists Jewish Australians must not be excluded or harassed for being supporters of Israel. Lowy, the former co-chief executive of Westfield Corporation, said universities, arts organisations and businesses must take tackling antisemitism as seriously as discrimination against Indigenous Australians, Muslim Australians or women to receive public funding. “I fear that Australian society is at a historic crossroads,” Lowy told a conference organised by the Jerusalem Post newspaper in Sydney on Thursday. “The royal commission now has the nation’s attention, and the world is watching.” Businessman Steven Lowy said antisemitism must be taken as seriously as prejudice against other minority groups. AAPIMAGE



Bell will hand down her final report on December 18, four days after the first anniversary of the Bondi attack which killed 15 people in the nation’s worst terror attack. Lowy said tackling antisemitism will require difficult decisions by private and public institutions. “Who receives public funding? Who gets a grant, a platform, or a seat at the table?” he asked. “Are codes of conduct enforced or quietly set aside when enforcement is awkward? “Ministers, vice chancellors, arts boards, chief executives and councils make those decisions every week. Each one sends a signal about what this country will tolerate.



“The principle is simple: public money should not support people or organisations who promote hatred against any group of Australians.” Lowy, who has previously spoken about the online attacks faced by his family, added that ordinary Australians such as teachers, nurses, tradies and small business owners will have the most important role in ensuring that antisemitism does not become normalised. University of Sydney chancellor and former Telstra chief executive David Thodey agreed with Lowy, telling the conference: “I worry about Australia. This is not what we stand for. We are about inclusion. We are not about antisemitism, and I just find it abhorrent.” The conference venue was heavily protected by armed police guards, but there was no sign of protest activity. Lowy said he believed the rise of antisemitism following the October 7 attacks in Israel, when 1200 people were killed, can be partly explained by a “willful corruption” of words such as genocide, colonisation, apartheid and Zionism “to turn a complex conflict into a license to demonise Jews”.



The word Zionist in particular, he said, “has been twisted and distorted beyond all reality” and “has become weaponised as a vicious slur”. “This brand of antisemitism reflects the hardest prejudice to confront. This is the prejudice that believes itself virtuous, that excluding Jews or denying Jewish self-determination as a stand against racism is somehow a moral and correct thing to be doing,” he said. Lowy argued in his speech that you “cannot separate support for Zionism or the right of Israel to exist from the Jewish people generally”. “I am a proud Jew, and I am a proud Zionist, and the vast majority of Jewish Australians feel responsible for ensuring that Israel continues to exist,” he said. “When an institution says Zionists are not welcome on a panel at a music, art, or literary festival, or in a workplace, Jewish Australians overwhelmingly and understandably interpret that as Jews not being welcome.” Lowy’s stance differs from groups such as the progressive Jewish Council of Australia and non-Zionist Jews, who argue that Jewish identity and support for Israel’s existence should not be conflated.



Related Article Opinion

Antisemitism The abomination on Bondi Beach is a failure that extends beyond any politician or party Steven Lowy Businessman and philanthropist Lowy said Zionism simply describes a “belief in the right of self-determination of the Jewish people in the historic, spiritual, religious, and physical homeland, Israel”. “Zionism does not necessitate any views about borders of Israel, settlements, the legal status of Jerusalem or Palestinian statehood,” he said. Israel’s global standing has plummeted since the war in Gaza began in 2023, with Pew Research polling released in June showing 79 per cent of Australians now hold an unfavorable view of Israel. More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza since the war began according to the Gazan health ministry, a figure that includes Hamas combatants.



Israel has been accused of genocide at the International Court of Justice and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has been charged with war crimes by the International Criminal Court. Related Article Updated

Israeli-Palestinian conflict Australia sanctions Israeli settlers, construction company Lowy said he supported a two-state solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict and that he believed a new government in Israel not led by Netanyahu could help improve relations between Israel and Australia and reduce divisions within Israeli society. “Personalities do matter,” he told this masthead on the sidelines of the conference. He said he opposed the sanctions on Israeli settlers and settler organisations Foreign Minister Penny Wong announced this week, arguing they would damage the Australia-Israel relationship but have no practical impact on settlement building in the West Bank.



“It is in Australia’s interest to have close ties to Israel,” Lowy said, pointing to co-operation between spy agencies ASIO and Mossad on national security as well as technological and business links. World.title: The new Parks and Recreation? Inside Amy Poehler’s long-awaited return to TV
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

When Amy Poehler called Parks and Recreation co-creator Mike Schur and said she had a new idea for a show and wanted to act again, he said yes before he even knew what it was. “It kind of didn’t matter,” he says, speaking to me before the premiere of their new comedy-mystery, Dig, Poehler’s first major TV series in more than a decade. “This is going to sound corny, but the magic [that turned Parks and Recreation into a phenomenon] is Amy. The experience of working with her on that show and creating the character of Leslie Knope was so fun and so formative for me. Editor's pick Australian TV ‘What the hell have I done?’: The crisis that inspired Nazeem Hussain’s new comedy “Especially at this point in our careers and in our lives, the people you do things with matter as much or more than what those things are.” It’s a line that sounds almost exactly like one Leslie uttered to her colleagues in the Parks and Rec finale, co-written by Schur and Poehler 11 years ago: “Teddy Roosevelt once said far and away the best prize that life has to offer is the chance to work hard at work worth doing. I would add that what makes work worth doing is getting to do it with people that you love.” The sentiment isn’t a world away from Poehler’s new character either – another hard-working and often idealistic woman who finds strength in female friendship, this time an archaeologist gearing up to take over the dig site she’s been working on for years in Greece. Although Elise (Poehler) is someone who’s had her spirit broken more than Pawnee’s perkiest public servant. Loading



Amy Poehler (third from right) in the 2015 finale of Parks and Recreation. Divorced and well accustomed to disappointment, this talented archaeologist has been toiling in a “dying field” without the credit she deserves when she comes across an impressive find that could change everything. Unfortunately, Elise is quickly confronted with the reality that good work alone is rarely enough to get ahead. It’s a less hopeful vision of the world than the one Parks and Recreation, the definitive show of the Obama era, gave us – but it’s much more resonant for 2026. Editor's pick Streaming How do you follow-up Adolescence? Stephen Graham went full psycho “As she’s dreaming about taking over a dig, moving up in the world, she starts having to dip her toes into the worlds of [fundraising and glad-handing] and encountering a lot of deeply unpleasant people,” Schur says. Her haughty boss Neville, played by Hugh Laurie, who studied archaeology in his uni days while getting into comedy with the Cambridge Footlights, is great at it. “He loves holding court, orating and basking in the glow of the admiration of the people who surround him,” Schur says of the character. But even he is challenged through the series – especially by the rise of a new guard, including the vacuous heir of a benefactor who cares less about the excavation and discovery of ancient human history and more about dancing on boats and innovation in T-shirt design. “There are two ways to try to make your way in the world: one of them is through stuff that doesn’t really matter, and one of them is through stuff that does matter,” Schur says. “The hard fact is, the people who do the glad-handing and the superficial stuff often are the ones who are getting ahead.” Fina Strazza as Patty, Antonia Thomas as Clare and Geraldine Viswanathan as Dylan in new comedy Dig. Colleen Hayes/Peacock



Based on Kate Myers’ 2023 novel Excavations, the series is both a mystery and an ensemble comedy. It kicks off with a White Lotus-style flash forward in the first episode, with Poehler’s character advising her young cohorts to “tell the right story for the rest of their lives” before biting, kicking and shooting each other – and much of the series is dedicated to what inspired that chaos. Adding that element of mystery is an increasingly common tactic to keep audiences bingeing. But the pleasure of Dig, like the other workplace comedies Schur has worked on, including Parks and Recreation and Brooklyn Nine-Nine, is in its quirky character dynamics. Related Article Streaming Hollywood can’t get enough of this Aussie star. Why is she overlooked at home? Elise isn’t down in the dirt on her own. She’s joined by Dylan (Australia’s Geraldine Viswanathan), a flighty twenty-something who has returned to the site to make amends; Clare (Antonia Thomas, Lovesick), a well-to-do lab tech in her 30s who she’s had beef with for years; and Patty (Fina Strazza, Paper Girls), a dweeby but knowledgeable young assistant overwhelmed on her first dig. “Each of these characters has their strengths and weaknesses,” Viswanathan says. “They take [cues] from each other and grow stronger that way. Dylan’s strength is her fearlessness. She’s down to try anything. And I think she helps embolden Elise, Amy’s character. “I feel like my generation is like, ‘Get it, girl!’ And she’s like, ‘Well, you have to earn it, and you need to do it right.’” Loading



With such a broad range of ages in the main cast, there are plenty of intergenerational gags throughout. Elise, Gen X through and through, is dismayed Dylan has never heard of Pretty Woman and thinks Watergate is a book. But the relationships between her and all the younger women are never condescending or shallow – a fact that reflects Poehler’s respect for younger talent off-screen, too. Viswanathan met Poehler (who is also a creator and executive producer of the series) well before she was hand-picked for the role. Poehler’s production company, Paper Kite, which developed Broad City from a low-budget web series into a hit sitcom in the early 2010s, asked for a meeting with the rising star a while back. “They just wanted to meet me and see what’s up,” she says. “I think Paper Kite keeps their finger on the pulse, especially around women in comedy.” Geraldine Viswanathan as Dylan, Fina Strazza as Patty. Colleen Hayes/Peacock It was a surreal moment for the now 31-year-old, who started doing stand-up at the student bar at the University of Sydney and sketches with local group Freudian Nip (Jenna Owens and Vic Zerbst) before her Hollywood breakthrough in the 2018 sex comedy Blockers. Though now well established on screen – with Thunderbolts last year, she even has a Marvel movie under her belt – working with Poehler is a bucket-list item. “Amy has been on my Mount Rushmore of comedy heroes since I could remember,” she says. “I was such a comedy nerd growing up with Parks and Rec and SNL. She, Tina [Fey] and Mindy [Kaling] were my heroes. I have a really embarrassing Instagram post that’s archived from 2012 of their books, and it’s like ‘#church’. I was studying them. I just wanted to be them so badly.”

World.content:
BusinessCompaniesWall Street ‘It doesn’t get better than this’: Wall Street is about to mint thousands of instant millionaires Sabrina Valle November 19, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Anthropic’s initial public offering is poised to create thousands of paper millionaires among current and former employees, in what could rank among the largest employee wealth windfalls in Silicon Valley history. The offering is expected to unleash a wave of new wealth across the AI sector, rewarding everyone from early researchers and engineers to administrative staff who received stock grants as the Claude maker raced from startup to one of the world’s most valuable companies. Siblings and Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei. Bloomberg The IPO filing shows the amount of wealth embedded in employee stock awards, but not how that wealth is distributed among workers. As a result, outside estimates vary widely. Hill, a San Francisco marketplace for private-company shares, estimates 598 non-founder employees will hold at least $US100 million ($150 million) in equity after the initial public offering. Anthropic has priced its initial public offering at $US83 per share, above its targeted range of $US70 to $US78, giving it a value of around $US1.5 trillion.



Private-markets research firm Sacra estimates that roughly 2800 current and former Anthropic employees could hold at least $US1 million of pre-tax vested equity at a $US1.35 trillion valuation. Related Article Wall Street How infamous fraudster Sam Bankman-Fried missed out on a $52 billion jackpot The firms say their estimates are model-based and use public information. Reuters could not independently verify the estimates, which reflect factors including vesting periods, exercises, tender transactions, option awards, restricted stock units, award timing, headcount and employee retention rates. The filing does not disclose sums due individuals. But the wealth potentially shared by employees is vast. Anthropic option-holders were sitting on $US119 billion of paper gains as of September 30, at a weighted average exercise price of $US2.91 per share, the company disclosed. About $US73 billion of that amount had vested through service and could be exercised immediately. Anthropic did not respond to a comment request on the estimates.



“The idea of equity appreciating to an amount that is life-changing is something that people strive for,” Hill CEO Andrew Benson said. “It doesn’t get better than this.” In a letter to potential shareholders, Anthropic’s co-founders said that AI and Anthropic “represents one of the greatest economic opportunities in history”. Bloomberg Equity at entry level Workers who joined the firm when it started five years ago — even in administrative positions and entry-level jobs — could be sitting on life-changing wealth, reflecting their holdings of stock options that carry exercise prices of less than $US1.



Options granted through 2023 and still outstanding at the end of that year carried an average exercise price of 52 cents, the filing shows. Related Article Opinion

AI Nvidia’s result is gobsmacking, but a sideshow to its CEO spy scandal Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist At SpaceX, which was founded in 2002 and went public in June in a record-busting IPO, many of the employees who became millionaires had worked there for more than a decade. “Early employees who started in a very junior role should have actually a better financial outcome than somebody who joined in a very senior role right before the IPO,” Benson said, referring to Anthropic. Non-founder Anthropic employees can sell up to 10 per cent of their holdings on the first trading day, and up to another 35 per cent after fiscal 2026 earnings.



Early hires reap rewards Founded in 2021, the Claude maker expanded its workforce rapidly alongside the AI boom, growing to about 5300 employees as of September 30 from roughly 940 at the end of 2024. As it hired aggressively, the company used stock-based compensation as a key recruiting tool. Wall Street is bracing for the Anthropic IPO. Bloomberg A May 2024 job posting for an administrative business partner role shows how the benefits of Anthropic’s stock awards extended beyond AI researchers and engineers. The position, which involved scheduling and managing calendars for company leaders, coordinating conference logistics and handling expense claims and reimbursements, paid an annual salary of $US140,000 to $US190,000.



The posting added that equity would be “a major component of the total compensation” beyond the salary, indicating that administrative and support staff were also eligible for stock awards alongside cash pay. Related Article AI Australia’s largest media companies to unite against AI giants That year, Anthropic said it granted employees options at an average exercise price of $US1.30 per share. “And as we know from several anecdotes after the SpaceX IPO, this is often enough to help people down the organisation chart do quite well in IPO,” said Marcelo Ballve, head of research at Sacra. Anthropic granted CFO Krishna Rao 14 million stock options in 2024, also with a $US1.30 exercise price, according to the filing. At the IPO price range, those options would carry roughly $US1 billion in gross intrinsic value, before exercise costs and taxes.



Ballve said that equity awards for administrative, support and entry-level roles are not uncommon at venture capital-backed companies. Historically, though, many companies phased out equity grants at hiring for these roles as they scaled up and salaries became more competitive, moving to performance- and tenure-based grants instead. After Anthropic goes public, the company will likely reserve upfront equity grants solely for recruiting top talent, he said. World.content:
WorldSouth AmericaBrazil ‘Crisis moment’: Rare encounter with isolated Indigenous people in Brazilian rainforest Steven Grattan November 19, 2026 — 3:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Bogota, Colombia: A rare encounter between Indigenous people living in isolation in Brazil’s Amazon rainforest and members of a neighbouring community has prompted government protections amid concerns about the group’s health and threats to its forest home. The encounter began earlier this week near a government access control post and the Guajajara Indigenous village of Tawari in the north-eastern state of Maranhao, according to a statement from Brazil’s Ministry of Indigenous Peoples. An uncontacted Awa man and others filmed in the Brazilian Amazon in November. Guajajara, Survival International The ministry said about 20 members of the isolated Awa people had been sighted approaching the area in the Arariboia Indigenous Territory, but cautioned that information remained preliminary as authorities assessed the situation. The encounter has raised concerns about why members of a group that has spent decades hunting, fishing and gathering food while avoiding outsiders would suddenly approach a neighbouring community, particularly as illegal logging, hunting and other intrusions threaten their forest territory.



Sarah Shenker, head of Survival Brasil, part of Survival International, an organisation that advocates for Indigenous peoples’ rights, called the encounter “a crisis moment, really, and a wake-up call”, urging Brazilian authorities to crack down on illegal intrusions into Awa territory. She said the images of the encounter could help reinforce the existence of isolated Indigenous groups, whose presence was sometimes disputed by those seeking access to their lands. But she warned that the circumstances surrounding the encounter were troubling. A still from footage of the Awa people who approached a neighbouring Indigenous community. Guajajara, Survival International Footage recorded by members of the neighbouring Guajajara Indigenous community and shared by Survival International shows Awa adults and children gathered amid dense vegetation, some carrying bows and arrows and wearing feathered headdresses and necklaces. The reason for the group’s approach remains unclear, but Survival International says the Awa apparently approached a government team, asked for yams and took them back into the forest.



The Arariboia territory had faced decades of pressure from illegal intruders, Shenker said, leaving isolated communities increasingly vulnerable as surrounding forests had been cleared. The Brazilian government said the Awa group was already registered in the official database of isolated Indigenous peoples and was monitored by a protection team from Funai, the federal Indigenous affairs agency. Funai personnel and Indigenous health workers were in the area, and authorities had activated an emergency co-ordination mechanism to assess potential contact situations and health risks. Survival International has previously estimated that about 100 Awa remain uncontacted, although that is not necessarily a current population count; other Awa live in settled villages and maintain contact with outsiders. One of the most immediate concerns is the risk of disease. Indigenous peoples living in isolation can be particularly vulnerable to infectious illnesses because of their limited previous exposure to pathogens common in the wider population.



The ministry stressed that its policy was not to encourage contact but to protect the Awa’s right to remain isolated and determine for themselves whether to establish relations with outsiders. It also cautioned that a brief encounter did not necessarily mean a group had abandoned its isolation or chosen to establish permanent contact. Related Article Analysis

Paris Agreement What Lula’s win in Brazil means for the Amazon and the warming world The Arariboia territory is also home to the Guajajara people, whose Indigenous forest guardians have spent years monitoring their lands and confronting illegal intrusions. Shenker said those efforts had led to violence against the community, including killings of some community members, while responsibility for protecting the territory ultimately rested with the Brazilian government. “The only way that they will survive is if intruders are kept out of their forest once and for all,” she said. Despite the attention generated by the rare images, Shenker said she would rather the Awa had remained out of sight, living undisturbed in their forest. “We would rather not have images and not have video footage of the uncontacted Awa when that means that they are living in the way that they choose in their forest, able to get on with their lives, hunting, fishing, gathering,” she said.

World.title: A matter of ‘faith’: Speaker admits no one checking WA’s MP declarations
World.content:
PoliticsWAWA Parliament A matter of ‘faith’: Speaker admits no one checking WA’s MP declarations Hamish Hastie November 19, 2026 — 3:42pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Parliamentary speaker Stephen Price has admitted no one checks the veracity of members’ disclosures, but said it was something that should be “looked at”. The extraordinary admission came as beleaguered Riverton MP Jagadish “Dr Jags” Krishnan confirmed to this masthead he sought external legal advice, after conferring with the clerk of parliament, because of his “financial arrangements”. Riverton MP Jagadish Krishnan, AKA “Dr Jags”. Hamish Hastie WA Parliament’s declaration rules have come under the spotlight in the past fortnight after questions emerged over whether Krishnan had met his obligations, despite not declaring several loans he secured over the past few years. This masthead revealed Krishnan, who co-owns a large network of GP clinics, has several alleged debts and legal demands for money owed totalling nearly $4 million.



Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas used parliamentary privilege on Tuesday to suggest the total figure Krishnan owed was close to $15 million. Labor defeated a motion by the opposition on Tuesday to send Krishnan’s financial affairs and declarations to the powerful Procedures and Privileges Committee, and Premier Roger Cook has deflected further questions to parliament’s presiding officers – of which Price is one. Speaker Stephen Price’s press conference Journalist: Is it your job to ensure that annual returns are accurate? Speaker Stephen Price: No, it’s not. J: So, whose job is it, and what’s the point of those declarations? SP: That’s actually a good question. J: Do you know the answer? SP: I don’t know whose responsibility it is. The clerk is the registrar who collects and holds the record. J: Is public confidence in politicians’ annual returns undermined if there’s an open question whether they’re accurate? SP: Everyone has the same responsibility to ensure that financial returns are as accurate as required under the appropriate legislation. J: But how do we know that responsibility is actually being discharged properly? How does the public know that? SP: That’s a good question. I don’t know the answer. J: Was the premier wrong in to suggest that it was up to presiding officers to deal with this? SP: Look, it’s not our responsibility, but most people think it is. Speaking outside Parliament on Thursday, Price said he had not been asked to check Krishnan’s declarations. He said it was not his job to ensure MP declarations, known as annual returns, were accurate and was asked in response whose job it was to ensure this and what the point of those declarations were.



“That’s actually a good question,” he said. Related Article Updated

WA Parliament Zempilas accuses WA Labor MP of owing as much as $15 million in heated debate When asked whether he knew the answer he replied: “I don’t know whose responsibility it is. The clerk is the registrar who collects and holds the record.” When asked by journalists whether he said the situation was “farcical”, Price said he wouldn’t use those terms. “It has highlighted that we need to have a look at it,” he said.



Declarations are required by the Members of Parliament (Financial Interests) Act 1992, which requires MPs to disclose things including debts, gifts and contributions to travel. Krishnan’s annual return currently only notes a loan with Commonwealth Bank. Stephen Price’s press conference (continued) Journalist: The government of the day needs to take the lead, don’t they? Speaker Stephen Price: I’m not sure. As I said, we have to ... I have to have a look at it. J: I don’t mean any disrespect here, Speaker, but you’re very vague. SP: I don’t have the answers that you want. J: Doesn’t someone need to be able to answer these questions? SP: Now that has come up, yes. On multiple occasions, Krishnan said he was adamant he had met his obligations, citing legal advice he has received. He revealed to this masthead he sought that legal advice because of advice he received from parliament officers.



“After my re-election as the Member for Riverton at the last election, I sought advice from the Clerk of the Legislative Assembly, to ensure my declarations were correct,” he said. “The Clerk advised that given my financial arrangements I should seek further legal opinion. “As I have said previously, that advice provided last year has confirmed my disclosures are correct. Given it is a privileged legal opinion, it will not be released.” But the privilege over legal advice only operates in litigation. Privilege can also be waived by the person’s conduct, such as disclosing the substance of the advice. Zempilas acknowledged there was an element of “faith” in declarations, but threw his support behind an inquiry of some kind into MP disclosures.



“The reason the declarations exist are, for example, if I owe money to that person over there, and there’s a matter surrounding that person over there in parliament, and I’m advocating for them or in support of them, people can see that I might be taking a position because actually I owe that person money,” he said. “In its simple form, that’s what these declarations are about. But if it is impossible to be able to substantiate them, or nobody is in effect policing them, what is the point of them?” WA Opposition Leader Basil Zempilas. Trevor Collens Zempilas then turned the blowtorch on the government for voting down his effort to send Krishnan to the Procedures and Privileges Committee. “The very different issue here is there have been legitimate questions asked in the Parliament of Western Australia through the proper forums and techniques about the member for Riverton’s declarations,” he said.



“When given the opportunity to refer that on to the Privileges and Procedures Committee, the one body within our parliament that can look at these things, the government said no. Related Article Exclusive

WA Parliament WA Police receive complaints about embattled Labor MP’s alleged debts “That’s because they’re running a protection racket around their member for Riverton, and that is unacceptable. “I don’t know if it passes Labor’s tests. It doesn’t pass the pub test.” Deputy Premier Rita Saffioti again defended Krishnan and said the opposition did not bring any evidence to parliament to suggest he had not met his obligations.



Saffioti suggested all of Krishnan’s loans were related to his companies, and said all MPs were held to account by media and the opposition. “It’s been a system that has existed, and as I’ve said, when people haven’t told the truth, that’s normally found out,” she said. Saffioti said if the presiding officers wanted to look at disclosures she would be “very happy to support that”.

World.title: One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalInterest rates One foot in recession: The unemployment numbers that blow up the RBA’s case for hikes Shane Wright November 19, 2026 — 3:33pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

It was only a fortnight ago that Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock declared “we don’t see the economy cracking at this point”. Explaining the RBA’s 6-3 decision to deliver a fifth quarter percentage point rate rise in nine months, Bullock said the unemployment rate was “still relatively low” with the country enjoying jobs growth. RBA governor Michele Bullock said the bank thought the labour market was a bit tight. Renee Nowytarger In fact, she argued, “We think that the labour market’s a little bit tight.” After Thursday’s jobs report, that argument – about the strength of the jobs market and the overall economy – has to be revisited.



After the country lost 36,400 jobs in September, the bureau of statistics revealed a further 43,600 positions disappeared in October. It was the worst back-to-back result since 2021 during the pandemic. As Betashares chief economist David Bassanese noted, back-to-back monthly drops in employment seems to suggest “the economy has one foot in recession”. It’s not as if the RBA had not been warned that its aggressive tightening of monetary policy this year might have unwanted economic consequences. The minutes of its November meeting noted the pushback from the three people who voted against the increase. They were worried that, with four rate rises already working their way through the economy, including one inflicted on the country at the end of September, it was too early to tighten the monetary policy screws further. The slowdown in the property market, they said, might reduce economic activity more than expected which, in turn, would feed into employment growth. They were also not persuaded by the argument by the bank’s staff that the labour market was a little tight.



Related Article Employment Unemployment hits five-year high as RBA squeezes jobs market “These members expressed their concern that the economy might be near the point of entering a materially sharper downturn and pointed to the costs in terms of unemployment,” those minutes showed. The Reserve first lifted rates this year on February 4. On that day, unemployment was 4.1 per cent. Over the previous eight months, the country had added 155,000 jobs and the total number of unemployed was up by just 1100. In the eight months since that February rate rise, the number of unemployed has climbed by 91,700 while total jobs growth has slowed to just 20,500. Since that February decision, US President Donald Trump launched his ill-fated war against Iran while the AI construction boom – something that surprised the Reserve if its forecasts are anything to go by – has accelerated and deepened.



Inflation was too high in February and justified the bank’s move that month and the subsequent rate rises in March and May. But, as Bullock and the bank often remind the public, changes in interest rates take up to 12 months to work their way through the economy. That means those rate rises in the first half of the year have yet to fully work their anti-inflation magic. That doesn’t include the impact of the turmoil in the property market caused in part by the rate rises and the federal government’s overhaul of negative gearing and capital gains tax. Unsurprisingly, NSW, the state with the most expensive and disconnected-from-reality property market in the country, has suffered the biggest jobs hit. Since February, it has shed more than 31,000 workers. That’s occurred before the September 30 and November 4 rate rises have even begun to hit the economy.



Bullock and her team may soon be hearing a cracking noise outside their windows. Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

World.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon trial live updates: Crown prosecutor delivers closing address ahead of jury deliberations
World.content:
Crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield, SC, shows the jury a draft of a long message Lamarre-Condon sent to Baird in November 2023.

In the message, the accused falsely denied blocking a man on Baird’s phone and posting a story on Instagram to give the mistaken impression that Baird had sent him flowers. Lamarre-Condon told the court that he later admitted both of these things to Baird.

This is an extract of the message.

Jesse, I’m literally sitting here in tears trying to piece this all together. Firstly I want to validate how you would be feeling. You feel as if I possibly blocked someone on your Instagram, as I was with you this morning, which would be a massive betrayal of your trust and I hear, understand and see why you would have thought that, being as we were just together. I 100% agree it doesn’t go in my favour/look good for due to the timing and if I was in your situation, I would see why you may have those thoughts/suspicions based on that ...

There is no excuse to violate someone’s privacy and do that period!

I’m still so confused about the flower situation and why that got brought up/or is an issue,or how it even relates to this? You’re in my close friends, why didn’t you just reply to the story instead of taking a screenshot then sending it to me today? You mentioned that a few examples have been brought to your attention and I will happily own anything I’ve done wrong and will be honest about those things.

You know me Jesse, the real Beau, I’ve never done anything “crazy” with/to you and I’ve always been proud the way we could communicate openly and honestly with one another as grown adults, who have a lot of respect for one another. You know I always believe in taking the high road and not doing “petty” things to people … and this shit is simply out of character for me because I would never even have the thought to want to do anything to betray your trust or think of doing this.

World.content:
SportRacingHorse racing Grima hoping stars align again with long-shot chance in rich race Craig Kerry November 19, 2026 — 3:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. A lightweight, Chris Waller-trained long-shot in a rich race from a wide gate. It’s a familiar and memorable scenario for champion Sydney apprentice Siena Grima. Only this time, Grima will not be on God’s Window. Siena Grima salutes on God’s Window in the Epsom Handicap. Getty Images With her first group 1 ride, Grima scored a dream victory in the $1.5 million Epsom Handicap (1600m) with $26 hope God’s Window last month at Randwick.



On Saturday at Kembla, premier jockey James McDonald takes over on God’s Window in the $1 million The Gong (1600m), where the six-year-old was a $6 chance from gate nine. “When the best jockey in the world wants to jump on, you can’t really say no, can you?” Grima said. The 24-year-old, though, still has a job to do for her boss, Waller, who has four in the race. She rides Osipenko, a $34 chance, from gate 13. The seven-year-old, which has just 53 kilograms, has been less than two lengths away at his past two runs, in the Filante Handicap (1600m) and listed Ladies Day Cup (1500m). “I’ve been happy with him,” said Grima, who has ridden Osipenko in a trial only.



“I’ve done a little bit of his work recently and I think a lightweight will bring him into it and if it all goes to plan, I think he’ll be well enough in the finish. “He always tries hard and he’s an older horse so he knows how to get the job done.” Grima also rides for Waller in the third race, where she takes two kilograms off topweight Medatsu ($12). The pair were fifth last start in a benchmark 78 handicap over 2400m and drop to 2000m in the same grade on Saturday. “He’s always there, but he’s very one pace,” she said. “If he wants to do it, he will, but he’s pretty smart. He carries a big weight, which always makes things harder.”



Grima was happy to stick with Jason Coyle-trained Lulumon ($34) in the sixth, a 1000m benchmark 78 handicap after taking her to second place at her past two starts. She believed Danny Williams-trained Chemtrail ($31) would also run well in the final race after they finished third last time out. “I’ve been looking forward to getting back on her,” she said. “She just can’t really seem to draw a gate, but she’s really tough. I think a bit of give in the ground will help her out, and I think the freshen up will do her well. “It’s good. I’ve got a lot of rides. Chemtrail last start was super and he carries the lightweight again and I don’t think he’s drawn terribly. If he runs up to last start, he’ll be really, really good.” Grima has been among the grieving friends of 22-year-old Scone apprentice Izzy Neale, who died following a race fall at Warren on November 8. A celebration of Neale’s life will be held on Wednesday at Merriwa Showground from 12pm.



Last Saturday at Newcastle, Grima was an emotional winner aboard Ertijaaj of the Izzy’s Gift race, held to honour Neale and her organ donation. Siena Grima winning on Ertijaaj at Newcastle last week. Getty Images “Saturday was still pretty raw, and then winning her race, I was a bit upset,” she said. “But I’m just pushing through and trying to ride as best as I can because she died doing what she loved, and I get to do it every day, which I’m very blessed to do.”
