World.title: More than 3000 bird flu tests carried out since July
World.content:
The Ministry of Primary Industries (MPI) will test a little penguin that died in Kaikōura to rule out bird flu as the cause.

New Zealand has had three individual detections of H5 bird flu since July and there have been no positive cases since August.

Chief veterinary officer Dr Mary van Andel said it could take two rounds of testing at a specialist animal health laboratory in Wellington to rule it out.

"Since the first detection of bird flu in New Zealand on 15 July this year, MPI has received more than 3500 public reports, and has carried out more than 3180 tests," she said.

"We're grateful to everyone that takes time to report sick or dead birds. All reports play an important role in our surveillance for bird flu in New Zealand."

Each report was carefully reviewed and assessed.

While the kororā death was unfortunate, she said it was not uncommon for penguins to die for a variety of reasons.

People should report seeing three or more sick or dead wild birds in a group to the exotic pest and disease hotline on 0800 80 99 66 or online at report.mpi.govt.nz

World.title: Man accused of sexual offending against four young boys named as Christchurch man Tahu Paki
World.content:
A man accused of sexual offending against four young boys can now be named as Christchurch man Tahu Paki.

Paki faces 18 charges including nine of sexual violation by unlawful sexual connection, two of attempted sexual violation by unlawful sexual violation, two of indecent assault on a young person under 16 and five charges of indecent assault. Paki denies the allegations.

On Thursday, the Court of Appeal released a judgment declining his leave to bring a second appeal against name suppression.

In March, Christchurch District Court Judge Michael Crosbie declined Paki's name suppression.

Judge Crosbie said Paki's application was premised on publication of his name causing extreme hardship to himself and his family.

Crosbie's judgment said the Crown opposed interim name suppression, submitting that none of the grounds relied on by Paki reached the level of "extreme hardship".

The Crown also said there were "positive reasons" for not allowing suppression to continue, including that suppression of his name was "impeding the investigation into the alleged offending and is likely impeding additional complainants from coming forward and reporting similar experiences with the defendant".

The Crown said there was "significant public interest" in Paki's name being published.

Judge Crosbie said none of the matters raised by Paki reached the threshold of extreme hardship.

"There is a significant public interest in Mr Paki's name being published and the proceedings being open so that if there are other complainants ... they may feel as though they can safely come forward."

He said he was "not satisfied that publication of his name will result in any hardship beyond that which is an ordinary consequence of alleged offending like this".

"The threshold for "extreme hardship" is very high, and it has not been met in this case."

Paki then appealed to the High Court. Justice Rachel Dunningham declined the appeal in June, and Paki then went to the Court of Appeal.

On Thursday, the Court of Appeal rejected his application for leave to appeal.

World.title: Airlines make it difficult for passengers to understand their rights: Consumer NZ
World.content:
Audio player for " Commerce Commission files charges against Air New Zealand " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2687624%2Fairlines-make-it-difficult-for-passengers-to-understand-their-rights-consumer-nz

Commerce Commission files charges against Air New Zealand Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

Consumer NZ Chief Executive Jon Duffy says airlines are making it difficult for passengers to understand their rights when flight cancellations or delays disrupt their travel plans.

It comes after the Commerce Commission announced it was filing charges against Air New Zealand under the Fair Trading Act, alleging the airline misled passengers about their rights to compensation when flights were disrupted for reasons within its control.

Speaking to Checkpoint on Thursday, Duffy said passengers in other territories were proactively advised of refund rights when preventable problems incurred extra costs.

"Because [in New Zealand] there's no mandatory requirement for airlines to disclose passengers rights to them when a disruption occurs there's ample opportunity for airlines to either mislead, sow confusion or omit to tell people what their rights are," he said.

Duffy said the Governent had regulation making powers to compel the airlines to do better for affected customers.

"New Zealand is actually an outlier in not doing this.

"If a passenger is put to expense because of a cancellation or a disruption that is within control of the airline, things like mechanical failure [or] crew sickness they are entitled to be reimbursed for any extra espenses that they're put to," Duffy said

He said Jet Star was recently fined $2.25 million by the Commerce Commission in a similar case.

Frequent concerns

The commission said over the past five years, consumers have often raised concerns about Air New Zealand.

Its deputy chair Anne Callinan claimed Air New Zealand made statements that led some passengers to incorrectly assume they weren't entitled to compensation, and rejected legitimate reimbursement claims.

Callinan said the commission believed passengers missed out on money they were entitled to under the law.

She said New Zealand's Civil Aviation Act is clear that airlines have a responsibility to reimburse domestic passengers for losses caused by cancellations or delays that are within the airline's control.

Responding to the charges, Air New Zealand said it was disappointed court proceedings had been started and had approached the commission's investigation in good faith.

It undertook a voluntary review of more than 62,000 claims relating to disruptions within its control, and identified mistakes in less than one percent of cases.

It said all affected customers have been contacted and the mistakes put right.

World.title: Corrections still tackling almost 7000 prison cell risks
World.content:
Content warning: This article discusses suicide.

Four years into a nationwide effort to make prison cells safer, almost 7000 known suicide risks remain in high-security and remand cells across the country.

Data released under the Official Information Act shows Corrections initially identified 2350 risks, before further inspections pushed the total to 13,335.

Corrections said it was committed to preventing self-harm and unnatural deaths and was prioritising cells based on risk as it continued the $6.79 million programme.

Just under half the risks - 6429 - had been removed or remediated to date.

The pace of progress has been criticised as deeply concerning by human rights monitors at Amnesty International and the mother of a prisoner who died in his cell in 2022.

Corrections said building constraints, high cell occupancy and other factors meant it would not be feasible to eliminate all of the risks, but said it was taking the programme seriously.

Audio player for " Thousands of suicide risks in prison cells not addressed " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/crime-and-justice/2687617%2Fcorrections-still-tackling-almost-7000-prison-cell-risks

Thousands of suicide risks in prison cells not addressed Checkpoint Download MP3 4m

Mother says action cannot wait

In findings released in August about the death of 30-year-old Nukuroa "Nuku" Strange in an Invercargill Prison cell in 2022, coroner Amelia Steel said it was unacceptable that Corrections had failed to act with urgency to mitigate a known risk.

Strange, who was on remand, had attempted suicide twice in the months before he died.

Although details of his death cannot be reported for legal reasons, the circumstances were the same as the death of another prisoner in the cell six years earlier.

Strange's mother, Kerry Ann Pink, said she remembered the moment during the inquest when she learnt about the previous death.

"It made me angry. I sort of had to hold on to my husband's leg and he had my fingernail imprint on his leg because I was just so angry. They could have prevented it but they didn't," she said.

Pink said she still regularly listened to an audio recording of her last phone call with her son and thought about all of the milestones he was missing.

Pink, who has organised suicide awareness events in Invercargill, said it should not take Corrections years to mitigate thousands of other known cell risks around the country.

"That is honestly piss poor. These are lives that they're playing with. It makes you angry. What happens if this is your child?" she said.

Corrections said staff were managing a growing number of people who had mental health and disability needs. RNZ / Cole Eastham-Farrelly

Every risk cannot be eliminated - Corrections

Deputy commissioner for men's prisons Neil Beales said Corrections was taking the programme seriously and staff were investing significant time, effort and attention to make cells safer.

"This isn't something we're doing on the side. It isn't something to do when we can. It's about not only looking at our existing infrastructure, particularly the older infrastructure where those risks were more prominent but embedding those lessons into how we build future infrastructure," he said.

Beales said the programme had grown in scope partly because officials had decided to take a more expansive view of cell risks rather than just removing the obvious hazards.

He said Corrections wanted to keep prisoners safe but also avoid making every cell "pretty much sterile".

"Where the department have done things for all of the best intentions - like putting televisions in cells or putting better toilet facilities - sometimes these things end up then presenting a risk that was not intended. We do want to try to make the living environments for people in prison as normal as we possibly can," he said.

"This is a challenge that I think every single Department of Corrections in every single country will face - how do you balance the ability to normalise an environment but at the same time remove every single risk in a prison?"

The programme would not result in every risk being removed from every cell, Beales said.

Preventing suicide and self-harm also involved proper at-risk and cell-sharing risk assessments, as well as ensuring vulnerable prisoners had the right placement, supervision and oversight, he said.

"Personally, I don't think we're ever going to be done at stopping trying to stop people from harming themselves. I can't see a time when we will ever turn around as a department and say 'okay, we've cracked this'."

Corrections declined to provide further details of where the remaining 6906 risks were located, saying doing so could inadvertently inform vulnerable prisoners where to find them.

27 apparent suicides since 2023

Reports published by Corrections showed 27 apparent suicides in prisons since 2023, after the programme began.

In the eight years before that, there were 55 apparent suicides, with the annual number ranging from one to 11.

Amnesty International Aotearoa movement building and advocacy director Lisa Woods said New Zealand owed prisoners dignity and care.

"This is a horrific situation that I think people would expect Corrections and the minister to be addressing urgently," she said.

Woods said she was deeply concerned by how long it was taking Corrections to make cells safer and how little the department had initially known about the number of risks.

Almost 7000 hazards presented a "significant amount of risk", she said.

"It's not good enough. Corrections must provide the funding to address this issue immediately," she said.

Corrections said staff were managing a growing number of people who had mental health and disability needs.

It said all deaths in custody were referred to the coroner and investigated by the independent Office of the Inspectorate, which provided detailed recommendations.

The department said it had recently refreshed and extended its suicide prevention and postvention action plan and expanded its prison mental health teams.

The programme to make cells safer, which was initially intended to run until 2027, had also been funded until 2028, Corrections said.

World.title: Commerce Commission files charges against Air  New Zealand
World.content:
Audio player for " Commerce Commission files charges against Air New Zealand " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/business/2680040%2Fcommerce-commission-files-charges-against-air-new-zealand

Commerce Commission files charges against Air New Zealand Checkpoint Download MP3 8m

The Commerce Commission is filing charges against Air New Zealand under the Fair Trading Act.

It alleges the airline misled passengers about their rights to compensation when flights were disrupted for reasons within the airline's control.

Delays that would be considered within an airline's control include engineering issues, crew sickness, and operational delays.

The commission said over the past five years, consumers have frequently raised concerns about Air New Zealand.

Its deputy chair Anne Callinan claimed Air New Zealand made statements that led some passengers to incorrectly assume they weren't entitled to compensation, and rejected legitimate reimbursement claims.

Callinan said the commission believed passengers missed out on money they were entitled to under the law.

She said New Zealand's Civil Aviation Act is clear that airlines have a responsibility to reimburse domestic passengers for losses caused by cancellations or delays that are within the airline's control.

Responding to the charges, Air New Zealand said it was disappointed the Commerce Commission has decided to start court proceedings.

A spokesperson said the airline approached the commission's investigation in good faith.

It undertook a voluntary review of more than 62,000 claims relating to disruptions within its control, and identified mistakes in less than one percent of cases.

It said all affected customers have been contacted and the mistakes put right.

The airline has apologised and said it has improved internal guidance and training to ensure it doesn't happen again.

Consumer NZ chief executive, Jon Duffy, said airlines were making it difficult for passengers to understand their rights when flight cancellations or delays impacted travel plans.

Duffy said passengers in other territories were proactively advised of refund rights when preventable problems incurred extra costs.

"Because [in New Zealand] there's no mandatory requirement for airlines to disclose passengers rights to them when a disruption occurs there's ample opportunity for airlines to either mislead, sow confusion or omit to tell people what their rights are," he said.

Duffy said the government had regulation making powers to compel the airlines to do better for affected customers.

"New Zealand is actually an outlier in not doing this.

"If a passenger is put to expense because of a cancellation or a disruption that is within control of the airline, things like mechanical failure [or] crew sickness they are entitled to be reimbursed for any extra expenses that they're put to," Duffy said

World.title: Tonnes of asbestos pulled from $1b Queenstown development site
World.content:
Thousands of tonnes of asbestos has been removed from the site of a more than $1 billion Queenstown development, according to newly-released council documents.

Lakeview is a residential, hospitality and retail precinct being built by Australian property developer 94 Feet as an extension of the town centre.

Queenstown Lakes District Council approved an extra $6.3 million to clear asbestos from the site in 2021, bringing the forecast site clearance cost to $12m.

Documents published by the council on Thursday suggest it was aware asbestos was present before demolition work began.

The initial plan was for excavation and off-site disposal of affected soil after environmental reporting confirmed asbestos fibres in the soil at four locations in 2020, with two above the relevant guidelines.

"As demolition and site-clearance progressed, considerably more asbestos was encountered than had been identified through the earlier investigations," the council said.

The final demolition report recorded 64.56 tonnes of asbestos-containing building material and 12,669 tonnes of asbestos-contaminated soil were removed over 12 months.

The council said the contractor reported the "significant" amount of contaminated soil was related to historic work at the site.

Lakeview 2020 Supplied/94Feet

While the land under a development agreement had been remediated, other council-retained land including Lynch Block, the proposed hot pool site and Market Square might need further investigation and possible mitigation or remediation, the council said.

"On Lot 9, remediation work has been completed and measures are in place for the ongoing management of encapsulated asbestos-contaminated soil," the council said.

The wider infrastructure bill hit $74m in a January 2025 forecast, comprising $42m in subdivision costs, $14m for subdivision site clearance, $2m for ancillary site clearance and $16m for ancillary projects.

The extra work included additional transport and water infrastructure projects alongside the subdivision but with benefits for the wider network.

Supplied/94Feet

Of the forecast spending, $23 million was funded through rates and development contributions and $52m was reported as cost of sale, the council said.

The council said $48m had been invested in subdivision infrastructure in subsequent reports, with an additional $7m in deferred infrastructure.

The Lakeview land was initially valued at $42m.

The council planned to progressively sell "super lots" to the developer in stages, which would then develop them in line with an agreed plan for the entire precinct.

The council said the land deal provided for $75m in staged base land payments and it was also entitled to a share of the profit.

"This mechanism allows council to share in additional value realised over the life of the development," the council said.

In 2018, the council asked for pitches to develop the Lakeview Precinct, saying it wanted to maximise the financial return in way that minimised risk for ratepayers, create a thriving residential-focused mixed-used precinct and complete the project in eight to 10 years, subject to market conditions.

The council noted there should be a range of housing price points and types of homes, although affordable housing was not a requirement.

Housing insecurity, affordability and shortages have plagued Queenstown for years, with some people resorting to sharing rooms, hot-bedding, and living in garages, tents or cars.

About 300 people at a former Queenstown camping ground, many of whom were low-wage migrant workers, were evicted in 2019 to make way for the development

World.title: Person injured in dog attack at Dunedin park
World.content:
Dunedin City Council is investigating reports of two dogs attacking a person at a park.

Emergency services were called to Kettle Park on Victoria Road at 9.30am on Thursday following reports that a person had been injured.

Council staff have been in touch with the person but are yet to find the dogs' owner.

The council wanted to hear from the dogs' owner or anyone who witnessed the attack.

"Our investigation is ongoing and we will be speaking to witnesses," the council said.

"Our animal control officers have an increased presence in the area until the dogs are located."

St John was notified but paramedics were not needed.

World.title: ‘Reputational damage’: Queenstown council warned over risks from Wānaka sludge deal
World.content:
Queenstown's mayor and two councillors were warned that a deal to spread Wānaka's sewage sludge on farmland in Central Otago would degrade the land and could pose a reputational risk for the council.

Details of the council's five-year agreement with contractor SJ Allen Holdings were revealed in documents released under the Local Government Official Information and Meetings Act and published by the council.

The documents show a council staff member told Mayor John Glover and councillors Gavin Bartlett and Cody Tucker that the contract would keep the council at "arm's length" from the risks.

Otago Regional Council granted non-notified resource consent in January allowing the district council to spread the sludge - a by-product of the wastewater treatment process - onto farmland near Lauder.

When Lauder locals discovered what was happening in September, there was an outcry over odour, dust, and potential effects on waterways.

Otago Regional Council has since been reviewing the consent, while Central Otago's mayor and councillors have written to their Queenstown counterparts asking them to reconsider the deal.

The documents show Glover, Bartlett and Tucker were first told about the potential arrangement in February, once SJ Allen had secured the regional council discharge consent.

Deal done under time pressure

The district council already had an arrangement with SJ Allen to truck Wānaka's sewage sludge to a landfill near Winton in Southland.

In the February letter, a staff member told Glover, Bartlett, and Tucker that the arrangement was becoming increasingly costly and that SJ Allen had come forward with an unsolicited alternative offer that could deliver a "magnitude of savings".

"SJ Allen approached us late last week advising that they had secured Resource Consent to dispose of wastewater sludge to land at a property located in Central Otago. They have offered to accept up to 2000 tonnes of material from our Wānaka WWTP [wastewater treatment plant] ...on the basis that we enter into a five-year commitment for this arrangement," the letter said.

The costs were redacted in the documents, but Glover previously told RNZ the arrangement saved the council about $1 million.

The staff member, whose name was redacted, said the district council would need to move quickly with a sunset clause in SJ Allen's conditional agreement to purchase the land at Lauder.

"Unfortunately, we are being put under some time pressure to advise SJ Allen of our interest in this offer," they said.

Otago Regional Council granted non-notified resource consent in January allowing the district council to spread the sludge onto farmland near Lauder. Supplied

The staff member told Glover, Bartlett, and Tucker that the deal came with "real and perceived" risks.

They said there was a notable difference between taking sewage sludge to landfill and spreading it on farmland.

"Wastewater sludges include contaminants and the land will be subject to degradation as a result of the application of these materials. The resource consent will have considered these within the assessment of environmental effects, and we will be at arm's length from this due to the contractual arrangement," they wrote.

"Risks associated with contamination and consent compliance will sit with the consent holder, but should issues occur, these could lead to reputational damage for QLDC."

The council sent a final contract to SJ Allen in April.

Glover previously told RNZ his council had relied on the consent in good faith, but he was open to discussing alternative arrangements.

High E coli readings, less-than-minor adverse effects

The documents also reveal high levels of pathogens in the wastewater sludge, with E coli concentrations of 650,000 units per 100mL.

The material was being trucked straight from the plant without undergoing heat-drying, composting or microbial stabilisation, an Otago Regional Council report said.

That meant instead of being categorised as a biosolid, which could be beneficially used as a soil fertiliser or conditioner, it was considered raw sewage sludge.

Regional council planners considering the consent application wrote that spreading the sludge on Lauder farmland was a "relatively novel approach to disposing of the proposed waste" but determined that any adverse effects on the nearby environment including soil, groundwater, wetlands, air quality and human health would be less than minor.

The planners said potential odour or surface run-off would not extend beyond the property boundaries.

They noted that written approval had been provided by Kā Rūnaka via its company Aukaha Ltd.

The documents showed that sludge spreading would be restricted to a 50-hectare trial block for the first year.

The contract also included a clause stating that the waste would need to be diverted to the Southland landfill if winter weather or saturated soil made spreading unsafe.

The documents showed regional council staff did not visit the Lauder site before granting the consent.

"There was considered to be sufficient photographic evidence, plans and aerial mapping information of the site...the scale and the nature of the activity proposed means that a site visit was not required in this instance."

While SJ Allen had sought a 35-year consent, Otago Regional Council opted to grant a 15-year consent.

Council responds

Queenstown Lakes District Council has been contacted for comment.

In a statement, Otago Regional Council said the consent application followed requirements set out by the Resource Management Act.

The effects were not expected to extend beyond the property boundary so public notification was not required, a spokesperson said.

"The consent includes conditions requiring management and monitoring to manage potential effects on human health and the environment.

"If monitoring results demonstrate a rising trend across three consecutive samples, SJ Allen is required to investigate the cause of the trend and provide a report to ORC outlining the cause, any actual or potential effects and any proposed remedial actions."

World.title: Wallabies looking for attacking spark against Wales
World.content:
The eternally upbeat Wallabies are relishing the promise of a rare northern-hemisphere dry track on which to fight fire with Wales in a pivotal spring tour showdown in Cardiff.

Looking to avert a ninth successive loss in Europe and a first season whitewash at the hands of the four UK home nations in 68 years, the Wallabies are intent on taking the fight to the suddenly formidable Welsh.

Strike forward Tom Hooper admits Les Kiss's side were too passive on attack in the tour-opening 45-22 defeat to England, before leaving their run too late in a defensively improved 15-12 loss to Scotland on Sunday.

With Wales on a high after downing the All Blacks for the first time since 1953, the Wallabies know a more clinical attacking display will be required this Sunday (AEDT).

"That first English game, we probably didn't move the ball around well enough, and when you're versing quality oppositions with quality defences, you've got to keep them guessing on what you've got to do," Hooper said on Wednesday, local time.

"We've got to make sure that we've got multifaceted weapons that we can throw at the Welsh this weekend and that's something that we'll be looking to do."

Australia's misfiring attack again proved costly in Edinburgh with Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii squandering an opportunity to set up a match-winning try after the bell at Murrayfield.

Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii has misfired this spring. (AP Photo: Scott Heppell)

Instead of going through the hands, which probably would have resulted in Max Jorgensen clinching victory down the right sideline, Suaalii threw a cut-out pass straight to Jorgensen rather than drawing the last defender for fullback Tom Wright.

The backline's lack of execution under pressure has been a common occurrence during Australia's run of four successive defeats, including back-to-back trouncings from New Zealand.

"Sometimes we're trying too hard to maybe force something that's maybe not there," said playmaker Ben Donaldson, one of the best after coming on late against the Scots.

Worrying signs as Wallabies leave it too late to fire in Scotland defeat The Wallabies once again show precious little in an attacking sense, as Scotland edge a "turgid" encounter at Murrayfield.

"So we're doing a lot of drills and training around that skill execution: short passing, long passing, ID-ing what's in front of us. We're trying to find cues to then attack off that.

"Sometimes you can go through the motions of running a play or throwing a pass, but not actually looking at what's in front of you."

Donaldson is hoping the Wallabies' attack will be sharper under a closed roof at Principality Stadium.

"It's a bit challenging — we trained today in the wet, on a muddy field," he said.

"But we know we've played in a lot of dry-weather conditions this year, so I feel like that's when we play our best footy. When we move the ball, we've got some great skilful forwards, some backs who like to get the ball in space.

"So it's really going to help us. Under the roof, I think you'll see some pretty good footy."

Coach Kiss will name his match day 23 on Friday.

The ABC of SPORT Sports content to make you think... or allow you not to. A newsletter delivered each Saturday.
