World.title: Bancroft says he is 'freed' as Cummins hits nets with captaincy in question
World.content:
Cameron Bancroft has made his first public statement since alleging the entire Australian cricket team knew of the 2018 ball-tampering plot.

Bancroft, who was the player caught using sandpaper on the ball in the infamous Test match against South Africa in Cape Town, claimed the entire team knew what he was doing on the field, and said then-coach Darren Lehmann was part of discussions about ball tampering.

Cameron Bancroft's bomb is Australian cricket's point of no return Cameron Bancroft's statement is the atom bomb Cricket Australia has always feared. For so many of the game's key figures, there is no turning back now.

The article, more than 4,000 words long, contradicts Test captain Pat Cummins's claim last week that he did not know sandpaper was being used during that match.

"Obviously, yeah, I've been carrying a lot of this stuff for a long period of time," Bancroft told the Nine Network outside his home in Perth.

"So I feel really freed and really happy to be able to do that."

Earlier on Wednesday, Cricket Australia had announced a forum would be launched for players and staff to discuss their recollections and perspectives of the infamous tour, but ruled out a new investigation.

Bancroft, who was suspended along with then-captain Steve Smith and vice-captain David Warner, said he wanted to be part of the CA forum.

"Now there's a process in place which Cricket Australia has put in … I look forward to being a part of that process," he said.

Loading...

Cummins hits the nets as former Black Cap questions his captaincy

In his article, Bancroft said he wrote the piece after watching Cummins's 70-minute press conference last week, where the current Test captain refuted suggestions he and the bowlers knew about the use of sandpaper.

A new memoir by retired player Usman Khawaja, who in his book said the entire team needed to take responsibility for Sandpapergate, brought the saga back into the limelight.

Cummins said Khawaja had been "casual" with people's lives and reputations.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote in an article that originally appeared in the West Australian before being sent out to all media.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins's press conference."

In the wake of Bancroft's allegations, Cummins was training at the Sydney Cricket Ground with the NSW team ahead of its Sheffield Shield match against Queensland, which begins on Sunday.

Cummins is not expected to play in that match, but bowled in the nets alongside fellow Australian quick Josh Hazlewood as they get ready for the first of four Tests against New Zealand.

With Australian cricket in turmoil, a former Black Cap Simon Doull has publicly questioned whether Cummins can carry on as captain following Bancroft's published article.

“He [Bancroft] felt Pat Cummins blatantly lied to everybody,” Doull said while commentating for Sky Sports during New Zealand's first Test against India in Wellington.

"I don't know how Pat Cummins survives from this. We all knew what was going on. I'm not sure how many of those guys survive moving forward to that New Zealand series."

Meanwhile, David Warner, who has been vocal about Cricket Australia's handling of the 2018 investigation, said he was happy Bancroft was able to "get some stuff off his chest".

"Obviously, he has told the truth. I think it's been weighing on him heavily for a long time; I think it's great to get it off his chest," he told the Seven Network.

"I'm here to support him as well, as I am to support Usman Khawaja as well. I just think it's a relief for him and that's his truth, and I respect that."

World.title: When is the AFL draft and how does it work? Here's what you need to know
World.content:
It is that time of the year again where hope springs eternal for all AFL clubs.

It is draft day and all 18 clubs are dreaming of selecting players who might play in their next premiership.

The draft can be a complicated beast these days, with academies and father-son selections muddying the waters for clubs looking to secure the best talent.

Here is everything you need to know about the 2026 AFL draft.

When is the AFL draft?

This year's draft will be held across two nights on November 19 and November 20.

November 19 will see the first round of prospects having their names called before the second round and beyond takes place on the following night.

How can I follow the AFL draft?

ABC Sport will have live blogs running on both nights of the draft, bringing you news and analysis of every pick.

The draft will also be broadcast live on Fox Footy and Kayo Sports.

What time is the AFL draft?

Both nights of the draft will start at 7pm AEDT.

Here are the corresponding times for other regions of Australia.

6:30pm ACDT: South Australia

South Australia 6pm AEST: Queensland

Queensland 5:30pm ACST : Northern Territory

: Northern Territory 4pm AWST: Western Australia

Who are the players expected to be selected early?

Dougie Cochrane is expected to be the first name called out at the top of the 2026 draft. (Josh Chadwick/AFL Photos/via Getty Images)

The top few picks of this year's draft appear to be set in stone as night one approaches.

Two prospects — Dougie Cochrane and Cody Walker — are already tied to clubs and are expected to go within the first five picks.

Cochrane is eligible to join Port Adelaide as a part of its Next Generation Academy (NGA), while Walker is tied to Carlton under the father-son rule after his father, Andrew, played 202 games for the club.

In the open pool, Ethan Drever is expected to have his name called by Essendon after its bid on Cochrane is matched by Port at the top of the draft.

The draft will get interesting when Richmond selects after Essendon, with names such as Arki Butler, Harry Van Hattum and Heath Mellody all in consideration at that spot.

What is the current order of picks in the first round?

Essendon

Richmond

West Coast

Melbourne (received from Port Adelaide via trade)

Richmond (received from Port Adelaide via trade)

Sydney (received from North Melbourne via trade)

Port Adelaide (received from Melbourne via trade)

Gold Coast (free agency compensation pick)

GWS Giants

St Kilda

Collingwood

Port Adelaide (received from Melbourne via trade)

Carlton

Melbourne (received from Western Bulldogs via trade)

Adelaide

St Kilda (received from Geelong via trade)

Essendon (received from Hawthorn via trade)

Carlton (received from Sydney via 2025 Curnow trade)

Fremantle

GWS Giants (received from Brisbane via trade)

How does the bidding system work in the AFL draft?

The AFL assigns each draft pick with a points value. The first pick in the draft has the most value, with 3,000 points, and the points value of each pick decreases all the way down until pick 54, the final pick of the third round, which is worth 14 points. Any picks from then onwards have no points value.

There have been several changes to the bidding system this year to make it tougher for clubs that finish higher up the ladder to match a bid on one of their academy prospects:

Clubs can now only use two picks to match a bid, up to and including pick 36

A discount or loading will be applied when clubs match a bid, depending on where that club finishes on the ladder

The previous year's grand finalists have to pay 20 per cent extra to match any bid, while teams that made the preliminary final have to pay 10 per cent extra

Teams that finished between 5th and 10th have no discount or loading, while teams that finished outside the top 10 receive a 10 per cent discount on bids

Clubs that finish in the bottom five on the ladder and have their top pick pushed back due to a matched bid will be compensated with an extra pick in the second round

Can teams do trades during the draft?

They sure can!

Since being introduced in 2018, the ability for teams to trade during the draft has added an extra wrinkle to the whole process.

Teams can trade with each other using their own picks in the current draft as well as using picks in the 2027 or 2028 drafts.

Which players have been selected with the first pick in recent years?

Willem Duurmsa (left) was selected first overall by West Coast in last year's draft. (AAP)

Here is a look at the top pick from each of the last 10 drafts:

2025: Willem Duursma (West Coast)

2024: Sam Lalor (Richmond)

2023: Harley Reid (West Coast)

2022: Aaron Cadman (GWS Giants)

2021: Jason Horne-Francis (North Melbourne)

2020: Jamarra Ugle-Hagan (Western Bulldogs)

2019: Matt Rowell (Gold Coast)

2018: Sam Walsh (Carlton)

2017: Cam Rayner (Brisbane)

2016: Andrew McGrath (Essendon)

World.title: Four Aussies chasing biggest payday in history of women's golf
World.content:
Major winners Hannah Green and Grace Kim are among four Australians chasing the biggest payday in women's golf history at the mega-money Tour Championship in Florida.

Tournament debutants Cassie Porter and Karis Davidson are also hunting the monstrous $US4 million ($5.96 million) winner's cheque as world number one Nelly Korda and two-time defending champion Jeeno Thitikul seek to add to their growing legacies.

Korda would be elevated to the LPGA Hall of Fame with a maiden victory at the season-ending showpiece — which would be her fifth win of a prolific 2026 campaign.

The American captured two majors among her four titles, and also finished runner-up three times to become the first woman to secure player-of-the-year honours before the Tour Championship.

Korda nominated her US Open triumph in June as her undoubted season highlight, but issued a warning to her rivals that she hoped more was to come this weekend in Naples.

"It was definitely a dream come true because that dream started when I was 14 years old, and to finally get that win there at the US Women's Open, and honestly at such an iconic venue like Riviera was so, so special," the 28-year-old said.

"But I'm super motivated every week. If I wasn't getting frustrated at the weeks that I was just not playing well, then that means there is something wrong for me.

"I want to win every single week. Knowing one of the biggest wins I wanted in my career was checked off, that doesn't mean I have less motivation. It's actually the opposite. I want to be in that position more and more."

The second-ranked Thitikul has also won four times this year and now has the chance to become the first player to complete a Tour Championship hat-trick.

"It's phenomenal for me," the Thai said.

"We're not going to take four wins in just one season, right?"

The field includes 17 of the 19 winners on tour this season with Porter and Davidson among 11 players on debut at the $US11 million ($16.4 million) showpiece at Tiburon Golf Club.

Australia's triple major champion Minjee Lee will be conspicuously absent after failing to make the elite 60-strong field for the first time since 2014.

AAP

World.title: Cummins stands firm despite Bancroft's Sandpapergate allegation
World.content:
Australia Test captain Pat Cummins has responded to Cameron Bancroft's sensational claims that everyone knew about the use of sandpaper in 2018, in a statement through his manager.

Yesterday night, Bancroft released a 4,500-word piece detailing the events of the infamous 2018 tour of South Africa, where he was caught using sandpaper on the ball during a Test in Cape Town.

Last week, Cummins held a 70-minute press conference in the wake of the saga being brought back into the spotlight following the release of Usman Khawaja's memoir, Sabr.

Cameron Bancroft's bomb is Australian cricket's point of no return Cameron Bancroft's statement is the atom bomb Cricket Australia has always feared. For so many of the game's key figures, there is no turning back now.

Cummins maintained he, and the bowling unit, did not know sandpaper was being used on the field.

Bancroft's article directly contradicts Cummins's statement, but the Test captain has maintained his position.

"Pat’s position hasn't changed in eight years," Cummins's manager, Neil Maxwell, said.

"He's been consistent and adamant from day one. Pat feels for Cam, of course. He has been through a lot.

"We would urge people to again read Pat's interview transcript. There is nothing he hasn't answered. And that includes in response to what Cam has now said.

"Pat has rebuilt the Australian cricket team. That 24-year-old in Cape Town resolved to fix the team and spent eight years doing it."

Bancroft said Cummins's press conference last Friday, where the Test captain said any suggestion bowlers knew of the sandpaper use was "utter nonsense", was the catalyst for his tell-all piece.

"It was not just the three of us — Steve Smith, David Warner and I — who knew about me using sandpaper on the ball in South Africa. It was the whole team," Bancroft wrote in an article that originally appeared in the West Australian before being sent out to all media.

"I withheld important details, including when the use of sandpaper began, how long it went on for, and the involvement and awareness of others.

"The final straw for me to write this account was Australian cricket captain Pat Cummins's press conference."

Darren Lehmann, who was Australian coach at the time of the incident, was commentating for ABC Sport when Bancroft's article was published on Wednesday.

Bancroft said Lehmann was present during conversations about using sandpaper on the ball to help it reverse-swing.

The former coach said he would need to "work through each allegation" before making any comment.

"The allegations … I've got to sit back. It's only just come to light. So I just need to sit back and process all that and work through each allegation. That's what I will be doing over the next few days," Lehmann said on ABC Radio.

"I need to have a really good read of it, don't I? What's been transpired, speaking to people, and just make sure I'm saying what I want to say and answer the questions you want to ask."

Earlier on Wednesday, Cricket Australia (CA) had announced a forum for players to come forward and discuss their recollections and perspectives of the infamous period in Australian cricket history.

However, CA chief executiveTodd Greenberg said the forum was not an investigation, and CA would decide what information from the forum would be made public.

World.title: Alexander Zverev officially notified of lawsuit by ex-partner in abuse case
World.content:
Top-ranked tennis player Alexander Zverev has officially been notified of a lawsuit filed by his former partner during the middle of the season-ending ATP Finals.

The latest legal case alleges that Zverev violated the terms of an out-of-court settlement between the pair after the woman accused him of assaulting her.

The lawsuit brought by Brenda Patea in Germany takes issue with Zverev reportedly saying in an interview with French sports daily L'Equipe earlier this year that "it has been proven that the accusations were false" and "my innocence has been proven".

Zverev's Berlin-based lawyers, Christian Schertz and Anna Sophie Heuchemer, confirmed in a statement shared with The Associated Press that they were formally served with Patea's lawsuit on Wednesday.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit," Zverev's lawyers said. "If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion" protected by the German constitution.

They said there had been no breach of any contractual obligations.

Patea's lawyer, Michael Scheele, told The AP that Zverev's claim over his innocence "triggered a veritable storm of criticism against our client".

He said the backlash was damaging to her business as an influencer and that she also felt her honour had been violated.

"Quite apart from the fact that Zverev's claim is false, he was not permitted to make any public statements whatsoever, in any form," he said. "Both Brenda Patea and Alexander Zverev had agreed to this in a settlement."

Patea is seeking an order that Zverev not repeat such comments and that he be fined up to 250,000 euros ($408,600) each time he does.

Zverev faced a charge of causing bodily harm to Patea during an argument in Berlin in May 2020. He always denied any wrongdoing.

The case ended in a district court in Berlin in 2024 after the settlement. Zverev agreed to pay fines to the state and charitable organisations.

Brenda Patea arrives at court in 2024 after making her allegations against Alexander Zverev. (Getty Images: Jens Kalaene/picture alliance)

Zverev this month ascended to the number one ranking for the first time. He also won his first two Grand Slam titles this year and is competing this week at the ATP Finals in Turin. His next match is on Thursday.

Zverev has not commented on the lawsuit.

It is not the first time that legal affairs have clashed with Zverev's tennis schedule. The settlement with Patea was decided while Zverev was playing the 2024 French Open. He did not appear in court then.

He previously denied abuse allegations from another former girlfriend, Olga Sharypova, who first made the accusations in 2020 and followed up in 2021 with a detailed account in a Slate.com article that was taken down because of a preliminary injunction issued by a German court. Slate said it stood by the article.

The allegations prompted the men's professional tennis tour, the ATP, to investigate her claims.

It ended 15 months later, in January 2023, with the ATP saying there was "insufficient evidence" to substantiate the claims.

AP

World.title: GWS Giants desperate to draft young star
World.content:
It's a sign of the precarious position of Australian Rules Football in Western Sydney that Ethan Matthews' father, Cameron, took to bribing kids to join his son at the Ingleburn Magpies.

"Definitely got lots of players across from softball at times, in rugby league, a few soccer," Ethan told ABC Sport.

"When we were younger, not too much, five, 10 bucks, but then as we started to get a bit older, we started to demand a bit more, so I probably got up to $25, $50 at times, depending on how talented the athlete was."

Bribing kids to play Aussie Rules in rugby league heartland gives some indication about why the GWS Giants are so keen to bring their Academy player through their door in Thursday night's AFL draft.

Ethan Matthews is the most talented product to come out of western Sydney in the Giants' history. (Supplied: Phil Hillyard)

Drafting a gifted Aussie Rules player is important not just for the Giants' playing list but also for the message that they are still trying to sell 16 years down the track: that the club can build a local Aussie Rules culture so that more kids like Ethan Matthews take up the game and follow the Giants.

The job of winning the hearts and minds of rugby league and soccer fans in western Sydney is a constant work in progress for the Giants.

While the Giants made the Grand Final in 2019 only to get thrashed by Richmond, the impact of COVID the following year put a halt to the team's momentum that they're still struggling to recover from.

So, Matthews is much more than the most talented player to come out of western Sydney in the club's short history; he's the poster child for the region and what local boys and girls can achieve.

The Giants are expected to take Matthews with their pick nine, but there's every chance that he could be bid on prior to that, which would mean GWS would have to match the bid.

Ethan Matthews could be one of the top picks at the 2026 AFL Draft. (Getty Images: Graham Denholm)

The local boy from the village of Appin, south of Campbelltown, would be just the fifth western Sydney local drafted to the Giants since the team entered the AFL in 2012 and the highest draft pick of those by a country mile.

When he's picked, it will be the culmination of a dream for the politely spoken 18-year-old who'll be in Melbourne on draft night.

"I just expected it to be a great get-together with all my family and friends," Matthews said.

"Just a moment to celebrate the journey. It's been a great, not a few years; it's been 10 years now of hard work and effort put in."

Matthews knows that there's every chance another club could snaffle him, but the Giants have given him enough reassurance that he's heading to Sydney Olympic Park come Friday morning.

"They've certainly told me as much as they can; they would love to have me," he said.

"I'm not going to lie and say they aren't my preferred team to go to; [I've] been there since I was 12 and love the Giants very much."

Ethan Matthews with his father, Cameron, mother, Melissa and sister, Ava before the AFL draft in Melbourne. (Supplied)

The journey began even earlier at just four when his footy-loving dad and mad Collingwood supporter took him down to join the Ingleburn Magpies Auskick side.

From there, he progressed through to the Giants' development side in the under-12s to the Academy at 16 and then this year played a starring role for the Giants Talent League side and then the Allies in the National Under-18s Championships.

The highlight for the 186cm left-footer was a best-on-ground game against Vic Country, where he racked up plenty of disposals plus nine score involvements, six tackles and eight marks playing in the midfield.

The highlights of that game were a recruiter's dream as Matthews glided around the field dodging tackles and delivering pinpoint left-foot passes to leading forwards.

"I like to think I'm quite a fundamental and skilful footballer; I like to use my Footy IQ," he said.

Unfortunately, Matthews injured his foot later in the Championships, which brought his season to an end, but not before he picked up the Hunter Harrison medal as the best player from the northern states' academy programs.

And while his close footy mates were following his progress closely thanks to Cameron's bribes, that wasn't the case for his other school friends who were wondering where he'd disappeared to.

"Not too many people, I guess, especially at school, had too much of an idea about a national champs game, and no-one knows where you've been or what you've done, and I've kind of liked that," he said.

"But yeah, all my close friends and all my mates that play footy certainly do know, and I'm lucky enough with Dad bribing people to come across, most of my friends have at some stage played footy with me in younger years and are very interested."

Once at the Giants, Matthews is determined to work hard and break into the team, which is coming off a disappointing 2026 season highlighted by injuries to key players.

"It's going to be very hard to crack into the AFL team," Matthews said.

"So, first [I've] just got to get into the side, but once I do, I reckon I would start on a wing or a half back, and then ultimately in a few years' time I see myself as a midfielder."

Ethan Matthews says he wants to be a role model for young Australian Rules footballers in western Sydney. (Supplied: Phil Hillyard)

Matthews also sees himself as a role model to help grow the game in Western Sydney.

"It's an honour and a privilege, especially to represent this area," he said.

"I'd love to be a role model for many kids, especially out in this area, to keep striving and play footy, and have a dream, I think, being a role model out here would be something very special to me."

Come Thursday night, Matthews will almost certainly be decked in orange and charcoal, and while that's been his destiny for six years, it will mean permanently abandoning his childhood team and first love, Collingwood.

"I definitely love the Giants just as much, but yeah, [I'm a] Collingwood fan," he said.

"Dad signed me up before birth, didn't have much choice there."

World.title: Opetaia's fight with former heavyweight champion called off
World.content:
Jai Opetaia's eyebrow-raising move to heavyweight to fight Deontay Wilder is over after the Australian withdrew from their bout.

The Gold Coast-based Opetaia (31-0) was set to move up from cruiserweight to face former world champion Wilder on the undercard to Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua's Cardiff blockbuster next month.

"Fighter to fighter, I know the feeling, and it's frustrating. I've ‌always prided myself on fighting anyone, anyplace," Opetaia posted on social media on Wednesday night.

He rubbished suggestions he'd pulled out of the fight because of Wilder's "big right hand".

"The goal has never changed and still, like I've always said, remains the same. Undisputed," he said.

"They all said I couldn't after signing with Zuffa Boxing, everything always against us, stripped and vacated multiple times … but you watch.

"I'm coming to spoil the party."

The fight was seen as a lucrative, profile-raising option — albeit a risky one given the power of Wilder — to stay busy before a potential cruiserweight clash with David Benavidez next year.

Jai Opetaia (left) and David Benavidez (right) could potentially fight in 2027. (Getty Images: Zuffa Boxing/Ed Mulholland/)

Opetaia's co-promoter Mick Francis said Opetaia had aggravated a hand injury first sustained during his September bout against Noel Mikaelian.

"This is a disappointing setback for Jai, who was looking forward to what promised to be a cracking fight. His focus now is on making a full recovery and continuing his quest to become the undisputed cruiserweight champion of the world," he said.

Benavidez and Opetaia agreed in the ring after Opetaia's last win to face each other next May.

The two-division champion holds the WBO and WBA's cruiserweight belts and will face WBC strap-holder Michal Cieslak in a unification battle next month.

And the WBC had installed the Australian as the mandatory challenger for the winner of that fight.

Opetaia was stripped of his IBF title for fighting for the unsanctioned Zuffa belt he now holds, alongside his enduring Ring champion status.

The Australian beat former WBC champion Mikaelian, who gave up his belt for a shot at Opetaia.

Opetaia remains in a court battle with the IBF to reclaim that belt and, if successful, could walk into a clash with Benavidez with all four major organisations' belts on the line.

Meanwhile, contenders have lined up to replace Opetaia on the card, with Derek Chisora, Richard Riakporhe and even fellow Australian and Tasman Fighters stablemate Justis Huni floated as options.

AAP

Tech.title: Elon Musk tries to explain what’s going on with Ukraine and Starlink
Tech.content:
is a senior reporter covering technology, gaming, and more. He joined The Verge in 2019 after nearly two years at Techmeme.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Elon Musk said Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy is lying about disruptions to Starshield in Ukraine and that he’s trying to misuse SpaceX’s consumer service, Starlink, for military purposes. Musk made the comments at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday as he tried to explain the conflict following weeks of back and forth between Zelenskyy, Musk, and the US government.

“From the beginning, I’ve said that Starlink is a civilian system,” Musk said. “It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people. If you want to do that, you need to do Starshield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government. But do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions.”

Musk also said that “if they want to do something that’s an offensive military action, it needs to be the Starshield system where the kill decision is that of the War Department, perhaps ultimately the president, and not mine.”

The interviewer, Andrew Ross Sorkin, said that President Zelenskyy refers to the system as Starshield and is claiming that is the system that was slowed down. “That’s false,” Musk said, claiming that Zelenskyy is “not always truthful.”

Sorkin asked, “So when President Zelenskyy talks about using Starshield, he is not using Starshield, or he’s lying?”

“He is lying,” Musk said. “What he is actually saying is he wants to use Starlink for offensive military operations.”

Tech.title: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”

Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”

In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”

Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

Tech.title: Democrats skip a vote on adding Brendan Carr’s adviser to the FCC
Tech.content:
Senate commerce committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-TX) began a meeting Wednesday meant to confirm President Donald Trump’s nominee to the Federal Communications Commission with a lopsided dais. To his right sat all 14 Republican members of the panel, including Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-SD). To his left were about a dozen empty chairs — every Democratic member of the panel was absent.

Cruz said he’d learned the night before that Democrats intended to boycott the vote, though Democrats say they’d repeatedly raised their concerns about advancing a Republican FCC nominee without a Democratic one. “The administration has shown it’s willing to move Democrats,” Cruz said, pointing to Senate votes scheduled on bipartisan pairs of nominations to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and the Securities and Exchange Commission. And even though the Supreme Court confirmed his power to do so, Cruz said, Trump has not moved to fire any Democrats from the FCC, as he did at the Federal Trade Commission. “This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party,” Cruz said.

“This is an ordinary nomination to fill a vacancy previously held by someone in the same party”

But in statements and comments to reporters outside the committee room, Democrats said that the process has been far from normal. Senate committees often vote on nominations to historically independent agencies in bipartisan pairs. Confirming Danielle Thumann Severs, senior counsel to FCC Chair Brendan Carr, to become a commissioner at the agency would put the FCC at four total members — three Republicans and one Democrat, Anna Gomez. Gomez’s term has technically expired, though she can remain on the commission through next year unless she’s replaced. But Democrats fear that by confirming a third Republican to the FCC, Trump might finally fire Gomez, because he’d no longer need her present for a quorum to vote on key actions.

Democrats asked for Thumann’s confirmation vote to be withheld until her nomination could be paired with a Democratic nomination. One way to do that would be to renominate Gomez. But so far, the president has not offered any Democratic nominees for the commission. Democrats said they made their concerns clear to Cruz, and added, “This is not a problem we created, but a problem that the White House can solve.” The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In addition to the procedural concerns, Democrats worry about Thumann’s work as an adviser to Carr, and whether she was truthful about the matters she worked on. In a letter asking Cruz to delay her confirmation vote, Sen. Ben Ray Luján (D-NM) detailed his concerns. At the November 10th hearing where Thumann answered committee members’ questions, she testified that she had “not worked with the Chairman on any media-related issues,” Luján noted in the letter. But documents obtained via a Freedom of Information Act request show that Thumann was “looped in” on various media matters, and “helped draft Skydance’s commitments that facilitated the 2 FCC’s approval of the Skydance-Paramount merger,” Luján wrote. “She also played a role in processing informal complaints related to CBS 60 Minutes alleged news distortion and she apparently orchestrated the Commission’s response to consumers regarding the Jimmy Kimmel controversy.” The FCC did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the matter.

Even Cruz admitted concerns with Carr’s handling of Kimmel’s comments in the aftermath of conservative activist Charlie Kirk’s killing. But at Wednesday’s meeting, he said he “emphatically agree[s]” that Thumann had resolved any lingering worries about that. He added that his JAWBONE Act, which the committee previously passed, could directly address First Amendment violations by government agencies of either party. The bill would let individuals sue government officials if they illegally try to compel social media or broadcast companies to remove their speech. Sen. Jerry Moran (R-KS), who’d similarly expressed concern over the Kimmel incident, said he found Thumann’s responses on the subject “comforting,” including in a phone call earlier that morning where he said he’d expressed his “serious interest in how the FCC protects and promotes free speech, including free speech on broadcast.” On the call, he said, “she was able to satisfy me once again in her answers, including an explanation for her role at the FCC and her lack of engagement on this type of issue as the FCC made decisions.”

“If she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?”

Speaking to reporters outside of the hearing room ahead of the meeting, Luján accused Thumann of lying to the committee. “The questions that I have is if she was lying about this, what else is she lying about and what else is she hiding?” he said. Luján said he wants both Thumann and Carr to appear before the committee by the end of the year to answer lawmakers’ questions. Asked if he’d support using the committee’s subpoena power or even pursuing impeachment against Carr when Democrats regain power next year, Luján said his vote to confirm Carr as a commissioner under President Joe Biden is among his biggest regrets, and that while he hopes Carr will testify voluntarily, “everything should be on the table here to be able to get answers for the American people.”

When it came time to vote on whether to advance Thumann’s nomination for a final step of a vote on the Senate floor, all 15 Republicans voted “aye.” That gave Thumann enough votes for her nomination to advance to the Senate floor, where it’s expected to pass along party lines once scheduled. Still, the clerk listed off the names of the 13 Democratic committee members whose seats remained empty. There was no response.

Tech.title: Absolute Batman can save DC Studios
Tech.content:
is a reporter focusing on film, TV, and pop culture. Before The Verge, he wrote about comic books, labor, race, and more at io9 and Gizmodo for almost five years.

This drastic shift in priorities will likely change what the DCU looks like in the coming years as Skydance attempts to parlay its comics IP into projects that can help it get on top of the $80 billion of debt the company is now responsible for after acquiring WBD. Ellison’s instinct to whip out the A-list superheroes is probably right from a business perspective. Most casual DC movie fans are more interested in stories about the Trinity than obscure characters like Gorilla Grodd. But after two iffy attempts at creating interconnected DC movie franchises, that audience might not have much of an appetite for yet another full-on reboot.

Rather than starting from scratch, DC Studios should probably keep some of the things that worked well during Gunn and Safran’s tenure, like presenting Superman as a compassionate person with a strong moral compass. But if the studio really wants to take this franchise in a new direction that gets people excited, it should also be thinking about tapping into the energy of some of DC’s most successful recent comics. Though the WBD merger prompted Skydance to begin laying off almost 2,000 employees last month, DC Comics — which Skydance gained control of as part of the deal — was reportedly left unscathed because the publishing arm’s business has been performing surprisingly well. Much of that success seems to have been driven by strong sales of comics created by DC’s Absolute Universe imprint.

Image: DC Comics / Mark Spears

Launched in 2024, the Absolute Universe comics reimagine DC’s heroes and villains as wildly different versions of their classic selves. Absolute Wonder Woman is a witch raised in Hell, Absolute Superman first arrives on Earth as a teenager who remembers his childhood on Krypton, and Absolute Batman is a working-class civil engineer rather than a socialite born into immense wealth. The Absolute characters’ worldviews and approaches to enacting justice are all distinct from their mainstream universe counterparts. But as much as the Absolute comics diverge from established canon, they each capture the essence of what makes their central characters iconic pillars of the DC brand.

Wonder Woman aside, there have been so many cinematic portrayals of DC characters based on their classic selves that it has often seemed like Warner Bros. was stuck in a kind of rut. There have been slight stylistic differences between the various big-screen iterations of Superman and Batman over the years, but for the most part, they have all come across as the products of a studio that’s averse to trying new things.

Absolute Batman is compelling because it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics.

That’s part of what made Matt Reeves’ The Batman— which didn’t bother to rehash Bruce Wayne’s tragic origin story — feel somewhat like a breath of fresh air when it debuted in 2022. Robert Pattinson will reprise his role as the Dark Knight in The Batman Part II, but it’s not really clear whether that version of the character will have any bearing on the DCU’s future.

Between Reeves’ Batman films existing in their own universe (similar to Todd Phillips’ Joker features) and Pattinson presumably being busy now that he’s been cast as Amazon’s new James Bond, it doesn’t seem likely that that version of the character will be incorporated into the DCU. Ellison obviously intends to put out more projects featuring Batman, though, and DC Studios could tell a riveting story if it took some cues from the hero’s Absolute incarnation. What makes Absolute Batman such a compelling series is the way it inverts the established power structures that define most classic Batman comics. In those books, Bruce Wayne is part of Gotham’s marginalized underclass, while the Joker is a moneyed elite whose villainy is highlighted in the way he manipulates various industries.

Previous Next



1 / 3 Batman taking on crooked cops in Absolute Batman Annual. Image: DC Comics / Daniel Warren Johnson, Mike Spicer, Clayton Cowles

This inversion puts Absolute Batman in a position to operate as a vigilante with a much deeper connection to the ordinary people he has sworn to protect. Monstrous supervillains like Poison Ivy and Bane are still major threats, but the comics also spend time pitting Absolute Batman against more ordinary evils like corrupt police departments infested with white nationalists fixated on terrorizing minorities. Absolute Batman’s progressive political overtones might not gel with Ellison’s personal sensibilities, and the comic’s brutality probably doesn’t align with Latcham’s approach to making films. But Absolute Batman’s phenomenal sales have made it abundantly clear that readers are enjoying these stories, which is likely a big part why DC Studios announced earlier this year that it has plans to produce an animated series based on the comics.

Those plans might change in the wake of Skydance acquiring WBD, but an Absolute Batman series would give DC Studios an organic way to introduce the character into its tentpole films. Having characters jump back and forth between TV and the big screen was one of the stronger ideas Gunn introduced to the DCU, and it’s a strategy that could continue to benefit DC Studios under Latcham’s leadership. Turning Absolute Batman into the next flagship Bruce Wayne would be a bold move on Skydance’s part. But if the studio really wants to prove that this megamerger was the right decision, it needs to show the public that it has the guts to take exciting chances.

Tech.title: Trump’s latest land grab is an AI hub in the Philippines
Tech.content:
President Donald Trump was greeted by no less than five beauty queens when he landed in the Philippines on Tuesday, according to local news outlet Rappler. As he stepped onto the tarmac, a child handed him small US and Philippine flags. A band played “YMCA,” a staple at Trump rallies, as more girls in traditional bell-sleeved blouses and young men in wide-brimmed hats danced to the song.

Outside the airport, hundreds of protesters packed streets bearing signs — and at least one prop casket — saying “Trump out.” Others say “Reject Pax Silica,” the name for the US-led international initiative to secure chips and critical minerals used in the hardware fueling the AI boom.

Peace and prosperity for whom?

“Pax” comes from the Latin word for “peace, stability, and long-term prosperity,” the Pax Silica website proudly says. Yet the unspoken question — peace and prosperity for whom? — explains the whiplash between the Philippine government’s warm welcome of Trump and the public fury raging outside.

Trump says he wants to “win AI” — whatever that means. As such, the US needs data centers full of GPUs to do it. With Americans increasingly opposed to data centers and chip factories being built in their communities, the US is now recruiting less affluent nations to take up some of the slack. Lawmakers from both the US and the Philippines are promising a slice of the riches that advances in generative AI are supposed to create. And that’s supposed to be worth the land razed, homes destroyed, and natural resources lost in the name of technological progress. In the Philippines, that’s taking the shape of a proposed 1,620-hectare (4,000 acres) hub for chip factories, processing plants for critical minerals, and data centers.

At least two dozen countries have signed on to the Pax Silica initiative, and Trump was expected to pressure more to join while in the Philippines for events related to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit. With Pax Silica, the US aims to insulate itself from China’s dominance in manufacturing semiconductors and processing critical minerals needed to make those chips. Trump held a bilateral meeting with President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. Wednesday before heading to Shenzhen to meet with China’s President Xi Jinping and Russia’s President Vladimir Putin.

Philippine and US officials are expected to sign a framework agreement by the end of the year for the jointly developed Pax Silica Economic Security Zone. The details are still murky and shrouded in NDAs. The Philippines’ Bases Conversion and Development Authority (BCDA) overseeing the plan expects an economic boom from minerals processing and chip manufacturing, with perhaps a data center or two on site. Meanwhile, human rights advocates who oppose the project warn that it will displace Indigenous residents, cutting them off from water resources on which they rely.

“How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood?”

“We do not want to give up our community,” Petronila Capiz-Muñoz, chieftain of the Indigenous Aeta Hungey tribe, told Human Rights Watch. “How do we give up our burial grounds, our church, our livelihood? This is where we source our water, this is where we plant.” Capiz-Muñoz said BCDA officials have told residents that they’ll need to relocate by December to make way for development. Small farmers are also afraid the semiconductor hub will push them off their lands, according to Lian Buan, Southeast Asia researcher at Human Rights Watch.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here.

The Aeta are among the first people to inhabit the Philippines, believed to have arrived around 30,000 years ago. And yet the Aeta Hungey tribe has been trying since 1994 to secure an official certificate recognizing its ancestral domain in one of the areas now facing industrial development. But since the tribe hasn’t been granted that certificate, the BCDA can still claim the AI hub will be built “outside titled ancestral domains.”

The agency says the project will be on public land located at the former Clark Air Base built in the early 1900s when the Philippines was a US territory. The Philippine constitution now only allows its own citizens to own private land. But the BCDA can offer leases lasting as long as 99 years to foreign developers. The agency expects to rake in close to $1 billion USD (about 60 billion in PHP Peso) from lease income over the first 25 years.

There are layers of land-grabbing to unpack here

The BCDA was in talks with around 30 different companies interested in setting up shop in Clark’s proposed AI hub, then-BCDA President and CEO Joshua Bingcang told reporters in July. He couldn’t name names, he said, because of NDAs — creating the same kind of opacity that has turned Americans against data centers on their home turf.

He did mention, however, that an American energy company was conducting a feasibility study into building a liquefied natural gas (LNG) line and plant to meet the hub’s enormous electricity demand. Bingcang called LNG a clean fuel, but that’s provably false. LNG is primarily methane, a smog-forming pollutant that is an even more potent greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide.

Bingcang said in September that the Philippine government wanted to invite Nvidia, TSMC, and Apple. While one or two data center developers had expressed interest, according to Bingcang, most of the companies interested were “high tech” manufacturing firms. He has also described chip manufacturing as a “clean” industry, echoing corporate spin that’s been around since the start of Silicon Valley.

At the first chip fabs in California, workers — many of them Filipino immigrants — donned “bunny suits” to assemble sensitive chips in environmentally controlled “clean rooms.” Little did they know that the gear they wore offered little protection against the harsh chemicals used in manufacturing, which also leaked out of storage tanks to contaminate soil and groundwater. When studies came out in the ’90s documenting disproportionately high rates of miscarriages among workers, companies pledged to phase out some of the chemicals linked to reproductive health risks. Around the same time, chip manufacturing started to move out of the US to Asia, where similar health problems stemming from the same chemicals cropped up even decades later.

Chipmakers say their fabs have gotten much safer over the years, in part because more work is automated. Even so, the BCDA estimates that the AI hub will create up to 190,000 direct jobs. The BCDA, White House, and Philippine’s Malacañang Palace did not immediately respond to questions from The Verge.

“I don’t want to date myself, but I knew your parents very well. They were great,” Trump told President Marcos during his visit. Marcos’ parents are estimated to have stolen up to $30 billion from government coffers over decades of rule before a people power movement ousted the current president’s father from the same office in the 1980s. But public memory, it seems, can be short.

And skyrocketing demand for more powerful chips used for generative AI has raised fears among environmental and labor groups that history might repeat itself. Companies move fast and break things, leaving a toxic mess in their wake. And when Americans decide they’ve had enough in their own back yards, the industry sets up shop somewhere else where they think their customers aren’t paying attention and politicians are happy to look the other direction.

Tech.title: Nvidia’s rise, visualized
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

If someone handed you $8,300 every second, what would you do? That’s how much pure profit Nvidia now makes. By the time you finish reading this paragraph, Nvidia will likely have cleared $45,000 and change.

But I want you to understand: Nvidia isn’t your average semi-successful company that might tempt a new CEO to fix things that are broken. It is a company so staggeringly, mind-bogglingly successful it’ll do everything in its power not to rock the boat. There is so much money at stake.

It’s so much money that when I heard about Jensen Huang’s resignation, my first thought was: I need a way to visualize this jaw-dropping amount of money for you. I want to show you that Nvidia has risen so far, so fast, that rival chipmakers AMD, Intel, and Qualcomm barely qualify as competition now.

If you’re on a desktop OS, you could mouse over each dot in our chart above to see the staggering sums. But we built another way to visualize the rise of Nvidia I like even better. It’s a horizontal bar graph that not only puts Nvidia’s revenue growth in perspective, but shows you its monster profits right alongside them — plus the world events that made Nvidia a star.

TL;DR: The crypto boom and the great GPU shortage have nothing on the AI boom. Those earlier periods saw Nvidia’s profits briefly peak at $1.24 billion and $3 billion a quarter respectively, while the rise of data centers has driven them to $65 billion per quarter with no sign of stopping.

Yes, Jensen may have set a trillion dollars of Nvidia’s market cap on fire — from around $5 trillion at the start of November to “only” $3.6 trillion now — but the smoldering company is raking in $700 million in profit a day on average.

Put another way: Nvidia could give a $1 million bonus to every one of its 42,000 employees, every three months, without running out of cash. Or, you know, Nvidia could end world hunger or provide clean water for everyone, now that it’s making over $200 billion in pure profit a year.

Maybe that’d make people feel differently about data centers?

But even if we stick to self-serving capitalism, you’re probably still a happy investor if you bought Nvidia a decade ago. A $1,000 investment 10 years ago is now worth over $67,000. You’d have over $1 million if you invested $15,000 back then.

And make no mistake, Nvidia is sticking to capitalism. Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress just promised to return as much money to investors as possible on the company’s November 17th earnings call. “Going forward, we intend to return all excess free cash flow net of strategic uses to shareholders,” she announced. “All” is a lot more than the 50 percent baseline that Jensen promised five months ago.

Nvidia isn’t the only company whose fortunes have risen this dramatically. RAMageddon revealed that just three companies — Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron — controlled nearly 90 percent of the entire global DRAM market, and those three have repeatedly signaled that they’d prefer to celebrate record profits instead of ramping up production too fast.

But while their revenues and profits have been skyrocketing even faster over the past year or so, even Big RAM hasn’t caught the AI wave quite the same way as Nvidia. Samsung, of course, doesn’t just make memory — its revenue numbers include phones, tablets, TVs, home appliances, chips, displays, camera sensors, audio, networking equipment, medical equipment, and more.

In the most recent quarter, Micron made $37.7 billion in profit, SK Hynix made $29.8 billion, and Samsung came in at around $55.3 billion, but they’re all shy of Nvidia’s $65.3 billion. Historically, RAM has also been a bit more cyclical: Both Micron and SK Hynix actually lost money in 2023 because they produced too much memory.

On its latest earnings call, the first since cofounder Jensen Huang’s resignation, interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress reinforced the idea that Nvidia expects the good times to keep on rolling.

Asked how things might change under new management, she suggested that they wouldn’t: “From a business perspective, it’s business as usual,” she said. She added that the company has secured the backing of customers and suppliers including TSMC, the all-important firm that actually fabricates Nvidia’s chips.

“Our momentum is real, our demand is accelerating, our supply is growing. Our customers and partners are with us, and employees are committed,” she claimed. “We’ve got this.”

Nvidia claims it’ll rake in even more money next quarter, with projected revenue of $130 billion. Profit may be proportionally smaller since gross margins are estimated to drop to 71–72 percent (compared to nearly 75 percent), but Kress said Nvidia intends to get them up as high as 73 percent next year.

In other words: This astounding gravy train isn’t going anywhere. At least that’s the plan.

Stevie Bonifield contributed to this story.

Tech.title: Sony’s impressive Bravia 8 II OLED hits a new low price ahead of Black Friday

Black Friday is a great time to save on a new OLED television for your winter movie nights. Though, it turns out that you can already get a great deal on the 65-inch Sony Bravia 8 II, one of our favorite OLED televisions. My colleague John Higgins praised the Bravia 8 II for its excellent image quality and engaging picture, though those positive traits are consistent with almost all OLED TVs. What sets this one apart is its impressive image processing, the bold colors from its quantum dot-equipped OLED panel, and that it looks great right out of the box (although he recommends using Professional mode). The screen was awarded the top spot at 2025’s Value Electronics TV Shootout, beating out similar offerings from competitors like Panasonic, LG, and Samsung.
